source_file: 10005587_2024_Allentown Victory Church v. City of Allentown_ca3
case_name: Allentown Victory Church v. City of Allentown
accommodation_description: The church requested permission to house eighteen (later reduced to fifteen) rather than twelve residents in its transitional recovery home as a reasonable accommodation under the zoning ordinance's accommodation provision.
key_holding: The Third Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the City, holding that the church failed to demonstrate that housing more than twelve residents was 'necessary' rather than merely 'preferable' for the Home's operation, as required under the reasonable accommodation burden-shifting framework.
brief_summary: Allentown Victory Church, which operates a transitional recovery home for men exiting substance abuse treatment and incarceration, sued the City of Allentown and its Zoning Hearing Board after the Board denied its requests to classify the Home as either a Large Group Home or an Institution and to house more than twelve residents as a reasonable accommodation. The Third Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the City, finding that while the Church invoked the FHA's reasonable accommodation provision, it failed to produce evidence showing that housing eighteen (later fifteen) residents was 'necessary' rather than merely economically preferable.
key_cases_cited: Lapid-Laurel, LLC v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment of Twp. of Scotch Plains, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Vorchheimer v. Phila. Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
431 E. Palisade Ave. Real Est., LLC v. City of Englewood, 977 F.3d 277 (3d Cir. 2020)
Lakeside Resort Enters., LP v. Bd. of Supervisors of Palmyra Twp., 455 F.3d 154 (3d Cir. 2006)

source_file: 10006353_2024_David Q. Webb v. Miami-Dade County Government_ca11
case_name: David Q. Webb v. Miami-Dade County Government
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged defendants refused to provide a reasonable accommodation for his angina-related disability at Camillus House residential facility, but the specific accommodation requested was not described in the opinion due to dismissal on shotgun pleading grounds.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, holding that the district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing appellant's case because he failed to comply with the court's order to file a proper second amended complaint after being warned that failure to do so would result in dismissal.
brief_summary: Pro se appellant David Webb sued Miami-Dade County Government, Miami-Dade County Homeless Trust, Camillus House (a non-profit supportive housing provider), and individual defendants, alleging Fair Housing Act and ADA violations related to his removal from a Camillus House residential facility for his angina disability. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal without prejudice, finding no abuse of discretion because Webb failed to file a proper second amended complaint after the court identified his pleading as a shotgun complaint and warned that failure to comply would result in dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Off., 792 F.3d 1313 (11th Cir. 2015)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Vibe Micro Inc. v. Shabanets, 878 F.3d 1291 (11th Cir. 2018)
Foudy v. Indian River Cnty. Sheriff's Off., 845 F.3d 1117 (11th Cir. 2017)
Moon v. Newsome, 863 F.2d 835 (11th Cir. 1989)

case_name: Celia Litman; et al. v. Jennifer Guckin; Township of Towamencin
accommodation_description: Parents requested permission to add a room to their single-family home and use a trailer on the property to teach their autistic son independent living skills.
key_holding: The District Court's dismissal was affirmed because all claims were time-barred; the injury occurred in 2019 when zoning citations were issued, making the 2023 lawsuit four years after the alleged wrong and two years past the two-year statute of limitations.
brief_summary: The Litman family sued Towamencin Township and its zoning officer challenging zoning citations issued in 2019 for using a trailer on their property to accommodate their autistic son, alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act violations. The Third Circuit affirmed the District Court's dismissal, holding that all claims were time-barred because the alleged injury occurred in 2019 when the citations were issued, making the 2023 lawsuit well outside the applicable two-year statute of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Wallace v. Kato, 549 U.S. 384 (2007)
Cowell v. Palmer Township, 263 F.3d 286 (3d Cir. 2001)
Dique v. N.J. State Police, 603 F.3d 181 (3d Cir. 2010)

Pearson v. Sec'y Dep't of Corr., 775 F.3d 598 (3d Cir. 2015)

source_file: 10038254_2024_Gilead Community Services, Inc. v. Town of Cromwell_ca2
case_name: Gilead Community Services, Inc. v. Town of Cromwell
accommodation_description: Gilead sought to operate a group home for individuals with mental health disabilities in Cromwell, and the town's campaign of discrimination and retaliation was designed to prevent the group home from opening.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed the jury's liability findings under the FHA, including that municipalities can be held vicariously liable for discriminatory acts of officials and that punitive damages are available against municipalities under the FHA, but vacated the $5 million punitive damages award as unconstitutionally excessive and remanded for a new trial on damages unless plaintiffs accepted remittitur to $2 million.
brief_summary: Gilead Community Services and Connecticut Fair Housing Center sued the Town of Cromwell after the town engaged in a sustained campaign of discrimination, including discriminatory public statements, zoning threats, and police targeting, to prevent Gilead's group home for individuals with mental health disabilities from opening, forcing the home to close. The Second Circuit affirmed the jury's liability findings and $181,000 compensatory damages award but vacated the $5 million punitive damages award as unconstitutionally excessive, remanding for reduction to $2 million.
key_cases_cited: Cabrera v. Jakabovitz, 24 F.3d 372 (2d Cir. 1994)
Robinson v. 12 Lofts Realty, Inc., 610 F.2d 1032 (2d Cir. 1979)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. County of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)
State Farm Mut. Auto Ins. Co. v. Campbell, 538 U.S. 408 (2003)

case_name: Merck v. Walmart, Inc.
accommodation_description: This is not a Fair Housing Act case; it is a Fair Credit Reporting Act claim regarding Walmart's alleged failure to provide plaintiff with a full copy of his consumer report before revoking his conditional job offer.
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Walmart, holding that plaintiff Thomas Merck lacked Article III standing because his alleged informational injury under the Fair Credit Reporting Act did not bear a sufficiently close relationship to a harm traditionally recognized as providing a basis for lawsuits in American courts.
brief_summary: Thomas Merck sued Walmart under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, alleging Walmart violated 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(3)(A) by failing to provide him with a full copy of his consumer report before revoking his conditional job offer after a background check revealed an undisclosed misdemeanor conviction. The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Walmart, finding Merck lacked Article III standing because his claimed procedural injury did not resemble a harm traditionally recognized in American courts and he failed to demonstrate any concrete injury flowing from the statutory violation.
key_cases_cited: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)
Ward v. Nat'l Patient Acct. Servs. Sols., Inc., 9 F.4th 357 (6th Cir. 2021)
Ward v. NPAS, Inc., 63 F.4th 576 (6th Cir. 2023)
Gadelhak v. AT&T Servs., Inc., 950 F.3d 458 (7th Cir. 2020)

source_file: 10082236_2024_Joshua Debity v. Vintage Village Homeowners Ass'n_ca6
case_name: Joshua A. Debity, et al. v. Vintage Village Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: Request for a six-foot wooden privacy fence in the backyard instead of the HOA-approved wrought-iron fence to prevent the disabled child from eloping and to provide privacy when the child disrobes due to sensory processing disorder.
key_holding: The appellate court reversed summary judgment for the HOA, finding the district court improperly ignored evidence related to the privacy concern and erred in excluding the treating provider's testimony about the child's need for a privacy fence, creating genuine issues of material fact as to whether a wooden privacy fence was necessary to afford the disabled child equal opportunity to enjoy the property.
brief_summary: Joshua and Leah Debity sued their HOA after it refused to approve a wooden privacy fence for their autistic son G.D., instead requiring a wrought-iron fence; the district court excluded the child's medical provider's testimony and granted summary judgment for the HOA. The Sixth Circuit reversed, holding that genuine issues of material fact existed as to whether the wooden privacy fence was necessary to afford the child equal opportunity to use and enjoy the property, and the district court improperly limited the treating provider's testimony about the child's need for privacy accommodations.
key_cases_cited: Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Anderson v. City of Blue Ash, 798 F.3d 338 (6th Cir. 2015)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)

case_name: Katalin Bloodgood-Loper v. Lenard Loper; LVL Investments, LLC; Michelle L. Mercer
accommodation_description: The opinion does not identify any specific accommodation request; the FHA claims were dismissed for failure to plead facts showing defendants acted 'because of' plaintiff's protected class membership.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal because Bloodgood-Loper failed to allege facts sufficient to show defendants engaged in conduct made unlawful by the Fair Housing Act 'because of' her membership in a protected class under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a), (f).
brief_summary: Katalin Bloodgood-Loper, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's dismissal of her federal claims including Fair Housing Act claims against Lenard Loper, LVL Investments, LLC, and Judge Michelle Mercer. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that Bloodgood-Loper failed to plead sufficient facts showing the defendants' conduct was 'because of' her membership in a protected class under § 3604(a) and (f).
key_cases_cited: Hebbe v. Pliler, 627 F.3d 338 (9th Cir. 2010)
Schucker v. Rockwood, 846 F.2d 1202 (9th Cir. 1988)
Chudacoff v. Univ. Med. Ctr. of S. Nev., 649 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2011)

Karim-Panahi v. L.A. Police Dep't, 839 F.2d 621 (9th Cir. 1988)

case_name: Neway Mengistu v. Forestview Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an apartment with accessibility modifications, but defendants declined to rent due to the high cost of renovations.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants because plaintiff's FHA claims were barred by the two-year statute of limitations, having accrued when defendants informed him of their decision not to rent on May 11, 2017, and alternatively because plaintiff failed to raise a triable dispute that his requested accommodations were reasonable.
brief_summary: Neway Mengistu sued Forestview Apartments and its manager alleging Fair Housing Act violations after defendants decided not to rent him an apartment due to the high cost of accessibility renovations. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants, holding that the claims were time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations and alternatively failed on the merits because Mengistu did not raise a triable dispute that his accommodation requests were reasonable.
key_cases_cited: Soto v. Sweetman, 882 F.3d 865 (9th Cir. 2018)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)

source_file: 10099647_2024_Earlando Samuel v. Delaware County Housing Authority_ca3
case_name: Earlando Samuel v. Delaware County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for two-bedroom Section 8 voucher to accommodate a live-in aide assisting with disability-related impairments including osteoarthritis, cognitive impairment, depression, anxiety, and panic disorder
key_holding: The Third Circuit found no abuse of discretion in denying Samuel's motions for appointed counsel, concluding that despite his disabilities, Samuel demonstrated adequate ability to litigate his reasonable accommodation claim given his prior federal litigation experience, proactive engagement with housing regulations, and the relatively straightforward factual issues at summary judgment.
brief_summary: Earlando Samuel, a pro se appellant with multiple disabilities, appealed from the Third Circuit the District Court's denial of his three motions to appoint counsel in his Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation case against the Delaware County Housing Authority regarding his Section 8 voucher and live-in aide request. The Third Circuit affirmed, finding no abuse of discretion because Samuel demonstrated sufficient ability to represent himself despite his disabilities, citing his prior federal litigation experience and adequate presentation of his case.
key_cases_cited: Tabron v. Grace, 6 F.3d 147 (3d Cir. 1993)
Houser v. Folino, 927 F.3d 693 (3d Cir. 2019)
Parham v. Johnson, 126 F.3d 454 (3d Cir. 1997)

source_file: 10105570_2024_Adam U. Steines v. Westgate Palace, L.L.C._ca11
case_name: Adam U. Steines v. Westgate Palace, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request; it concerns a Military Lending Act challenge to mandatory arbitration clauses in timeshare loan documents.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that because the Military Lending Act overrides the Federal Arbitration Act, Section 16 of the FAA (authorizing interlocutory appeals from arbitration orders) does not apply; the court also affirmed that the MLA applies to the timeshare loan because the timeshare interest is more like a hotel room than a dwelling and thus does not qualify for the MLA's residential mortgage exception.
brief_summary: Adam and Miranda Steines, active-duty servicemembers, brought a class action against Westgate Resorts alleging violations of the Military Lending Act, including that Westgate's timeshare loan documents failed to provide required disclosures and unlawfully included mandatory arbitration clauses. The Eleventh Circuit dismissed the appeal, holding that because the MLA expressly overrides the FAA, Section 16 of the FAA—which permits interlocutory appeals from orders denying arbitration—does not apply, leaving the court without appellate jurisdiction.

case_name: J.W. Seals, Jr.; Vergie Seals; Marie L. Pace v. Itex Group L.L.C.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that uninhabitable conditions (mold, structural defects, pest infestations) in her apartment made it 'unavailable' under the FHA.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that Sections 3604(a) and 3604(f)(1) of the FHA provide relief for discrimination in the sale or rental of dwellings, not for claims that an apartment is uninhabitable.
brief_summary: Vergie Seals and her children sued ITEX Group under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and state law, alleging that deplorable conditions including mold, structural defects, and pest infestations made her apartment 'unavailable' under § 3604(a) and (f)(1). The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that these FHA provisions cover discrimination in the sale or rental of housing, not claims that existing housing is uninhabitable, and plaintiffs abandoned the appeal by failing to challenge this basis.
key_cases_cited: Cox v. City of Dallas, Tex., 430 F.3d 734 (5th Cir. 2005)
Grant v. Cuellar, 59 F.3d 523 (5th Cir. 1995)
Brinkmann v. Dallas Cnty. Deputy Sheriff Abner, 813 F.2d 744 (5th Cir. 1987)

case_name: In re: Nyah Sekel
accommodation_description: Petitioner seeks writ of mandamus directing district court to grant her motion for summary judgment in underlying Fair Housing Act case
key_holding: Petitioner is not entitled to mandamus relief because she has not demonstrated a clear right to the relief sought and mandamus cannot be used as a substitute for appeal.
brief_summary: Nyah Sekel petitioned the Fourth Circuit for a writ of mandamus directing the district court to grant her motion for summary judgment in her pending Fair Housing Act case. The court denied the petition, holding that mandamus is a drastic remedy available only in extraordinary circumstances and that Petitioner failed to demonstrate a clear right to the relief sought.

case_name: Nora Dunn v. Carter Manuel, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a temporary substitute apartment and time to gather assistance to move and separate her personal items while her unit was being repaired due to her hoarding disorder.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to dismiss because hoarding disorder does not qualify as a protected disability under the FHA since plaintiff failed to allege facts showing it substantially limits major life activities, and alternatively because plaintiff failed to plead that her requested accommodation was reasonable, proportional, or necessary to ameliorate her disability's effects.
brief_summary: Nora Dunn sued her landlord Sharon Hydinger alleging Fair Housing Act violations, including failure to accommodate her hoarding disorder, intentional discrimination, retaliation, and hostile environment harassment. The court granted the motion to dismiss, finding that hoarding disorder is not a protected disability under the FHA because it does not substantially limit major life activities, and alternatively that Dunn failed to plead the remaining elements of her accommodation claim.

case_name: Miller v. Coastline Management
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation requested; plaintiff mentions CPTSD and mother's walker use as basis for discrimination claim regarding delayed repairs and unlivable conditions.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claims fail because she cited 42 U.S.C. § 3601 (which merely states the FHA's general purpose) and § 3605 (which applies to real estate transactions like selling, brokering, or appraising), neither of which provides a cause of action for discrimination experienced while living in a condo unit.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Fredrika Miller sued Coastline Management and Beachcomber Homeowner Association alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on discrimination she and her mother experienced while living in their condo unit, citing her CPTSD and her mother's walker use as bases for discrimination. The court dismissed the FHA claims with prejudice, finding Miller failed to state a plausible cause of action under the cited statutory provisions (42 U.S.C. § 3601, which establishes only general FHA purpose, and § 3605, which applies to real estate transactions, not tenancy-related discrimination claims).
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

source_file: 10166836_2024_Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated_azd
case_name: Wayne Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated
accommodation_description: Disabled veteran requested permission to keep his garage door open while engaged in therapeutic woodworking inside his garage, as an accommodation from the HOA's rule requiring garage doors to remain closed at all times.
key_holding: The court reopened discovery to allow plaintiff to depose board members regarding emails about his accommodation request, finding that an email in which the board president called the garage door rule 'stupid' is relevant to whether the accommodation request was reasonable under § 3604(f)(3).
brief_summary: Wayne Hiatt, a disabled veteran, sued Sun City Festival Community Association under the Fair Housing Act alleging discrimination based on disability after the HOA denied his accommodation request to keep his garage door open while engaged in therapeutic woodworking. The court's order addressed discovery disputes, denying plaintiff's sanctions request, reopening discovery for limited depositions of board members regarding emails about the accommodation request, and denying defendant's motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel.

source_file: 10166885_2024_Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated_azd
case_name: Wayne Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled veteran with PTSD and claustrophobia, requested to keep his garage door open while woodworking/engaging in activities in his garage as a therapeutic accommodation.
key_holding: The court found that Plaintiff established four of five elements for a reasonable accommodation claim as undisputed facts, but denied summary judgment because a genuine dispute of material fact exists regarding whether keeping the garage door open was necessary to afford Plaintiff equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling, given evidence that Plaintiff could use a community woodworking facility and engaged in other activities without the door open.
brief_summary: Wayne Hiatt, a disabled veteran with PTSD and claustrophobia, sued Sun City Festival Community Association seeking partial summary judgment on his reasonable accommodation claim under the FHA, alleging the HOA's CC&Rs requiring garage doors to remain closed discriminated against his disability-related need to keep his garage door open while woodworking. The Court denied the motion, finding that while four of five elements were undisputed, a genuine dispute of material fact remains regarding whether the accommodation was necessary to afford Plaintiff equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)

case_name: TL Harvey v. Maxwell & Morgan P.C., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to install a window air conditioning unit despite HOA rules, framing it as an accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims because his complaint failed to identify his disability, explain how the requested accommodation was necessary for that disability, or allege facts plausibly showing the defendants were responsible for creating a discriminatory housing environment.
brief_summary: TL Harvey, a Black homeowner, sued his HOA (RED HOA), its law firm, property manager, and board members alleging they targeted him based on race and failed to accommodate his disability by refusing to allow a window air conditioner. The court granted the motions to dismiss, finding Harvey's FHA claims insufficiently pleaded because he failed to identify his disability or explain how the requested accommodation was necessary.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

source_file: 10167251_2024_Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated_azd
case_name: Wayne Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated
accommodation_description: Request to waive the HOA's closed-garage-door rule to keep garage door open while engaging in therapeutic woodworking and other activities to manage PTSD symptoms
key_holding: Plaintiff raised serious questions going to the merits of his FHA reasonable accommodation claim but failed to establish irreparable harm due to his 17-month delay in seeking preliminary injunctive relief and his ability to endure the alleged harm during that period.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Wayne Hiatt, a disabled veteran with PTSD, sued the Sun City Festival Community Association seeking a preliminary injunction to allow him to keep his garage door open while woodworking and engaging in other therapeutic activities as a reasonable accommodation under the Fair Housing Act. The court denied the motion, finding that while Hiatt raised serious questions on the merits of his reasonable accommodation claim, he failed to demonstrate immediate irreparable harm given his 17-month delay in seeking injunctive relief.

10167751_2024_United African-Asian Abilities Club v. Alexander C. Freiberg_cacd
case_name: United African-Asian Abilities Club et al v. Alexander C. Freiberg et al
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request is described; the claims arise from alleged construction-related accessibility standard violations at a place of public accommodation under the FHA, ADA, and California Unruh Act.
key_holding: The court issued an Order to Show Cause directing plaintiff to explain why the court should not decline to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state Unruh Act claim, given California's heightened pleading requirements and high-frequency litigant restrictions for construction-related accessibility claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff United African-Asian Abilities Club filed suit against Alexander C. Freiberg alleging violations of the federal Fair Housing Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, and California's Unruh Act based on construction-related accessibility violations. The court issued an Order to Show Cause regarding whether it should exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the Unruh Act claim, noting that California enacted heightened pleading requirements and financial restrictions on 'high-frequency litigants' to deter vexatious construction-related accessibility litigation, and that federal court filings can circumvent those state-law protections. The court ordered plaintiff to identify statutory damages sought and to submit declarations establishing whether plaintiff and counsel qualify as high-frequency litigants, warning that failure to respond adequately could result in dismissal of the Unruh Act claim or the entire action.
key_cases_cited: City of Chicago v. Int'l Coll. of Surgeons, 522 U.S. 156 (1997)

case_name: Emma Adams v. Aqua 388 Community Association et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a reasonable parking accommodation from the HOA (specifics not detailed in this sanctions order).
key_holding: The court issued an order to show cause against plaintiff's counsel for improper closing argument that exploited an evidentiary exclusion the counsel himself had successfully obtained, suggesting the jury should draw an adverse inference from the absence of a witness counsel had excluded from testifying.
brief_summary: Emma Adams sued the Aqua 388 Community Association alleging Fair Housing Act violations for failure to provide a reasonable parking accommodation, prevailing at summary judgment and trial; the court subsequently issued an order to show cause against Adams's counsel for attorney misconduct during closing argument, where counsel improperly argued the jury should draw an adverse inference from the absence of a witness whose testimony counsel had successfully moved to exclude.
key_cases_cited: Evon v. L. Offs. of Sidney Mickell, 688 F.3d 1015 (9th Cir. 2012)

key_holding: The court ordered plaintiff to show cause why it should not decline supplemental jurisdiction over plaintiff's Unruh Act and state law claims, and required plaintiff to identify statutory damages sought and provide declarations regarding high-frequency litigant status.
brief_summary: United African-Asian Abilities Club and another plaintiff sued 6335 Whitsett Ave LLC and related defendants asserting federal and California Fair Housing Act claims along with ADA and Unruh Act claims. case_name: Deepa Patel et al. v. City of Stanton et al.
accommodation_description: Motel owner and business entity allege City revoked motel permit and issued citations because City sought to drive out minority guests and Asian-Indian owner.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claim under § 3604(b) because the complaint failed to specify how plaintiffs themselves were injured by a discriminatory housing practice, what constituted the discriminatory practice, and which defendant was responsible, while also noting uncertainty whether the FHA applies to motels as temporary shelters.
brief_summary: Deepa Patel and California One Hospitality LLC, owners of Dixie Orange County Motel, sued the City of Stanton and unknown officials alleging the City revoked their motel permit and issued administrative citations because City officials sought to drive out low-income minority guests and the Asian-Indian owner. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to comply with Rule 8(a) pleading requirements, finding the FHA claim vague as to the discriminatory practice, injury, and responsible defendant, while granting leave to amend the federal claims and declining supplemental jurisdiction over state writ claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: United States of America v. Joel Lynn Nolen, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request at issue; this case involves sexual harassment of female tenants by landlord.
key_holding: The court granted the government's motion to compel discovery, requiring defendants to produce ESI, provide supplemental interrogatory responses, produce financial documents and tax returns, and produce insurance policies, while denying the motion as to certain property ownership document requests.
brief_summary: The United States sued landlords Joel and Shirlee Nolen alleging they subjected female tenants to sexual harassment in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court granted in part the government's motion to compel discovery, ordering defendants to produce ESI, supplemental interrogatory responses, financial documents, and insurance policies within 21 days, while denying the motion as to certain property ownership document requests.

source_file: 10169656_2024_Chhang v. West Coast USA Properties LLC_caed
case_name: Pharilyn Chhang v. West Coast USA Properties LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to keep a Pit Bull as a service animal, which Madrigal denied citing insurance concerns.
key_holding: The court denied reconsideration because the proposed allegations were not newly discovered, the plaintiff could have raised them earlier, and even with the proposed amendments, HACM still owed no legal duty to intervene in the private landlord's alleged discriminatory conduct since HACM did not own, operate, or manage the property.
brief_summary: Pharilyn Chhang, a Section 8 voucher holder, sued private landlord Sergio Madrigal and the Housing Authority of the City of Madera (HACM) alleging discrimination for denying her request to keep a Pit Bull as a service animal. The court granted HACM's motion to dismiss on the ground that HACM had no legal duty to intervene in the private landlord's alleged discriminatory acts, and denied reconsideration because the proposed amendments were not new evidence and amendment would remain futile.

case_name: United States of America v. Javier Salazar, Jr., et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was at issue in this case; the case concerns sex-based housing discrimination in the form of sexual harassment of a female tenant by the property manager, denial of necessary repairs as retaliation for rejecting his advances, and interference with the tenant's enjoyment of her home.
key_holding: The court recommends granting default judgment against defendants who subjected a female tenant to months of sexual harassment in violation of the Fair Housing Act, awarding $45,000 in compensatory and punitive damages and permanent injunctive relief.
brief_summary: The United States brought this FHA action on behalf of Angela McGinnis against property owner Ricardo Covarrubias and property managers Javier Salazar Sr. and Jr., alleging that Salazar Jr. subjected McGinnis to persistent sexual harassment during her tenancy at a Bakersfield, California single-family home, while Salazar Sr. failed to address the conduct after being informed, and all defendants retaliated by refusing to repair a gas leak and locking her out of the property. After all defendants failed to file any opposition and defaulted, the magistrate judge recommends granting default judgment awarding $30,000 in joint and several compensatory damages, $12,500 in punitive damages against Salazar Jr., and $2,500 in punitive damages against Salazar Sr., along with permanent injunctive relief including FHA training for all defendants and a harassment policy for the property owner.
key_cases_cited: Eitel v. McCool, 782 F.2d 1470 (9th Cir. 1986)
Fair Hous. v. Combs, 285 F.3d 899 (9th Cir. 2002)

case_name: Pharilyn Chhang v. West Coast USA Properties LLC

key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion for leave to file a second amended complaint to add the insurance broker for defendant West Coast USA Properties LLC as a new party, finding no bad faith, undue delay, or prejudice given defendants' non-opposition.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Pharilyn Chhang brought suit against West Coast USA Properties LLC, Sergio Madrigal, and the Housing Authority of the City of Madera alleging violations of the Federal Fair Housing Act, the Civil Rights Act of 1871, and state law claims. The Housing Authority of the City of Madera was previously dismissed with prejudice following two motions to dismiss. This order concerns plaintiff's unopposed motion for leave to file a second amended complaint to add the insurance broker for West Coast USA Properties LLC as an additional defendant, which the court granted after finding the Rule 15(a) factors weighed in favor of amendment.
key_cases_cited: Nunes v. Ashcroft, 375 F.3d 805 (9th Cir. 2004)
Eminence Capital, LLC v. Aspeon, Inc., 316 F.3d 1048 (9th Cir. 2003)
Washington v. Lowe's HIW Inc., 75 F. Supp. 3d 1240 (N.D. Cal. 2014)

case_name: United States v. Joel Lynn Nolen, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested in this case. The underlying FHA claims concern alleged sex discrimination in the form of sexual harassment by defendant Joel Nolen against female tenants and prospective tenants at rental properties; the instant order concerns a discovery dispute over the scope of a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition notice directed at the United States.
key_holding: The court granted the United States' motion for a protective order forbidding the Nolens from conducting a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition of a United States representative because the seven noticed topics — covering all allegations of sexual harassment, harm to aggrieved persons, and Mrs. Nolen's liability from 1999 to present — were overbroad, unduly burdensome, and disproportionate to the needs of the case given the availability of individual percipient witnesses and other appropriate discovery tools.
brief_summary: The United States brought a Fair Housing Act action under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604, 3617, and 3614(a) alleging that defendant Joel Nolen subjected female tenants and prospective tenants at properties he owned or managed to sex discrimination, including sexual harassment, and that his wife Shirlee Nolen was vicariously liable for failing to take corrective measures. During discovery, the Nolens served a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition notice on the United States listing seven topics that collectively encompassed all sexual harassment allegations, harm to aggrieved persons, and Mrs. Nolen's conduct from 1999 to the present. The court granted the United States' motion for a protective order, finding the notice overbroad, insufficiently specific, and disproportionate because the Nolens had failed to depose the nineteen aggrieved persons themselves and had not used interrogatories, making the Rule 30(b)(6) notice an improper catch-all substitute for targeted discovery.
key_cases_cited: Brazos River Auth. v. GE Ionics, Inc., 469 F.3d 416 (5th Cir. 2006)

case_name: Jacqueline Coleman v. Xiaoyan Fang and Ye Fang
accommodation_description: Not specified in the case text. The complaint alleges housing discrimination under the Fair Housing Act related to a rental unit plaintiff vacated in July 2021, but the specific nature of the discriminatory conduct or any accommodation request is not described in this order.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommended denying plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction because plaintiff failed to articulate any legal or factual basis for injunctive relief and failed to demonstrate a possibility of irreparable harm, having vacated the defendants' unit more than three years prior.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jacqueline Coleman filed a Fair Housing Act housing discrimination complaint against her former landlords, the Fangs, on the same day she filed a motion for preliminary injunction. The motion for injunction referenced a VAWA complaint and included an attached 2023 restraining order against plaintiff's ex-husband, who is not a party to this case. The magistrate judge found no basis for a preliminary injunction because plaintiff had not lived in the unit for over three years, showed no irreparable harm, and the restraining order was unrelated to the FHA claim against the defendant landlords.
key_cases_cited: Munaf v. Geren, 553 U.S. 674 (2008)

case_name: United States of America v. Javier Salazar, Jr., et al.
accommodation_description: Sexual harassment by property manager involving unwanted sexual solicitations, physical contact, and retaliation against female tenant Angela McGinnis.
key_holding: Default judgment entered against landlords for FHA sexual harassment violations, awarding $45,000 in damages and injunctive relief including a 10-year ban on Defendant Salazar Jr. from property management at residential properties.
brief_summary: The United States brought this action against landlords Javier Salazar Jr., Javier Salazar Sr., and Ricardo Covarrubias for Fair Housing Act violations involving sexual harassment of female tenant Angela McGinnis. After default judgment was entered, the court granted damages of $45,000 and injunctive relief including a 10-year ban on Salazar Jr. from property management activities at residential properties.
key_cases_cited: S. Cal. Hous. Rights.Ctr. v. Krug, 564 F. Supp. 2d 1138 (C.D. Cal. 2007)

source_file: 10171744_2021_Sam Sohn v. California Housing Financing Agency_cand
case_name: Sam Sohn v. California Housing Financing Agency
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reasonable accommodation through Keep Your Home California mortgage assistance program as a result of her disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed the second amended complaint without leave to amend because plaintiff's factual allegations were insufficient to state any viable claim, including her Fair Housing Act and reasonable accommodation claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sam Sohn, who is over sixty-five years old and claims disability status, filed suit against California Housing Financing Agency, Keep Your Home California, Senator Dianne Feinstein, and the U.S. Department of the Treasury alleging violations of 42 U.S.C. § 1985, the Fair Housing Act, and other federal statutes. The court dismissed the second amended complaint without leave to amend, finding that plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual matter to state any viable claim, including her reasonable accommodation claim which the court construed as an ADA Title I claim.
key_cases_cited: Watison v. Carter, 668 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 2012)
Foman v. Davis, 371 U.S. 178 (1962)

case_name: Heyward v. Mosser Properties, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought accommodation related to repeated elevator outages at his multi-story apartment complex; he alleged that when elevators were not in service he was forced to climb stairs on several occasions, aggravating and compounding his disability, and that no accommodations were provided for disabled residents to access the second and third levels of the building.
key_holding: The court, conducting a mandatory § 1915(e) screening of a pro se in forma pauperis complaint, found that plaintiff's racial discrimination claims lacked any factual support, his ADA/disability claim was potentially moot and likely inapplicable to private residential apartments, and many allegations appeared irrational in light of attached VA progress notes, ordering plaintiff to supplement his complaint by October 14, 2024 or face dismissal.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Marco Heyward sued his apartment property manager Mosser Properties alleging that property managers allowed unauthorized persons into his apartment who stole belongings, smeared feces, and smoked crack, and that Mosser discriminated against him based on his race (African American) and disability. The court conducted a mandatory screening of the in forma pauperis complaint and identified several deficiencies: racial discrimination claims contained no factual basis linking Mosser's conduct to race, the ADA claim was potentially moot because plaintiff no longer resided at the property and the ADA generally does not apply to private residences, the statute of limitations on elevator-outage claims was unclear, and several allegations appeared irrational when read alongside the attached VA progress notes. The court gave plaintiff until October 14, 2024 to file a supplement curing these deficiencies, or alternatively to voluntarily dismiss the case without prejudice to pursue state claims in state court.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Denton v. Hernandez

case_name: Erika Macias v. Myron Lange
accommodation_description: This is a post-judgment enforcement proceeding regarding assignment of rents, not a reasonable accommodation case; the underlying FHA sexual harassment judgment was obtained in 2016.
key_holding: The court adopted the magistrate judge's report and granted Judgment Creditor Brancart & Brancart's motion for assignment of rents and restraining order under California Code of Civil Procedure section 708.510, directing that rents from the judgment debtor's seven residential properties be assigned to satisfy the $93,788.52 judgment.
brief_summary: Erika Macias obtained a 2016 jury verdict and 2017 judgment against landlord Myron Lange for sexual harassment under the Fair Housing Act, with attorney's fees awarded in 2017. After years of unsuccessful collection efforts, Judgment Creditor Brancart & Brancart moved for assignment of rents and a restraining order under California law to satisfy the $93,788.52 judgment from the judgment debtor's seven San Diego-area rental properties, several of which are covered by Section 8 vouchers. The court granted the motion, ordering that rental payments be assigned directly to the judgment creditor until the judgment is satisfied.

case_name: Gilead Community Services, Inc. v. Town of Cromwell
accommodation_description: Group home operator challenged municipality's discriminatory opposition campaign including petitions to state health officials, cease-and-desist letters, tax exemption denial, and alleged harassment of disabled residents.
key_holding: The court denied the Town of Cromwell's post-trial motions for judgment as a matter of law and new trial, affirming the jury's verdict that the Town violated the FHA and ADA through discriminatory conduct designed to force the group home to close.
brief_summary: Gilead Community Services, a group home operator, and the Connecticut Fair Housing Center sued the Town of Cromwell alleging the municipality violated the Fair Housing Act by orchestrating a campaign of discriminatory opposition to force closure of a group home for people with mental health disabilities through petitions to state officials, cease-and-desist letters, tax exemption denial, and harassment. Following a six-day trial, the jury found for plaintiffs and awarded $181,000 in compensatory damages and $5,000,000 in punitive damages; the court denied the Town's post-trial motions challenging the verdict.
key_cases_cited: Gilead Cmty. Servs. v. Cromwell
Cobb v. Pozzi, 363 F.3d 89 (2d Cir. 2004)

source_file: 10176464_2024_Atlantic Housing Partners L.L.L.P. v. Brevard County_flmd
case_name: Atlantic Housing Partners L.L.L.P. v. Brevard County
subsidy_program: Tax-exempt bonds; tax credits; Live Local Act
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request; developers allege county's denial of tax-exempt bond financing application for affordable housing development has discriminatory effects under FHA.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' segregative effect and disparate impact claims because plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts—providing only conclusory allegations without statistical evidence to establish that the county's denial of bond financing perpetuated segregation or disproportionately impacted a racial minority group.
brief_summary: Atlantic Housing Partners and related development entities sued Brevard County alleging that the County Commission's denial of their tax-exempt bond financing application for an affordable housing complex violated the FHA and Florida FHA by perpetuating segregation and having a disparate impact on racial minorities. The court granted the County's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs' claims conclusory and unsupported by the statistical evidence required to plead segregative effect or disparate impact claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

source_file: 10177302_2024_Derhem v. Bay House Miami Condominium Association_flsd
case_name: Kanayo Derhem v. Bay House Miami Condominium Association
accommodation_description: This motion concerns spoliation of evidence sanctions, not a reasonable accommodation request; the underlying case involved sex and race discrimination claims under the FHA that were resolved by final judgment.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' motion for sanctions due to spoliation of evidence was denied as untimely, having been filed nearly four months after the close of discovery and approximately ten months after the Local Rules' deadline, violating both Local Rule 26.1 and the Court's Scheduling Order.
brief_summary: Kanayo Derhem and others sued Bay House Miami Condominium Association alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on sex and race discrimination; after final judgment was entered for defendants, plaintiffs filed a motion for sanctions alleging defendants destroyed emails demonstrating discriminatory animus. The Court denied the sanctions motion as untimely because plaintiffs filed it nearly four months after the discovery deadline and approximately ten months after the Local Rules' deadline had passed, violating both Local Rule 26.1(g)(2)(a) and the Court's Scheduling Order.

case_name: Edgar Willis v. Nelson Ng
accommodation_description: Willis alleged landlord harassment and lease non-renewal due to race, with a passing reference to denial of unspecified reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state an FHA claim because Willis's conclusory allegations of race-based harassment, retaliatory rent increases, and lease non-renewal lack sufficient factual detail to give the defendant fair notice of the claims and the grounds upon which they rest.
brief_summary: Edgar Willis, proceeding pro se, sued his landlord Nelson Ng asserting Fair Housing Act and Section 1981 race discrimination claims, alleging harassment, retaliatory rent increases, and lease non-renewal. The court dismissed the complaint as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) because the complaint failed to allege sufficient factual matter to state plausible claims for relief.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Ralph Tanksley v. Cedar Rock Plantation
accommodation_description: Plaintiff made only cursory reference to 'fair and safe housing acts' in removal petition; no specific accommodation request was substantively analyzed.
key_holding: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the underlying action was simply a state court dispossessory (eviction) proceeding where plaintiff raised only conclusory allegations of FHA violations without factual support, failing to establish federal question or diversity jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ralph Tanksley attempted to remove a state court dispossessory (eviction) action to federal court, citing Fair Housing Act and other federal statutes, but the Southern District of Georgia found no subject matter jurisdiction and remanded the case to state court.

case_name: Beverly Galarza and Steven Galarza v. Quam Properties Hawaii, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request described; this is a retaliation claim under § 3617 based on plaintiffs' assistance with a DOJ accessibility investigation
key_holding: The court dismissed Steven Galarza (who has disabilities) for failure to state a retaliation claim because he did not personally engage in protected activity, and dismissed defendants Quam, Tracy, and Deatrick because the FAC failed to plausibly allege that their participation in the dog leash policy change constituted an adverse action under the FHA or that they acted with sufficient causal connection to plaintiffs' protected activities.
brief_summary: Beverly Galarza and her son Steven Galarza sued Quam Properties Hawaii, Inc. and others for retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, alleging that defendants changed a dog off-leash policy at a neighboring condominium catchment basin in retaliation for plaintiffs' assistance with a DOJ investigation into accessibility deficiencies. The court dismissed Steven Galarza for failing to allege he personally engaged in protected activity, dismissed defendants Quam, Tracy, and Deatrick for failing to state a viable retaliation claim because the dog leash policy change did not constitute an adverse housing action and causation was not plausibly alleged, but declined to dismiss remaining defendants for untimely service.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Sunshine H. Hauanio v. The Michaels Organization
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendant placed two towing stickers on her vehicle while placing only one on others' vehicles, claiming discriminatory treatment in housing matters
key_holding: The FHA housing discrimination claim was dismissed because plaintiff failed to provide sufficient factual allegations to show that defendant's placement of two towing stickers on her vehicle (versus one on others' vehicles) was discriminatory or retaliatory rather than merely conclusory.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Sunshine H. Hauanio, proceeding pro se, sued her former employer and landlord The Michaels Organization alleging employment discrimination under Title VII, the ADA, and the Pregnancy Discrimination Act, along with housing discrimination under the Fair Housing Act. The court granted TMO's motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, finding that while the housing discrimination claim invoked the FHA, the SAC provided insufficient factual matter to support any plausible discriminatory motive regarding the placement of towing stickers on plaintiff's vehicle compared to others.
key_cases_cited: Peterson v. Hewlett-Packard Co., 358 F.3d 599 (9th Cir. 2004)
Young v. UPS, Inc., 575 U.S. 206 (2015)

case_name: Laurie Thorson v. Hawai'i Public Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation for challenging rent reasonableness determination and requests interference with housing accommodations including live-in aide, payment standard exception, and voucher continuation be restrained
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to make the required showing for a temporary restraining order because she did not establish likelihood of success on the merits of her retaliation claim and did not adequately demonstrate irreparable injury, as she failed to show she must vacate by September 30 or that suitable alternative housing is unavailable due to defendants' conduct.
brief_summary: Laurie Thorson, a disabled recipient of Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher assistance, moved for a temporary restraining order against the Hawai'i Public Housing Authority and its officials, alleging they retaliated against her by interfering with her reasonable accommodations including her live-in aide and payment standard exception, putting her at imminent risk of eviction. case_name: Les Bock and Dunnia E. Aplicano v. Brentwood Homeowners' Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested permission to relandscape their property with low-maintenance materials to accommodate mobility limitations from rheumatoid arthritis and complications from a childhood accident.
key_holding: Although plaintiffs adequately alleged injury-in-fact for standing purposes based on emotional distress damages, they failed to state a reasonable modification claim because they did not adequately allege that the Association knew or should have known of their disabilities, nor that the modification request was made because of disability.
brief_summary: Les Bock and Dunnia Aplicano, homeowners with mobility disabilities, sued the Brentwood Homeowners' Association after it rejected their architectural application to relandscape their property with low-maintenance materials. case_name: Jane Doe v. University of Idaho
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request analyzed; plaintiffs' FHA claims focus on alleged race, national origin, and sex discrimination affecting their ability to remain in the Moscow, Idaho community.
key_holding: The FHA does not abrogate Eleventh Amendment immunity, so claims against the state university are barred; additionally, plaintiffs failed to adequately plead housing discrimination claims because they did not allege any defendant committed discriminatory conduct related to actual rentals, negotiations, terms, or advertising of dwellings.
brief_summary: Jane Doe, Kelly Doe, and John Doe, former law students at the University of Idaho College of Law, sued the University, University officials, and a fellow student under the Fair Housing Act and other statutes, alleging discrimination based on race, national origin, and sex that made living in Moscow, Idaho unsafe and caused them to leave. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, ruling the Eleventh Amendment bars claims against the state university and that plaintiffs failed to state plausible FHA claims because they did not allege discriminatory conduct related to actual housing transactions.

case_name: Valencia v. City of Springfield, Illinois
accommodation_description: The underlying case involved a group home for persons with disabilities seeking reasonable accommodation from the City's 600-foot spacing rule and its definition of family, which prohibited disabled individuals from living together in the same manner as non-disabled individuals.
key_holding: The court granted in part Private Plaintiffs' motion for attorneys' fees and litigation expenses, awarding $380,350 in attorneys' fees and $33,072.19 in costs, finding the hours expended on zoning matters and discovery were reasonably necessary to advance the successful FHA claims.
brief_summary: Private Plaintiffs Mary B. source_file: 10178593_2022_County Of Cook v. Bank of America Corporation_ilnd
case_name: County of Cook v. Bank of America Corporation, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request - case involves claims of discriminatory lending and foreclosure practices targeting minority borrowers
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants because Cook County failed to produce evidence of an integrated equity stripping scheme, could not establish robust causality between defendants' policies and racial disparities in foreclosure rates, and offered no evidence of actual increased out-of-pocket costs from the alleged discriminatory foreclosures.
brief_summary: Cook County sued Bank of America Corporation, Countrywide, and related entities under the Fair Housing Act, alleging defendants engaged in an equity stripping scheme that targeted African American and Hispanic borrowers for predatory loans, resulting in disproportionate foreclosures that harmed the County. source_file: 10178987_2024_Connectors Realty Group Corporation, The v. State Farm Fire _ Casualty Company_ilnd
case_name: Connectors Realty Group Corporation v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Company
accommodation_description: Not applicable - this case involves alleged racial discrimination in insurance claim denials based on zip code demographics, not a disability accommodation request
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on the race discrimination claims (Counts I-II) because genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether State Farm's investigation and denial of insurance claims was motivated by race, but denied class certification because individual issues predominate and plaintiff Williams presented serious credibility problems making him inadequate as a class representative.
brief_summary: The Connectors Realty Group Corporation and Darryl Williams sued State Farm Fire & Casualty Company alleging the insurer violated the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981-1982 by discriminatorily investigating and denying insurance claims for properties located in majority African-American zip codes. The court denied State Farm's motion for summary judgment on the discrimination claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist based on evidence including a former manager's testimony about a discriminatory policy and statistical analysis showing correlation between zip code demographics and claim denials, but denied the plaintiffs' motion for class certification because individual causation questions predominate and Williams' credibility issues made him an inadequate class representative.
key_cases_cited: N.A.A.C.P. v. American Family Mutual Insurance Co., 978 F.2d 287 (7th Cir. 1992)
United Farm Bureau Mutual Insurance Co. v. Metropolitan Human Relations Commission, 24 F.3d 1008 (7th Cir. 1994)

source_file: 10179253_2024_Legal Aid Chicago v. Hunter Properties, Inc._ilnd
case_name: Legal Aid Chicago v. Hunter Properties, Inc.
accommodation_description: Fair housing organization challenges landlord's blanket no-evictions screening policy as having disparate impact on Black renters
key_holding: The court granted dismissal for lack of standing, finding Legal Aid Chicago failed to allege a concrete injury beyond ordinary program costs because the alleged injuries (sealing eviction records, litigating eviction cases, education) were precisely the organization's core mission activities rather than new burdens imposed by the defendant.
brief_summary: Legal Aid Chicago sued Hunter Properties, a Chicago property management company, alleging that its blanket no-evictions screening policy violated the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on Black renters. The district court granted the motion to dismiss, finding that Legal Aid Chicago lacked organizational standing because it failed to allege a concrete injury beyond ordinary program costs—the activities it claimed as injuries (litigating eviction cases, sealing records, providing education) were precisely the organization's core mission, not new burdens imposed by the defendant's policy.

source_file: 10179261_2024_Access Living of Metropolitan Chicago v. City Of Chicago_ilnd
case_name: Access Living of Metropolitan Chicago, Inc. v. City of Chicago
accommodation_description: Access Living alleges the City of Chicago's affordable housing funding and oversight program fails to ensure compliance with federal accessibility requirements, effectively excluding people with disabilities from affordable housing.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment for the City, finding genuine issues of fact on whether Chicago's affordable housing scheme is a 'program or activity' subject to ADA, Section 504, and FHA liability, and whether the City's role in funding, approving construction, and contracting for compliance makes it responsible for design-and-construction accessibility failures.
brief_summary: Access Living of Metropolitan Chicago sued the City of Chicago alleging that the City's affordable housing funding program discriminates against people with disabilities by failing to ensure housing developments comply with federal accessibility laws under the ADA, Section 504, and Fair Housing Act. The court denied the City's motion for summary judgment, finding triable issues of fact on whether Chicago's substantial involvement in funding, approving, and contracting for accessibility compliance renders the City liable for design-and-construction accessibility failures under the FHA and for program accessibility under the ADA and Section 504.

case_name: Gary Copeny v. Diana England, Matt Evans, Diana Wright
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in the purchase of his home and return of earnest money.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding no plausible federal claims against the named defendants including insufficient factual allegations connecting any defendant to racial discrimination in housing.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Gary Copeny filed suit against Diana England, Matt Evans, and Diana Wright alleging racial discrimination in the purchase of his home in Hancock County, Indiana, including claims that he was defrauded in the sale and subjected to ongoing mistreatment. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) and dismissed it for failure to state a plausible claim, finding the complaint lacked factual allegations connecting any named defendant to discriminatory conduct.

source_file: 10180547_2024_FAIR HOUSING CENTER OF CENTRAL INDIANA, INC. v. M_J MANAGEMENT COMPANY, LLC, d_b_a THE SEXTON COMPANIES_insd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, Inc. v. M&J Management Company, LLC, d/b/a The Sexton Companies
accommodation_description: Two-person-per-bedroom occupancy policy that excludes families with three or more minor children from renting two-bedroom units
key_holding: The court found that plaintiff established a prima facie case of disparate impact based on familial status, but denied both parties' summary judgment motions because genuine disputes exist regarding whether defendants' occupancy policy is necessary to achieve substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interests.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana sued M&J Management (Sexton Companies) alleging that defendants' two-person-per-bedroom occupancy policy has a disparate impact on families with minor children in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding that while plaintiff established a prima facie case, genuine disputes remain about whether defendants' occupancy standard is necessary to achieve substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interests.

source_file: 10180644_2024_FAIR HOUSING CENTER OF CENTRAL INDIANA, INC. v. M_J MANAGEMENT COMPANY, LLC, d_b_a THE SEXTON COMPANIES_insd

key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to preclude plaintiff's expert James Colbert from testifying at bench trial, finding his statistical methodology and qualifications sufficient for admissibility under Daubert, despite acknowledging valid concerns about his failure to consider extraneous variables.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana sued M&J Management Company and affiliated entities alleging that their two-occupants-per-bedroom occupancy standard discriminates against families with minor children in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied defendants' motion to preclude expert testimony by plaintiff's statistician James Colbert, finding his data analysis methodology sufficiently reliable for admissibility at the upcoming bench trial despite concerns about his failure to account for alternative explanatory variables.

source_file: 10180688_2024_FAIR HOUSING CENTER OF CENTRAL INDIANA, INC. v. M_J MANAGEMENT COMPANY, LLC, d_b_a THE SEXTON COMPANIES_insd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, Inc. v. M&J Management Company, LLC, d/b/a The Sexton Companies
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; this is a disparate impact challenge to occupancy restrictions affecting families with children.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motion to exclude evidence of rules governing children's use of common facilities, finding such evidence relevant to assessing whether occupancy restrictions constitute disparate impact; the court also denied Plaintiff's motion to preclude Defendants' Rule 30(b)(6) designee testimony but granted Plaintiff's motion to prevent Defendants from adding unidentified witnesses.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana sued M&J Management Company (d/b/a The Sexton Companies) alleging that Defendants' occupancy restrictions and rules governing children's use of common facilities violate the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on families with children. The court ruled on pre-trial evidentiary motions, denying Defendants' request to exclude evidence of their common facility rules and denying Plaintiff's motion to preclude supplemental Rule 30(b)(6) testimony, while granting Plaintiff's request to prevent Defendants from adding unidentified witnesses to their trial witness list.
key_cases_cited: Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

source_file: 10180724_2024_United States v. Fox Run Apartments, LLC_ksd
case_name: United States of America v. Fox Run Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Veteran with PTSD/ADHD/depression requested to keep his 70-pound Doberman Pinscher emotional support animal despite a 25-pound pet weight limit.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion for attorney's fees and costs under the EAJA, finding the government's FHA reasonable accommodation claim was neither frivolous nor lacking substantial justification, as there was a reasonable basis for the factual allegations and legal theories supporting the failure-to-accommodate claim.
brief_summary: The United States sued Fox Run Apartments and related defendants under the FHA alleging failure to accommodate a veteran's ESA request for a 70-pound Doberman Pinscher, but voluntarily dismissed the claims; the court then denied defendants' motion for attorney's fees and costs under the EAJA, finding the government's position was substantially justified because the record supported that the veteran had a disability, requested a reasonable accommodation, and defendants failed to offer alternatives before he withdrew his application.
key_cases_cited: Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)

case_name: Edwards v. Klinedinst
accommodation_description: The court does not analyze any specific accommodation request; this opinion addresses only whether the prior state-court eviction judgment has preclusive effect on the federal FHA claims, denying defendant's summary judgment motion on res judicata grounds.
key_holding: Kansas Stat. Ann. § 61-3802 limits the preclusive effect of prior eviction judgments under the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, allowing plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act and Section 1981 claims to proceed despite the prior state-court action.
brief_summary: Kenneth and Taaliba Edwards sued their landlord Betty Klinedinst alleging Fair Housing Act claims and Section 1981 claims for race discrimination arising from a residential tenancy in Lansing, Kansas. The court denied Klinedinst's motion for summary judgment on res judicata grounds, holding that Kansas's special eviction judgment statute (§ 61-3802) limits preclusion so that claims not included in the prior state-court eviction judgment—including federal FHA claims—may proceed.
key_cases_cited: Herington v. City of Wichita, 500 P.3d 1168 (Kan. 2021)

source_file: 10181821_2024_Military Road Revitalization Company, LLC v. St. Tammany Parish Government_laed
case_name: Military Road Revitalization Company, LLC et al. v. St. Tammany Parish Government et al.
accommodation_description: Developer sued municipality over moratorium ordinance allegedly blocking affordable housing development serving protected classes including persons with disabilities
key_holding: The court granted Safety National's motion to dismiss the intentional discrimination FHA claims as excluded from insurance coverage but denied the motion as to the disparate-impact FHA claim because it does not require a showing of intent and therefore does not fall within the policy's exclusion for intentional violations of law.
brief_summary: Military Road Revitalization Company sued St. Tammany Parish Government and its insurer Safety National, alleging that a municipal moratorium ordinance blocking an affordable housing development violated the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on protected classes including African Americans, Hispanics, and persons with disabilities. The court granted Safety National's motion to dismiss the intentional discrimination claims as excluded from insurance coverage but denied the motion as to the disparate-impact claim, finding it does not require a showing of intent and therefore may be covered.

source_file: 10181920_2024_Stennis v. The Moorings of Oak Harbor Property Owners' Association LLC_laed
case_name: Shalmon J. Stennis et al. v. The Moorings of Oak Harbor Property Owners' Association Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Black homeowners allege HOA defendants selectively enforced community restrictions, issued fines, deactivated entry decal, and engaged in coordinated harassment against plaintiffs because of their race.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims under §§ 3604(a) and (b), finding plaintiffs adequately alleged discriminatory enforcement of HOA restrictions based on race and a hostile environment claim, but granted dismissal of plaintiffs' intentional infliction of emotional distress claims as insufficiently pleaded.
brief_summary: Black homeowners sued their homeowners association, property management company, and board president alleging race-based discrimination and harassment including selective enforcement of community restrictions, excessive fines, and deactivation of entry access. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims under §§ 3604(a) and (b), finding sufficient factual allegations of discriminatory treatment and hostile environment, but dismissed plaintiffs' state law intentional infliction of emotional distress claims as insufficiently pleaded.

case_name: Believe TGH, LLC, et al. v. Pointe Coupee Parish
accommodation_description: Therapeutic group home operator seeks zoning variance to expand the definition of 'family' to allow more than four unrelated minors with disabilities to reside together in a Rural Agricultural zoning district.
key_holding: The court denied reconsideration of its prior ruling denying partial summary judgment because genuine disputes of material fact remain regarding whether the requested zoning accommodation is reasonable and necessary for the therapeutic group home to operate.
brief_summary: Believe TGH, LLC and related entities, which operate therapeutic group homes for minors with disabilities, sued Pointe Coupee Parish after the Parish denied their variance request to expand the zoning definition of 'family' to allow group homes with more than four unrelated residents. 10182858_2022_Estate of DaMon R. Fisher v. City of Annapolis_mdd
case_name: Estate of DaMon R. Fisher v. City of Annapolis
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request at issue; this case concerns HACA's policy of not inspecting and licensing public housing, which allegedly disproportionately harmed African American residents and contributed to tenant DaMon Fisher's death from mold-related respiratory illness.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of Fisher's FHA disparate impact claim, finding that the non-inspection policy bore more heavily on African Americans, historical background supported an inference of discriminatory intent, and Fisher adequately alleged injury from discriminatory housing conditions; however, the § 1986 claim was dismissed as untimely.
brief_summary: DaMon Fisher's estate sued the City of Annapolis and the Housing Authority of the City of Annapolis (HACA) alleging that the City's longstanding policy of exempting HACA public housing from inspection and licensing requirements violated the Fair Housing Act and civil rights laws, and that resulting mold conditions in Fisher's apartment caused his death. The court denied dismissal of Fisher's FHA disparate impact claim, finding sufficient allegations that the non-inspection policy disproportionately harmed African American public housing residents and supported an inference of discriminatory intent, while dismissing the § 1986 claim as untimely.

source_file: 10182954_2024_Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc._mdd
case_name: Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested various reasonable modifications and accommodations purportedly necessary due to his disability, including: (1) construction or use of a roof balcony ('Balcony Requests'); (2) installation of storage sheds on his front porch and in the back of his house; (3) installation of a brick patio over soil ('Yard/Storage Requests'); and (4) installation of a trellis. The court found the balcony, patio, and trellis requests insufficiently pleaded as 'necessary' under the FHA, while the storage shed modification claims survived dismissal as to KFCA and the BFMA Defendants.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's pro se motion for reconsideration of its prior interlocutory order largely dismissing his FHA claims, finding he failed to present new evidence, a change in applicable law, or clear error causing manifest injustice under the Carlson standard.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Edward Siguel brought FHA and ADA claims against his homeowners association (King Farm Citizens Assembly), individual board members, an attorney, and architects, alleging denial of reasonable modifications and accommodations including a roof balcony, storage sheds, a brick patio, and trellis. In an earlier ruling, the court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motions to dismiss, dismissing most counts but allowing Count VI (storage shed modification requests) to proceed against KFCA and the BFMA Defendants. In this opinion, the court denied plaintiff's motion for reconsideration of that prior ruling, holding that plaintiff failed to identify new litigation-produced evidence, a change in applicable law, or a clear error rising to the level of manifest injustice as required by Fourth Circuit precedent.

source_file: 10182963_2024_Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc._mdd
case_name: Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to install storage sheds on his front porch and in the back of his house as a reasonable modification and/or accommodation, asserting that the sheds were causally connected to and necessary due to his disability (handicap status) to afford him full enjoyment of his dwelling under the FHA.
key_holding: The court denied the BFMA Defendants' motion for reconsideration of the interlocutory order denying their motion to dismiss Count VI (reasonable modification claim for storage sheds), finding that the defendants failed to establish substantially different evidence, a change in applicable law, or clear error causing manifest injustice under the Carlson framework.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Edward Siguel sued King Farm Citizens Assembly and numerous other defendants, including architect Laurence Frank and Bennett Frank McCarthy Architects, Inc. (BFMA Defendants), alleging multiple Fair Housing Act violations arising from the denial of his requests to install storage sheds as a reasonable modification/accommodation for his disability. In a prior interlocutory order, the court granted motions to dismiss as to most counts but allowed Count VI (failure to permit reasonable modifications for storage sheds) to survive against Defendant KFCA and the BFMA Defendants. The BFMA Defendants then moved for reconsideration, arguing the court erred in not dismissing Count VI against them; the court denied that motion, finding the defendants were merely relitigating the prior ruling and had not met the high bar required for reconsideration of an interlocutory order.

source_file: 10183030_2024_Bailey v. The Queen's Landing Council of Unit Owners, Inc._mdd
case_name: Rosanna Bailey v. The Queen's Landing Council of Unit Owners, Inc.
accommodation_description: Dr. Bailey alleges she was denied repairs, maintenance, and services (including remediation for mold, door replacements, video cameras) because of her disability and race, while similarly situated non-disabled, white neighbors received these services.
key_holding: The court dismissed the sex discrimination claim for failure to state a claim, but denied the motion to dismiss on the race discrimination, disability discrimination, and retaliation claims, finding sufficient timely allegations that the Council treated Dr. Bailey differently because of her race and disability.
brief_summary: Dr. Rosanna Bailey, a Black woman with disabilities, sued her condominium association alleging race and disability discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, claiming she received inferior repair services and maintenance compared to white, non-disabled neighbors. The court granted the motion to dismiss the sex discrimination claim as conclusory, but denied dismissal on the race and disability discrimination and retaliation claims, finding she alleged sufficient facts to proceed past the pleadings stage.

case_name: Tamara Johnson, et al. v. City of Annapolis
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; this is a disparate impact challenge to the City's non-enforcement of rental licensing and inspection requirements for HACA public housing properties
key_holding: The plaintiffs' renewed motion for summary judgment on FHA disparate impact liability was denied because, although the City's non-enforcement policy and the poor conditions at HACA properties are undisputed, the plaintiffs failed to establish the necessary causal link between the City's illegal conduct and the plaintiffs' injury given that the causal inference is not ineluctable and additional discovery is warranted.
brief_summary: Black public housing tenants and the Estate of DaMon R. Fisher sued the City of Annapolis alleging that the City's decades-long non-enforcement of rental licensing and inspection requirements for Housing Authority of the City of Annapolis (HACA) properties violated the Fair Housing Act by disparately impacting almost exclusively Black renters. The court denied the plaintiffs' renewed motion for summary judgment on disparate impact liability because while the City's discriminatory policy and poor housing conditions were undisputed, the plaintiffs failed to establish proximate causation given the debatable causal inference and the need for additional discovery.
key_cases_cited: Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
