case_name: Ray A. Sandles et al v. Secretary of Veterans Affairs
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - complaint alleges FHA violations related to septic repair, water shutoff, and eviction, but order does not specify accommodation request
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for appointment of counsel because plaintiff failed to demonstrate exceptional circumstances, as the case did not present complex facts or law, plaintiff could articulate claims adequately pro se, and plaintiff had not shown likelihood of success on the merits
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Ray A. Sandles and Y.S. sued the Secretary of Veterans Affairs alleging Fair Housing Act violations related to failure to repair a septic system, shutting off water, and attempting to evict them from property in Oak Harbor, Washington. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for appointment of counsel, finding no exceptional circumstances warranting counsel because the case did not involve complex facts or law and plaintiffs had not demonstrated likelihood of success on the merits.

case_name: Sang W. Mendy v. Tracy L. Larson, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case; the order concerns only a procedural motion to extend the time for service of process.
key_holding: The court retroactively extended the service deadline to September 19, 2023, finding that plaintiff's delayed service was the result of excusable neglect given his pro se status and genuine misunderstanding of Rule 4's requirements, even though counsel's post-appointment delay was unexplained.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Sang W. Mendy filed an FHA complaint against his landlord and security companies, alleging violations of 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604(b) and 3617, but failed to properly effectuate service within the 90-day deadline. Proceeding initially pro se, Mendy personally served the corporate defendants (impermissible under Rule 4) and struggled to locate individual defendant Larson. After counsel was appointed, service was eventually completed between August and September 2023. The court found excusable neglect warranting a retroactive extension of the service deadline to September 19, 2023, while denying the forward-looking extension because all defendants had already been served and no further extension was justified.

case_name: Slaughter v. Valley View I LLP
accommodation_description: Plaintiff references 'denial of a reasonable accommodation' and 'disability (air quality)' but provides no specific details about what accommodation was requested.
key_holding: The court issued an Order to Show Cause requiring plaintiff to provide factual details supporting her claims, including the reasonable accommodation claim, or face dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Antoinette Slaughter filed her second lawsuit against Valley View I LLP (property management company) and others alleging discrimination, retaliation, harassment, and denial of a reasonable accommodation related to her disability and air quality. The court issued an Order to Show Cause requiring plaintiff to provide specific factual details supporting her claims, noting the complaint lacks sufficient detail for defendants to respond and that a prior case was dismissed for similar deficiencies.
key_cases_cited: Indep. Towers of Wash. v. Washington, 350 F.3d 925 (9th Cir. 2003)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

source_file: 10245021_2024_McIntire v. Housing Authority of Snohomish County_wawd
case_name: Shawna McIntire v. Housing Authority of Snohomish County
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to retain or be transferred housing assistance — specifically, the VASH (Veterans Affairs Supportive Housing) voucher held in her abuser-husband's name — as a non-veteran victim of domestic violence following a family breakup, and also sought VAWA-required notices, documentation forms, and a grievance hearing upon the termination of her assistance.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion for partial summary judgment on liability for all four claims — VAWA violation, procedural due process under § 1983, breach of contract, and conversion — finding that HASCO's repeated failures to follow VAWA's procedural safeguards, its policy of not transferring VASH vouchers to non-veteran domestic violence victims, and its unlawful disposal of plaintiff's property without required notice each entitled plaintiff to judgment as a matter of law.
brief_summary: Shawna McIntire, a domestic violence victim and beneficiary of her veteran husband's VASH housing voucher, sued the Housing Authority of Snohomish County (HASCO) after HASCO secretly removed her from the voucher at her abuser's request, failed to provide VAWA-mandated notices and forms at any point during her tenancy or eviction proceedings, and then destroyed her personal property the day after she inquired about retrieving it without giving the 30-day statutory notice required under Washington law. The court granted plaintiff's motion for partial summary judgment on liability as to her VAWA, procedural due process (§ 1983), breach of contract, and conversion claims, finding undisputed evidence of HASCO's deliberate indifference, lack of VAWA training, and unlawful customs. The court also struck a key defense declaration for failure to properly disclose the witness and lack of personal knowledge foundation.
key_cases_cited: Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976)
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Nozzi v. Hous. Auth. of City of Los Angeles, 806 F.3d 1178 (9th Cir. 2015)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

case_name: Antionette Slaughter v. Valley View I LLP
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint mentions 'denial of a reasonable accommodation' but provides no factual details describing the specific accommodation requested.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed with prejudice because it failed to provide sufficient factual detail to state any claims, including the reasonable accommodation claim, following the same deficiencies identified in plaintiff's earlier dismissed case.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Antionette Slaughter filed a second federal lawsuit against Valley View I LLP (her apartment building's management company) alleging discrimination, retaliation, harassment, and denial of reasonable accommodation. The court dismissed the case with prejudice because the complaint failed to provide sufficient factual detail to state any claims, following the same deficiencies identified in her earlier dismissed case.
key_cases_cited: Indep. Towers of Wash. v. Washington, 350 F.3d 925 (9th Cir. 2003)

case_name: Sang W. Mendy v. Tracy L. Larson et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; the case concerns alleged racial discrimination in the terms, conditions, and privileges of tenancy, specifically a security guard's pattern of harassing and profiling Black residents, culminating in a false assault allegation against the plaintiff.
key_holding: The court denied defendant ASP's motion for summary judgment without prejudice because ASP failed to adequately support its interpretation of the stock purchase agreement's Retained Liabilities provision, granted plaintiff's Rule 56(d) motions to continue to allow further discovery, and granted plaintiff's motion for leave to file an amended complaint.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Sang Mendy, a Black resident of the Modera Jackson apartment complex, alleged that a security guard employed by Northwest Security Services repeatedly harassed him and other Black residents, and made a false assault allegation against him in October 2020 that resulted in his arrest and a year of lost work. After Northwest merged into American Security Programs, Inc. (ASP), Mendy sued under the Fair Housing Act's Sections 3604(b) and 3617. The court denied ASP's motions to dismiss and for summary judgment, finding Mendy had adequately pleaded successor liability and that genuine issues of material fact remained regarding whether the Retained Liabilities provision of the stock purchase agreement insulated ASP from liability, and granted Mendy leave to file an amended complaint to add clarifying facts.
key_cases_cited: Ohana v. Marriott, 2016 WL 11760169 (C.D. Cal. 2016)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)

case_name: Sang W. Mendy v. Tracy L. Larson et al.
accommodation_description: The underlying case involves Fair Housing Act claims, but this discovery order does not describe the specific accommodation request at issue.
key_holding: This discovery order grants in part and denies in part three motions: ASP's motion to seal is granted for purchase price and financial information but denied for litigation summaries in Schedule 3.23; ASP's motion for protective order is granted for financial information in the Agreement schedules; and Mendy's motion to compel is granted as to ASP's balance sheets and income statements from 2021, 2023, and 2024 for purposes of assessing punitive damages.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Sang Mendy filed Fair Housing Act claims against American Security Programs, Inc. and others arising from an October 2020 incident, and this discovery order addresses competing motions regarding sealing of documents and disclosure of financial information for punitive damages purposes. The court granted ASP's requests to seal purchase price and financial information from the Agreement while requiring disclosure of litigation summaries, and granted Mendy's motion to compel production of ASP's balance sheets and income statements from 2021, 2023, and 2024.

case_name: Eddie L. Hatch, Jr. and Michelle Davis-Hatch v. Barrett
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged race-based refusal to sell a commercial building they sought to purchase for a food service training facility; no disability accommodation was requested.
key_holding: The FHA does not apply because the property is a commercial building, not a dwelling as defined by 42 U.S.C. § 3602(b), and the moving defendants were not sellers in the transaction.
brief_summary: Eddie and Michelle Hatch sued the City of Milwaukee and various development entities alleging racial discrimination in the sale of a commercial building, claiming the DCD favored a white developer over Black entrepreneurs in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice, holding that the FHA does not apply because the property is a commercial building rather than a dwelling as defined by the Act, and the moving defendants were not sellers in the transaction.

case_name: Eddie L. Hatch, Jr. and Michelle Davis-Hatch v. City of Milwaukee, Tom Barrett, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged racial discrimination in the sale of a commercial building, claiming the City favored a white developer over Black entrepreneurs.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims because the commercial building at issue does not constitute a 'dwelling' under the FHA, as plaintiffs intended to use it as a food service training facility for commercial purposes rather than for residential occupancy.
brief_summary: Eddie and Michelle Davis-Hatch, proceeding pro se, sued the City of Milwaukee and various city officials alleging racial discrimination in connection with the City's refusal to sell them a commercial building for use as a food service training facility. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that the commercial property did not constitute a 'dwelling' under the FHA and therefore fell outside the statute's coverage.

case_name: Debra Lee Huzjak v. Kim Ellis, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges neighbors harassed her and her mother based on age, disability, race, and religion through break-ins, theft, bank fraud, and reports to the Department of Aging.
key_holding: The court recommends dismissal because Huzjak has not alleged that she personally experienced discrimination rising to the level of actual or constructive eviction, and any claims belonging to her mother cannot be pursued by Huzjak without authorization from the estate.
brief_summary: Debra Lee Huzjak sued her neighbors, the corporate owner of her apartment building, and the manager of the building, alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on discriminatory harassment by neighbors motivated by age, disability, race, and religious animus toward her mother. The court recommends dismissing all claims because Huzjak failed to allege personal discrimination that rose to the level of constructive eviction and cannot assert claims belonging to her mother's estate.

case_name: Shyanne Tubbs v. PMI of Greater Milwaukee, Monica Steller, David Grisamore, and Peter Hintz
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; plaintiff alleges mistreatment following apartment fire and speculates about racial discrimination.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissal because plaintiff's amended complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible Fair Housing Act claim, containing only speculative assertions about racial motivation without factual support.
brief_summary: Shyanne Tubbs, proceeding pro se, filed suit against her property management company and related defendants alleging mistreatment after a fire at her apartment and claiming Fair Housing Act violations based on race. The court screened the amended complaint and recommended dismissal, finding that Tubbs failed to allege sufficient facts to state a plausible claim for relief, offering only speculative assertions about racial motivation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

source_file: 10250032_2022_McFarland v. Housing Authority of Racine County_wied
case_name: McFarland v. Housing Authority of Racine County
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, mother of two disabled children including a physically-disabled son requiring a wheelchair-accessible home, sought an increase in Section 8 Vouchers and an extension of time to find suitable housing, which HARC denied.
key_holding: The court denied Schattner's motion to dismiss, finding plausible Plaintiff's state law retaliation claim under Wis. Stat. § 704.45 for terminating her tenancy after she complained about foundation issues; however, Plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 failed because she did not allege retaliation based on a protected class.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Nakreisha McFarland sued her landlord Michael Schattner and the Housing Authority of Racine County alleging, inter alia, that Schattner evicted her in retaliation for complaining about dangerous foundation conditions, and that HARC denied her request for an extension of time on her Section 8 Voucher without considering her disabled children's needs. The court denied Schattner's motion to dismiss, finding plausible her state law retaliation claim but rejecting her FHA retaliation claim for failure to allege retaliation based on a protected class.

case_name: Eddie L. Hatch, Jr. and Michelle Davis-Hatch v. City of Milwaukee, Tom Barrett, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege they were denied the opportunity to purchase city-owned property because of their race, as defendants allegedly rigged the selection process and inflated asbestos estimates to favor a white purchaser over minority bidders.

brief_summary: Black prospective property purchasers sued the City of Milwaukee and numerous officials and entities alleging they were denied the opportunity to purchase city-owned property because of their race, as defendants allegedly rigged the selection process and inflated asbestos estimates to favor a white purchaser over minority bidders. accommodation_description: Request to keep a five-pound chihuahua named Roxy as an assistance animal prescribed by a psychologist for anxiety, depression, schizoaffective disorder, and PTSD
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motions to compel a Rule 35 psychological examination of McLean and a Rule 34 examination of her assistance animal, finding both requests relevant and proportional to the needs of the Fair Housing Act case and that good cause exists for the examinations.

brief_summary: Relators James Dieter and Karen Schwenke brought a False Claims Act qui tam action alleging that the City of Milwaukee, Housing Authority of the City of Milwaukee, and Milwaukee County falsely certified compliance with federal anti-discrimination laws and the Fair Housing Act's affirmatively furthering fair housing mandate while knowingly creating and maintaining racially-segregated containment zones for low-income, minority, and disabled residents. source_file: 10252595_2023_United States of America v. City of Milwaukee_wied
case_name: United States of America ex rel. James Dieter and Karen Schwenke v. City of Milwaukee, City of Milwaukee Community Development Grants Administration, Housing Authority of the City of Milwaukee, and Milwaukee County
subsidy_program: CDBG, HOME, Emergency Shelter Grant, Housing Opportunities for People with AIDS, Section 8
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it is a False Claims Act case alleging defendants falsely certified compliance with the AFFH mandate and anti-discrimination laws to obtain federal housing funding.
key_holding: The court dismissed the False Claims Act complaint with prejudice because relators failed to adequately plead the 'what' and 'how' of falsity under Rule 9(b), failing to tie specific misconduct to specific statutory standards or show how certifications were misleading; relators' focus on only one neighborhood (Near West Side) was insufficient for a disparate impact theory, and their AFFH mandate allegations merely parroted regulatory text without explaining why specific certifications were false.
brief_summary: Relators James Dieter and Karen Schwenke sued the City of Milwaukee, Housing Authority of the City of Milwaukee, and Milwaukee County under the False Claims Act, alleging defendants falsely certified compliance with the Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing mandate and anti-discrimination laws to obtain federal HUD funding. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss with prejudice, finding relators failed to plead falsity with the required particularity under Rule 9(b) and failed to adequately allege a disparate impact theory showing how specific certifications were misleading.

case_name: Suan D. Kendrick v. Oakbrook Corporation et al.
accommodation_description: Criminal background screening denial based on felony conviction over 20 years old
key_holding: The plaintiff stated sufficient facts to proceed with a racial discrimination claim under the Fair Housing Act by identifying the type of discrimination (racial), the defendants (Oakbrook Corporation, Lindley, Gerensky, and Resident Check LLC), and when the discrimination occurred (February 4, 2019).
brief_summary: Suan D. Kendrick, an African American plaintiff, sued Oakbrook Corporation, Rebecca Lindley, Heather Gerensky, and Resident Check LLC alleging that they denied his rental application at Beerline B in Milwaukee because of his race and a criminal conviction over 20 years old, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915A and found that the plaintiff stated sufficient factual allegations to proceed with a racial discrimination claim.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Conley v. Gibson, 355 U.S. 41 (1957)

case_name: Shawanda V. Collins v. Team Management LLC et al.
subsidy_program: Section 42 Low Income Housing Tax Credits
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested; this case involves denial of a rental application based on a blanket criminal history exclusion policy and an income minimum advertising policy, not a request for modification of rules or policies to accommodate a disability.
key_holding: At the IFP screening stage, the court allowed Collins's FHA racial disparate impact claim (based on defendants' blanket criminal history exclusion policy) and her Wisconsin statutory disability discrimination claim (based on discriminatory income advertising) to proceed, but dismissed her federal disability and income discrimination claims for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Shawanda Collins, an African American woman with disabilities and a prior felony record over 19 years old, alleged that defendants' blanket pre-screening ban on applicants with criminal histories had a disparate impact on African Americans in violation of the FHA, and that their advertising of a 40% income minimum policy deterred and excluded disabled low-income individuals. The court conducted IFP screening applying Rule 8/Twombly/Iqbal pleading standards and found Collins's FHA racial disparate impact claim plausible given her statistical allegations and controlled testing of the application process, and her Wisconsin Stat. § 106.50 disability advertising claim sufficient, while dismissing her federal disability discrimination claim because she failed to allege defendants knew of her disability or denied her housing because of it, and her income discrimination claim because income alone is not a protected class under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Metropolitan Housing Development Corp. v. Village of Arlington Heights, 558 F.2d 1283 (7th Cir. 1977)

case_name: Kendrick v. Oakbrook Corporation
accommodation_description: Housing discrimination claim severed to separate case; accommodation type not analyzed in this order.
key_holding: The court construed the plaintiff's letter as a motion to sever under Fed. R. Civ. P. 21 and granted it, separating employment discrimination claims against postal service employees (remaining in Case No. 20-cv-1884) from housing discrimination claims (transferred to a new case with Oakbrook Corporation as defendant).
brief_summary: Suan D. Kendrick filed a pro se complaint that initially contained employment discrimination claims against postal service employees, then filed an amended complaint alleging housing discrimination against Oakbrook Corporation and related defendants. The court granted plaintiff's motion to sever, ordering that employment claims remain in Case No. 20-cv-1884 while housing discrimination claims are transferred to a new case.

case_name: Suan D. Kendrick v. Oakbrook Corporation
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges denial of rental application based on race and criminal conviction policy constitutes racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The court found that the plaintiff adequately alleged a housing discrimination claim by identifying the type of discrimination (racial), who committed it (defendants), and when it occurred (February 4, 2019), thereby stating the bare minimum facts to survive screening and require defendants to respond.
brief_summary: Suan D. Kendrick, an African American male, sued Oakbrook Corporation, Rebecca Lindley, Heather Gerensky, and Resident Check LLC under the Fair Housing Act, alleging that his rental application was denied at an apartment in Milwaukee because of his race and a felony conviction from over twenty years ago. The court, in a screening order, determined that the plaintiff had met the minimal pleading requirements by identifying the type of discrimination (racial), the actors (defendants), and the date of the denial, and therefore allowed the case to proceed to service and responsive pleading.

case_name: Kendrick v. Brennan
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's amended complaint alleges Fair Housing Act housing discrimination in rental context, but specific accommodation request not detailed in this severance order.
key_holding: The court construes plaintiff's letter as a motion to sever under Fed. R. Civ. P. 21 and grants severance, opening a new case for the housing discrimination claims against Oakbrook Corporation, Rebecca Lindley, Heather Gerensky, and Resident Check LLC, while retaining the employment discrimination claims against USPS defendants in this case.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Suan D. Kendrick filed an amended complaint alleging housing discrimination claims against Oakbrook Corporation, Rebecca Lindley, Heather Gerensky, and Resident Check LLC, which the court previously screened and allowed to proceed. The court now grants Kendrick's motion to sever his employment discrimination claims (against USPS defendants) from his housing discrimination claims, opening a new case for the housing discrimination matter while retaining the employment claims in this case.
key_cases_cited: UWM Student Assoc. v. Lovell, 888 F.3d 854 (7th Cir. 2018)

source_file: 10256152_2022_Barilani, Sherilyn v. Housing Authority of the City of Eau Claire_wiwd
case_name: Barilani v. Housing Authority of the City of Eau Claire
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the housing authority investigate and remediate toxic mold in her public housing unit after she and her children suffered serious health effects from mold exposure.
key_holding: Section 1437d(f) of the Federal Housing Act does not create an enforceable federal right to housing of a particular quality or condition that can be asserted under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, because the statute addresses HUD's contracting requirements rather than conferring rights directly on tenants.
brief_summary: Sherilyn Barilani and her minor children sued the Housing Authority of the City of Eau Claire alleging the housing authority violated the Federal Housing Act and her constitutional rights by failing to remediate toxic mold in their public housing unit, causing serious illness. The court granted the housing authority's motion to dismiss, holding that § 1437d(f) does not create an enforceable federal right to housing of a particular condition because it directs HUD's contracting requirements rather than conferring rights on individual tenants, and that the housing authority's negligent conduct did not shock the conscience to support a substantive due process claim.
key_cases_cited: Gonzaga Univ. v. Doe, 536 U.S. 273 (2002)
Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997)

case_name: Andrew Kummerow v. Ohawcha.org, Wendy Fromm, and Her Supervisors
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; plaintiff alleged discrimination based on sexual orientation and retaliation for complaints about housing conditions.
key_holding: Plaintiff's complaint failed to state a viable FHA claim because his allegations of discrimination based on sexual orientation did not give rise to an inference of discriminatory intent, and his retaliation claim failed because his complaints about habitability were not protected activity under the FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Andrew Kummerow sued the Oshkosh/Winnebago County Housing Authority and its property manager alleging discrimination based on sexual orientation, substandard housing conditions, and retaliation for complaints. The court dismissed his amended complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding that his allegations did not support an inference of discriminatory animus and that his habitability complaints did not constitute protected activity under the FHA.

case_name: John Gardner v. Harvard University et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint references Fair Housing Act claims against New England Center for Veterans and Boston Housing Authority regarding housing placement issues but does not articulate a specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because he failed to allege intentional discrimination based on a protected ground under the FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff John Gardner filed suit against Harvard University and numerous other defendants alleging wrongful removal from a graduate program and housing-related grievances at a veterans' center. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915A and dismissed Gardner's FHA claim for failure to allege intentional discrimination based on a protected ground, while granting leave to amend the complaint on other claims.

case_name: John Gardner v. Harvard University, Harvard University Police, Robert Neugeboren, Sergio Imparato, Susan Donnelly, Chris Bavitz, Tanna Wise, John Wise, John Hopkins, Father Phil Merdinger, New England Center and Home Veterans, Boston Housing Authority, Tim Murphy, Dianee Kreibich, Milton Gardner, Dr. Keith May, Dr. Gary Anderson, and Veterans Incorporated
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Fair Housing Act violations regarding housing decisions at a veterans' facility in Boston, though the specific accommodation request is not clearly articulated in the screening order.
key_holding: The court dismissed Gardner's Fair Housing Act claim because his conclusory allegations failed to suggest that any defendant intentionally discriminated against him based on his race or sex in any housing-related decision.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff John Gardner, a recovering alcoholic, sued Harvard University and multiple other defendants alleging wrongful removal from a master's degree program and Fair Housing Act violations related to housing difficulties at a veterans' facility in Boston. The court dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice for failure to comply with court orders and for failure to state plausible claims, finding Gardner's FHA allegations too conclusory to establish intentional discrimination based on race or sex.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Lavela v. Peloquin
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial harassment by a neighbor, including verbal disputes about parking and staring, but does not request any disability-related accommodation.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state a claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 because two isolated disputes with a neighbor did not allege a pattern of racial harassment or statements explicitly about race sufficient to suggest racially motivated conduct.
brief_summary: Gormidou Lavela, a Black tenant at Romeis Apartments in Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin, sued his neighbor Aaron Peloquin under the Fair Housing Act, alleging that Peloquin engaged in racial harassment during two disputes about parking and staring. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding that the allegations described only isolated acts without explicit references to race or facts suggesting racial motivation.

case_name: Lashunda Louvenia Dotson v. Kathy Toon Huser and Oakbrook Corporation
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request - case concerns alleged refusal to renew lease based on race and disability status
key_holding: The court held that issue preclusion barred Dotson's FHA discrimination claim because the state court eviction action had already determined that Dotson didn't have a valid lease, which constituted a nondiscriminatory reason for refusing to renew her lease, and Dotson's conclusory allegations of unfair proceedings were insufficient to overcome summary judgment.
brief_summary: Lashunda Dotson sued her former landlord and property management company, alleging they refused to renew her lease because she is Black and disabled in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The federal court granted summary judgment for defendants, holding that issue preclusion barred Dotson's claim because a prior state court eviction judgment had already determined that Dotson lacked a valid lease—a nondiscriminatory reason for the refusal to renew—and Dotson failed to present specific facts showing the state proceedings were unfair.

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Gormidou Lavela sued defendant Aaron Peloquin in federal court alleging racial harassment under the Fair Housing Act based on two neighbor encounters. case_name: Gormidou Y. Lavela v. Rodney Tapp, Valicia Gilbert, Shirley Severson, Mark Klein, and Jane/John Doe
accommodation_description: The underlying accommodation or discrimination claim is not described in this order; the text addresses only the procedural question of removal jurisdiction and does not detail the substance of plaintiff's housing claims.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion to remand, holding that defendants properly removed the FHA and Wisconsin Open Housing Act claims to federal court because FHA actions are within original federal jurisdiction and defendants timely filed their notice of removal within 30 days of being served.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Gormidou Lavela, proceeding pro se, originally filed suit in Chippewa County Circuit Court against a property management company and its employees under the Fair Housing Act, the Wisconsin Open Housing Act, and other federal and state law provisions. Defendants removed the case to federal court based on federal-question and supplemental jurisdiction, and plaintiff moved to remand. The court denied remand, finding that: (1) concurrent state court jurisdiction over FHA claims does not defeat a defendant's right to remove; (2) the notice of removal was timely filed within 30 days of service; and (3) plaintiff's ability to re-draft a state-only complaint did not render the existing removal improper.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges race-based mistreatment by white residents and failure by property management to investigate his complaints; also alleges retaliation and defamation for filing complaints.
key_holding: The court treated plaintiff's motion for voluntary dismissal as a notice of dismissal and dismissed the case on the merits under Rule 41(a)(1)(B) because plaintiff had previously voluntarily dismissed a federal action against the same defendants based on the same claims, preventing plaintiff from refiling the same federal claims in federal court.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Gormidou Lavela, a Black resident at Romeis Apartments in Chippewa Falls, Wisconsin, brought this second federal action against Meridian Group, Inc. (a property management company) and its employees alleging race-based mistreatment, failure to investigate complaints, retaliation, and defamation. The court dismissed the case on the merits under Rule 41(a)(1)(B) because Lavela had previously voluntarily dismissed an earlier federal action raising the same claims against the same defendants, operating as an adjudication on the merits that bars refiling the federal claims.

case_name: The City of Huntington v. The Lifehouse, Inc.
accommodation_description: The Lifehouse, a sober living home operator, claims federal disability statutes exempt its fourteen properties from all Huntington zoning ordinances, building codes, fire codes, and inspection requirements as a reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The court denied The Lifehouse's motion to dismiss, holding that federal question jurisdiction exists under the coercive action doctrine because The Lifehouse could bring claims under federal disability statutes, and the declaratory judgment action would serve a useful purpose in settling whether the federal accommodation claims provide a blanket exemption from local laws.
brief_summary: The City of Huntington sued The Lifehouse, Inc., a sober living home operator, seeking declaratory judgment that federal disability statutes (including the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act) do not exempt The Lifehouse's fourteen properties from the City's rental registry inspections and WVARR certification requirements. The Lifehouse moved to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction, ripeness, mootness, and discretionary refusal to hear the declaratory judgment action. The court denied the motion, holding it has federal question jurisdiction under the coercive action doctrine because The Lifehouse could bring affirmative claims under federal disability statutes, and exercising declaratory judgment jurisdiction would serve a useful purpose.

source_file: 10266023_2024_Legacy Recovery Svc v. City of Monroe_ca5
case_name: Legacy Recovery Services, L.L.C. v. City of Monroe
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought to purchase city-owned property — a two-story, 56-bedroom building at 1400 and 1401 Stubbs Avenue in Monroe, Louisiana — to operate a low-level residential substance abuse treatment center for Medicaid recipients recovering from substance abuse disorders (alcoholism and substance use disorders), thereby providing housing and treatment access to persons with those disabilities.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of appellate jurisdiction because the district court's order partially granting and partially denying motions to dismiss was neither a final decision under 28 U.S.C. § 1291 nor an appealable collateral order.
brief_summary: Legacy Recovery Services and individual plaintiffs sued the City of Monroe and city officials after the city council refused to pass an ordinance approving the sale of city-owned property intended for use as a residential substance abuse treatment facility, alleging discrimination against the facility's future residents on the basis of their disabilities (alcoholism and substance abuse disorders) under the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, ACA, and 42 U.S.C. § 1983, as well as several Louisiana state law claims. The district court granted in part and denied in part the defendants' motions to dismiss, retaining equal protection, Open Meetings Law, and non-failure-to-accommodate ADA/RA claims while dismissing the FHA claims and failure-to-accommodate theories. The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal, holding that the partial dismissal was not a final order and did not satisfy the narrow collateral-order doctrine because the dismissed and retained claims were intertwined, would require piecemeal review, and would be fully reviewable after final judgment.

Swint v. Chambers Cnty. Comm'n, 514 U.S. 35 (1995)

key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Pickard's TRO motion because Pickard failed to provide the hearing transcript necessary for meaningful appellate review, and the available record did not demonstrate the district court applied an incorrect legal standard, followed improper procedures, or made clearly erroneous findings.
brief_summary: William Pickard appealed the district court's denial of his motion for a temporary restraining order to prevent his eviction from disputed property, asserting Fair Housing Act and § 1983 discrimination claims. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the denial because Pickard failed to provide the transcript of the hearing where the district court explained its reasoning, preventing meaningful appellate review, and the district court did not abuse its discretion based on the incomplete record.

case_name: Deandre Bradley v. Ronald Hain, individually and in his official capacity as the Sheriff of Kane County; Kane County, Illinois; Rochelle Stockman; A. Keaty; S. McKanna; M. Azemi; J. Directo; L. Aguirre; S. Flowers; P. Osmani; Dr. Kul Sood; Wellpath LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a pretrial detainee with paralysis who uses a wheelchair, requested an accessible cell with grab bars, accessible toilet and shower, and an emergency alert button near those fixtures.
key_holding: The Fair Housing Act does not apply to a jail because a jail cell is not a 'dwelling' under 42 U.S.C. § 3602(b), as the FHA's purpose of promoting freedom of choice in housing has no application in the prison context where inmates are subject to strict regulation of where and how they live.
brief_summary: Deandre Bradley, a pretrial detainee with paralysis who uses a wheelchair, sued the Sheriff of Kane County, Kane County, correctional officers, and Wellpath LLC (healthcare contractor) alleging they failed to provide disability accommodations and proper medical care at the Kane County Adult Justice Center. The court granted Defendants' motions to dismiss, dismissing Bradley's FHA claims with prejudice because the court found that a jail cell does not constitute a 'dwelling' under the FHA, and therefore the FHA does not apply to detention facilities.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Garcia v. Condarco

case_name: Lynette Cooper v. Housing Authority Baltimore City et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation by housing authorities and conspirators for unspecified prior activities.
key_holding: Plaintiff's complaint alleging retaliation by HABC, BCHA, former attorneys, elected officials, and foreign nations based on delusional conspiracy theories about chemical releases and device hacking fails to state a plausible claim and is frivolous.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Lynette Cooper, proceeding in forma pauperis, brought a rambling complaint alleging that HABC, BCHA, and numerous other parties engaged in a vast criminal conspiracy involving chemical releases, device hacking, and home breakages in retaliation against her. The Court dismissed the complaint as frivolous and for failure to state a claim upon which relief can be granted, finding Plaintiff's allegations 'irrational [and] wholly incredible.'

case_name: Larry L. Henderson v. Cornelius Bryant, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested modifications to bathroom doors, bedrooms, entry doors, and other areas of his apartment unit to accommodate his mobility disability requiring a powered wheelchair, which defendants failed to complete.
key_holding: The Court found plaintiff stated plausible FHA claims against the property owner, management company, and several individual defendants for failing to make reasonable accommodations and modifications, while dismissing claims against one defendant and dismissing ADA claims for failure to establish defendants were public entities.
brief_summary: Larry L. Henderson, a disabled tenant in St. Louis, Missouri who uses a powered wheelchair due to a neurological disorder, sued his apartment complex, property management company, and individual employees alleging they failed to make reasonable accommodations and modifications to his unit and restricted his caregivers' access. The Court granted his in forma pauperis application and allowed his FHA claims to proceed against all defendants except one leasing associate, while dismissing his ADA claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Erickson v. Pardus, 551 U.S. 89 (2007)

case_name: Dan Chacko v. Melissa Preston
accommodation_description: FHA claim referenced but no specific accommodation request described in the opinion
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, finding that Chacko failed to show how his property was substantially similar to proffered comparator properties for his Fair Housing Act claim.
brief_summary: Dan Chacko appealed the district court's dismissal of his civil action against his homeowners association and related defendants, raising various claims including a Fair Housing Act claim. The Fourth Circuit affirmed, finding that Chacko failed to adequately plead how his property was substantially similar to comparator properties, and rejecting his claims under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act and constitutional challenges.

case_name: Evans-Williams v. Sunstates Management Corporation

brief_summary: Plaintiff Karren Evans-Williams, proceeding pro se, sued Sunstates Management Corporation and Cypress Lakes Apartments alleging retaliation under the Fair Housing Act and a Fourteenth Amendment due process violation. The court sua sponte dismissed the case for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding that the FHA retaliation claim was not well-pleaded because plaintiff failed to allege any underlying discrimination on a protected basis, and the Fourteenth Amendment claim failed because defendants are private actors not bound by constitutional restrictions.

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Deborah Morris sued Amtrak and Baltimore City seeking relief regarding the Frederick Douglass Tunnel construction and alleged segregation, citing the Fair Housing Act among other statutes. Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Sydney Ellerbe v. Tuscan Highlands Apartments
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case; the plaintiff sought relief from a racially discriminatory eviction, alleging that defendant used false assault allegations as a pretext to evict him because of his race in violation of FHA § 3604(b).
key_holding: On IFP screening under 28 U.S.C. § 1915, the court allowed plaintiff's FHA disparate treatment claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) and wrongful eviction claim under NRS 118A.390 to proceed, while dismissing without prejudice the negligence and defamation per se claims for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sydney Ellerbe, an African American man, sued Tuscan Highlands Apartments alleging that after two racially-motivated incidents at a restaurant located within the apartment community, the defendant evicted him based on false assault allegations fabricated as a pretext to cover up the underlying racial discrimination. The court screened the complaint on an IFP application, finding that plaintiff adequately stated a claim for FHA disparate treatment under § 3604(b) and wrongful eviction under Nevada law, but dismissed negligence and defamation per se claims without prejudice and with leave to amend due to pleading deficiencies.
key_cases_cited: Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Pac. Shores Properties, LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)

case_name: Donell L. Prince v. Priscilla Pajela et al.
accommodation_description: Unspecified Fair Housing Act claim based on protected activity; accommodation request not clearly identified in opinion
key_holding: The magistrate judge did not err in denying leave to amend the complaint because plaintiff's proposed FHA claims were futile—they failed to identify the protected activity or connect proposed defendants to discrimination as required.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Donell L. Prince appealed magistrate judge orders denying his motion for leave to amend the complaint to add defendants and motion for reconsideration. The court affirmed, finding plaintiff's proposed FHA claims were futile because they failed to identify any protected activity or connect proposed defendants to discriminatory conduct.
key_cases_cited: Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)

case_name: Ernestine McKnight v. United Management II, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; case involves claims of racial harassment by neighbors and alleged unlawful retaliation eviction for complaining about racial discrimination.
key_holding: The court deferred ruling on the FHA claim to allow limited discovery on whether plaintiff's HUD administrative complaints were pending and tolled the limitations period, while granting the motion to dismiss plaintiff's claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, and 2000d as untimely because the discriminatory acts and her tenancy ended in December 2018.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Ernestine McKnight, a 72-year-old Black woman, sued United Management II, Inc. and related defendants alleging racial harassment by neighbors and unlawful retaliation eviction at Watauga Green Apartments in Boone, North Carolina. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, and 2000d as untimely because her tenancy and the discriminatory acts ended in December 2018, while deferring ruling on the FHA claim pending limited discovery on whether her HUD administrative complaints were pending and tolled the two-year limitations period.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Chardon v. Fernandez, 454 U.S. 6 (1981)
Jones v. R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co., 541 U.S. 369 (2004)

case_name: Jose Antonio Ramos v. Breaking Ground and City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's primary claims concern racial discrimination in housing placement (disparate treatment), with passing references to unspecified handicaps affecting use of showers/bathrooms
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss because plaintiff failed to plead a qualifying disability substantially limiting major life activities and failed to allege similarly situated comparators for his racial discrimination claim.
brief_summary: Jose Antonio Ramos, a pro se plaintiff and formerly homeless Hispanic man residing in temporary supportive housing at 123 East 15th Street, sued Breaking Ground and the City of New York alleging racial discrimination in housing placement and disability-related claims under the FHA. The court granted both motions to dismiss, finding plaintiff's disability allegations insufficient because he failed to plead a qualifying disability substantially limiting major life activities, and his racial discrimination claim failed because he did not allege he was similarly situated to the non-Hispanic individuals who allegedly received housing before him.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

source_file: 10284094_2024_Timothy Whiting v. the Coachella Valley Housing Coalition_ca9
case_name: Timothy Lewis Whiting v. The Coachella Valley Housing Coalition
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged racial discrimination in housing under the Fair Housing Act, including claims of harassment, interference with FHA rights, and retaliation.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal because Whiting failed to allege facts sufficient to show severe or pervasive harassment based on race, interference with FHA rights, a distinct and palpable injury from discriminatory conduct, or retaliation for protected activity.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Timothy Lewis Whiting appealed the dismissal of his housing discrimination suit against the Coachella Valley Housing Coalition, alleging racial discrimination, hostile housing environment, and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act and related state laws. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the dismissal, holding that Whiting failed to plead sufficient facts to establish any cognizable claim under the FHA or related statutes.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Morris v. W. Hayden Ests. First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)
Walker v. City of Lakewood, 272 F.3d 1114 (9th Cir. 2001)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)

case_name: Kesha Lennon v. NVR Mortgage, et al.
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation request was made; plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in mortgage lending and housing transactions.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because her complaint contained only vague, conclusory allegations of racial discrimination without factual matter sufficient to plausibly suggest she suffered adverse action for a discriminatory reason.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Kesha Lennon sued NVR Mortgage Finance, Ryan Homes, and Legacy Title Agency alleging fraud, RICO violations, and discrimination claims including Fair Housing Act claims related to her failed attempt to purchase a townhouse in Sicklerville, New Jersey. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support any of her federal claims, including vague allegations of racial discrimination under the FHA and ECOA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic v. Twombly
Mt. Holly Gardens Citizens in Action, Inc. v. Township of Mount Holly
Shahin v. PNC Bank
White v. Barbe

case_name: Brooklynn C. Clark v. GSL Properties, Inc., CBRE GWS Real Estate Services, Inc., One & Three Centerpointe Drive, Monica Ulrig, Anthony Doe, John Doe, Jon/Jane Does 1-20, Bryce Siebenthall, and Kimberly Carpenter
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an accommodation related to her anxiety, which defendants requested documentation for but never responded to or honored.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's sex, race, and disability discrimination claims but found she pleaded sufficient facts to survive dismissal on her failure to make reasonable accommodations claim based on anxiety, as she requested an accommodation, provided supporting documentation, and defendants never responded.
brief_summary: Brooklynn C. Clark, a Black transgender woman with anxiety, sued GSL Properties and related defendants alleging housing discrimination based on race, sex, gender, and disability including disparate rent increases, false reports to law enforcement, and security deposit retention. The court dismissed most claims but held that plaintiff pleaded sufficient facts to proceed on her failure to make reasonable accommodations claim, finding she requested an accommodation for her anxiety, provided supporting documentation from her doctor, and defendants failed to respond.
key_cases_cited: McGary v. City of Portland, 386 F.3d 1259 (9th Cir. 2004)
Gilligan v. Jamco Dev. Corp., 108 F.3d 246 (9th Cir. 1997)
Gibson v. Cmty. Dev. Partners, 2022 WL 10481324 (D. Or. 2022)
Myers v. Highlands at Vista Ridge Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 2022 WL 4452414 (D. Or. 2022)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)

source_file: 10286748_2024_Jett v. The Country Acres Association of Columbus County LTD_nced
case_name: Raymond A. Jett, Jr. and Tara S. Jett v. George Parker Coleman and Michael P. Coleman
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought to add FHA claims in an HOA dispute but provided no specific accommodation request described in the opinion; court found the proposed amendment futile for failure to allege discriminatory purpose.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' proposed amendment to add FHA claims was denied as futile because the proposed second amended complaint failed to allege the purported violations were motivated by a discriminatory purpose, containing only conclusory assertions that the court need not accept as true.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Raymond and Tara Jett sued individual landlords George and Michael Coleman in an HOA dispute, seeking to amend their complaint to add Fair Housing Act and ADA claims; the court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to deny the motion to amend as futile because plaintiffs failed to allege discriminatory purpose.
key_cases_cited: Edwards v. City of Goldsboro, 178 F.3d 231 (4th Cir. 1999)

source_file: 10286804_2024_Dogbe v. The Lakes at Lemmon Valley, LLC_nvd
case_name: John Dogbe and Alberta Dogbe v. The Lakes at Lemmon Valley, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege they were subjected to discriminatory treatment based on race when asked to cease a clubhouse party and subsequently served with an eviction notice.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiffs' FHA claims under § 3604(b) and § 3617 because the complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to plausibly establish that Defendant's actions were motivated by racial discrimination rather than legitimate concerns about the party size and conduct.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs John and Alberta Dogbe, who are of African descent, sued their landlord The Lakes at Lemmon Valley, LLC alleging racial discrimination after being required to end a clubhouse party and receiving an eviction notice. The court granted Defendant's motion to dismiss the FHA claims, finding the complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to plausibly allege discrimination because of race, though the court granted leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
McGary v. City of Portland, 386 F.3d 1259 (9th Cir. 2004)
Ave. 6E Investments, LLC v. City of Yuma, Ariz., 818 F.3d 493 (9th Cir. 2016)
Morris v. West Hayden Estates First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)

case_name: Deborah Morris v. Amtrak, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's vague complaint references housing-related issues and 'segregation in housing' but does not articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed because plaintiff lacked standing (failed to allege particularized injury), and the complaint constituted impermissible shotgun pleading that failed to provide fair notice of any cognizable claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Deborah Morris filed a sprawling 63-page complaint against Amtrak and Baltimore City alleging various claims including fair housing, civil rights, and constitutional violations arising from housing segregation and related issues. The court dismissed the entire case sua sponte, finding Morris lacked standing because she failed to allege any particularized injury, and her complaint constituted impermissible shotgun pleading that failed to give defendants fair notice of any cognizable claim.
key_cases_cited: Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Dorothy Dumay v. WinnResidential California L.P.
accommodation_description: Reasonable accommodation request by plaintiff Dorothy Dumay based on her disabilities, but the specific accommodation requested is not detailed in this order striking affirmative defenses.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion to strike certain affirmative defenses (Third, Fourth, Fifth, One, Two, Six through Fifteen, Eighteenth, Seventeen, Nineteen, and Twenty) either without leave to amend (those plainly inapplicable or not true affirmative defenses) or with leave to amend, finding that defendants' failure to timely respond waived defenses that are legally defective, but allowing amendment for remaining defenses.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Dorothy Dumay sued defendants WinnResidential California L.P. and Menlo Westridge Affordable Partners, LP alleging disability discrimination for failing to provide requested reasonable accommodations under the Fair Housing Act and related state laws. The court granted in part plaintiff's motion to strike twenty-one affirmative defenses, striking several defenses without leave to amend for being legally inapplicable or not constituting true affirmative defenses, while allowing defendants to amend certain other defenses.
key_cases_cited: Zivkovic v. S. Cal. Edison Co., 302 F.3d 1080 (9th Cir. 2002)
Whiting v. City of Palm Desert, No. EDCV 17-01395, 2018 WL 6034968 (C.D. Cal. May 17, 2018)

case_name: Tony L. Hill v. Roger Hester
accommodation_description: No accommodation request identified; complaint challenges prison conditions (mold, flooding, no heat/AC) and retaliation for filing lawsuit
key_holding: The court dismissed the fourth amended complaint as a shotgun pleading for failing to specify which defendant was responsible for which conduct, without reaching the merits of the FHA or other claims.
brief_summary: Tony L. Hill, a pro se prisoner at Zephyrhills Correctional Institution, sued prison officials alleging unconstitutional living conditions (mold, flooding, no heat/AC) and retaliation for filing this lawsuit, asserting claims under the FHA, RICO, and constitutional amendments. The court granted the motion to dismiss as a shotgun pleading because the complaint failed to specify which defendant was responsible for which conduct, and granted Hill one final opportunity to amend.

source_file: 10287865_2024_The Ohio House, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa_ca9
case_name: The Ohio House, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa
accommodation_description: Ohio House requested a waiver of the 650-foot separation requirement that would allow it to operate its sober-living facility in the multi-family residential zone despite being within 650 feet of other group homes.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed that Ohio House's requested accommodation—a waiver of the City's separation requirement—was unreasonable because the jury had an evidentiary basis to find that granting such a waiver would cause a fundamental alteration of the City's zoning scheme designed to prevent overconcentration of sober living facilities.
brief_summary: The Ohio House, LLC, a sober-living facility operator, sued the City of Costa Mesa challenging zoning ordinances requiring conditional-use permits and a 650-foot separation requirement for group homes serving disabled individuals in recovery from substance abuse. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment for the City, holding that Ohio House failed to prove disparate treatment and disparate impact claims, and that the jury had sufficient evidence to find Ohio House's requested waiver of the separation requirement was unreasonable as it would fundamentally alter the City's zoning scheme.
key_cases_cited: Pac. Shores Props., LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)
Socal Recovery, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa, 56 F.4th 802 (9th Cir. 2023)
Community House, Inc. v. City of Boise, 490 F.3d 1041 (9th Cir. 2007)
Giebeler v. M & B Properties, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)

case_name: Shauna Alvanos and Stephen Alvanos v. Heartland Credit Union, Jeff Rauch, Shay Santos, April Oshiro, Property Services of Madison, Phil Kleiboer, and Phil and Heather Revocable Trust Dated March 2015
accommodation_description: No discrete accommodation was formally requested; rather, plaintiffs alleged that Heartland Credit Union refused to consider Social Security Disability Income (SSDI) as income when evaluating their mortgage eligibility and required them to obtain a co-signor, which plaintiffs characterized as disability-based discrimination in lending.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA, Title VI, and Rehabilitation Act complaint without prejudice for failure to satisfy Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a)(2) because plaintiffs did not identify their protected class, specify what each defendant did to discriminate against them, or articulate the basis of the alleged discrimination, while granting leave to amend within thirty days.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Shauna and Stephen Alvanos alleged that Heartland Credit Union and three of its employees conspired with a property management company owner to purchase their home for below-market value and discriminated against them in mortgage lending by refusing to consider Social Security Disability Income when evaluating their mortgage eligibility. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) and found it failed to state a claim under the FHA, Title VI, or the Rehabilitation Act because plaintiffs did not allege their race, disability, or any other protected ground, nor did they specify the particular discriminatory acts of each defendant. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice and granted plaintiffs until January 3, 2025, to file an amended complaint, warning that failure to do so would result in dismissal with prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Kummerow v. Ohawcha.org, 2022 WL 873599 (W.D. Wis. 2022)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)
Felton v. City of Chi., 827 F.3d 632 (7th Cir. 2016)
Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181 (2002)

source_file: 10288346_2024_Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated_azd
case_name: Hiatt v. Sun City Festival Community Association Incorporated
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled veteran with PTSD, requested accommodation to keep his garage door open while woodworking in his garage to avoid triggering PTSD symptoms, as an exception to the HOA CC&R rule requiring garage doors to remain closed.
key_holding: The court struck defendant's MSJ on necessity and reasonableness for failure to comply with local rules governing motions for reconsideration, but denied defendant's MSJ on damages, finding genuine issues of material fact exist as to causation of emotional distress damages and whether punitive damages are warranted based on defendant's failure to engage in the interactive process.
brief_summary: Wayne Hiatt, a disabled veteran with PTSD, sued Sun City Festival Community Association HOA after it denied his request to keep his garage door open while woodworking as an accommodation for his disability-related need to avoid triggering PTSD symptoms. The court granted Hiatt's motion to strike portions of defendant's MSJ on procedural grounds and denied defendant's MSJ on damages, allowing both actual and punitive damages claims to proceed to trial.
key_cases_cited: Pac. Shores Props., LLC v. City of Newport Beach, 730 F.3d 1142 (9th Cir. 2013)
Fair Hous. Ctr. of Wash. v. Breier-Scheetz Props., LLC, 743 F. App'x 116 (9th Cir. 2018)
Montano v. Bonnie Brae Convalescent Hosp., Inc., 79 F. Supp. 3d 1120 (C.D. Cal. 2015)
Sw. Fair Hous. Council v. WG Scottsdale LLC, No. CV-19-00180-TUC-RM (D. Ariz. 2022)

source_file: 10289143_2024_HINKSON v. THE CITY OF NEW YORK PRINCIPAL MUNICIPALITY_njd
case_name: Frederick Roger Hinkson v. The City of New York Principal Municipality
accommodation_description: Plaintiff raised the Fair Housing Act among numerous other federal statutes in connection with a 1980 childhood injury at a park, but no actual housing accommodation request was made and the FHA claim was dismissed as inapplicable to the facts.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because the FHA applies in the context of housing, and Plaintiff's allegations relate to a 1980 childhood injury sustained while playing in a park, not a housing matter.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Frederick Roger Hinkson sued the City of New York and related agencies over a 1980 childhood injury sustained when he was struck by a swing while playing in a park, asserting numerous federal statutes including the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the complaint in its entirety for failure to state a claim, finding that the FHA and other statutes cited do not apply to the facts alleged, which concern a park injury rather than housing discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

source_file: 10289147_2024_HUMPHRIES v. U.S. DEPARTMENT OF HOUSING _ URBAN DEVELOPEMENT_paed
case_name: Jacqueline R. Humphries v. U.S. Department of Housing & Urban Development, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to respond in writing or via electronic communication instead of telephone interviews as an accommodation for disabilities including memory loss, anxiety, and depression during HUD's investigation of her discrimination complaints.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims because the ADA does not apply to the federal government, the Rehabilitation Act does not waive sovereign immunity for money damages against HUD, the FHA provides no private right of action against HUD for failure to investigate, and plaintiff failed to state plausible constitutional claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jacqueline Humphries sued HUD and its employees alleging they denied her reasonable accommodation requests (to communicate in writing/electronically instead of by phone) during the investigation of her housing discrimination complaints against multiple housing authorities. The court dismissed all claims, finding the ADA and Rehabilitation Act inapplicable to the federal government due to sovereign immunity, the FHA provides no private right of action against HUD, and plaintiff failed to state viable constitutional claims under Bivens.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Lane v. Pena, 518 U.S. 187 (1996)
Turner v. Sec'y of U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 449 F.3d 536 (3d Cir. 2006)
Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, 403 U.S. 388 (1971)
Marinoff v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 892 F. Supp. 493 (S.D.N.Y. 1995)

source_file: 10290500_2024_Guidry v. H U D Church Point Housing_ca5
case_name: Troy B. Guidry v. HUD Church Point Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; the plaintiff alleged discriminatory eviction by the HUD Church Point Housing Authority in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 1982 and the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit dismissed Guidry's pro se appeal as frivolous because he made no legal arguments challenging the district court's rulings that dismissed his FHA discriminatory eviction claim as time-barred and his other claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Troy Guidry, proceeding pro se, brought claims against HUD Church Point Housing Authority for discriminatory eviction under 42 U.S.C. § 1982 and the Fair Housing Act, against Rayne State Bank for state-law fraud claims, and against the Church Point Police Department for wrongful arrest. The district court dismissed the bank claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and the remaining claims as time-barred. On appeal, Guidry restated only factual allegations without challenging the legal bases for dismissal, leading the Fifth Circuit to dismiss the appeal as frivolous and entirely without merit.

case_name: Renée D. White et al. v. The GHS Group et al.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion to strike defendants' answer and affirmative defenses, finding plaintiffs failed to meet their burden to show the answers were scandalous, impertinent, or immaterial under Rule 12(f), and declined to assess the legal sufficiency of affirmative defenses at the motion to strike stage.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Renée White and Sharon Ricks sued The GHS Group and related defendants in July 2024, raising Fair Housing Act claims that appear to involve requests for accommodations or services. The court denied plaintiffs' motion to strike defendants' answer and affirmative defenses, finding plaintiffs failed to establish that the challenged pleadings were scandalous, impertinent, or immaterial under Rule 12(f).

source_file: 10292117_2024_Alliance for Fair Board Recruitment v. SEC_ca5

case_name: Sophia Loftis v. Progress Residential and Tiffany Green
accommodation_description: No accommodation request described; plaintiff alleges race-based housing discrimination regarding property purchases in Black neighborhoods and withholding of rental deposit.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint as frivolous and for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual details connecting Progress Residential's alleged conduct—purchasing properties in predominantly Black neighborhoods and using race-based statistics to withhold her deposit—to a plausible Fair Housing Act violation.
brief_summary: Sophia Loftis sued Progress Residential and Tiffany Green under the Fair Housing Act, alleging that Progress Residential engaged in racial discrimination by purchasing properties in predominantly Black neighborhoods, making homes unavailable, and driving up prices, and that a leasing agent used race-based statistics to withhold her deposit. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a plausible FHA claim, finding the allegations too conclusory to establish intentional discrimination or disparate impact.
key_cases_cited: Jackson v. Okaloosa Cnty., 21 F.3d 1531 (11th Cir. 1994)
Bonasera v. City of Norcross, 342 F. App'x 581 (11th Cir. 2009)
Hallmark Devs., Inc. v. Fulton Cnty., 466 F.3d 1276 (11th Cir. 2006)

Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Shaniqua Newkirk v. Douglas Elliman, Inc.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges racial discrimination through refusal to rent based on housing voucher status (source of income) with disparate impact on African Americans
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss plaintiff's FHA claim as time-barred because discriminatory acts occurred in February and June 2021, beyond the two-year limitations period, and neither the discovery rule nor continuing violation doctrine applies; discriminatory advertisements published within the limitations period did not injure plaintiff who merely viewed them.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Shaniqua Newkirk, an African American housing voucher holder, sued Douglas Elliman and individual brokers alleging racial discrimination under the FHA, claiming that defendants' refusal to rent to voucher holders and publication of income-restrictive advertisements disparately impacted Black and Hispanic renters. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claim as time-barred, finding the alleged discriminatory acts occurred in 2021, beyond the two-year statute of limitations, and dismissed the remaining state law claims without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
McDermott v. New York Metro LLC, 664 F. Supp. 2d 294 (S.D.N.Y. 2009)
Ragin v. Harry Macklowe Real Estate Company, 6 F.3d 898 (2d Cir. 1993)

source_file: 10296263_2024_Inova Health Care Services, for Inova Fairfax Hospital and Its Department, Life With Cancer v. Omni Shoreham Corporation_dcd

10297777_2024_Plainview Mobile Home Park v. City of Oak Grove, Kentucky_kywd
case_name: Plainview Mobile Home Park v. City of Oak Grove, Kentucky
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; the underlying claims concern the alleged discriminatory denial of water utility service to manufactured home communities and their residents.
key_holding: The magistrate judge denied defendants' motion to strike plaintiffs' expert accountant Missy DeArk, finding the deficient disclosure was not a fatal surprise warranting exclusion, and instead ordered plaintiffs to supplement their expert disclosure with a written report complying with Rule 26 within thirty days.
brief_summary: Mobile home park owners and individual prospective tenant Sarina Shannon sued the City of Oak Grove, Kentucky and its public works director, alleging that defendants denied water utility service to manufactured home communities with discriminatory intent to eliminate those communities and their residents from the city, in violation of the FHA, equal protection, civil rights statutes, and the Takings Clause. The present opinion addresses defendants' motion to strike plaintiffs' expert accountant Missy DeArk under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26 and 37 for failure to provide a written expert report by the disclosure deadline. The court denied the motion, finding the omission was likely an honest misunderstanding between counsel rather than gamesmanship, and directed plaintiffs to supplement the disclosure with a compliant written report within thirty days.

case_name: Andrea Ortiz v. Beverly Valasek, Donald E. Loudner, Douglas County Housing Authority, Gretna Crown, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested installation of a handicap ramp at the rental property for her mother who could not use stairs due to disability.
key_holding: The federal district court dismissed plaintiff's complaint without prejudice, finding it lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because plaintiff's claims arose from and sought to reverse a state court eviction judgment, and alternatively would abstain under Younger given the ongoing state court proceedings.
brief_summary: Andrea Ortiz, proceeding pro se, sued Douglas County Housing Authority, its Section 8 manager, an attorney, and a property owner alleging disability discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act and due process violations under § 1983, arising from her eviction from public housing for unpaid rent; the court dismissed the case without prejudice on jurisdictional grounds, holding that Rooker-Feldman barred review of claims seeking to reverse the state court eviction judgment and that Younger abstention applied given ongoing state proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Rooker v. Fid. Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)

case_name: Michael John Ryall, Sr. v. Normandy Village Apartments, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; plaintiff claims general discrimination from lease non-renewal under the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The magistrate recommended dismissal because the plaintiff, a white male with no disabilities, failed to plead that he is a member of a protected class under the Fair Housing Act, and the lease dispute is a state contract matter lacking federal jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Michael John Ryall, Sr. sued Normandy Village Apartments, Inc. claiming the landlord discriminated against him under the Fair Housing Act by failing to properly notify him of lease non-renewal. The magistrate recommended dismissal, finding the plaintiff is a white male with no disabilities and failed to allege membership in any protected class required to state an FHA claim, and the underlying lease dispute is a state contract matter.
key_cases_cited: Roberson v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., No. CV 23-4022, 2023 WL 10406019 (E.D. La. Dec. 12, 2023)
Treece v. Perrier Condo. Owners Ass'n, Inc., 593 F. Supp. 3d 422 (E.D. La. 2022)
L & F Homes & Dev., LLC v. City of Gulfport, Miss., 2012 WL 2863481 (S.D. Miss. July 11, 2012)

source_file: 10299281_2024_Semper v. Hawaii Life Real Estate Services, LLC_hid
case_name: Jehan Semper v. Hawaii Life Real Estate Services, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: N/A - plaintiff alleges religious discrimination (based on Judaism) in real estate transactions, not an accommodation request
key_holding: The First Amended Complaint failed to state plausible claims for religious discrimination under the FHA because plaintiff's conclusory allegations of discriminatory intent were insufficient without factual allegations supporting an inference that defendants' conduct was motivated by her Jewish faith.
brief_summary: Jehan Semper, who is Jewish, sued multiple real estate agencies and agents alleging they conspired to prevent her from purchasing vacant land in Hawaii County because of her religion, and later retaliated by interfering with her HUD complaint. The court recommended dismissing the First Amended Complaint with prejudice because plaintiff failed to plead sufficient factual allegations to support a plausible inference of discriminatory intent, offering only conclusory assertions that defendants discriminated against her because she is Jewish.
