case_name: Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi v. Edward Pec, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that the landlord remediate mold and repair water leaks in their basement apartment to accommodate Angel Lopez's asthma and COPD.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiffs failed to adequately allege what disability entitled them to accommodation, what specific accommodation they requested, whether defendants knew of the disability, or how refusing to repair water leaks constituted discrimination based on disability.
brief_summary: Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi, tenants in a Palisades Park, New Jersey apartment, sued their landlord Edward Pec and The Palisades LLC, as well as a law firm, alleging Fair Housing Act claims (including reasonable accommodation), ADA violations, and state law claims arising from habitability disputes. The District of New Jersey granted both motions to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to adequately plead their federal claims—the FHA reasonable accommodation claim was dismissed because plaintiffs made only conclusory allegations without stating what accommodation was requested, what disability entitled them to accommodation, or how defendants' failure to repair discriminated against them—and abstained from exercising jurisdiction over related state court matters.

source_file: 10308231_2025_Washington v. DHS Department of Homeless Services_nysd
case_name: Sandra A. Washington v. NYC DHS; WIN Shelter
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a Home Bound Individual with a disability residing in a homeless shelter, alleges that DHS failed to secure permanent housing for her and failed to provide adequate services needed for a person with a disability to obtain housing in a timely manner.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's federal claims with leave to amend because she failed to plead facts about what disability she suffers, what services were denied, and whether she alleges intentional discrimination or a failure to accommodate; the court further noted uncertainty about whether the FHA applies to homeless shelters.
brief_summary: Sandra A. Washington, a pro se plaintiff residing at WIN homeless shelter, sued NYC Department of Homeless Services and WIN Shelter alleging disability discrimination, failure to provide adequate services to obtain housing, and constitutional violations under § 1983. The court dismissed all federal claims with leave to amend, finding the complaint failed to allege facts specifying her disability, what accommodations were denied, and the nature of the discrimination claim.

case_name: Gerald Cymbalsky v. 522 Shore Road Owners, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff did not specifically request a reasonable accommodation but appears to challenge the cooperative's commencement of a state court 'furniture eviction' action against him while he was hospitalized.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim fails because he did not allege that he requested and was denied a reasonable accommodation, and the commencement of the state court eviction action was motivated by profit-seeking rather than discriminatory animus based on his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Gerald Cymbalsky sued his cooperative housing corporation, property managers, and attorneys for Fair Housing Act violations, RICO, constitutional privacy violations, and FDCPA violations arising from a state court action seeking access to clean his apartment while he was hospitalized. The court dismissed all claims, finding that the FHA claim failed because Cymbalsky did not request any accommodation and alleged no discriminatory animus, while the other claims failed for failure to state a viable claim.

case_name: Sarah Nathreen v. Denver Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to halt an imminent eviction and compel the Denver Housing Authority to fulfill its obligations under the Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program by paying past-due rent to her landlord, effectively requesting eviction defense relief premised in part on her severe physical and mental health conditions.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's Emergency Motion for TRO and Preliminary Injunction because her seven-month delay in seeking relief undermined a finding of irreparable harm, and her conclusory allegations failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits of her FHA and civil rights claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sarah Nathreen sued the Denver Housing Authority alleging it failed to pay her Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher rent for the entirety of her lease, resulting in eviction proceedings initiated by her landlord, Holland Residential, LLC (Sabine Apartments). She sought an emergency TRO to halt the eviction, compel DHA to remit past-due rent, and facilitate porting of her voucher, asserting eight claims including FHA violations, Title VI, Section 1981/1982, and constitutional claims. The court denied the TRO, finding that Plaintiff's seven-month delay in seeking relief undercut irreparable harm and that her bare, conclusory allegations—including the absence of specific facts showing DHA was obligated to pay rent or that any failure was discriminatory—failed to establish a likelihood of success on the merits.

source_file: 10311847_2025_Fair Hous. Ctr. of Metro. Detroit v. Am. House Grosse Pointe_ca6
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Metropolitan Detroit v. American House Grosse Pointe, LLC
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit vacated the district court's summary judgment and remanded for further proceedings on the issue of standing, in light of FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024), without expressing any view on the merits of the Fair Housing Act claims.
brief_summary: The Fair Housing Center of Metropolitan Detroit sued American House Grosse Pointe, a senior living facility, alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The district court granted summary judgment to the defendant on November 28, 2023. The Sixth Circuit vacated and remanded because the district court's standing analysis predated the Supreme Court's decision in FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine (2024), and the appellate court declined to rule on the merits, leaving standing for the district court to reassess on a fully developed record.

case_name: Miriam Millan-Heffner, et al. v. Gemcraft Homes Group, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Home purchasers alleged race-based steering and discriminatory treatment during home construction process based on Ms. Millan-Heffner's Puerto Rican identity.
key_holding: The court granted in part plaintiffs' motion for leave to amend, finding the proposed breach of contract and UTPCPL claims were not futile, but denied leave to add quasi-contract and third-party beneficiary claims as futile.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Millan-Heffner (Puerto Rican) and her husband sued their homebuilder alleging race-based discrimination, claiming they were treated with less respect than white clients and steered to a separate area of the development. The court granted in part plaintiffs' motion for leave to amend the complaint, allowing breach of contract and UTPCPL claims to proceed while denying leave to add quasi-contract and third-party beneficiary claims as futile.

source_file: 10313209_2025_Tiffany Simone Fulton v. City of New York_nysd
case_name: Tiffany Simone Fulton v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, as Black and Brown Harlem residents, allege defendants discriminated against them by failing to offer apartment units at a vacant property for rent to immediate community members instead of migrants.
key_holding: Plaintiffs lack Article III standing because they failed to allege a concrete and particularized injury in fact—the proposed plan to house migrants at the property was abandoned, and plaintiffs' objection is a generalized grievance about keeping housing available for Harlem residents generally rather than a personal injury.
brief_summary: Three Harlem residents sued the City of New York and property owners alleging racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act for allegedly planning to house migrants at a vacant property instead of offering housing to Black and Brown community members. The court dismissed all claims without prejudice for lack of Article III standing, finding plaintiffs failed to allege a concrete and particularized injury since the proposed plan was abandoned and plaintiffs' grievance was generalized rather than particularized.
key_cases_cited: Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)

source_file: 10314069_2025_(PS) Roberts v. Sacramento Housing _ Redevelopment Agency_caed
case_name: Sydney Brooke Roberts and David Tyrone Samuel v. Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency, et al.
accommodation_description: Request for an additional bedroom added to plaintiffs' Housing Choice Voucher to accommodate David Samuel's and AIMS's disabilities, including separate bedrooms for each.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment was denied because the evidence was insufficient to establish that defendants violated the FHA, ADA, or Rehabilitation Act, particularly given that the additional bedroom accommodation was ultimately granted in March 2023.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Sydney Brooke Roberts and David Tyrone Samuel, a family with disabilities (David and their minor child AIMS both have qualifying disabilities), sued the Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act for denying their reasonable accommodation request for an additional bedroom added to their Housing Choice Voucher. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment, finding that plaintiffs failed to meet their burden to show they were entitled to judgment as a matter of law, particularly given that the accommodation was ultimately granted in March 2023.

source_file: 10314802_2024_Xi v. BES Kessler Park Fund X11 LLC_txnd
case_name: K'in Way Xi, et al. v. BES Kessler Park Fund X11 LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege employment discrimination based on race and color, claiming they were fired for stealing Amazon packages while a white employee was given the benefit of the doubt.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a plausible disparate treatment claim because it does not allege that the adverse employment action was taken because of protected status; all employees, regardless of race, were fired for the same conduct after video evidence confirmed their participation.
brief_summary: Four plaintiffs sued their employer under Title VII, Section 1981, and the Fair Housing Act, alleging they were discriminated against based on race and color when they were fired for stealing Amazon packages while a white employee was initially given the benefit of the doubt. The court recommends granting the motion to dismiss because the complaint fails to plausibly allege that the adverse employment action was taken because of a protected status, as all employees were ultimately fired for the same conduct.

case_name: Michael Feliciano v. Andres Aguirre
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an emergency transfer to a different unit due to worsening medical and mental health conditions caused by unsafe living conditions with his current landlord.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because he failed to allege sufficient facts showing he has a covered disability or that he explained the connection between his disability and the requested emergency transfer accommodation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Michael Feliciano sued Andres Aguirre, a Section 8 program representative, under the Fair Housing Act and ADA, alleging Aguirre refused to process his reasonable accommodation request for an emergency transfer due to medical and mental health issues. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to adequately plead a covered disability or explain the nexus between his disability and the requested accommodation.

case_name: Eyvonne A. Webb v. Carrington Mortgage Services LLC
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request; it challenges mortgage escrow account handling and property tax credit calculations as source-of-income discrimination under the Maryland Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's Maryland Fair Housing Act claim because property tax credits applied directly to reduce tax obligations do not constitute 'source of income' under the statute, which requires money paid to or on behalf of a buyer or renter.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eyvonne A. Webb sued Carrington Mortgage Services LLC alleging the mortgage servicer discriminated against her by failing to account for property tax credits in her escrow account statements, violating the Maryland Fair Housing Act's prohibition on source-of-income discrimination. The court granted Carrington's motion to dismiss, finding that property tax credits applied directly to reduce tax liability are not a 'source of income' under the MFH statute because they are not money paid to or on behalf of the homeowner.

case_name: Carmencita María Pedro, et al. v. Hilton Worldwide, Inc., et al.
race_if_mentioned: Pedro is Puerto Rican; Fisher is Afro-Latino
accommodation_description: Request for a $60 laundry credit as a reasonable accommodation for Fisher's schizophrenia
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims because the complaint failed to allege facts supporting a plausible inference of race or disability discrimination, including dismissing the $60 laundry credit accommodation request as failing to state a nexus between Fisher's schizophrenia and the requested financial accommodation.
brief_summary: Pedro and Fisher, a mother and son with schizophrenia, sued Hilton and related entities alleging they were ejected from a hotel where Fisher was residing while awaiting permanent supportive housing, claiming discrimination based on race and disability and failure to accommodate. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state plausible claims, finding no facts supporting an inference of discrimination and that the $60 laundry credit request lacked a nexus to Fisher's disability.

case_name: Sydney Ellerbe v. Tuscan Highlands, LLC; Schulman Properties; and Winnie Schulman
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; plaintiff alleges race-based disparate treatment and eviction as cover-up for racially motivated removals from a restaurant
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's constructive eviction, disparate impact, negligence, and defamation claims but allowed plaintiff's claim for wrongful eviction under Nevada law and his FHA disparate treatment claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) to proceed because plaintiff sufficiently alleged that defendants used false assault allegations as a pretext to evict him in retaliation for or to cover up racially discriminatory conduct.
brief_summary: Sydney Ellerbe, an African American tenant, sued Tuscan Highlands LLC and related defendants alleging he was discriminatorily removed from a restaurant twice due to his race and then wrongfully evicted using false assault allegations as a pretext. The court granted leave to proceed on his wrongful eviction claim under Nevada law and his Fair Housing Act disparate treatment claim, but dismissed his constructive eviction, disparate impact, negligence, and defamation claims.

case_name: Eugene Davis v. Holly Negaard; Holly Negaard as Trustee of the Holly Negaard Revocable Living Trust; Jessica Purdy a/k/a Jessica Shanafelt; and Purdy Investments, LLC d/b/a/ Western Apartments
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants (landlord and property manager) timely cooperate by providing him with a rent ledger and other tenant information necessary to qualify for the Community Action/Emergency Rent Bridge rental assistance program so he could avoid falling into arrears and face eviction.
key_holding: The court dismissed Count 3 of plaintiff's complaint seeking declaratory relief because the Rooker-Feldman doctrine barred federal review of the state court eviction judgment, and the Declaratory Judgment Act does not provide relief for past conduct where no ongoing or future controversy exists.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eugene Davis, a tenant at Western Apartments in Minot, North Dakota, sued his landlord and property manager alleging housing discrimination under the FHA and North Dakota law, negligence/property damage, and seeking declaratory relief after defendants allegedly failed to timely provide rental documents needed for the Community Action/Emergency Rent Bridge assistance program, leading to eviction. Defendants moved to partially dismiss Count 3, which sought a court order requiring defendants to file stipulations in state court acknowledging the eviction was wrongfully obtained through discrimination and to satisfy the state court judgment. The federal court granted the motion, holding that such relief would effectively void the state court's eviction ruling in violation of the Rooker-Feldman doctrine and that the Declaratory Judgment Act does not provide a remedy for purely past conduct.

brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center sued Pelican Management and related entities (Goldfarb) alleging that their minimum income policy requiring prospective renters to earn 43 times monthly rent violated the FHA and NYCHRL by disparately impacting disabled applicants who rely on rental subsidies. brief_summary: Eddy J. Philippeaux, a disabled veteran, sued Miami Apartments Investors, LLC, Baron Residential Management, and related defendants alleging they unlawfully refused to renew his lease in retaliation for filing a prior fair housing lawsuit against them. case_name: Robert L. Hatcher v. Sylvain Yang and Travis Smith
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Fair Housing Act claims against landlord Yang arising from forcible entry and detainer action, though specific accommodation request not detailed in this order.
key_holding: Claims against Defendant Smith, an attorney who represented the landlord in state court eviction proceedings, are dismissed with prejudice based on litigation privilege; any discrimination claim against Smith is too conclusory to withstand dismissal.
brief_summary: Robert Hatcher, proceeding pro se, sued his landlord Sylvain Yang and Yang's attorney Travis Smith alleging claims including Fair Housing Act violations arising from a forcible entry and detainer action in state court. brief_summary: Plaintiff Latonia Black, a Black tenant, sued Royal American Management and related defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations including disparate treatment and failure to reasonably accommodate under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3), along with retaliation claims. brief_summary: Kiontay Smith, an African-American bisexual woman employed as a maintenance technician at Kittle Property Group, sued the company alleging Title VII race and sex discrimination and Fair Housing Act claims after she was terminated for allegedly making threats of gun violence and subsequently evicted from her employee housing within seven days. case_name: Clark v. Blueprint Investments, LLC
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested in this proceeding. The underlying state court cases involved landlord-tenant disputes including allegations of retaliatory evictions and discriminatory practices by the landlord, but no discrete accommodation request was at issue before the federal court.
key_holding: The court remanded all four state court cases because it lacked subject matter jurisdiction: plaintiff could not remove cases as a plaintiff under 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a) (which permits only defendants to remove), and the Municipal Court eviction and escrow cases were founded on state law without a properly pleaded federal question.
brief_summary: Plaintiff April Clark attempted to remove four Franklin County state court cases — two eviction cases against her, one rent escrow case she filed, and one Common Pleas case she filed alleging breach of contract, retaliation, and discrimination — to federal court, claiming FHA, ADA, RICO, and constitutional violations. The court held that removal is statutorily available only to defendants, not plaintiffs, and the Municipal Court cases presented no properly pleaded federal question sufficient to confer jurisdiction.

case_name: Concern for Independent Living, Inc. v. Town of Southampton, New York
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - The complaint alleges the Town's denial of a zone change application for a 50-unit supportive housing development for disabled and low-income persons constitutes disability discrimination under the FHA.
key_holding: The court granted the parties' joint motion to stay discovery pending resolution of Defendants' anticipated motion to dismiss, finding that Defendants made a strong showing that Plaintiff's claims may be unmeritorious, discovery would be voluminous and burdensome, and Plaintiff would suffer little prejudice from a stay.
brief_summary: Concern for Independent Living, Inc., a non-profit developer, sued the Town of Southampton and its Town Board alleging the denial of its zone change application to construct Liberty Gardens, a 50-unit affordable supportive housing development for disabled and low-income persons, violated the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and NYSHRL. The court granted the parties' joint motion to stay discovery pending resolution of Defendants' anticipated motion to dismiss, finding a stay warranted based on the factors of likely unmeritorious claims, breadth of discovery, and lack of prejudice to Plaintiff.

case_name: Naketia Johnson v. FirstKey Homes LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves alleged race-based refusal to rent and lease termination.
key_holding: Johnson adequately stated a claim under the FHA because she alleged the defendant terminated her lease four minutes after she took possession and informed her the cancellation was based on reasons related to her race.
brief_summary: Naketia Johnson sued FirstKeyHomes LLC alleging the landlord violated the Fair Housing Act by canceling her lease four minutes after she took possession, citing reasons related to her race. The court denied the motion to dismiss the FHA claim, finding Johnson adequately alleged race-based discrimination under § 3604(a), while dismissing her § 1983 claim for failure to state that defendant acted under color of law.

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Evan Miranda and Evelyn Perez filed suit against their landlord Yorkhill Housing Inc., building-management agent First Service Residential, and the NYC Department of Housing, Preservation, and Development, asserting claims construed under the Fair Housing Act, the Rehabilitation Act, and state law. The court granted IFP status but dismissed without prejudice any claims Miranda attempted to assert on Perez's behalf, as a non-lawyer cannot represent another party in federal court under 28 U.S.C. § 1654. The order directs the Clerk and U.S. Marshals Service to effectuate service on all three defendants.

case_name: Shedrick Bowes-Northern v. Herman Patel, et al.
accommodation_description: Whether Fair Housing Act applies to hotel guest claiming illegal eviction constitutes discrimination under FHA
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants because the plaintiff was a hotel guest rather than a tenant and the hotel was not a 'dwelling' under the Fair Housing Act, thus the FHA provided no protection to the plaintiff.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Shedrick Bowes-Northern sued hotel defendants Herman Patel and Comfort Inn and Suites, along with Town of Porter and police officials, alleging he was illegally evicted from a hotel during COVID-19 and that the hotel owner's statement about Black Americans constituted defamation. The court granted summary judgment for all defendants, finding that as a hotel guest rather than a tenant, the plaintiff had no rights under the Fair Housing Act because a hotel does not qualify as a 'dwelling' under the statute, and the plaintiff's constitutional due process rights were not violated because hotel guests are not entitled to eviction procedures under Indiana law.

case_name: Mari Rodriguez v. City of Chicago
accommodation_description: Rodriguez requested that the City preserve the driveway apron so she could continue using it as a safe pick-up location for medical transportation due to her mobility disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed Rodriguez's FHA reasonable modification claim because the driveway apron was not within the 'premises' of her dwelling unit—it was on an adjacent commercial property—and thus did not fall within the scope of § 3604(f)(3)(A) protection.
brief_summary: Mari Rodriguez, a tenant with mobility disabilities, sued the City of Chicago alleging that the removal of a driveway apron she used for safe medical transportation pickup violated the ADA and FHA. The court granted the City's motion to dismiss, holding that the driveway was not a City service subject to ADA Title II and was not part of Rodriguez's 'premises' under the FHA's reasonable modification provision.

brief_summary: Jermaine Anderson, a pro se plaintiff, filed a complaint against Bill Whiteside and Shreveport City Court Building alleging racial discrimination, civil rights violations, and Fair Housing Act violations, seeking $20,000 in damages. accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an accommodation for her mobility disability related to navigating a gravel parking lot, including difficulty bringing groceries into her apartment and falling in the parking area.
key_holding: Because default was entered, all well-pleaded allegations except those relating to damages were deemed admitted, and the Court found sufficient allegations to support liability under the Fair Housing Act, awarding $20,000 in damages plus attorney fees.
brief_summary: Spring Hill sued Provident Asset Management LLC under the Fair Housing Act alleging the property management company failed to provide a reasonable accommodation for her mobility disability related to parking lot accessibility. The Court granted default judgment in favor of plaintiff after defendant failed to plead or defend, finding well-pleaded allegations sufficient to establish liability, and awarded $20,000 in damages plus $6,370.32 in attorney fees.

case_name: Deborah Morris v. City of Baltimore
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, an elderly disabled resident of a private apartment building, sought building-wide accessibility improvements including functioning elevators and emergency chair lifts, allegedly required to make the building accessible housing.
key_holding: The court granted the City's motion to dismiss because the City of Baltimore is not a proper legal entity subject to suit, Plaintiff lacks Article III standing as any alleged harm is traceable to her private landlord rather than the City, and Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts showing the City took any discriminatory action against her based on disability.
brief_summary: Deborah Morris, a pro se plaintiff and disabled resident of a private apartment building in Baltimore, sued the City of Baltimore alleging violations of the ADA, Section 504, and the Fair Housing Act due to the building's inaccessible conditions. The court granted the City's motion to dismiss because Plaintiff sued the wrong defendant (the City rather than her private landlord), lacked Article III standing as her alleged harm was not traceable to the City, and failed to state plausible claims showing the City acted with discriminatory intent.

case_name: Sean A. Clark v. NYCHA
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request is described in the case text; the plaintiff alleged general race and disability discrimination by NYCHA arising from conduct in 2006, 2015, 2018, and 2020 without specifying the nature of any requested accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and § 1983 claims against NYCHA with prejudice and without leave to amend because the complaint was nearly identical to claims dismissed in two prior cases and all claims were time-barred given that more than three years elapsed between NYCHA's most recent alleged actions in 2020 and the 2024 filing.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sean Clark filed his third action in the Southern District of New York against NYCHA alleging race and disability discrimination under the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and 42 U.S.C. § 1983, based on NYCHA's alleged conduct in 2006, 2015, 2018, and 2020. The court granted NYCHA's Motion to Dismiss, finding the complaint nearly identical to complaints dismissed by two prior judges (Judge Koeltl in 2022 and Judge Torres in 2024), both of whom had also offered plaintiff leave to amend that he declined to use. Dismissal was with prejudice because plaintiff had already been given two prior amendment opportunities he did not use, and because the applicable statutes of limitations (two years under the FHA, three years under the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and § 1983) had all expired.

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ruth McLean filed suit against PNC Bank and others challenging a state court foreclosure action on her New Jersey property, asserting claims under consumer protection statutes including FDCPA, RESPA, TILA, and various state laws. The court granted PNC Defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding the complaint failed to state viable claims, was barred by the Anti-Injunction Act, and was untimely, while also dismissing improperly joined defendants without leave to amend.

case_name: John Doe v. James V. McDonald, M.D.
accommodation_description: Doe sought readmission to Oceanview Manor Home for Adults, a Transitional Adult Home in Coney Island where he had previously resided, after being denied readmission under New York State regulations that prohibited TAHs from accepting new residents with serious mental illness until those facilities achieved sufficient integration between disabled and non-disabled residents; he also sought, by implication, either a waiver or exception to those regulations to allow his return.
key_holding: The Second Circuit held that John Doe's FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act claims against New York's regulations blocking readmission of seriously mentally ill individuals to Transitional Adult Homes were moot because post-filing events—including his return to Oceanview, the State's promulgation of a Waiver Rule permitting case-by-case readmissions, and Oceanview's removal from TAH classification—completely eradicated the effects of the alleged violation and Doe lacked any continuing personal stake in the outcome.
brief_summary: John Doe, an individual with serious mental illness, filed suit in 2016 alleging that New York State regulations violated the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act by blocking his readmission to Oceanview Manor Home for Adults (a Transitional Adult Home) solely because of his mental illness. After suit was filed, the State consented to a TRO allowing Doe to return, promulgated a Waiver Rule permitting case-by-case readmissions of former TAH residents with serious mental illness, and ultimately removed Oceanview's TAH designation entirely. The Second Circuit, reviewing an interlocutory appeal from the district court's denial of the State's summary judgment motion on standing, recharacterized the issue as mootness, found the case moot, dismissed the appeal, vacated the district court's order, and remanded with instructions to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.

key_holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed the jury verdict for eight Black homeowners, finding their reverse redlining claims timely under equitable tolling, rejecting challenges to jury instructions on disparate impact and disparate treatment, and upholding the district court's ruling that a loan modification release provision was unenforceable.

case_name: Constance Swanston, Women's Elevated Sober Living LLC, and Shannon Jones v. City of Plano, Texas
accommodation_description: WESL sought a variance from Plano's zoning ordinance to operate a sober living home with 15 residents instead of the maximum permitted 8 unrelated individuals, arguing therapeutic necessity for substance use disorder recovery.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for new trial, finding that under the Fifth Circuit's newly articulated standard, plaintiffs' expert testimony failed to prove that 15 residents was 'indispensable or essential' to recovery rather than merely 'preferable,' since the expert acknowledged therapeutic benefit exists at lower occupancy levels and even with as few as two residents.
brief_summary: WESL, a sober living home operator, sued the City of Plano challenging the city's denial of a reasonable accommodation request to allow 15 residents instead of the zoning-permitted maximum of 8, arguing therapeutic necessity for residents with substance use disorders. case_name: Bernard T. Anderson Bey v. Roc Nation LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff did not request a traditional reasonable accommodation. His FHA-related claim against NYCHA alleged that NYCHA discriminated against him in violation of the Fair Housing Act by 'deliberately overlooking' his repeated requests for intervention—through NYCHA's grievance policy—to stop NYCHA's XRF lead testing of his apartment, which he alleged was a pretext to falsify test results and wrongfully evict him and his daughter.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motions for a preliminary injunction and TRO in their entirety because plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable harm as to any requested relief, the court lacked jurisdiction over claims involving non-defendant parties (NYPD and Albany County Family Court), and any compensable harms could be adequately remedied through monetary damages at trial.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Bernard T. Anderson Bey sued Roc Nation, Jay-Z, Live Nation, NYCHA, Coinbase, REDC, and the IRS, alleging a sweeping conspiracy in which the music industry defendants exerted financial and political influence over the other defendants to exclude him from the hip hop industry, destroy his cryptocurrency holdings, block his business financing, and engineer his eviction from his NYCHA apartment. Plaintiff moved for a preliminary injunction and TRO seeking, among other things, rescission of his Coinbase contract and return of crypto assets, access to Live Nation's essential facilities, and an order barring NYCHA from entering his apartment. The court denied all injunctive relief, finding it lacked jurisdiction over claims concerning the NYPD and Albany County Family Court, that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine barred review of the family court child support order, and that plaintiff failed to show irreparable harm because the alleged injuries were either speculative or fully compensable through money damages.

accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged that defendants selectively enforced zoning code against them based on race, resulting in criminal prosecution for operating a two-family home in a single-family zone.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants on plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claim because plaintiffs failed to present evidence that defendants knew of plaintiffs' race or were motivated by racial discrimination in enforcing the zoning code.
brief_summary: Darren and Marlene Thomas appealed the Eastern District of New York's grant of summary judgment to defendants, including the Town of Oyster Bay and code-enforcement officials, in their lawsuit alleging racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act regarding enforcement of zoning codes against their two-family home. The Second Circuit affirmed, finding that plaintiffs failed to produce evidence that defendants knew of their race or were motivated by racial discrimination in initiating enforcement proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Mitchell v. Shane, 350 F.3d 39 (2d Cir. 2003)

source_file: 10338763_2025_Wiggins v. Omaha Housing Authority Foundation Inc._ned
case_name: Toni Wiggins v. Omaha Housing Authority Foundation Inc.
accommodation_description: The complaint vaguely alleged that Wiggins and her husband were present at Henry Lee's OHA housing unit doing 'what was best for him to receive a reasonable accommodation for his disabilities,' but did not specify the nature of Henry's disability, what accommodation was being sought or from whom, or whether Wiggins was requesting a reasonable accommodation from the OHA or was simply providing personal care to Henry as his power of attorney and caregiver.
key_holding: The court finds that Wiggins' pro se complaint fails to state a plausible claim under the FHA or 42 U.S.C. § 1983 because she does not allege sufficient facts establishing a protected activity, a nexus to a protected characteristic, or a causal link between any protected activity and the OHA's adverse actions, and grants her 30 days to file an amended complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Toni Wiggins sued the Omaha Housing Authority after its CEO called police to have Wiggins and her husband arrested and removed from a property where they were serving as power of attorney and caregivers for a disabled OHA tenant (Henry Lee), and thereafter filed a false eviction action against them. Wiggins alleged violations of the FHA (retaliation under § 3617, disparate treatment/harassment under § 3604), 42 U.S.C. § 1983, 18 U.S.C. § 1001, and various Nebraska statutes. On initial review under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e), the court determined the complaint failed to state any plausible federal claim—finding no factual allegations tying the OHA's conduct to a protected characteristic, no adequate causal link between any protected activity and the adverse actions, and no private right of action under 18 U.S.C. § 1001—and granted Wiggins 30 days to file an amended complaint.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Gallagher v. Magner, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
Neudecker v. Boisclair Corp., 351 F.3d 361 (8th Cir. 2003)

source_file: 10338845_2025_Lee v. Omaha Housing Authority Foundation Inc._ned
case_name: Lee v. Omaha Housing Authority Foundation Inc.
accommodation_description: Hasani Lee, as power of attorney for his father Henry Lee, alleges he was attempting to obtain a reasonable accommodation for Henry's disabilities when the OHA had him arrested and removed from the property.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state plausible FHA claims because he made no allegations regarding his own protected characteristics and failed to allege facts showing a causal connection between any protected activity and the OHA's adverse actions, as his allegations about reasonable accommodation were vague and conclusory.
brief_summary: Hasani Lee, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued the Omaha Housing Authority alleging it violated the Fair Housing Act by making false police reports and filing a false eviction action against him after he was acting as power of attorney for his disabled father. The court dismissed Lee's FHA claims at initial review, finding he failed to plead facts establishing a retaliation claim because his allegations were vague, failed to specify what reasonable accommodation was being sought, and failed to allege a causal connection between any protected activity and the adverse actions.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Neudecker v. Boisclair Corp.
Gallagher v. Magner
United States v. Edmunds

case_name: Dawn Chappel v. Adams County Children's Services, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requests injunctive relief to prevent enforcement of a state court eviction order and allow her to return to the property at 211 Sunshine Ave, Winchester, Ohio.
key_holding: The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to review the state court eviction judgment, and alternatively, plaintiff fails to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits of her FHA retaliation claim or entitlement to preliminary injunctive relief.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Dawn Chappel, proceeding pro se, filed a request for injunctive relief seeking to prevent enforcement of a state court eviction order and return to her property at 211 Sunshine Ave, Winchester, Ohio, which she ties to an FHA retaliation claim. The court granted defendant Moore's motion to strike the unauthorized response to the answer and recommended denial of the injunctive relief request, finding the court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine and alternatively that plaintiff fails to meet preliminary injunction requirements.
key_cases_cited: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Rooker v. Fid. Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)
Liberty Coins, LLC v. Goodman, 748 F.3d 682 (6th Cir. 2014)

case_name: Quintin J. Ballentine v. Postgraduate Center for Mental Health and Jacob Barak
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - complaint broadly asserts disability-based housing discrimination but accommodation request specifics not analyzed in this service order
key_holding: Court grants plaintiff in forma pauperis status and directs service on defendants; complaint construed to assert disability-based housing discrimination claims under the Fair Housing Act
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quintin J. Ballentine sues the Postgraduate Center for Mental Health and CEO Jacob Barak asserting disability-based housing discrimination claims under the Fair Housing Act and other statutes. This is a procedural service order granting in forma pauperis status and directing the U.S. Marshals Service to effect service on defendants; the Court has not yet substantively analyzed the merits of any accommodation request.

source_file: 10347143_2025_Lopez v. The YWCA of North East New York_nynd
case_name: Lopez v. YWCA of Northeast New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested multiple reasonable accommodations while enrolled in the YWCA housing program: (1) an exemption from the no-smoking policy to permit cannabis use for relief of PTSD and chronic acute pain symptoms; (2) permission to keep service dogs in her unit; (3) an exemption from the YWCA's policy of using police intervention, due to her PTSD arising from prior law enforcement abuse; and (4) use of independent contractors rather than defendant Yunis Alloush to perform apartment repairs, to avoid contact with him—an accommodation that was eventually granted in writing but later violated when Alloush appeared at her apartment in November 2024.
key_holding: On initial IFP review, the court allowed FHA and ADA disability discrimination, reasonable accommodation, sex-based discrimination, hostile housing environment, and retaliation claims against the YWCA and certain defendants to proceed, while dismissing race and religion-based FHA claims without prejudice to repleading, dismissing ADA damages claims and individual-defendant Rehabilitation Act claims with prejudice, and granting leave to amend on several other dismissed claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mariah Lopez, an Afro-Latina transgender woman with disabilities (PTSD, chronic pain) enrolled in the YWCA of Northeast New York's 'Rosie's House' housing program, filed an amended complaint alleging disability, race, sex, and religious discrimination under the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and other federal and state laws, arising from alleged failures to honor reasonable accommodations, a hostile housing environment, uninhabitable conditions, and retaliation for filing a lawsuit. The court granted IFP status and conducted an initial screening review, allowing core FHA and ADA disability accommodation, sex-based discrimination, hostile housing environment, and retaliation claims to proceed against the YWCA, its officers, and the Alloush landlord defendants. Race and religion-based FHA claims were dismissed without prejudice, and certain ADA claims for monetary damages and against individual defendants were dismissed with prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Meyer v. Holley
Francis v. Kings Park Manor
Littlejohn v. City of New York

case_name: Ronald D. Leonard v. Hocking Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Leonard requested to keep an emotional support dog as a reasonable accommodation for his disability
key_holding: Leonard failed to state a failure-to-accommodate claim because he did not plead facts showing HMHA refused to permit his ESA—he merely received routine letters requesting documentation about his animal and pet agreement, which does not constitute a refusal of his accommodation request.
brief_summary: Leonard sued Hocking Metropolitan Housing Authority and its employees alleging they failed to accommodate his disability by sending letters requesting ESA documentation and pet agreement information, constituting harassment and constructive eviction. The court dismissed his claims, finding he failed to plead that HMHA refused his accommodation or acted with discriminatory animus toward disabled persons.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
HDC, LLC v. City of Ann Arbor, 675 F.3d 608 (6th Cir. 2012)
Burns v. City of Columbus, Dep't of Pub. Safety, Div. of Police, 91 F.3d 836 (6th Cir. 1996)

source_file: 10347542_2025_Gurevitch v. Emerald Green Property Owners Association Inc._nysd
case_name: Gurevitch v. Emerald Green Property Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; this case involves claims of religious discrimination through HOA enforcement actions rather than a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to state FHA discrimination or retaliation claims because they offered no factual allegations demonstrating that Defendants were motivated by discriminatory intent, including no comparator showing non-Jewish residents were treated more favorably.
brief_summary: Alexander and Irina Gurevitch, a Hasidic Jewish couple, sued the Emerald Green Property Owners Association and its attorney alleging FHA religious discrimination and retaliation claims based on HOA fines, stop-work orders, and foreclosure actions targeting them after they purchased property in the HOA community. The court granted Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that Plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts to plausibly infer discriminatory intent, as they provided no comparator showing non-Jewish residents were treated differently.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Dickerson v. BPP PCV Owners LLC, 2022 WL 4538281 (S.D.N.Y. 2022)
Favourite v. 55 Halley St., Inc., 381 F. Supp. 3d 266 (S.D.N.Y. 2019)

case_name: Debbie Johnson v. Montage North America, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that Montage (1) reposition outdoor event speakers so they pointed away from her residential unit, (2) lower the volume of amplified music and speaking during outdoor events, or (3) grant her access to the Residential Lounge or other quieter areas of the Hotel—all to alleviate the debilitating noise caused by her Ramsay Hunt Syndrome, which creates extreme sensitivity to sound.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's ADA claims without prejudice because her privately-owned condominium unit within the Montage Hotel is not a 'place of public accommodation' under the ADA, and her complaint failed to plead sufficient facts establishing that Defendant discriminated against her in the enjoyment of the hotel's public areas (as opposed to her private residential unit), while her FHA claims were not at issue in the partial motion and remain pending.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Debbie Johnson, who suffers from Ramsay Hunt Syndrome causing extreme sound sensitivity, sued Montage North America under both the FHA and ADA after Defendant refused to accommodate her disability by modifying the placement or volume of speakers used during outdoor events at the Montage Hotel at Deer Valley Resort, where she resided in a privately-owned condominium (Unit 960). Defendant moved to partially dismiss only the ADA claims, arguing that Unit 960 is a long-term private residence rather than a 'place of public accommodation' under 42 U.S.C. § 12182. The court granted the partial motion to dismiss, finding that the complaint's allegations centered on Plaintiff's use and enjoyment of her private residential unit rather than any of the hotel's public goods or services, and therefore failed to state an ADA claim; the FHA claims survive and remain pending.
key_cases_cited: Phibbs v. Am. Prop. Mgmt., 2008 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 21879 (D. Utah 2008)
Indep. Hous. Servs. v. Fillmore Ctr. Assocs., 840 F. Supp. 1328 (N.D. Cal. 1993)
Regents of the Mercersburg College v. Rep. Franklin Ins. Co., 458 F.3d 159 (3d Cir. 2006)

source_file: 10349111_2025_Durham v. Liberty Park Terrace Property Management_waed
case_name: John Michael Ray Durham v. Liberty Park Terrace Property; Cliff Butler; Tenets of Apartment #4; and Spokane Police Department
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested. Plaintiff sought injunctive relief to stop retaliation, harassment, and discrimination by the property manager and to halt eviction proceedings, but did not request any specific housing accommodation related to a disability or other protected characteristic under the FHA.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's emergency motion for preliminary injunction because plaintiff failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits of his Equal Protection, Due Process, negligence, and Fair Housing Act claims, including failing to allege facts showing defendants discriminated against him on any protected basis.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff John Durham, a tenant at Liberty Park Terrace in Spokane, sought emergency preliminary injunctions against his property management company, property manager Cliff Butler, neighboring tenants, and the Spokane Police Department, alleging ongoing noise harassment, retaliation by Butler (including a retaliatory 30-day notice to comply or vacate), police inaction, and violations of the Fair Housing Act (42 U.S.C. § 3601) and constitutional equal protection and due process rights. The court denied all preliminary injunction requests, finding plaintiff had not shown likelihood of success on any claim because he failed to allege facts establishing membership in a protected class, a custom or policy of municipal negligence, or discrimination on any FHA-protected basis. The court further found no irreparable harm given plaintiff had relocated to a hotel and eviction appeared avoidable.
key_cases_cited: City of Cleburne, Tex. v. Cleburne Living Ctr., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Winter v. Natural Resources Defense Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)

case_name: Noureddine Ecasali v. Scott McMillin, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants refused to lease to her based on national origin, religion, race, and Section 8 voucher status, but has not articulated a specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed for failing to state a claim because it does not give defendants fair notice of what claims are being asserted, does not identify which defendant committed which act, and lacks information about where plaintiff attempted to lease or why she believes the defendants discriminated against her.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Noureddine Ecasali, proceeding in forma pauperis, sued eighteen defendants including Scott McMillin and various McMillin entities alleging violations of the Federal and California Fair Housing Acts, claiming defendants refused to lease to her because of her national origin, religion, race, and Section 8 voucher status. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding it failed to give defendants fair notice of the claims against them, did not identify what role each defendant played, and lacked basic information about the alleged discriminatory conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Susan Lloyd v. Manbel Devco I LP et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested multiple disability-related accommodations including: (1) accessible entry through the front electronic keypad door, which she could not operate on her mobility scooter before it relocked; (2) installation of a handicap ramp on her back patio (which took two months to install and was then rendered unusable by other tenants' dogs defecating on it); and (3) unspecified bathroom accommodations — all of which she alleged were denied or inadequately provided despite repeated requests.
key_holding: The court partially denied the Manbel defendants' motion to dismiss, allowing the FHA/RA/PHRA claim to proceed on reasonable accommodation and modification grounds related to handicap accessibility, while granting all other motions to dismiss for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Tenant Susan Lloyd, who uses a mobility scooter and has heart and respiratory problems, sued the owner and employees of the Eclipse at Belmont Apartments, among others, asserting claims under the FHA, Rehabilitation Act, PHRA, and numerous state-law theories arising from alleged handicap accessibility failures, pesticide exposure, smoking, ERAP payment disputes, and harassment by other tenants. The court granted motions to dismiss by the law firm defendants, LCHA, and Greenscapes in full, and granted in part and denied in part the Manbel defendants' motion, allowing the FHA/RA/PHRA accessibility and accommodation claims, a UTPCPL claim, a negligence claim, a nuisance claim, and a breach of contract claim to proceed. The court noted that Lloyd's surviving FHA claims face significant challenges at summary judgment.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center
Olmstead v. L.C.
Lapid-Laurel v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment

source_file: 10350993_2025_Deitch v. Medstar Medical Group Southern Maryland LLC_mdd
case_name: Ronald S. Deitch v. Medstar Medical Group, Southern Maryland LLC
subsidy_program: St. Mary's County Department of Housing affordable housing program for disabled veterans
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Habitat's property managers made a false police report that led to his arrest and eviction from his apartment, claiming this was in retaliation for his advocacy on behalf of himself and neighbors, not because of his disability.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state an FHA discrimination claim because his own allegations negated any plausible inference that the defendants' adverse actions (false police report and eviction) were taken because of his disability, as he alleged the motive was retaliation for his advocacy unrelated to disability.
brief_summary: Ronald Deitch, a disabled tenant with multi system atrophy, sued Habitat America LLC (his landlord) and others alleging Fair Housing Act violations after Habitat's property managers allegedly made a false police report that led to his arrest and eviction. The court granted Habitat's motion to dismiss, finding Deitch failed to state an FHA claim because his own allegations showed the alleged retaliation was motivated by his advocacy for himself and neighbors, not by his disability, and the claim was also time-barred.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Thomas v. The Salvation Army of S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)
Lokhova v. Halper, 995 F.3d 134 (4th Cir. 2021)
Indep. Hous. Srvs. of S.F. v. Fillmore Ctr. Assocs., 840 F. Supp. 1328 (N.D. Cal. 1993)
Want v. Shindle Props., LLC, No. PWG-18-2833 (D. Md. Oct. 29, 2018)

case_name: Al Tudor DuPont; Aurelia Anderson v. Sterling Family Trust
accommodation_description: Request for a two-bedroom apartment at the same reduced rent as a reasonable accommodation for disability during rent stabilization-ordered relocation, rather than the one-bedroom comparable unit specified by municipal code.
key_holding: The district court did not abuse its discretion in denying preliminary injunction because the requested two-bedroom apartment at one-bedroom rent does not constitute a reasonable accommodation—it does not meet the ordinance's definition of a comparable unit and imposes an undue financial burden.
brief_summary: Al Tudor DuPont and Aurelia Anderson sued their landlord seeking a preliminary injunction to compel transfer to a two-bedroom apartment at reduced rent as a reasonable accommodation under the FHA. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the denial, holding that the accommodation request failed because it did not meet the municipal code's definition of a comparable unit and imposed an undue financial burden on the landlord.
key_cases_cited: Ohio House, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa, 122 F.4th 1097 (9th Cir. 2024)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
Giebeler v. M & B Assoc., 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)
Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)

source_file: 10351946_2025_Canoe Creek Neighborhood Association, Inc. v. Douse_flmd
case_name: Canoe Creek Neighborhood Assn., Inc. v. Douse
accommodation_description: Defendant alleges HOA failed to provide him a copy of the Declarations due to his race, constituting Fair Housing Act discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3605.
key_holding: The federal court lacks subject matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff's complaint arises exclusively under state law and does not present a federal question on its face; the defendant's Fair Housing Act defense and any potential counterclaim do not confer federal question jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule.
brief_summary: Canoe Creek Neighborhood Homeowners Association sued homeowner James Douse in Florida state court for violating HOA covenants; Douse removed the case to federal court, arguing the HOA discriminated against him based on race in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The magistrate judge recommends granting the motion to remand because the federal court lacks subject matter jurisdiction—the plaintiff's complaint arises entirely under state law, and a federal defense or counterclaim does not establish federal question jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule.
key_cases_cited: Caterpillar Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386 (1987)
Home Depot U.S.A., Inc. v. Jackson, 587 U.S. 435 (2019)
In re Bethesda Mem'l Hosp., Inc., 123 F.3d 1407 (11th Cir. 1997)

case_name: United States v. Petties
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case. The case involves a pattern or practice of sex-based discrimination through sexual harassment of female tenants, including unwanted sexual advances, physical assault, unauthorized entry into bedrooms, non-consensual photographing and filming, offers of housing benefits in exchange for sexual acts, denial of housing benefits upon refusal, and adverse actions such as eviction or lockout upon refusal of sexual advances.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that the United States adequately stated a pattern or practice claim of sex-based discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(a) by alleging a longstanding pattern of sexual harassment of female tenants, that the § 3610 administrative prerequisites do not apply to a § 3614(a) government enforcement action, and that the statute of limitations does not bar the claims on the face of the complaint.
brief_summary: The United States brought a Fair Housing Act enforcement action against landlord Shevis Petties and related entities, alleging a pattern or practice of sex-based discrimination through sexual harassment of female tenants from at least 2016 to the present, in violation of 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604(a), 3604(b), and 3617. Defendants moved to dismiss on grounds that individual tenants failed to exhaust administrative remedies under § 3610, that various statutes of limitations barred the claims, and that certain factual allegations were implausible. The court denied the motion in full, finding the complaint adequately pled a § 3614(a) pattern or practice claim, that § 3610's administrative procedures do not govern a § 3614(a) action brought by the Attorney General, and that defendants failed to demonstrate any applicable statute of limitations barred the claims on the face of the complaint.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
United States v. Pelfrey
United States v. Pedaline
United States v. Hames

case_name: Rickey Banks v. Ryan Ross et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged various disabilities (arthritis, wheelchair use, anxiety) and claimed he was denied housing services and access to a donated vehicle program at a transitional housing facility, but did not articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claims were dismissed because he failed to identify which specific disability formed the basis of discrimination and failed to establish a nexus between his alleged handicaps and Defendants' actions.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Rickey Banks, a disabled veteran residing in transitional housing operated by Open Door Ministries following his release from prison, brought claims against the facility's director, executive director, and fellow residents alleging discrimination on the basis of race and disability, ADA violations, and constitutional claims. The court granted Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that Plaintiff failed to state viable federal claims because his pleadings were conclusory, failed to establish the required nexus between his disabilities and Defendants' actions, and sought monetary damages under Title III of the ADA which only provides for injunctive relief.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Thomas v. The Salvation Army S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)
PGA Tour, Inc. v. Martin, 532 U.S. 661 (2001)

case_name: Banks v. Ross
defendant_type: OTHER: Non-profit transitional housing program operator and its employees
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged he was denied transportation services and receipt of a donated vehicle under a veterans' donation program as a reasonable accommodation for his disabilities.
key_holding: The court recommended granting motions to dismiss because plaintiff's complaints, even liberally construed, fail to state plausible federal claims under the ADA, Fair Housing Act, or constitutional provisions, as plaintiff failed to establish the requisite nexus between his alleged disabilities and the defendants' actions.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Rickey Banks sued Ryan Ross and other employees of Open Door Ministries' Arthur Cassell Memorial Transitional House, alleging disability and race discrimination in violation of the ADA and FHA, including claims that defendants denied him transportation services and a donated vehicle as accommodations for his mobility disabilities. The court recommended granting defendants' motions to dismiss because plaintiff failed to state plausible federal claims, as his complaints failed to establish any nexus between his disabilities and the allegedly discriminatory actions.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
PGA Tour, Inc. v. Martin, 532 U.S. 661 (2001)
Thomas v. The Salvation Army S. Territory, 841 F.3d 632 (4th Cir. 2016)

case_name: Osborne v. Belton
accommodation_description: Request to keep a service dog as an accommodation for mental health disability (anxiety and depression related to being mentally challenged)
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Belton's Rule 60(b) motion, holding that Belton failed to establish any grounds for relief under Rule 60(b)(1)-(6), including inadvertence, newly discovered evidence, fraud, or void judgment, and therefore the district court did not abuse its discretion in denying the motion.
brief_summary: Tenants Clifford Osborne and Deborah Olsen sued their former landlord Kevin Belton for disability discrimination under the FHA after Belton refused to accept a physician's letter recommending a service dog and proceeded with their eviction. The district court granted summary judgment for plaintiffs, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed the denial of Belton's Rule 60(b) motion to set aside the judgment, finding no abuse of discretion in rejecting his arguments based on attorney neglect, newly discovered evidence, fraud, and lack of jurisdiction.

case_name: Eshawn Jessica Scipio v. Housing Authority of Hartsville
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was made; plaintiff alleged she was denied access to her tenant file and EIV reports and was subjected to rent increases and eviction.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on plaintiff's FHA claims because she failed to provide evidence that she was treated differently from similarly situated individuals or that defendants acted with intentional or purposeful discrimination.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eshawn Jessica Scipio, an African-American tenant of the Housing Authority of Hartsville, sued the housing authority and its officials alleging racial discrimination and Fair Housing Act violations arising from denial of access to her tenant records, rent increases, Section 8 voucher termination, and eviction. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding plaintiff failed to provide evidence of discriminatory intent or that she was treated differently from similarly situated individuals.

case_name: Danny Carlson v. Carrington Square et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested safety grab bars in his bathroom as a reasonable accommodation for his disability, which was denied, allegedly leading to injuries from a fall.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's Motion to Compel Discovery as untimely under Local Rule 37-1, which requires parties to file motions to compel within 45 days of the prompt written communication identifying discovery deficiencies; Plaintiff's eleven-month delay in challenging Carrington's discovery responses violated this requirement.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Danny Carlson sued Carrington Square et al. alleging disability discrimination and fair housing violations arising from his eviction and denial of requested accommodations including grab bars and unit transfer. The court denied his Motion to Compel Discovery as untimely because he waited eleven months after receiving Carrington's discovery responses to raise objections, violating Local Rule 37-1's 45-day filing requirement for motions to compel.

case_name: Lakeisha C. Green v. Allied First Bank SB
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; case involves claims that bank discriminated in mortgage servicing and foreclosure prevention based on protected classes including race, sex, and marital status.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie disparate treatment claim because she admitted Servbank offered her loss mitigation options, could not show similarly situated applicants were treated differently, and offered only conclusory allegations that the bank discriminated based on her protected characteristics without evidence that race, sex, or other traits were a significant factor in its decisions.
brief_summary: LaKeisha C. Green sued Allied First Bank SB alleging the bank discriminated against her in mortgage servicing and foreclosure proceedings based on her race, sex, marital status, and other protected characteristics under the FHA and ECOA. The court granted summary judgment for the bank, finding Green failed to establish a prima facie case because she admitted the bank offered her loss mitigation options, could not show similarly situated borrowers were treated differently, and provided only conclusory allegations of discrimination without evidence that her protected traits were a significant factor in the bank's decisions.

case_name: AGVR Property Owner LLC v. Rowe
accommodation_description: Defendant removed a state court eviction proceeding asserting ADA and FHA rights, but the court did not reach the merits of any accommodation request due to lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
key_holding: The court lacked jurisdiction to reconsider the remand order under 28 U.S.C. § 1447(d), which bars review of remand orders based on subject matter jurisdiction.
brief_summary: AGVR Property Owner LLC sued to evict Jasper Calhoun Rowe in Dallas County, Texas, and Rowe removed the eviction proceeding to federal court claiming ADA and Fair Housing Act rights. The federal court lacked subject matter jurisdiction to adjudicate the removed action and remanded it, then denied Rowe's motion for reconsideration of that remand order under 28 U.S.C. § 1447(d) as barred from appellate or collateral review.
key_cases_cited: Powerex Corp. v. Reliant Energy Servs., Inc., 551 U.S. 224 (2007)
New Orleans Public Serv., Inc. v. Majoue, 802 F.2d 166 (5th Cir. 1986)

case_name: Carlos Turner, et al. v. Henley Appraisals, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request was made; this case involves claims of intentionally discriminatory appraisals and lending practices based on race and national origin.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims against Henley Appraisers for failure to plead sufficient factual allegations of discriminatory intent, but allowed discrimination claims against U.S. Bank to proceed based on allegations that the bank's lending decision-making process was discriminatory.
brief_summary: Carlos and Diana Davoli Turner, along with the Miami Valley Fair Housing Center, sued Henley Appraisals, U.S. Bancorp, and U.S. Bank alleging that appraisals and lending decisions discriminated against the Turners based on race and national origin, claiming a 'whitewashed' appraisal showed their home was worth $185,000 more than the appraisals ordered by U.S. Bank. The court dismissed all claims against Henley and U.S. Bancorp for failing to allege sufficient facts showing discriminatory intent, but allowed the discrimination claims against U.S. Bank to proceed based on allegations that the bank's loan decision-making process involved a discriminatory policy.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Art Reyes v. Harris County, Christopher Ross, Amanda Fry, Alexzander French Michael, and Joseph M. Douglass
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged deputies discriminated against him based on race by arresting and jailing him while his neighbors were not arrested or charged for similar conduct, and interfered with his right to use HOA common amenities.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim because he failed to allege that Harris County discriminated in the sale or rental of housing, real estate transactions, brokerage services, or otherwise coerced, intimidated, or interfered with his fair housing rights under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604, 3605, 3606, or 3617.
brief_summary: Art Reyes, proceeding pro se, sued Harris County and individual deputies under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, alleging that deputies discriminated against him based on race by repeatedly detaining, arresting, and charging him while declining to arrest his white neighbors for similar conduct. The court granted Harris County's motion to dismiss, dismissing all claims because Plaintiff failed to adequately plead a Monell claim against the County and because his FHA claim fell outside the statute's scope as he alleged police misconduct rather than discrimination in housing transactions.

case_name: Art Reyes v. Harris County, Christopher Ross, Amanda Fry, Alexzander French Michael, and Joseph M. Douglass
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested. Plaintiff's FHA claim alleged that law enforcement officers discriminated against his right to access and use Deerfield Village community common amenities (swimming pool, bike trail) on the basis of his race (Asian), by issuing trespass warnings and making arrests while declining to arrest or charge his white neighbors for similar or more severe conduct.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to dismiss all claims, finding that plaintiff's § 1983 false arrest, malicious prosecution, equal protection, and double jeopardy claims each failed to satisfy their required elements, and that plaintiff's FHA claim failed because the deputies' conduct—interfering with access to HOA common amenities—did not fall within the FHA's prohibitions on discrimination in housing sales, rentals, real estate transactions, or brokerage services.
brief_summary: Art Reyes, an Asian male proceeding pro se, sued Harris County and individual sheriff's deputies under § 1983 and the FHA, alleging he was repeatedly arrested and charged while his white neighbors engaged in similar or worse conduct without consequence, arising from an ongoing neighborhood dispute within the Deerfield Village HOA. The court dismissed all § 1983 claims, finding the false arrest claims defeated by probable cause, the malicious prosecution claims deficient for lack of unlawful seizure and malice, the equal protection claim unsupported because Reyes failed to identify similarly situated comparators outside his protected class who were treated more favorably, and the double jeopardy claim inapplicable because the three charges arose from three discrete incidents. The FHA claim was dismissed because none of the FHA's enumerated provisions—covering discrimination in housing sales/rentals, real estate transactions, brokerage services, or interference with rights thereunder—applied to law enforcement conduct affecting access to HOA amenities.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

case_name: United States v. Nolen
accommodation_description: Sexual harassment and retaliation by landlord against tenants; not a disability accommodation case
key_holding: The court granted partial summary judgment on vicarious liability for Shirlee Nolen under the FHA's vicarious liability framework (24 C.F.R. § 100.7(b)) but denied summary judgment on punitive damages and alter ego/corporate veil piercing as premature prior to adjudication of underlying merits.
brief_summary: The United States sued Joel and Shirlee Nolen and Nolen Properties, LLC under the FHA alleging that Joel Nolen engaged in a pattern or practice of sex discrimination through sexual harassment and retaliation against tenants. The court's partial summary judgment ruling addressed vicarious liability, punitive damages, and alter ego theories—granting vicarious liability for Shirlee Nolen but denying summary judgment on punitive damages and corporate veil piercing as premature pending adjudication of the underlying claims.

case_name: Morris v. Baltimore Municipal
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that housing at 301 McMechen Street be rendered ADA and Rehabilitation Act compliant, that 'Brand New Elevators' be installed, that various bathroom remodeling and technology infrastructure upgrades be completed, and that Defendants act 'in good faith and protect all the elderly and disabled people at 301 McMechen Street,' including the implementation of emergency response plans.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint in its entirety without prejudice because it rested entirely on conclusory assertions without plausible factual allegations sufficient to state a claim under Rule 12(b)(6), and because the 55-page complaint violated Rule 8's requirement for a short and plain statement and Local Rule 103.1.d's 40-page limit.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Deborah Morris and Arnell Mason filed a sprawling 55-page complaint against Baltimore Municipal and various housing entities alleging eight counts of civil rights violations—including racial segregation in housing, discriminatory refusals to transact, disparate treatment, and failure to provide ADA- and Rehabilitation Act-compliant conditions at 301 McMechen Street. The defendants moved to dismiss under Rules 12(b)(1) and 12(b)(6). The court dismissed the complaint in its entirety without prejudice, finding that while it retained subject matter jurisdiction and standing was not clearly lacking, the complaint offered only generalized, conclusory assertions of wrongdoing unsupported by plausible factual allegations, and the pleading grossly exceeded the page limits required by local rule.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly

case_name: United States of America and Fair Housing Partnership of Greater Pittsburgh, Inc. et al. v. AION Management, LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Fair housing testers requested assigned parking spaces near building entrances as reasonable accommodations for prospective tenants with mobility disabilities (using walkers and crutches).
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that Plaintiffs sufficiently alleged all three elements of a § 3604(f)(3)(B) reasonable accommodation claim (refusal, reasonable accommodation, and necessity/equal opportunity) and that Defendants' statements about refusing to assign parking spaces violated § 3604(c).
brief_summary: The United States and fair housing organizations sued AION Management and affiliated property owners for denying assigned parking spaces to prospective tenants with mobility disabilities, alleging violations of §§ 3604(c), 3604(f)(1), 3604(f)(2), and 3604(f)(3)(B) of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that Plaintiffs established Article III standing and sufficiently stated claims that Defendants refused to make reasonable accommodations in their parking policies and made discriminatory statements regarding housing availability.
