source_file: 10360316_2025_Ellis v. NAICA Housing Development Fund Company, Inc._nysd
case_name: Jaezon Ellis v. NAICA Housing Development Fund Company, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination based on a staff member calling him a slur, but no disability-related accommodation request is made in this case.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because one incident of offensive name-calling is not sufficiently severe or pervasive to create a hostile housing environment, and plaintiff's other federal claims fail because NAICA is a private entity not acting under color of state law.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jaezon Ellis sued NAICA Housing Development Fund Company, a nonprofit homeless prevention organization, and two employees for negligence, property loss, and discrimination after being called a slur by a staff member at a transitional housing facility. The court dismissed all federal claims, finding NAICA is a private entity not subject to Section 1983 liability, the single incident of name-calling is insufficient to state a hostile housing environment claim under the Fair Housing Act, and plaintiff has no constitutional due process claim for the property loss.

source_file: 10361008_2025_Reese v. Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association I_dcd
case_name: Reese v. Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association I
accommodation_description: Reese alleged that PPCA permitted white unit-owners to use the master insurance policy to cover repairs while denying her similar requests.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for PPCA because Reese failed to produce any evidence rebutting PPCA's legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for denying her insurance coverage claims, instead relying on unsupported allegations and speculation.
brief_summary: Allison Reese, an African American condominium owner, sued Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association alleging race discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 3605, claiming the association permitted white unit-owners to use the master insurance policy for repairs but denied her similar requests. The court granted summary judgment for PPCA, finding Reese failed to produce any evidence rebutting PPCA's legitimate, non-discriminatory justification for denying coverage and instead relied on unsupported assertions and speculation about differential treatment.

case_name: Will J. Belton v. Regions Bank NA, et al.
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it involves business partnership disputes, alleged race-based discrimination in financial transactions, RICO claims, and banking regulation violations regarding limited partnerships.
key_holding: The court denied multiple procedural motions (stay of state court proceedings, protective order, motions to consolidate) as the underlying removed state court actions were recommended for remand and the parties were required to communicate through counsel.
brief_summary: Will J. Belton, proceeding pro se and then with counsel, sued Regions Bank NA and related entities alleging race-based discrimination, Fair Housing Act violations, RICO violations, and banking regulation breaches related to limited partnership interests and business opportunities for African American businesses. The court denied all procedural motions including requests to stay state court proceedings, consolidate cases, and obtain a protective order, while remanding improperly removed state court actions and staying discovery pending resolution of pending motions to dismiss.

case_name: Nadia Winston v. HON Partners II LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff raises general discrimination and disability allegations but does not articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request that the court analyzes.
key_holding: The court granted Defendant Mulvaney's motion to dismiss because the plaintiff's complaint and amended complaint failed to allege any cognizable claim against her specifically, as all alleged wrongful conduct was attributed to other parties (HON Partners, Dallas Housing Authority), and plaintiff had already been given an opportunity to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Nadia Winston sued HON Partners II LLC and property manager Marissa Mulvaney in federal court alleging discrimination, retaliation, breach of lease, negligence, defamation, and Violence Against Women Act violations. The court granted Mulvaney's motion to dismiss with prejudice because the plaintiff's amended complaint failed to allege any actions taken by Mulvaney specifically, instead attributing all alleged misconduct to other parties, and plaintiff had already been afforded an opportunity to amend her complaint.

case_name: Victor Ortiguerra, et al. v. Grand Isle Shipyard, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation is at issue; the underlying FHA claim alleges that defendants discriminatorily segregated Filipino workers in employer-provided housing and COVID-19 quarantine facilities and refused to permit them to evacuate during Hurricane Ida, while non-Filipino workers were allowed to leave.
key_holding: The magistrate judge denied defendants' motion to modify the protective order covering T visa applications, holding that the motion was effectively an improperly grounded request for reconsideration of a prior discovery ruling under Rule 54(b) and that defendants failed to present any persuasive justification for revisiting that ruling.
brief_summary: Filipino welders and fitters employed by Grand Isle Shipyard sued their employers under the FLSA, TVPA, and FHA, alleging they were segregated in housing, forced to remain in a hurricane-damaged bunkhouse without utilities while non-Filipino co-workers were permitted to evacuate, and subjected to threats of termination and deportation. During discovery, defendants moved to modify a protective order entered in August 2024 to compel production of plaintiffs' T visa applications and all supporting documents, a request the court had substantially denied in a prior June 2024 ruling. The magistrate judge denied the motion, finding it was a thinly disguised reconsideration motion under Rule 54(b) that lacked new evidence or identification of error in the prior ruling, and that all four factors governing protective order modification weighed in plaintiffs' favor.

case_name: Yolanda E. Quewon v. Philadelphia Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for a handicap-accessible ramp outside her home as a reasonable accommodation for hip and knee pain.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim because she failed to adequately plead the elements of a reasonable accommodation claim: she did not describe her disability, did not allege whether she requested the accommodation from the defendant, and did not explain how the ramp was necessary for her to use and enjoy her dwelling.
brief_summary: Yolanda Quewon, a public housing tenant with hip and knee pain, sued the Philadelphia Housing Authority alleging harassment about rent payments and requesting a handicap-accessible ramp as a reasonable accommodation. The court dismissed her Amended Complaint without prejudice, finding she failed to state a plausible FHA claim because she did not adequately describe her disability, did not allege whether she requested the accommodation from defendants, and did not explain how the ramp was necessary for her to use and enjoy her dwelling.

case_name: Manson v. Fresno Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that defendants maintain a functioning elevator to provide equal access to their apartments, arguing that 21 months of elevator outages and entrapments constituted a constructive denial of reasonable accommodation for their mobility disabilities.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the 21-month delay in repairing the malfunctioning elevator constituted a constructive denial of reasonable accommodation and whether defendant Cipro had a disability known to defendants.
brief_summary: Three mobility-disabled tenants at a supportive housing project for homeless and disabled veterans in Fresno sued their housing provider for failing to reasonably accommodate their disabilities by delaying over 20 months to repair a frequently malfunctioning elevator that trapped passengers, including plaintiff Manson. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether the delay constituted a constructive denial of reasonable accommodation and whether one plaintiff had a disability known to defendants.

key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendant because plaintiff failed to present competent evidence of discriminatory intent or identify a specific policy, procedure, or practice with a discriminatory effect on a protected class; plaintiff's conclusory assertions that defendant leased him an infested apartment because of his race did not constitute competent summary judgment evidence.

case_name: C.R., an individual, by and through his next friend Tracey Joffe v. PLB Management, LLC, DBA Park La Brea Management; et al.
accommodation_description: Request to reserve the parking space directly in front of C.R.'s apartment for exclusive use by his mother as caretaker to accommodate his severe autism spectrum disorder.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's grant of judgment as a matter of law, holding that substantial evidence supported the jury's verdict that PLB failed to provide a reasonable accommodation, but affirmed the conditional new trial order because the district court did not abuse its discretion in finding the jury's verdict on reasonable alternatives was against the weight of evidence.
brief_summary: C.R., a nonverbal individual with severe autism spectrum disorder, sued PLB Management, LLC under the Fair Housing Act after the property manager refused his mother's request to reserve a parking space directly in front of their apartment for his disability-related needs. Following a jury trial verdict for C.R., the district court granted PLB judgment as a matter of law and conditionally ordered a new trial. The Ninth Circuit reversed the judgment as a matter of law, finding substantial evidence supported the jury's verdict that the reserved parking space further away was not a reasonable alternative, but affirmed the conditional new trial on reasonable alternatives and damages as within the district court's discretion.

case_name: McGrath v. Dunecrest Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Request for approval to construct a balcony extension with stairs to provide additional space and a secondary exit for adult autistic children
key_holding: The court granted the Association's motion for attorney's fees because the plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims were frivolous, unreasonable, or groundless from the outset—the balcony extension accommodation failed because autism was not the but-for cause of the need, the familial status claim failed because disabled adults do not constitute protected familial status, and the retaliation claim failed because the emails did not constitute coercive conduct.
brief_summary: The McGraths sued their condominium association seeking approval for a balcony extension with stairs as a reasonable accommodation for their adult autistic children, plus familial status discrimination and retaliation claims. The court granted summary judgment for the Association in May 2024 and, in this March 2025 ruling, awarded the Association $86,562.50 in attorney's fees after finding the plaintiffs' claims were frivolous and groundless from the outset because the disability accommodation failed the causation requirement, the familial status claim did not fit the FHA's definition, and the retaliation claim lacked evidentiary support.

key_holding: The complaint failed to state a racial discrimination claim under § 1981, Title VI, or the FHA because it did not plead facts showing discriminatory intent, only conclusory assertions about a 'medical industrial complex' exploiting Black men.

case_name: Resources for Human Development, Inc. v. Lower Providence Township

brief_summary: Resources for Human Development, Inc. accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiffs made general demands for ADA-compliant housing, elevator installation, bathroom remodeling, and housing conditions improvements at 301 McMechen Street, framed as civil rights violations rather than specific accommodation requests.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim and for failing to comply with Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8 and Local Rule 103.1.d (79-page complaint exceeding the 40-page limit), noting plaintiffs had filed a nearly identical action that was dismissed less than two weeks prior.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Deborah Morris and Arnell Mason filed a 79-page civil rights complaint against Baltimore City and related housing entities alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act violations regarding housing conditions at 301 McMechen Street. case_name: Jennifer Dixon v. Silva-Markham Partners and Koelbel & Co.
accommodation_description: Ms. Dixon sought a live-in aide accommodation for her autoimmune disorder that affects her cognition and mobility, and separately sought a transfer from a one-bedroom to a two-bedroom apartment unit facilitated through her housing voucher from the Colorado Division of Housing.
key_holding: The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation granting defendants summary judgment on all FHA claims—discrimination, hostile housing environment, and retaliation—because plaintiff's objections were insufficiently specific to trigger de novo review and the court found no clear error in the recommendation, while dismissing the state law security deposit claim without prejudice.
brief_summary: Jennifer Dixon, a tenant with an autoimmune disorder living in a Colorado apartment complex managed by Silva-Markham Partners and Koelbel & Co., brought FHA claims for housing discrimination under § 3604, hostile housing environment, and retaliation under § 3617, as well as a state law claim for failure to return her security deposit. The magistrate judge recommended—and the district court adopted—summary judgment for defendants, concluding that a prior settlement barred pre-January 2021 conduct, the statute of limitations barred pre-June 2020 conduct, and plaintiff failed to establish genuine disputes of material fact on the merits of any FHA claim. Plaintiff's pro se objections were overruled as too vague and non-specific to warrant de novo review.

case_name: Eldridge v. City of Alton, Illinois
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested disability accommodations from the City of Alton related to trash/waste collection services, as co-plaintiff Eldridge is disabled and physically struggles to pull full trash bins back toward the house after collection; they also sought the City's intervention to stop their neighbor from disrupting waste collection and requested that an outstanding trash bill be voided due to the City's failure to provide the paid-for services.
key_holding: The court dismissed the pro se complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding that plaintiffs' FHA and ADA claims failed because they did not connect the alleged interference with trash collection services or the denial of reasonable accommodations to disability-based discrimination, and their constitutional and other federal claims were similarly deficient.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Elliander Eldridge and Melissa Scharfinski, both disabled homeowners in Alton, Illinois, sued the City of Alton alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and various constitutional and criminal statutes arising from a contentious ongoing dispute involving a well-connected neighbor who allegedly disrupted their trash collection, the City's selective ordinance enforcement against them rather than the neighbor, and the City's failure to provide disability accommodations related to waste collection services. The court granted both plaintiffs IFP status but screened and dismissed the entire complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2), finding that claims under criminal statutes lacked a private right of action, ESA and CAA claims failed for lack of pre-suit notice compliance, and FHA/ADA claims failed because plaintiffs never connected the alleged conduct to disability discrimination. Plaintiffs were granted leave to file an amended complaint by April 28, 2025.

accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged they were discriminated against in the administration of ERAP funds and in NYCHA's failure to recertify incomes, based on race, national origin, disability, and source of income.

brief_summary: Black and Hispanic NYCHA public housing residents and Residents to Preserve Public Housing sued OTDA, NYCHA, and its commissioner alleging racial and disability discrimination in the state's ERAP program, which allegedly deprioritized public housing tenants, and NYCHA's failure to recertify incomes during the pandemic. case_name: Merriilee Turnbull v. Frankenmuth Insurance Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, an insurance agent, alleges she was terminated in retaliation for whistleblowing about Defendant's bundled insurance policy requirement that she claimed discriminated against disabled homeowners.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim because she failed to plead a causal connection between any protected whistleblowing activity and her termination, and lacked standing to bring a disparate impact claim on behalf of disabled homeowners.
brief_summary: Merriilee Turnbull, an independent insurance agent, sued Frankenmuth Insurance Company and Matthew Hillborg alleging they terminated her agency appointment in retaliation for whistleblowing about a sales policy she claimed discriminated against disabled homeowners, along with state law claims for negligent misrepresentation, promissory estoppel, defamation, and tortious interference. The court dismissed the FHA retaliation claim for failure to plead causation and lack of standing, dismissed most claims against both defendants, but allowed one defamation claim against Hillborg to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Robert Ricketts v. Westwood Condo Assoc.
accommodation_description: Repair of roof leaks and carbon monoxide hazards to allow Plaintiff and his children with asthma to occupy the condo safely
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim was properly dismissed because he failed to allege sufficient facts showing that his or his children's asthma constitutes a 'handicap' as defined under the FHA, which requires that the condition substantially limit a major life activity such as breathing.
brief_summary: Robert Ricketts, a Connecticut attorney and condo owner, sued Westwood Condominium Association and related parties alleging they violated the FHA by failing to repair roof leaks and carbon monoxide hazards after learning of his and his children's asthma. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding Ricketts failed to state a plausible FHA claim because his allegations did not establish that his or his children's asthma substantially limits a major life activity as required to qualify as a handicap under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

source_file: 10369794_2025_Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Goldfarb Properties, Inc._nysd
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Pelican Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested by an individual plaintiff. FHJC, as a fair housing organization, challenged defendants' facially neutral minimum annual income policy (43x monthly rent) as discriminatory in its application to applicants with rental subsidies or vouchers, disproportionately harming disabled persons who rely on such assistance.
key_holding: The court granted in substantial part FHJC's motion for attorneys' fees and costs following its successful bench trial and Second Circuit affirmance on disability discrimination and source of income discrimination claims, applying a 15% across-the-board reduction and reducing paralegal billing rates to $200/hour, while rejecting defendants' remaining objections to the fee application.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center (FHJC) challenged defendants' 2015 policy requiring prospective renters to earn an annual income of at least 43 times their monthly rent as discriminatory under the FHA and New York City Human Rights Law. After a bench trial, the court found in FHJC's favor on all three claims—disability discrimination under the FHA, disability discrimination under the NYCHRL, and source of income discrimination under the NYCHRL—and awarded $240,540 in compensatory damages, $750,000 in punitive damages, and injunctive relief; the Second Circuit affirmed in January 2025. This opinion resolves FHJC's post-appeal motion for attorneys' fees and costs totaling $1,582,286.61, directing an amended fee application incorporating a reduced paralegal rate of $200/hour, re-rating of entries identified as entirely clerical at $200/hour, and a 15% across-the-board reduction.
key_cases_cited: Farrar v. Hobby
Hensley v. Eckerhart
Fox v. Vice
Green v. Torres
Lilly v. City of New York

source_file: 10369809_2025_Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Goldfarb Properties, Inc._nysd
case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Pelican Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: The case did not involve a traditional reasonable accommodation request; rather, FHJC challenged defendants' company-wide minimum income policy (43x monthly rent) as unlawfully screening out applicants with disabilities who rely on partial rental subsidies or housing vouchers, and sought an injunction prohibiting defendants from applying minimum income requirements to applicants with rental subsidies or vouchers.
key_holding: The court granted FHJC's motion for attorneys' fees and costs, directing submission of an amended fee application reflecting adjustments including reduction of paralegal hourly rates to $200, compensation of fully clerical entries at $200/hour, and a 15% reduction to all pre-settlement fees to account for work performed on behalf of a dismissed co-plaintiff, vague entries, and unrelated work.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center (FHJC) brought suit against the owners of New York City rental buildings alleging that defendants' minimum income policy—requiring prospective renters to earn at least 43 times monthly rent—unlawfully discriminated based on disability and source of income under the FHA and NYCHRL. After a bench trial, the court found for FHJC on all three claims, awarded $240,540 in compensatory damages, $750,000 in punitive damages, and injunctive relief; the Second Circuit affirmed on January 21, 2025. This amended opinion resolves FHJC's motion for $1,582,286.61 in attorneys' fees and costs, largely granting the award while applying targeted adjustments to paralegal rates, clerical entries, and pre-settlement hours.
key_cases_cited: Farrar v. Hobby, 506 U.S. 103 (1992)
Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424 (1983)
Green v. Torres, 361 F.3d 96 (2d Cir. 2004)
Lilly v. City of New York, 934 F.3d 222 (2d Cir. 2019)

source_file: 10369893_2025_Haymarket DuPage, LLC v. Village of Itasca_ilnd

case_name: Carol Noe v. Ray Realty et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants perform necessary repairs to her apartment in a manner that accommodated her disability—i.e., that repairs be made in a particular way as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The court adopted the magistrate judge's Report and Recommendation in its entirety, granting all four motions to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6) and dismissing all claims with prejudice except FHA discrimination and retaliation claims against the Original Defendants (Ray Realty and the Zecevic/Militec individuals), which were dismissed without prejudice with leave to replead within 30 days.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Carol Noe filed suit in 2019 against her landlord Ray Realty and numerous other defendants, alleging violations of the FHA, ADA, and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 based on disability discrimination and retaliation—specifically that defendants refused to perform apartment repairs in a manner accommodating her disability. Magistrate Judge Tarnofsky issued a 51-page Report and Recommendation recommending that all four motions to dismiss be granted, with the specific FHA reasonable accommodation claims dismissed with prejudice and broader FHA discrimination and retaliation claims against the Original Defendants dismissed without prejudice. The district court overruled plaintiff's objections (which merely reiterated prior arguments and did not address particular findings), adopted the R&R in full, and gave plaintiff 30 days to file a second amended complaint limited to FHA discrimination and retaliation claims against the Original Defendants.

case_name: Stern v. Highland Lake Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege HOA amendments (rental ban, religious structure restrictions, Sunday viewing restrictions) and individualized harassment by HOA members were motivated by religious animus toward Hasidic Jews.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants because plaintiffs failed to establish that the alleged discriminatory conduct—HOA by-law amendments and individualized harassment—was sufficiently severe and pervasive to create a hostile housing environment under § 3604(b), and defendants articulated legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their policies.
brief_summary: Hasidic Jewish homeowners sued their HOA and individual defendants alleging religious discrimination based on hostile by-law amendments (rental ban, religious structure restrictions, Sunday commercial restrictions) and individualized harassment intended to create a hostile housing environment. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding plaintiffs failed to demonstrate the conduct was sufficiently severe and pervasive under § 3604(b), and defendants proffered legitimate non-discriminatory reasons for their policies that plaintiffs did not rebut with sufficient evidence of pretext.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Mitchell v. Shane, 350 F.3d 39 (2d Cir. 2003)

Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

source_file: 10373175_2025_CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor and City Council Of Baltimore_mdd
case_name: CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore
accommodation_description: CMDS sought a use-and-occupancy permit to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility, which the City denied based on zoning requirements that CMDS claims were discriminatorily applied.
key_holding: The Court held that punitive damages are unavailable against the City under the FHA and that CMDS cannot recover lost profits if it never had a legal right to open its facility, making the outcome of parallel state-court zoning litigation critical to determining actual damages.
brief_summary: CMDS Residential, LLC sued the City of Baltimore alleging the City discriminatorily denied a use-and-occupancy permit to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility in violation of the FHA and ADA. This Court ruling addressed a motion in limine on damages, holding that punitive damages are unavailable against the municipality under the FHA and that CMDS cannot recover lost profits unless it first establishes a legal entitlement to operate the facility in pending parallel state-court zoning litigation.
key_cases_cited: City of Newport v. Fact Concerts, Inc., 453 U.S. 247 (1981)
Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181 (2002)

case_name: Sherri Strole v. Mark Wirth, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B) was at issue; plaintiff sought equal enforcement of park policies and equal access to amenities and community events on the same terms afforded to male tenants, constituting a sex/gender disparate-treatment discrimination claim rather than an accommodation request.
key_holding: On IFP screening under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2), plaintiff's FHA sex discrimination (disparate treatment), retaliation, and interference claims state plausible claims for relief and proceed, while her IIED claim is dismissed without prejudice for failure to allege sufficiently extreme and outrageous conduct.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sherri Strole, a tenant at Fairgrounds RV LLC's RV park, brought FHA claims for sex/gender discrimination, retaliation, and coercion/interference, along with an IIED claim, alleging discriminatory enforcement of park policies, arbitrary rent increases, vandalism to her property, and exclusion from community activities based on her gender as compared to male tenants. The court conducted mandatory IFP screening and found the three FHA claims plausible on their face — allowing them to proceed — but dismissed the IIED claim without prejudice because the alleged conduct did not rise to the level of extreme and outrageous conduct required under Arizona law, granting leave to amend within thirty days. The court also denied plaintiff's motions for permanent anonymity and to compel arbitration without prejudice, while partially granting her motion to compel by ordering service by a U.S. Marshal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Harris v. Itzhaki, 183 F.3d 1043 (9th Cir. 1999)

source_file: 10373318_2025_Spraggins v. Ironwood Crossing Public Facility Corporation_txnd
case_name: Lasae D. Spraggins v. Ironwood Crossing Public Facility Corporation, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought a preliminary injunction to enjoin state court eviction proceedings and stay the writ of possession, arguing intervention was authorized by the Fair Housing Act and ADA.
key_holding: The court held that the Anti-Injunction Act bars federal jurisdiction to enjoin state court proceedings and that Younger abstention applies, thus denying plaintiff's motions for preliminary injunction and to stay the writ of possession.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Lasae D. Spraggins, a pro se litigant facing eviction in state court, filed a federal action seeking to enjoin the state eviction proceedings and stay the writ of possession, arguing this intervention was authorized under the Fair Housing Act and Americans with Disabilities Act. The court accepted the magistrate judge's recommendation and denied the motions, holding that the Anti-Injunction Act bars federal jurisdiction over the state court proceedings and that Younger abstention applies.
key_cases_cited: Mitchum v. Foster, 407 U.S. 225 (1972)
Ex Parte Young, 209 U.S. 123 (1908)

case_name: Robert A. Johnson v. Raven Wood Homeowners Association, et al.
accommodation_description: Request that the HOA provide virtual/remote attendance option via Zoom at annual meetings as an accommodation for disability-related health risks during the COVID-19 pandemic
key_holding: Genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether Mr. Johnson is disabled within the FHA's definition, whether the accommodation was necessary and reasonable, and whether the HOA denied his request by failing to provide virtual meeting access, precluding summary judgment.
brief_summary: Disabled combat veteran Robert Johnson sued Raven Wood Homeowners Association alleging failure to provide reasonable accommodation under the FHA by denying his request to attend annual HOA meetings virtually via Zoom due to his health conditions. The court denied Defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact on all elements of the reasonable accommodation claim including disability status, necessity of the accommodation, reasonableness, and whether the HOA's actions constituted a denial.

source_file: 10373706_2025_Sara Watts v. Joggers Run Property Owners Association, Inc._ca11
case_name: Sara Watts v. Joggers Run Property Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: HOA's alleged discriminatory enforcement of rules targeting Watts and her family based on race, including forcing her to give up her service dog after a neighbor's complaint.
key_holding: Section 3604(b) applies to post-acquisition HOA conduct affecting housing-related contractual rights under HOA rules, and Watts plausibly stated claims for racial discrimination under the FHA and Civil Rights Act by alleging the HOA selectively enforced rules against her and denied access to community amenities because of her race.
brief_summary: Sara Watts, an African American woman, sued her HOA alleging racial discrimination in post-acquisition enforcement actions including towing her son's car without proper notice, restricting basketball court access citing concerns about people of color, and subjecting her guests to false accusations. The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that Section 3604(b) covers HOA conduct affecting housing-related contractual rights under HOA rules, and Watts sufficiently alleged plausible claims for racial discrimination under the FHA and Civil Rights Act.

case_name: Frazier v. Luther
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation requested; case centers on racial discrimination claim involving alleged statement 'Ain't no black man going to owe me money' and subsequent eviction
key_holding: The court found plaintiff's race-based disparate treatment claims under § 3604(a)-(c) plausible under the McDonnell Douglas framework based on his membership in a protected class, qualification to rent, eviction as comparable rejection, and inference that housing remained available to others, while dismissing the § 3617 retaliation claim for failure to plead protected activity and the trespass claim because defendant had legal right to enter under the lease.
brief_summary: Lance Frazier, a Black man, sued landlord Justin Luther and Luther Properties LLC for Fair Housing Act violations based on race discrimination, claiming he was evicted after Luther stated 'Ain't no black man going to owe me money' and changed his locks; Frazier also asserted state law claims for trespass, conversion, and breach of contract against the Kennedys. The district court partially granted the motion to dismiss, allowing the race-based discrimination claims under § 3604(a)-(c) and conversion claim to proceed while dismissing the retaliation claim under § 3617 and trespass claim, finding no protected activity was pled and the landlord had contractual right to enter the premises.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Housing Opportunities Made Equal of Greater Cincinnati v. Count X LLC
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation request is described in this opinion; the underlying claims concern discriminatory lease provisions based on familial status, disability-related harassment of Carter (who is disabled), and retaliation for filing complaints with HUD, while the opinion itself addresses only defendants' state-law counterclaims.
key_holding: The court granted the FHA plaintiffs' unopposed motion to dismiss defendants' counterclaims for tortious interference with a business relationship and defamation without prejudice, finding that defendants failed to plausibly allege the required elements of either counterclaim under Rule 12(b)(6).
brief_summary: Housing Opportunities Made Equal of Greater Cincinnati (HOME), along with tenants Sophia Smith and her disabled son Demeirakle Carter, sued Count X LLC and its managing member M. Aaron Taylor for discriminatory housing practices under the Fair Housing Act, Ohio Civil Rights Act, and other laws, alleging familial status and disability discrimination, harassment, and retaliation. Defendants denied the allegations and filed counterclaims for tortious interference with their Section 8 business relationship with CMHA and defamation. The court granted plaintiffs' motion to dismiss both counterclaims without prejudice, holding that defendants' sparse allegations failed to plausibly allege the elements of either claim and that defendants had waived opposition by failing to respond to the motion.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Allfrey v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association, Inc.

key_holding: Both cross-motions for summary judgment were denied because genuine issues of material fact exist regarding whether Plaintiff provided sufficient information to evaluate her accommodation request and whether the requested accommodation was necessary, requiring resolution at trial.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Shearldine Marie Allfrey sued Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association alleging ADA discrimination and FHA reasonable accommodation denial based on being denied the right to bring her service dog into common areas. Both parties filed cross-motions for summary judgment, which the Court denied because material facts remain genuinely disputed regarding whether Plaintiff provided adequate documentation and whether the accommodation was necessary, precluding summary judgment resolution.

case_name: Cedric Willis v. U.S. Bank National Association, as Trustee, Igloo Series Trust; LoanCare LLC; and Security National Mortgage Company, Inc.
accommodation_description: Case involves removal jurisdiction; FHA cited as basis for federal question jurisdiction but no accommodation claim is substantively analyzed in this procedural ruling on motions to remand.
key_holding: The court denied the motions to remand because federal question jurisdiction exists based on non-frivolous FHA allegations, all defendants properly joined in or consented to removal, and a state court default judgment does not bar removal.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Cedric Willis sued defendants U.S. Bank, LoanCare LLC, and Security National Mortgage Company in Texas state court, and after defendants removed the case to federal court, Willis filed two motions to remand. The court denied both motions, holding that it has federal question jurisdiction based on non-frivolous Fair Housing Act allegations in the complaint, that all defendants properly consented to removal, and that a state court default judgment does not prevent removal.

key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal of the FHA disparate impact claim because plaintiffs' allegations were too conclusory to demonstrate discriminatory effect, lacking any statistics or proof of discriminatory impact.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Bhavin Patel and Jerubha Life LLC, owner and operator of the New Bay Motel in Los Angeles, appeal the dismissal of their constitutional claims and Fair Housing Act disparate impact claim challenging the City of Los Angeles' nuisance closure of their motel. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that the FHA claim failed because the complaint contained only conclusory allegations without statistics or other proof demonstrating discriminatory impact.

case_name: Nikeshkumar Ahir; Pintuben Nikeshkumar Ahir; Pawanputra 108, Inc. v. City of Los Angeles
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; FHA claim based on discriminatory impact from closure of motel property
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal of the FHA claim because the complaint's allegations were too conclusory and lacked statistics or other proof demonstrating discriminatory impact.
brief_summary: Owners of the 108 Motel sued the City of Los Angeles and related entities under § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, challenging the City's 2023 physical closure of the motel. case_name: Meredith Twyman v. Recap PA Holdings, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a designated handicapped parking space closer to her apartment unit due to arthritis-related mobility limitations.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's reasonable accommodation claim because she failed to plead sufficient facts showing (1) when, how, and to whom she made the accommodation request, and (2) why the handicapped parking space was necessary to afford her an equal opportunity to enjoy her dwelling given her arthritis.
brief_summary: An African American woman with arthritis sued her property manager under the Fair Housing Act alleging race and disability discrimination, including a claim that she requested a handicapped parking space as a reasonable accommodation. The court granted the defendant's motion to dismiss, finding the plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts to support a reasonable accommodation claim because she did not adequately explain when her request was made or why the parking space was necessary given her disability.

brief_summary: Aaron Sanders, a pro se disabled veteran plaintiff, sued real estate agent Anna Marie Stephens alleging she refused to sell him property at 3264 Collins Ferry Road in Morgantown, West Virginia because of his disability, in violation of the FHA. case_name: Darryl West v. Marc Landau and Drinda Osborne
accommodation_description: West did not request a specific accommodation; he alleged disability discrimination in eviction proceedings based on retaliation for cooperating with law enforcement.
key_holding: The FHA claim was properly dismissed because West failed to allege that his disability was the basis for the alleged eviction—his claim was based on alleged retaliation for reporting criminal conduct to police and cooperating with law enforcement, not disability discrimination.
brief_summary: Darryl West, proceeding pro se, sued his landlord Drinda Osborne and her attorney Marc Landau alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and state law violations arising from an alleged lifetime housing agreement and attempted eviction. case_name: Fontaine v. CGI

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Matiya Fontaine, a disabled Black woman residing in Brooklyn, sued CGI, Lineage Properties, Empire State Management Co., La Cabana Apartments, and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations, Section 1981, and Title VI claims based on being refused apartment renovations and an ADA upgrade to a larger unit, and being threatened with termination from her housing assistance program. source_file: 10381039_2025_United African-Asian Abilities Club v. ASP Mohawk, LLC_casd
case_name: United African-Asian Abilities Club, James Lee v. ASP Mohawk, LLC
accommodation_description: The complaint alleges Fair Housing Act and ADA violations, but the Court's ruling addresses only supplemental jurisdiction over the state Unruh Act claim; the merits of any accommodation request are not reached.
key_holding: The Court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over Plaintiffs' Unruh Act claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1367(c)(4) because exceptional circumstances exist (high-frequency litigants bypassing California's procedural safeguards) and compelling reasons of fairness and comity weigh in favor of dismissal without prejudice.
brief_summary: United African-Asian Abilities Club and James Lee sued ASP Mohawk, LLC alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and California's Unruh Act. case_name: United States of America v. Javier Salazar, Jr., et al.
accommodation_description: Sexual harassment claim by tenant Angela McGinnis against landlords - not a reasonable accommodation case
key_holding: Defendants' motion to set aside default judgment was denied because defendants acted culpably (willfully failed to participate in litigation despite repeated notice) and failed to identify any meritorious defense to the underlying sexual harassment claims.
brief_summary: The United States brought this action on behalf of tenant Angela McGinnis against private landlords and property managers Javier Salazar Jr., Javier Salazar Sr., and Ricardo Covarrubias, alleging sexual harassment in violation of the Fair Housing Act. After defendants failed to appear or defend, default judgment was entered against them, and the magistrate judge recommends denying their motion to set aside the default judgment because their delay was willful and they presented no meritorious defense.
key_cases_cited: United States v. Aguilar, 782 F.3d 1101 (9th Cir. 2015)

source_file: 10384281_2025_The Ohio House, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa_ca9
case_name: The Ohio House, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa
accommodation_description: Ohio House requested a waiver of the City's 650-foot separation requirement between sober living homes as a reasonable accommodation for disabled persons recovering from addiction.
key_holding: The court affirmed that Ohio House's requested accommodation—granting an exception to the separation requirement—was unreasonable because a jury could find it would cause a fundamental alteration of the City's zoning scheme designed to prevent overconcentration of sober living facilities and institutionalization of disabled persons.
brief_summary: The Ohio House, LLC, operator of a sober living facility in Costa Mesa, California, appealed the district court's partial summary judgment and post-verdict rulings in its action challenging the City's zoning ordinances requiring conditional-use permits and separation requirements for group homes serving disabled persons recovering from addiction. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that the differential treatment under the zoning code benefits the protected class of disabled persons, that Ohio House failed to prove disparate impact, and that Ohio House's requested accommodation (waiver of the separation requirement) was unreasonable because it would fundamentally alter the City's zoning scheme.
key_cases_cited: Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)

case_name: Michaela Nash v. A B C Insurance, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Nash requested transfer to another accessible apartment after rat infestation, but was denied; her original petition included Fair Housing Act discrimination claims which she voluntarily dismissed prior to this ruling.
key_holding: Following Royal Canin U.S.A., Inc. v. Wullschleger, the court lacks federal question jurisdiction because Nash voluntarily dismissed her Fair Housing Act claims in her Second Supplemental Petition, and the remaining state law tort claims do not present a substantial federal question under Grable; therefore, the court recommends granting the motion to remand.
brief_summary: Michaela Nash, a wheelchair-bound amputee residing at Cooper Road Plaza low-income housing complex, filed suit alleging rat infestation caused severe injuries including toe amputations, asserting Fair Housing Act discrimination claims along with state law tort claims. The court recommends granting Nash's motion to remand because she voluntarily dismissed her FHA claims in her Second Supplemental Petition, eliminating federal question jurisdiction under Royal Canin, and the remaining state law tort claims do not present a substantial federal question.

case_name: Cedric Willis v. U.S. Bank National Association, as Trustee, Igloo Series Trust; Loancare LLC; and Security National Mortgage Company, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought preliminary injunction to prevent foreclosure sale of his home, though no specific reasonable accommodation request was identified or analyzed by the court.
key_holding: The court denied the TRO/preliminary injunction because plaintiff failed to show substantial likelihood of success on his unspecified claims, there was no nexus between the monetary relief sought and the injunctive relief requested, monetary damages cannot constitute irreparable harm, and no imminent foreclosure sale was established.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Cedric Willis sued U.S. Bank National Association and related mortgage entities seeking monetary damages for breach of contract, negligence, fraud, and Fair Housing Act violations related to a foreclosure notice on his home, and moved for a preliminary injunction to prevent the foreclosure sale. The court denied the motion, finding Willis failed to establish the requirements for preliminary injunctive relief, including substantial likelihood of success on unspecified claims, irreparable harm, and imminent foreclosure threat.

case_name: Justin Baker v. Avenue5 Residential et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested several disability-related accommodations from Avenue5, including installation of exterior pest vent grills to prevent birds from entering his unit and disturbing his sleep, silencing of a noisy storage room, transfer to a quieter apartment unit, adjustment of toilet seats, noise enforcement against barking dogs and screaming neighbors, and repair of his heater and HVAC unit.
key_holding: The court partially dismisses Baker's amended complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e), allowing only his FHA reasonable accommodation and hostile housing environment claims to proceed while dismissing all other claims with or without prejudice.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Justin Baker, a tenant at Walton Lofts in Seattle with multiple severe disabilities, brought his fourth federal lawsuit against property manager Avenue5 Residential and numerous other defendants alleging various FHA violations, ADA retaliation, and other claims arising from management's alleged failure to respond to his accommodation requests, harassment by staff, and initiation of eviction proceedings. The court conducted mandatory IFP screening under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) and dismissed most claims, including FHA retaliation, reasonable modification, design and construction, and discriminatory advertising, either with or without prejudice for failure to state a claim, while allowing Baker's FHA reasonable accommodation claim and hostile housing environment claim to survive because he adequately alleged denial of accommodations (such as exterior pest vent grills and unit transfers) in his current apartment since 2024, and alleged staff physically threatened him and entered his unit without permission. The court also applied the two-dismissal rule to bar claims arising from Baker's prior apartment unit, as he had voluntarily dismissed two previous federal suits raising the same claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: LaSae D. Spraggins v. Ironwood Crossing Public Facility Corporation
accommodation_description: The case text does not describe the specific accommodation requested; the plaintiff alleged FHA and ADA violations in the context of a pending eviction without the opinion detailing the nature of any particular accommodation sought.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommended denying plaintiff's motions for a preliminary injunction and stay of writ of possession because the Anti-Injunction Act and Younger abstention doctrine deprive the federal court of jurisdiction to enjoin the pending state court eviction proceedings.
brief_summary: Plaintiff LaSae Spraggins filed suit against Ironwood Crossing Public Facility Corporation alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act and ADA arising from a pending eviction in Tarrant County, Texas, and sought emergency injunctive relief to stay enforcement of a writ of possession issued by the state court. The magistrate judge recommended denying both motions, concluding that the Anti-Injunction Act (28 U.S.C. § 2283) and the Younger abstention doctrine barred the federal court from enjoining or staying the state eviction proceedings. The court did not reach the merits of the underlying FHA or ADA claims.

source_file: 10397530_2025_Ward v. Blue Canyon Property Management LLC_kywd
case_name: Timothy A. Ward v. Blue Canyon Property Management LLC; and Madrid KY, LLC
accommodation_description: Timothy Ward requested to pay rent after receiving his monthly Social Security Disability payment rather than by the standard lease deadline.
key_holding: Ward failed to establish causation between his requested rent payment timing accommodation and his disabilities, and Defendants articulated a legitimate non-discriminatory reason (Ward failed to pay any rent) for denying the accommodation.
brief_summary: Timothy Ward, a tenant with advanced congenital heart failure, diabetes, PTSD, and other conditions, sued Blue Canyon Property Management LLC and Madrid KY, LLC claiming the landlords violated the FHA by denying his request to pay rent after receiving his Social Security Disability payment. The court granted summary judgment for Defendants, finding Ward failed to establish the required nexus between the accommodation and his disabilities, and Defendants proffered legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for denial based on Ward's failure to pay any rent.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)

case_name: Meredith Twyman v. Recap PA Holdings, LLC, 963 Street Road LLC
accommodation_description: Tenant requested a private handicapped parking space with a blue ADA-compliant sign; landlord provided a reserved parking spot for her exclusive use but did not install a blue handicapped placard.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's reasonable accommodation claims with prejudice because plaintiff received a private parking spot designated exclusively for her use—which is a better accommodation than a general handicapped spot—and plaintiff failed to allege how her scoliosis and anxiety necessitate brighter parking lot lighting, as brighter lighting applies to everyone regardless of disability.
brief_summary: Meredith Twyman, an African American woman with disabilities including scoliosis, chronic disc pain, and anxiety disorder, sued her property manager and landlord alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on race and disability discrimination and failure to accommodate her requests for a specially marked parking space and improved parking lot lighting. The court dismissed all federal claims with prejudice after four attempts, finding plaintiff failed to plead facts showing the requested accommodations were necessary to afford her equal housing opportunity and that plaintiff received an adequate parking accommodation.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)

accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's summary judgment in favor of the defendant, finding no reversible error in the FHA violation allegations.
brief_summary: Raymond Earl May, Jr. and Angela Dolores May appealed the Eastern District of North Carolina's grant of summary judgment to their landlord, Martin Fein Interest Ltd., in their Fair Housing Act case. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's decision, finding no reversible error in its rejection of the plaintiffs' FHA claims.

case_name: Yolanda E. Quewon v. Philadelphia Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff allegedly suffers from hip and knee pain from walking up stairs and cannot afford assistance, but no specific accommodation was formally requested or described in the complaint.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because she failed to allege any disability, any request for accommodation, or any connection between her hip and knee pain and the landlord's demands for rent.
brief_summary: Yolanda Quewon, a tenant of the Philadelphia Housing Authority, sued PHA and an individual for breach of contract, due process violations, and Fair Housing Act discrimination, alleging she was harassed to pay rent and utilities despite a lease that did not require such payments. The court dismissed her case with prejudice because her Second Amended Complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to state a viable federal claim, including failing to allege disability, any accommodation request, or a nexus between her conditions and the alleged discriminatory conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Dawn N. Earle v. Manchester Village Owners Association Inc, et al.

key_holding: The filing of an amended complaint moots any pending motion to dismiss the original complaint, so defendants' motion to dismiss was denied as moot without reaching the merits of the ADA or FHA claims.
brief_summary: Dawn Earle sued Manchester Village Owners Association Inc. and individual defendants alleging disability discrimination, failure to accommodate her disabilities in housing and parking, and retaliation in violation of the ADA and FHA. Defendants moved to dismiss for failure to state a claim. The court denied the motion as moot because Earle filed an amended complaint, which superseded the original complaint and rendered the pending motion to dismiss moot, without reaching the substantive merits of either claim.

accommodation_description: Fox generally alleged she requested 'repairs and reasonable accommodations' but did not plead specific accommodation requests with sufficient detail.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim fails because she did not plead facts establishing a causal link between protected activity and alleged adverse actions, and her disability discrimination claim was dismissed because she failed to adequately allege her disability or identify what reasonable accommodations she requested.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Marcella Fox sued her landlord Ryan Kovacs, property management entities, and HopeLink of Southern Nevada alleging habitability violations, negligence, and Fair Housing Act claims including retaliation for requesting repairs and disability discrimination. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding Fox failed to plead sufficient facts to establish her retaliation claim's causation element and failed to adequately allege her disability or identify specific reasonable accommodation requests.

case_name: Jacqueline Buckholz v. Kelso Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for informal hearing to appeal housing voucher termination, or extension of tenancy, as reasonable accommodation for mental health disabilities affecting ability to meet appeal deadlines
key_holding: Plaintiff demonstrated serious questions going to the merits of her reasonable accommodation claim, irreparable harm from imminent eviction and homelessness, and the balance of hardships and public interest favored granting the preliminary injunction to reinstate her housing voucher.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Jacqueline Buckholz, an individual with mental health disabilities receiving Section 8 housing assistance, sued Kelso Housing Authority alleging the termination of her housing voucher violated the Fair Housing Act's reasonable accommodation requirement because her disability affected her ability to meet the deadline for requesting an informal hearing. The court granted Plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction, finding she showed serious questions going to the merits, faced irreparable harm from imminent eviction, and the balance of equities and public interest favored enjoining the defendant from refusing to make housing assistance payments while the case proceeds.

case_name: Newman v. State of Delaware
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Newman filed multiple incoherent complaints alleging a 'double dipping' rent scheme and various conspiracies, with one complaint mentioning the Fair Housing Act in connection with housing voucher payments but not asserting a cognizable reasonable accommodation claim.
key_holding: The Court dismissed all five Complaints as frivolous pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i) because they relied on indisputably meritless legal theories and fantastic or delusional factual scenarios, with Plaintiff Newman having filed twenty-six previously dismissed complaints demonstrating a pattern of groundless litigation.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Shantell D. Newman filed five separate civil actions against various defendants including the State of Delaware, private landlords, and courthouse security officers, alleging federal criminal statutes, § 1983 civil rights claims, and Fair Housing Act violations stemming from an alleged rent scheme while she was homeless and pregnant. The Court dismissed all five Complaints as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(i), finding the allegations were clearly baseless, relied on fantastic or delusional scenarios, and noting Plaintiff had filed twenty-six previously dismissed complaints demonstrating a pattern of groundless litigation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

case_name: Stansly T. Maponga v. Hall Park Hotel, et al.
accommodation_description: Maponga alleged generally that the hotel 'failed to accommodate' his 'back disability and cognitive impairments' under the ADA, but did not identify what specific accommodation was requested, denied, or needed, nor did he allege what major life activity was substantially limited.
key_holding: The court held that pro se plaintiff Maponga's amended complaint failed to state a claim upon which relief could be granted under the ADA, FHA, and all state law claims due to insufficient factual allegations, but granted leave to file a second amended complaint within 30 days.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Stansly Maponga sued Hall Park Hotel and two individuals alleging violations of the ADA and FHA, breach of contract, unjust enrichment, and intentional infliction of emotional distress, arising from his removal from the hotel 21 days into a 32-night stay after paying only $2,000 of a $12,000 agreed rate. Screening the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), the court found all claims deficient: the ADA and FHA claims lacked any factual allegations establishing a disability, discriminatory conduct, or how the defendants interfered with fair housing, while the state law claims failed for independent reasons. Rather than dismissing outright, the court afforded Maponga one additional opportunity to amend and cure the identified deficiencies.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

case_name: Quintin J. Ballentine v. Bowery Residence Committee
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: This transfer order does not address the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claim; the court transferred venue to the Eastern District of New York because the operative events occurred in Brooklyn, making EDNY a more convenient forum.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quintin J. Ballentine, a shelter resident, brings Fair Housing Act and ADA claims against Bowery Residence Committee and government officials alleging violations at a Brooklyn shelter. The S.D.N.Y. court transferred this action to the Eastern District of New York, finding that venue was proper in EDNY where the underlying events occurred and that transfer served the convenience of parties and witnesses.

case_name: National Urban League et al. v. Trump
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case. Plaintiffs are nonprofit organizations challenging executive orders restricting DEI programs in federal contracts and grants on constitutional grounds (First and Fifth Amendment).
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to show likelihood of success on the merits of their constitutional challenges to executive orders restricting DEI programs; the government's decision not to fund certain activities does not violate the First Amendment, and the challenged provisions are not facially invalid.
brief_summary: Three nonprofit organizations (National Urban League, National Fair Housing Alliance, AIDS Foundation of Chicago) sued President Trump and federal agencies to preliminarily enjoin enforcement of executive orders restricting DEI programs in federal contracts and grants, alleging First and Fifth Amendment violations. The court denied the preliminary injunction motion, finding plaintiffs lacked standing for some claims and failed to show likelihood of success on their facial constitutional challenges because the government may decline to fund certain activities and the executive orders do not facially violate constitutional rights.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Agency for Int'l Dev. v. Alliance for Open Soc'y Int'l, Inc., 570 U.S. 205 (2013)

case_name: Katherine Trujillo v. Amity Plaza, LLC, Housing Authority of the City of Littleton, d/b/a South Metro Housing Options, and Frank Martinez
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; claims involve alleged sexual assault/harassment by maintenance employee and individual liability under the FHA for discriminatory housing practices.
key_holding: The court properly granted sua sponte summary judgment in favor of Frank Martinez because he is not a 'housing provider' under the FHA, had no authority over rental decisions as a maintenance employee, and no evidence established any quid pro quo relationship or discriminatory housing practice connected to his role.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Katherine Trujillo sued Amity Plaza LLC, the Housing Authority of the City of Littleton, and maintenance employee Frank Martinez for Fair Housing Act violations under §§ 3604(b) and 3617, alleging discriminatory conduct and seeking individual liability against the employee. The court denied Trujillo's motion to amend judgment and confirmed sua sponte summary judgment in favor of Martinez, finding that as a maintenance employee with no authority over housing decisions, he could not be held individually liable as a 'housing provider' under the FHA.

case_name: Heather Hogrobrooks Harris v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
accommodation_description: This case concerns mortgage foreclosure proceedings and does not involve any disability accommodation request; plaintiff raised claims under Reconstruction Era civil rights statutes (§§ 1981, 1982, 1985(3)) and state consumer protection law.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's claims as barred by res judicata because the same claims had been raised and rejected in two prior lawsuits (Harris I and Harris II), and plaintiff failed to demonstrate any basis to overcome the res judicata bar.
brief_summary: Heather Hogrobrooks Harris filed her third lawsuit against Wells Fargo Bank and Wilson & Associates, raising claims under §§ 1981, 1982, and 1985(3) related to mortgage foreclosure proceedings that she had previously brought and lost in Harris I and Harris II. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that the claims were barred by res judicata because they had been raised and rejected in prior litigation, and ordered Harris to show cause why she should not be subject to a pre-filing restriction for her repetitive, frivolous lawsuits.

case_name: Luis Ricardo Munroe v. New York University, Erin Jane Lynch, Legal Affairs Department, Office of Faculty Housing
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - complaint asserts FHA claims but specific accommodation request not described in this service order
key_holding: No merits determination; Court granted Plaintiff in forma pauperis status and ordered service of process on Defendants New York University, Erin Jane Lynch, Legal Affairs Department, and Office of Faculty Housing.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Luis Ricardo Munroe, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, filed a complaint against New York University and related defendants asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act, Americans with Disabilities Act, and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act regarding faculty housing. The Court granted IFP status and issued this order directing the U.S. Marshals Service to effect service on Defendants — this is a procedural service order that does not address the merits of any claim.

case_name: Green v. Allied First Bank SB
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint references Fair Housing Act but does not articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request; the case concerns mortgage loss-mitigation and foreclosure, not a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: The court granted Servbank's motion to dismiss because claim preclusion bars Green's second lawsuit, which involves the same parties, same court, same judgment on the merits, and the same nucleus of operative facts (loss-mitigation process and foreclosure) as her first lawsuit.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff LaKeisha C. Green filed her second lawsuit against Allied First Bank SB (Servbank) challenging the bank's loss-mitigation process and foreclosure on her home, invoking the Fair Housing Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The court granted Servbank's motion to dismiss with prejudice, holding that claim preclusion bars the lawsuit because it involves the same parties, the same prior judgment on the merits, and the same nucleus of operative facts as Green's earlier lawsuit.

case_name: Michael-Zahir David Fleming v. Westwood Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested in this case. Fleming challenged a new parking policy requiring residents to park miles away from the apartment complex, framing this as a constitutional taking and due process violation rather than any accommodation request under the FHA.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss because plaintiff failed to allege state action for his constitutional claims and failed to allege membership in a protected class for his FHA and § 1982 claims.
brief_summary: Pro se tenant Michael-Zahir David Fleming sued his apartment complex and property manager alleging violations of the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1982 and 1983, the Fair Housing Act, and state conversion law, primarily challenging a new parking policy that he claimed infringed his property rights. The court dismissed all federal constitutional claims because Westwood, a private company, was not a state actor, and dismissed the FHA and § 1982 claims because Fleming explicitly failed to allege membership in any protected class or any discriminatory animus. The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law conversion claim, and all claims were dismissed without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jimmy Avila sued NYCHA and CIDNY alleging disability, race, and gender discrimination under the FHA, Rehabilitation Act, ADA, and Section 1983, claiming defendants failed to provide housing accommodating his disabilities and terminated needed services. brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Charles Sexton, a homeless individual, sued the NYC Department of Homeless Services, multiple private shelter operators (VOA, Westhab, Project Renewal, Breaking Ground), and numerous individual defendants claiming constitutional violations, FHA discrimination, and other federal claims arising from his stays at three homeless shelters. case_name: Tyeashia M. Blackburn; Lezlie E. Freeman v. Kelly Webb; Rent King, LLC
accommodation_description: No FHA accommodation was requested or at issue as a substantive claim. Plaintiffs raised for the first time on appeal an argument that the district court should have provided them ADA litigation accommodations for disabilities affecting their capacity to meet procedural requirements during periods of worsening health; this argument was forfeited because plaintiffs never requested such accommodations, a continuance, or any extension of time before the district court.
key_holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal with prejudice of plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act racial discrimination and retaliation claims as a sanction for repeated litigation misconduct, including failure to cooperate with discovery and chronic noncompliance with procedural rules and court orders.
brief_summary: Tyeashia Blackburn and Lezlie Freeman sued landlord Kelly Webb and Rent King, LLC under 42 U.S.C. § 3604 alleging racial discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act. The district court dismissed the case with prejudice pursuant to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 16(f), 37(b)(2)(A), and 41(b) based on a pattern of discovery failures, unauthorized filings, and repeated noncompliance despite prior warnings. The Tenth Circuit affirmed, finding no abuse of discretion in the district court's application of the Ehrenhaus factors and declining to consider plaintiffs' forfeited ADA-accommodations argument raised for the first time on appeal.
key_cases_cited: Ehrenhaus v. Reynolds, 965 F.2d 916 (10th Cir. 1992)
Richison v. Ernest Grp., Inc., 634 F.3d 1123 (10th Cir. 2011)
Garrett v. Selby Connor Maddux & Janer, 425 F.3d 836 (10th Cir. 2005)
Clark v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 590 F.3d 1134 (10th Cir. 2009)

case_name: Dawn M. Chappel v. Adams County Children's Services, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested injunctive relief preventing enforcement of a state court eviction order and allowing her to return to property at 211 Sunshine Ave., Winchester, Ohio, as relief for alleged FHA retaliation.
key_holding: The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation to deny preliminary injunction on the FHA retaliation claim because plaintiff failed to establish a substantial likelihood of success on the merits, presented no evidence of discriminatory animus beyond speculation, and the requested relief would not preserve the status quo.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Dawn Chappel, a Section 8 voucher holder, sued Adams County Children's Services, a police chief, and a housing authority official alleging FHA retaliation under § 3617, seeking preliminary injunctions to prevent enforcement of a state court eviction order and to obtain housing-related relief. The court adopted both Magistrate Judge R&Rs, denying the preliminary injunction motions because plaintiff failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on her retaliation claim, offered only speculation of discriminatory animus related to her status as a recovering drug addict, and sought relief inconsistent with the status quo.
key_cases_cited: Liberty Coins, LLC v. Goodman, 748 F.3d 682 (6th Cir. 2014)
Kooman v. Boulder Bluff Condos., 833 F. App'x 623 (6th Cir. 2020)
HDC, LLC v. City of Ann Arbor, 675 F.3d 608 (6th Cir. 2012)

source_file: 10581724_2025_U.S. Bank, National Association as legal title trustee v. Valeria Taveras_ca11
case_name: U.S. Bank, National Association as Legal Title Trustee for Truman 2016 SC6 Title Trust v. Taveras
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested. The Fair Housing Act was invoked solely as a predicate for civil-rights removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1443; the Taverases argued that Florida's foreclosure procedures reflected a systemic policy of racial discrimination that denied them rights under the FHA, the Civil Rights Acts of 1866 and 1964, and the Equal Protection Clause.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's remand of a state foreclosure action and its award of costs and fees to U.S. Bank, holding that the Taverases failed the second prong of the Rachel test for § 1443 civil-rights removal because they could not demonstrate that their federal civil rights would be predictably denied by Florida courts, and that their second removal attempt on the eve of a dispositive hearing was objectively unreasonable.
brief_summary: The Taverases defaulted on their Florida mortgage in 2008 and faced a state-court foreclosure by U.S. Bank. Two days before a 2023 summary-judgment hearing, they attempted for the second time to remove the case to federal court, asserting jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1331, 1332, and 1443, and alleging that Florida's foreclosure system embodied a policy of racial discrimination that violated the Civil Rights Acts and the Fair Housing Act. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's remand, finding the Taverases failed both prongs of the Rachel civil-rights-removal test and that no diversity or federal-question jurisdiction existed, and affirmed the award of costs and fees because the removal lacked an objectively reasonable basis.
key_cases_cited: Georgia v. Rachel, 384 U.S. 780 (1966)
Greenwood v. Peacock, 384 U.S. 808 (1966)
Johnson v. Mississippi, 421 U.S. 213 (1975)
Sofarelli v. Pinellas County, 931 F.2d 718 (11th Cir. 1991)
BP P.L.C. v. Mayor of Balt., 593 U.S. 230 (2021)

case_name: Tony Cole v. Joseph Faulkner, et al.
accommodation_description: Cole alleged retaliation under the Fair Housing Act for asserting his legal rights related to the property at issue in eviction proceedings.
key_holding: Cole's FHA retaliation claim fails because he failed to allege what specific right under §§ 3603, 3604, 3605, or 3606 he was exercising that triggered the anti-retaliation provision of § 3617, merely alleging he was asserting 'legal rights related to the property' generally.
brief_summary: Tony Cole sued Joseph Faulkner and others alleging retaliatory eviction under the Fair Housing Act and constitutional claims after being evicted from a building in Chicago through state court proceedings. The court granted reconsideration on jurisdictional grounds but ultimately maintained dismissal of Cole's claims, finding his FHA retaliation claim failed because he did not adequately allege the specific right he was exercising under the Act, and his § 1983 claim failed because private defendants did not act under color of state law.
key_cases_cited: Gilbank v. Wood Cnty. Dep't of Hum. Servs., 111 F.4th 754 (7th Cir. 2024)

source_file: 10583019_2025_Dogbe v. The Lakes at Lemmon Valley, LLC_nvd
case_name: John Dogbe and Alberta Dogbe v. The Lakes at Lemmon Valley, LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - case concerns alleged racial discrimination in eviction and enforcement of clubhouse policies
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of plaintiffs' racial discrimination claims under § 1981, § 1982, § 3604(b) disparate treatment, and § 3617 because plaintiffs sufficiently alleged that but-for their race, the party would not have been shut down and they would not have received an eviction notice.
brief_summary: African American tenants John and Alberta Dogbe sued their landlord The Lakes at Lemmon Valley, LLC alleging racial discrimination after their clubhouse party was shut down and they received an eviction notice while similarly-situated white residents had not faced such actions. The court granted in part and denied in part defendant's motion to dismiss, dismissing disparate impact claims but allowing disparate treatment claims under § 3604(b) and § 3617 to proceed because plaintiffs sufficiently alleged race was a but-for cause of the eviction notice.
