case_name: Christopher K. Andersen v. Olympus at Daybreak
accommodation_description: Plaintiff seeks TRO to enjoin unlawful detainer action and prevent eviction as reasonable accommodation for disability-related claims (water-heater repair requests and mental health impacts).
key_holding: The court denied the TRO because Andersen failed to demonstrate irreparable harm—he voluntarily surrendered his apartment and obtained alternative housing, undercutting his claim of imminent injury from the pending unlawful detainer action.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Christopher K. Andersen, a tenant facing eviction from Olympus at Daybreak apartments, moved for a temporary restraining order to enjoin the unlawful detainer action, prevent reporting of eviction records, and halt collection of early termination fees, asserting Fair Housing Act and ADA claims based on disability-related repair requests and retaliation. The court denied the motion without prejudice, finding Andersen failed to demonstrate irreparable harm because he voluntarily surrendered the apartment and obtained alternative housing, mooting his claim of imminent injury from the pending state court eviction proceedings.

case_name: United States of America v. Javier Salazar, Jr., et al.
accommodation_description: The underlying accommodation or FHA violation at issue is not described in this order, which addresses only the procedural motion to set aside default judgment; the complaint references enforcement of the FHA on behalf of Angela McGinnis but no specifics of the alleged violation or requested accommodation are disclosed in the text of this order.
key_holding: The court adopted the magistrate judge's findings and recommendations and denied defendants' motion to set aside the default judgment previously entered in favor of the United States in this Fair Housing Act enforcement action, holding that the relevant factors weighed in favor of maintaining the default judgment.
brief_summary: The United States filed a Fair Housing Act enforcement action on behalf of Angela McGinnis against Javier Salazar Jr., Javier Salazar Sr., and Ricardo Covarrubias, and obtained a default judgment against defendants in October 2024. Defendants, through newly retained counsel, moved to set aside the default judgment in November 2024. The court adopted the magistrate judge's findings and recommendations — to which no party filed objections — and denied the motion, concluding that the factors governing relief from a default judgment weighed in favor of maintaining it.

case_name: 8214 Wilson Drive, LLC v. Daugherty
accommodation_description: The underlying eviction dispute allegedly involves disability and familial status discrimination under the FHA, but no specific accommodation request is identified in the record.
key_holding: The court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction because removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1443(1) requires reliance on laws providing equal civil rights in terms of racial equality, and Daugherty's claims of disability and familial status discrimination did not satisfy this requirement; additionally, the Rooker-Feldman doctrine and Younger abstention barred federal review.
brief_summary: Daugherty, acting as trustee of RLD Ministry Trust, removed a Nebraska landlord-tenant eviction proceeding to federal court alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on disability and familial status discrimination, along with constitutional claims. The court granted in forma pauperis status but remanded the case to state court for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, holding that 28 U.S.C. § 1443(1) only authorizes removal for racial equality claims, and alternatively that Rooker-Feldman and Younger abstention doctrines barred federal review of the state court proceedings.

subsidy_program: City Family Homelessness and Eviction Prevention Supplement (City FHEPS)
accommodation_description: This screening order does not substantively analyze any reasonable accommodation request; it addresses municipal liability under state law and service of process issues.
key_holding: The Court dismissed claims against municipal agencies (NYC HPD, DHS, APS, City FHEPS) because NYC agencies are not suable entities under N.Y. City Charter ch. 17, § 396, but ordered service on remaining private and individual defendants.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Jimmy Avila and Mezie Oduka sued numerous defendants including private landlords, property management companies, and NYC municipal agencies for alleged violations of the ADA and Fair Housing Act. The Court dismissed claims against municipal agencies on the ground that NYC agencies cannot be sued as separate entities, while ordering service on remaining named defendants.

case_name: Pamela Shomo & DeJa Shomo v. Karen Cooksey, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support animal (dog named King) in the apartment as a reasonable accommodation, which was allegedly not considered before eviction.
key_holding: The FHA failure to accommodate claim was dismissed because the amended complaint failed to allege any qualifying disability, any request for reasonable accommodation, how the accommodation was reasonable and necessary, or that defendants refused any such request.
brief_summary: Pamela and DeJa Shomo sued Columbia Glade Apartments and its manager Karen Cooksey alleging that their eviction violated the Fair Housing Act on both racial discrimination and failure to accommodate an emotional support animal grounds. The court granted Cooksey's motion to dismiss, finding the amended complaint failed to state plausible FHA claims because it did not allege a qualifying disability, did not allege a request for accommodation was made, and did not allege defendants refused such a request.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

source_file: 10587034_2025_APPELGREN v. ISLAND HOSPITALITY MANAGEMENT VII, LLC_njd
case_name: Mark Appelgren v. Island Hospitality Management VII, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought a quiet, stress-free environment and room modifications during a hotel stay to manage his anxiety disorder, IBS, and other disabilities, but he did not inform hotel staff of his disabilities.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA and ADA reasonable accommodation claims fail because he never informed hotel staff of his disabilities, so Defendants could not have known why he made any requests and cannot be liable for refusing accommodations they were unaware were sought.
brief_summary: Mark Appelgren, a federal agent with severe anxiety, depression, and IBS, sued Island Hospitality Management and Hilton alleging discrimination during an attempted hotel stay where he experienced delays, hostile interactions, and a chaotic lobby environment that triggered his anxiety and IBS symptoms. The Court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that because Plaintiff never informed hotel staff of his disabilities, Defendants could not be held liable for failing to accommodate those disabilities.

case_name: Patsy Jay v. Grand Management Services, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff made a verbal request to keep her mobility walker on her porch as a disability accommodation, which defendants did not respond to, and later cited the walker as a lease violation in the eviction notice issued after plaintiff reported McKnight's sexual assault.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on plaintiff's hostile living environment and retaliation claims because genuine issues of material fact existed regarding whether defendants' failure to evict McKnight and issuance of an eviction notice to plaintiff constituted disability discrimination and unlawful retaliation under § 3617.
brief_summary: Patsy Jay, a mobility-disabled elderly tenant, sued Grand Management Services and related defendants alleging they failed to protect her from a neighbor who sexually assaulted and stalked her, issued a retaliatory eviction notice after she reported the assault, and discriminated against her based on disability by failing to accommodate her need to keep a walker on her porch. The court denied summary judgment on plaintiff's hostile living environment and retaliation claims, finding genuine disputes of material fact regarding defendants' knowledge of the neighbor's dangerous behavior toward women and whether the eviction notice was retaliation for plaintiff's protected activity.

case_name: Robert L. Hatcher v. Sylvain Yang and Travis Smith
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to continue parking his vehicle in the back yard of the duplex property due to his disability-related limitations.
key_holding: The court denied Defendant Yang's motion to dismiss because he failed to demonstrate that dismissal was proper, as he submitted unsworn statements outside the pleadings and cited no legal authority addressing the FHA.
brief_summary: Robert L. Hatcher, a 74-year-old disabled African American man, sued his private landlord Sylvain Yang alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, including that Yang refused to make reasonable accommodations for his disability (allowing him to park in the back yard and be excused from lease maintenance obligations) and discriminated against him based on disability and race by showing favorable treatment to a new tenant. The court denied Yang's motion to dismiss because he failed to meet his burden, submitting only unsubstantiated facts outside the pleadings without supporting legal authority.
key_cases_cited: North Mill Street, LLC v. City of Aspen, 6 F.4th 1216 (10th Cir. 2021)

case_name: Deepa Patel et al. v. City of Stanton et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs are motel business operators challenging revocation of their motel permit and business license by the City of Stanton as violating procedural due process; the case does not involve a reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' procedural due process claim with prejudice because plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the permit revocation, received constitutionally adequate notice and hearing for the business license revocation, failed to adequately plead a Haas claim regarding hearing officer bias, and had no protected property interest in their business license under the Stanton Municipal Code's discretionary revocation provisions.
brief_summary: Motel operators Ahir and Megha Hospitality LLC sued the City of Stanton alleging violations of their Fourteenth Amendment procedural due process rights when the City revoked their motel permit and business license without adequate notice. The court granted the City's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge the permit revocation, received constitutionally adequate process for the business license revocation, failed to state a Haas claim for hearing officer bias, and had no protected property interest in their business license.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

case_name: Dennis Turner and Darlene Brooks v. Autumn Lake Property Owners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; this is an HOA fee overcharge dispute where plaintiffs attempted to invoke the FHA in their objection without pleading any discrimination in the complaint.
key_holding: The case was dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to plead any discrimination allegations in their complaint, and their objection attempting to invoke the Fair Housing Act was meritless.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Dennis Turner and Darlene Brooks sued Autumn Lake Property Owners Association Inc. alleging the HOA overcharged them fees. The court dismissed the case for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to plead any discrimination allegations in their complaint, and their attempt to invoke the Fair Housing Act in an objection was insufficient to establish jurisdiction.

case_name: Dennis Turner and Darlene Brooks v. Autumn Lake Property Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request — case concerns HOA fee disputes, not disability accommodations; plaintiffs improperly invoked FHA for fee challenge
key_holding: Plaintiffs' federal claims citing the Fair Housing Act are wholly insubstantial and frivolous because their actual allegations concern homeowners' association fees, which have no connection to the FHA's provisions governing housing discrimination.
brief_summary: Two homeowners sued their property owners association over alleged overcharging of HOA fees for over a decade, invoking the Fair Housing Act as the sole basis for federal jurisdiction. The court recommends granting the motion to dismiss because plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims are wholly insubstantial and frivolous — their fee dispute has no connection to the FHA's provisions governing housing discrimination.

case_name: Daniel St. Clair v. Leonard Bernard George
accommodation_description: The opinion does not describe any specific accommodation request; it only addresses whether the case was properly removed to federal court.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommends denying the motion to remand because the defendant timely removed the case within 30 days of receiving the amended petition that first stated a federal claim, and none of the prior exhibits qualified as 'other paper' under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(3) to trigger earlier removal.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Daniel St. Clair sued landlord Leonard Bernard George in Texas justice court; after plaintiff amended his petition to add a Fair Housing Act claim, defendant removed the case to federal court, and plaintiff moved to remand. The magistrate judge recommends denying the remand motion because defendant's removal was timely under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b)(3).

case_name: Anne Lauren Krause v. KCG Development, LLC and Landsman Real Estate Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendants failed to make repairs to her apartment as a reasonable accommodation for her physical and mental impairments under the FHA.
key_holding: Because Defendants filed timely Answers to the Complaint, default has not been entered and Plaintiff's motion for default judgment, treated as a motion for entry of default, is denied; separately, the court found insufficient merit to appoint counsel under the relevant factors.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Anne Lauren Krause, proceeding pro se, sued KCG Development and Landsman Real Estate Company alleging they failed to make repairs to her apartment as a reasonable accommodation for her physical and mental impairments in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied Plaintiff's motion for default judgment because Defendants had filed timely Answers, finding no default had occurred; the court also denied Plaintiff's request for appointed counsel, finding insufficient merit to warrant counsel assignment.

case_name: Charity Mainville v. Anna De Santis and De Santis Rentals, LLC
accommodation_description: This opinion addresses a motion to recuse the assigned Magistrate Judge under 28 U.S.C. § 455(a), not a substantive fair housing accommodation claim.
key_holding: The magistrate judge's motion to recuse was denied because plaintiff failed to comply with local rules requiring a supporting brief, and alternatively, plaintiff failed to establish any valid basis for recusal as her dissatisfaction with adverse rulings does not create a reasonable question of impartiality.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Charity Mainville filed a motion seeking recusal of the assigned Magistrate Judge under 28 U.S.C. § 455(a), asserting bias based on his denial of her motion for electronic filing authorization. The court denied the motion to recuse because plaintiff failed to file a required supporting brief under local rules and, alternatively, because plaintiff's disagreement with adverse rulings does not establish a valid basis for recusal under objective standards.
key_cases_cited: Liteky v. United States, 510 U.S. 540 (1994)

case_name: Mirlande Dina Michel-Wiggins v. Jes Holdings, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested two apartments under a single housing voucher to accommodate a live-in aide arrangement, because she does not wish to share living space with an aide.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that requiring two apartments under a single housing voucher imposed an undue financial burden and did not constitute a reasonable accommodation under the FHA.
brief_summary: Mirlande Michel-Wiggins, a disabled individual using a Section 8 housing voucher, sued Jes Holdings LLC and Fairway Management alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to rent her two apartments under a single voucher to accommodate a live-in aide, and by declining to provide trash pickup and mail delivery as disability accommodations. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, holding that requiring two apartments under one housing voucher constituted an undue financial burden and was not a reasonable accommodation, and that the ancillary service requests failed because the primary accommodation claim failed.

case_name: April Elisha Randle v. Shardai Pearson, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; complaint broadly alleges housing conditions and retaliation under FHA § 3617.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim fails because she does not claim to belong to any protected class enumerated in the FHA, and her complaint does not identify which FHA rights she seeks to enforce.
brief_summary: April Randle, proceeding pro se, sued her property manager, property management company, and corporate officer over housing conditions (cockroaches, mold, leaking pipes) and alleged Fourth Amendment violations from security cameras. The court dismissed her complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding her FHA claim deficient because she did not claim membership in a protected class and her Fourth Amendment claim failed for lack of state action.

case_name: Karla Hunt v. Volare Health LLC
accommodation_description: Employee terminated for advocating against discrimination of a prospective patient with a mental health diagnosis who was denied admission to a nursing facility
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim was dismissed because she did not allege that she aided or encouraged the prospective patient in exercising his FHA rights, as the patient was unaware of the dispute, but she was granted leave to amend; Plaintiff's Oregon whistleblower retaliation claim survived because the close temporal proximity between her advocacy and her termination, combined with the factual setting, was sufficient to plead causation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Karla Hunt, an employee at a nursing and rehabilitation facility operated by Volare Health LLC, sued alleging she was terminated in retaliation for advocating that the facility admit a prospective patient with a mental health diagnosis, which she believed constituted disability discrimination under the FHA. The court granted Volare's motion to dismiss the FHA retaliation claim because Hunt failed to allege she aided the patient in exercising his FHA rights, but dismissed with leave to amend; the court denied dismissal of Hunt's Oregon whistleblower retaliation claim finding sufficient temporal proximity and factual support for causation.

case_name: Delroy Askins v. Prestige Management Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who receives medical supplies via mail and has a home health aide, alleges he was assaulted by the building superintendent, his medical supplies were taken, and he was denied access to the community room.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because he failed to allege facts showing he has a disability as defined by the FHA or that any adverse actions taken against him were motivated by his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Delroy Askins sued Prestige Management Inc. and building superintendent Lowell Hendricks alleging disability discrimination under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act based on being assaulted, having his medical supplies taken, and being denied access to the community room. case_name: Alberto James Santiago Sr. v. Elishia Chill, et al.
accommodation_description: Santiago alleges disability and national origin discrimination based on derogatory comments about Puerto Ricans, eviction threats, and failure to repair a door latch, but no specific accommodation request is substantively analyzed.
key_holding: The court dismissed Santiago's claims with prejudice for improper service of process (Santiago served defendants personally as a party, violating Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(c)(2)) and failure to prosecute (Santiago failed to respond to discovery, ignored court orders, and engaged in contumacious conduct).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Santiago sued Key Property Management and property manager Chill alleging national origin and disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, claiming derogatory comments about Puerto Ricans, eviction threats, and failure to repair his door. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding Santiago improperly served process himself as a party and failed to prosecute by ignoring discovery obligations and court orders over three years of litigation.

case_name: Nathaniel Manny Ballantyne v. Guenther Management LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in rental denial based on claim that defendant changed credit score requirement from 600 to 700 after his application.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment or disparate impact because he was not the first qualified applicant (another applicant applied two days earlier and was approved), the credit score requirement was always 700, and the property was ultimately rented to a Black individual.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Nathanial Ballantyne sued Guenther Management LLC, a property management company, alleging racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act after he was not selected as a tenant for a rental property in Spokane, Washington. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding plaintiff failed to establish a prima facie case because he was not the first qualified applicant, the credit score requirement was always 700, and evidence showed the property was rented to another Black individual.

case_name: Quintin J. Ballentine v. Bowery Residence Committee
accommodation_description: The case text does not specify the particular accommodation or modification requested; it states only that plaintiff alleges Defendants violated his rights at a shelter operated by BRC in Brooklyn, New York.
key_holding: The Southern District of New York transferred plaintiff's pro se FHA and ADA action to the Eastern District of New York because the events giving rise to the claims occurred in Brooklyn, which falls within the Eastern District, making it the more convenient forum under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quintin Ballentine filed suit under the FHA and ADA against Bowery Residents' Committee (a nonprofit shelter operator), BRC Chair Julie Salamon, NYC Mayor Eric Adams, and NY Governor Kathy Hochul, alleging violations of his rights at a BRC-operated shelter in Brooklyn, New York. The SDNY court did not reach the merits but determined that because the locus of operative facts — the Brooklyn shelter — lies within the Eastern District of New York, transfer was appropriate under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) for the convenience of the parties and witnesses and in the interest of justice. The case was transferred to the Eastern District of New York with all further determinations, including in forma pauperis status, left to the transferee court.

case_name: Claran Lundgren v. Ashton Glenn H.O.A. c/o Wacammaw Management, and Bob Sauthoff
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; plaintiff alleges harassment, discrimination, retaliation, and selective enforcement by HOA officials
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims under the doctrine of res judicata, finding the claims arose from the same operative facts and subject matter adjudicated in prior state court proceedings; alternatively, the claims failed to plausibly allege discrimination in the terms, conditions, or privileges of housing.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Claran Lundgren sued the Ashton Glenn HOA and its president Bob Sauthoff alleging Fair Housing Act claims based on harassment, discrimination, retaliation, and selective enforcement related to HOA fines and property violations. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss under res judicata, finding the federal claims were barred because they arose from the same operative facts litigated in prior state court proceedings, and alternatively because the allegations failed to plausibly state a discrimination claim under the FHA.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation by housing provider for engaging in protected activity, including reporting habitability issues to code enforcement, HUD, and local authorities; plaintiff mentions disabilities (cancer survivor, heart problems, depression) and her son's respiratory issues.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act because plaintiff failed to identify specific protected actions she took or any adverse actions by defendants, providing only threadbare conclusory assertions insufficient under the pleading standards.
brief_summary: Danell Scoggins, proceeding pro se, sued Falcon Court and Turning Point of Central California (a permanent supportive housing provider), alleging retaliation under the Fair Housing Act for reporting habitability issues to code enforcement and federal authorities. The magistrate judge recommended dismissal without leave to amend, finding the complaint failed to plead a prima facie retaliation claim because plaintiff did not identify specific protected actions or adverse actions, providing only conclusory allegations insufficient under Twombly and Iqbal standards.

case_name: Charlesetta Moore, SR. v. C.F.Y. Development Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; complaint alleges poor treatment and discriminatory conduct including a racial slur directed at plaintiff.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class and failed to plead facts showing different treatment because of protected class status, as a single racial slur and generalized allegations of poor treatment are insufficient to state a disparate treatment claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Charlesetta Moore, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued C.F.Y. Development Inc. and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on discriminatory treatment at Galt Place Senior Apartments, including rent increases, service failures, and a racial slur. The court dismissed the first amended complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class and failed to plead facts showing she was treated differently because of protected class status.

case_name: Gorawara v. Caprio
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested in this case. The claims centered on alleged racial intimidation and discrimination by the landlords under FHA § 3617 and deceptive practices under CUTPA in connection with renting and evicting Gorawara from an apartment.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment, holding that the court properly exercised its inherent docket-management authority, did not err in rejecting jury instructions lacking a factual predicate or proper pleading basis, and did not abuse its discretion in denying leave to amend the complaint for a fourth time at the jury charge conference.
brief_summary: Rahul Gorawara, a pro se attorney, sued his former landlords John and Carolyn Caprio alleging intimidation and racial discrimination under Fair Housing Act § 3617 and deceptive-practices claims under the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act (CUTPA), arising from his tenancy and eviction. Following a jury trial, the jury found for the defendant on all but two state-law claims (slander and negligent infliction of emotional distress against Carolyn Caprio's estate). On appeal, Gorawara challenged the district court's pre-trial scheduling order, rejection of two proposed jury instructions, and denial of leave to file a fourth amended complaint; the Second Circuit rejected all three challenges and affirmed.

case_name: Yolanda Calhoun v. The Greens at Lake Overholser
accommodation_description: The case text does not describe any specific accommodation requested; it refers only generically to 'claims of discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act' without further elaboration on the underlying allegations.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA action without prejudice because plaintiff failed to effect timely service of process under Fed. R. Civ. P. 4(m) and failed to respond to the court's order to show cause, with no permissive extension warranted under the Espinoza factors.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Yolanda Calhoun filed a Fair Housing Act complaint against The Greens at Lake Overholser and Jessica Jeffries alleging discrimination and retaliation arising from events beginning in November 2022 and culminating in her eviction in March 2023. After plaintiff failed to serve defendants within the 90-day period required by Rule 4(m), the court issued a show cause order, which plaintiff also failed to answer. The court dismissed the action without prejudice both for failure to effect timely service and for failure to comply with a court order, finding no Espinoza factors favored a permissive extension and that the Ehrenhaus factors supported dismissal.

source_file: 10599577_2025_ROSADO v. THE CITY OF CHESTER COUNTY PENNSYLVANIA_paed
case_name: Geronimo F. Rosado, Jr. v. The City of Chester County, Pennsylvania, et al.
accommodation_description: Rosado, who has a visual impairment, alleges he was discriminated against due to his disability and was not provided reasonable accommodation during property retrieval after eviction, but no specific accommodation request is clearly articulated in the opinion.
key_holding: The court dismissed Rosado's federal claims with prejudice for failure to state a claim, including ADA Title II and Section 504 claims which failed because the private defendants (Kurtas Defendants, police officers) are not public entities and do not receive federal financial assistance as required for RA claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Geronimo Rosado, a Section 8 HCVP participant with visual impairment, sued the City of Chester, Chester County Housing Authority, private landlords, police officers, and others alleging wrongful eviction and failure to accommodate his disability during property retrieval after an August 2024 eviction. The court dismissed all federal claims with prejudice, finding Rosado failed to state viable ADA Title II or Section 504 claims because the private defendants are not public entities and do not receive federal financial assistance.

case_name: Laurie Thorson v. Hawaii Public Housing Authority, Hakim Ouansafi, Ryan Akamine, and Lyle Matsuura
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested continuation of a two-bedroom voucher reasonable accommodation to permit her son to serve as her live-in aide for epilepsy and transient epileptic amnesia.
key_holding: Defendants are entitled to summary judgment because HPHA's investigation into whether Thorson's son actually resided with her as a live-in aide was motivated by legitimate compliance concerns under HUD regulations, and Thorson failed to present sufficient evidence that this explanation was pretextual for disability-based retaliation.
brief_summary: Laurie Thorson, a Section 8 voucher recipient with epilepsy, sued the Hawaii Public Housing Authority and its officials alleging disability discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, claiming HPHA improperly investigated her live-in aide arrangement and used flawed comparables in rent reasonableness determinations. The court granted summary judgment for Defendants, finding Thorson failed to establish that HPHA's legitimate, nondiscriminatory justification for investigating whether her son actually resided with her was pretext for retaliation.

case_name: El Camino, LLC v. City of South Saint Paul, Minnesota
accommodation_description: Request to house up to ten unrelated adults in recovery from substance use disorders in a single-family residential zone that otherwise limits occupancy to three unrelated persons
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment because El Camino lacked Article III standing, having failed to demonstrate concrete injury in fact—the company sold the property at a profit, and its claims of monetary harm were speculative, while its requests for declaratory and injunctive relief were moot after the property sale.
brief_summary: El Camino, LLC, a group sober home operator, sued the City of South Saint Paul alleging the city violated the Fair Housing Act and ADA by twice denying its requests for a zoning accommodation to house up to ten unrelated adults in recovery from substance use disorders in a single-family residential zone. The court granted the city's motion for summary judgment, holding that El Camino lacked Article III standing because its claims for declaratory and injunctive relief were moot after it sold the property, and El Camino failed to demonstrate any concrete monetary injury attributable to the city.

case_name: Albert Pickett, Jr. et al. v. City of Cleveland, Ohio
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - case involves disparate impact challenge to municipal water lien policy allegedly making housing unavailable to Black homeowners
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed class certification, holding that plaintiffs' disparate-impact claim under § 3604(a) presents a common question—whether Cleveland's water lien policy violates the FHA by disproportionately affecting Black homeowners—that predominates over individualized damages issues, and that plaintiffs have Article III standing based on the FHA's congressional authorization of housing discrimination claims.
brief_summary: African American homeowners and residents in Cuyahoga County, Ohio sued the City of Cleveland alleging that its water lien policy, which places liens on properties with delinquent water bills, has a disparate impact on Black homeowners in violation of § 3604(a) of the Fair Housing Act. The Sixth Circuit affirmed class certification under Rules 23(b)(2) and 23(b)(3), finding that plaintiffs' common question—whether the disproportionate placement of water liens on Black homeowners violates the FHA—predominates over individualized damages issues and that plaintiffs have Article III standing based on the cognizable harm of housing discrimination claims.

brief_summary: Heidi Grossman Lepp, associated with Sugarleaf Church, sued Detroit officials and private parties alleging defendants conducted raids, inspections, and parking restrictions that violated her constitutional and federal statutory rights. Horton and Mike Douglas alleging claims under the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act and Fair Housing Act related to their new home purchase, including workmanship defects and discriminatory refusal to make repairs. accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged a general denial of Fair Housing Act and ADA protections in connection with their eviction from Temecula Senior Apartments, but did not specify or detail any particular accommodation request; the claim appears incidental to their broader challenge of the state court's unlawful detainer ruling.
key_holding: The district court denied plaintiffs' TRO and sua sponte dismissed all claims with prejudice as frivolous and violating Rule 8, finding the complaint was essentially an improper attempt to challenge a state court unlawful detainer ruling barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine.

brief_summary: Peter and Denise Benvin sued neighbor William Garrett and the City of Inkster alleging that Garrett engaged in racially-motivated harassment (calling Benvin a racist, white trash, and making other racial comments over five years), and that the City failed to respond to complaints. case_name: Lynya Cooper v. Chicago Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request to transfer Ms. Talbert, who had a progressive neurological disease rendering her unable to walk, from a second-floor apartment to a wheelchair-accessible ground floor unit
key_holding: The court approved a $525,000 settlement and allocated 95% to Lynya Cooper individually ($498,750) and 5% to the Estate of Trebora Talbert ($26,250), finding the settlement fair and reasonable after thorough negotiation.

case_name: Marcus Hinton, et al. v. County of Cochise, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request alleged; plaintiffs claim they were illegally evicted and subjected to racial epithets, alleging housing discrimination based on race under § 3604(a).
key_holding: Plaintiffs fail to state a Fair Housing Act claim because they do not plausibly allege that the County Defendants, who are not alleged to have had any authority to sell or rent the property, engaged in housing discrimination based on race; the vague allegation that racial epithets were directed at them does not support an inference of housing discrimination under § 3604(a).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Marcus, Vanessa, and Veronica Hinton sued Cochise County and numerous other defendants alleging they were illegally evicted from their rental property, subjected to racial slurs, and had their property stolen by law enforcement officials. The Court granted the County Defendants' motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act claim, finding that plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege that county officials with no authority to rent property engaged in housing discrimination based on race under § 3604(a), though the Court granted leave to amend the complaint.
key_cases_cited: Benavidez v. County of San Diego, 993 F.3d 1134 (9th Cir. 2021)

case_name: T&R Properties, Inc. v. Berlin Township
accommodation_description: No accommodation request—this case involves a developer's challenge to municipal zoning denial based on racial discrimination and disparate impact under the FHA.
key_holding: The Fair Housing Advocates Association lacks standing to intervene because its alleged injuries—resource diversion and frustration of organizational mission—do not constitute a concrete, particularized injury caused by the Township's actions, and its proposed claims are duplicative of the original plaintiff's claims.
brief_summary: T&R Properties sued Berlin Township alleging the municipality denied zoning approval for affordable housing with discriminatory intent against racial minorities. Fair Housing Advocates Association moved to intervene, asserting its own intentional discrimination and disparate impact claims. The court denied the motion to intervene, finding FHAA lacks Article III standing because its alleged injuries—resource expenditure investigating the Township and frustration of its anti-discrimination mission—do not constitute a concrete injury traceable to the Township's conduct, and its claims are duplicative of T&R's.
key_cases_cited: FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine, 602 U.S. 367 (2024)

case_name: Anthony Alexander James v. Matzger Management Company
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The magistrate recommends dismissal without prejudice because plaintiff, proceeding pro se, failed to file a Second Amended Complaint after being granted leave to amend and failed to respond to an order to show cause regarding failure to prosecute.
brief_summary: Anthony Alexander James, proceeding pro se, sued Matzger Management Company alleging Fair Housing Act violations and other claims. Following a prior order granting defendant leave to amend, the Court issued findings and recommendations recommending dismissal without prejudice because plaintiff failed to file a Second Amended Complaint or respond to an order to show cause for failure to prosecute.

case_name: McLain v. Sedgwick County Sheriff's Office
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs request extended time for filings, clear written instructions, and accommodations for disability-related communication barriers during legal proceedings due to Michael McLain's PTSD, TBI, and cognitive impairments affecting cognitive processing, memory, and communication.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for appointed counsel after evaluating the four relevant factors, finding that while plaintiff Michael McLain has documented cognitive disabilities (PTSD, TBI, stroke-related impairment), his filings in this litigation have been articulate and well-organized, and plaintiffs failed to demonstrate diligent efforts to obtain counsel on their own.
brief_summary: Michael S. McLain and Janette McLain, proceeding pro se, sued Sedgwick County Sheriff's Office and other defendants asserting civil rights claims including ADA and Fair Housing Act violations, and filed a motion seeking appointed counsel and disability accommodations (extended time, clear instructions, communication support) for Michael McLain's PTSD, TBI, and cognitive impairments. The court denied the motion for appointed counsel, finding plaintiffs' filings were articulate and organized despite their claimed disabilities, and declined to issue prospective accommodations, indicating it would address accommodation requests on an as-needed basis.

case_name: Joy Lucretia Clark v. PNC Bank
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case concerns denial of a business trust account application at a bank.
key_holding: The FHA claim was dismissed with prejudice because the statute does not apply to business bank account applications—the FHA applies only to dwellings, and Clark alleged no facts connecting her claim to housing discrimination.
brief_summary: Joy Lucretia Clark sued PNC Bank for denying her business trust account application, invoking the Fair Housing Act, Consumer Financial Protection Act, and Equal Credit Opportunity Act. The court dismissed her complaint with prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), finding the FHA inapplicable to banking transactions with no connection to dwellings, the CFP Act provides no private right of action, and the ECOA claim lacked any factual allegations of prohibited discrimination.

case_name: White Lake Caddis, LLC v. Charter Township of White Lake
accommodation_description: Developer seeks to place a three-quarter transitional living facility for individuals recovering from addiction without being required to comply with all ordinances applicable to adult foster care congregate facilities.
key_holding: The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the breach of contract claim because it did not relate to the federal discrimination claims and would substantially expand the scope of litigation, and therefore denied the preliminary injunction motion without prejudice.
brief_summary: White Lake Caddis, LLC sued Charter Township of White Lake alleging discriminatory zoning practices that prohibited development of a three-quarter transitional living facility for individuals in recovery from addiction. The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the plaintiff's breach of contract claim and denied without prejudice the motion for preliminary injunction on that state law claim, which the court found unrelated to the federal Fair Housing Act and ADA claims that remain pending.

case_name: Mills Pond Grp., LLC v. Town of Smithtown
accommodation_description: Developer sought special exception approval to build an assisted living facility in a residentially-zoned district, asserting that denial of such approval violates the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that the developer's Fair Housing Act claims were unripe because the developer failed to apply for a variance with the Zoning Board of Appeals before seeking federal judicial review, and failed to demonstrate that such an application would be futile.
brief_summary: Mills Pond Group LLC, a real estate developer, and putative future residents of a planned assisted living facility sued the Town of Smithtown after the Town passed an ordinance amendment preventing assisted living facilities in residential zones and denied the developer's special exception application without prejudice. The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding the claims were unripe because the developer failed to apply for a variance with the Zoning Board of Appeals and did not demonstrate that such an application would be futile.

case_name: Danell R. Scoggins v. Falcon Court and Turning Point of Central California
citation: No reporter citation (E.D. Cal. Case No. 1:24-cv-00188-KES-SKO)
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff alleged some form of retaliation by housing providers, but failed to identify protected activity or adverse action with sufficient specificity
key_holding: The second amended complaint was dismissed because plaintiff failed to plead facts sufficient to state a retaliation claim under the Fair Housing Act, specifically failing to identify any protected activity in which she engaged and any sufficiently adverse action taken by defendants.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Danell Scoggins sued Falcon Court and Turning Point of Central California alleging retaliation under the Fair Housing Act. The district court adopted the magistrate judge's findings and recommendations and dismissed the case without leave to amend because the second amended complaint failed to plead facts sufficient to state a retaliation claim under the FHA, as plaintiff did not identify protected activity or sufficiently adverse actions by defendants.

source_file: 10615091_2025_Affinity Recovery Center LLC v. Town Commissioners of Sudlersville_ca4
case_name: Affinity Recovery Center LLC v. Town Commissioners of Sudlersville
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation requested is not described in this brief appellate opinion; however, given the plaintiff's identity as a recovery center LLC suing a municipality under the FHA and ADA, the accommodation likely involved a request for a zoning exception, variance, or permit to operate a substance use recovery/sober living facility within the Town of Sudlersville.
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's order granting the Town Commissioners of Sudlersville's motion to dismiss or, in the alternative, for summary judgment on Affinity Recovery Center LLC's claims under Title II of the ADA and the Fair Housing Act, finding no reversible error.
brief_summary: Affinity Recovery Center LLC, a substance use recovery center operator, sued the Town Commissioners of Sudlersville asserting claims under Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Fair Housing Act. The district court granted defendant's motion to dismiss or, in the alternative, for summary judgment. The Fourth Circuit affirmed without oral argument, finding no reversible error in the district court's ruling.

case_name: Arocho v. Chicopee Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; the case concerns the housing authority's alleged failure to protect tenants from a violent neighbor based on race/national origin discrimination.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA claims because they failed to plead facts showing they were personally subjected to discriminatory conduct, failed to identify similarly situated comparators treated differently based on race, and because the claims were barred by the FHA's two-year statute of limitations.
brief_summary: Relatives and visitors of a murder victim sued the Chicopee Housing Authority and its executive director, claiming the housing authority violated the FHA by failing to evict a violent tenant with a known criminal history while making derogatory comments about Hispanic residents, thereby discriminating based on race and national origin. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the visitor plaintiffs lacked standing under the FHA, the tenant plaintiffs failed to plead a plausible disparate treatment claim, and all FHA claims were time-barred.

case_name: Amanda Craven v. Karyn Knaak and Dane County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested participation in a HUD homeownership program and an 'exception to payment standard grants' as reasonable accommodations for her disability, and requested office space as a reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim because plaintiff did not identify what her disability is, what specific actions each defendant took, or how those actions constituted discrimination, though the court assumed her requests to participate in a homeownership program and for office space as reasonable accommodations related to her disability.
brief_summary: Amanda Craven, a disabled resident of Dane County with a Section 8 housing choice voucher, sued Dane County Housing Authority alleging disability discrimination for denying her request to participate in a HUD homeownership program and interfering with her ability to use her voucher. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a plausible claim because Craven did not identify what her disability is, what specific acts each defendant committed, or how those acts constituted discrimination, though the court granted her leave to amend.

case_name: Donna Calloway v. Kenyon Morgan, as agent of Prime Time Housing, LLC, and individually, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; case involves alleged housing discrimination based on sex and religion, discriminatory statements, and retaliation.
key_holding: The court rejected defendants' attempt to invoke FHA exemptions as a jurisdictional challenge, characterizing the exemptions as affirmative defenses rather than matters affecting subject matter jurisdiction, and found the court has jurisdiction over claims under §§ 3604(c) and 3617 which are not subject to the exemptions at § 3603(b).
brief_summary: Donna Calloway sued Kenyon Morgan and Prime Time Housing, LLC alleging Fair Housing Act violations including sex discrimination, religious discrimination, discriminatory statements, and retaliation in connection with a home purchase arrangement. Defendants moved to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, arguing the FHA's exemptions under § 3603(b) applied. The court denied the motion, holding that FHA exemptions are affirmative defenses rather than jurisdictional defects and that the court has jurisdiction over claims under §§ 3604(c) and 3617, which are not subject to the exemptions.

case_name: Tekeva Shaw v. Habitat for Humanity, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request identified; plaintiff alleged discrimination, breach of contract, privacy violations, and construction defects related to home purchase.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissal with prejudice of Shaw's Fair Housing Act claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3605 because Shaw failed to plead membership in any protected class, failed to plead she met all relevant qualifications, and failed to plead defendants continued similar transactions with others of similar qualifications.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Tekeva Shaw filed suit against Habitat for Humanity, Regions Bank, and various other corporate defendants alleging breach of contract, privacy violations, construction defects, and Fair Housing Act claims stemming from her home purchase. The court recommended dismissing Shaw's federal claims with prejudice for failure to state a claim upon which relief may be granted, finding she failed to plead any protected class membership required under § 3605.

case_name: Sehra Waheed v. Molly Wasow Park, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reasonable accommodation in eviction proceedings due to disability-related medical injuries affecting her ability to work and financial hardship.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim as beyond the scope of the leave to amend granted, without substantive analysis of the accommodation request.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sehra Waheed sued her former landlord Trinity Bui and various City of New York officials and agencies, asserting claims including Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation based on her alleged disability affecting her ability to work and pay rent during eviction proceedings. The court dismissed this FHA claim as beyond the scope of the limited leave to amend granted, and dismissed the entire action for failure to state a claim and lack of standing.

brief_summary: Shenoa Gilbert, a Section 8 voucher holder with a back injury and Stage 3 kidney disease, sued her property management company alleging violations of the Fair Housing Amendments Act and Rehabilitation Act for denying her accommodation requests for a first-floor unit and exemption from pesticide use. The Court dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, finding plaintiff failed to sufficiently plead the elements of her reasonable accommodation and retaliation claims.

case_name: Valentine v. Granville Realty, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Valentine, a disabled U.S. Army veteran, requested emergency injunctive relief to halt eviction proceedings, which he alleges were initiated in retaliation for his disability-related ESA and protected activity.

brief_summary: Plaintiffs Valentine and Hubbard, including a disabled U.S. Army veteran with an ESA, moved for a temporary restraining order to halt eviction proceedings at their Fresno residence, alleging disability discrimination, retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, and Civil RICO violations. brief_summary: Plaintiffs KC and MC, residents of the Monarch Condominium since 2000, sued the Condo Defendants and a retained psychiatrist after their August 2021 request for a service dog (emotional support animal) was denied in September 2021 following an independent psychiatric evaluation. The court denied Defendant Dr. First's motion for a stay of discovery pending his motion to dismiss, ruling based on its assessment of the merits of the pending motions that discovery should proceed.

case_name: TL Harvey v. Maxwell & Morgan P.C., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff filed Fair Housing Act claims against a homeowners association and related defendants, but the specific accommodation requested is not detailed in this attorneys' fees order.
key_holding: Defendants' motion for attorneys' fees was denied because plaintiff's FHA claims were not frivolous and defendants failed to identify which fees were incurred exclusively in defending non-frivolous federal claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff TL Harvey sued a law firm, property management company, and homeowners association alleging multiple federal and state claims including Fair Housing Act violations and racial discrimination under 42 U.S.C. § 1981. This order addresses only defendants' motion for attorneys' fees, denying the motion because plaintiff's federal claims were not frivolous under the demanding federal standard and defendants failed to segregate recoverable from non-recoverable fees.

case_name: Smith v. ResiPro, LLC
subsidy_program: Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher; Choose to Own Homeownership Program
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; case centers on alleged discriminatory housing practices based on race and disability in connection with home purchase
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim (Count II) as time-barred under the two-year limitations period, finding no basis to apply the continuing violations doctrine to extend the deadline, and dismissed the ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims (Count III) on the same timeliness grounds.
brief_summary: Ronetta Smith, individually and as guardian for two disabled adults, sued ResiPro LLC and ResiCap LP alleging they performed deficient construction work on her home purchased through the CHA Choose to Own program in Chicago's south side, with claims including FHA discrimination, ADA, and state law torts. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act claims as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations, finding no continuing violation exception applied, and dismissed most state law claims for factual insufficiency or failure to state a claim.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a homeless individual, does not request a disability accommodation but rather challenges the City's housing system for allegedly treating homeless U.S. citizens differently from migrants/asylum seekers, asserting this violates the FHA.

brief_summary: Jason Calderon, a pro se plaintiff, sued the City of New York alleging that the City's shelter system violated equal protection and the Fair Housing Act by providing hotels to migrants and asylum seekers while forcing homeless U.S. citizens to use the general shelter system. case_name: Dawn N. Earle v. Manchester Village Owners Association Inc, et al.

brief_summary: Dawn N. brief_summary: Sarah Brockway sued her former landlord (Arlene L. Petschke Trust No. 102) alleging the landlord violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to accommodate her Ehlers-Danlos syndrome mobility disability. The court denied Defendants' motion for summary judgment, holding that a reasonable jury could find the October 12 Letter provided adequate notice of her disability and accommodation needs for handicap parking, handrails, and ramps, distinguishing Watters because Plaintiff requested disability-specific modifications that a non-disabled tenant would not typically request and Defendants completely ignored the request.

key_holding: Plaintiff's fourth amended complaint fails to state any colorable claim because she did not specifically allege what her disability is, how her requested accommodation was reasonable, what adverse actions were taken against her, or how any alleged denial was causally connected to her protected activity.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Shirley M. key_holding: The Court stayed all open motions pending resolution of Defendants' motion to dismiss based on improper service, lack of personal jurisdiction, and lack of subject matter jurisdiction, directing Defendants to file their reply brief by July 18, 2025.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sehra Waheed filed suit against a law firm, individual attorneys, an asset management LLC, and other individuals alleging legal malpractice, tortious interference, constitutional violations, Title VII, Fair Housing Act, ADA, and ECOA claims. case_name: Oliver A. Lee v. HUD Housing Attorney
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; plaintiff alleges misuse of government housing funds, racketeering, and suppression of Black community in Milwaukee
key_holding: The complaint failed to state a claim because it did not identify who violated the plaintiff's rights, what actions each defendant took, when the violations occurred, or how the plaintiff personally suffered harm, leaving the court unable to determine jurisdiction or standing.
brief_summary: Oliver A. Lee sued HUD Housing Attorney, Milwaukee Housing Attorney, Milwaukee Representative Willie Heinz, Smart Reality Management, MPI Property Management, Rental Assistance Program Community Advocate, and Zillow Reality alleging they misused federal housing funds, committed racketeering, and discriminated against the Black community in Milwaukee in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding the allegations too vague and conclusory to establish standing or provide defendants fair notice of the claims against them, but granted Lee leave to amend.

Cal. court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claims because the complaint contained no factual allegations to support a claim of discrimination based on sex or any other protected class, and dismissed the remaining federal claims without prejudice.

brief_summary: Four individual plaintiffs sued Cepco Management Services and Lantana Crossing HOA asserting Fair Housing Act, civil rights, and state law claims related to allegedly discriminatory HOA rule enforcement. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to prosecute, finding plaintiffs engaged in dilatory conduct including failing to comply with court orders, repeated cancellation of depositions, and causing counsel withdrawal, warranting dismissal with prejudice.

key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint because he failed to allege facts showing he is disabled, that any defendant discriminated against him based on disability in a housing matter, or that any defendant violated his constitutional rights
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Bobby Felicie sued various government officials including Assistant Inspector General Octavia Hill, state court judges, and HRA officials alleging constitutional violations, disability discrimination, and violations of the ADA, FHA, HIPAA, Privacy Act, CFAA, and ECPA. source_file: 10634417_2025_Group Home on Gibson Island, LLC v. Gibson Island Corporation_ca4
case_name: Group Home on Gibson Island, LLC v. Gibson Island Corporation
accommodation_description: Request for waiver of business-purpose covenant to operate assisted living group home for seniors with disabilities on Gibson Island
key_holding: The court held that the accommodation was 'necessary' because without the covenant waiver, disabled persons could not live on Gibson Island, but reversed summary judgment because genuine disputes existed as to whether the defendant's four conditions rendered the accommodation 'unreasonable' or were pretextual.
brief_summary: Craig Lussi, through two LLCs, sued Gibson Island Corporation (a homeowners association) alleging the HOA violated the FHA by refusing to waive its business-purpose covenant as a reasonable accommodation for an assisted living group home for seniors with disabilities, and by retaliating and discriminating against him for advocating FHA-protected housing rights. The Fourth Circuit vacated summary judgment for the Corporation, holding that Lussi's accommodation request was necessary to afford disabled persons equal housing opportunity on Gibson Island, and that genuine disputes of material fact existed as to whether the HOA's four conditions (septic monitoring, arbitration, escrow, and guarantor requirements) rendered the accommodation unreasonable or were pretextual for discrimination and retaliation.

brief_summary: Anna White Ferraraccio sued New Peoples Bank alleging discrimination in her attempts to obtain financing. case_name: Dawn Thompson v. Evolve Bank & Trust and PennyMac Loan Services, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permanent loan modifications from PennyMac and asked both defendants to consider waiting and modifying the mortgage terms while her Social Security disability application was pending following a December 2016 car accident that she alleged rendered her unable to return to work.
key_holding: The court granted both defendants' motions to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), dismissing PennyMac because it had no involvement in the mortgage origination and no actual foreclosure was initiated, and dismissing Evolve because origination-related claims were time-barred and remaining post-assignment claims failed to state a plausible claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Dawn Thompson sued original mortgagee Evolve Bank & Trust and successor mortgagee PennyMac Loan Services alleging discriminatory mortgage origination, FHA underwriting standard violations, ADA disability discrimination in loan modifications, CARES Act violations, and various state law claims arising from her 2015 residential mortgage on a Worcester, Massachusetts property. The court granted PennyMac's motion to dismiss because PennyMac was not involved in origination and no actual foreclosure proceedings were ever initiated (plaintiff sold the home voluntarily). The court granted Evolve's motion to dismiss because the origination claims were barred by the applicable statute of limitations (the complained-of conduct occurred more than seven years before suit was filed) and the remaining post-assignment claims failed because Evolve had no involvement after assigning the mortgage to PennyMac in January 2019.

source_file: 10634783_2025_McCready v. Unity Sober Living Homes, LLC_paed
case_name: John McCready v. Unity Sober Living Homes, LLC, RE/MAX Achievers
accommodation_description: Disabled residents receiving SSDI sought to pay rent on the same weekly schedule as non-disabled residents rather than being required to pay monthly under Unity's facially discriminatory rent policy.
key_holding: Unity's written rent policy violated the Fair Housing Act as a matter of law because it facially discriminated against disabled residents receiving SSDI by requiring them to pay rent monthly while non-disabled residents could pay weekly, and Unity failed to rebut this discriminatory intent with evidence beyond self-serving, uncorroborated testimony.
brief_summary: John McCready, a recovering drug addict with depression receiving SSDI benefits, sued Unity Sober Living Homes and its property manager Re/Max Achievers alleging Unity's rent policy that required only SSDI recipients to pay monthly while non-disabled residents paid weekly violated the Fair Housing Act. The court granted partial summary judgment to McCready, holding Unity's written policy facially discriminated against disabled individuals in violation of § 3604(f)(2), and also found Unity liable for wrongful eviction and failure to return security under Pennsylvania law, while dismissing McCready's intentional infliction of emotional distress claim.

case_name: Joshua Derby, Alyssia Warren, and Z.D., a minor v. Pleasant Beach Mobile Home Resort, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs vaguely referenced 'a request for accommodation under the ADA' in their amended complaint but provided no specific facts identifying any disability, what accommodation was requested, or how the Fair Housing Act applied; the court found these references entirely conclusory and insufficient to state a claim.
key_holding: The court dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice because plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts to support any of their four federal claims, including a § 3617 Fair Housing Act interference/retaliation claim based on alleged retaliatory eviction, which consisted only of legal conclusions unsupported by factual allegations.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Joshua Derby, Alyssia Warren, and minor Z.D. sued their mobile home park operator for alleged threatened eviction, asserting claims under Title II of the ADA, the Fair Housing Act (§ 3617), 42 U.S.C. § 1982, and the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause. The court granted plaintiffs' motion for reconsideration to allow review of their amended complaint, but dismissed all four counts with prejudice: the ADA Title II claim failed because the defendant is a private entity; the § 3617 FHA claim failed for lack of factual allegations; the § 1982 claim failed for absence of any racial discrimination allegation; and the due process claim failed because the defendant is a private actor. The court also invoked Younger abstention and the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to bar any federal interference with ongoing or concluded state eviction proceedings.

case_name: Connolly v. Lanham
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; the case concerns alleged racial discrimination in a home appraisal valuation.
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to establish pretext because although the appraiser made some inconsistent adjustments, Defendants' expert testimony demonstrated the appraisal methodology complied with professional standards, and no genuine issue of material fact existed showing the valuation result was motivated by racial discrimination rather than legitimate appraisal considerations.
brief_summary: Black homeowners sued an appraiser and his company alleging racial discrimination after their home was appraised at $472,000, then re-appraised at $750,000 by a different appraiser after removing evidence of Black occupancy. The court granted summary judgment to defendants on all discrimination claims, finding plaintiffs failed to establish pretext because defendants' expert testimony showed the appraisal methodology complied with professional standards and the challenged adjustments did not demonstrate discriminatory intent.

case_name: Stephanie Haywood v. Warner Robins Housing Authority, Africa Porter, Reginald Early, Robert Gidney, Andre Washington, Kesha Bray, Betty Ann Faulks, and John Does 1-10
accommodation_description: No specific disability-related accommodation was requested. Plaintiff's FHA claims arise from alleged retaliation by housing authority staff for her protected activities, including requesting repairs, reporting code violations, and filing grievance complaints.
key_holding: The court granted Plaintiff's motion to proceed in forma pauperis but found her complaint to be an impermissible shotgun pleading, ordering her to file a recast complaint within 21 days or face dismissal without prejudice.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Stephanie Haywood, a public housing tenant at Warner Robins Housing Authority, sued the housing authority and several of its employees alleging that Defendants retaliated against her for engaging in protected activities such as requesting repairs, reporting code violations, and filing complaints, subjecting her to repeated lease termination threats, fabricated charges, unlawful entry, and a baseless 'probation' status. The complaint also raised claims under the Fair Housing Act, VAWA, the Georgia Open Records Act, and the Fourteenth Amendment, along with various state tort claims. The court granted IFP status but dismissed John Does 1-10 sua sponte under the fictitious party pleading rule and found the complaint to be a shotgun pleading that failed to specify which claims were asserted against which defendants, directing Plaintiff to file a recast, conforming complaint within 21 days.

source_file: 10638097_2025_National Fair Housing Alliance v. Bank of America, National Association_mdd
case_name: National Fair Housing Alliance, et al. v. Bank of America, N.A., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; this is a systemic disparate impact challenge to Bank of America's maintenance and marketing of real estate owned (REO) properties in majority-minority neighborhoods.
key_holding: Organizational plaintiffs lack Article III standing under the Supreme Court's Hippocratic Medicine framework, and on the merits, defendants are entitled to summary judgment because plaintiffs failed to propose equally effective alternatives to the challenged policies under step three of the disparate impact framework.
brief_summary: A coalition of fair housing organizations and three individual homeowners sued Bank of America and its property servicer alleging that their maintenance and marketing of bank-owned foreclosure properties in minority neighborhoods violated the Fair Housing Act's disparate impact and disparate treatment provisions. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of standing and summary judgment on the merits, finding organizational plaintiffs failed to establish concrete injury after Hippocratic Medicine and that plaintiffs' proposed alternatives to defendants' policies were not equally effective.

case_name: Valentine v. Granville Realty, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Valentine had been prescribed an emotional support animal (ESA) by the Department of Veterans Affairs on July 9, 2019, as medically necessary to mitigate his disabilities; after plaintiffs informed defendants on April 9, 2025 that the ESA had been diagnosed with terminal kidney failure, defendants issued a notice of sale initiating eviction proceedings fourteen days later, which plaintiffs alleged constituted denial of the ESA accommodation and retaliation in violation of the FHA.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommended denying pro se plaintiffs' motion for a temporary restraining order and/or preliminary injunction because plaintiffs failed to comply with Rule 65(b) and Local Rule 231's procedural requirements and failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits or irreparable harm on their FHA, RICO, and state law claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Michael Valentine and Amanda Hubbard, tenants at 1371 N. Roosevelt Avenue in Fresno, California, sought emergency injunctive relief against their landlord and related entities, alleging disability discrimination, retaliation, and RICO violations. Plaintiffs alleged that defendants issued a notice of sale initiating eviction proceedings just fourteen days after being informed that Valentine's VA-prescribed emotional support animal had been diagnosed with terminal kidney failure, which plaintiffs contended demonstrated retaliatory intent and disability-based discrimination under the FHA. The magistrate judge recommended denying the TRO and preliminary injunction on both procedural grounds (failure to notify defendants or justify the omission, non-compliance with Local Rule 231) and on the merits (no likelihood of success, no showing of imminent irreparable harm given plaintiffs' own ten-week delay in seeking relief), and additionally ordered docket corrections to conform to the operative first amended complaint.

case_name: Fussell v. Sun Vista RV Resort LLC

race_if_mentioned: Not explicitly identified; complaint alleged racial discrimination and plaintiff Derhem (a transgender individual) was referred to with a racial slur ('monkey'), but plaintiff's specific race is not stated in the text
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested; the case involved claims of disparate treatment in housing based on race and transgender/gender identity, including alleged discriminatory delays in a condominium unit purchase and hostile post-acquisition conduct such as repeated gender-identity comments, confronting Derhem with a pre-transition photo, and racial slurs.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part defendant Brumsted's motion for attorneys' fees, awarding fees for the Florida Condominium Act claims (Counts II, III, V) but denying fees for the Fair Housing Act claim (Count I) because plaintiff's discrimination claim, though unsuccessful on the merits, was not frivolous given that plaintiff established a prima facie case and presented some evidentiary support.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Kanayo Derhem (a transgender individual) and Mojtaba Koosej brought housing discrimination claims based on race and gender identity against Bay House Miami Condominium Association and others, including defendant Charles Brumsted Jr., resulting in a final judgment for defendants after summary judgment. In this post-judgment attorneys' fees order, the magistrate judge found Brumsted entitled to fees under Florida's Condominium Act (Counts II, III, V) because he was the clear prevailing party on those claims, but denied fees on the FHA discrimination claim (Count I) because plaintiff established a prima facie case and presented supporting evidence—including affidavits and anti-transgender Facebook posts—sufficient to render the claim non-frivolous even though it ultimately failed.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Fair Hous. Ctr. of Greater Palm Beaches, Inc. v. Shutters Condo. Ass'n, Inc., No. 08-81566-CIV, 2011 WL 13172602 (S.D. Fla. Feb. 9, 2011)
Bonner v. Mobile Energy Servs. Co., 246 F.3d 1303 (11th Cir. 2001)
