source_file: 10644815_2025_Derhem v. Bay House Miami Condominium Association_flsd
case_name: Kanayo Derhem et al. v. Bay House Miami Condominium Association et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested; the case involved direct housing discrimination claims based on race and gender/transgender identity, including alleged hostile housing environment, wrongful fines, bans from common areas, and interference with lease approval processes.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motion for attorneys' fees and costs, holding that defendants are not entitled to fees on the FHA claim (Count I) because they failed to show it was frivolous, but are entitled to fees as prevailing party under Florida's Condominium Act (Chapter 718) for Counts II–IV, and are entitled to costs on all five claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Kanayo Derhem and Mojtaba Koosej, a Black transgender woman and her co-plaintiff, sued a Miami condominium association and individual defendants alleging racial and gender-based housing discrimination under the FHA and violations of Florida's Condominium Act (Chapter 718), among other claims. Defendants obtained final judgment in their favor via a combination of dismissal and summary judgment, and subsequently moved for attorneys' fees and costs. The court granted the motion in part, awarding fees for the Florida condominium law claims (Counts II–IV) under the mandatory fee-shifting provision of § 718.303, denying fees for the FHA claim because defendants failed to demonstrate it was frivolous or groundless, denying fees for the negligence claim for lack of statutory or contractual basis, and awarding costs to defendants on all five claims.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Rothenberg v. Sec. Mgmt. Co., 677 F.2d 64 (11th Cir. 1982)
Hamilton v. Sheridan Healthcorp, Inc., 700 F. App'x 883 (11th Cir. 2017)

case_name: Jacqueline Peters v. Cafton Towers Owners Corp.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendant stay her eviction until she completes medical treatment as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The court denied the TRO because plaintiff failed to show likelihood of success on her reasonable accommodation claims, as her requested accommodations (environmental screening, washer/dryer, restrictions on other residents, and eviction stay) were not shown to be reasonable without undue burden, and the two-month delay in responding did not constitute a constructive denial absent evidence of bad faith.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jacqueline Peters sued Cafton Towers Owners Corp. alleging the cooperative building violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to provide reasonable accommodations for her disability and by terminating her lease in retaliation for requesting accommodations. The court denied Peters' motion for a temporary restraining order, finding she failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits because she did not show her requested accommodations were reasonable without undue burden and did not adequately plead pretext for the eviction.
key_cases_cited: Austin v. Town of Farmington, 826 F.3d 622 (2d Cir. 2016)
Logan v. Matveevskii, 57 F. Supp. 3d 234 (S.D.N.Y. 2014)
Basank v. Decker, 449 F. Supp. 3d 205 (S.D.N.Y. 2020)
Shang Hai Zhenglang Tech. Co. v. Mengku Tech. Co., 2020 WL 6826257 (E.D.N.Y. 2020)

source_file: 10645226_2025_(PS) Roberts v. Sacramento Housing _ Redevelopment Agency_caed
case_name: Sydney Brooke Roberts and David Tyrone Samuel v. Sacramento Housing & Redevelopment Agency
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested an extra bedroom added to their Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher as a reasonable accommodation for disabilities including ADHD, autism, PTSD, and depression.
key_holding: The motion to compel discovery was denied because plaintiffs failed to identify specific discovery responses that were wrongfully withheld, instead making broad challenges to defendants' overall discovery conduct, and defendants had made substantial document productions exceeding 10,000 pages.
brief_summary: Two disabled plaintiffs with two children sued Sacramento Housing and Redevelopment Agency alleging disability discrimination and failure to accommodate under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act, stemming from the denial of their request to add an extra bedroom to their Section 8 voucher. The court denied plaintiffs' motion to compel discovery, finding they failed to identify specific responses that were wrongfully withheld and that defendants had made substantial document productions.

case_name: Mary Anne Sause v. Mid America Management, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was formally requested; plaintiff, who alleged she is elderly and disabled, sought renewal and recertification of her government-subsidized apartment lease and alleged defendants failed to follow proper eviction procedures before locking her out.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's second amended complaint without prejudice for failure to comply with Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a) because she listed statutes without connecting them to specific factual allegations or identifying which defendant took which actions.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mary Anne Sause sued the owners, operators, and managers of Cedar Run Apartments, alleging she was locked out of her government-subsidized apartment and rendered homeless. Her second amended complaint listed a lengthy array of federal and state statutes—including the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and VAWA—but failed to connect those statutes to specific factual allegations or identify which defendant committed which acts. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss without prejudice, holding the complaint did not satisfy Rule 8(a)'s pleading requirements despite multiple opportunities to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Lillian Gonzalez v. Cheryl Mongo, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants failed to keep premises safe during her tenancy, causing safety risk and emotional distress to herself and her minor child, in violation of the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to articulate specific tortious conduct attributable to any defendant and failed to ascribe any wrongful conduct to named defendants.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Lillian Gonzalez sued multiple defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations, claiming defendants failed to keep Southlawn Palm Apartments safe during her tenancy, resulting in stalking and assault. The court granted all pending motions to dismiss, finding Gonzalez failed to state a plausible claim because she did not articulate specific tortious conduct attributable to any named defendant or provide facts putting defendants on notice of the claims against them.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Anderson v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev.

case_name: K.F., a Minor, by and through His Legal Guardian Sandra Fernandez v. Hines Corporation, et al.
accommodation_description: Specific accommodation request not identifiable from the complaint; the case concerns unsafe housing conditions and 2024 eviction but no specific accommodation is described.
key_holding: The court denied pending motions without prejudice, abstaining from substantive review under Younger and Rooker-Feldman doctrines due to parallel state court proceedings, and ordered plaintiff to file an amended complaint or pay filing fees.
brief_summary: Sandra Fernandez, proceeding pro se on behalf of her minor son K.F., filed a 79-page complaint against Hines Corporation and other defendants alleging unsafe housing conditions and 2024 eviction, invoking the FHA, ADA, and civil rights statutes. The court denied pending motions without prejudice, abstaining under Younger and Rooker-Feldman doctrines from interfering with state court proceedings, and ordered plaintiff to either pay the filing fee or file a fee application and submit an amended complaint by August 29, 2025.

case_name: Allen Feingold v. Erie Insurance Exchange
accommodation_description: No housing accommodation was requested; plaintiff merely invoked the Fair Housing Act as a purported basis for federal jurisdiction in an automobile insurance dispute.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's third amended complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding plaintiff failed to establish diversity jurisdiction (by not pleading Erie Insurance's citizenship) and failed to plead any valid federal claim, including a Fair Housing Act claim which the court found insufficient because plaintiff did not allege Erie is his landlord or that Erie provides housing covered by the statute.
brief_summary: Allen Feingold sued Erie Insurance Exchange asserting claims arising from an alleged 2018 assignment of his former client's rights to uninsured/underinsured motorist claims from automobile accidents; he invoked the Fair Housing Act and other federal statutes to establish federal question jurisdiction. The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding Feingold failed to plead Erie's citizenship for diversity jurisdiction and failed to state any valid federal claim, including an insufficient Fair Housing Act claim because he did not allege Erie is a landlord or housing provider.

case_name: Jasmine Hill v. Philadelphia Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff seeks damages and injunctive relief for alleged race discrimination (failure to maintain lead-safe housing) and retaliation for complaining about housing conditions.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a FHA or Title VI claim because plaintiff's allegations of race discrimination are conclusory and provide no factual basis to infer discriminatory intent, and plaintiff's retaliation claim fails because her complaints concerned housing conditions rather than prohibited discrimination.
brief_summary: Jasmine Hill, an African-American Section 8 voucher holder, sued the Philadelphia Housing Authority and HUD alleging she was discriminated against based on race and retaliated against for complaining about lead paint exposure in her subsidized unit. The Court dismissed her complaint for failure to state plausible claims, finding her race discrimination allegations conclusory and her retaliation claim deficient because her complaints concerned housing conditions rather than prohibited discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Mt. Holly Gardens Citizens in Action, Inc. v. Twp. of Mount Holly, 658 F.3d 375 (3d Cir. 2011)
White v. Barbe, 767 F. App'x 332 (3d Cir. 2019)

case_name: Sharon Lee, et al. v. Twin Hawks Airpark LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Not determinable from the case text; the order addresses only service-of-process procedure and does not describe the underlying Fair Housing Act claim or any accommodation requested.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motions for an extension of time to complete service of process and for alternative service by mail to defendants' addresses and their known attorney, finding that unique circumstances including a gated rural property, a frequently absent defendant, and the risk of statute-of-limitations bar on the Fair Housing Act claim constituted good cause or excusable neglect.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Sharon Lee and Tommy Wessel filed a Fair Housing Act complaint against Twin Hawks Airpark LLC and Harold Duane Lambeth in February 2025 but were unable to complete traditional service of process due to a gated rural property accessible only by keypad code and a defendant who frequently traveled by private plane, leaving his home vacant. The court authorized alternative service by First Class Mail to defendants' home and work addresses and by certified mail to attorney Craig Cline, who had represented Twin Hawks in ongoing related litigation and had actual or near-certain notice of the suit. The court also extended the service deadline to September 3, 2025, noting that dismissal would bar plaintiffs' FHA claims under the statute of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Bank of N.Y. Mellon v. Dodev, 433 P.3d 549 (Ariz. Ct. App. 2018)
Lemoge v. United States, 587 F.3d 1188 (9th Cir. 2009)

case_name: Cindy Adams v. Consuelleo Anderson, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request is identified in the opinion; the complaint alleges general racial discrimination and various tort claims against HUD.
key_holding: The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1) because plaintiff failed to establish subject matter jurisdiction over her claims against HUD, as sovereign immunity bars suits against federal agencies absent an express waiver, and plaintiff did not identify any applicable waiver for her discrimination, tort, or other claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Cindy Adams, who alleges she lived in HUD-owned public housing, sued HUD along with nineteen other defendants asserting racial discrimination, premise liability, civil rights, and tort claims. The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding that sovereign immunity bars plaintiff's claims against HUD because she failed to identify any statutory waiver of sovereign immunity applicable to her claims for money damages, including under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Kelly v. Wilson, 426 F. App'x 629 (10th Cir. 2011)
Unimex, Inc. v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urb. Dev., 594 F.2d 1060 (5th Cir. 1979)
Ramming v. United States, 281 F.3d 158 (5th Cir. 2001)
Moore v. Bryant, 853 F.3d 245 (5th Cir. 2017)

case_name: Gregory Austin Gadson v. Riverbay Corporation
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; plaintiff pro se complaint was incomprehensible and failed to allege any specific accommodation request
key_holding: The court dismissed the action for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to allege facts demonstrating a federal law claim, and even if FHA retaliation claims were analyzed, plaintiff failed to allege facts showing FHA-protected activity, defendant's awareness, adverse action, and causal connection.
brief_summary: Gregory Austin Gadson, proceeding pro se, sued Riverbay Corporation in federal court seeking injunctive and declaratory relief related to an eviction proceeding in Housing Court, invoking the FHA and other federal statutes. The court dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding plaintiff's complaint alleged no facts demonstrating a federal law claim, and granted plaintiff 30 days leave to amend.

case_name: Dominic Son v. Oakmont Properties-Azure, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges disability discrimination related to his adjustment disorder but does not specify what accommodation was requested or needed.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA disability claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing his adjustment disorder substantially limited major life activities or explaining what accommodation he needed and was refused.
brief_summary: Dominic Son, a Vietnamese-American tenant at Azure Apartments in Sparks, Nevada, sued Oakmont Properties, FPI Management, and the Housing Authority of the City of Reno alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on race and disability discrimination, along with state law claims. The court dismissed the federal claims for failure to state a claim, finding the complaint contained only conclusory allegations of racial discrimination without supporting facts and failed to adequately plead the disability accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Giebeler v. M & B Assocs.

source_file: 10648578_2025_(PS) Holmstrand v. Mercy Housing of California_caed
case_name: Holmstrand v. Mercy Housing of California
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint is too vague to identify a specific accommodation request; plaintiff alleges housing discrimination related to an eviction and prior assault by another resident.
key_holding: Plaintiff's complaint was dismissed for failure to state a claim because it lacked sufficient factual allegations describing the specific actions or omissions by defendants and failed to comply with Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2) pleading requirements.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sue Ellen Holmstrand sued Mercy Housing entities alleging Fair Housing Act and VAWA violations related to her eviction from a Section 202 supportive housing property in Encinitas, California, and a prior assault by another resident. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice for failure to state a claim because the complaint lacked sufficient factual detail to identify specific causes of action or explain what each defendant did to violate her rights, granting plaintiff leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Bolima Tafah v. Lake Village Townhomes et al.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested; plaintiffs sought a temporary restraining order to prevent their eviction from their residence at 1806 Long Leaf Way, Severn, Maryland, which they characterized as a retaliatory eviction taken in response to their filing of a federal lawsuit.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' emergency TRO motion to stop an eviction because (1) plaintiffs failed to comply with Rule 65(b)(1)'s procedural prerequisites, (2) plaintiffs failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits, and (3) the Anti-Injunction Act and Younger abstention doctrine bar federal courts from enjoining ongoing state court eviction proceedings, even where FHA claims are asserted; the original motion to dismiss was denied as moot following the filing of an amended complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Bolima Tafah and co-plaintiff filed a complaint and subsequently an amended complaint against their landlord, property manager, and a credit reporting company, alleging fifty federal and state law violations spanning 2021–2025, including claims related to ongoing eviction proceedings, vehicle repossession, and negative credit reporting. Plaintiffs filed an emergency TRO motion seeking to halt an eviction scheduled for August 13, 2025, arguing it was retaliatory for having filed their federal lawsuit. The court denied the TRO on procedural grounds under Rule 65(b)(1), for failure to demonstrate the Winter factors, and on jurisdictional grounds under the Anti-Injunction Act and Younger abstention doctrine, which bar federal interference with ongoing state court eviction proceedings even when FHA claims are raised.
key_cases_cited: Hoechst Diafoil Co. v. Nan Ya Plastics Corp., 174 F.3d 411 (4th Cir. 1999)

case_name: Chrysanthus v. Stedke
accommodation_description: No coherent disability accommodation request identified; complaint alleges 'terrorism' claims and social media retaliation in connection with a lease
key_holding: Plaintiff's in forma pauperis complaint was dismissed as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) because the allegations were incomprehensible, failed to meet basic pleading standards, and asserted fantastical terrorism theories unrelated to any cognizable legal claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Philip Chrysanthus filed an in forma pauperis complaint against Daven E. Stedke alleging terrorism and social media retaliation in connection with a property lease at 4610 South Dixie Highway in Lima, Ohio, invoking Title VIII of the Fair Housing Act but asserting no coherent disability-based claims. The court sua sponte dismissed the complaint as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), finding the allegations were incomprehensible and failed to state any plausible claim upon which relief could be granted.

source_file: 10649340_2025_McBride v. Housing Authority of the County of Jackson, Illinois_ilsd
case_name: Shelby McBride v. Housing Authority of the County of Jackson, Illinois
accommodation_description: McBride requested to remain in her home during repairs rather than transfer, have belongings relocated, stay with her daughters temporarily, and receive expedited repairs with regular progress reports.
key_holding: Because the original complaint contained substantial federal claims under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the Housing Authority was required to remove within thirty days of receiving the complaint; their failure to do so rendered the removal untimely, requiring remand.
brief_summary: Shelby McBride sued the Housing Authority of the County of Jackson, Illinois alleging discrimination under the Fair Housing Act after the Authority delayed repairs to her home following storm damage and ignored her written requests for reasonable accommodations. The Court granted McBride's Motion to Remand, finding the removal was untimely because the original complaint contained substantial federal claims under the FHA and 42 U.S.C. § 1983, triggering the thirty-day removal deadline long before the Authority filed its notice of removal.
key_cases_cited: Loper Bright v. Raimondo
Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Allapatthah Services, Inc.
Johnson v. Orr
Williams v. Aztar Indiana Gaming Corp.
Walker v. Trailer Transit, Inc.

case_name: Jimmy Avila v. ACACIA Network, Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Request to transfer from an apartment with mold that exacerbates tenant's chronic rhinitis and rhinosinusitis, a condition worsened by mold exposure.
key_holding: Avila's claims were properly dismissed because he failed to plead sufficient factual allegations establishing that defendants discriminated against him based on disability or that there was a causal connection between his protected activity (filing lawsuits) and the termination of his tenancy.
brief_summary: Jimmy Avila, a tenant with schizoaffective disorder living in supportive housing managed by ACACIA Network, sued ACACIA and 1212 Grant Realty for disability discrimination and retaliation under the FHA, ADA, and state laws, claiming he was denied a reasonable accommodation in the form of a transfer from a moldy apartment and was evicted in retaliation for filing lawsuits. The court granted motions to dismiss both actions, finding Avila failed to plead sufficient facts to support a causal connection between his lawsuits and tenancy termination, or to support a disability discrimination claim.

case_name: Siddharth Kode v. Joseph Pargin; Kimberly Pargin
accommodation_description: No accommodation request — case involves alleged racially motivated conspiracy to drive plaintiff out of neighborhood
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal of Kode's Fair Housing Act and other civil rights claims against the Pargins as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations, finding no actionable conduct within the limitations period to support his claims of racially motivated conspiracy and racketeering.
brief_summary: Siddharth Kode, proceeding pro se, sued his neighbors Joseph and Kimberly Pargin and others alleging a racially motivated conspiracy and racketeering enterprise to drive him out of his Williamson County, Texas neighborhood, asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act, Civil Rights Acts, Ku Klux Klan Act, and RICO. The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal of all claims against the Pargins, agreeing with the district court that the claims were time-barred under the applicable two-year statute of limitations because Kode failed to identify any actionable conduct within the relevant limitations period.

case_name: Larry Johnson v. Thomas Brenneke; Guardian Management, LLC; Guardian Real Estate Services; Uptown Tower Apartments; Lisa Simonson; Kelly Paine; et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff seeks Rule 60 relief to reopen three previously dismissed Fair Housing Act cases
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's Rule 60 motion as untimely, noting the judgment was entered in August 2022 and plaintiff offered no compelling reason for delaying nearly three years to seek reopening.
brief_summary: Larry Johnson, proceeding pro se, filed three consolidated Fair Housing Act actions that were dismissed with prejudice in August 2022; after the Ninth Circuit affirmed the judgment, Johnson filed a Rule 60 motion seeking to reopen the cases. The District Court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Findings and Recommendation and denied the motion as untimely, finding no compelling reason for the nearly three-year delay.

case_name: Larry Johnson and Michelle Hume v. Guardian Management, LLC; Lisa Simonson; Kelly Paine; et al.
accommodation_description: The underlying accommodation request is not described in this document. The order is entirely procedural, addressing only the timeliness of a Rule 60 motion for relief from judgment; no details of the original FHA accommodation or modification claims appear in the text.
key_holding: The court adopts the magistrate judge's Findings and Recommendation and denies plaintiff's Rule 60 motion seeking leave to amend or file an independent action as untimely, finding no extraordinary circumstances to justify relief from a judgment entered nearly three years prior.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Larry Johnson and Michelle Hume brought two consolidated Fair Housing Act actions that were dismissed with prejudice in September 2022, a judgment subsequently affirmed by the Ninth Circuit on appeal. Plaintiff Johnson then filed a Rule 60 motion seeking leave to amend his pleadings, claiming he was unaware until April 2025 that he had been granted leave to amend in a March 2022 order, and that health issues impaired his ability to participate in the litigation. The district court adopted the magistrate judge's Findings and Recommendation denying the motion as untimely under Rule 60(c)(1), concluding that plaintiff's health difficulties did not constitute extraordinary circumstances where he had nonetheless been able to file and vigorously litigate an appeal.
key_cases_cited: Ashford v. Steuart, 657 F.2d 1053 (9th Cir. 1981)

case_name: John L. Roseman v. 1900 Capital Trust II
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff seeks temporary restraining order to stay state court eviction order and prevent removal from his home at 24823 Cobblestone Court.
key_holding: The court denied the TRO motion because it lacked subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, which bars federal courts from reviewing state court decisions, and because plaintiff failed to comply with Rule 65(b)(1)(B)'s notice certification requirements.
brief_summary: John L. Roseman, proceeding pro se, sued 1900 Capital Trust II seeking a temporary restraining order to prevent his eviction from property in Farmington Hills, Michigan, asserting fraud, contract, and race discrimination claims under the Fair Housing Act. The court denied the TRO motion on procedural grounds (failure to certify notice to defendant) and for lack of jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, which bars federal courts from reviewing state court eviction orders.

case_name: Damia Bjurling v. Alec Johnson, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges that defendant Alec Johnson denied 'reasonable accommodations related to her disability' (autism); the complaint also references her service dog, which was allegedly injured by defendant Holder. The specific nature of the reasonable accommodation requested is not described with any particularity in the complaint.
key_holding: The court dismisses pro se plaintiff's amended complaint without prejudice and with leave to amend because it fails to plead sufficient facts showing how defendants injured plaintiff and her service dog, instead improperly relying on approximately 500 pages of attached exhibits.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Damia Bjurling filed an amended complaint under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act against a private individual (Alec Johnson), a police chief (Shelby Parker), and another individual (Calvin Earl Holder III), alleging harassment, intimidation, retaliation for asserting FHA rights, denial of reasonable accommodations related to her autism, and injury to herself and her service dog. The court dismissed the original complaint for failure to state a claim, and the amended complaint likewise failed to articulate specific facts as to each defendant's conduct, instead incorporating roughly 500 pages of exhibits. The court dismissed the amended complaint without prejudice, granting plaintiff leave to file a second amended complaint by August 25, 2025 that specifically pleads the underlying factual bases for her claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

case_name: Pamela Crawford v. Douglas M. Milner et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was denied rental of an apartment because of her race (African American); no accommodation request is involved.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA disparate treatment claim because she failed to plead facts supporting her belief that defendants rented the apartment to a non-African American tenant, stating only conclusory allegations about motivation without factual support.
brief_summary: African American plaintiff Pamela Crawford sued landlords Douglas and Michelle Milner alleging they refused to rent an apartment to her because of her race, claiming the unit was rented to a non-African American applicant after she submitted documentation. case_name: Dalila Agiza v. Bexar County, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff referenced an emotional support horse named Beautie in her amended complaint; the horse was seized during an alleged unlawful entry on May 30, 2025. No formal accommodation request or denial is described in detail—the FHA claim was included only as a conclusory allegation and was dismissed for failure to state a claim.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommends dismissal of nearly all claims—including conclusory FHA, ADA, and RICO claims—for failure to state a claim under § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii), while recommending that a new § 1983 unlawful-seizure claim against a Bexar County constable, accompanying officers, and attorney Alex Perez be allowed to proceed based on the alleged warrantless seizure of personal property, including an emotional support horse named Beautie, from Plaintiff's home on May 30, 2025.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Dalila Agiza brought § 1983 civil rights claims against Bexar County, a county judge, clerk's office staff, private attorneys, and LVNV Funding, LLC, arising from state court eviction and consumer-debt proceedings. After a show-cause order, Plaintiff amended her complaint to add claims under the ADA, FHA, and RICO, but all were dismissed as conclusory and legally deficient. The one surviving claim is a § 1983 cause of action alleging that a Bexar County Precinct 1 Constable (badge 1114), accompanying officers, and attorney Alex Perez unconstitutionally entered Plaintiff's property and seized personal items, including her emotional support horse Beautie, without legal authority.

case_name: Manuel James Gonzalez, as legal guardian of REG, a minor v. Royse Services LLC d/b/a LaVida Vacations
accommodation_description: Request to waive pet deposit fee for minor daughter's service dog trained to prevent panic attacks and destructive tantrums associated with autism
key_holding: The court granted default judgment for plaintiff, finding that Royse Services violated both the ADA and FHA by refusing to waive a pet deposit for the minor daughter's service dog, despite knowledge of her disability and the dog's necessity to mitigate her autism symptoms.
brief_summary: Manuel James Gonzalez sued Royse Services LLC on behalf of his minor daughter R.E.G., who has autism and requires a service dog, alleging the vacation rental company violated the ADA and FHA by refusing to allow the service dog unless he paid a $150 pet deposit. The court granted default judgment for plaintiff, finding Royse Services discriminated against R.E.G. based on her disability by refusing to waive its pet fee policy despite knowing of her disability and the service animal's necessity.

source_file: 10651719_2025_Joe v. Olive Branch Assisted Living LLC_azd
case_name: Hailei Joe v. Olive Branch Assisted Living LLC
accommodation_description: No formal accommodation was requested by Plaintiff; the issue arose as Defendant argued that its duty to provide a reasonable accommodation was never triggered because Plaintiff made no request. The court rejected this defense, noting that the duty to explore reasonable accommodations can arise without a formal request when the need is obvious, and analyzed whether Defendant should have explored accommodations enabling Plaintiff to remain in the facility following her HIV-positive disclosure rather than discharging her.
key_holding: The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment on FHA, AFHA, and ADA discrimination claims because a genuine issue of material fact remains as to whether Plaintiff's HIV-positive status was the but-for cause of her discharge, while granting Defendant summary judgment on Plaintiff's retaliation claims (for lack of a distinct and palpable injury), public disclosure of private facts claim (for insufficient publicity), and prayer for punitive damages.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Hailei Joe sued Olive Branch Assisted Living LLC after being discharged from its residential addiction treatment facility three days after disclosing an HIV-positive diagnosis, alleging discrimination under the FHA, AFHA, and ADA, retaliation based on Defendant's threatening emails and defamation counterclaim, and public disclosure of private facts under Arizona common law. On cross-motions for summary judgment, the court found genuine disputes of material fact as to whether HIV status was the but-for cause of Plaintiff's discharge, allowing the discrimination claims to proceed to a jury trial on the FHA and AFHA counts (with ADA injunctive relief reserved for the court). The court granted Defendant summary judgment on retaliation (Plaintiff suffered no distinct and palpable injury from the non-frivolous defamation counterclaim), public disclosure (informing a small group of residents does not satisfy the 'public at large' publicity requirement), and punitive damages (insufficient evidence of reckless indifference or evil mind).

case_name: Chapuis v. Forest Hill Group LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a wheelchair user, seeks injunctive relief to access an apartment property he alleges contains over forty inaccessibility barriers that deterred him from renting.
key_holding: An individual FHA plaintiff who visited an apartment complex, observed inaccessibility barriers, felt discriminated against, and was deterred from renting has alleged a concrete and particularized injury-in-fact sufficient for Article III standing; the Supreme Court's Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine decision on organizational standing does not apply to individual plaintiffs bringing their own civil rights claims.
brief_summary: Charles Chapuis, a wheelchair user, sued Forest Hill Group LLC alleging that an apartment property he visited in Germantown, Tennessee contained over forty inaccessibility barriers in violation of the Fair Housing Act, causing him to feel discriminated against and deterring him from renting. The court denied Forest Hill's motion to dismiss for lack of standing, holding that Chapuis sufficiently alleged a concrete and particularized injury-in-fact based on his firsthand experience of accessibility barriers at the property.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges Oregon's rent increase statute (ORS § 90.323) as having disparate impact on disabled individuals on fixed incomes by allowing rent increases that outpace Social Security COLA adjustments.
key_holding: The court granted in forma pauperis status but identified multiple pleading deficiencies including Eleventh Amendment immunity barring FHA claims against the state, failure to adequately allege ADA-qualifying disability, lack of personal involvement by state official defendants for § 1983 claims, and inability to pursue class action without counsel.
brief_summary: James Jacobson, a 69-year-old pro se plaintiff receiving Social Security benefits, sued the State of Oregon and its housing agency challenging Oregon's rent increase statute (ORS § 90.323) as creating disparate impact on disabled tenants on fixed incomes. case_name: The King/Morocco v. Greystar Corporation
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; the plaintiff's FHA claims centered on retaliation for unspecified prior complaints of discrimination and alleged improper threats of eviction for non-payment of rent.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal with prejudice of a pro se FHA complaint as frivolous and failing to state a claim, where the plaintiff's allegations amounted to no more than petty slights by apartment-complex staff and a conclusory assertion of retaliatory eviction for discrimination complaints.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Myron Simms sued his apartment complex and its owner/manager (Greystar/Eleve' Apartments) under the Fair Housing Act, alleging he was threatened with eviction for non-payment of rent and that an eviction proceeding was filed in retaliation for his complaints of discrimination. The district court, screening the in forma pauperis complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), dismissed the case with prejudice as both frivolous and failing to state a plausible claim. The Fifth Circuit affirmed, finding that Simms's allegations amounted to no more than petty slights insufficient to establish FHA liability.

brief_summary: Peter Gakuba sued the City of Baltimore and city officials alleging violations of constitutional rights and the Fair Housing Act in connection with delay in disbursement of $24,000 in COVID-19 Emergency Rental Assistance funds. accommodation_description: Request to waive the Florida Building Code's automatic fire sprinkler system requirement to operate a community residential group home for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities

The court granted in part and denied in part the City's motion to dismiss, dismissing MBSC's spot zoning, tax, contract rights, and vested rights claims, but allowed MBSC's Fair Housing Act disparate treatment and disparate impact claims to proceed.

brief_summary: Plaintiffs Treasured Homes LLC and its sole member Kimberly Cunningham sued the City of Toledo and Commissioner Ken Fischer alleging the City violated the FHA by denying their request to waive the 500-foot spacing requirement between group homes to open a second adult care facility at 3442 Woodley Road. The court denied cross-motions for summary judgment on the failure-to-accommodate claim, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to reasonableness, while granting summary judgment for Defendants on the disparate treatment claim for insufficient evidence of discriminatory intent.

brief_summary: Sang Mendy, a Black tenant at Modera Jackson apartments in Seattle, sued security guard Tracy Larson, his employer Northwest Security Services, property management company Mill Creek Residential Services, and American Security Programs, alleging they created a hostile housing environment based on race under § 3604(b) and interfered with his Fair Housing Rights under § 3617. key_holding: The § 3604(b) racial discrimination claim survived against Goncharko/5120 based on allegations of using a racial slur, disparate maintenance denial, and targeted eviction, but Coldwell Banker was dismissed for failure to plead racial motivation; the § 3604(f) accommodation claim failed because requests for repairs are modifications, not accommodations under § 3604(f)(3)(B), and the § 3617 retaliation claim failed for lack of alleged protected activity.
brief_summary: Steven Hobbs, a Black commercial mortgage broker and Chicago tenant, sued property owners Igor Goncharko and 5120 South LLC, property management company Coldwell Banker, and prior owner The Stewardship Group, alleging racial discrimination, disability discrimination, and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, plus a § 1981 breach of contract claim related to an alleged purchase agreement for affordable housing. accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested under the FHA; plaintiffs sought to prevent eviction from 1740 E. 54th Street, Brooklyn, NY and obtain a declaratory judgment that their equitable ownership interest in the property was superior to and enforceable against defendants' interests.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for injunctive relief and ordered plaintiffs to show cause why the action should not be dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding that neither the Contracts Clause claim nor the bare FHA reference established federal jurisdiction, and that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine independently barred review of the underlying state court eviction proceedings.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Heron and Blake, facing eviction from a Brooklyn property, filed a federal action asserting equitable ownership superior to defendants' interests, invoking the Contracts Clause, the Fair Housing Act, and UCC § 9-317(a)(2) to challenge defendants' eviction and ejectment proceedings. The court found the Contracts Clause inapplicable because no legislative act was alleged, and the FHA claim failed because plaintiffs did not allege discrimination based on any protected characteristic—merely characterizing an eviction as 'housing discrimination.' The court denied plaintiffs' emergency motion for a preliminary injunction, noted Rooker-Feldman as an independent jurisdictional bar, and directed plaintiffs to show cause within 30 days why the action should not be dismissed without prejudice.

brief_summary: Plaintiff Brian Legge sued Clarke County, Virginia and its officials seeking to enjoin demolition of a garage that violated the County's 50-foot setback zoning requirement, alleging Fair Housing Act discrimination based on his medical conditions (cancer, gastrointestinal complications) and retaliation under § 3617. The court denied Legge's motion for preliminary injunction, finding he failed to show a likelihood of success on his FHA claims because he did not establish the required nexus between his variance requests and his alleged handicap, and because he did not engage in protected FHA activity to support his retaliation claim.

brief_summary: Ruth Castro, a pro se Hispanic tenant with severe asthma, sued her landlord and property management entities under the Fair Housing Act, alleging that defendants discriminated and retaliated against her by refusing to enforce non-smoking provisions in the lease despite her disability-related need for a smoke-free environment, and ultimately evicting her after she requested accommodations and sought assistance from government agencies. key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for a writ of mandamus directing the SDNY to transfer the case to a neutral federal district, denied the motion for an immediate hearing as moot, and denied any implicit motion for recusal, finding no valid legal basis for any of the requested relief.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Brendalis Roldan filed an underlying complaint in New York state court against Bronx Pro Realty and Unimac Developers LLC alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which defendants removed to the Southern District of New York. The court denied all motions, holding that a district court lacks authority to issue mandamus against a co-equal court, plaintiff failed to meet the statutory requirements for venue transfer, and plaintiff failed to articulate any factual basis supporting recusal of the assigned judges.

case_name: Heimkes v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested reasonable accommodation to bring their respective service dogs into the common areas of Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium, and challenged the defendant's refusal to permit service dogs in those areas as well as the delay in ruling on the accommodation request.
key_holding: The court denied all three of Plaintiffs' motions to recuse Judge Moorer, finding that none of the alleged grounds—including adverse rulings, handling of counsel withdrawals, denial of continuances, and an allegedly improper ex parte communication—demonstrated personal bias or prejudice distinguishable from the court's ordinary judicial role.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Mark Heimkes and Shearldine Allfrey brought consolidated FHA and ADA claims against Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association, alleging denial of reasonable accommodation for their service dogs in common areas, interference/coercion, disparate treatment, and retaliation. During the course of a non-jury trial, Plaintiffs filed three successive recusal motions against Judge Moorer, citing adverse rulings, the granting of co-counsel withdrawal motions over objection, denial of continuances related to counsel's health issues, and an alleged ex parte communication regarding the Loper Bright decision. The court denied all three motions, finding the grounds were based entirely on adverse judicial rulings and procedural management decisions, not personal bias.

case_name: Jeff Olley, et al. v. Adrianne S. Todman, et al.
accommodation_description: No traditional accommodation was requested; plaintiffs sought proper investigation and timely enforcement of their underlying housing discrimination complaint by HUD and TWC, including issuance of a charge against their landlord, access to the full investigative file, and reconsideration of the no-cause determination.
key_holding: The court recommends dismissal with prejudice of all claims because claims against HUD are barred by sovereign immunity (plaintiffs failed to identify any waiver), claims against TWC and its officials are barred by Eleventh Amendment immunity without a viable Ex parte Young exception, the County cannot be held liable under Monell for lack of any alleged policy or final policymaker, and official-capacity claims against Judge Lawton-Evans and Clerk Hudspeth are duplicative of the claims against Harris County.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Jeff Olley, Aderonke Aderemi, and their minor child brought this housing discrimination action alleging that HUD, the Texas Workforce Commission, Harris County officials, and a state court judge conspired to fraudulently close out their underlying housing discrimination complaint and to wrongfully evict them, invoking 42 U.S.C. § 3617, § 1983, § 1985, and various constitutional provisions. The magistrate judge analyzed each defendant group separately, finding federal sovereign immunity barred monetary claims against HUD, Eleventh Amendment immunity barred claims against TWC and its officials because plaintiffs failed to allege an ongoing federal law violation sufficient for Ex parte Young, and the Monell claims against Harris County failed because plaintiffs alleged neither an official policy nor a final policymaker for any of the challenged actions. All claims were recommended for dismissal with prejudice.

case_name: Isis Rudolph v. Harrison Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reasonable accommodations from HMHA including extensions of time and alternative communication methods to allow her to participate in the Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program given her cognitive, memory, and communication limitations; she also requested accommodation from Cedar One regarding her disability. Additionally, she filed a request with the court for accommodations pertaining to in-person appearances and accessibility-enhancing document formatting.
key_holding: On initial § 1915(e)(2) screening, the court allows plaintiff to proceed on her FHA reasonable accommodation, retaliation, Rehabilitation Act, ADA (against HMHA only), due process, and state-law claims, but recommends dismissal of her ADA claim against Cedar One (private landlord is not a public entity), her discriminatory renter's insurance enforcement claim (insufficient factual pleading), and her § 1985(3) civil rights conspiracy claim (vague and conclusory allegations of coordination).
brief_summary: Isis Rudolph, a pro se plaintiff with PTSD, ADHD, and traumatic brain injury, sued Harrison Metropolitan Housing Authority and Cedar One Property Management under the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, § 1985(3), and state law, alleging denial of reasonable accommodations in her Section 8 voucher program, retaliatory non-renewal of her lease shortly after she requested disability accommodations, and repeated unauthorized entries into her unit. On mandatory § 1915(e)(2) screening of the amended complaint, the magistrate judge permitted the core FHA, Rehabilitation Act, due process, and state-law claims to proceed but recommended dismissal of the ADA claim against Cedar One (private landlord not subject to ADA), the FHA renter's insurance discrimination count (naked assertion of hardship without factual enhancement), and the § 1985(3) conspiracy count (no plausible allegation of coordination between defendants). The court also denied plaintiff's motion to stay eviction proceedings without prejudice and denied her miscellaneous PACER fee-exemption motion as moot.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: James E. Jacobson, Jr. v. AH Gresham Park, LLC
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Court denied Plaintiff's motion for appointment of pro bono counsel, finding no exceptional circumstances warranting appointment because Plaintiff had not demonstrated likelihood of success on the merits and had shown adequate ability to represent himself despite the complexity of the legal issues.
brief_summary: Plaintiff James Jacobson, Jr., a self-represented litigant proceeding in forma pauperis, moved for appointment of pro bono counsel in this Fair Housing Act and Americans with Disabilities Act case. The Court denied the motion, finding no exceptional circumstances because Plaintiff had not demonstrated likelihood of success on the merits and had shown adequate ability to represent himself despite the complexity of the legal issues, granting leave to renew the motion at a later stage.

case_name: Isaiah Hunter-Bey v. Allen Miller, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with mental health conditions seeks litigation accommodations including extended deadlines, simplified communications, remote participation, private hearing room, morning scheduling, and assistive technology access to participate meaningfully in court proceedings.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motions for reasonable accommodations without prejudice, finding them premature since no hearings are scheduled, service on all defendants is not complete, and plaintiff has demonstrated ability to participate in the case through numerous filings.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Isaiah Hunter-Bey, who has mental health conditions, sued his landlord Community Property Solvers LLC and property manager Allen Miller alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and state law violations, and separately requested Title II ADA accommodations from the court for litigation participation. The magistrate judge denied the accommodation requests without prejudice, finding them premature since service on all defendants is incomplete and no hearings are scheduled, while noting plaintiff may raise accommodations on a case-by-case basis as proceedings progress.

case_name: Dalila Agiza v. Bexar County, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was described; plaintiff asserted Fair Housing Act violations only in conclusory terms without providing any factual basis for the claim.
key_holding: The court accepted the magistrate judge's recommendation and dismissed all of plaintiff's claims—including her conclusory FHA, ADA, and RICO claims—for failure to state a claim, preserving only her § 1983 unlawful seizure claim against the Bexar County Precinct 1 Constable and associated officers.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Dalila Agiza filed § 1983 civil rights claims against Bexar County, a county judge, clerk's office staff, private attorneys, and LVNV Funding LLC, arising from an eviction and consumer-debt proceeding in state court. In response to a show cause order, she added new claims including conclusory allegations under the ADA, the Fair Housing Act, and RICO. The court adopted the magistrate judge's report, dismissing all claims except a new § 1983 unlawful seizure claim stemming from the alleged seizure of her property on May 30, 2025.

source_file: 10672101_2025_Prendergast v. Wode Cooper Companies Atcheson Place Lofts_ohsd
case_name: Carla Prendergast v. Woda Cooper Companies Atcheson Place Lofts, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendant Triumph passed over her Section 8 housing voucher application in favor of other applicants, characterizing this as source-of-income discrimination under the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: Source of income is not a protected characteristic under the Fair Housing Act, which prohibits discrimination only because of race, color, religion, sex, handicap, familial status, or national origin, so plaintiff fails to state an FHA claim.
brief_summary: Carla Prendergast, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued her former and prospective landlords Woda Cooper Companies/Atcheson Place Lofts and Metropolitan Holdings/Triumph Apartments, along with the Legal Aid Society of Columbus and Ohio Adult Parole Authority, alleging Fair Housing Act violations, due process violations under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and state law claims stemming from her loss of housing. The court dismissed all federal claims, including her FHA source-of-income discrimination claim, because source of income is not a protected characteristic under the FHA, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.

source_file: 10672251_2025_Daniel Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees_ca11
case_name: Daniel A. Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees
accommodation_description: Student with disability requested to keep an emotional support cat in his university dorm room and common areas as a reasonable accommodation for his disability.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of FHA and state law claims based on Eleventh Amendment immunity but vacated and remanded to allow the plaintiff leave to amend to add Rehabilitation Act claims, which would not be barred by sovereign immunity.
brief_summary: Daniel Frishberg, a University of South Florida student with a disability, sued the university and building owner after his emotional support animal waiver was revoked when he repeatedly brought his cat into dorm common areas in violation of the accommodation terms. The district court dismissed his Fair Housing Act and state law claims based on Eleventh Amendment immunity. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the dismissal of those claims but vacated and remanded, holding the district court erred by not giving the pro se plaintiff an opportunity to amend to add Rehabilitation Act claims, which are not barred by sovereign immunity when the state receives federal funding.

case_name: Kelvin Simmons v. Jason Woo, Esq., et al.
accommodation_description: Simmons, a legally blind individual, requested accessible communications, maintenance coordination, and alternative dispute resolution as reasonable accommodations for his disability.
key_holding: The court stayed the federal case under the Colorado River doctrine, finding that parallel state court proceedings involving the same parties and substantially similar claims—including an ongoing ICA appeal and counterclaim proceeding—weighed in favor of abstaining from exercising jurisdiction; the IFP application was denied as moot.
brief_summary: Kelvin Simmons, a legally blind tenant, filed a federal action alleging disability discrimination and reasonable accommodation denials against Stott Property Management LLC, property owners, and other defendants, seeking to vacate an eviction judgment and obtain damages. The district court stayed the federal case under the Colorado River doctrine, finding that parallel state court proceedings involving the same parties and substantially similar claims—including an ongoing ICA appeal and a counterclaim proceeding—warranted abstention to avoid duplicative litigation and inconsistent results.

case_name: Shawanda V. Collins v. Team Management LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Collins raised, for the first time in her opposition to summary judgment, a claim under FHA Section 3604(f) that defendants failed to reasonably accommodate her disability-related need for a unit with a bathtub after she rejected the unit offered during her March 2024 tour; the court declined to consider this claim because it was never pleaded in her complaint and was improperly raised for the first time at the summary judgment stage.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' summary judgment on all Fair Housing Act claims because plaintiff Collins voluntarily withdrew her own rental application after being approved for and offered a unit, meaning defendants never denied her housing for any discriminatory or retaliatory reason, and dismissed her state law claim for lack of standing because she did in fact apply for housing.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Shawanda Collins, a physically disabled African American woman with a dated felony conviction, alleged that defendants violated the FHA by racially discriminating against her and retaliating against her for invoking her Fair Housing rights during her attempt to secure a subsidized apartment in Milwaukee. The court granted summary judgment for all defendants because the undisputed record showed that Collins was approved for a unit, given a tour, and offered a lease, but she herself chose to withdraw her application before defendants could act further, thereby negating any claim that she was denied housing. Her state law claim under Wis. Stat. § 106.50 alleging that defendants' advertising deterred disabled persons from applying was dismissed for lack of standing because Collins herself did apply for housing and suffered no deterrence injury.

case_name: Jacqueline Peters v. Caton Towers Owners Corp.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff seeks to prevent her eviction as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for TRO and preliminary injunction because the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal review of the state-court eviction judgment, and plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable harm from any injury other than eviction.
brief_summary: Jacqueline Peters, a pro se plaintiff residing at Caton Towers, sued the building's management company alleging denial of disability accommodations and retaliatory eviction under the Fair Housing Act. The court denied her motion for a TRO and preliminary injunction, holding that Rooker-Feldman bars federal review of her eviction claims because a state court already issued a final judgment and warrant of eviction, and she showed no irreparable harm from any other alleged discrimination.

case_name: Anthony Jackson v. S2 Residential
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation requested; claims involve housing assignment to pest-infested unit, differential security deposit requirement, and delayed pest remediation as discriminatory housing practices.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for S2 Residential because Jackson failed to present competent evidence that his apartment was pest-infested at the time of rental, that other tenants paid lower security deposits (S2 Residential offered a legitimate credit-score justification), or that S2 Residential had a policy causing a discriminatory effect.
brief_summary: Anthony Jackson appealed summary judgment for S2 Residential in this Fair Housing Act case, alleging he was assigned a pest-infested apartment, charged a higher security deposit than other tenants, and experienced delay in pest remediation. The Fifth Circuit affirmed, finding Jackson failed to produce competent evidence that his apartment was pest-infested at the time of rental, that the security deposit differential was discriminatory (S2 Residential offered a credit-score justification), or that S2 Residential had any challenged policy causing a discriminatory effect.

brief_summary: Plaintiffs Victor Cagara Ortiguerra et al. sued Defendants Grand Isle Shipyard, LLC and GIS, LLC under the Fair Housing Act, Trafficking Victims Protection Act, and other claims arising from housing conditions during employment-related quarantine. The court denied Defendants' motion for reconsideration of its prior order refusing to compel arbitration of Plaintiffs' FHA claims, holding that the claims did not arise from employment because Plaintiffs had no work duties during quarantine when the alleged housing violations occurred.

case_name: Fuller v. Christine Apartments LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges eviction proceedings as discriminatory retaliation and fraudulent landlord practices; no specific reasonable accommodation request identified
key_holding: Plaintiff's complaint fails to state a plausible FHA claim because it does not allege facts showing plaintiff belongs to a protected class or that defendants' facially neutral practices had a discriminatory impact; the TRO motion was denied because plaintiff cannot show likelihood of success on the merits.
brief_summary: Pro se tenant Thomas Fuller sued Christine Apartments LLC and related defendants alleging fraud and unlawful eviction under the Fair Housing Act, Section 1983, and Section 1985, and sought a temporary restraining order to stop eviction proceedings. The district court denied the TRO motion and dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, holding that Fuller failed to allege sufficient facts establishing that he belongs to a protected class or that defendants' practices had a discriminatory effect, and that the court lacked jurisdiction to review the state court eviction proceedings under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine.

case_name: Woodard v. State of Missouri
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who claims to be homeless, does not articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request; his complaint broadly alleges harassment by the State of Missouri related to his child being taken away.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint for failure to state a claim because the State of Missouri is not a 'person' under § 1983 and is protected by Eleventh Amendment immunity, and plaintiff's FHA claim failed because he did not allege discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, or national origin.
brief_summary: Self-represented plaintiff Michael Woodard sued the State of Missouri under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, claiming harassment related to his child being taken away and seeking $15,000,000 in damages while stating he is now homeless. The court dismissed the action under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) for failure to state a claim because the State is immune from suit under § 1983 and the Eleventh Amendment, and plaintiff failed to allege any FHA-protected basis for discrimination.

case_name: Gregory Austin Gadson v. Riverbay Corporation
accommodation_description: Plaintiff seeks to prevent eviction, renew his lease, and obtain a certified stock certificate from Riverbay, framing these as remedies for alleged FHA violations based on familial status and disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims for failure to state a claim because plaintiff's factual allegations show Riverbay's adverse actions were motivated solely by non-payment of rent arrears, not by familial status or disability, and plaintiff failed to plead protected activity for retaliation claims.
brief_summary: Gregory Austin Gadson, proceeding pro se, sued Riverbay Corporation (a Mitchell-Lama cooperative housing provider) to prevent his eviction from a Bronx apartment and obtain lease renewal and stock certificate issuance, alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on familial status and disability. The court dismissed the action because Gadson failed to state plausible claims—his allegations show Riverbay's adverse actions were motivated solely by unpaid rent arrears, not protected characteristics, and he failed to plead protected activity for retaliation.

case_name: Mirlande Dina Michel-Wiggins v. Department of Housing and Urban Development, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to use Housing Choice Voucher to pay for extended stay hotel room as a reasonable accommodation for PTSD and agoraphobia
key_holding: The court dismissed claims because HUD was not responsible for the local housing agency's denial of the hotel accommodation request, and HUD's offer of video conferencing or written questions as alternatives to an in-person interview at the hotel room constituted a reasonable accommodation under the Rehabilitation Act even though it was not the plaintiff's preferred option.
brief_summary: Michel-Wiggins, a Section 8 voucher recipient with PTSD and agoraphobia, sued HUD alleging disability discrimination for the denial of her request to use her voucher at an extended stay hotel and HUD's refusal to conduct an in-person interview at her hotel room during a fair housing investigation. The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss, holding that HUD could not be liable for the local housing agency's denial of the voucher accommodation, and that HUD provided a reasonable accommodation by offering video conferencing and written interview questions as alternatives to an in-person interview.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discriminatory remarks about her race and gender and retaliation for reporting discrimination; FHA claim dismissed at screening.
key_holding: The court granted Airbnb's motion to compel arbitration because Sita had constructive notice of the arbitration clause through repeated acceptance of Airbnb's Terms of Service, and she failed to argue that the agreement was inapplicable or invalid.
brief_summary: Keren Sita sued Airbnb alleging Fair Housing Act violations (discriminatory remarks about race and gender and retaliation), breach of contract, negligence, and negligent misrepresentation after booking a Vermont rental property. The FHA claim was dismissed at initial screening, and the court granted Airbnb's motion to compel arbitration on the remaining state law claims because Sita had constructive notice of the arbitration clause through repeated acceptance of the Terms of Service.

case_name: Latarsha Williams v. Navy Federal Credit Union
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiff alleges discriminatory loan denials based on being labeled an 'Outside Risk'
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA, ECOA, and § 1981 claims because she failed to allege membership in a protected class (race, national origin, or gender) and failed to establish discriminatory intent under the McDonnell Douglas framework.

source_file: 10677224_2025_Meyer v. Ten Mile Island Condominium Association_cod
case_name: Scott Meyer v. Ten Mile Island Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested exclusive assignment of the parking spot outside his condominium unit for his use due to his wheelchair mobility needs.
key_holding: The court granted defendants summary judgment because the parties' prior Settlement Agreement signed during CCRD conciliation proceedings released defendants from 'any and all claims' arising from the same facts, and plaintiff's current claims arise from the same operative facts resolved in those proceedings.
brief_summary: Scott Meyer, a wheelchair user who owns a condominium in the Ten Mile Island Condominium Association in Frisco, Colorado, sued the HOA alleging Fair Housing Act violations for denying his request for a reserved parking spot as a reasonable accommodation and for retaliation. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment, holding that plaintiff's claims are barred by a prior Settlement Agreement the parties signed during CCRD conciliation proceedings, which expressly released defendants from any and all claims arising from the same underlying facts.

case_name: Luis E. Ogando v. John J. Napolitano, Esq.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested. Plaintiff mentioned being disabled (from a 2016 vehicle accident), Hispanic, and of Jewish Israeli messianic religion, but expressly did not allege that any defendant discriminated against him on those bases, and no reasonable accommodation or modification was sought or denied.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims by a pro se plaintiff arising from a 2006 home purchase and subsequent foreclosure and eviction because claims related to state court proceedings were barred by the Eleventh Amendment, Rooker-Feldman doctrine, and res judicata, and the remaining federal statutory claims under the FHA, ECOA, TILA, RESPA, and § 1983 failed on the merits because plaintiff never alleged discrimination on any protected characteristic, lacked standing as a non-borrower, and filed well outside applicable statutes of limitations.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Luis Ogando sued multiple defendants—including mortgage lenders, attorneys, a realtor, and the New York Supreme Court—arising from a 2006 home purchase in which he used a credit-worthy intermediary (Mateo) as the nominal borrower, was allegedly promised the deed would be transferred to him, and was ultimately evicted after Mateo entered a short sale. The court first dismissed claims related to state court proceedings under the Eleventh Amendment (as to the NY Supreme Court), Rooker-Feldman (as to the eviction judgment), and res judicata (as to the foreclosure). The court then dismissed all remaining federal claims—under the FHA, ECOA, TILA, RESPA, and § 1983—because plaintiff failed to allege discrimination based on any protected characteristic, was not a borrower under TILA or RESPA, the TILA limitations period had expired in 2007, and the named private parties were not state actors, before declining supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.

case_name: McKay Burley and Tyson Thomas v. Charles J. Chapman
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case involves neighbor harassment based on sexual orientation and sex, not a reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The court denied default judgment on plaintiffs' FHA discriminatory statements claim (§ 3604(c)) because defendant's alleged statements were not made 'with respect to the sale or rental of a dwelling,' and denied default judgment on the § 3617 interference claim because defendant is merely a neighbor whose conduct may not implicate FHA-protected housing rights; however, the court granted default judgment on the state IIED claim, finding plaintiffs alleged extreme and outrageous conduct sufficient to state that claim.
brief_summary: Two gay men sued their next-door neighbor for discriminatory harassment including anti-gay slurs and threats of violence, asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act for discriminatory statements (§ 3604(c)) and interference (§ 3617), as well as state law claims. The court granted default judgment on the state intentional infliction of emotional distress claim, finding extreme and outrageous conduct, but denied default judgment on the FHA claims, holding that the discriminatory statements claim failed because the neighbor's statements were not made in connection with the sale or rental of a dwelling, and that the interference claim failed because the alleged conduct did not sufficiently implicate FHA-protected housing rights.

case_name: T&R Properties, Inc. v. Berlin Township
accommodation_description: Developer T&R Properties claims Berlin Township denied zoning permits for a mixed-use development in a manner that discriminates against racial minorities by restricting high-density housing.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs leave to take four additional depositions beyond the ten-deposition limit and extended case management deadlines, finding good cause shown that individualized deposition testimony regarding motives and rationales for zoning decisions is not discoverable through less burdensome means such as meeting minutes.
brief_summary: T&R Properties, Inc. sued Berlin Township challenging the denial of zoning permits for a mixed-use development, alleging the denials were arbitrary and discriminatory based on race. The court granted plaintiffs' motion for leave to take four additional depositions and extended case deadlines, finding the individualized testimony regarding zoning decision-makers' motives is not available through other sources.

source_file: 10679704_2025_Walker v. U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Development_dcd
case_name: Angie Walker v. U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Development
accommodation_description: Walker did not request a discrete reasonable accommodation. Her complaints centered on the USDA's alleged failure to enforce a no-smoking policy against neighboring tenants, failure to remediate hazardous conditions (including nicotine-stained walls and a severely rusted bathroom sink), selective enforcement of rules against her and her son, and ultimately the discriminatory and retaliatory eviction she and her son suffered in 2021.
key_holding: The court dismissed Walker's FHA and civil rights claims against USDA for lack of standing because her alleged injuries—including discriminatory and retaliatory eviction—were fairly traceable only to her private landlord, Grand Management Services, not to the USDA, and mere government subsidy of a private entity does not convert that entity's actions into government action.
brief_summary: Angie Walker, a former tenant in a USDA Rural Development-subsidized apartment complex in Gold Beach, Oregon, sued the USDA alleging that her 2021 eviction and years of discriminatory treatment and retaliation beginning in 2014 violated the FHA and her civil rights. The court dismissed the case sua sponte for lack of standing under Rule 12(b)(1), finding that Walker's own documentary exhibits demonstrated that her landlord, Grand Management Services, not the USDA, was responsible for the eviction, inspection notices, and failure to address maintenance and smoking complaints. Because Walker's injuries were traceable to an independent third party not before the court, she could not satisfy the traceability element of Article III standing, and the case was dismissed without prejudice.

case_name: Larry Johnson v. Lisa Simonson and Kelly Paine

key_holding: Plaintiff's retaliation claims failed because he could not establish causation between protected activity and adverse actions, and his parking accommodation claim failed because he previously agreed in a settlement that the commercial parking space provided by defendants met his accessibility needs.
brief_summary: Larry Johnson, a pro se tenant at Uptown Tower Apartments (a HUD Section 8 property managed by Guardian Management), sued property managers Lisa Simonson and Kelly Paine alleging Fair Housing Act retaliation under § 3617 and reasonable accommodation claims for accessible parking and paperwork delivery procedures. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment on all claims, finding no evidence of causation for the retaliation claims and concluding that the parking accommodation was resolved by a prior settlement agreement.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a wheelchair user, alleges that Defendants failed to design and construct the 174-unit apartment complex in compliance with FHA accessibility and usability requirements for covered multifamily dwellings.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that Plaintiff sufficiently alleged Article III standing as an individual plaintiff who was deterred from renting due to accessibility barriers, and that Plaintiff plausibly alleged FHA design-and-construction violations against all Defendants including the architect.
brief_summary: Amy Burnett, a wheelchair user, sued Rutledge Flats LLC and related development entities alleging the 174-unit Nashville apartment complex was designed and constructed in violation of FHA accessibility requirements, deterring her from renting. case_name: Frantz Neptune v. Cobble Ridge Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges harassment, trespassing, and property destruction at his residence in Cobble Ridge community and seeks relief for discriminatory housing practices.
key_holding: The court granted the State Defendants' motion to dismiss on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds because the Fair Housing Act does not create a private right of action against state agencies for their handling of investigations into discriminatory housing practices, and plaintiff failed to state a cognizable due process or equal protection claim under § 1983.

key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims were properly dismissed because they relate to an unlawful foreclosure rather than to the sale or rental of a dwelling or any real estate transaction, and the statute does not apply to foreclosure matters.

case_name: Be the Bush Recovery Ministries v. Coffee County, Tennessee
accommodation_description: BTB requested permission to operate its residential addiction recovery program in an RS-1 Low Density Residential zone through a zoning amendment or special exception.
key_holding: The RS-1 zoning ordinance is not facially discriminatory because it applies a neutral distinction between single-family dwellings and other residential uses rather than singling out group homes for the disabled, and BTB failed to establish standing for injunctive relief due to speculative future plans.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to complete income recertification after the deadline and to have her counsel assist her with the recertification process as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment to defendants on plaintiff's reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B), finding that plaintiff failed to establish she was disabled or that defendants denied a requested accommodation, noting defendants granted several accommodation requests and ultimately resolved the recertification dispute in December 2020.
brief_summary: Stephany Webster, a resident of Walnut Park Manor senior apartment complex in Sapulpa, Oklahoma (a LIHTC/LOW-Income Housing Tax Credit property managed by Fairway Management), sued the defendants claiming disability discrimination, sex discrimination, and retaliation under the FHA, alleging defendants failed to grant reasonable accommodations, made housing unavailable based on disability and sex, and retaliated against her for filing a 2019 lawsuit.
