source_file: 10716560_2025_Felice Lazae Martin, et al. v. Michael Castillo, et al._caed
case_name: Felice Lazae Martin, et al. v. Michael Castillo, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested to be excused from rent payments during a search period for alternative housing while relocating from a property with toxic mold and no functioning heat; plaintiffs also alleged they sought electronic filing accommodations from the Kern County Superior Court due to their disabilities during a 43-day e-filing shutdown.
key_holding: The court found that pro se plaintiffs failed to plead any cognizable federal claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the ADA, or the Fair Housing Act, and granted leave to file an amended complaint within 21 days.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Felice Lazae Martin and Hector Joseph Borges sued their landlord Michael Castillo and his attorney for toxic mold habitability violations, an illegal lockout, and disability discrimination under the FHA, ADA, and constitutional provisions. On IFP screening, the court found the complaint failed to state any cognizable federal claim, noting plaintiffs made only cursory references to the FHA without supporting facts, failed to identify a proper ADA defendant, and did not adequately allege any constitutional violations under § 1983. The court ordered plaintiffs to file an amended complaint or a notice of voluntary dismissal within 21 days.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Lopez v. Smith, 203 F.3d 1122 (9th Cir. 2000)
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)

source_file: 10730094_2025_Eric Crouse v. Housing Works, Deschutes County, and the State of Oregon_ord
case_name: Eric Crouse v. Housing Works, Deschutes County, and the State of Oregon
accommodation_description: Request that payment standard be increased and utility allowance be raised to allow access to suitable housing under the Section 8 voucher program
key_holding: The State of Oregon's motion to dismiss was granted because the court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under Oregon's APA (which provides the exclusive remedy for review of final agency orders) and because Plaintiff failed to allege any affirmative acts by the State that caused injury, as opposed to mere failures to act.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eric Crouse, a person with disabilities represented by the Deschutes County IDD program, sued Housing Works (the local housing authority), Deschutes County, and the State of Oregon alleging failures to provide reasonable housing accommodations including increased payment standards and utility allowances under Section 8. The State of Oregon moved to dismiss, and the court granted the motion on jurisdictional grounds (Oregon APA provides exclusive review mechanism) and for failure to state a claim because Plaintiff alleged no affirmative acts by the State causing injury.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Wyatt B. v. Kotek, 146 F.4th 1267 (9th Cir. 2025)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

source_file: 10730134_2025_Mikel James Gueltzau v. Derek Warehime, Property Manager and Owner; and Cathy Warehime, Property Manager and Owner_ned
case_name: Mikel James Gueltzau v. Derek Warehime, Property Manager and Owner; and Cathy Warehime, Property Manager and Owner
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation request is not described in this procedural order.
key_holding: The court struck two improperly filed documents, revoked the pro se plaintiff's CM/ECF electronic filing privileges due to persistent non-compliance with procedural rules, and ordered plaintiff to show cause why future submissions should not be pre-screened by the court.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mikel James Gueltzau, who alleges Fair Housing Act discrimination against private landlords Derek and Cathy Warehime, filed additional improperly docketed documents despite prior court warnings; the court struck the filings, revoked plaintiff's electronic filing privileges, and ordered plaintiff to show cause why future submissions should not require pre-filing court review due to abusive litigation practices.

source_file: 10730290_2025_Yifan Shen v. Commissioner, Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services_ca11
case_name: Yifan Shen v. Commissioner, Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege SB 264's purchase restriction, registration requirement, and affidavit requirement constitute discriminatory housing practices under the Fair Housing Act based on race and national origin, though no individualized accommodation request is at issue.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the denial of preliminary injunction as to registration and affidavit requirements but reversed as to the purchase restriction because no plaintiff had standing to challenge it; the court applied rational basis review under Terrace v. Thompson, finding the purchase restriction did not violate Equal Protection as applied to noncitizens, and rejected federal preemption arguments regarding CFIUS.
brief_summary: Chinese citizens and a real estate brokerage firm sued Florida officials to enjoin enforcement of SB 264, which restricted Chinese noncitizens from purchasing Florida real property, required registration of property owned by Chinese persons, and mandated compliance affidavits. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the denial of preliminary injunction for the registration and affidavit requirements but reversed and remanded for the purchase restriction because no plaintiff had standing to challenge it, applying rational basis review and finding the statute did not facially violate Equal Protection.
key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Plyler v. Doe, 457 U.S. 202 (1982)
Yick Wo v. Hopkins, 118 U.S. 356 (1886)
Terrace v. Thompson, 263 U.S. 197 (1923)
Crosby v. Nat'l Foreign Trade Council, 530 U.S. 363 (2000)

source_file: 10730691_2025_Maria Guadalupe Aguilera v. Capital One, N.A., Jack Johnson, Kristina Nevel, Joanne Tucker, Suzanne Drotman, and Judith Williams_oknd
10730883_2025_Mikel James Gueltzau v. Derek Warehime, Property Manager and Owner; and Cathy Warehime, Property Manager and Owner_ned
case_name: Mikel James Gueltzau v. Derek Warehime, Property Manager and Owner; and Cathy Warehime, Property Manager and Owner
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to file documents via email or fax and to attend hearings via Zoom or telephone as ADA accommodations to court filing requirements.
key_holding: The Court denied Plaintiff's ADA accommodation requests for email/fax filing and remote hearings because such accommodations are not reasonably necessary—email and fax filing would be inappropriate given Plaintiff's past abuse of electronic filing privileges, and the Court already considers parties' circumstances when setting hearings.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff filed multiple improper and frivolous documents in a Fair Housing Act discrimination case, prompting the Court to impose filing restrictions requiring paper submissions by mail. Plaintiff then sought ADA accommodations to file documents via email or fax and attend hearings remotely, which the Court denied because such accommodations were not reasonably necessary given his past abuse of electronic filing and his demonstrated ability to file documents quickly in person.
key_cases_cited: In re Tyler, 839 F.2d 1290 (8th Cir. 1988)
Williams v. McKenzie, 834 F.2d 152 (8th Cir. 1987)
Hall v. Higgins, 77 F.4th 1171 (8th Cir. 2023)
Fletcher v. Brown Cnt'y, 2008 WL 752661 (D. Neb. 2008)

source_file: 10731021_2025_Asya Weston, et al. v. WIP 800 J Lofts, et al._caed
case_name: Asya Weston, et al. v. WIP 800 J Lofts, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege the unlawful detainer action and eviction were retaliatory and discriminatory based on race, familial status, and disability, but do not specify a particular accommodation request being denied.
key_holding: The FHA claim was dismissed because plaintiffs failed to sufficiently allege they suffer from a qualifying handicap under § 3602(h), that defendants knew of their impairments, or that defendants refused to make an accommodation.
brief_summary: Two Black tenants sued WIP 800 J Lofts and associated individuals alleging the unlawful detainer action against them was fraudulent and retaliatory, targeting their race, familial status, and disabilities in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, finding plaintiffs failed to state an FHA claim because they did not adequately allege a qualifying handicap or discriminatory conduct based on protected characteristics.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Harris v. Itzhaki
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co.

source_file: 10731555_2025_Daniel Reeves v. United States of America et al._gasd
10731564_2025_United States of America v. Five Properties, LLC et al._laed
case_name: United States of America v. Five Properties, LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support dog as a reasonable accommodation for a mental disability
key_holding: The Government's action is not barred by res judicata because the Government has an independent interest in enforcing the FHA and seeks broader public interest remedies beyond what the private plaintiff sought, and laches does not apply to bar the Government's suit.
brief_summary: The United States government filed suit on behalf of Dory Turnipseed against Five Properties, LLC and Tonti Management alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act for refusing to accommodate Turnipseed's mental disability by denying her emotional support dog. The court denied the defendants' motion for summary judgment, holding that the Government's action is not barred by res judicata because the Government has independent enforcement interests seeking broader public remedies, and laches does not apply to bar suits brought by the United States in its sovereign capacity.
key_cases_cited: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
E.E.O.C. v. Waffle House, Inc., 534 U.S. 279 (2002)
United States v. East Baton Rouge Par. Sch. Bd., 594 F.2d 56 (5th Cir. 1979)
United States v. Popovich, 820 F.2d 134 (5th Cir. 1987)
Test Masters Educ. Servs., Inc. v. Singh, 428 F.3d 559 (5th Cir. 2005)

source_file: 10731635_2025_Troy King v. Julia Owner LLC, et al._azd
case_name: Troy King v. Julia Owner LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request; plaintiff alleges intentional racial discrimination in rental terms, lease renewal denial, and eviction proceedings.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims were properly dismissed because his amended complaint failed to allege sufficient facts connecting the defendant's alleged discriminatory statements and actions to his race, despite having been given specific guidance on what factual allegations were required.
brief_summary: Troy King, a Black tenant at an apartment complex managed by Julia Owner LLC and later Greystar Management, sued alleging racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 1981, and the Arizona Civil Rights Act, claiming he witnessed staff quote a White family a lower rate, was denied lease renewal, and faced retaliatory eviction and fraudulent court filings. The court dismissed his claims without leave to amend, finding his amended complaint still failed to allege sufficient facts showing the defendant's alleged discriminatory conduct was connected to his race.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
In re Cloudera, Inc., 121 F.4th 1180 (9th Cir. 2024)
United States v. United Healthcare Ins. Co., 848 F.3d 1161 (9th Cir. 2016)
Kendall v. Visa U.S.A., Inc., 518 F.3d 1042 (9th Cir. 2008)

source_file: 10731728_2025_Irish Horton v. Beacon Woods East Master Association, Inc., Ronnie Armstrong, and Christopher Skene_flmd
case_name: Irish Horton v. Beacon Woods East Master Association, Inc., Ronnie Armstrong, and Christopher Skene
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a Black man with a physical disability requiring a service dog, alleged he was expelled from the clubhouse when Defendants refused entry based on his service animal.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Plaintiff's race-based discrimination claims under the FHA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, finding that the Amended Complaint failed to plead sufficient facts showing that Defendants' discriminatory conduct stemmed from racial animus rather than animus toward Plaintiff's disability and use of a service dog.
brief_summary: Irish Horton, a Black/African American man with a physical disability who uses a service dog, sued Beacon Woods East Master Association, Inc. and two HOA officers alleging they expelled him from a clubhouse in May 2023 because of both his race and disability. The Court granted Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that Plaintiff's factual allegations showed discriminatory animus stemmed from his disability and use of a service dog rather than his race, and that Plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts showing he was treated differently than similarly situated non-Black residents.
key_cases_cited: Watts v. Joggers Run Prop. Owners Ass'n, Inc., 133 F.4th 1032 (11th Cir. 2025)
Ziyadat v. Diamondrock Hosp. Co., 3 F.4th 1291 (11th Cir. 2021)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Plowright v. Miami Dade Cnty., 102 F.4th 1358 (11th Cir. 2024)

source_file: 10731759_2025_Toby Masse v. Clark County, et al._wawd
case_name: Toby Masse v. Clark County, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination based on race, sex, and sexual orientation, denial of homeless services, and seizure of personal property, claiming Fair Housing Act violations.
key_holding: The Court found the complaint deficient under Rule 8 for failing to provide factual allegations showing the who, what, where, when, and why of each claim, and granted plaintiff 21 days to file an amended complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Toby Masse filed an in forma pauperis complaint against Clark County, City of Vancouver, and others alleging discrimination based on race, sex, and sexual orientation, denial of homeless services, and unconstitutional seizure of property in violation of the Fair Housing Act, Civil Rights Act, and Fourteenth Amendment. The Court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) and found it deficient for failing to provide sufficient factual allegations to state plausible claims, ordering plaintiff to file an amended complaint within 21 days or face dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

source_file: 10732345_2025_Ronald Satish Emrit and Presidential Committee_Political Action Committee_Separate Segregated Fund Number C00569897 d_b_a United Emrits of America v. Erin Burnett, et al._nmd
case_name: Ronald Satish Emrit and Presidential Committee/Political Action Committee/Separate Segregated Fund Number C00569897 d/b/a United Emrits of America v. Erin Burnett, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendants failed to provide Section 8 housing voucher and violated Fair Housing Act
key_holding: The complaint failed to state Fair Housing Act or ADA claims because it did not identify the specific statutory provisions violated or allege sufficient facts showing the claims arose under those statutes, and plaintiff failed to comply with the court's order to show cause.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ronald Satish Emrit sued television personalities, BMW Cars of North America, and Congresswoman Nancy Mace alleging Fair Housing Act and ADA violations based on defendants' failure to provide a Section 8 housing voucher and defamatory statements. The court dismissed the case without prejudice for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted and for plaintiff's failure to comply with the magistrate judge's order to show cause.

source_file: 10732441_2025_Anthony George Bell v. Weinreb Management LLC; Abraham Reiss of Weinreb Management LLC; Pitor Piwowarczyk of 455 Ocean Associates LLC; 455 Ocean Associates LLC_nyed
case_name: Anthony George Bell v. Weinreb Management LLC; Abraham Reiss of Weinreb Management LLC; Pitor Piwowarczyk of 455 Ocean Associates LLC; 455 Ocean Associates LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges housing quality issues (roach infestation, inoperable vents, electrical problems) without requesting any disability-related accommodation or alleging discrimination based on his HIV and asthma
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a Fair Housing Act claim because plaintiff does not allege any acts of discrimination—merely mentioning health conditions (HIV and asthma) without linking defendants' conduct to discriminatory treatment based on disability is insufficient to invoke FHA protections.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Anthony George Bell sued Weinreb Management LLC and 455 Ocean Associates LLC alleging housing quality issues including roach infestation, broken vents, and electrical problems at his Brooklyn apartment; Bell mentioned having HIV and asthma but did not request any disability accommodation. The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, finding that merely citing the Fair Housing Act is insufficient where plaintiff fails to allege any discriminatory conduct based on his protected characteristics.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Rivera v. Inc. Vill. of Farmingdale, 784 F. Supp. 2d 133 (E.D.N.Y. 2011)
Gamarra v. Paul, 2024 WL 4515286 (E.D.N.Y. Oct. 17, 2024)
Scoggins v. Turning Point of Cent. Cal., Inc., 2023 WL 2354820 (E.D. Cal. Mar. 3, 2023)

source_file: 10734040_2025_Elewood Torres, on behalf of himself and all others similarly situated v. MMS Group LLC. d_b_a MMS Group, New York City Housing Preservation and Development, New York State Division of Housing and Community
case_name: Elewood Torres, on behalf of himself and all others similarly situated v. MMS Group LLC. d/b/a MMS Group, New York City Housing Preservation and Development, New York State Division of Housing and Community Renewal
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs sought accessible building features and accommodations necessary for deaf and hearing-impaired individuals to independently use and access the residential premises, including modifications and design features at two residential buildings that would enable deaf or hard-of-hearing residents and visitors to use the buildings without barriers.
key_holding: The district court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Report and Recommendation in full, granting class certification under Rule 23 for a class of deaf and hearing-impaired residents and visitors as to Counts Three, Four, Five, Six, Seven, Eight, Ten, and Eleven with modifications narrowing the class period to on or after July 19, 2019 (or 2020 for Count Ten), while denying certification as to Counts One and Two.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Elewood Torres filed FHA and state law claims on behalf of himself and similarly situated individuals, alleging that Defendants—including property owners, managers, and related entities—failed to maintain two residential buildings to be independently usable by deaf and hearing-impaired persons and failed to provide access to housing for individuals with disabilities. Magistrate Judge Figueredo issued a Report and Recommendation recommending class certification as to most counts with modifications to the proposed class period and class definition. The district court reviewed Defendants' and Plaintiff's objections, applying de novo review to newly raised arguments and clear error review to rehashed arguments, and adopted the R&R in full, certifying the class with the narrowed time period and also granting Defendants' motion to seal sensitive medical information.
key_cases_cited: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc., 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Comcast Corp. v. Behrend, 569 U.S. 27 (2013)
Amchem Products, Inc. v. Windsor, 521 U.S. 591 (1997)
Consolidated Rail Corp. v. Town of Hyde Park, 47 F.3d 473 (2d Cir. 1995)
Tyson Foods, Inc. v. Bouaphakeo, 577 U.S. 442 (2016)

source_file: 10734407_2025_Farrial Mercer v. Kristopher Brewer, et al._almd
10734421_2025_Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc._flsd
case_name: Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a condominium owner with medical conditions limiting her tolerance to demolition-related environmental hazards, requests a 90-day extension of pretrial and trial deadlines in the underlying state court action as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The Anti-Injunction Act bars the federal court from granting the requested injunction because neither the Fair Housing Act nor the Americans with Disabilities Act expressly authorizes injunctive relief to stay state court proceedings, and the Plaintiff's objection regarding the court's consideration of medical evidence is without merit since the AIA prohibition is a legal threshold issue independent of the quantum of disability evidence.
brief_summary: Valery Kantsepolsky, a condominium owner with health conditions affecting her tolerance to environmental hazards from demolition, sued the River Shores Association, Inc. (her HOA) under the FHA and ADA seeking a preliminary injunction to enjoin the HOA from proceeding with exploratory demolition in her unit and to obtain a 90-day extension of trial deadlines in a related state court action. The federal court denied the TRO because the Anti-Injunction Act prohibits enjoining state court proceedings, and neither the FHA nor ADA expressly authorizes such relief as an exception to the AIA's general prohibition.
key_cases_cited: Mitchum v. Foster, 407 U.S. 225 (1972)
Mercer v. Sechan Realty, Inc., 569 F. App'x 652 (11th Cir. 2014)
Atl. Coast Line R. Co. v. Bhd. of Locomotive Eng'rs, 398 U.S. 281 (1970)
Schiavo ex. rel. Schindler v. Schiavo, 403 F.3d 1223 (11th Cir. 2005)
Burr & Forman v. Blair, 470 F.3d 1019 (11th Cir. 2006)

source_file: 10734581_2025_N. Clark LLC, ET AL v. UNITED STATES DEPARTMENT OF HOUSING AND URBAN DEVELOPMENT, ET AL_laed
case_name: N. Clark LLC v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs (property owners accused of FHA violations) requested that HUD dismiss the discrimination complaint and charge against them and issue a corrective press release vindicating them.
key_holding: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiffs failed to exhaust their FTCA claims (no sum-certain monetary claim presented), their intentional tort claims were barred by the FTCA's intentional tort exception, HUD's decision to close the case without determination was committed to agency discretion, and HUD's press release was not a final agency action subject to APA review.
brief_summary: N. Clark LLC and Kathleen Cresson sued HUD and DOJ under the FTCA and APA seeking to have HUD dismiss a discrimination complaint and charge filed against them by the Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, and to compel HUD to issue a corrective press release. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding plaintiffs failed to exhaust FTCA administrative remedies, their intentional tort claims were barred, and HUD's actions were either committed to agency discretion or did not constitute final agency action subject to judicial review.
key_cases_cited: Hui v. Castaneda, 559 U.S. 799 (2010)
FDIC v. Meyer, 510 U.S. 471 (1994)
Millbrook v. U.S., 569 U.S. 50 (2012)
Bennett v. Spears, 520 U.S. 154 (1997)
Texas v. Cardona, 743 F. Supp. 3d 824 (N.D. Tex. 2024)

source_file: 10734649_2025_Michael Troy Wilkes v. San Mateo County Transit District (SAMTRANS), et al._cand
case_name: Michael Troy Wilkes v. San Mateo County Transit District (SAMTRANS), et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested court facility access accommodations and modifications to security policies to allow use of prosthetic inline skates as a mobility aid rather than wheelchair.
key_holding: The court dismissed the case as frivolous under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) because plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint curing deficiencies, failed to establish subject matter jurisdiction, violated local rules by filing motions without leave, and repeatedly ignored court orders despite warnings.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Michael Troy Wilkes, who uses prosthetic inline skates as a mobility aid for severe pelvic injuries, sued San Mateo County Transit District and numerous other defendants alleging ADA and Fair Housing Act violations related to access denials. The court dismissed the case with prejudice as frivolous under § 1915(e)(2) screening because plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint establishing jurisdiction, violated local procedural rules, and repeatedly ignored court orders despite warnings.

source_file: 10735679_2025_Delroy Askins v. Prestige Management Inc.; Lowell Hendricks_nysd
case_name: Delroy Askins v. Prestige Management Inc.; Lowell Hendricks
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was assaulted by building superintendent, denied access to community room, and had medical supplies stolen, all because of his disability (paraplegia/wheelchair use); no specific accommodation request was made.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because, even assuming he has a disability, he alleged no facts suggesting his disability motivated any adverse actions—the claim that the assault occurred 'because of his disability' was speculative without supporting facts from which a reasonable inference of discriminatory motivation could be drawn.
brief_summary: Delroy Askins, a paraplegic wheelchair user, sued Prestige Management and building superintendent Lowell Hendricks alleging assault, denial of community room access, and theft of medical supplies as discrimination because of his disability. The court dismissed the amended complaint, finding that plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting his disability motivated any adverse action—his conclusory assertion that the assault occurred 'because of his disability' was speculative and insufficient to state a FHA claim.
key_cases_cited: Palmer v. Fannie Mae, 755 F. App'x 43 (2d Cir. 2018)
Rodriguez v. Vill. Green Realty, Inc., 788 F.3d 31 (2d Cir. 2015)
Gladstone, Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Amato v. McGinty, 2022 WL 226798 (N.D.N.Y. 2022)

source_file: 10736151_2025_Jana Smith v. Mark Downey; Charles Olsen; Ariell Hartwell; Mark Simon; and Sherman Smith_ord
case_name: Jana Smith v. Mark Downey; Charles Olsen; Ariell Hartwell; Mark Simon; and Sherman Smith
accommodation_description: Not described in this order; the specific nature of the housing discrimination or accommodation at issue is not detailed in this procedural ruling, which addresses only the summary judgment motion and scheduling.
key_holding: The court denied Defendant Downey's motion for summary judgment because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding plaintiff's housing rights claims, and denied the parties' joint motion for a trial extension, maintaining the December 15, 2025 trial date limited to plaintiff's two federal claims under the Fair Housing Act and § 1985.
brief_summary: Jana Smith brought suit against Mark Downey and others alleging violation of the Fair Housing Act under 42 U.S.C. § 3604 and conspiracy to interfere with civil rights under 42 U.S.C. § 1985, among twelve total claims. Defendant Downey moved for summary judgment, arguing that Smith followed a pattern of destroying residences and then claiming housing rights violations, supporting his motion with declarations from a plumber, handyman, neighbor, and real estate agent. The court denied summary judgment because Smith's competing declaration created genuine disputes of material fact, denied the joint motion for a trial extension due to the age of the case, and ordered trial to proceed on December 15, 2025 limited to the two federal law claims.
key_cases_cited: Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)
Clicks Billiards, Inc. v. Sixshooters, Inc., 251 F.3d 1252 (9th Cir. 2001)

source_file: 10737104_2025_Dyshawn Underwood, individually, and as guardian of minor child K.U. v. Blue Leaf Residential Management, LLC, et al._ohsd
case_name: Dyshawn Underwood, individually, and as guardian of minor child K.U. v. Blue Leaf Residential Management, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: The complaint alleges refusal to accommodate K.U.'s disabilities but the specific accommodation request is not described in this procedural ruling.
key_holding: The court granted Cyclone's motion for leave to file a counterclaim because futility determinations are better made through a motion to dismiss than at the pleading stage.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Dyshawn Underwood, on behalf of herself and minor child K.U., sued defendants Blue Leaf Residential Management and Cyclone Columbus Park for refusing to accommodate K.U.'s disabilities and for retaliation under the Fair Housing Act. This opinion only addresses Cyclone's motion for leave to file a counterclaim for breach of contract and declaratory judgment, which the court granted without reaching the merits of the FHA claims.

source_file: 10737236_2025_Alicia Paschall v. Amber Andrade and Julie Hardison_waed
case_name: Alicia Paschall v. Amber Andrade and Julie Hardison
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request was made; the case involves a child custody dispute and constitutional claims against CPS and probation officials, with a brief FHA retaliation claim dismissed for failure to plead protected activity.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim because she failed to adequately plead she engaged in protected FHA activity or that defendants caused an adverse housing consequence causally linked to such activity, and failed to plausibly allege retaliatory motive.
brief_summary: Alicia Paschall, proceeding pro se, sued Federal Probation Officer Amber Andrade and CPS Supervisor Julie Hardison alleging constitutional violations, civil rights claims, and federal statutory claims stemming from the removal of her child in a Washington dependency proceeding. The district court dismissed her Third Amended Complaint for failure to state a claim, finding defendants immune from suit, plaintiff's claims barred by Rooker-Feldman doctrine and lack of standing, and her FHA retaliation claim deficient for failure to plead protected activity.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Food & Drug Admin. v. All. for Hippocratic Med.
San Pedro Hotel Co. v. City of Los Angeles

source_file: 10739169_2025_Asia Martin, et al. v. Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. and Ansonia Property Management, LLC_ilnd
case_name: Asia Martin, et al. v. Federal Home Loan Mortgage Corp. and Ansonia Property Management, LLC
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation request is identified in the opinion. The FHA and Rehabilitation Act claims are framed as disability discrimination arising from the allegedly uninhabitable and poorly maintained conditions of the apartment complex, with plaintiffs seeking injunctive relief to ensure they are not discriminated against due to their disabilities or left 'unable to sufficiently utilize the Property.'
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to stay proceedings, finding that neither Burford nor Colorado River abstention applied because the parallel state court building code enforcement action could not provide plaintiffs with monetary relief, eviction protection, or redress for disability discrimination and retaliation claims, and because defendants had themselves chosen the federal forum by removing several plaintiffs' cases.
brief_summary: Over twenty tenants of Ellis Lakeview Apartments in Chicago's Kenwood neighborhood sued Freddie Mac (the owner) and Ansonia Property Management for allegedly failing to maintain the complex in habitable condition, asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act (disability discrimination), the Rehabilitation Act, the Illinois Human Rights Act, the Chicago RLTO (including retaliation and security deposit violations), the Illinois Landlord Retaliation Act, the Illinois Consumer Fraud Act, breach of implied warranty of habitability, and breach of lease. Defendants moved to stay the federal action pending a longstanding City of Chicago building code enforcement lawsuit in state court, invoking Burford and Colorado River abstention doctrines. The court denied the stay, finding no real risk of disrupting the state proceeding, no adequacy of state-court relief for plaintiffs' monetary and disability-related claims, and noting that defendants had affirmatively chosen the federal forum by removing several plaintiffs' cases.
key_cases_cited: Burford v. Sun Oil Co., 319 U.S. 215 (1943)
Colorado River Water Conservation District v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Tyrer v. City of S. Beloit, 456 F.3d 744 (7th Cir. 2006)
Hartford Cas. Ins. Co. v. Borg-Warner Corp., 913 F.2d 419 (7th Cir. 1990)
Int'l Coll. of Surgeons v. City of Chicago, 153 F.3d 356 (7th Cir. 1996)

source_file: 10739282_2025_Trestle Creek Association v. Stephen R. Schooley, Jody F. Schooley_mtd
10740192_2025_Connie D. Parker v. PulteGroup, Inc., et al._mdd
case_name: Connie D. Parker v. PulteGroup, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request; case involves allegations of racial discrimination in home pricing and terms, with plaintiff claiming she was charged more than white neighbors for comparable homes.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motions to compel arbitration, finding the Home Purchase Agreement's broad arbitration clause enforceable and applicable to all of Parker's claims, including her Fair Housing Act and Civil Rights Act discrimination claims, despite Parker's arguments that she did not intend to arbitrate statutory discrimination claims.
brief_summary: Connie D. Parker, a 74-year-old Black U.S. Army veteran, sued PulteGroup, Inc. and related defendants alleging racial and age-based discrimination in the sale of a townhome in the Watershed community, claiming she was charged higher prices and down payments than white neighbors for comparable homes. The court granted defendants' motions to compel arbitration, finding the Home Purchase Agreement's broad arbitration clause was enforceable and covered all of Parker's claims including her Fair Housing Act and Civil Rights Act discrimination claims.
key_cases_cited: Adkins v. Lab. Ready, Inc., 303 F.3d 496 (4th Cir. 2002)
Green Tree Fin. Corp.-Ala. v. Randolph, 531 U.S. 79 (2000)
Hill v. Peoplesoft USA, Inc., 412 F.3d 540 (4th Cir. 2005)
Cheek v. United Healthcare of the Mid-Atlantic, Inc., 835 A.2d 656 (Md. 2003)
Stone v. Wells Fargo Bank, N.A., 361 F.3d 539 (D.Md. 2019)

source_file: 10740678_2025_John R. Fouts v. United States of America et al._kywd
case_name: John R. Fouts v. United States of America et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought ADA housing accommodations including prevention of eviction while holding a valid mainstream housing voucher, remediation of toxic mold and water leakage in his unit, safe housing with storage of medications and oxygen equipment outside a homeless shelter, housing for two certified registered emotional support animals, and access to medically necessary treatment and diet.
key_holding: The court dismissed the entire pro se action under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) for failure to state a claim, finding FHA and ADA allegations conclusory and lacking specific factual support, constitutional claims barred by sovereign and judicial immunity, and § 1983 claims against private defendants unsupported by state-actor allegations.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff John R. Fouts filed suit against a sprawling list of defendants—including the United States, Commonwealth of Kentucky, Louisville Metro Housing Authority, a private apartment complex (Station J-Town/New Chestnut Ridge Apts LLC), multiple technology companies, and three federal judges—alleging violations of the FHA, ADA, § 1983, Bivens, RICO, the False Claims Act, and state law, arising from his alleged eviction while holding a valid mainstream housing voucher, denial of ADA housing accommodations, and a wide range of other grievances including medical denial and digital surveillance. The court dismissed all federal claims on initial review under § 1915(e): claims against the United States and Commonwealth of Kentucky were barred by sovereign immunity; Bivens claims against the three federal judges were barred by judicial immunity; § 1983 claims against private defendants failed for lack of state-actor allegations; the Louisville Metro Housing Authority was not a suable 'person' under § 1983; and FHA/ADA claims against the housing authority and apartment complex were dismissed for being purely conclusory without supporting factual allegations. State-law claims were dismissed without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.

source_file: 10740712_2025_United States of America ex rel. Eric J. Russell v. The City of Columbus_ohsd
10740783_2025_Hlevictor A. Hoskins, Jr. and Tracey R. Young v. Plaza Place Owners Association, Inc. and Associa Principal Management Group of Houston_txsd
case_name: Hlevictor A. Hoskins, Jr. and Tracey R. Young v. Plaza Place Owners Association, Inc. and Associa Principal Management Group of Houston
accommodation_description: The order does not detail the specific accommodation request; the complaint alleges FHA and ADA violations but the ruling only addresses procedural requirements for TRO.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' emergency motion for temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction because plaintiffs failed to demonstrate substantial likelihood of success on the merits through unsubstantiated allegations and failed to show irreparable harm beyond speculative consequences from non-payment of disputed charges.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Hlevictor Hoskins and Tracey Young sued their homeowners association and property management company for ADA and FHA violations, also bringing state law claims for breach of fiduciary duty and negligence. The court denied their emergency motion for temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, finding they failed to meet the requirements for extraordinary relief.
key_cases_cited: Guillory v. PPG Industries Inc, 434 F.3d 303 (5th Cir. 2005)
United States v. Wilson, 864 F.2d 1219 (5th Cir. 1989)

source_file: 10741156_2025_Jessica Berk v. Ritz Condominium Association, et al._njd
case_name: Jessica Berk v. Ritz Condominium Association, et al.
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation or modification requested by plaintiff is not described in this opinion; the court dismissed the matter on procedural grounds and noted that a fuller recounting of plaintiff's allegations appears at ECF No. 40.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA and 42 U.S.C. § 3617 claims with prejudice for lack of prosecution under Rule 41(b) because plaintiff willfully abandoned her case by repeatedly failing to appear for court conferences and comply with court orders, rendering Poulis balancing unnecessary.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Jessica Berk filed suit against Ritz Condominium Association and Stanley Maragoudakis asserting claims under 42 U.S.C. § 3617, fraud, Fair Housing Act violations, and civil rights violations. Over a six-month period, plaintiff failed to attend multiple court-ordered conferences, failed to respond to an order to show cause, and failed to move to reinstate the case within the court's 90-day deadline. The court dismissed the case with prejudice for lack of prosecution under Rule 41(b), finding that plaintiff's willful abandonment rendered the Poulis balancing analysis unnecessary.
key_cases_cited: Poulis v. State Farm Fire & Cas. Co., 747 F.2d 863 (3d Cir. 1984)
Spain v. Gallegos, 25 F.3d 439 (3d Cir. 1994)
Ricks v. Udijohn, No. 14-04079, 2017 WL 53706 (D.N.J. Jan. 4, 2017)
Mindek v. Rigatti, 964 F.2d 1369 (3d Cir. 1992)

source_file: 10741255_2025_Jimmy Keels Williamson v. Christian Recovery Centers, Inc._nced
case_name: Jimmy Keels Williamson v. Christian Recovery Centers, Inc.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff's complaint, which was screened for failure to state a claim, referenced disability accommodation in housing context at a recovery center.
key_holding: Upon reviewing the magistrate judge's recommendation with no objections filed, the district court dismissed plaintiff's FHA disability discrimination claim without prejudice for failure to state a claim, while allowing plaintiff's FHA racial discrimination claim to proceed.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jimmy Keels Williamson sued Christian Recovery Centers, Inc., a recovery center operator, alleging race discrimination and disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, Title VII, and ADA. Upon screening under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e), the court dismissed plaintiff's disability discrimination claims (including FHA reasonable accommodation claim) without prejudice for failure to state a claim, but allowed the FHA racial discrimination claim to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Diamond v. Colonial Life & Acc. Ins. Co., 416 F.3d 310 (4th Cir. 2005)
Camby v. Davis, 718 F.2d 198 (4th Cir. 1983)

source_file: 10741283_2025_Concern for Independent Living, Inc. v. Town of Southampton, New York, and Town Board of the Town of Southampton_nyed
case_name: Concern for Independent Living, Inc. v. Town of Southampton, New York, and Town Board of the Town of Southampton
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought permission and the opportunity to construct Liberty Gardens, an affordable housing development intended for persons with disabilities, in the unincorporated community of Tuckahoe within the Town of Southampton—construction that Defendants allegedly blocked through unlawful and discriminatory conduct.
key_holding: The magistrate judge denied plaintiff's motion to lift the stay of discovery, finding no change in circumstances justified vacating the stay while the motion to dismiss remained pending with oral argument already scheduled.
brief_summary: Concern for Independent Living, Inc., a non-profit organization, sued the Town of Southampton and its Town Board for allegedly using unlawful and discriminatory conduct to prevent the construction of Liberty Gardens, an affordable housing development in the unincorporated community of Tuckahoe, in violation of the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and New York Human Rights Law. Discovery had been stayed pending resolution of a motion to dismiss. The magistrate judge denied plaintiff's motion to lift the stay, concluding that no changed circumstances existed to warrant vacating it, particularly given that oral argument on the motion to dismiss was already scheduled before the district judge for January 9, 2026.

source_file: 10742406_2025_David D. Crossett v. Douglas Shumway, and Carriage Crossing Homeowners Association, Inc._utd
case_name: David D. Crossett v. Douglas Shumway and Carriage Crossing Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for two additional live-in aides beyond the one already approved by the HOA, to assist with daily movement, glucose monitoring, insulin preparation, and safety needs due to legal blindness, diabetes, and bipolar disorder.
key_holding: The court denied Crossett's emergency motions for injunctive relief because he failed to show the requested accommodation of two additional live-in aides is reasonable, a required element of an FHA reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
brief_summary: Plaintiff David Crossett, a condominium owner with legal blindness, diabetes, and bipolar disorder, sued his homeowners association seeking to compel approval of two additional live-in aides beyond the one already permitted. The court denied Crossett's emergency motions for temporary injunctive relief, finding he failed to establish a likelihood of success on the merits because he did not demonstrate the requested accommodation of two additional live-in aides is reasonable under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Carlson v. Carrington Square LLC, 2025 WL 1017536 (D. Utah Apr. 4, 2025)
Courage to Change Ranches Holding Co. v. El Paso Cnty., 73 F.4th 1175 (10th Cir. 2023)
Arnal v. Aspen View Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 226 F. Supp. 3d 1177 (D. Colo. 2016)

source_file: 10743592_2025_JAMES B. HERRERA v. MADDOX MANAGEMENT, LLC_nmd
case_name: James B. Herrera v. Maddox Management, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendant submitted false rental verifications to prospective landlords, interfering with his Section 8 voucher use, and ignored his requests for reasonable accommodations for his disabilities.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims fail because he failed to plausibly allege a connection between his disability or protected activity and the alleged adverse action, and he did not adequately plead disability status, causation, or discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: James Herrera sued Maddox Management, LLC alleging Fair Housing Act violations, procedural due process claims, and Rehabilitation Act claims stemming from the landlord's alleged submission of false rental verifications and failure to accommodate his disabilities. The court denied Defendant's motion to dismiss but ordered Plaintiff to show cause why his case should not be dismissed for failure to state plausible claims, finding the complaint failed to adequately plead disability, causation, or discriminatory intent.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Morgan v. Carrington Mortg. Servs., 719 F. App'x 735 (10th Cir. 2017)
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr., Inc. v. St. George City, 685 F.3d 917 (10th Cir. 2012)
Hatfield v. Cottages on 78th Cmty. Ass'n, No. 21-4035 (10th Cir. 2022)

source_file: 10743632_2025_Raphael Jackson, et al. v. Mills Properties, Inc., et al._moed
case_name: Raphael Jackson, et al. v. Mills Properties, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs' email to landlord requesting accommodation for high-risk pregnancy and suicidal ideation, characterizing it as a request for reasonable accommodation to avoid eviction.
key_holding: The Court dismissed the federal action without prejudice under Rooker-Feldman doctrine and other abstention doctrines because parallel state-court proceedings involving the same eviction and FHA claims were already pending, depriving the federal court of subject-matter jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Individual tenants Raphael Jackson and Chaley Grant sued Mills Properties, Inc. and related entities alleging Fair Housing Act violations arising from eviction proceedings they claim were discriminatory retaliation for requesting accommodations related to high-risk pregnancy and suicidal ideation. The Court dismissed the federal action without prejudice under Rooker-Feldman, Younger, and Colorado River abstention doctrines because parallel state-court proceedings involving identical eviction and FHA claims were already pending, depriving the federal court of jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Hageman v. Barton, 817 F.3d 611 (8th Cir. 2016)
Jacobs v. Gear Prop., 2 F. App'x 617 (8th Cir. 2001)
Newell v. Rolling Hills Apartments, 134 F. Supp. 2d 1026 (N.D. Iowa 2001)

case_name: Desiree Knight v. Macon Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for minimum rent hardship adjustment as a reasonable accommodation for anxiety and ADHD
key_holding: Knight's FHA failure-to-accommodate claim was dismissed because she failed to plausibly allege how her requested accommodations (special inspection, rent hardship adjustment) were necessary to alleviate the effects of her anxiety and ADHD, as she did not explain how these impairments limit her major life activities.
brief_summary: Desiree Knight, a Section 8 voucher holder with anxiety and ADHD, sued Macon Housing Authority alleging failures to accommodate, FHA retaliation, Section 504 discrimination, and due process violations. The court dismissed her FHA failure-to-accommodate and retaliation claims without prejudice, finding she failed to plead sufficient facts showing how her requested special inspection, rent hardship adjustment, and VAWA transfer were necessary accommodations for her disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Philippeaux v. Apartment Inv. & Mgmt. Co., 598 F. App'x 640 (11th Cir. 2015)
Wright v. City of Roanoke Redevelopment & Housing Auth., 479 U.S. 418 (1987)

source_file: 10744240_2025_Irvin G. Murray v. U.S. Treasury, et al._paed
case_name: Irvin G. Murray v. U.S. Treasury, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested. Murray sought restoration of his housing voucher and housing rights at 5138 Reno Street in Philadelphia, claiming he had been denied housing and evicted in retaliation for attempting to reclaim a purported $43 million inherited FHA judgment, not based on any disability or other protected characteristic.
key_holding: The court dismissed Murray's complaint in its entirety as factually frivolous and for failure to state a claim, including his FHA retaliation claim, because Murray failed to allege that he was discriminated against or retaliated against on account of membership in a protected class rather than for attempting to reclaim a purported $43 million inheritance.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Irvin Murray sued numerous federal, state, and local government entities and private individuals alleging a broad conspiracy to steal his claimed $43 million inheritance and to retaliate against him—including by denying him housing—for attempting to recover it. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915 and dismissed all claims as factually frivolous, finding the allegations wholly incredible, and alternatively as legally baseless on sovereign immunity, Eleventh Amendment, Monell, statute of limitations, and state-action grounds. The court also dismissed a liberally construed FHA retaliation claim because Murray predicated it solely on retaliation for pursuing an inheritance rather than on discrimination tied to a protected class, which is an essential element of any FHA claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Holley v. Dep't of Veteran Affairs, 165 F.3d 244 (3d Cir. 1999)
Lloyd v. Presby's Inspired Life, 251 F. Supp. 3d 891 (E.D. Pa. 2017)
Davis v. Rubin, 2020 WL 7624833 (E.D. Pa. Dec. 22, 2020)

source_file: 10744257_2025_Robert A. Johnson v. Raven Wood Homeowners Association, et al._wawd
case_name: Robert A. Johnson v. Raven Wood Homeowners Association, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to participate in HOA meetings virtually as a reasonable accommodation for disability
key_holding: The court set aside the entry of default against Mr. Krieger, finding he did not act in bad faith or with culpable intent, has a meritorious defense (including an argument that he reasonably accommodated plaintiff's request to participate in HOA meetings virtually), and plaintiff would not suffer prejudice.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Robert Johnson brought Fair Housing Act claims against the HOA and its former president Mr. Krieger; after default was entered against Krieger, he moved to set aside the default. The Court granted Krieger's motion, finding no culpable conduct, a meritorious defense that he reasonably accommodated Johnson's request to participate in meetings virtually, and no prejudice to Johnson.

case_name: Anthony Alfieri v. Cortland Management LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiff alleges discrimination based on familial status (having a minor child) and retaliation for filing a HUD complaint.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims under § 3604(b) and § 3617 because plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual facts showing concrete adverse action or causal link between the alleged harms and his protected class status.
brief_summary: Anthony Alfieri sued Cortland Management LLC alleging the landlord discriminated against him based on familial status by targeting his four-year-old daughter with repeated noise complaints and threatened eviction, and retaliated against him by raising his rent after he filed a HUD complaint. The court dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, finding Alfieri failed to allege sufficient facts showing concrete adverse action or a causal connection between the alleged harms and his protected class status.
key_cases_cited: Morris v. W. Hayden Ests. First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
United States v. City of Hayward, 36 F.3d 832 (9th Cir. 1994)
Ohio House, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa, 135 F.4th 645 (9th Cir. 2025)

source_file: 10745833_2025_Mekal Faruki v. Housing Authority for the County of Sacramento, et al._caed
case_name: Mekal Faruki v. Housing Authority for the County of Sacramento, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reasonable accommodation in processing his Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher application, including consideration of his certified disability, after defendants allegedly lost his application and failed to respond for years.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim was dismissed for failure to state a claim because his allegations were speculative and lacked specific supporting facts necessary to state a claim for relief, and his claim that a similarly situated friend was treated more favorably failed to suggest disability discrimination since that friend is also disabled.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Mekal Faruki, an elderly individual with Multiple Myeloma, sued the Housing Authority for the County of Sacramento and related entities alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by losing his Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher application and failing to accommodate his disability over years of follow-up. The magistrate judge recommended dismissing the complaint without leave to amend for failure to state a plausible FHA claim, finding the allegations speculative and failing to plead facts showing disability-based discrimination since plaintiff's friend who received more favorable treatment was also disabled.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Lovell v. Chandler, 303 F.3d 1039 (9th Cir. 2002)
Duvall v. County of Kitsap, 260 F.3d 1124 (9th Cir. 2001)

source_file: 10746118_2025_Sean Murphy v. Brixworth Homeowners Ass'n, Inc._ca6
case_name: Sean Murphy; Denise Pagels, et al. v. Brixworth Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; Murphy alleged that the HOA violated the FHA and ADA by enforcing its covenant prohibiting yard signs and banning him from community amenities (pool and common spaces) as a result of his non-compliance, claiming membership in a protected class under the FHA.
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment on the pleadings, holding that Murphy's complaint's explicit invocation of the Fair Housing Act and ADA gave the district court proper federal-question jurisdiction, and that the district judge committed no reversible error in accepting the related case or refusing to recuse.
brief_summary: Sean Murphy sued the Brixworth HOA after it told him to remove large political yard signs and banned him and his family from community amenities until he complied. Murphy's complaint in Tennessee state court alleged breach of contract and violations of the Fair Housing Act and Americans with Disabilities Act; the HOA removed the case to federal court. The Sixth Circuit affirmed the district court's grant of judgment on the pleadings, rejecting Murphy's arguments that no federal claims existed in his complaint, that reassignment to Chief Judge McDonough was improper, and that the judge should have recused himself.
key_cases_cited: Smolarek v. Chrysler Corp., 879 F.2d 1326 (6th Cir. 1989)
Davet v. City of Cleveland, 456 F.3d 549 (6th Cir. 2006)
Liteky v. United States, 510 U.S. 540 (1994)

source_file: 10746417_2025_T_R PROPERTIES, INC., et al. v. BERLIN TOWNSHIP, et al._ohsd
case_name: T&R Properties, Inc., et al. v. Berlin Township, et al.
accommodation_description: This discovery ruling does not involve a reasonable accommodation request; the underlying case involves challenges to zoning decisions allegedly motivated by racial discrimination and familial status.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motion to stay discovery because their Rooker-Feldman jurisdictional arguments were fairly debatable rather than certain to bar the case, and Defendants overstated the hardship of resuming limited depositions.
brief_summary: T&R Properties sued Berlin Township alleging the Township engaged in intentional and disparate impact racial discrimination in zoning decisions and denied housing to families with children in violation of the Fair Housing Act. This Opinion & Order denies Defendants' motion to stay discovery, finding their jurisdictional objections were fairly debatable and did not warrant pausing the case.
key_cases_cited: Ohio Valley Bank Co. v. MetaBank
Shanks v. Honda of Am. Mfg.
Hahn v. Star Bank
Seattle House, LLC v. City of Delaware
Ohio Bell Tel. Co., Inc. v. Global NAPs Ohio, Inc.

case_name: Manal Farhan v. 2715 NMA LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to display a Palestinian flag in her apartment window to express her heritage, and was evicted when she refused to comply with defendants' neutrality policy.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that Farhan's complaint failed to plausibly allege that defendants enforced a neutrality policy against her because of her national origin rather than her political expression in support of the Palestinian cause, and that her disparate impact claim failed without any statistical evidence showing the policy disproportionately affected Palestinian tenants.
brief_summary: Manal Farhan, a Palestinian American, sued her apartment building's owner and operator after they ordered her to remove a Palestinian flag from her window pursuant to a neutrality policy regarding the Israel-Palestine conflict and then terminated her tenancy when she refused. The Seventh Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, finding Farhan's complaint failed to plausibly allege intentional national origin discrimination or disparate impact because the eviction was motivated by her political expression rather than her protected status, and she provided no statistical evidence of disparate impact.
key_cases_cited: Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)

case_name: Manal Farhan v. 2715 NMA LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff is a Palestinian American who was told to remove a Palestinian flag from her apartment window and was subsequently evicted under a 'neutrality' policy.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal because Farhan failed to plead facts showing defendants' neutrality policy was created or applied 'because of' her national origin rather than viewpoint neutrality regarding the Israel-Palestine conflict, and she effectively pleaded herself out of court by characterizing her claim as viewpoint discrimination.
brief_summary: Manal Farhan, a Palestinian American tenant, sued her landlord under the Fair Housing Act alleging national origin discrimination after being told to remove a Palestinian flag from her apartment window and subsequently evicted under a 'neutrality' policy. The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that Farhan failed to plead facts showing defendants enforced the policy because of her national origin rather than viewpoint neutrality, and that she effectively pleaded herself out of court by characterizing her claim as viewpoint discrimination rather than protected-class discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Swanson v. Citibank, N.A., 614 F.3d 400 (7th Cir. 2010)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

source_file: 10748104_2025_61 East Main Street Associates, LLC, and Moche Halpern v. The Village of Washingtonville, Thomas Devinko, in his official and individual capacities, Donna Jacaruso, in her official and individual capacities
case_name: 61 East Main Street Associates, LLC, and Moche Halpern v. The Village of Washingtonville
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, an Orthodox Jewish developer and LLC, allege discriminatory denial of approval for a multi-unit residential development based on anti-Semitic animus.
key_holding: The Court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that Plaintiffs' claims were not ripe because no final determination was issued on their site plan application and Plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that the futility exception applied to excuse the finality requirement.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs, an Orthodox Jewish real estate developer and his LLC, sued the Village of Washingtonville and individual officials alleging Fair Housing Act, Equal Protection, Due Process, and civil conspiracy claims based on alleged anti-Semitic animus motivating delays and denial of their multi-unit residential development project. The Court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the claims were not ripe because the Village had not issued a final determination on the site plan application and Plaintiffs failed to meet the high standard required to invoke the futility exception to the finality requirement.
key_cases_cited: Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton Bank, 473 U.S. 172 (1985)
Vill. Green at Sayville, LLC v. Town of Islip, 43 F.4th 287 (2d Cir. 2022)
Murphy v. New Milford Zoning Comm'n, 402 F.3d 342 (2d Cir. 2005)
Sherman v. Town of Chester, 752 F.3d 554 (2d Cir. 2014)
Sunrise Detox V, LLC v. City of White Plains, 769 F.3d 118 (2d Cir. 2014)

source_file: 10748138_2025_Williams Victor Funes Nunez v. Morgan Properties LLC, et al._njd
case_name: Williams Victor Funes Nunez v. Morgan Properties LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to be moved to a first-floor unit for five-year-old child with autism
key_holding: The court denied the TRO/preliminary injunction because the Anti-Injunction Act bars federal courts from enjoining state court eviction proceedings, and plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable harm for his other requested relief.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Williams Victor Funes Nunez filed an emergency motion seeking to halt state court eviction proceedings and obtain FHA/ADA accommodations for his autistic child, including transfer to a first-floor unit. The court denied the motion under the Anti-Injunction Act, which bars federal courts from enjoining state eviction proceedings absent narrow statutory exceptions that do not apply here, and found plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable harm.
key_cases_cited: In re Prudential Ins. Co. of Am. Sales Pracs. Litig., 314 F.3d 99 (3d Cir. 2002)
Poussaint v. Mendlowitz, No. 24-5387, 2024 WL 4543062 (E.D. Pa. Oct. 22, 2024)
In re Diet Drugs, 282 F.3d 220 (3d Cir. 2002)
Reilly v. City of Harrisburg, 858 F.3d 173 (3d Cir. 2017)
Ferring Pharms., Inc. v. Watson Pharms., Inc., 765 F.3d 205 (3d Cir. 2014)

source_file: 10748519_2025_Karen Denise Price, individually and as executor and sole beneficiary of the Estate of Dennis H. Buie v. FCI Lender Services, et al._gand
case_name: Karen Denise Price, individually and as executor and sole beneficiary of the Estate of Dennis H. Buie v. FCI Lender Services, et al.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - No reasonable accommodation claim analyzed; this is a transfer order addressing venue.
key_holding: The Court transferred the action to the Northern District of Georgia because the property at issue is located there, all defendants are found or transact business there, and a substantial portion of alleged events occurred in that district, making it the proper and more convenient venue.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Karen Denise Price, proceeding pro se and seeking in forma pauperis status, filed this action in the Southern District of New York against 50 defendants asserting eleven federal claims including Fair Housing Act claims arising from real property located in Atlanta, Georgia. The Court transferred the action to the Northern District of Georgia under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) because venue was proper there (property location, defendant contacts, and locus of operative facts) and that forum was more convenient for all parties and witnesses.

source_file: 10748536_2025_Lance Frazier v. Justin Luther, Individually and d_b_a Luther Properties, LLC, Phillip Kennedy, and Angie Kennedy_msnd
case_name: Lance Frazier v. Justin Luther, Individually and d/b/a Luther Properties, LLC, Phillip Kennedy, and Angie Kennedy
accommodation_description: Racial discrimination claim under the Fair Housing Act, not a reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court granted the motion to quash because the subpoenas seeking all text messages, phone calls, photos, and videos over a six-month period were grossly overly broad and sought irrelevant information that would capture private communications entirely unrelated to the case.
brief_summary: Lance Frazier sued Luther Properties, LLC and others for racial discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, along with state law claims for conversion, trespass, and negligent infliction of emotional distress. This order grants the motion to quash overly broad subpoenas served on telecommunications companies seeking six months of all text messages, calls, photos, and videos from multiple phone numbers, as the subpoenas captured volumes of irrelevant private communications unrelated to the case.
key_cases_cited: Crescent City Remodeling, LLC v. CMR Constr. & Roofing, LLC, 643 F. Supp. 3d 613 (E.D. La. 2022)

source_file: 10748635_2025_Duc L. Trinh and Sally Y. Ly v. La Jolla Racquet Club Condominium Owners’ Association, Inc., et al._casd
case_name: Duc L. Trinh and Sally Y. Ly v. La Jolla Racquet Club Condominium Owners' Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested reasonable accommodations for safe ingress and egress due to Plaintiff Ly's wheelchair-bound disability after the parking garage—the sole accessible route to her unit—was closed.
key_holding: The court found Plaintiffs' reasonable accommodation claims survived the low threshold for IFP screening, while dismissing the Elder Abuse Act claim for failure to allege Defendants were care custodians.
brief_summary: Vietnamese tenants in a La Jolla condominium allege the HOA refused reasonable accommodations for wheelchair access after closing the parking garage—the only accessible route to their unit—and demanded invasive residency verification while allegedly targeting them based on their race/ethnicity. The court granted IFP status and e-filing, dismissed only the Elder Abuse Act claim without leave to amend, and allowed the Fair Housing Act and other claims to proceed past screening.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

source_file: 10749500_2025_Shyane Harden v. Kier Management; Michelle Tipplette; and Lindsay Borke_utd
case_name: Shyane Harden v. Kier Management; Michelle Tipplette; and Lindsay Borke
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was retaliated against for complaining about not receiving an income-based rent subsidy or reduction despite completing required certifications.
key_holding: Plaintiff fails to state an FHA retaliation claim because she did not allege she was engaged in the exercise of fair housing rights or that defendants were motivated by discriminatory intent; her complaint about not receiving a rent subsidy despite completing certifications does not constitute protected activity under the FHA.
brief_summary: Shyane Harden, a tenant at Bramblewood Apartments in Ogden, Utah, sued Kier Management and two employees for retaliatory eviction under the Fair Housing Act, claiming they attempted to evict her in retaliation for her complaints about not receiving a rent subsidy despite completing required certifications. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a plausible FHA claim because Harden did not allege she engaged in protected fair housing activity or that defendants were motivated by discriminatory intent, and granted her leave to amend by December 29, 2025.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Hatfield v. Cottages on 78th Cmty. Ass'n

case_name: McCready v. Re/Max Achievers
accommodation_description: This opinion addresses discovery sanctions for late document production; the underlying FHA claim concerns Re/Max's management of the property where a sober home operated that led to plaintiff's eviction.
key_holding: The court denied default judgment as disproportionate but imposed alternative sanctions including attorneys' fees, prohibition on Re/Max blaming co-defendants for negligence, and allowing plaintiff to control use of late-produced documents at trial.
brief_summary: John McCready sued Re/Max Achievers and other defendants for Fair Housing Act violations arising from his eviction from a sober home in Pottstown; this opinion addresses Re/Max's motion for sanctions due to discovery failures including the late production of over 600 pages of text messages and documents.
key_cases_cited: Poulis v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Co.
Hildebrand v. Allegheny County
Briscoe v. Klaus

10752477_2025_Cahail v. United States of America, The_ksd
case_name: Karen Cahail and Rachel Cahail v. United States of America, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs request appointment of counsel as an accommodation for disabilities including PTSD and physical impairments.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' renewed motion for appointment of counsel, finding that while plaintiffs cannot afford counsel and have disabilities, these factors do not distinguish them from other pro se litigants and do not establish exceptional circumstances warranting appointment.
brief_summary: Karen and Rachel Cahail, proceeding pro se, filed a renewed motion requesting the appointment of counsel as an accommodation for their disabilities (PTSD and physical impairments). The court denied the motion, finding that plaintiffs' inability to afford counsel and their disabilities did not establish exceptional circumstances to distinguish them from other self-represented litigants.
key_cases_cited: McLain v. Sedgwick Co. Sheriff's Office, No. 25-4036-JWB-BGS, 2025 WL 1696525 (D. Kan. June 17, 2025)
Beaudry v. Corr. Corp. of Am., 331 F.3d 1164 (10th Cir. 2003)

George v. Payne-Delano, No. 24-2132-JWL, 2024 WL 3826124 (D. Kan. Aug. 14, 2024)

source_file: 10754293_2025_Stephen Gray, et al. v. Warren Verbanec, et al._cand
case_name: Stephen Gray, et al. v. Warren Verbanec, et al.
race_if_mentioned: Not specified; complaint references race, color, sex, national origin, and age generally without identifying plaintiff's specific race
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; the case involved allegations of ongoing harassment, racial discrimination, intimidation, and financial exploitation by a private HOA and associated individuals over an eleven-year period.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint with prejudice because pro se plaintiffs failed to allege facts showing that defendant Warren Verbanec, a private HOA member, acted under color of state law as required for a §1983 claim, and the complaint lacked any specific factual allegations supporting the conclusory claims of conspiracy and discrimination.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Stephen and Mikyong Gray filed suit against Warren Verbanec and others, alleging an eleven-year conspiracy to deprive Ms. Gray of civil rights through harassment and discrimination based on race, color, sex, national origin, and age, invoking 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1983, 1985(3), and 3601–3619 (Fair Housing Act). The court construed the complaint as a single §1983 claim on behalf of Ms. Gray only. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding that the complaint failed to allege facts showing Verbanec acted under color of state law—since the Sunset Ridge Road Association is a private HOA and not a governmental entity—and that the complaint was entirely devoid of specific factual allegations to support its conclusory claims of conspiracy and discrimination.

source_file: 10754314_2025_Jacqueline Huskey and Ritan Wynn, on behalf of themselves and all others similarly situated v. State Farm Fire _ Casualty Company_ilnd
case_name: Jacqueline Huskey and Ritan Wynn, on behalf of themselves and all others similarly situated v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Company
accommodation_description: Class action alleging State Farm's algorithmic decision-making tools for homeowners insurance claims have a disparate impact on Black policyholders
key_holding: The court granted in part State Farm's motion to compel production of survey data but protected counsel-expert communications as work product, and denied discovery of third-party litigation funding documents as irrelevant to the claims.
brief_summary: Black homeowners brought a class action against State Farm alleging its algorithmic insurance claims handling tools have a disparate impact on Black policyholders in violation of the FHA. The court ruled on a discovery motion, ordering plaintiffs to produce survey data but protecting counsel-expert communications as work product and denying discovery into litigation funding arrangements.
key_cases_cited: In re Turkey Antitrust Litig., 2022 WL 797180 (N.D. Ill. Mar. 16, 2022)
Trs. of Chicago Reg'l Council of Carpenters Pension Fund v. Drive Constr., Inc., 2022 WL 2341290 (N.D. Ill. June 29, 2022)
Sandra T.E. v. S. Berwyn Sch. Dist. 100, 600 F.3d 612 (7th Cir. 2010)
OTR Transportation, Inc. v. Data Interfuse, LLC, 2022 WL 296056 (N.D. Ill. Feb. 1, 2022)
Dover v. British Airways, PLC, 2014 WL 5090021 (E.D.N.Y. Oct. 9, 2014)

source_file: 10754452_2025_Michael S. McLain and Rosalee Janette McLain v. Board of County Commissioners of Sedgwick County, Kansas, et al._ksd
case_name: Michael S. McLain and Rosalee Janette McLain v. Board of County Commissioners of Sedgwick County, Kansas, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Michael McLain alleges he was blocked from the City of Goddard's Facebook page in retaliation for exercising rights under the ADA and FHA, including requests for PTSD accommodations during an arrest.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 fails because the Goddard Defendants do not engage in any regulated activities under §§ 3603-3606 (sale/rental of housing, residential real estate transactions, or brokerage services), so blocking Plaintiffs from a Facebook page cannot constitute retaliation for exercising Fair Housing Act rights.
brief_summary: Michael and Rosalee McLain sued the City of Goddard and other defendants alleging, inter alia, that the City blocked Mr. McLain from its Facebook page in retaliation for exercising rights under the ADA and FHA. The court granted the Goddard Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that Plaintiffs failed to plead a plausible FHA retaliation claim because the City does not engage in any regulated housing activities under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Monell v. Dep't of Social Serv. of City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Zhu v. Countrywide Realty, Co., 165 F. Supp. 2d 1181 (D. Kan. 2001)

case_name: Desiree Knight v. Macon Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Knight requested inspection accommodations, unit transfer, and a minimum rent hardship exemption from Macon Housing Authority as reasonable accommodations.
key_holding: The Court denied the TRO because Knight failed to establish substantial likelihood of success on the merits, as the alleged due process violation (a hearing presided over by a non-impartial MHA employee) had not yet occurred when the motion was filed.
brief_summary: Desiree Knight, proceeding in forma pauperis, filed a motion for a temporary restraining order against Macon Housing Authority alleging reasonable accommodation denials related to inspection, transfer, and minimum rent hardship requests. The Court denied the TRO motion and had previously dismissed Knight's Fair Housing Act and Rehabilitation Act claims, allowing only her due process claim to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Cate v. Oldham, 707 F.2d 1176 (11th Cir. 1983)
Fernandez-Roque v. Smith, 671 F.2d 426 (11th Cir. 1982)
Parker v. State Bd. of Pardons & Paroles, 275 F.3d 1032 (11th Cir. 2001)

Four Seasons Hotels & Resorts, B.V. v. Consorcio Barr, S.A., 320 F.3d 1205 (11th Cir. 2003)

10755748_2025_Dominic Son v. Oakmont Properties-Azure, LLC, et al._nvd
case_name: Dominic Son v. Oakmont Properties-Azure, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested assistance with his account and late fees via email to the property manager, communicating his adjustment disorder diagnosis as a basis for the requested help.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's federal claims with prejudice because the allegations were too conclusory and speculative to state plausible claims for relief under the pleading standards of Ashcroft v. Iqbal and Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Dominic Son, an Asian-American with adjustment disorder, sued Oakmont Properties-Azure LLC and FPI Management (property owners/managers) and Reno Housing Authority, alleging race and disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and constitutional claims arising from his apartment lease at Azure Apartments in Sparks, Nevada. The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation and dismissed all federal claims with prejudice, finding Plaintiff's allegations too conclusory and speculative to state plausible claims for relief.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
