source_file: 10755962_2025_Bernard T. Anderson Bey v. Roc Nation LLC, et al._nysd
case_name: Bernard T. Anderson Bey v. Roc Nation LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged NYCHA discriminated against him by conducting lead testing as a guise to illegally evict him and his daughter from his public housing residence.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim against NYCHA because his allegations were conclusory and failed to provide factual support showing adverse treatment based on a protected classification, in addition to dismissing the entire action based on violations of an anti-filing injunction from a prior case.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Bernard T. Anderson Bey sued Roc Nation LLC, Sean Carter, Live Nation, Coinbase, NYCHA, REDC, and the IRS alleging antitrust violations, discrimination, and fraud, claiming music industry defendants conspired to sabotage his career and influenced government agencies including NYCHA to evict him from his public housing unit. The court dismissed the entire action with prejudice based on violations of an anti-filing injunction from a prior case, and alternatively dismissed the FHA claim against NYCHA for failure to state plausible factual allegations of intentional discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Avila v. New York City Hous. Auth., No. 24-CV-6680 (LTS) (S.D.N.Y. Oct. 25, 2024)

source_file: 10756321_2025_Anthony Montero v. New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA), et al._nysd
case_name: Anthony Montero v. New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA), et al.
accommodation_description: The order does not describe any specific accommodation request; it addresses only service of process and party addition under Rule 21.
key_holding: The court directed service on most defendants in this pro se IFP action asserting FHA retaliation and disability discrimination claims, added Yolanda Padilla as a defendant under Rule 21, and withheld service on four defendants pending a fourth amended complaint with sufficient factual allegations about their involvement.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Anthony Montero, a Bronx resident, filed suit against NYCHA, Building Management Associates, and numerous individual officials, asserting claims of retaliation and disability discrimination under the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, FHA, and 42 U.S.C. § 1983, as well as state law claims. The court, having granted IFP status, issued this Order of Service directing the Clerk to add Yolanda Padilla as a defendant under Rule 21 because Plaintiff clearly intended to name her but inadvertently omitted her from the caption. The court directed USMS service on most defendants but withheld service on Gigante, Diaz, Warren, and Mikrut due to the absence of any factual allegations about their involvement, granting leave to file a fourth amended complaint.

source_file: 10756893_2025_Felice Lazae Martin, et al. v. Michael Castillo, et al._caed
case_name: Felice Lazae Martin, et al. v. Michael Castillo, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested to be excused from rent payments during the period they searched for alternative housing after one plaintiff became bedridden due to autistic burnout, catatonia, and neurological effects from alleged toxic mold exposure, and later contracted pneumonia that prevented her from working and earning income, rendering them unable to afford immediate relocation from the uninhabitable property.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommended dismissal without prejudice with leave to amend because plaintiffs failed to establish federal subject matter jurisdiction, failed to plead state action required for § 1983 claims against private defendants, failed to state cognizable ADA claims, and made only two cursory references to the Fair Housing Act without any supporting facts.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Felice Lazae Martin and Hector Joseph Borges sued their landlord Michael Castillo and his attorney for claims arising from toxic mold conditions and lack of heating in their rental property, an alleged illegal lockout, failure of law enforcement to intervene, and a 43-day shutdown of the Kern County Superior Court's e-filing system. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915 and found that § 1983 claims failed because neither defendant was a state actor, ADA claims failed because the proper defendant (the County) was not named and no accommodation request was adequately pled, and FHA claims were supported only by two cursory references with no specific facts. The magistrate judge recommended dismissal without prejudice with leave to amend after plaintiffs failed to file an amended complaint within the ordered 21-day period.
key_cases_cited: Kokkonen v. Guardian Life Ins. Co. of Am., 511 U.S. 375 (1994)
Caterpillar, Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386 (1987)
Monell v. Dep't of Social Servs. of City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
McGary v. City of Portland, 386 F.3d 1259 (9th Cir. 2004)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)

source_file: 10756942_2025_Anita Valladores, et al. v. Ashtree Apartments, LLC_caed
case_name: Anita Valladores, et al. v. Ashtree Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: This case involves policies allegedly harassing children and restricting their activities (bikes, skateboards, outdoor play), not a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommended denying the motion for minor's compromise because the petition failed to comply with Local Rules—it did not explain how settlement amounts were determined, disclose attorney compensation/terms, or justify the $2,000 differential between minor plaintiffs.
brief_summary: Minor plaintiffs (D.C., K.C., E.J., M.J.) sued Ashtree Apartments alleging the landlord violated the Fair Housing Act by harassing children for outdoor activities and restricting bikes, skateboards, and play. The parties settled at mediation; the magistrate judge recommended denying the minor's compromise petition because it failed to comply with local rules regarding disclosure of settlement amount determination and attorney compensation arrangements.

source_file: 10757113_2025_Mezie Oduka v. Danisha Davis, et al._nysd
case_name: Mezie Oduka v. Danisha Davis, et al.
accommodation_description: Not specified in this procedural order; the case text does not describe the specific accommodation or modification requested or denied — it references only that plaintiff has raised FHA, ADA, and NYCHRL claims without setting out the underlying factual allegations.
key_holding: The court grants plaintiff's request for pro bono counsel to assist him during settlement negotiations and at the upcoming settlement conference, finding that plaintiff qualifies as indigent and that his claims under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and NYCHRL are of sufficient substance to warrant appointment.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Mezie Oduka filed suit against Danisha Davis and others, asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the New York City Human Rights Law. At the October 15, 2025 Case Management Conference, plaintiff—who had already been granted in forma pauperis status—requested pro bono counsel. The Magistrate Judge granted the request, directing the Clerk of Court to locate volunteer counsel to represent plaintiff during settlement negotiations and at the upcoming settlement conference.
key_cases_cited: Hodge v. Police Officers, 802 F.2d 58 (2d Cir. 1986)
Mallard v. U.S. Dist. Court, 490 U.S. 296 (1989)
Cooper v. A. Sargenti Co., Inc., 877 F.2d 170 (2d Cir. 1989)

source_file: 10757487_2025_Sehra Waheed v. MLMIC Insurance Company; Sonia Kim; Michael Terrani; Garden OBGYN of East 67th Street; Bethpage Medical, PLLC, d_b_a Garden OBGYN_nysd
case_name: Sehra Waheed v. MLMIC Insurance Company; Sonia Kim; Michael Terrani; Garden OBGYN of East 67th Street; Bethpage Medical, PLLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that her doctors' insurer pay her rent as a 'reasonable accommodation' for disability-related financial constraints arising from a medical procedure.
key_holding: The FHA claim was dismissed because the plaintiff sued an insurance company and medical providers rather than a housing provider, and her claims concerned monetary compensation for alleged insurance bad faith rather than any actual housing discrimination.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sehra Waheed sued her doctors' insurer (MLMIC Insurance Company) and medical providers under the ADA and FHA, seeking rent payments as a 'reasonable accommodation' for disability-related financial harm following a medical procedure. The court dismissed both federal claims, holding that ADA Title III does not apply because plaintiff was not seeking access to a public accommodation, and the FHA does not apply because her claims concerned insurance bad faith litigation rather than housing discrimination by a housing provider.
key_cases_cited: Gladstone, Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)
Palmer v. Fannie Mae, 755 F. App'x 43 (2d Cir. 2018)
Littlejohn v. City of New York, 795 F.3d 297 (2d Cir. 2015)

10757978_2025_Susan Suarez; Delailah Perez; Andre Rojas v. Park Lane Management Corporation, et al._nysd
case_name: Susan Suarez; Delailah Perez; Andre Rojas v. Park Lane Management Corporation, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Susan Suarez, who is blind, requested rescheduling of a housing inspection as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed Suarez's FHA claims because, assuming she is disabled, she failed to allege facts showing she suffered adverse treatment or that defendants discriminated against her because of her disability, granting 30 days' leave to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs sued Park Lane Management Corporation, Kahen Properties, and individual landlords under the ADA and FHA, alleging defendants failed to accommodate Plaintiff Susan Suarez's disability (she is blind) by refusing to reschedule a housing inspection. The court dismissed ADA claims because private landlords are not subject to the ADA, dismissed FHA claims for failure to state a plausible discriminatory motive claim, and granted 30 days' leave to amend.

source_file: 10758666_2025_Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing _ Redevelopment Commission_sdd
case_name: Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing & Redevelopment Commission
accommodation_description: Request for protective order prohibiting BHRC from verifying income with employer; underlying FHA claim concerns income deduction calculations for housing assistance
key_holding: The magistrate judge denied the protective order motion because Rule 26(c) does not apply when no discovery has been served, and plaintiff failed to certify that she conferred with defendant in good faith before filing the motion.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat sued Brookings Housing & Redevelopment Commission alleging Fair Housing Act and Rehabilitation Act violations related to income deduction calculations for housing assistance. The magistrate judge denied plaintiff's motion for a protective order prohibiting BHRC from contacting her employer for income verification because Rule 26(c) does not authorize protective orders when no discovery has been served and plaintiff failed to satisfy the good faith conferral requirement.
key_cases_cited: General Dynamics Corp. v. Selb Mfg. Co., 481 F.2d 1204 (8th Cir. 1973)
Pansy v. Borough of Stroudsburg, 23 F.3d 772 (3d Cir. 1994)
United States v. Becerra, 73 F.4th 966 (8th Cir. 2023)
Thompson v. Nix, 897 F.2d 356 (8th Cir. 1990)

source_file: 10760654_2025_Richard Renfroe v. Burlington Capital Properties, L.L.C._ned
10762371_2025_Domonique Cornell Wilson, et al. v. Holiday Estates, et al._mied
case_name: Domonique Cornell Wilson, et al. v. Holiday Estates, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case. Plaintiffs sought relief for uninhabitable housing conditions (a gas leak and malfunctioning HVAC unit) and alleged retaliatory eviction after lodging complaints about those conditions with the defendants.
key_holding: The court summarily dismissed plaintiffs' federal Fair Housing Act and § 1983 claims for failure to state a claim because plaintiffs failed to allege discrimination or retaliation based on any protected category under the FHA and all defendants were private parties not subject to § 1983, then declined supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Wilson filed suit on behalf of himself and his minor children against his mobile home landlord Holiday Estates and related defendants, alleging that a gas leak and HVAC problems made his family ill, that he complained about these conditions, and that defendants retaliated by attempting to evict the family. The court granted in forma pauperis status but, after issuing a show cause order that plaintiffs failed to adequately answer, summarily dismissed all federal claims because plaintiffs had not alleged discrimination or retaliation tied to any protected category under the FHA, and because § 1983 does not apply to private parties. The court then declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state law negligence and emotional distress claims, dismissing them without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Tahfs v. Proctor, 316 F.3d 584 (6th Cir. 2003)

source_file: 10762570_2025_Shirley Drummer v. Southern Nevada Regional Housing Authority, et al._nvd
case_name: Shirley Drummer v. Southern Nevada Regional Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a live-in aide and an extra bedroom for medical supplies, supported by medical documentation from her licensed physician and therapist, due to her primary progressive multiple sclerosis, anxiety, depression, cognitive issues, and need for ongoing behavioral therapy.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's fifth amended complaint with leave to amend because it failed to satisfy Rule 8's pleading requirements by lumping all defendants together without specifying which particular defendant was responsible for which violation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Shirley Drummer, who suffers from primary progressive multiple sclerosis and related conditions, sued the Southern Nevada Regional Housing Authority and four individual employees alleging denial of reasonable accommodations (a live-in aide and an extra bedroom for medical supplies), disability discrimination, and retaliation under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act. The court screened the fifth amended complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) and dismissed it with leave to amend, finding that the complaint failed to comply with Rule 8 by lumping defendants together under claims without a short and plain statement tying specific conduct to specific defendants. Plaintiff was granted until January 12, 2026 to file a sixth and final amended complaint.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Cai v. Enter. Leasing Co.-W. LLC, 2024 WL 810885 (D. Nev. 2024)

case_name: Eve Escobedo v. Rogelio Carlos Gonzalez
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a property seller, alleged defendant realtor made discriminatory statements to a buyer regarding a death at the property and pressured her to reduce the sale price based on race and gender.
key_holding: Plaintiff fails to state a viable FHA claim because she was not renting or selling housing, and she has not alleged any act committed on account of her membership in a protected class under the FHA.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eve Escobedo sued defendant Rogelio Carlos Gonzalez, a realtor, alleging he made false statements to a potential buyer about a death at her property and pressured her to accept a lower offer based on her race and gender, invoking the Fourteenth Amendment and Fair Housing Act. The Magistrate Judge recommended granting the motion to dismiss, finding no viable federal claims because the plaintiff failed to allege state action for constitutional claims and failed to state any claim under the Fair Housing Act as she was not renting or selling housing and alleged no act committed because of her protected class status.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

source_file: 10763487_2025_Dornnel Locke, et al. v. Wayne J. Griffin Electric, Inc., et al._ctd
10763543_2025_Tyree Moore v. Office of Economic Opportunity, Zugely Ortiz, Danielle Majted_njd
case_name: Tyree Moore v. Office of Economic Opportunity, Zugely Ortiz, Danielle Majted
accommodation_description: No traditional FHA accommodation was requested; plaintiff sought financial rental assistance (payment of rental arrears) from OEO, a government-funded economic assistance office, to prevent eviction.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint without prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) because plaintiff failed to allege membership in a protected class under Title VI or FHA § 3604, and failed to identify a protected activity or adverse action sufficient to state a retaliation claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Tyree Moore sued the Office of Economic Opportunity and two individual employees alleging discrimination and retaliation arising from OEO's denial of rental assistance to help pay his rental arrears and avoid eviction. The court granted his IFP application but screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915 and dismissed it without prejudice, finding that plaintiff did not allege he was a member of any protected class under Title VI (race, color, national origin) or FHA § 3604 (race, color, religion, sex, familial status, national origin), and failed to identify a protected activity or adverse action for his retaliation claim. Plaintiff was granted 30 days to amend the complaint to cure these deficiencies.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Conley v. Gibson, 355 U.S. 41 (1957)

source_file: 10763627_2025_Anthony Alfieri v. Cortland Management LLC, et al._azd
case_name: Anthony Alfieri v. Cortland Management LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: No disability-related accommodation requested; claims involve familial status discrimination (noise complaints when daughter present) and retaliation for filing HUD complaint
key_holding: This procedural order addresses service requirements and case management procedures; the court did not substantively analyze the merits of the familial status discrimination or retaliation claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Anthony Alfieri sued Cortland Management LLC alleging the property management company discriminated against him based on familial status by issuing noise complaints only when his daughter visited and then raised his rent, and further alleged retaliation after he filed a complaint with HUD. The court dismissed the original complaint for failure to allege concrete harm, but allowed amendment; in this procedural order the court found the amended complaint sufficient to proceed with service and issued case management instructions.

source_file: 10763692_2025_Nicole Furnas v. Tierra Luna and Sol Enterprises, LLC; et al._azd
case_name: Nicole Furnas v. Tierra Luna and Sol Enterprises, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: This order does not address a reasonable accommodation request; it addresses a discovery protective order concerning ex parte contact with former employees in a sexual harassment case.
key_holding: The court granted in part the motion for protective order, holding that ex parte contact with former employees is prohibited only where the acts or omissions of the former employee gave rise to the underlying litigation, adopting the 'gave rise to' test from Lang v. Superior Court rather than the broader 'may be imputed to' standard advocated by defendants.
brief_summary: Nicole Furnas sued her former landlords (Tierra Luna and Sol Enterprises, LLC and related entities) alleging that a maintenance worker demanded sexual favors in exchange for lease renewal. The court ruled on a protective order motion concerning ex parte contact with former employees, holding that such contact is prohibited only for former employees whose acts or omissions gave rise to the underlying litigation.
key_cases_cited: Lang v. Superior Ct., In & For Cnty. of Maricopa, 170 Ariz. 602, 826 P.2d 1228 (Ct. App. 1992)
Phillips ex rel. Ests. of Byrd v. Gen. Motors Corp., 307 F.3d 1206 (9th Cir. 2002)
Lois Grunow Mem'l Clinic v. Davis, 49 Ariz. 277, 66 P.2d 238 (1937)

case_name: Carlos A. Alonso Cano v. 245 C&C, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested a reserved handicapped parking space for their son Angie who has hearing loss and mobility issues.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed that the parking spot accommodation claim was barred by the FHA's two-year statute of limitations because the request was made in 2012-2013 and the suit was filed in 2019, and the bathroom modification claim failed because Appellees approved the modification request the day after it was made.
brief_summary: Carlos Alonso Cano and family sued 245 C&C, LLC and CFH Group, LLC (their landlords) alleging Fair Housing Act violations, including failure to provide a reserved handicapped parking space and bathroom modification for their son with hearing loss. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court, finding the parking claim time-barred by the two-year statute of limitations and the bathroom modification claim failed because defendants approved the request the next day.
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Sailboat Bend Sober Living, LLC v. City of Fort Lauderdale, 46 F.4th 1268 (11th Cir. 2022)

source_file: 10764500_2025_South Carolina State Conference and Georgetown County Branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, FourSix Development, and We Do Good Work, LLC v. Georgetown County, a politica
case_name: South Carolina State Conference and Georgetown County Branch of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, FourSix Development, and We Do Good Work, LLC v. Georgetown County
accommodation_description: Zoning denial for affordable housing development Porter's Landing on land owned by Georgetown Memorial Hospital
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss because NAACP Plaintiffs lacked both associational standing (no identified member with concrete injury) and organizational standing (no concrete injury beyond generalized frustration of mission and resource diversion under Alliance for Hippocratic Medicine), and Plaintiffs lacked standing to pursue declaratory or injunctive relief due to speculative future injury.
brief_summary: NAACP organizations and housing developers sued Georgetown County alleging the County's denial of a zoning application for Porter's Landing, an affordable housing development, violated the Fair Housing Act and Equal Protection Clause. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the NAACP Plaintiffs lacked standing because they failed to identify any member with concrete injury from the zoning denial and failed to establish organizational standing under recent Supreme Court precedent requiring a direct injury beyond frustration of mission and resource diversion.
key_cases_cited: Food & Drug Admin. v. All. for Hippocratic Med., 602 U.S. 367 (2024)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021)
N.A.A.C.P. v. City of Kyle, Tex., 626 F.3d 233 (5th Cir. 2010)

source_file: 10765213_2025_Mark Patrick Gansert v. Residences at Landon Ridge LP, AP Companies, Housing Authority of the City of San Antonio_txwd
case_name: Mark Patrick Gansert v. Residences at Landon Ridge LP, AP Companies, Housing Authority of the City of San Antonio
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation for distributing flyers about tenant rights and complaining about fraudulent billing and front door repairs, not a request for accommodation of disability.
key_holding: The Magistrate Judge recommended dismissal of Plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 because Plaintiff's complaints to Defendants concerned fraudulent billing for trash services and failure to repair a front door, which fell outside the scope of activity protected by the FHA as they did not relate to discriminatory treatment based on a protected characteristic.
brief_summary: Section 8 voucher holder Mark Patrick Gansert sued his landlords (Landon Ridge LP, AP Companies) and the San Antonio Housing Authority alleging First Amendment retaliation under § 1983, FHA retaliation, breach of HAP contract, and HUD regulations violations. The Court adopted the Magistrate Judge's recommendation and dismissed the case for failure to state a claim, finding the FHA retaliation claim failed because plaintiff's complaints about billing and repairs were not protected activity under § 3617.

source_file: 10765243_2025_Justin Baker v. The Emerald Condos et al._wawd
case_name: Justin Baker v. The Emerald Condos et al.
accommodation_description: Baker requested a parking spot at the Emerald for his physical therapist who periodically visits for appointments, and sought accommodations for his inability—due to his disabilities—to comply with certain HOA physical-task policies such as recycling and trash disposal. He also sought, via preliminary injunction, a transfer from his current condo unit to a different unit within the same building (which was resolved by settlement and denied as moot).
key_holding: On IFP review under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2), the court dismissed most of Baker's claims with prejudice for failure to state a claim, while allowing FHA claims for reasonable accommodation (24 C.F.R. § 100.204), discrimination (24 C.F.R. § 100.65; 42 U.S.C. § 3604(b),(f)), prohibited interference/coercion/intimidation (24 C.F.R. § 100.400), and hostile environment harassment (24 C.F.R. § 100.600) to survive, ordering Baker to file a third amended complaint limited to those surviving claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Justin Baker, a disabled resident of The Emerald condominiums in Seattle, sued HOA management company CWD Group and its employees for violations of the FHA, ADA, and other statutes, alleging denial of disability accommodations (including a parking spot for his physical therapist), discriminatory enforcement of HOA policies, retaliation for filing complaints with city authorities, and stalking/harassment. On IFP screening under § 1915(e)(2), the court dismissed the majority of claims with prejudice—including defamation, ADA claims, FHA § 3617 coercion, and numerous FHA regulatory claims—for failure to state a claim or absence of a private right of action, while permitting claims for reasonable accommodation, disability discrimination, prohibited interference/coercion, and hostile environment harassment to proceed. Baker was ordered to file a third amended complaint by January 13, 2026, addressing only the surviving claims in compliance with Rule 8(a)(2).
key_cases_cited: Baker v. Avenue5 Residential, No. C24-01862JHC, 2025 WL 1207666 (W.D. Wash. Apr. 25, 2025)
Slaughter v. Valley View I LLP, No. C23-1360JLR, 2023 WL 6461058 (W.D. Wash. Oct. 4, 2023)

source_file: 10765288_2025_Johnny Moffett v. Columbia Manor et al._wawd
case_name: Johnny Moffett v. Columbia Manor et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges racial harassment by white supremacy group and failure of property manager to intervene.
key_holding: Plaintiff's amended complaint fails to state an FHA claim because it contains only conclusory allegations of racial bias without specific facts from which the court could infer that defendants were motivated by racial discrimination or engaged in conduct prohibited by 42 U.S.C. § 3604(a).
brief_summary: Johnny Moffett, an African American man with disabilities, sued Columbia Manor (Smith Towers) and individual defendants alleging racial harassment by a white supremacy group and claiming the property manager failed to intervene. The court dismissed the amended complaint sua sponte under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim, finding the complaint contained only conclusory allegations of race-based discrimination without specific facts demonstrating discriminatory intent or conduct prohibited by the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Barren v. Harrington, 152 F.3d 1193 (9th Cir. 1998)
Missouri ex rel. Koster v. Harris, 847 F.3d 646 (9th Cir. 2017)
Watison v. Carter, 668 F.3d 1108 (9th Cir. 2012)

source_file: 10766204_2025_Mary E. Martinez v. ABQ Code Enforcement, Angelo Matzer, Ray Velarde, and William (Josh) Gallegos_nmd
case_name: Mary E. Martinez v. ABQ Code Enforcement, Angelo Matzer, Ray Velardez, and William (Josh) Gallegos
accommodation_description: Unable to determine; complaint too incoherent and non-compliant with Rule 8(a) to identify any specific accommodation request
key_holding: Magistrate recommended declining to accept plaintiff's 64-page filing as an amended complaint and dismissing all federal claims without prejudice for failure to comply with Rule 8(a) pleading requirements, remanding remaining state-law claims to state court.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mary E. Martinez filed suit against ABQ Code Enforcement and city employees alleging Fair Housing Act, ADA, and constitutional claims related to code enforcement actions and her Section 8 housing. The Magistrate recommended dismissing all federal claims without prejudice because plaintiff's complaint failed to comply with Rule 8(a), being rambling, non-compliant with formatting requirements, and failing to identify specific claims or factual allegations against defendants.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Nasious v. Two Unknown B.I.C.E. Agents
McNamara v. Brauchler
Robbins v. Oklahoma
Smith v. City of Enid ex rel. Enid City Comm'n

source_file: 10766223_2025_Maurice Dosso v. The Coventry Group Community Management, Inc. et al._vawd
case_name: Maurice Dosso v. The Coventry Group Community Management, Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Vehicle towing enforcement; plaintiff alleges selective enforcement of parking rules against him as a Black homeowner compared to white homeowners, constituting race-based housing discrimination.
key_holding: The court transferred the case to the Northern District of West Virginia because venue was improper in the Western District of Virginia—all alleged events (towing, HOA citations, property management decisions) occurred in West Virginia, and the court lacked personal jurisdiction over defendant ZZ Auto, a West Virginia corporation.
brief_summary: Maurice Dosso, a Black homeowner in Stonebrook Village, West Virginia, sued Coventry Group Community Management, Stonebrook Village HOA, property manager Keila Navarro, and ZZ Auto alleging race-based discrimination after his vehicle was towed while white neighbors' similarly parked vehicles were not towed. The court transferred the case to the Northern District of West Virginia because venue was improper in the Western District of Virginia—all events occurred in West Virginia and the court lacked personal jurisdiction over defendant ZZ Auto—and declined to reach the merits of any claims.

source_file: 10766369_2025_Justin Baker v. The Emerald Condos et al._wawd
case_name: Justin Baker v. The Emerald Condos et al.
citation: UNDETERMINED (W.D. Wash. Order, Case No. C25-1989JLR)
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an exception to the condominium building's policy requiring residents to break down cardboard boxes before disposal, which he characterized as a reasonable accommodation for his disability. He claimed he had such an accommodation 'on file with the city of Seattle,' but defendants, particularly Mr. Page, told him he was 'not allowed to have his reasonable accommodation for the cardboard.'
key_holding: The court dismissed with prejudice pro se plaintiff's third amended FHA complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failure to comply with Rule 8(a) and failure to state claims for disparate treatment, reasonable accommodation, interference/coercion, and harassment, finding further amendment futile after four opportunities to plead.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Justin Baker, proceeding in forma pauperis, filed a third amended complaint against property management company CWD Group and individual defendants Joe Majewski and Zach Page, alleging violations of the FHA (42 U.S.C. § 3604(b) and (f)) and related regulations concerning disability-based discrimination at his condominium. Baker's central allegation was that defendants refused to honor his reasonable accommodation—an exemption from the building's policy requiring residents to break down cardboard boxes for disposal—despite his claim of federal disability status. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice, finding the complaint violated Rule 8(a)'s pleading requirements and failed to allege sufficient facts to support any of the asserted claims, and denied further leave to amend as futile.

source_file: 10766412_2025_Randy Dewayne Pittman v. Landsphere Property Management, et al._cand
case_name: Randy Dewayne Pittman v. Landsphere Property Management, et al.
accommodation_description: Creation of an accessible parking space for the plaintiff at his apartment building.
key_holding: The court dismissed the plaintiff's FHA claim with prejudice for failure to state a claim after the plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint, and dismissed the state-law claims without prejudice for lack of supplemental jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Randy Dewayne Pittman sued his landlord and property manager under the FHA and California state law, alleging they failed to create an accessible parking space at his apartment building. The court had previously dismissed his complaint with leave to amend after screening it pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2), finding it failed to state an FHA claim. Because Pittman did not file an amended complaint by the December 1, 2025 deadline, the court dismissed the federal FHA claim with prejudice and the state-law claims without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic v. Twombly

source_file: 10766939_2025_Blakelick Properties, LLC v. The Village of Glen Ellyn_ilnd
case_name: Blakelick Properties, LLC v. The Village of Glen Ellyn
accommodation_description: This is not a disability accommodation case; Blakelick Properties challenges a municipal ordinance banning short-term rentals as a regulatory taking, with FHA cited as one of several claims but not substantively analyzed.
key_holding: The Court granted preliminary injunction against Glen Ellyn's short-term rental ban as applied to Blakelick, finding Blakelick likely succeeded on its regulatory takings claim and would suffer irreparable harm from loss of its short-term rental business.
brief_summary: Blakelick Properties LLC, owner of a short-term rental property in Glen Ellyn, Illinois, sued the Village of Glen Ellyn challenging Ordinance No. 7180-VC which bans short-term rentals, arguing it constitutes a regulatory taking under the Fifth Amendment. The Court granted preliminary injunction, finding Blakelick demonstrated likelihood of success on the merits of its regulatory taking claim, would suffer irreparable harm from loss of its entire short-term rental business, and the balance of equities favors enjoining enforcement against Blakelick while litigation proceeds.
key_cases_cited: Whitaker v. Kenosha Unified Sch. Dist. No. 1 Bd. of Educ., 858 F.3d 1034 (7th Cir. 2017)

source_file: 10766941_2025_Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc._flsd
case_name: Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a 90-day extension of pretrial and trial deadlines in the pending state court action as a reasonable accommodation for her medical conditions affecting her ability to tolerate demolition-related environmental hazards.
key_holding: The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to stay the federal case pending resolution of the state court action under Colorado River abstention, while allowing the FHA reasonable accommodation claim to proceed and dismissing the ADA claim for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Valery Kantsepolsky, a condominium unit owner with medical conditions limiting her tolerance for demolition-related environmental hazards, sued the River Shores Association, Inc. alleging the HOA failed to provide reasonable accommodations and engaged in retaliation when she sought a 90-day extension of deadlines in underlying state court litigation. The court adopted the magistrate judge's report, staying the federal case under Colorado River abstention doctrine while allowing the FHA reasonable accommodation claim to survive dismissal and dismissing the ADA claim for failure to state a claim.
key_cases_cited: Colorado River Water Conservation District v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
A.L. by and through D.L. v. Walt Disney Parks & Resorts US, Inc., 900 F.3d 1270 (11th Cir. 2018)

source_file: 10767062_2025_Marcos Isaac Rojas v. Shelter Corporation and Kyle Didier_mnd
case_name: Marcos Isaac Rojas v. Shelter Corporation and Kyle Didier
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; claims involve race-based tenant harassment and alleged retaliation via camera installation.
key_holding: The court dismissed Rojas's FHA disparate impact and retaliation claims because he failed to allege sufficient facts to plausibly support either claim, failing to adequately plead that defendants' policies disproportionately harmed minorities or that the camera installation constituted actionable retaliation.
brief_summary: Rojas, a Mexican national origin tenant, sued his property manager and company president alleging they failed to protect him from race-based tenant harassment and retaliated by installing a camera near his parking spot. The court dismissed his FHA claims (disparate impact and retaliation) without prejudice, finding he failed to plead sufficient facts to state plausible claims under either theory.

source_file: 10767770_2025_Maurice Dosso v. The Coventry Group Community Management, Inc. et al._wvnd
case_name: Maurice Dosso v. The Coventry Group Community Management, Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in towing of his vehicle from HOA community parking, claiming Black residents are selectively targeted compared to White residents.
key_holding: The court found venue improper in the Western District of Virginia because ZZ Auto (a West Virginia corporation) was not subject to personal jurisdiction there, and a substantial part of the events giving rise to the claims occurred in West Virginia; accordingly, the court transferred the case to the Northern District of West Virginia rather than dismissing it.
brief_summary: Maurice Dosso, a Black homeowner in Stonebrook Village HOA community in West Virginia, sued Coventry Group Community Management, Inc., Stonebrook Village HOA, HOA agent Keila Navarro, and ZZ Auto Service Center alleging racial discrimination under the Civil Rights Act and Fair Housing Act after his vehicle was towed from community parking. The court transferred the case to the Northern District of West Virginia after finding that venue in the Western District of Virginia was improper because defendant ZZ Auto was a West Virginia corporation not subject to personal jurisdiction in Virginia and the events giving rise to the claims occurred in West Virginia.

source_file: 10767804_2025_Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing _ Redevelopment Commission_sdd
case_name: Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing & Redevelopment Commission
accommodation_description: Request that the housing authority extend and preserve plaintiff's Housing Choice Voucher without interruption and process her portability packet as an accommodation for disability
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's emergency TRO and preliminary injunction motion because she failed to establish a likelihood of success on the merits of her disability accommodation claims against the housing authority.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat sued Brookings Housing & Redevelopment Commission alleging Fair Housing Act violations, seeking an emergency TRO and preliminary injunction to prevent expiration of her Housing Choice Voucher and to compel the housing authority to process her portability request as a disability accommodation. The court denied the motion, finding that Jeffcoat failed to demonstrate a likelihood of success on the merits of her claims.

source_file: 10767808_2025_James E. Jacobson, Jr. v. AH Gresham Park, LLC; AH Albion House, LLC; TMG Property Management Services NW, LLC; and Atlas Property Management_ord
case_name: James E. Jacobson, Jr. v. AH Gresham Park, LLC; AH Albion House, LLC; TMG Property Management Services NW, LLC; and Atlas Property Management
accommodation_description: Jacobson requested a 'simple space swap' to obtain a wheelchair-accessible parking spot that GPA management had assigned to other tenants.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Jacobson's federal action with prejudice because his claims were barred by res judicata, as they arose from the same factual transactions underlying his previously filed state court action that resulted in a final judgment with prejudice.
brief_summary: Jacobson, a wheelchair-using tenant at Gresham Park Apartments, sued his landlords and property managers claiming they denied his request for a wheelchair-accessible parking spot and engaged in various retaliatory and discriminatory conduct. The federal court dismissed the case with prejudice based on res judicata, finding that Jacobson's claims arose from the same factual transactions that were or could have been litigated in a prior state court action that resulted in a final judgment with prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

source_file: 10767966_2025_Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi v. Edward Pec, et al._njd
case_name: Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi v. Edward Pec, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Angel Lopez requested a handicapped parking space near his apartment as a reasonable accommodation for his asthma and COPD disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed Lopez's FHA reasonable accommodation claim with prejudice because his allegations were conclusory—he failed to plead specific facts showing how a handicapped parking space was necessary to afford him an equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling, as opposed to merely being something he would prefer.
brief_summary: Angel Lopez and Kazue Koizumi sued their landlord Edward Pec and The Palisades LLC, as well as attorneys Brandon Broderick and Christopher Karounos, alleging Fair Housing Act violations including failure to provide a reasonable accommodation (handicapped parking space) for Lopez's asthma and COPD, along with claims of harassment, invasion of privacy, and discrimination based on race and disability. The Court granted both motions to dismiss, dismissing the FHA reasonable accommodation claim with prejudice because Lopez failed to plead specific facts demonstrating how the requested parking accommodation was necessary to afford him an equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

source_file: 10768029_2025_Scott Robert Moore v. Amy C. Yerkey, et al._cacd
case_name: Scott Robert Moore v. Amy C. Yerkey, et al.
accommodation_description: The underlying accommodation request is not described in this order; the opinion only references that plaintiff raised housing discrimination and retaliation claims against his landlord following an eviction proceeding.
key_holding: The Court accepted the Magistrate Judge's Report, dismissing Claims One through Four without further leave to amend, while authorizing service on Defendant Rosanna Domingo as to Claim Two (housing discrimination and retaliation) only.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Scott Robert Moore, a tenant, filed a pro se complaint against his landlord and state court officials following an eviction proceeding, raising Fair Housing Act and ADA claims. The Magistrate Judge recommended dismissing most claims based on Eleventh Amendment immunity, judicial immunity, and the Anti-Injunction Act, but recommended allowing Claim Two (housing discrimination and retaliation against the landlord) to proceed. The District Court accepted this Report and Recommendation, dismissing Claims One through Four without leave to amend while authorizing service on Defendant Domingo as to the surviving Claim Two.

case_name: Charles Ray Johnson v. Norman Rinehart
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was described; plaintiff's complaint was too vague and conclusory to identify any particular accommodation sought.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA and ADA claims were dismissed without prejudice because his complaint contained only conclusory statements and general legal references without specific factual allegations establishing that he is disabled, that he was discriminated against based on race, or that defendant took retaliatory action against him.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Charles Ray Johnson sued landlord Norman Rinehart alleging ADA discrimination, race-based housing discrimination, disability discrimination, and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act. key_holding: Plaintiff failed to plead facts plausibly establishing that defendants discriminated against him based on his Middle Eastern ancestry; his FHA claim was dismissed along with other federal claims for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Dr. Ayman Adeeb, a property owner and contractor of Middle Eastern descent, sued the City of Marina and its officials alleging discriminatory and retaliatory code enforcement against his properties based on his race and in retaliation for his public records requests. case_name: Antony Montero v. New York City Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: The case text does not describe any specific accommodation request; this is a purely procedural order of service and provides no factual detail about the underlying nature of the disability discrimination or any accommodation sought.
key_holding: The court issued an amended order of service directing the Clerk to issue summonses and effect service through the U.S. Marshals Service on all sixteen named defendants in plaintiff's FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and § 1983 retaliation and disability discrimination action.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Antony Montero, a NYCHA resident in the Bronx, brought suit alleging retaliation and disability discrimination under the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, Fair Housing Act, and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 against NYCHA and its private management contractor BMA and their respective employees and officers. After plaintiff filed an amended complaint adding and renaming several defendants, the magistrate judge issued this amended order of service directing the Clerk of Court to add the newly named defendants, issue summonses for all sixteen defendants, and deliver all necessary paperwork to the USMS to effect service on plaintiff's behalf given his IFP status.

source_file: 10769132_2026_Judy Shaw Foundation v. City of Howard, South Dakota_sdd
case_name: Judy Shaw Foundation v. City of Howard, South Dakota
accommodation_description: The City enacted zoning ordinances requiring a special exception for group homes and residential chemical dependency treatment centers, allegedly discriminating against disabled individuals with substance use disorders.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for JSF on the issue that a residential chemical dependency treatment center was a permissible use under existing zoning ('service establishment') without needing a special exception, denied the City's motion on the FHA disparate treatment claim finding evidence of discriminatory intent in enacting the ordinances, and denied JSF's motion on the City's advice-of-counsel defense which remains for jury determination.
brief_summary: Judy Shaw Foundation (JSF), which owned property in Howard, South Dakota, sued the City of Howard after the city enacted ordinances requiring a special exception to operate a residential chemical dependency treatment center on property JSF was selling to iRecover US, Inc. The court granted summary judgment for JSF on its ADA claim (for lack of standing), denied summary judgment for both parties on JSF's FHA disparate treatment claim (finding evidence of discriminatory intent), granted JSF partial summary judgment on the interpretive question of whether the treatment center was a permissible use under existing zoning, and denied JSF's motion on the City's advice-of-counsel defense.

source_file: 10769187_2026_Judy Shaw Foundation v. City of Howard, South Dakota_sdd
case_name: Judy Shaw Foundation v. City of Howard, South Dakota
accommodation_description: JSF alleged the City enacted discriminatory zoning ordinances (745 and 746) to exclude residential chemical dependency treatment centers serving disabled individuals (those recovering from substance use disorders), requiring them to obtain a special exception permit.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the City on JSF's ADA claim for lack of standing, but denied the City's motion on JSF's FHA disparate treatment claim, finding genuine issues of material fact exist regarding the City's discriminatory intent in enacting the zoning ordinances, including what advice of counsel the City received and whether the treatment center was already a permitted use under the existing ordinance.
brief_summary: Judy Shaw Foundation (JSF), which owned the Howard Hotel property in Howard, South Dakota, sued the City of Howard after iRecover backed out of purchasing the property to operate a residential chemical dependency treatment center, allegedly due to the City's enactment of zoning Ordinances 745 and 746 requiring a special exception permit for group homes and treatment facilities. The court granted summary judgment for the City on JSF's ADA claim (lack of standing), but denied summary judgment on JSF's FHA disparate treatment claim, finding genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding the City's discriminatory intent, including whether the treatment center was already a permitted use under existing zoning and what advice of counsel the City received before enacting the ordinances.

source_file: 10769217_2026_Gerard Torres, + 2 Children v. Alexis Winnell, Property Manager, et al._mad
case_name: Gerard Torres, + 2 Children v. Alexis Winnell, Property Manager, et al.
accommodation_description: Torres requested accommodations for participation in court proceedings—specifically, clear plain-language explanations of filings, motions, and orders; extra time to read, understand, and respond to court documents; assistance from court staff or an appointed advocate if necessary; and any other accommodations the court deemed appropriate—asserting a mental impairment and invoking Title II of the ADA and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
key_holding: The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction over the plaintiff's complaint because his pleading fails to identify any disability, discriminatory conduct, or how he exercised rights under the Fair Housing Act or other federal statutes, and complete diversity of citizenship is absent.
brief_summary: Gerard Torres, a self-represented disabled tenant in Roslindale, Massachusetts, filed suit against his property manager and fellow residents alleging harassment, defamation, car tampering, and—in a later TRO motion—retaliation under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act after receiving a 7-Day Notice to Quit. The court found it lacked both federal question and diversity subject matter jurisdiction because Torres's complaint contained no well-pleaded federal claim (he identified no disability, no discriminatory conduct tied to that disability, and no exercise of federal statutory rights), and the parties lacked complete diversity. The court denied Torres's motions for IFP status, a temporary restraining order, and court-proceeding accommodations, and directed him to file an amended complaint within 28 days if he wished to proceed.

source_file: 10769390_2026_Dewanna Johnson, et al. v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc.; McKinney Housing Authority v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc
case_name: Dewanna Johnson, et al. v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc.; McKinney Housing Authority v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this is a discriminatory policy case involving a ban on rentals to tenants who use Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers to pay rent, which the court analyzes as a facially neutral policy alleged to be motivated by racial animus against the predominantly Black voucher-holding population.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss plaintiffs' disparate treatment, hostile housing environment harassment, racial intimidation, and retaliation claims, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged that the Section 8 voucher ban was racially motivated, while dismissing with prejudice the disparate impact claims of the Johnson Plaintiffs and McKinney Housing.
brief_summary: Three consolidated Fair Housing Act cases challenge a 2022 Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher ban enacted by the Providence Homeowners Association (PHOA) and managed by FirstService Residential Texas in a Dallas suburb, which displaced a predominantly Black voucher-holding tenant population. The court denied most motions to dismiss, holding that plaintiffs plausibly alleged racial discriminatory intent behind the facially neutral voucher ban based on Board members' use of racially coded language, procedural departures in rule-making, and the fact that 93% of affected voucher holders were Black—distinguishing the case from the Fifth Circuit's Lincoln Property decision. The disparate impact claims of the Johnson Plaintiffs and McKinney Housing were dismissed with prejudice, while all other claims, including hostile housing environment harassment, racial intimidation, and retaliation, survived.
key_cases_cited: Lincoln Property Co. v. Rankin, 920 F.3d 900 (5th Cir. 2019)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Cicalese v. Univ. of Tex. Med. Branch, 924 F.3d 762 (5th Cir. 2019)
Swierkiewicz v. Sorema North America, 534 U.S. 506 (2002)
Ames v. Ohio Dep't of Youth Servs., 605 U.S. 303 (2025)

source_file: 10769396_2026_Dewanna Johnson, et al. v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc.; McKinney Housing Authority v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc
case_name: Dewanna Johnson, et al. v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc.
accommodation_description: Not applicable. This is not a reasonable accommodation or modification case. The central issue is defendants' categorical ban on renting to tenants who use federal Housing Choice Vouchers (Section 8) to pay rent, which plaintiffs allege was enacted because of the race of the voucher-holding population (93% Black) rather than the payment mechanism itself.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss disparate treatment, hostile housing environment, and retaliation claims, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged that racial animus motivated the HOA's Section 8 voucher ban, but dismissed disparate impact claims for the Johnson and McKinney plaintiffs with prejudice.
brief_summary: Three consolidated Fair Housing Act cases arise from a 2022 decision by Providence Homeowners Association and its property manager FirstService to implement a ban on rentals to tenants using Housing Choice Vouchers (Section 8) in Providence Village, Texas, where 93% of voucher-holding households were Black. Individual tenants, fair housing nonprofits, and two government housing authorities allege the ban was racially motivated, supported by Board members' racially coded social media comments, procedural departures from normal voting processes, and continued racial hostility after the ban's enactment. The court denied the bulk of defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motions, holding that plaintiffs plausibly alleged intentional race discrimination under a flexible pleading standard, while dismissing disparate impact claims for the Johnson and McKinney plaintiffs.
key_cases_cited: Lincoln Property Mgmt. Co. v. C. Ventures, 920 F.3d 900 (5th Cir. 2019)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

source_file: 10769412_2026_Dewanna Johnson, et al. v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc.; McKinney Housing Authority v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc
case_name: Dewanna Johnson, et al. v. Providence Homeowners Association and FirstService Residential Texas, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request—case involves challenge to HOA's ban on Section 8 voucher holders (the 'Voucher Ban') as racially discriminatory housing policy
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of plaintiffs' disparate-treatment claims, finding they plausibly alleged that the Voucher Ban was enacted because of the race of the predominantly Black voucher holders rather than the means of payment, while dismissing plaintiffs' disparate-impact claims with prejudice.
brief_summary: Current and former Providence Village tenants and two public housing authorities sued the HOA and its property manager alleging the HOA's ban on Section 8 voucher holders (implemented in 2022) constituted intentional race discrimination under § 3604(a). The court denied defendants' motions to dismiss the disparate-treatment claims, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged racially coded language and procedural irregularities suggesting race motivated the policy, while dismissing the disparate-impact claims with prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Lincoln Property Co. v. Kinnebrew, 920 F.3d 900 (5th Cir. 2019)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Cicalese v. Univ. of Tex. Med. Branch, 924 F.3d 762 (5th Cir. 2019)
Swierkiewicz v. Sorema North America, 534 U.S. 506 (2002)
Ames v. Ohio Dep't of Youth Servs., 605 U.S. 303 (2025)

source_file: 10769863_2026_Marceline Hope Engler v. The Salvation Army_arwd
case_name: Marceline Hope Engler v. The Salvation Army
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a transgender woman, alleges she was prevented from using the women's bathroom and was evicted from The Salvation Army facility based on gender identity.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed because it failed to allege sufficient facts establishing that The Salvation Army's facility qualified as a 'dwelling' under the FHA, and the damages claim of $900 fell below the jurisdictional minimum for diversity jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Marceline Hope Engler, a pro se transgender plaintiff, sued The Salvation Army alleging sex/gender-identity discrimination after being prevented from using the women's bathroom and being evicted from the facility. The court dismissed the complaint without prejudice, finding the plaintiff failed to allege facts establishing the Salvation Army facility qualified as a 'dwelling' under the Fair Housing Act, and the claim fell below the jurisdictional threshold for diversity jurisdiction.

source_file: 10769944_2026_James B. Herrera v. Maddox Management, LLC_nmd
case_name: James B. Herrera v. Maddox Management, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged in his Amended Complaint that he suffered from documented medical and psychological disabilities and had requested reasonable accommodations from Defendant, which were ignored; however, he did not specify in either the Amended Complaint or the Second Amended Complaint the nature or content of the accommodations requested.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims in Plaintiff's Second Amended Complaint with prejudice for failure to state a claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e), finding that Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege disability discrimination or retaliation under the Fair Housing Act and the Rehabilitation Act, with the sole exception that the portion of Count I challenging the state court damages award was dismissed without prejudice under Rooker-Feldman.
brief_summary: Plaintiff James Herrera sued his former landlord, Maddox Management, LLC, alleging that during eviction proceedings Defendant responded to rental verification inquiries from prospective landlords with false or misleading information, causing him to lose housing at Tesoro Apartments and forfeit his Section 8 voucher, and that Defendant retaliated against him by seeking inflated damages in state court. The court conducted a sua sponte review under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) and found that Plaintiff's Second Amended Complaint failed to plausibly allege causation (the rental verification predated his HUD complaint by months), failed to plead sufficient factual allegations of disability status or Defendant's discriminatory intent, and failed to allege that the rental verification forms actually contained the false information Plaintiff claimed. After two prior opportunities to amend, the court dismissed all claims with prejudice, declining to grant a third leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Morgan v. Carrington Mortg. Servs., 719 F. App'x 735 (10th Cir. 2017)
Wilkerson v. Shinseki, 606 F.3d 1256 (10th Cir. 2010)
Hall v. Bellmon, 935 F.2d 1106 (10th Cir. 1991)

source_file: 10770206_2026_Telvon Taylor v. Westland Real Estate Group, LLC., et al._nvd
case_name: Telvon Taylor v. Westland Real Estate Group, LLC., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was evicted despite paying rent in violation of the Fair Housing Act because of his disabilities, requesting that the eviction be prevented as a reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: At the § 1915(e) screening stage, the court found that plaintiff adequately alleged a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim because he sufficiently alleged he is disabled, defendants knew of his disability, the accommodation to address hazardous conditions was necessary to afford equal enjoyment of the dwelling, and defendants refused to make such accommodation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Telvon Taylor, a disabled tenant, sued Westland Real Estate Group, LLC and Hacienda Hills Apartment alleging disability discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and wrongful eviction after he complained about hazardous conditions including mold exposure. The court granted Taylor's in forma pauperis application and, at the § 1915(e) screening stage, found his complaint stated a plausible FHA reasonable accommodation claim sufficient to proceed past screening.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Dubois v. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of 2987 Kalakaua, 453 F.3d 1175 (9th Cir. 2006)
United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)

source_file: 10770715_2026_Cincinnati Insurance Company v. Lost Run Farm Community Association, Inc., Armour Property Management, LLC, Vincent Kroon, Ben Wheat, Scott Bruns, Ashlee Wheat, Edward Kowlowitz, Rebecca Kiell, John Garcia,
case_name: Cincinnati Insurance Company v. Lost Run Farm Community Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: The Garcias requested a fence to contain their dogs as an accommodation for Mary Kay Garcia's disability, which the Board denied.
key_holding: The insurer had no duty to defend or indemnify because the CGL coverage did not apply (the intentional discriminatory acts were not an 'occurrence') and the Wrongful Acts coverage exclusions barred coverage (dishonest/malicious acts, civil rights violations, emotional distress).
brief_summary: Cincinnati Insurance Company sought declaratory judgment that it had no duty to defend or indemnify Lost Run Farm HOA, its board members, and property management company Armour against the Garcias' discrimination claims in underlying state litigation. The court granted Cincinnati's summary judgment motion, finding no coverage under the CGL policy (intentional discriminatory acts did not constitute an 'occurrence') and no coverage under the Wrongful Acts policy (exclusions for dishonest/malicious acts and civil rights violations applied).
key_cases_cited: Jim Barna Log Sys. Midwest, Inc. v. Gen. Cas. Ins. Co. of Wisconsin, 791 N.E.2d 816 (Ind. Ct. App. 2003)
Auto-Owners Ins. Co. v. Harvey, 842 N.E.2d 1279 (Ind. 2006)

source_file: 10770839_2026_United States of America v. Juliet Payseur and 20-22 McGregor Avenue, LLC_njd
case_name: United States of America v. Juliet Payseur and 20-22 McGregor Avenue, LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; case involves race-based housing discrimination and retaliation claims.
key_holding: The court granted in part Doyle's motion to strike, striking Defendants' second, fifth, eighth (unclean hands portion), thirteenth, and fourteenth affirmative defenses as insufficient, while denying the motion as to the first (failure to state a claim) defense and denying Defendants' request for sanctions.
brief_summary: Brittany Doyle, a Black woman, intervened as a plaintiff in this Fair Housing Act enforcement action alleging that Defendants discriminated against her based on race by imposing discriminatory lease terms and retaliating against her after she filed a HUD complaint. The court ruled on Doyle's motion to strike Defendants' affirmative defenses, striking several as legally insufficient while denying others and also denying Defendants' request for sanctions.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal

source_file: 10770867_2026_Hector Salvatori v. The Huntington National Bank_ohsd
10772814_2026_Karen Sam _ Robert Sam v. Dekalb Housing Authority, et al._ilnd
case_name: Karen Sam & Robert Sam v. DeKalb Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs did not specifically identify what reasonable accommodations were requested, beyond vague references to accommodations that could have prevented their eviction and delay in processing a port request for their Section 8 voucher.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiffs failed to allege what specific accommodations were requested or how their disabilities connected to the alleged wrongs, and failed to state plausible disparate treatment or disparate impact claims.
brief_summary: Karen and Robert Sam, proceeding pro se, sued the DeKalb Housing Authority, HUD, and the City of Sycamore alleging Fair Housing Act violations and other claims arising from their eviction from Section 8 voucher housing and alleged delays in processing their request to port their voucher. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to state what specific accommodations were requested or how they related to plaintiffs' disabilities, and failed to adequately plead disparate treatment, disparate impact, or reasonable accommodation claims.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Tex. Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc.

Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. Of City of New York

source_file: 10773145_2025_Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc._flsd
case_name: Valery Kantsepolsky v. River Shores Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with chemical sensitivities requested that defendant use disability-related precautions during any entry into her unit for exploratory demolition and repairs.
key_holding: The court recommended staying the FHA claims under Colorado River abstention doctrine rather than dismissing them, finding the parallel state proceedings involve substantially similar parties and issues, while dismissing the ADA claim because residential condominiums are not places of public accommodation subject to ADA Title III.
brief_summary: Valery Kantsepolsky, a condominium owner with chemical sensitivities, sued the River Shores Association alleging the HOA violated the FHA by denying her requests for disability-related precautions during unit inspections and by refusing to engage in an interactive process. The magistrate judge recommended granting the motion to dismiss in part, dismissing the ADA claim and staying the FHA claims pending resolution of parallel state court proceedings involving the same parties and substantially similar issues.
key_cases_cited: Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)

source_file: 10773598_2026_Brittany M. Chandler v. LoanCare, LLC; Lakeview Loan Servicing, LLC; and Trustee Corps_ord
case_name: Brittany M. Chandler v. LoanCare, LLC; Lakeview Loan Servicing, LLC; and Trustee Corps
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges LoanCare refused to provide financial assistance (forbearance, loan modification, or other mortgage relief) after learning of her disability, while offering such assistance to her non-disabled ex-boyfriend for the same property.
key_holding: The court found that plaintiff raised serious questions as to the merits of her Fair Housing Act disability discrimination claim alleging that the mortgage servicer offered financial assistance to her ex-boyfriend but refused to extend such assistance to her after learning of her disability, warranting a TRO to prevent foreclosure.
brief_summary: Brittany Chandler, a disabled homeowner with a neuromuscular autoimmune disease and mental health conditions, sued her mortgage servicer and foreclosure trustee alleging Fair Housing Act disability discrimination after LoanCare refused to provide financial assistance following her disability disclosure while offering assistance to her non-disabled ex-boyfriend. The court granted a temporary restraining order enjoining the foreclosure sale after finding serious questions on the merits of her disability discrimination claim and that the balance of hardships favored the plaintiff.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
All. for the Wild Rockies v. Cottrell, 632 F.3d 1127 (9th Cir. 2011)

source_file: 10774111_2026_Jacob O’Connor v. Collett’s Mountain Resorts, Inc. d_b_a Flaming Gorge Resort and Maretta Bair_utd
case_name: Jacob O'Connor v. Collett's Mountain Resorts, Inc. d/b/a Flaming Gorge Resort and Maretta Bair
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to keep his trained diabetic alert dog, Smokey, in employer-provided shared employee housing. Smokey was trained to alert O'Connor or another human when O'Connor's blood glucose levels dropped or spiked, and O'Connor contended the dog was medically necessary to prevent unnoticed nocturnal hypoglycemic episodes that could result in coma or death.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss all seven causes of action, holding that plaintiff plausibly alleged ADA and FHA claims for failure to accommodate, wrongful termination/denial of housing, discriminatory statement, and retaliation based on defendants' refusal to allow his diabetic alert service dog in employer-provided housing and his subsequent termination.
brief_summary: Jacob O'Connor, a front desk clerk with Type 1 diabetes, sued his former employer Collett's Mountain Resorts after it refused to allow his trained diabetic alert dog in employer-provided employee housing and then terminated his employment when he protested the denial and mentioned seeking legal advice. The court held that employer-provided housing qualifies as a 'privilege of employment' under the ADA, that O'Connor's requests to multiple managers constituted protected activity, and that the close temporal connection between his accommodation requests and his firing supported plausible claims. The court denied defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss all seven causes of action arising under the ADA, the FHA, and the Utah Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Courage to Change Ranches Holding Co. v. El Paso
Cinnamon Hills Youth Crisis Ctr., Inc. v. Saint George City
Arnal v. Aspenview Condo. Ass'n

source_file: 10775296_2026_Jennifer Phillips v. Beckley Police Department and Officer Gregory and Officer Atterson and Officer Murray and Officer Birchfield and Officer Christian, in their individual and official capacities._wvsd
case_name: Jennifer Phillips v. Beckley Police Department et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested; the FHA claim was based on allegations that the Beckley Police Department's pattern of inaction in response to racially motivated harassment by neighbors, and Officer Murray's falsified or delayed police reports submitted to the Beckley Housing Authority, interfered with and discriminated against Phillips in the enjoyment of her federally protected housing rights.
key_holding: The court dismissed Jennifer Phillips' complaint against the Beckley Police Department and five officers, finding she failed to state a claim for § 1983 municipal liability, constitutional defamation, or Fair Housing Act violations, and overruled all objections to the magistrate judge's proposed findings and recommendation.
brief_summary: Jennifer Phillips, a pro se tenant at a Beckley Housing Authority property, sued the Beckley Police Department and five officers under § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, alleging that officers falsified police reports, failed to protect her from racially motivated harassment by neighbors, subjected her to unlawful detention, and ignored her requests to correct official reports. The district court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation, finding that Phillips failed to plead an official policy or custom for municipal liability, failed to allege a constitutionally cognizable deprivation for her defamation/stigma claim, and failed to allege a sufficient causal connection between any protected FHA activity and an adverse housing action. The court dismissed the complaint but held dismissal in abeyance until January 30, 2026, to allow Phillips an opportunity to file a curative amended complaint.
key_cases_cited: Paul v. Davis, 424 U.S. 693 (1976)
