source_file: 10776090_2026_Ernesto Varela, et al. v. William Harold Hill, et al._moed
case_name: Ernesto Varela, et al. v. William Harold Hill, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; this case concerns alleged race-based harassment and threats (§ 3617 retaliation claim) rather than a reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The court sua sponte identified a potential statute of limitations bar for Count III under the FHA (§ 3617) because plaintiffs filed their action approximately five years after the alleged discriminatory conduct ended, beyond the two-year limitations period, and ordered plaintiffs to show cause why the claim should not be dismissed.
brief_summary: Ernesto Varela and others sued William Harold Hill and others alleging race-based harassment and threats that made their housing unavailable and caused them to move; Count III under the Fair Housing Act's anti-retaliation provision survived earlier motions but the court sua sponte ordered plaintiffs to show cause why this claim should not be dismissed as untimely because it was filed approximately five years after the alleged discriminatory conduct ended, beyond the two-year FHA statute of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Buckley v. Ray, 848 F.3d 855 (8th Cir. 2017)
Smith v. Boyd, 945 F.2d 1041 (8th Cir. 1991)
Smithrod v. City of St. Paul, 746 F.3d 391 (8th Cir. 2014)

source_file: 10776210_2026_Bolima Tafah et al. v. Lake Village Townhomes et al._mdd
case_name: Bolima Tafah et al. v. Lake Village Townhomes et al.
accommodation_description: The complaint contains only conclusory allegations including 'refusal to accommodate postpartum recovery' and 'retaliation after request for accommodation' without specifying the nature of any accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed the amended complaint for failure to state plausible claims because plaintiffs' allegations were merely conclusory statements lacking sufficient factual content to support any cause of action, including FHA reasonable accommodation claims.
brief_summary: Bolima Tafah and Akwi Suna Epse Tafah sued Lake Village Townhomes, Orchards at Severn, LLC, RentGrow, Inc., and Equifax alleging over 50 violations of federal and state law including Fair Housing Act claims. The court granted all defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the amended complaint failed to state plausible claims because it contained only conclusory legal conclusions without supporting factual allegations.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

source_file: 10776283_2026_Akosua AaeBo-Akhan v. Kwesi Akhan, et al._ksd
case_name: Akosua Aaebo-Akhan v. Kwesi Akhan, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought one million dollars in damages and reinstatement of her Section 8 housing status after the cancellation of her Section 8 voucher in 2022.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim against HUD was dismissed because the United States has not waived sovereign immunity for claims under § 3617, and Plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to state a claim that HUD violated the Fair Housing Act.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Aaebo-Akhan, proceeding pro se, sued HUD seeking $1 million in damages and reinstatement of her Section 8 housing status after her voucher was cancelled in 2022, alleging her traffickers prevented her from submitting documents to HUD. The court dismissed her complaint against HUD under § 3617 of the Fair Housing Act because the United States has not waived sovereign immunity for such claims and Plaintiff failed to state facts sufficient to allege a FHA violation.
key_cases_cited: Kelly v. Wilson, 426 F. App'x 629 (10th Cir. 2011)

source_file: 10776300_2025_Min Huang, Qiong Dai, and Jiayin Dong v. Ken Paxton, Attorney General of Texas, in his Official Capacity_txwd
case_name: Min Huang, Qiong Dai, and Jiayin Dong v. Ken Paxton, Attorney General of Texas, in his Official Capacity
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this case involves a constitutional and statutory preemption challenge to Texas Senate Bill 17, which prohibits non-U.S. citizens and non-permanent residents domiciled in designated countries (including China) from purchasing or renting property in Texas for more than one year.
key_holding: The court dismissed the claims of the two foreign-domiciled plaintiffs (Min Huang and Quiong Dai) because foreign citizens outside U.S. territory lack standing to assert constitutional rights under both Rule 12(b)(1) and Rule 12(b)(6), denied the preliminary injunction for lack of irreparable harm as to plaintiff Jiayin Dong, and stayed Dong's remaining claims pending the Fifth Circuit's ruling in Wang v. Paxton.
brief_summary: Three Chinese nationals challenged Texas Senate Bill 17, which makes it unlawful for non-U.S. citizens or permanent residents domiciled in China and certain other countries to purchase or rent property in Texas for more than one year, asserting claims including FHA preemption, Equal Protection, and Supremacy Clause violations. The court dismissed the claims of plaintiffs Min Huang and Quiong Dai—both domiciled outside the United States—holding that foreign citizens outside U.S. territory cannot assert constitutional rights under either 12(b)(1) or 12(b)(6), and rejected their argument that Supremacy Clause and Equal Protection claims could survive on alternative facts. The court denied the preliminary injunction as to plaintiff Jiayin Dong, a Baylor University student on an F-1 visa whose lease is not yet expired, finding no irreparable harm at the time, and stayed his remaining claims pending the Fifth Circuit's opinion in the related case Wang v. Paxton.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Agency for Int'l Dev. v. All. for Open Soc'y Int'l, Inc., 591 U.S. 430 (2020)
United States v. Verdugo-Urquidez, 494 U.S. 259 (1990)
Boumediene v. Bush, 553 U.S. 723 (2008)

source_file: 10776301_2025_Rosanna Barrera v. LDG Riverstone LP, ET AL._txwd
case_name: Rosanna Barrera v. LDG Riverstone LP, ET AL.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants provide accessible design and construction including safe, accessible routes from the parking garage to her residential unit, and requested a reserved accessible parking spot in front of her unit due to her mobility limitations.
key_holding: The magistrate recommended dismissing plaintiff's Section 1983 claims for failure to plead state action, but found she stated non-frivolous FHA claims for design and construction violations under § 3604(f)(3)(C) and for failure to accommodate under § 3604(f)(3)(B) by denying her request for an accessible parking spot.
brief_summary: Rosanna Barrera, a tenant with mobility impairments, sued LDG Riverstone LP and related entities alleging the apartment complex's design lacked accessible routes from the parking garage to her unit and that defendants denied her request for a reserved accessible parking spot in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The magistrate recommended dismissing her Section 1983 constitutional claims for failing to plead state action, but found she adequately stated claims under the FHA for design and construction violations and failure to accommodate, allowing those FHA claims to proceed past in forma pauperis screening.
key_cases_cited: Providence Behav. Health v. Grant Rd. Pub. Util. Dist., 902 F.3d 448 (5th Cir. 2018)
Bowman v. RLB Inv. Partners, LLC, 2016 WL 7326622 (E.D. Tex. 2016)
Whitaker v. W. Vill. Ltd. P'ship, 2004 WL 2008502 (N.D. Tex. 2004)
Neitzke v. Williams, 490 U.S. 319 (1989)
Priester v. Lowndes Cnty., 354 F.3d 414 (5th Cir. 2004)

source_file: 10776422_2026_Daniel T. Doria v. Yavapai College District Governing Board, et al._azd
case_name: Daniel T. Doria v. Yavapai College District Governing Board, et al.
accommodation_description: The case text does not specify the particular accommodation requested in the underlying FHA claim; the opinion addresses only the attorneys' fees motion following dismissal, noting the FHA claim arose from defendants' enforcement of a lease governing plaintiff's tenancy at the Verde Valley RV Park and subsequent eviction proceedings.
key_holding: The court granted in part defendants' motion for attorneys' fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988(b) and A.R.S. § 12-349, awarding $7,500 of the requested $31,446 after finding plaintiff's FHA, ADA, retaliation, and Due Process claims were frivolous and brought without substantial justification, but reducing the award due to plaintiff's pro se status and limited financial resources.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Daniel Doria brought claims under the FHA, ADA, Arizona state law retaliation, and Due Process arising from defendants' enforcement of a lease and eviction proceedings at the Verde Valley RV Park. The court had previously dismissed all claims with prejudice based on res judicata and collateral estoppel because the same claims had already been adjudicated in state court. Defendants then sought $31,446 in attorneys' fees, which the court reduced to $7,500 based on plaintiff's in forma pauperis status, pro se status, and minimal income of approximately $300/month.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. Equal Emp. Opportunity Comm'n, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Miller v. L.A. Cnty. Bd. of Educ., 827 F.2d 617 (9th Cir. 1987)

source_file: 10776430_2026_Nicole Furnas v. Tierra Luna and Sol Enterprises, LLC; et al._azd
case_name: Nicole Furnas v. Tierra Luna and Sol Enterprises, LLC; et al.
accommodation_description: Sexual harassment claim - tenant alleges maintenance worker demanded sexual favors in exchange for lease renewal
key_holding: The court granted the motion for protective order in part, limiting discovery to relevant topics and requiring each party to bear their own costs.
brief_summary: Nicole Furnas sued Tierra Luna and Sol Enterprises and its maintenance worker Jesus Santos Caceres, alleging sexual harassment in violation of the Federal Fair Housing Act after Caceres allegedly demanded sexual favors in exchange for lease renewal. The court resolved a discovery dispute by granting in part the defendants' motion for protective order to limit the scope of depositions and discovery requests to relevant matters.
key_cases_cited: Phillips ex rel. Ests. of Byrd v. Gen. Motors Corp., 307 F.3d 1206 (9th Cir. 2002)

source_file: 10776572_2026_Steven E. Hobbs, Sr. v. Igor Goncharko, et al._ilnd
case_name: Steven E. Hobbs, Sr. v. Igor Goncharko, et al.
accommodation_description: Hobbs requested expedited rodent remediation as a disability accommodation because his mobility impairment prevented him from cleaning infested areas without re-injury risk, and eviction settlement/payment plan due to disability-related financial hardship.
key_holding: The court granted Coldwell Banker's motion to dismiss the racial disparate impact claim with prejudice, but denied Landlord Defendants' motion on the failure-to-accommodate claim, finding that rodent remediation is plausibly a service accommodation rather than a modification, while eviction-related requests fail because financial hardship is not unique to disabled persons.
brief_summary: Steven Hobbs, an African American tenant with a mobility disability from spinal fractures, sued his Chicago landlords and Coldwell Banker under the Fair Housing Act alleging racial discrimination, disability discrimination, and retaliation. The court granted Coldwell Banker's motion to dismiss his disparate impact racial discrimination claim with prejudice for failure to plead causation, but denied the landlords' motion on Hobbs's failure-to-accommodate claim regarding rodent remediation, which the court found plausibly alleges a service accommodation necessary due to his disability.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Watters v. Homeowners' Ass'n at Pres. at Bridgewater, 48 F.4th 779 (7th Cir. 2022)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Oconomowoc Residential Programs v. City of Milwaukee, 300 F.3d 775 (7th Cir. 2002)

source_file: 10776828_2025_FDA v. R. J. Reynolds Vapor Co._scotus
10777793_2026_Kevin Brown v. Cornerstone Realtors, LLC, et al._moed
case_name: Kevin Brown v. Cornerstone Realtors, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Claim that developers, architects, builders, contractors, and/or owners of an apartment complex violated the FHAA's design and construction accessibility requirements.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to prosecute, finding that while plaintiff's counsel engaged in improper conduct by allowing deadlines to lapse due to a busy schedule, dismissal would be a disproportionate sanction where there was no bad faith and defendants had not been prejudiced by failure to engage in discovery.
brief_summary: Kevin Brown sued Cornerstone Realtors, LLC, LC Lafayette Partners, LLC, and The Hinrichs Group, Inc. under the Fair Housing Act alleging that the developers, architects, builders, contractors, and/or owners of an apartment complex at 2200 LaSalle Street in St. Louis, Missouri violated the FHAA's accessibility and usability requirements. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss for failure to prosecute under Rule 41(b), finding that dismissal would be too harsh a sanction absent a clear record of delay or contumacious conduct and warning plaintiff that future dilatory conduct would result in sanctions including dismissal.

source_file: 10777846_2026_Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc., et al._mdd
case_name: Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Siguel requested, as a reasonable modification under the FHA, that he be permitted to leave the roof of his front porch without a decorative balustrade (a fake balcony composed of columns, posts, and railings), or alternatively, that King Farm install and maintain the balustrade for him, on the ground that his physical disability causes pain, bleeding, and fatigue that make installing and maintaining the structure burdensome and harmful.
key_holding: The court denied Siguel's motion to vacate the dismissal of his 2025 lawsuit because both his 2022 and 2025 complaints arise from the same ongoing dispute over King Farm's demand that he reinstall a balustrade, and under the doctrine against claim splitting, all claims arising out of a single wrong must be presented in one action.
brief_summary: Edward Siguel, a disabled homeowner in a planned community, filed a second federal lawsuit in 2025 against his HOA, King Farm Citizens Assembly, alleging FHA violations related to the association's repeated demands that he reinstall a decorative balustrade on his front porch roof, which he removed in 2019 due to roof damage and the difficulty of maintaining it given his disability. The court sua sponte dismissed the 2025 case as duplicative of Siguel's still-pending 2022 lawsuit, which involved substantively identical allegations about the same balustrade dispute. Siguel's motion to vacate the dismissal and for leave to amend were denied because the 2025 claims arise from the same continuing wrong as the 2022 case and must be pursued in that proceeding, whether through a motion to supplement or for reconsideration.
key_cases_cited: Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Sensormatic Sec. Corp. v. Sensormatic Elecs. Corp., 452 F. Supp. 2d 621 (D. Md. 2006)
Katyle v. Penn Nat'l Gaming, Inc., 637 F.3d 462 (4th Cir. 2011)
JTH Tax, Inc. v. Aime, 984 F.3d 284 (4th Cir. 2021)
Hodges v. Meletis, 109 F.4th 252 (4th Cir. 2024)

source_file: 10778453_2026_New Beginning Sanctuary, A Missouri Not-For-Profit Corporation, Jaam Properties LLC, A Missouri Limited Liability Company, and Alon Fisch, An Individual v. City of Springfield, Missouri, A Missouri Municipa
case_name: New Beginning Sanctuary, A Missouri Not-For-Profit Corporation, Jaam Properties LLC, A Missouri Limited Liability Company, and Alon Fisch, An Individual v. City of Springfield, Missouri, A Missouri Municipal Corporation
accommodation_description: Request to operate a residential recovery home for persons in recovery from substance use addiction in an R-SF residential zone as a reasonable accommodation from the City's zoning ordinance that prohibits group homes within a quarter mile of an existing group home.
key_holding: Plaintiffs' expert testimony may be admitted under Daubert for disparate impact and disparate treatment claims, but must be excluded from the failure to accommodate claim under One Love Housing because the experts' opinions were not presented to the City as part of Plaintiffs' accommodation request.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs New Beginning Sanctuary and Jaam Properties sued the City of Springfield seeking to operate a residential recovery home for individuals recovering from substance use addiction, requesting a reasonable accommodation from the City's zoning ordinance that prohibited group homes within a quarter mile of an existing group home. The Court ruled on a motion to exclude expert testimony, allowing the experts' opinions to be considered for disparate impact and disparate treatment claims but excluding them for the failure to accommodate claim because the plaintiffs did not present this evidence to the City during the administrative process.
key_cases_cited: One Love Hous., LLC v. City of Anoka, Minnesota, 93 F.4th 424 (8th Cir. 2024)
Lapid-Laurel, L.L.C. v. Zoning Bd. of Adjustment, 284 F.3d 442 (3d Cir. 2002)
Tsombanidis v. W. Haven Fire Dep't, 352 F.3d 565 (2d Cir. 2003)
Gallagher v. Magner, 619 F.3d 823 (8th Cir. 2010)
Daubert v. Merrell Dow Pharmaceuticals, 509 U.S. 479 (1993)

source_file: 10779646_2026_Orane M. Cornish Jr. v. Cheyanne Tripp et al._ctd
case_name: Orane M. Cornish Jr. v. Cheyanne Tripp et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges his landlord conditioned continued housing on submission to unwanted sexual advances, creating a hostile housing environment.
key_holding: The court denied Defendant Tripp's motion to dismiss Plaintiff's FHA hostile housing environment claim, finding Plaintiff sufficiently alleged that his landlord conditioned housing on submission to unwanted sexual advances on the basis of sex, but granted Defendant Paris's motion to dismiss because Paris, as a non-landlord associate, lacked sufficient connection to Plaintiff’s housing arrangement.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Orane Cornish, proceeding pro se, sued Defendant Tripp (his landlord) and Defendant Paris (Tripp's associate) under the Trafficking Victims Protection Act and Fair Housing Act, alleging he was coerced into unpaid labor and sex trafficking, and that his landlord created a hostile housing environment by conditioning housing on submission to unwanted sexual advances. The court denied both defendants' motions to dismiss the TVPA claims and denied Tripp's motion to dismiss the FHA hostile housing environment claim, but dismissed the FHA claim against Paris without leave to amend because he was not the plaintiff's landlord.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Texas Dep't of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)
Cain v. Rambert, No. 13-CV-5807 (MKB), 2014 WL 2440596 (E.D.N.Y. May 30, 2014)

source_file: 10779681_2026_Justin Thomas Fanty v. Greater Dayton Premier Management, et al._ohsd
case_name: Justin Thomas Fanty v. Greater Dayton Premier Management, et al.
accommodation_description: The opinion does not describe the specific accommodation request; the complaint alleging Fair Housing Act violations was dismissed as time-barred and failing to state a claim.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims fail because they are time-barred and fail to state a claim upon which relief can be granted, and the case was dismissed with prejudice for failure to prosecute after plaintiff failed to respond to the motion for judgment on the pleadings despite being given multiple opportunities to do so.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Justin Thomas Fanty, proceeding pro se, sued Greater Dayton Premier Management (a public housing authority) and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations during his tenancy. The court granted defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings on the merits, finding the claims time-barred and insufficient, and also dismissed the case with prejudice for failure to prosecute after Fanty failed to respond to the motion despite receiving multiple extensions.

source_file: 10779805_2026_Ellen Burke v. AP Atherton Limited Partnership, Tomlinson _ Associates Inc., Teri Giacomino, Glen Kyle, Tim Beery and Tom Mannschreck_mtd
case_name: Ellen Burke v. AP Atherton Limited Partnership, Tomlinson & Associates Inc., Teri Giacomino, Glen Kyle, Tim Beery and Tom Mannschreck
accommodation_description: The opinion does not describe any specific accommodation request; the court merely notes plaintiff was granted leave to amend her Fair Housing Act claims.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' Motion to Dismiss as moot because plaintiff filed an amended complaint, which superseded the original complaint and rendered the pending motion to dismiss non-justiciable.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Ellen Burke sued AP Atherton Limited Partnership, Tomlinson & Associates Inc., and individual defendants for Fair Housing Act claims. The court initially dismissed all defendants except AP Atherton Limited Partnership and Tomlinson & Associates Inc. and granted leave to amend, then denied the pending Motion to Dismiss as moot upon the filing of an Amended Complaint.
key_cases_cited: CDK Global LLC v. Brnovich, 16 F.4th 1266 (9th Cir. 2021)
Morgan v. LexisNexis Risk Solutions, Inc., 2025 WL 2986630 (E.D. Cal. Oct. 23, 2025)

source_file: 10780289_2026_Heidi Erickson v. Michael Inman, et al._ilcd

10781059_2026_Christine Carroll, individually and on behalf of residents of “A Fortress,” v. Town of Manchester, City of Hartford, Roger Thrall, Nancy Navarretta, and Advanced Behavioral Health, Inc._ctd
case_name: Christine Carroll, individually and on behalf of residents of "A Fortress," v. Town of Manchester, City of Hartford, Roger Thrall, Nancy Navarretta, and Advanced Behavioral Health, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to enjoin enforcement of zoning, building, and fire code ordinances against her substance abuse recovery group homes, arguing that selective enforcement against facilities housing individuals with disabilities (persons recovering from addiction) constituted discrimination, and she requested that defendants be enjoined from enforcing any directives or ordinances requiring cessation of operations at 510 New Britain Avenue, Hartford and 101-103 Cedar Street, Manchester.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for a preliminary injunction because she failed to demonstrate irreparable harm or a clear likelihood of success on the merits of her FHA and ADA claims alleging discriminatory enforcement of municipal zoning, building, and fire codes against her substance abuse recovery group homes.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Christine Carroll, owner and operator of multiple substance abuse recovery group homes operating as 'A Fortress,' sued the Town of Manchester, City of Hartford, state DMHAS commissioner, and a behavioral health contractor, alleging they enforced zoning, building, and fire codes in a discriminatory manner against her properties in violation of the FHA, ADA, and the Fourteenth Amendment. Plaintiff sought a TRO and preliminary injunction to prevent enforcement of ordinances that could result in closure of her properties and eviction of disabled residents. The court denied the motion, finding no irreparable harm (residents remained housed with no imminent eviction) and no clear likelihood of success on the merits, and further concluding the balance of equities favored defendants given the compelling public interest in ensuring safe, code-compliant housing.
key_cases_cited: Stewart B. McKinney Found., Inc. v. Town Plan & Zoning Comm'n of Town of Fairfield, 790 F. Supp. 1197 (D. Conn. 1992)
Step By Step, Inc. v. City of Ogdensburg, 176 F. Supp. 3d 112 (N.D.N.Y. 2016)

source_file: 10781103_2026_KORTNEY DONAVON v. RICHMOND-HENRICO ARMS LIMITED PARTNERSHIP_vaed
case_name: Kortney Donavon v. Richmond-Henrico Arms Limited Partnership
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation requested is not described in the federal court opinion; plaintiff invoked FHA § 3604(f) as a defense to eviction in state court proceedings, suggesting a disability-related accommodation was asserted before the state court, but the nature of the accommodation is not detailed in this federal court record.
key_holding: The court dismissed the action for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the state court eviction proceeding was not properly removable, the claims were moot after execution of the writ of eviction, and the Anti-Injunction Act barred the requested injunctive relief.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Kortney Donavon attempted to remove a state court eviction proceeding to federal court after a writ of eviction issued by Henrico County General District Court, asserting Fair Housing Act claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604(f) and 3617 and civil rights claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1983 and 1985(3). The federal court dismissed the action on three independent grounds: the writ had already been executed rendering the matter moot, the state court action was not removable because no pending controversy existed when plaintiff filed, and the Anti-Injunction Act precluded the court from enjoining state court proceedings. The court granted plaintiff's IFP application but dismissed without reaching the merits of any claims.
key_cases_cited: Porter v. Clarke, 852 F.3d 358 (4th Cir. 2017)
Atlantic C. L. R. Co. v. Bhd. of Locomotive Eng'rs, 398 U.S. 281 (1970)
Denny's Inc. v. Cake, 364 F.3d 521 (4th Cir. 2004)

source_file: 10781650_2026_Sharon Lee, et al. v. Twin Hawks Airpark LLC, et al._azd
case_name: Sharon Lee, et al. v. Twin Hawks Airpark LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege Twin Hawks filed an easement lawsuit in retaliation for Lee's housing discrimination complaint filed with the Arizona Attorney General.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' retaliation claims with leave to amend, finding plaintiffs failed to plead facts showing Twin Hawks' easement lawsuit would not have occurred without intentional race-based retaliation, particularly when a plausible nonretaliatory explanation (enforcing prescriptive easements) was supported by deposition testimony, the timing of events, and the large number of community members believing easements existed.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Sharon Lee and Tommy Wessel sued Twin Hawks Airpark LLC and Managing Committee member Harold Duane Lambeth, alleging Twin Hawks filed state court easement litigation in retaliation for Lee's housing discrimination complaint filed with the Arizona Attorney General, asserting claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, and 3617. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege but-for causation for their retaliation claims given the compelling alternative explanation that Twin Hawks legitimately pursued easement enforcement against community members who had barricaded roads and obstructed property.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

source_file: 10782307_2026_Jesse Lewis Walker v. Lukrom REIT LLC, et al._azd
case_name: Jesse Lewis Walker v. Lukrom REIT LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's dog was left in the apartment during eviction; the accommodation request is not clearly articulated as a reasonable accommodation but is framed as familial status discrimination and retaliation for requesting repairs.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims for failure to state a claim because the conclusory allegations of familial status discrimination and retaliation lacked sufficient factual matter to make the claims plausible under Ashcroft v. Iqbal and Bell Atlantic v. Twombly; the court granted leave to amend the FHA claims but denied leave to amend the PTFA claim as futile.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jesse Walker, who was evicted for non-payment of rent, sued his landlord Lukrom REIT LLC alleging Fair Housing Act claims for familial status discrimination and retaliation for requesting repairs. The court screened the complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) and dismissed it for failure to state a claim, finding the FHA allegations were conclusory and unsupported by sufficient factual matter, but granted leave to amend the FHA claims against Lukrom while denying leave to amend the PTFA claim as futile.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Tami Huston; Justin Huston v. Willamette Valley Rentals, LLC; Nick Sharifi; Roya Sharifi
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case involves refusal to rent to foster parents with disabled children based on familial status and disability
key_holding: Plaintiffs, who are foster parents of children with disabilities, are entitled to summary judgment on their Fair Housing Act claims because the landlord's treatment of their rental application changed adversely after learning of their familial status and children's disabilities, while a similarly situated applicant without children or disabilities was offered more favorable terms.
brief_summary: Foster parents with disabled children sued a property management company for housing discrimination after their rental application was denied following disclosure of their family composition and children's disabilities. The court granted plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment on federal and state Fair Housing Act claims, finding that defendants discriminated against plaintiffs based on familial status and disability by refusing to rent and offering less favorable terms compared to applicants without children or disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Morris v. West Hayden Estates First Addition Homeowners Ass'n, Inc., 104 F.4th 1128 (9th Cir. 2024)

source_file: 10784337_2026_Shasta Partee, on behalf of herself and all other occupants v. Powers Properties_scd
case_name: Shasta Partee, on behalf of herself and all other occupants v. Powers Properties
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodation to allow her son with mental health disabilities (ADHD, bipolar disorder, emotional dysregulation) to remain in the apartment despite behavioral incidents rather than having her lease non-renewed.
key_holding: The court held that plaintiff failed to establish the accommodation was necessary to afford an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling because the requests neither specified what accommodation was sought nor identified how it would ameliorate the son's mental impairments, and alternatively that the direct threat exception applied given documented evidence of the son posing safety risks.
brief_summary: Shasta Partee sued Powers Properties, the property manager of Briar Grove Apartments, alleging the landlord failed to accommodate her adult son's mental health disabilities and retaliated against her after she requested accommodations to prevent lease non-renewal based on the son's behavioral incidents. The court granted summary judgment for the defendant, finding plaintiff failed to establish the requested accommodation was necessary and that the direct threat exception applied given evidence of the son pointing a realistic weapon at people, jumping from a balcony, and committing arson.

source_file: 10784366_2026_Laura Saitta v. Greystar Real Estate Partners, LLC; et al._casd
case_name: Laura Saitta v. Greystar Real Estate Partners, LLC; et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; claim is for gender-based discrimination in housing terms and conditions
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act sex discrimination claim because the SAC contained only conclusory allegations without factual content sufficient to plausibly infer gender-based discriminatory animus, and plaintiff was currently renting a two-bedroom penthouse unit contradicting her theory that women were being forced into one-bedroom apartments.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Laura Saitta, proceeding pro se, sued Greystar Real Estate Partners (property manager), Kilroy Realty (property owner), and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act sex discrimination and Section 1985 conspiracy claims related to her rental at One Paseo Village in San Diego, claiming she was discriminatorily subjected to unequal housing terms and pricing because she is a woman. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss without leave to amend, finding plaintiff's FHA sex discrimination claim conclusory and factually unsupported, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.

source_file: 10784453_2026_Lori Robins v. Waterford at Aberdeen Association, Inc., et al._flsd
case_name: Lori Robins v. Waterford at Aberdeen Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Visually impaired plaintiff requested to submit HOA work orders via email as an alternative to the inaccessible website.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff summary judgment on her reasonable accommodation claim for email work order submission, finding that Waterford constructively rejected the request by ignoring it after reviewing it; however, the court denied summary judgment on her pool gate lock modification claim because she failed to offer to pay for the modification as required under § 3604(f)(3)(A).
brief_summary: Plaintiff Lori Robins, who is visually impaired, sued Waterford at Aberdeen Association, Inc. (an HOA) for discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, alleging the HOA failed to accommodate her disability by refusing to provide accessible alternatives to its inaccessible website. The court granted partial summary judgment for Robins on her claim that the HOA constructively rejected her reasonable accommodation request to submit work orders via email, while denying her modification claim for the pool gate lock because she failed to offer to pay for it as required under § 3604(f)(3)(A).
key_cases_cited: Bhogaita v. Altamonte Heights Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 765 F.3d 1277 (11th Cir. 2014)

source_file: 10784485_2026_My Thi Nhu Tran, et al. v. Gulf Coast Bank _ Trust Co., et al._laed
case_name: My Thi Nhu Tran, et al. v. Gulf Coast Bank & Trust Co., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged defendants engaged in mortgage fraud against Vietnamese immigrants with limited English proficiency, and during settlement negotiations, defendants threatened foreclosure to coerce plaintiffs into abandoning their federal housing claims.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motions for reconsideration and leave to supplement because plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts to support a § 3617 retaliation claim (no causal connection between protected activity and adverse action), failed to allege state action for § 1983 claims, and failed to state a cognizable claim under § 1985 for conduct at a settlement conference.
brief_summary: Vietnamese immigrant homeowners sued Gulf Coast Bank, their mortgage broker, realty company, and closing agent alleging mortgage fraud and seeking to add claims for Fair Housing Act retaliation under § 3617 based on alleged foreclosure threats during settlement conference. The court denied plaintiffs' motions for reconsideration, finding plaintiffs failed to plead causation for the § 3617 retaliation claim, failed to allege state action for § 1983 claims, and failed to state a cognizable claim under § 1985 for settlement conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

case_name: Hemphill v. St. Mary's County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to appear virtually in all court proceedings as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's TRO and reasonable accommodation motions because plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits—she did not adequately demonstrate she has a disability, that defendant knew of her disability, or that any adverse action was caused by her disability status.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Larisha Hemphill, proceeding pro se, filed for a temporary restraining order and reasonable accommodation under the ADA and FHA against St. Mary's County Housing Authority. The court denied both motions because Hemphill failed to establish a likelihood of success on the merits—her filings did not adequately establish her disability status, causation linking any adverse action to disability, or imminent irreparable harm warranting emergency relief.

source_file: 10785456_2026_New Hampshire Youth Movement v. David M. Scanlan, in his official capacity as New Hampshire Secretary of State; Coalition for Open Democracy et al. v. David Scanlan in his official capacity as New Hampshire
10785621_2026_Vladik Uchikura, et al. v. Clark County Properties LP, et al._azd
case_name: Vladik Uchikura, et al. v. Clark County Properties LP, et al.
accommodation_description: Wheelchair user plaintiff requested accommodation to access the leasing office, laundry room, and ground floor apartments which were allegedly inaccessible to people with physical disabilities.
key_holding: The court granted CPA's motion to dismiss because the TAC failed to allege any facts establishing successor liability—CPA purchased the property over three years after plaintiffs' tenancy ended, and there were no allegations of CPA's specific conduct, express assumption of liabilities, consolidation, mere continuation, or fraudulent transfer.
brief_summary: Vladik Uchikura and Cindy Mateer, individuals with disabilities including wheelchair use, sued Clark County Properties LP, management companies, and successor owner Copper Point Apartments LLC alleging Fair Housing Act violations for discrimination based on disability and failure to accommodate accessibility barriers at CopperPoint Apartments during their 2019-2021 tenancy. The court granted CPA's motion to dismiss on successor liability grounds, finding the TAC failed to allege any facts plausibly establishing that CPA assumed liability for the predecessor owners' alleged misconduct occurring years before CPA's 2024 property purchase.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

source_file: 10785674_2026_Kathleen Bankhead, individually and on behalf of all others similarly situated v. Wintrust Financial Corporation and Barrington Bank _ Trust Co., N.A._ilnd
case_name: Kathleen Bankhead v. Wintrust Financial Corporation and Barrington Bank & Trust Co., N.A.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves alleged race discrimination in mortgage lending terms and access to favorable loan products (float-down option, interest rates).
key_holding: The court dismissed the Second Amended Complaint with prejudice because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination (no factual allegations of discriminatory animus connecting Wintrust's policies to racial disparities) or disparate impact (statistics alone, without identifying a specific 'artificial, arbitrary, and unnecessary' policy causing the disparity, cannot satisfy the robust causality requirement under Texas Dept. of Housing v. Inclusive Communities Project).
brief_summary: African American plaintiff Kathleen Bankhead sued Wintrust Financial Corporation and Barrington Bank alleging racial discrimination in mortgage lending, claiming she was denied favorable loan terms (float-down option, lower interest rates) because of her race and because she was purchasing property in Bronzeville, a majority-Black Chicago neighborhood. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding the complaint failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination (no allegations of discriminatory animus connecting policies to disparities) and disparate impact (statistics alone, without identifying a specific policy causing disparity, cannot satisfy the causal requirements under Inclusive Communities).

source_file: 10785877_2026_Linda C. Chase v. Arbor Properties Development Inc., et al._flnd
case_name: Linda C. Chase v. Arbor Properties Development Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; plaintiff alleges retaliation for having filed a prior fair housing complaint alleging disability discrimination.
key_holding: Plaintiff fails to state a plausible FHA retaliation claim because the temporal sequence—Arbor decided in June 2021 not to lease to Plaintiff before she filed her discrimination complaint in August 2021—irrefutably negates causation, and the ten-month gap between the protected activity and the adverse action is insufficient without additional factual allegations.
brief_summary: Linda C. Chase sued Arbor Properties Development Inc. and individual property managers alleging defendants denied her lease application at Arbor Landing Mill Bayou in retaliation for her having filed a fair housing complaint based on disability. The magistrate judge recommends dismissal, finding the second amended complaint is an impermissible shotgun pleading and alternatively that plaintiff failed to state a retaliation claim because the timeline negates causation.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Philippeaux v. Apartment Inv. & Mgmt. Co., 598 F. App'x 640 (11th Cir. 2015)

source_file: 10786318_2026_Lorin Grossman v. B_J Services of Miami, LLC, et al._flsd
case_name: Lorin Grossman v. B&J Services of Miami, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a wheelchair user, alleges landlord refused to show or lease property to her because of her physical disability.
key_holding: The court entered default judgment on Counts III–XI (Florida FHA claims and federal § 3604(c), (d), and (f)(1) claims) based on disability discrimination, but denied default judgment on Counts I and II because federal § 3604(a) and (b) do not cover disability-based discrimination.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Lorin Grossman, a wheelchair user, sued B&J Services of Miami and its agent alleging they refused to show or lease a rental property to her because of her disability after representing the property was unavailable while showing it to able-bodied prospective tenants. The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to enter default judgment on most claims under the Florida Fair Housing Act and federal § 3604(c), (d), and (f)(1), awarding $132,200 in damages, but denied default judgment on federal § 3604(a) and (b) claims because those provisions do not cover disability discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Banai v. Sec'y, U.S. Dept. of Hous. & Urban Dev., 102 F.3d 1203 (11th Cir. 1997)
Eagle Hosp. Physicians, LLC v. SRG Consulting, Inc., 561 F.3d 1298 (11th Cir. 2009)

source_file: 10786786_2026_Laquita Oliver v. Navy Federal Credit Union_ca4
case_name: Oliver v. Navy Federal Credit Union
accommodation_description: Class action alleging Navy Federal Credit Union's semi-automated underwriting algorithm produces discriminatory results against African American, Latino, and other minority mortgage applicants through disparate treatment and disparate impact.
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit held that district courts may deny class certification before discovery only if the complaint's allegations fail to satisfy Rule 23(a) and (b) as a matter of law, affirmed the denial of Rule 23(b)(3) class certification for lack of commonality due to significant variation across mortgage products, minority groups, and adverse outcomes, but vacated the Rule 23(b)(2) denial as premature.
brief_summary: Nine minority mortgage applicants sued Navy Federal Credit Union individually and on behalf of a putative class alleging that its semi-automated underwriting algorithm produces discriminatory results against African Americans, Latinos, and other racial minorities in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Rule 23(b)(3) class certification, finding the proposed class lacked commonality because statistical evidence showed disparate impact varied significantly across different mortgage products, minority groups, and adverse outcomes with no single practice uniformly affecting all class members, but vacated the Rule 23(b)(2) certification denial as premature.
key_cases_cited: Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. Dukes, 564 U.S. 338 (2011)
Goodman v. Schlesinger, 584 F.2d 1325 (4th Cir. 1978)
General Telephone Co. of Southwest v. Falcon, 457 U.S. 147 (1981)
Eisen v. Carlisle & Jacquelin, 417 U.S. 156 (1974)
Microsoft Corp. v. Baker, 582 U.S. 23 (2017)

source_file: 10786933_2026_Judy Shaw Foundation, Inc. v. City of Howard, South Dakota_sdd
case_name: Judy Shaw Foundation, Inc. v. City of Howard, South Dakota
accommodation_description: This is a procedural order striking defendant's untimely motion for partial summary judgment; no accommodation is analyzed as the court addressed only statutory standing and Rule 16(b) good cause.
key_holding: The City of Howard's partial summary judgment motion raised only statutory standing arguments (whether JSF qualifies as an 'aggrieved person' under the FHA and third-party standing under § 1983), which are non-jurisdictional merits issues subject to procedural deadlines; because the City failed to show good cause for filing nine months after the dispositive-motion deadline and was not diligent, the motion was properly stricken.
brief_summary: Judy Shaw Foundation, a fair housing organization, sued the City of Howard, South Dakota, under the Fair Housing Act (and § 1983); this order grants JSF's motion to strike the City's partial summary judgment motion as untimely. The court held that the City's motion raised only statutory standing issues (whether JSF is an 'aggrieved person' under the FHA) that are non-jurisdictional and subject to scheduling deadlines, and because the City failed to demonstrate good cause or diligence in filing nine months late, the motion was properly stricken.
key_cases_cited: Arbaugh v. Y & H Corp., 546 U.S. 500 (2006)
Bank of Am. Corp. v. City of Miami, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Env't, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)
Sherman v. Winco Fireworks, Inc., 532 F.3d 709 (8th Cir. 2008)
FW/PBS, Inc. v. City of Dallas, 493 U.S. 215 (1990)

10787023_2026_United States of America v. Douglas S. Waterbury, Carol A. Waterbury, E_A Management Co., and Ontario Realty, Inc._nynd
case_name: United States of America v. Douglas S. Waterbury, Carol A. Waterbury, E&A Management Co., and Ontario Realty, Inc.
accommodation_description: This is a procedural motion to dismiss based on the expiration of a consent decree, not a reasonable accommodation case; the underlying discrimination allegations are not substantively analyzed in this order.
key_holding: The consent decree, which was entered on August 9, 2019 with a five-year effective period, expired on August 9, 2024, and neither party moved to extend it, so the case must be dismissed with prejudice.
brief_summary: The United States government sued landlords and property management companies for Fair Housing Act violations, a consent decree was entered in 2019, and defendants were later held in contempt for violating it. On defendants' motion, the court dismissed the case with prejudice because the five-year consent decree expired on August 9, 2024, and neither party sought to extend it.

source_file: 10793996_2026_Chelsie Nitschke and Cynthia George v. 326 Welch Partners; Avenue Construction, LLC; Barnett Design Studio, LLC_tnmd
case_name: Chelsie Nitschke and Cynthia George v. 326 Welch Partners; Avenue Construction, LLC; Barnett Design Studio, LLC
accommodation_description: This is a design and construction accessibility case, not an individual accommodation request case; the plaintiffs alleged the apartment complex failed to meet FHA accessibility requirements.
key_holding: The court granted judgment on the pleadings and found defendants liable for violating 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C) and the ADA by failing to design and construct the apartment complex in compliance with federal accessibility standards.
brief_summary: Two disabled Tennessee residents sued the owner, construction company, and architectural firm of a Nashville apartment complex, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act's design and construction requirements. The defendants admitted most allegations and acknowledged violations of the FHA and Fair Housing Act Accessibility Guidelines, with the court granting judgment on the pleadings and finding defendants liable for failing to design and construct accessible covered multifamily dwellings under § 3604(f)(3)(C).
key_cases_cited: Meyer Nat. Foods, LLC v. Liberty Mut. Fire Ins. Co., 218 F. Supp. 3d 1034 (D. Neb. 2016)

10795232_2026_Rosalind Holmes v. Warren County Metropolitan Housing Authority_ohsd
case_name: Rosalind Holmes v. Warren County Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for a two-bedroom unit to permit plaintiff's mother, a disability-related live-in caregiver, to be included in the household
key_holding: The court recommended denying the TRO and preliminary injunction because plaintiff failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits, irreparable harm, or that the requested affirmative relief fell within the proper scope of preliminary injunctive relief.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Rosalind Holmes sued Warren County Metropolitan Housing Authority under the Fair Housing Act alleging the agency denied her reasonable accommodation request for a two-bedroom unit to permit her mother to live with her as a disability-related live-in caregiver. The court recommended denying plaintiff's motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, finding she failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits or irreparable harm warranting extraordinary relief.

source_file: 10795873_2026_Bianca Bates v. Amin Habeeb, Marisol Bassit, and Iron Valley Real Estate_pamd
case_name: Bianca Bates v. Amin Habeeb, Marisol Bassit, and Iron Valley Real Estate
accommodation_description: No accommodation request is described; the amended complaint is completely devoid of any factual allegations about what the defendants did.
key_holding: The court dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice because it failed to state any claims—the complaint was devoid of factual allegations detailing what the defendants allegedly did to violate the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, or constitutional rights.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Bianca Bates sued Amin Habeeb, Marisol Bassit, and Iron Valley Real Estate for alleged violations of the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and constitutional rights. The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Report and Recommendation and dismissed the case with prejudice because the amended complaint contained no factual allegations whatsoever about what the defendants did to harm Bates.

case_name: Eleanor McGinn v. Broadmead, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for gluten-free meals at a continuing care retirement community due to celiac disease
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit held that McGinn forfeited review of her Fair Housing Act claim by failing to address the district court's alternate ground for dismissal, and alternatively that her FHA claim was barred by the two-year statute of limitations since the alleged failure to accommodate occurred in January 2019 and she filed suit in September 2023.
brief_summary: Eleanor McGinn, who has celiac disease, sued Broadmead, Inc., her continuing care retirement community, alleging it failed to accommodate her dietary needs by repeatedly serving her meals containing gluten. The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Broadmead on McGinn's Fair Housing Act claim, holding that she forfeited review by failing to address the district court's alternative reasoning and that her claim was untimely under the two-year statute of limitations; the court vacated summary judgment on state law breach of contract and negligence claims arising from a January 2021 incident involving allegedly contaminated chicken marsala.
key_cases_cited: Laufer v. Naranda Hotels, LLC, 60 F.4th 156 (4th Cir. 2023)
Nanni v. Aberdeen Marketplace, Inc., 878 F.3d 447 (4th Cir. 2017)
Hill v. Hampstead Lester Morton Ct. Partners LP, 581 F. App'x 178 (4th Cir. 2014)
Frederick Rd. Ltd. P'ship v. Brown & Sturm, 756 A.2d 963 (Md. 2000)
Clapper v. Amnesty Int'l USA, 568 U.S. 398 (2013)

case_name: Connecticut Fair Housing Center and Carmen Arroyo v. CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, LLC
accommodation_description: Arroyo requested that CoreLogic accept her conservatorship certificate as proof of authority to access her son Mikhail's consumer file, rather than requiring a power of attorney which Mikhail, as a conservatee, could not execute.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed that CoreLogic did not violate the Fair Housing Act because it did not proximately cause the denial of housing, and Arroyo failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate impact or failure to accommodate since she never provided a facially valid conservatorship certificate even after being informed of the documentation requirement.
brief_summary: Connecticut Fair Housing Center and Carmen Arroyo sued CoreLogic Rental Property Solutions, which provides tenant screening reports to housing providers, alleging that CoreLogic violated the Fair Housing Act by facilitating housing denials based on criminal history and by refusing to accept a conservatorship certificate as documentation for accessing a disabled conservatee's consumer file. The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal of the FHA claims, holding that CoreLogic did not proximately cause housing denials because landlords made independent discretionary decisions, and that Arroyo's failure-to-accommodate claim failed because she never provided a facially valid conservatorship certificate despite being informed of the requirement.
key_cases_cited: Staub v. Proctor Hospital, 562 U.S. 411 (2011)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)
Texas Dept. of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

FDA v. Alliance for Hippocratic Med., 144 S. Ct. 1540 (2024)

source_file: 10797116_2025_Kiara S. Jones v. Chad Chronister, ET AL._flmd
case_name: Kiara S. Jones v. Chad Chronister, ET AL.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges the legitimacy of a writ of possession issued while her eviction appeal was pending, seeking to have her eviction reversed or enjoined.
key_holding: The Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal review of state court judgments, and Florida law permitted the trial court to issue the writ of possession while the underlying order was on appeal absent a stay.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Kiara Jones, proceeding pro se, sued Sheriff Chad Chronister, Deputy Harrison, landlord Earl B. Mason Sr., and attorney Jason Kao challenging the validity of a writ of possession executed during her appeal of an eviction judgment. The Magistrate Judge recommends denying Jones's in forma pauperis motion and dismissing the amended complaint with prejudice because the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal review of the state court judgment and Florida law permitted issuance of the writ pending appeal absent a stay.
key_cases_cited: Exxon Mobil Corp. v. Saudi Basic Indus. Corp., 544 U.S. 280 (2005)
Siegel v. LePore, 234 F.3d 1163 (11th Cir. 2000)
Carr v. U.S. Bank, 793 F. App'x 971 (11th Cir. 2019)

source_file: 10797202_2026_Leonor E Canales v. Phoenix Housing Authority, et al._azd
case_name: Leonor E Canales v. Phoenix Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Request that PHA accept alternative medical documentation instead of required physician-signed accommodation form to process her Section 8 reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's failure to accommodate claim because she failed to allege sufficient facts about what specific accommodation she requested, how it was necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling, and why it was reasonable, though granting leave to amend.
brief_summary: Leonor Canales, a Section 8 participant with multiple mental health disabilities including depression, anxiety, PTSD, and bipolar disorder, sued the Phoenix Housing Authority alleging it failed to provide reasonable accommodations by refusing to accept her medical records instead of a required physician-signed form and failed to engage in an interactive process. The court dismissed her reasonable accommodation claim without prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding she did not adequately allege what accommodation she requested or why it was necessary and reasonable, though it allowed her retaliation claim to proceed.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC, 988 F.3d 1185 (9th Cir. 2021)
Salisbury v. City of Santa Monica, 998 F.3d 852 (9th Cir. 2021)

10799433_2026_Joyce Ann Jefferson v. Landmark Apartment Associates; Ross Financial Services, Inc.; Cris Barnett_ilcd
case_name: Joyce Ann Jefferson v. Landmark Apartment Associates; Ross Financial Services, Inc.; Cris Barnett
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a request for reasonable accommodation or modification; the FHA claims concern hostile housing environment and constructive eviction based on race and disability discrimination.
key_holding: The court granted Jefferson's motion for leave to amend her complaint to add six individual defendants and three state-law claims, finding the proposed amendments were not futile because the amended complaint stated plausible claims for FHA racial and disability discrimination, § 3617 interference/intimidation, conversion, constructive eviction, Illinois Landlord Retaliation Act violation, and negligence.
brief_summary: Joyce Ann Jefferson, a tenant in a federally subsidized apartment in Peoria managed by Landmark Apartment Associates and Ross Financial Services, alleged that employees stole her belongings and sold them on Facebook Marketplace, then launched a campaign of racial slurs, harassment, threats, and intimidation that drove her from the property. She brought FHA claims for racial and disability discrimination (§§ 3604(b) and 3604(c)) and unlawful intimidation (§ 3617), along with state-law claims for conversion. Jefferson moved to amend her complaint to add six individual employee defendants and three additional state-law claims (constructive eviction, Illinois Landlord Retaliation Act, and negligence). The court granted leave to amend in full, rejecting defendants' futility arguments on every count.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009) (en banc)

10800666_2026_Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing _ Redevelopment Commission_sdd
case_name: Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat v. Brookings Housing & Redevelopment Commission
accommodation_description: Plaintiff filed a motion for protective order prohibiting defendant from contacting her employer about employment, income, or medical limitations, which the court analyzed as unrelated to discovery.
key_holding: The magistrate judge's denial of plaintiff's protective order motion was not clearly erroneous or contrary to law because the motion was unrelated to discovery requests and plaintiff failed to meet and confer with defendant before filing.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Estela Elizabeth Jeffcoat filed an objection to Magistrate Judge Duffy's order denying her motion for a protective order to prevent defendant housing authority from contacting her employer about her employment, income, or medical limitations. The district court overruled her objection, finding the protective order motion was not related to any discovery requests in the case and plaintiff failed to meet and confer with defendant before filing.

case_name: Brown v. Nationwide Mutual Insurance Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with disability affecting executive function requested that insurance claims adjuster explain water remediation procedures in simplified terms.
key_holding: All of plaintiff's claims, including FHA reasonable accommodation claims, were dismissed with prejudice as time-barred because the alleged discriminatory conduct occurred in 2016 but plaintiff did not file suit until 2024, well beyond the applicable statutes of limitations.
brief_summary: Randy Brown sued Nationwide Mutual Insurance Company eight years after a 2016 water damage claim, alleging violations of the ADA and FHA based on the insurer's failure to provide effective communication accommodations about water remediation procedures. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice as time-barred, finding no basis for statutory tolling or equitable exception.

source_file: 10802670_2026_Sandy Phillips v. Stoddard County Circuit Court, et al._moed
case_name: Sandy Phillips v. Stoddard County Circuit Court, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested telephonic appearance at court hearings as an ADA Title II accommodation due to a documented disability that prevents her from driving; she alleged she had previously requested this accommodation from the Missouri state court but was denied, and she renewed the request before the federal court. In the housing context, she also alleged denial of 'reasonable modifications and telephonic accommodations' in state court proceedings where she sought to litigate her housing claims.
key_holding: The court grants plaintiff in forma pauperis status but orders her to file a second amended complaint on the court-provided form, finding the amended complaint legally deficient for misjoining unrelated claims against different defendant groups and failing to plead essential elements for each cause of action under the FHA, ADA Title II, and § 1983.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sandy Phillips brought claims under the FHA, ADA Title II, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, and Missouri law against her landlord and associated agents (for habitability issues and retaliatory conduct) and against state court defendants (for denying telephonic hearing accommodations). The court granted IFP status and conducted an initial § 1915 review, identifying multiple deficiencies including misjoinder of unrelated claims arising from two separate factual situations, and failure to allege essential elements for each legal theory. The court ordered plaintiff to file a second amended complaint choosing which set of claims to pursue in this action, warning that failure to comply would result in dismissal.

source_file: 10803192_2026_Jermaine Capel v. Norfolk Redevelopment _ Housing Authority_ca4
case_name: Jermaine M. Capel v. Norfolk Redevelopment & Housing Authority
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), finding no reversible error in the dismissal of plaintiff's Fair Housing Act and § 1983 claims.
brief_summary: Jermaine M. Capel, proceeding pro se, appealed the Eastern District of Virginia's dismissal of his Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims against Norfolk Redevelopment & Housing Authority. The Fourth Circuit affirmed, finding no reversible error in the district court's § 1915(e)(2)(B) dismissal.

source_file: 10803438_2026_Tanesha A. Turner v. 3526-28 E 9TH AVE TRUST, et al._innd
case_name: Tanesha A. Turner v. 3526-28 E 9TH AVE TRUST, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiff alleges discrimination based on familial status, sex, and domestic violence history, and retaliation for reporting housing violations.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA discrimination claim for failing to allege facts connecting defendants' actions to her protected characteristics, and dismissed her retaliation claim for failing to adequately plead protected activity under Rule 8 and Twombly.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Tanesha A. Turner sued her landlord, a housing assistance organization (Continuum of Care Network), and related individuals alleging Fair Housing Act discrimination based on familial status, sex, and domestic violence history, as well as retaliation for reporting housing violations. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the complaint failed to state a plausible claim because it lacked factual allegations connecting defendants' conduct to any protected characteristic and failed to adequately plead protected activity for the retaliation claim.

10804696_2026_Karen DeMoor v. Freeman Webb Company, Realtors, et al._tnmd
case_name: Karen DeMoor v. Freeman Webb Company, Realtors, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; the plaintiff alleged disability-related discrimination in housing maintenance and eviction without requesting any accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because, although she alleged she was disabled and discriminated against, she failed to allege that she requested a reasonable accommodation related to her disability, and she did not allege that defendants' actions were taken in response to any accommodation request.
brief_summary: Karen DeMoor, a tenant in Lebanon, Tennessee receiving Social Security Disability benefits, sued Freeman Webb Company (property manager) and individuals alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on delayed repairs to her window and smoke detectors and subsequent eviction. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice, finding that while plaintiff adequately alleged disability, she failed to state a plausible FHA claim because she never requested a reasonable accommodation related to her disability.

case_name: Shannon Perry v. Encore At Boulevard One LLC
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation request is not described in this appellate order; the opinion focuses on procedural issues rather than the merits of the FHA claim.
key_holding: The Tenth Circuit affirmed the dismissal of the Fair Housing Act claim, holding that the tenant's substantive challenges to the dismissal were waived for being raised only in the reply brief and lacked merit even if considered.
brief_summary: Shannon Perry appealed the dismissal of her Fair Housing Act claim arising from an eviction dispute against Encore At Boulevard One LLC and individual defendants. The Tenth Circuit affirmed the dismissal, holding that Perry waived her substantive challenges by raising them only in a reply brief, and rejected her remaining procedural arguments regarding the TRO denial as moot, the ADA and Double Jeopardy claims, the timing of dismissal before discovery, and the denial of a guardian ad litem.

source_file: 10805225_2026_Elhadj Alpha Mahmound Souare v. Akron Metropolitan Housing Authority, et al._ohnd
case_name: Elhadj Alpha Mahmound Souare v. Akron Metropolitan Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges his eviction from public housing, asserting claims under the Fair Housing Act without specifying a particular accommodation request.
key_holding: The federal district court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine to review a state court eviction judgment, and therefore dismissed plaintiff's complaint without addressing the merits of his Fair Housing Act claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Elhadj Alpha Mahmound Souare sued Akron Metropolitan Housing Authority and Stephanie Pence in federal court, challenging his September 2024 eviction and raising Fair Housing Act claims. The federal court dismissed the complaint sua sponte for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, holding that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal district courts from reviewing state court judgments, and denied all pending motions as moot.

source_file: 10805293_2026_Darrell Bilbrey v. Oceana Oceanfront Condominium Association, Inc._flmd
case_name: Darrell Bilbrey v. Oceana Oceanfront Condominium Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: This order does not analyze the merits of any accommodation request; it is a discovery ruling denying Defendant's motions to compel.
key_holding: The court denied Defendant's motions to compel discovery because Defendant failed to provide legal authority in support of its requests, exceeded the 25-interrogatory limit without court approval, propounded overbroad document requests, and sought production of tax returns irrelevant to the damages actually claimed.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Darrell Bilbrey sued Oceana Oceanfront Condominium Association under the Fair Housing Act for claims including reasonable accommodation denial after being recalled from the Board of Directors, and Defendant removed the case to federal court. This order denies Defendant's motions to compel discovery responses because Defendant failed to provide legal authority, exceeded interrogatory limits, and propounded procedurally defective discovery requests.

source_file: 10805317_2026_Jameerah Ware, Amira Ware, and Cheryl Vaughn v. A and K Properties of SC, Inc. and Sheriff Phillip E. Thompson_scd
case_name: Jameerah Ware, Amira Ware, and Cheryl Vaughn v. A and K Properties of SC, Inc. and Sheriff Phillip E. Thompson
accommodation_description: Request that the eviction and ejectment process accommodate Plaintiff Amira Ware's disabilities as required under the Fair Housing Act
key_holding: Plaintiffs' FHA claim against Sheriff Thompson was dismissed because Plaintiffs failed to respond to his arguments for dismissal and therefore conceded the claim, and Plaintiffs failed to allege facts plausibly demonstrating that Sheriff Thompson deprived Plaintiff Amira Ware of due process or otherwise discriminated against her on the basis of disability.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Jameerah Ware, Amira Ware, and Cheryl Vaughn sued their landlord A&K Properties and Sheriff Phillip Thompson alleging, inter alia, that the eviction process failed to accommodate Plaintiff Amira Ware's disabilities under the Fair Housing Act. The district court granted Sheriff Thompson's motion to dismiss, adopting the magistrate judge's recommendation, because Plaintiffs failed to respond to his dismissal arguments and thus conceded the FHA claim, and because Plaintiffs failed to state a plausible claim for relief against him.

source_file: 10805479_2026_Jlyn Bryant et al. v. Tinker Federal Credit Union_okwd
case_name: Jlyn Bryant et al. v. Tinker Federal Credit Union
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested in this case. The dispute involved plaintiffs' application for a $1.5 million residential mortgage loan that defendant denied, and plaintiffs' theory that the signed loan application itself constituted a financial asset owed back to them.
key_holding: The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding plaintiffs' claims—premised on the legally frivolous 'vapor money' theory—failed to state a plausible claim under the FHA, ECOA, or any other cited statute, and that amendment would be futile.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Jlyn Bryant and Joecelyne Acuna applied to Tinker Federal Credit Union for a $1.5 million residential mortgage loan, which was denied due to delinquent payment history and insufficient income. Plaintiffs sued alleging breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, and violations of ECOA and FHA, advancing the 'vapor money' theory that their signed loan application was a financial asset they lent to defendant, which defendant was obligated to credit back to them. The court dismissed all claims with prejudice under Rule 12(b)(6), holding that the vapor money theory has been universally rejected by federal courts, and that plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege disparate treatment under the FHA or ECOA because they did not allege membership in a protected class or differential treatment compared to similarly qualified applicants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

source_file: 10806862_2026_William M. Pickard, III v. American Pride Properties, LLC, et al._alnd
case_name: William M. Pickard, III v. American Pride Properties, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges APP Defendants refused to sell him property due to his disability-related criminal and litigious history (depression and mania).
key_holding: The court dismissed SPM Defendants' claims because plaintiff's FHA claims were conclusory and failed to allege SPM took prohibited discriminatory action; the court dismissed APP Defendants' claims under Colorado River abstention because parallel state court proceedings involving the same parties and substantially similar issues regarding the property sale were already pending.
brief_summary: William Pickard sued American Pride Properties (APP) and SPM LLC (his former landlord) alleging they discriminated against him due to his mental health disability by refusing to sell him property and by sharing derogatory information. The court abstained from the APP claims under Colorado River due to pending state litigation, and dismissed SPM claims for failure to state an FHA claim because plaintiff provided only conclusory allegations without facts showing SPM took prohibited discriminatory action.

case_name: Metropolitan Fair Housing Council of Oklahoma, Inc., James McNamee, and Marta McNamee v. Frank Feiock and Glenna Feiock, both d/b/a Rockford Garden Apartments
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to enforce the prior attorney's fees and costs award, ordering plaintiffs to pay $6,055.50 in fees and $2,151.65 in costs plus post-judgment interest within 45 days.
brief_summary: Following the entry of judgment for defendants on all Fair Housing Act failure to accommodate claims, defendants moved to enforce the court order awarding them attorney's fees and costs; plaintiffs disputed responsibility for payment asserting MFHCO would pay. The court granted the motion to enforce, finding the award was joint and undisputed, and ordered plaintiffs to pay within 45 days plus post-judgment interest at the applicable Treasury rate.

source_file: 10806920_2026_Harmony Home of Huntington, Inc. v. Executive Director, Indiana Department of Homeland Security, The Members of the Fire Prevention and Building Safety Commission, Indiana Department of Homeland Security_in
case_name: Harmony Home of Huntington, Inc. v. Executive Director, Indiana Department of Homeland Security
accommodation_description: Request for governmental exemption from Class 1 building code requirements applied to group recovery home for persons with substance use disorders
key_holding: The court found DHS engaged in intentional discrimination by classifying the Home as a Class 1 structure while treating similarly situated nuclear family and foster homes as Class 2, using a flexible yet targeted definition of 'tenant' that functions as a proxy for discrimination against persons with disabilities.
brief_summary: Harmony Home of Huntington, Inc., which operates a group recovery home for men with substance abuse disorders, sued the Indiana Department of Homeland Security and the Fire Prevention and Building Safety Commission alleging that DHS unlawfully classified the Home as a Class 1 structure under Indiana building codes while treating similarly situated nuclear family and foster homes as Class 2, violating the Fair Housing Amendments Act, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act. The court granted summary judgment for Plaintiff, finding that DHS engaged in intentional discrimination by applying a facially neutral 'tenant' definition in a manner designed to impose Class 1 building requirements on group homes for persons with disabilities while exempting comparable family homes, and entered a permanent injunction requiring DHS to treat the Home as a Class 2 structure.
key_cases_cited: New Horizons Rehabilitation, Inc. v. State, 400 F. Supp. 3d 751 (S.D. Ind. 2019)

source_file: 10806943_2026_Gabriella Collette, for herself and on behalf of Channin Collette, an incapacitated person v. Utah State Developmental Center; Utah State Department of Human Services; State of Utah; Jarod Squire_utd
case_name: Gabriella Collette, for herself and on behalf of Channin Collette, an incapacitated person v. Utah State Developmental Center; Utah State Department of Human Services; State of Utah; Jarod Squire
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges State Defendants violated the FHA by failing to prevent and protect Plaintiff from sexual assault at the Center, but does not identify a specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim (Count II) on Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity grounds because Congress did not abrogate states' immunity when enacting the FHA, and Utah has not waived immunity under the circumstances.
brief_summary: Gabriella Collette, as legal guardian of incapacitated Channin Collette with intellectual disabilities and autism, sued Utah State Developmental Center, the Utah Department of Health and Human Services, the State of Utah, and employee Jarod Squire alleging, inter alia, an FHA violation for failure to protect Channin from sexual assault by a caregiver. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claim on Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity grounds, holding Congress did not abrogate state immunity in the FHA and Utah has not waived immunity where the injury arose from assault and battery.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
