source_file: 10808207_2026_Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc., et al._mdd
case_name: Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the HOA (KFCA) accommodate his disability by excusing him from its requirement to reinstall the decorative columns and railings (a 'fake balcony' or 'balustrade') on the flat roof above his open front porch, citing that maintaining the structure caused him physical pain and organ damage due to the need to clear accumulated snow and ice. He also sought accommodations/modifications allowing him to build a brick patio in his backyard, construct a backyard shed, install a 'horizontal shed' on his front porch, and install a plant trellis — all of which KFCA denied.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for a preliminary injunction/stay because plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits, finding that the Fourth Circuit's Gibson Island Corp. decision did not alter the Bryant Woods causation/amelioration standard for 'necessity' under the FHA, and that plaintiff's request to avoid reinstalling decorative columns and railings on his porch roof did not plausibly provide direct amelioration of the effects of his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Edward Siguel, a disabled homeowner in an HOA community, sought a preliminary injunction to prevent KFCA from requiring him to reinstall decorative columns and railings ('fake balcony' or 'balustrade') on the flat roof above his front porch, contending the reinstallation requirement violated the FHA's reasonable accommodation and modification provisions and arguing that the Fourth Circuit's 2025 Gibson Island Corp. decision established new, more favorable legal standards. The court carefully analyzed Gibson Island Corp. and concluded it did not overrule or modify the Bryant Woods requirement that a proposed accommodation must provide 'direct amelioration' of a disability's effects in order to be 'necessary' under the FHA. Because plaintiff could not demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits under that standard, the court denied the motion without reaching the other Winter preliminary injunction factors.
key_cases_cited: Bryant Woods Inn, Inc. v. Howard Cnty, Md., 124 F.3d 597 (4th Cir. 1997)

(apartment owner), alleging disability discrimination, retaliation, and hostile housing environment under the Fair Housing Act. case_name: Imani Lawson v. Dice Holdings LLC, Ozarks Communities, Theresa Knoth, and Daniel
accommodation_description: Plaintiff appears to allege retaliation for disputing Ameren utility bills, lease termination, and eviction proceedings, though no specific accommodation request is articulated in the complaint.
key_holding: The court found it lacked subject matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff failed to allege membership in any protected class and failed to allege she engaged in protected activity under the FHA, and the Rooker-Feldman doctrine barred review of the underlying state court eviction judgment.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Imani Lawson filed a complaint against her landlord/property management defendants seeking to vacate a state court eviction judgment, alleging Fair Housing Act violations including retaliation for disputing utility bills. key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish the required causal connection between his protected HUD complaints and defendants' alleged adverse conduct, and his claims of harassment and discrimination rested solely on conclusory assertions insufficient to survive summary judgment.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Terry Rockette sued Carpenter Management Company and its employees alleging racial and gender discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act, retaliation for filing HUD complaints, and other federal and state claims. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment, dismissing all federal claims with prejudice because plaintiff failed to establish causation between his protected activity and any alleged adverse action, and his conclusory assertions were insufficient to support his discrimination and harassment claims.

source_file: 10808878_2026_Plainview Mobile Home Park, et al. v. City of Oak Grove, et al._kywd

The court denied plaintiffs' motion to alter judgment under Rule 59(e), finding they failed to establish grounds for reconsideration and had previously lacked sufficient evidence of disparate treatment or statistical evidence of disparate impact to support their FHA claims.

case_name: Dickerson v. BPP PCV Owners LLC
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request; this is an appeal from dismissal of racial discrimination and retaliation claims arising from a baseless theft accusation by a building security officer.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that the complaint failed to plead intentional racial discrimination under the FHA because the security guard's accusation was based on the plaintiff's resemblance to the person in security footage, not racial animus, and the FHA retaliation claim failed for lack of allegations connecting the incident to prior complaints.
brief_summary: Gloria D. Dickerson, a 72-year-old Black woman residing at Peter Cooper Village in Manhattan, sued BPP PCV Owners LLC alleging racial discrimination after a building safety officer accused her of theft based on security camera footage. The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, finding that Dickerson failed to plead intentional discrimination because the accusation was based on physical resemblance to the person in the footage rather than racial animus, and her retaliation claim failed for lack of causal connection to any prior protected activity.
key_cases_cited: Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)

case_name: Steven Ray Collins; Sharon Lavette Collins v. Wells Fargo & Company; Wells Fargo Bank, N.A.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested or at issue in this case; the action was dismissed on res judicata grounds without reaching the merits of any FHA claim.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of plaintiffs' Fair Housing Act claims against Wells Fargo as barred by res judicata, because the action involved the same cause of action between the same parties after a final judgment on the merits in a prior state court proceeding.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Steven Ray Collins and Sharon Lavette Collins appealed the dismissal of their Fair Housing Act claims against Wells Fargo & Company and Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. The district court dismissed the action under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6) on the ground that it was barred by res judicata, applying California's claim preclusion doctrine to give effect to a prior state court judgment involving the same cause of action and the same parties. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, also rejecting plaintiffs' procedural objections regarding the lack of oral argument and the alleged consideration of matters outside the pleadings.
key_cases_cited: Holcombe v. Hosmer, 477 F.3d 1094 (9th Cir. 2007)

case_name: Miller v. Asset Living, LLC
accommodation_description: The case does not involve a discrete reasonable accommodation or modification request. Plaintiffs' disability-related claims arise from alleged failure to maintain habitable conditions—including functional elevators—that affected residents with disabilities, brought under the ADA (Title III) and the Fair Housing Amendments Act.
key_holding: The Magistrate Judge recommends granting defendants' partial motions to dismiss, dismissing Claims One (ADA) and Five (Denver Municipal Code) with prejudice on substantive legal grounds, and Claims Three (CCPA) and Eight ("Colorado CARES Act") without prejudice for pleading deficiencies and duplicativeness, while allowing Claims Two (FHA), Four (CADA), Six (warranty of habitability), and Seven (retaliation) to proceed.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs residing at Avantus Apartments in Denver sued their property owner and manager for severe habitability failures—including sewage backups, mold, pest infestations, and non-functional elevators—and for alleged retaliation after complaining about those conditions, bringing eight claims under federal and state law. Defendants filed partial motions to dismiss Claims One (ADA), Three (CCPA), Five (Denver Municipal Code), and Eight ("Colorado CARES Act"). The Magistrate Judge recommended granting all four dismissals: the ADA claim failed because residential apartment complexes are not "places of public accommodation"; the Denver Municipal Code claim failed because the cited provisions were reserved or conferred enforcement rights only on a government manager; the CCPA claim failed to meet Rule 9(b)'s heightened pleading particularity standard; and Claim Eight was both insufficiently pleaded and duplicative of surviving warranty-of-habitability and retaliation claims.

case_name: United States of America v. Five Properties, LLC et al.

key_holding: Turnipseed's motion to intervene was denied because all elements of res judicata were met: Five Properties and Tonti Management were in privity through a principal/agent relationship, and the Government's suit arose from the same nucleus of operative facts as Turnipseed's original suit, which was dismissed with prejudice for failure to prosecute.
brief_summary: Dory Turnipseed sought to intervene in the United States' Fair Housing Act lawsuit against Five Properties, LLC and Tonti Management Corporation, which alleged the defendants refused to accommodate her mental disability by prohibiting her emotional support dog. The district court sustained Defendants' objection, reversed the magistrate judge's order granting intervention, and denied Turnipseed's motion based on res judicata, finding that Turnipseed's dismissed suit and the Government's suit arose from the same nucleus of operative facts, and that the defendants were in privity through their principal/agent relationship.

source_file: 10815083_2026_Mark Heimkes v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association, Inc.; Shearldine Marie Allfrey v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association, Inc._alsd
case_name: Mark Heimkes v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association, Inc.; Shearldine Marie Allfrey v. Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Both plaintiffs requested accommodation to bring their service/assistance dogs into the pool and Owner's Lodge areas where pets were prohibited: Mr. Heimkes for his PTSD service dogs (Logan, Rex, Tatanka) and Mrs. Allfrey for her seizure alert dog (Dewey).
key_holding: The accommodation claims failed because plaintiffs refused to provide FMRCOA with reliable disability-related information linking their disabilities to the need for service animals, and Mr. Heimkes' dog Rex was properly excluded under the direct threat exception; additionally, Mrs. Allfrey failed to demonstrate Dewey was trained to perform a specific alerting task for her seizure condition.
brief_summary: Two condominium unit owners sued Fairhope Motorcoach Resort Condominium Owners Association seeking reasonable accommodations under the FHA to bring their service/assistance dogs into restricted common areas, and also brought ADA and interference claims. After a twelve-day bench trial, the court found for the defendant on all claims, holding that plaintiffs' refusal to provide reliable disability-related information prevented the defendant from conducting a meaningful review of the accommodation requests, one dog's behavior justified exclusion under the direct threat exception, and the facility was not a place of public accommodation under the ADA.

case_name: Christina G. Lyons v. Gene B. Glick Company, Inc.
accommodation_description: Lyons requested that Glick install in-unit laundry machines in her apartment to accommodate her unspecified disability when she moved in in 2015; Glick allegedly unlawfully delayed installation until January 2017.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of Fair Housing Act claims barred by Rooker-Feldman (eviction-related) and the two-year statute of limitations, but vacated and remanded for further proceedings on the subset of timely retaliation claims arising from conduct between October and December 2017.
brief_summary: Christina Lyons sued her former landlord, Gene B. Glick Company, under the Fair Housing Act after a state court evicted her, alleging that Glick unlawfully delayed installing in-unit laundry machines as a disability accommodation and then retaliated against her through ignored maintenance requests, unannounced unit entries, and hostile construction. The Seventh Circuit held that Rooker-Feldman barred claims whose injuries were caused by the state court eviction judgment, and that claims predating October 2017 were time-barred under the FHA's two-year limitations period. However, a narrow subset of retaliation claims based on conduct occurring between October and December 2017—attributed to Glick's lease consultant and construction subcontractor—survived both bars and required remand for further fact development on agency liability.

source_file: 4850760_2021_Benedict Mohit v. City of Haines City_ca11
case_name: Benedict Mohit v. City of Haines City
accommodation_description: Mohit did not articulate a specific accommodation request; his FHA claim broadly challenged Haines City's land development regulation and permit requirements as applied to his 20-acre property's agricultural and livestock use, asserting—without factual support—intentional discrimination, discriminatory impact, and refusal of a reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of plaintiff's FHA claim because he failed to plausibly allege intentional discrimination, discriminatory impact, or a refusal to make a reasonable accommodation, and separately failed to contest the district court's untimeliness ruling.
brief_summary: Benedict Mohit purchased a 20-acre property in Haines City, Florida intending to farm and raise livestock, but a city land development regulation adopted shortly after his purchase required him to obtain a conditional use permit for agricultural activities. Mohit filed suit in federal court alleging violations of the Fifth Amendment Takings Clause, substantive due process and equal protection, and the Fair Housing Act, after the city ultimately granted him a conditional use permit. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment on the Takings claim and dismissal of the FHA and constitutional claims, finding that Mohit failed to allege beyond conclusory statements any discriminatory animus, disparate impact, or basis for a reasonable accommodation under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Jackson v. Okaloosa Cnty., 21 F.3d 1531 (11th Cir. 1994)

case_name: Gary Hatter v. Gloria Williams, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to remain in a two-bedroom unit despite being required to downsize to a one-bedroom to match his one-person Section 8 voucher, citing need for physical-therapy equipment storage.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment because Hatter received the accommodation he requested (approval to remain in the two-bedroom unit), so he could not show a denial of reasonable accommodation; his subsequent removal from the voucher program was based on unreported property ownership, not disability discrimination or retaliation.
brief_summary: Gary Hatter, a disabled Section 8 voucher holder, sued the Housing Authority of Champaign County and its employees alleging disability discrimination, racial discrimination, and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act after the agency terminated his rental assistance based on his failure to disclose ownership interest in real estate. The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants, finding that Hatter's reasonable accommodation request was actually granted, and the subsequent voucher revocation was supported by evidence of program-rule violations unrelated to his disability.
key_cases_cited: Scheidler v. Indiana, 914 F.3d 535 (7th Cir. 2019)
Riley v. City of Kokomo, 909 F.3d 182 (7th Cir. 2018)
McCann v. Badger Mining Corp., 965 F.3d 578 (7th Cir. 2020)

case_name: Gary Hatter v. Gloria Williams, et al.
accommodation_description: Hatter requested to remain in a two-bedroom unit despite his one-person voucher, asserting he needed the extra space for physical-therapy equipment related to his back injury disability.
key_holding: Hatter received the exact accommodation he requested (to remain in his two-bedroom unit), so he cannot establish a denial of reasonable accommodation; the subsequent termination of his Section 8 subsidy was based on his failure to disclose an interest in real property, not on disability or retaliation.
brief_summary: Gary Hatter, a disabled Section 8 voucher holder, sued the Housing Authority of Champaign County and its employees alleging disability and racial discrimination and retaliation after his housing assistance was terminated for allegedly misrepresenting his assets. The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants, finding that Hatter received the reasonable accommodation he requested (to keep his two-bedroom unit) and lacked evidence that the subsequent termination of his voucher was discriminatory or retaliatory rather than based on his failure to disclose ownership interest in real estate.
key_cases_cited: Scheidler v. Indiana, 914 F.3d 535 (7th Cir. 2019)

source_file: 4852565_2021_Julie Wartluft v. Milton Hershey Sch and Sch Tru_ca3
case_name: Julie Ellen Wartluft, et al. v. The Milton Hershey School and School Trust
accommodation_description: Parents allege School barred student from graduation ceremony and house barbecue based on her mental illness.
key_holding: Third Circuit affirmed summary judgment because the boarding school is not a 'renter' under § 3604(f)(1) since Abbie provided no bargained-for consideration for her housing, and the graduation ceremony and barbecue are not services 'in connection with' housing under § 3604(f)(2).
brief_summary: Julie Wartluft and Frederick Bartels sued the Milton Hershey School after their daughter Abbie's suicide, claiming the School violated the Fair Housing Act by barring her from her eighth-grade graduation ceremony and a house barbecue due to her mental illness. The Third Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the School, holding that the FHA does not apply because Abbie was not a 'renter' under § 3604(f)(1) and the graduation/barbecue services were not provided 'in connection with' her housing under § 3604(f)(2).
key_cases_cited: Astralis Condominium Ass'n v. Sec'y, U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urb. Dev., 620 F.3d 62 (1st Cir. 2010)

source_file: 4853358_2021_Sharon Chavis v. State of New Jersey_ca3
case_name: Sharon Chavis v. State of New Jersey
accommodation_description: Denial of transfer request from psychiatric hospital to Kings Adult Care Center; plaintiffs' FHA claims stemmed from institutional psychiatric care rather than traditional housing
key_holding: The Third Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because the District Court's order dismissing the complaint without prejudice did not dispose of defendants' outstanding cross-claims for indemnification and contribution, and the District Court did not certify the order under Rule 54(b).
brief_summary: Sharon and Mya Chavis, proceeding pro se, appealed from a District Court order dismissing without prejudice their complaint against the State of New Jersey, former Governor Chris Christie, Jersey City Medical Center, and Meadowview Psychiatric Hospital stemming from psychiatric institutionalization care. The Third Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of appellate jurisdiction because the District Court's order did not dispose of the defendants' outstanding cross-claims and was not certified as a final judgment under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b).
key_cases_cited: Borelli v. City of Reading, 532 F.2d 950 (3d Cir. 1976)

source_file: 4856976_2021_De La Fuente v. Sherry Netherland, Inc._ca2
case_name: Roque De La Fuente v. The Sherry Netherland, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; this case involves alleged refusal to permit purchase of cooperative apartment based on race (Mexican-American)
key_holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for defendants because De La Fuente failed to rebut defendants' legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for denying his cooperative apartment purchase application, and the alleged remark by a non-board member was insufficient to establish pretext for racial discrimination.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Roque De La Fuente, a Mexican-American, sued The Sherry Netherland, Inc. and its board members alleging they denied his application to purchase a cooperative apartment because of his race. The Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants, finding that defendants proffered legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons (plaintiff's history of being overly litigious and dishonest) and plaintiff failed to present evidence that these reasons were pretext for discrimination.

case_name: Glenn Howard; Gale Howard; Christine Howard v. HMK Holdings, LLC; Hovik M. Khaloian
accommodation_description: Request to extend the tenancy termination date from July 15, 2017 to January 22, 2018 as an accommodation for Glenn Howard's brain injury requiring 24-hour care while his neurologist optimized his medication regimen.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the landlord, holding that plaintiffs failed to establish a causal link between Glenn Howard's medical condition and the requested tenancy extension—physicians only restricted 'long travel' to Florida, not relocation within or near Los Angeles, so the extension was not necessary to afford an equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.
brief_summary: The Howards, tenants in a month-to-month rental property, sued their landlord under the Fair Housing Amendments Act seeking to extend their tenancy as a reasonable accommodation for Glenn Howard's brain injury requiring 24-hour care while his neurologist optimized his medication. The landlord initially granted a two-month extension but denied a second extension through January 2018. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the landlord, finding no causal link between Howard's disability and the requested accommodation because his physicians only restricted long-distance travel to Florida, not local relocation, meaning the extension was not necessary to afford equal opportunity to use and enjoy housing.
key_cases_cited: Giebeler v. M & B Associates, 343 F.3d 1143 (9th Cir. 2003)

case_name: Metropolitan Omaha Property Owners Association, Inc. v. City of Omaha
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; property owners challenge the Rental Property Registration and Inspection Ordinance as having discriminatory disparate impact on minority tenants under § 3604(a).
key_holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed dismissal because plaintiffs failed to plausibly plead discriminatory intent for a disparate treatment claim, and failed to allege facts demonstrating a causal connection between the ordinance and any housing disparity for a disparate impact claim.
brief_summary: Metropolitan Omaha Property Owners Association and two member property owners sued the City of Omaha, challenging the Rental Property Registration and Inspection Ordinance as violating the Fair Housing Act by resulting in disparate treatment and disparate impact on minority tenants. case_name: Craig Steven MacKenzie v. Marcia L. Fudge, Secretary, U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; plaintiff is a developer who sued federal agencies (HUD, DOJ) alleging they mishandled a fair housing discrimination investigation against the City of Dallas
key_holding: Plaintiff's claims are barred by res judicata because he previously litigated identical claims against HUD and DOJ in the Northern District of Texas, which resulted in final judgments dismissing his claims with prejudice
brief_summary: Craig MacKenzie, a developer who previously sued HUD and DOJ in the Northern District of Texas over their handling of a fair housing investigation against the City of Dallas, filed a substantially similar suit in D.C. federal court. The D.C. court dismissed all claims as barred by res judicata and collateral estoppel, finding that MacKenzie had a full and fair opportunity to litigate his claims in Texas and failed to appeal the adverse judgment.

source_file: 4865835_2021_Rodney Green, Sr. v. Mercy Housing, Inc._ca9
case_name: Rodney Green, Sr. v. Mercy Housing, Inc.
accommodation_description: Green alleged that Mercy Housing refused to provide him with reasonable accommodations for his mobility impairment/disability, though the specific nature of the accommodations requested is not detailed in this published opinion (those merits are addressed in a separate concurrently-filed memorandum disposition).
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit held that the Christiansburg standard—requiring a finding that the plaintiff's claim was frivolous, unreasonable, or groundless—applies to the award of both attorney's fees and costs to a prevailing defendant under the Fair Housing Act's fee-shifting provision, 42 U.S.C. § 3613(c)(2).
brief_summary: Rodney Green, Sr., a Black and mobility-impaired former tenant, sued Mercy Housing for race- and disability-based discrimination under the Fair Housing Act; the district court granted summary judgment to Mercy Housing and taxed costs of $5,962.11 against Green. In this published opinion, the Ninth Circuit addressed solely the costs question, holding that the Christiansburg standard applies to fee and cost awards under the FHA's fee-shifting provision, joining the First, Second, Fourth, and Fifth Circuits. The court vacated the costs award and remanded, instructing that costs may only be assessed against a non-prevailing FHA plaintiff upon a finding that the claim was frivolous, unreasonable, or groundless.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. EEOC, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)

case_name: Donahue Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Landlord's alleged failure to respond to race-based tenant-on-tenant harassment constitutes intentional racial discrimination under the FHA
key_holding: Landlords cannot be presumed to exercise the degree of control over tenants necessary to impose FHA liability for tenant-on-tenant harassment; Francis failed to plausibly allege that KPM had substantial control over Endres or that KPM acted with discriminatory intent in declining to intervene.
brief_summary: Black tenant Donahue Francis sued his landlord Kings Park Manor and property manager Corinne Downing under the FHA, Sections 1981 and 1982, and NYSHRL, alleging they intentionally discriminated against him by failing to respond to race-based harassment by fellow tenant Raymond Endres. The Second Circuit, sitting en banc, affirmed dismissal of all claims, holding that landlords cannot be presumed to have the substantial control over tenants necessary to impose FHA liability for tenant-on-tenant misconduct, and Francis failed to plausibly allege the landlords acted with discriminatory intent.

source_file: 4868335_2021_Myers v. District of Columbia Housing Authority_dcd
case_name: Belinda Myers et al. v. District of Columbia Housing Authority et al.
accommodation_description: Underlying complaint alleged sexual harassment by property manager in violation of the Fair Housing Act and Equal Protection Clause, not a reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: Oliver's defamation and false light counterclaim against plaintiffs' law firm website posting fails because the fair report privilege applies to the posting, which fairly and accurately summarized the judicial complaint, and Oliver failed to adequately plead falsity or overcome the privilege with actual malice allegations.
brief_summary: Female public housing tenants sued D.C. Housing Authority and its property manager Oliver alleging sexual harassment in violation of the Fair Housing Act and Equal Protection Clause; after plaintiffs' counsel published a website announcement about the lawsuit, Oliver filed a defamation and false light counterclaim. The court granted plaintiffs' motion to dismiss the counterclaim, holding that the fair report privilege barred the claims because the website posting was a substantially accurate summary of the complaint and Oliver failed to adequately plead falsity or actual malice.

key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal because plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge mortgage assignments as void rather than voidable, and rejected the Fair Housing Act continuing violations doctrine argument without substantive analysis of a specific FHA provision.
brief_summary: The Estate of Catherine Brown Morris and trustee Toddella A. Brown appealed the district court's dismissal of claims against The Bank of New York Mellon regarding mortgage assignments and foreclosure proceedings on a San Bernardino property, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act and various consumer protection statutes. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that plaintiffs lacked standing to challenge mortgage assignments as voidable rather than void, that the FHA claim failed under the continuing violations doctrine, and that other federal and state claims were time-barred or failed to state a claim.

case_name: Harmony Haus Westlake, L.L.C. v. Parkstone Property Owners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request to operate a sober-living home with 12 unrelated residents recovering from alcoholism and drug addiction, and to park 8 vehicles, in a single-family residential subdivision subject to HOA deed restrictions limiting occupancy to single families and vehicles to garage/driveway.
key_holding: Harmony Haus failed to prove that allowing 12 unrelated residents at the Catorce house is 'necessary' under the FHA's reasonable accommodation requirement, because evidence showed that sober-living homes with six to eight residents are effective, and Harmony Haus did not establish that 12 residents is essential for therapeutic or financial viability.
brief_summary: Harmony Haus Westlake, a sober-living home operator, sued Parkstone HOA seeking to operate a 12-resident facility at a house in its Austin, Texas gated community, arguing the HOA's single-family residential use and parking restrictions violated the FHA's reasonable accommodation requirement. The Fifth Circuit vacated the district court's injunction for Harmony Haus, holding that Harmony Haus failed to prove 12 residents is a necessary accommodation because Parkstone presented evidence that effective sober-living homes operate with six to eight residents.

key_holding: The complaint failed to state a disparate treatment claim because it contained no facts suggesting animus against persons with disabilities was a significant factor in the zoning variance denial, and failed to state a reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiff did not argue her requests were related to her disabilities.
brief_summary: Barbara Perricone-Bernovich and family sued the Village of Head of the Harbor and individual officials under the Fair Housing Act, alleging that the denial of her zoning variance application constituted disability discrimination. accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged sex discrimination when defendant refused to offer him a one-bedroom apartment while offering one to a less-qualified female applicant.
key_holding: The court held that Webb qualified as an 'aggrieved person' under the FHA because his claim that U.S. Vets made housing 'unavailable' due to sex fell within § 3604(a)'s plain text, regardless of whether he paid rent.

key_holding: The Third Circuit affirmed dismissal because Dew failed to allege sufficient factual matter to state plausible disparate treatment and disparate impact claims under the FHA; his bare allegations that SCT had not rented to Black or Hispanic tenants lacked any statistical analysis or identified policy causing the disparity.

The court granted the government's motion to dismiss, finding the Northern District action was stayed but not closed, making this case an impermissible duplicate that should be adjudicated in Texas.

case_name: Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs request tenant protection vouchers and relocation assistance as relief for inadequate housing conditions at their PBRA-subsidized complex, plus release from existing leases.
key_holding: The court denied HUD's motion to transfer venue to the Southern District of Texas, finding that HUD failed to carry its burden of demonstrating that the Southern District of Texas is a substantially more convenient forum than the District of Columbia, particularly because HUD headquarters in D.C. will have final approval authority over any decision to issue tenant protection vouchers or terminate housing assistance payments.
brief_summary: Sandpiper Residents Association and individual residents sued HUD seeking tenant protection vouchers, relocation assistance, and release from leases at their allegedly substandard PBRA-subsidized apartment complex in Galveston, Texas. The court denied HUD's motion to transfer venue to the Southern District of Texas, finding that HUD failed to establish that forum was more convenient, given that HUD headquarters in D.C. retains final approval authority over the requested relief.

case_name: Gregory Selden v. Airbnb, Inc.
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a disability accommodation request; Selden alleged race discrimination in housing on Airbnb's platform.
key_holding: The arbitrator correctly concluded that neither the host's single-family residence nor Airbnb's online platform qualified as a 'dwelling' under the Fair Housing Act or a 'public accommodation' under Title II, so Selden's discrimination claims failed as a matter of law; the arbitrator did not commit misconduct by limiting discovery because Selden failed to request interrogatories or depositions before the close of discovery and failed to show prejudice from the exclusion of his expert report.
brief_summary: Gregory Selden, an African American man, sued Airbnb alleging race discrimination after a host allegedly denied his rental request based on his race visible from his profile picture; Selden claimed violations of Title II, the Civil Rights Act of 1866, and the Fair Housing Act based on Airbnb's photo and true name policies having a disparate impact on Black users. The D.C. Circuit affirmed the district court's order compelling arbitration and denial of Selden's motion to vacate the arbitration award, holding that Selden agreed to arbitrate by signing up for Airbnb, Title II claims are arbitrable, and the arbitrator properly dismissed Selden's claims because neither the host's single-family residence nor Airbnb's platform qualified as a public accommodation or dwelling under the applicable statutes.

case_name: Rita Fox v. Lucille F. Gaines
accommodation_description: Sexual harassment by property manager in exchange for reduced rent and culminating in eviction after plaintiff ended the relationship.
key_holding: Sexual harassment—both hostile housing environment and quid pro quo sexual harassment—is actionable under the Fair Housing Act's prohibition on sex discrimination, provided the plaintiff demonstrates that she would not have been harassed but for her sex.
brief_summary: Rita Fox sued her property manager and landlord after being forced out of her apartment when she ended a sexual relationship with the property manager who had been reducing her rent in exchange for sexual favors. The Eleventh Circuit vacated the district court's dismissal, holding for the first time in the circuit that sexual harassment is actionable as sex discrimination under the Fair Housing Act when the harassment would not have occurred but for the plaintiff's sex.

case_name: Rita Fox v. Lucille F. Gaines
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification; it concerns claims of quid pro quo sexual harassment and hostile housing environment as forms of sex discrimination under the FHA.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit held for the first time in the circuit that sexual harassment—both hostile housing environment and quid pro quo—is actionable as sex discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, provided the plaintiff demonstrates she would not have been harassed but for her sex, and vacated the district court's dismissal of Fox's complaint.
brief_summary: Rita Fox, a single mother renting an apartment at Rose Bush Apartments in Jupiter, Florida, was subjected to a three-and-a-half-year pattern of quid pro quo sexual harassment by property manager Dana Gaines, who conditioned rent reductions on sexual favors and, after Fox ended the relationship, initiated fraudulent eviction proceedings that forced her to vacate. Fox sued Gaines and property owner Lucille Gaines under the FHA and Florida FHA for sex discrimination, but the district court dismissed the complaint, holding that sexual harassment claims were not actionable under the FHA despite acknowledging the 'overwhelming weight of federal authority' to the contrary. The Eleventh Circuit reversed, joining its sister circuits in holding that sexual harassment constitutes sex discrimination prohibited by the FHA when the plaintiff can show that but for her sex she would not have been harassed, and remanded for the district court to assess whether Fox's complaint adequately stated a claim.

case_name: Patrina Harrison v. Wells Fargo Bank
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged racial discrimination in a loan application/credit transaction by Wells Fargo Bank.
key_holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for defendant because plaintiff failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact as to whether she was qualified for the loan she sought or whether Wells Fargo's reason for denying her loan application was pretextual.
brief_summary: Patrina Harrison, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's summary judgment in favor of Wells Fargo Bank on her claims of racial discrimination under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and the Fair Housing Act related to a loan denial. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that Harrison failed to raise a genuine dispute of material fact as to whether she was qualified for the loan or whether Wells Fargo's proffered reason for denial was pretextual.

case_name: Brnovich v. Democratic National Committee
court: Supreme Court of the United States
accommodation_description: This is a Voting Rights Act case, not a Fair Housing Act case. It challenges Arizona's out-of-precinct ballot policy and third-party ballot-collection restriction under Section 2 of the VRA.
key_holding: The Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit, holding that Arizona's out-of-precinct policy and HB 2023 do not violate Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act because they impose only the usual burdens of voting, have small disparate impacts, and are supported by important state interests in election integrity.
brief_summary: The Democratic National Committee and affiliates sued Arizona under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, challenging two voting regulations: the state's policy of not counting ballots cast in the wrong precinct, and HB 2023 which prohibits third-party collection of early ballots. The Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit's en banc decision, holding that neither regulation violates the VRA because they impose only modest burdens, have small disparate impacts on minority voters relative to total votes cast, and serve important state interests in election integrity.

case_name: Oudree S. Ellis v. Eisenman Family Trust
accommodation_description: Plaintiff appealed district court judgment dismissing her Fair Housing Act race discrimination claim based on settlement preclusion from prior unlawful detainer stipulation.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal because the stipulation entered in the underlying unlawful detainer action constituted a binding settlement that precluded the current action, and plaintiff failed to demonstrate any basis for relief under Rule 59(e).
brief_summary: Oudree Ellis appealed the district court's dismissal of her Fair Housing Act race discrimination claim against the Eisenman Family Trust. accommodation_description: Wilson alleged defendants violated the FHA by artificially inflating her property's value relative to her white neighbors through discriminatory property tax assessments and discriminatory inspection practices.
key_holding: The Third Circuit affirmed the District Court's dismissal based on res judicata, finding that Wilson's claims were precluded because they were identical or could have been brought in her prior action against the same municipal defendants, and the prior case resulted in a final judgment on the merits.
brief_summary: Pro se appellant Gwendolyn Wilson appealed from the District Court's dismissal of her Fair Housing Act and § 1983 claims against Hillsborough Township and its departments, alleging discriminatory property tax assessments and inspection practices. The Third Circuit affirmed, holding that Wilson's claims were barred by res judicata because they were identical to claims raised or that could have been raised in a prior action that resulted in a final judgment on the merits.

key_holding: The eviction notice issued October 18, 2017 was motivated by the jury verdict in Friedel I, not George Friedel's disability, and the requested accommodation of keeping Maggie was not reasonable because a prior jury found Maggie posed a direct threat to other residents.
brief_summary: George and Kathleen Friedel appealed the dismissal of their second lawsuit against Sun Communities and Park Place Community, LLC regarding their emotional support dog Maggie, after a prior jury found the dog posed a direct threat. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding that the eviction notice was issued the day after the first trial ended (not because of disability) and that the requested accommodation was not reasonable on its face given the jury's direct-threat finding.

case_name: Webb v. United States Veterans Initiative
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled veteran, alleges that U.S. VETS discriminated against him based on sex by refusing to offer him a one-bedroom apartment while offering one to a less-qualified female applicant.
key_holding: The plaintiff's Fair Housing Act sex discrimination claim is not time-barred because the administrative tolling during the OHR proceeding preserved his right to sue, and the complaint was filed within the remaining limitations period.
brief_summary: Stanley Webb, a disabled veteran, sued U.S. VETS under the Fair Housing Act alleging sex discrimination in housing placement, claiming he was denied a one-bedroom apartment while a less-qualified female applicant received one. brief_summary: A.L.M., a minor suing through her parent, sued the Board of Managers of the Vireum Schoolhouse Condominium alleging that the Board and Vireum residents subjected her to a hostile housing environment based on her race (Chinese), national origin, sex, and age in violation of the FHA and Civil Rights Act. case_name: Julie Ballou v. James McElvain
accommodation_description: Julie Ballou, a police officer, alleges that Police Chief James McElvain denied her promotion to sergeant on the basis of her sex and subjected her to repeated internal affairs investigations as pretext for sex discrimination.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit held that Ballou established a prima facie case for sex discrimination under the Equal Protection Clause and that McElvain was not entitled to qualified immunity because discriminatorily denying a promotion based on sex violates clearly established law under Lindsey v. Shalmy and Bator v. State of Hawai'i.
brief_summary: Julie Ballou, a Vancouver, Washington police officer, sued Police Chief James McElvain under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 alleging that he violated her Equal Protection rights by discriminatorily denying her promotion to sergeant based on her sex and violated her First Amendment rights by retaliating against her for opposing sex discrimination. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the denial of qualified immunity, holding that Ballou presented sufficient circumstantial evidence of discriminatory intent and that any reasonable officer would have known that sex-based denial of promotion violates clearly established constitutional law.

case_name: City of Oakland v. Wells Fargo & Company
accommodation_description: Discriminatory mortgage lending practices that steered African-American and Latino borrowers into predatory loans with worse terms than similarly situated white borrowers
key_holding: Under Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, the en banc court held that Oakland's claimed economic injuries—lost property tax revenue and increased municipal expenditures—were too attenuated from Wells Fargo's discriminatory lending practices to satisfy the FHA's proximate cause requirement, as the downstream ripples of harm traveled too far beyond the first-step injury to minority borrowers.
brief_summary: The City of Oakland sued Wells Fargo alleging that its discriminatory mortgage lending practices against African-American and Latino borrowers caused higher default and foreclosure rates, which in turn decreased property values and resulted in lost tax revenue and increased municipal expenditures. The Ninth Circuit en banc, applying the Supreme Court's decision in Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, held that these downstream economic injuries were too attenuated from the discriminatory lending to establish proximate cause under the Fair Housing Act, reversing the district court's denial of Wells Fargo's motion to dismiss as to the tax revenue and injunctive/declaratory relief claims.

case_name: Southwest Fair Housing Council, Inc. v. Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement District
race_if_mentioned: African American, Native American, Hispanic, White
accommodation_description: The case concerns a water utility district's security deposit policy that imposed a $180 deposit on public housing customers versus $55 for other customers, alleged to discriminate based on race, national origin, sex, and familial status.
key_holding: Although the Ninth Circuit held the district court erred in its prima facie disparate impact analysis, it affirmed summary judgment for the District because the Security Deposit Policy served legitimate business interests in recovering unpaid water bills from public housing tenants whose landlord (Pinal County) refused to pay, and plaintiffs failed to demonstrate an equally effective, less discriminatory alternative.
brief_summary: Southwest Fair Housing Council and two public housing residents appealed summary judgment against the Maricopa Domestic Water Improvement District, challenging as discriminatory under the Fair Housing Act a policy requiring a $180 refundable security deposit from public housing customers versus $55 for other customers. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that although plaintiffs established a prima facie disparate impact case, the District proved the policy served its legitimate business interest in recovering delinquent water bills from tenants whose public-entity landlord refused to pay, and plaintiffs failed to present evidence of an equally effective, less discriminatory alternative.

brief_summary: Female Yale students sued fraternities and their housing corporations alleging sex discrimination in membership practices that prevented them from accessing fraternity housing, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. case_name: Gatling v. Jubilee Housing, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants repair or replace the wheelchair ramp at the front entrance of the Mozart apartment building (which was too steep, non-compliant with architectural standards, and had caused plaintiff to fall from her wheelchair) and repair or replace the wheelchair lift on the side of the building that had been inoperable for years, so that plaintiff—a wheelchair user—could safely access and exit her building and reach the mailroom.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the Rehabilitation Act reasonable accommodation claim because it could not determine at the pleading stage whether plaintiff's November 2020 request was a new discrete accommodation request (restarting the limitations clock) or merely a reconsideration of a prior denial, but granted dismissal of the DCHRA design and construction claims because those adaptive-design provisions apply only to multifamily buildings first occupied after April 20, 1999, and the Mozart was built in the 1930s.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Cynthia Gatling, a wheelchair user, sued her landlord Jubilee Housing for failing to repair an unsafe, overly steep wheelchair ramp and an inoperable wheelchair lift despite her repeated requests spanning several years, including a specific request following a November 2020 fall requiring emergency medical care. The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motion to dismiss: it allowed the Rehabilitation Act failure-to-accommodate claim to survive because it was unclear whether the November 2020 accommodation request was a new discrete act restarting the statute of limitations or a mere reconsideration of a prior denial, while dismissing the DCHRA design and construction claims because those provisions do not apply to a building constructed in the 1930s. The breach of contract and covenant of good faith and fair dealing claims were also dismissed because the lease contained no provision obligating defendants to provide reasonable accommodations.

brief_summary: Josephine Guion, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's grant of summary judgment in favor of Bonner Homeless Transitions on her Fair Housing Act claims of discrimination and retaliation, as well as state law claims for fraud, defamation, and intentional infliction of emotional distress. accommodation_description: Freedom's Path requested that GDPM amend its Administrative Plan to allow GDPM to apply for VASH project-based vouchers on Freedom's Path's behalf to enable development of supportive housing for disabled homeless veterans.

source_file: 5310802_2021_S. Baxter Jones v. City of Detroit, Mich._ca6
case_name: S. Baxter Jones v. City of Detroit, Michigan
accommodation_description: Request for wheelchair-accessible transportation vehicle rather than cargo van to safely transport plaintiff who uses a wheelchair during arrest by police officers
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit held that vicarious liability (respondeat superior) is not available for Title II of the ADA claims, because Title II incorporates the remedial framework of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, which does not permit vicarious liability following Gebser v. Lago Vista.
brief_summary: Baxter Jones, a wheelchair user, sued the City of Detroit alleging police officers failed to provide reasonable accommodation when they transported him in a cargo van rather than an accessible vehicle during his 2014 arrest, causing injuries. The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the City, holding that Title II of the ADA does not permit vicarious liability claims because it incorporates Title VI's remedial framework, which Gebser held does not allow respondeat superior liability.
key_cases_cited: Gebser v. Lago Vista Ind. Sch. Dist., 524 U.S. 274 (1998)
Barnes v. Gorman, 536 U.S. 181 (2002)
Hiler v. Brown, 177 F.3d 542 (6th Cir. 1999)
Foster v. Michigan, 573 F. App'x 377 (6th Cir. 2014)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)

source_file: 5343691_2022_Constance George v. House of Hope Recovery_ca9
case_name: Constance George v. House of Hope Recovery
accommodation_description: George alleges Barcroft and House of Hope Recovery discriminated against her on the basis of her race and religion in violation of the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Barcroft and House of Hope because George failed to present any comparator evidence establishing a prima facie case of religious discrimination under the McDonnell Douglas framework.
brief_summary: Constance George sued Patricia Barcroft, House of Hope Recovery, and other defendants alleging discrimination on the basis of race and religion under the Fair Housing Act. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Barcroft and House of Hope because George failed to present comparator evidence establishing a prima facie case of religious discrimination, and dismissed her appeal against Bridges to Change and Washington County for lack of jurisdiction due to inadequate notice of appeal.
key_cases_cited: Gamble v. City of Escondido, 104 F.3d 300 (9th Cir. 1997)
Bodett v. CoxCom, Inc., 366 F.3d 736 (9th Cir. 2004)
Lyons v. England, 307 F.3d 1092 (9th Cir. 2002)
Smith v. Barry, 502 U.S. 244 (1992)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green framework

source_file: 6225633_2022_Karen C. Yeh Ho v. Valencia Isles Homeowners Association, Inc._ca11
case_name: Karen C. Yeh Ho v. Valencia Isles Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Nature of accommodation request is undeterminable; complaint dismissed on procedural grounds before substantive FHA analysis.
key_holding: The district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing the complaint without prejudice for failure to timely respond to the motion to dismiss, where the plaintiff continued to file other documents and was properly warned of potential dismissal.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Karen Yeh-Ho appealed the dismissal without prejudice of her Fair Housing Act complaint against Valencia Isles Homeowners Association and related defendants; the Eleventh Circuit affirmed, holding the district court did not abuse its discretion in dismissing the complaint for the plaintiff's failure to timely respond to the motion to dismiss despite continued filings and proper notice.

case_name: Gatling v. Jubilee Housing, Inc.
accommodation_description: Wheelchair user tenant requests repair/replacement of building's wheelchair ramp and wheelchair lift to provide accessible entry and exit from the building.
key_holding: The court granted leave to amend for DCHRA reasonable accommodation claims under § 2-1402.21(d)(2)(A) and (d)(3)(B) because Gatling adequately alleged she is disabled, defendants knew of her disability, the requested accommodations (wheelchair ramp and lift repair) are necessary for equal use and enjoyment of the property, and defendants refused the accommodation; but the court denied claims requiring intentional discrimination or aiding-and-abetting theories as futile.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Cynthia Gatling, a wheelchair user, sued Jubilee Housing, Inc. and Jubilee Housing Limited Partnership alleging they failed to accommodate her disability by refusing to repair or replace an unsafe wheelchair ramp and inoperable wheelchair lift at her low-income apartment building. The court granted in part and denied in part her motion to file a second amended complaint, allowing her to proceed on DCHRA reasonable accommodation and breach of warranty of habitability claims but rejecting claims requiring intentional discrimination or aiding-and-abetting as futile.
key_cases_cited: United States v. District of Columbia, 538 F. Supp. 2d 211 (D.D.C. 2008)
Parham v. CIH Properties, Inc., 148 F. Supp. 3d 5 (D.D.C. 2015)
Hunter v. District of Columbia, 64 F. Supp. 3d 158 (D.D.C. 2014)
Killingham v. Wilshire Inv. Corp., 739 A.2d 804 (D.C. 1999)
Javins v. First Nat'l Realty Corp., 428 F.2d 1071 (D.C. Cir. 1970)

case_name: Doe v. Tonti Management Company, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: Request for accommodation from the one-animal-per-apartment policy to keep a second cat (GiGi) as an emotional support animal for major depressive disorder and anxiety.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the district court's order denying Doe’s motion to re-open the case and sever the cost-splitting provision of the arbitration agreement was an unappealable interlocutory order under § 16 of the FAA, and neither the collateral order doctrine nor mandamus jurisdiction applied.
brief_summary: Jane Doe sued Tonti Management Company, the operator of her apartment complex, under the Fair Housing Act seeking to keep a second emotional support animal despite a one-animal-per-apartment policy. After the district court compelled arbitration and denied Doe’s motion to sever the arbitration agreement’s cost-splitting provision, Doe appealed. The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the district court’s order was an unappealable interlocutory order under § 16 of the FAA.
key_cases_cited: Al Rushaid v. Nat’l Oilwell Varco, Inc., 814 F.3d 300 (5th Cir. 2016)
Apache Bohai Corp., LDC v. Texaco China, B.V., 330 F.3d 307 (5th Cir. 2003)
Green v. Serv. Corp. Int’l, 236 F. App’x 898 (5th Cir. 2007)
Vantage Health Plan, Inc. v. Willis-Knighton Med. Ctr., 913 F.3d 443 (5th Cir. 2019)

case_name: Ahmad Ajaj v. Federal Bureau of Prisons
accommodation_description: Prisoner requests religious accommodations including adjusted medication delivery during Ramadan fasting, halal diet, access to an imam, and ability to pray with others five times daily
key_holding: The Tenth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal of the group-prayer claim as moot because the court's finding that the plaintiff could pray with others five times daily was clearly erroneous, and reversed dismissal of individual-capacity RFRA damages claims because Tanzin v. Tanvir held such damages are available, though qualified immunity applies to RFRA damages claims.
brief_summary: Ahmad Ajaj, a Muslim prisoner at ADX Florence Colorado, sued BOP and individual BOP officials under RFRA alleging violations of his free exercise rights through denial of Ramadan fasting accommodation, halal diet, access to an imam, and group prayer. The Tenth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal of his group-prayer claim as moot (finding the record did not support that he could pray five times daily in the Life Connections Program) and reversed dismissal of individual-capacity damages claims under RFRA, holding that qualified immunity applies to RFRA damages claims.
key_cases_cited: Tanzin v. Tanvir, 141 S. Ct. 486 (2020)
Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800 (1982)
City of Boerne v. Flores, 521 U.S. 507 (1997)
Employment Division v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872 (1990)
Werner v. McCotter, 49 F.3d 1476 (10th Cir. 1995)

source_file: 6377422_2022_Smita Sanghvi v. County of San Bernardino_ca9
case_name: Smita Sanghvi and Mountain View Centers, Inc. v. County of San Bernardino
accommodation_description: Appellants alleged the County's decision to remove conservatees from Mountain View Centers was discriminatory, but the court found no protected status under the FHA was alleged.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal because Appellants' complaint failed to allege how the County's decision to remove residents was based on a protected status under the FHA, and the complaint itself demonstrated non-discriminatory reasons (an alleged sexual assault report) for the removal.
brief_summary: Smita Sanghvi and Mountain View Centers, Inc. (a conservatorship facility operator) appealed the dismissal of their claims against San Bernardino County, which had removed conservatees from their facility based on an alleged sexual assault report. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, finding that Appellants failed to allege how the County's decision was based on a protected status under the Fair Housing Act, and the complaint itself demonstrated non-discriminatory reasons for the removal.

source_file: 6433397_2022_Secretary, United States Department of Housing v. Welch_ca10
case_name: The Secretary, United States Department of Housing and Urban Development, on behalf of Denver Metro Fair Housing Center v. David B. Welch, et al.
accommodation_description: Not a reasonable accommodation case; the complaint alleged discrimination against families with children based on familial status, with respondents marketing the property as an 'adult condominium community' and making dwellings unavailable to families with children.
key_holding: The Tenth Circuit granted HUD's Petition for Enforcement of the administrative consent order, requiring respondents to pay $800 to the Denver Metro Fair Housing Center, adopt a non-discrimination policy, undergo fair housing training, and engage in affirmative advertising indicating families with children are welcome.
brief_summary: The Secretary of HUD, on behalf of the Denver Metro Fair Housing Center, petitioned the Tenth Circuit to enforce an administrative consent order against David B. Welch, John H. Welch, and Ruth E. Welch, who allegedly discriminated against families with children at their Westwood Cove Condominiums in Gunnison, Colorado. The court granted the enforcement petition, ordering respondents to comply with all terms of the consent order including monetary payment, adoption of non-discrimination policies, fair housing training, and affirmative advertising welcoming families with children.

source_file: 6444370_2022_Abolfazl Hosseinzadeh v. Bellevue Park Homeowners Assn._ca9
case_name: Abolfazl Hosseinzadeh v. Bellevue Park Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; claims involve alleged race, national origin, and religion discrimination through document withholding and board election invalidation
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants because plaintiff failed to establish pretext for discrimination, presenting no facts showing BPHOA's legitimate reasons for withholding documents and invalidating the board election were pretextual.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Hosseinzadeh, an Iranian immigrant and Muslim, sued the Bellevue Park Homeowners Association alleging race, national origin, and religion discrimination under the FHA, CRA, and WLAD based on BPHOA's withholding of personal records and invalidation of a board election in which he was elected. The Ninth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants, finding Hosseinzadeh failed to demonstrate that BPHOA's legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons for these actions were pretextual.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Gamble v. City of Escondido
Phiffer v. Proud Parrot Motor Hotel, Inc.
Mikkelsen v. Pub. Util. Dist. No. 1 of Kittitas Cnty.

case_name: Minnie McCall v. Montgomery Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged discriminatory inspection practices, unannounced apartment entry, and interference with 'porting out' (transferring to another apartment) based on her race and in retaliation for prior litigation against the Housing Authority.
key_holding: Summary judgment was proper because the racially derogatory comments were made by a third-party inspector and apartment maintenance worker—not Housing Authority employees—and the Housing Authority could not be held vicariously liable for their statements; moreover, McCall failed to establish an adverse action for her retaliation claim as her Section 8 benefits were never terminated and she never submitted a written request to transfer.
brief_summary: Minnie McCall, a Section 8 voucher holder, appealed the district court's summary judgment for the Montgomery Housing Authority on her Fair Housing Act claims alleging racial discrimination in inspection practices and retaliation for her prior lawsuit. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding that racially derogatory comments by a third-party inspector and apartment maintenance worker were not attributable to the Housing Authority under vicarious liability principles, and that McCall failed to establish an adverse action for her retaliation claim.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Dixon v. Hallmark Cos., Inc., 627 F.3d 849 (11th Cir. 2010)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)

source_file: 6449993_2022_Kenny Simelton v. Alexander County Housing Auth_ca7
case_name: Kenny Wayne Simelton v. Alexander County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged the housing authority discriminated against him and other former residents based on race and familial status at two Alexander County housing developments.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Simelton's Rule 60(b) motion to reinstate, finding no abuse of discretion in dismissing the case for failure to prosecute after Simelton repeatedly failed to comply with discovery requests and court orders.
brief_summary: Kenny Simelton sued the Alexander County Housing Authority and four former directors under the Fair Housing Act, Title VI, and the Illinois Civil Rights Act, alleging discrimination based on race and familial status at two county housing developments. The case was dismissed under Rule 41(b) for Simelton's failure to comply with discovery requests and court orders, and the Seventh Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of his Rule 60(b) motion to reinstate, finding no abuse of discretion in the dismissal.
key_cases_cited: Krivak v. Home Depot U.S.A., Inc., 2 F.4th 601 (7th Cir. 2021)
Shaffer v. Lashbrook, 962 F.3d 313 (7th Cir. 2020)
Kasalo v. Harris & Harris, Ltd., 656 F.3d 557 (7th Cir. 2011)
United States v. Hassebrock, 21 F.4th 494 (7th Cir. 2021)
Sroga v. Huberman, 722 F.3d 980 (7th Cir. 2013)

case_name: Jean Paraison v. Nationstar Mortgage, LLC
accommodation_description: N/A - case involves claim of race/nationality discrimination in real estate auction transaction rather than reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court affirmed dismissal of Paraison's FHA discrimination claim because his allegations were conclusory and speculative, failing to establish any factual connection between his race/nationality and the real estate agent's statements advising him to back out of the deal.
brief_summary: Jean Paraison, an African American male with a Haitian accent, sued Nationstar Mortgage alleging the company's real estate agent attempted to dissuade him from completing a real estate purchase based on his race and national origin. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal, finding Paraison's discrimination allegations were conclusory and speculative under Twombly/Iqbal standards, failing to allege facts connecting his protected characteristics to the agent's conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

source_file: 6455250_2022_Eddie Hatch, Jr. v. City of Milwaukee_ca7
case_name: Eddie L. Hatch, Jr. and Michelle Davis-Hatch v. City of Milwaukee
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged defendants gave unfair preference to a white developer over Black entrepreneurs in sale of city-owned commercial building.
key_holding: The appellate court vacated the dismissal with prejudice because the district court erred in not giving pro se plaintiffs at least one opportunity to amend their complaint to cure deficiencies in pleading intentional race-based discrimination under § 1982.
brief_summary: Black plaintiffs sued the City of Milwaukee and other defendants alleging racial discrimination in the sale of a city-owned commercial building under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1982. The district court dismissed with prejudice, finding the commercial property was not a "dwelling" under the FHA and plaintiffs failed to allege intentional race-based discrimination. The Seventh Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that pro se plaintiffs should have been given leave to amend to attempt to cure the pleading deficiencies.
key_cases_cited: Jones v. Alfred H. Mayer Co., 392 U.S. 409 (1968)
Shaikh v. City of Chicago, 341 F.3d 627 (7th Cir. 2003)
Becker v. Montgomery, 532 U.S. 757 (2001)

case_name: Hawkins v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: African-American Section 8 tenants sought relocation assistance (tenant protection vouchers) from HUD to move from substandard housing conditions at Coppertree Village, alleging the denial of such assistance constituted race-based discrimination.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding (1) it lacked jurisdiction over the APA and FHA claims because tenants failed to allege a final agency action, and (2) the Fifth Amendment equal protection claim failed because the allegations showed at most that HUD was aware of varying housing conditions but did not support an inference that HUD made decisions 'because of' race.
brief_summary: African-American tenants at Coppertree Village, a Section 8 project in Houston, sued HUD alleging that the agency's failure to provide relocation assistance (tenant protection vouchers) while maintaining a HAP contract with a substandard housing complex violated the Fair Housing Act and Fifth Amendment equal protection. The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding it lacked jurisdiction over the APA and FHA claims due to no final agency action, and that the equal protection claim failed because the tenants did not plausibly allege discriminatory purpose—only that HUD was aware of disparate housing conditions, which is insufficient to show decisions were made 'because of' race.
key_cases_cited: Bennett v. Spear, 520 U.S. 154 (1997)
Washington v. Davis, 426 U.S. 229 (1976)
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metro. Hous. Dev. Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)
Personnel Adm'r of Mass. v. Feeney, 442 U.S. 256 (1979)
Veasey v. Abbott, 830 F.3d 216 (5th Cir. 2016)

case_name: Birch Family Services, Inc. v. Wlody
accommodation_description: Neighboring homeowners allegedly harassed a group home for disabled adults by photographing and videotaping residents and staff based on disability and race animus.
key_holding: Affirming summary judgment for defendants because Birch failed to establish pretext—the Wlodys' legitimate reasons for photographing and videotaping (documenting alleged staff misconduct) were supported by evidence, and the discriminatory animus evidence (derogatory texts and epithets) combined with failure to show pretext was insufficient to survive summary judgment.
brief_summary: Birch Family Services, Inc., operator of a group home for disabled adults, sued neighboring homeowners under the FHA, alleging the neighbors' extensive photographing and videotaping of residents and staff constituted disability and race-based housing discrimination. The Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the defendants, finding that Birch failed to meet its burden of demonstrating pretext—the neighbors articulated legitimate reasons (documenting staff misconduct, noise, blocked driveway) supported by evidence, and Birch's evidence of discriminatory animus was insufficient to create a genuine dispute of material fact.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Mhany Mgmt., Inc. v. County of Nassau
Mitchell v. Shane
Frazier v. Rominger
McElwee v. County of Orange

source_file: 6470766_2022_Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_dcd
case_name: Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Tenants sought Tenant Protection Vouchers to transfer from substandard Sandpiper Cove apartments to decent, safe, and sanitary housing elsewhere.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims—including APA and intentional discrimination claims under § 3604(a)—as moot because the transfer of ownership to a new owner resolved the Notice of Default, eliminating HUD's statutory authority to issue Tenant Protection Vouchers and making the requested relief unavailable.
brief_summary: Two tenants and the Sandpiper Cove tenant association sued HUD seeking Tenant Protection Vouchers to relocate from substandard project-based Section 8 housing in Galveston, Texas, alleging HUD's refusal to issue vouchers violated the APA and constituted intentional race discrimination under § 3604(a). The court granted HUD's motion to dismiss, holding that intervening events—the sale to a new owner who had not received a Notice of Default—mooted the claims and rendered the requested relief unavailable.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
City of Los Angeles v. Lyons
Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Environment
Marino v. Nat'l Oceanic & Atmospheric Admin.

source_file: 6471218_2022_Michael Earl Van Cleve v. U.S. Secretary of Commerce_ca11
6472320_2022_Gene Phillips v. Acacia on the Green Condo Ass'n_ca6
case_name: Gene B. Phillips; Babette R. Krause v. Acacia on the Green Condominium Association, Inc.; Scott D. Cohen; Richard N. Dettlebach; John F. Klein; James N. Kleinfelter; Diane E. Lombardy; Nina H. Rothman; Amy W. Wachs
accommodation_description: Two disabled residents requested permission to use personal gas grills on their patios despite the condominium association's rule prohibiting grills on patios and balconies.
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed that Phillips's requested accommodation was not 'necessary' because she regularly walked to the pool next to the grilling area despite her arthritis, and Acacia offered an alternative accommodation; further, neither Phillips's nor Weiss's requested accommodation was 'reasonable' because permitting individual patio grills would impose significant administrative burdens on the association, including insurance liability risks.
brief_summary: Gene Phillips and Stephen Weiss, disabled residents of the Acacia on the Green Condominium Association in Lyndhurst, Ohio, sued the association after being denied permission to use personal gas grills on their patios, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Amendments Act. The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the association, holding that Phillips's request was not necessary to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling because she regularly walked past the grilling area to reach the pool, and both residents' requests were not reasonable because permitting individual patio grills would impose significant administrative and insurance burdens on the condominium association.
key_cases_cited: Vorchheimer v. Philadelphian Owners Ass'n, 903 F.3d 100 (3d Cir. 2018)
Howard v. City of Beavercreek, 276 F.3d 802 (6th Cir. 2002)
Anderson v. City of Blue Ash, 798 F.3d 338 (6th Cir. 2015)
Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Groner v. Golden Gate Gardens Apts., 250 F.3d 1039 (6th Cir. 2001)

source_file: 6472707_2022_Commissiong v. US Dept. Housing _ Urban Development_ca2
case_name: Commissiong v. US Dept. Housing & Urban Development
accommodation_description: Undetermined; Commissiong filed a HUD administrative complaint alleging discrimination in violation of the FHA regarding her apartment, but the specific accommodation requested is not detailed in the opinion.
key_holding: The court affirmed dismissal based on sovereign immunity, holding that HUD and its officials are immune from suit under the FHA and that Commissiong failed to identify a valid waiver of sovereign immunity.
brief_summary: Carol Commissiong filed a HUD administrative complaint alleging housing discrimination in violation of the FHA regarding her apartment; after HUD issued a finding of no reasonable cause, she filed an Article 78 petition against HUD and HUD employees in state court. The court affirmed dismissal, holding that sovereign immunity bars suit against HUD and its officials because the FHA does not create a private right of action against federal agencies and Commissiong failed to identify any valid waiver of sovereign immunity.
key_cases_cited: Green v. Dep't of Educ. of New York, 16 F.4th 1070 (2d Cir. 2021)

case_name: Mary E. Chambers v. District of Columbia
accommodation_description: This is a Title VII employment discrimination case, not a Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation case. The accommodation at issue is a job transfer request.
key_holding: The D.C. Circuit sitting en banc overruled Brown v. Brody, holding that discriminatory denial of a job transfer request violates Title VII's antidiscrimination provision without requiring proof of 'objectively tangible harm' because the statutory requirement that the discrimination relate to 'terms, conditions, or privileges of employment' provides the necessary limiting principle.
brief_summary: Mary Chambers sued the District of Columbia under Title VII alleging sex discrimination, claiming her employer denied her repeated transfer requests while granting similar requests to male employees. The en banc court overruled Brown v. Brody, holding that discriminatory denial of job transfers violates Title VII without requiring proof of 'objectively tangible harm' because the statutory text already provides the necessary limiting principle through the requirement that discrimination relate to 'terms, conditions, or privileges of employment.'
key_cases_cited: Brown v. Brody, 199 F.3d 446 (D.C. Cir. 1999)
