case_name: Hatfield v. Cottages on 78th Community Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged HOA retaliated against her for filing housing discrimination complaints with UALD and threatened legal action.
key_holding: The HOA's communications (September 6th Letter, September 10th Letter, notice of assessment, and statements at annual meeting) did not constitute coercive, threatening, intimidating, or interfering conduct under § 3617 because a person of normal fortitude would not find them objectively coercive.
brief_summary: Wendi Hatfield, a homeowner, sued her HOA and related defendants alleging FHA retaliation under § 3617 based on communications (cease-and-desist letter, fines, September letters, and meeting statements) that she claimed were coercive responses to her filing housing discrimination complaints. The Tenth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, holding that the HOA's conduct did not rise to the level of coercive, threatening, intimidating, or interfering conduct required for a § 3617 claim because the communications were merely informational and not objectively severe enough to deter a person of normal fortitude from exercising fair housing rights.
key_cases_cited: Bloch v. Frischholz, 587 F.3d 771 (7th Cir. 2009)
Geraci v. Union Square Condo. Ass'n, 891 F.3d 274 (7th Cir. 2018)
Revock v. Cowpet Bay Western Condominium Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Tony Staton v. Vesta Corporation
accommodation_description: Request for an accessible apartment unit suitable for his disability
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss on procedural process grounds but dismissed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim for failure to state sufficient factual allegations, granting plaintiff leave to amend.
brief_summary: Tony Staton, proceeding pro se, sued Vesta Corporation alleging the defendant denied him an accessible apartment suitable for his disability under the Fair Housing Act. The court denied the motion to dismiss on procedural process grounds but dismissed the FHA claim without prejudice for failure to plead sufficient factual content, including the nature of his disability and what accommodation he sought.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc., 514 U.S. 725 (1995)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

source_file: 7441118_2022_The School of the Ozarks, Inc. v. Joseph Biden, Jr._ca8
case_name: The School of the Ozarks, Inc. v. Joseph Biden, Jr.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; the case concerns College of the Ozarks' challenge to a HUD enforcement memorandum as applied to its religiously-based policy of assigning students to single-sex dormitories by biological sex, and its related communications about that housing policy under § 3604(c).
key_holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed dismissal of College of the Ozarks' pre-enforcement challenge to a HUD memorandum directing full enforcement of the Fair Housing Act's sex-discrimination prohibition to include sexual orientation and gender identity, holding that the College lacked Article III standing because its alleged injuries—both enforcement of its housing policies and chilling of its speech—were too speculative and not certainly impending.
brief_summary: College of the Ozarks, a private Christian college maintaining single-sex dormitories on religious grounds, brought a pre-enforcement challenge against a HUD memorandum that directed agency offices to fully enforce the Fair Housing Act's sex-discrimination provisions to cover sexual orientation and gender identity following Bostock v. Clayton County. The district court dismissed for lack of Article III standing, and the Eighth Circuit affirmed, finding that any threatened enforcement injury was highly speculative given that HUD had never charged a Title IX-exempt college with such a violation and that any liability would flow from the statute itself rather than the internal memorandum. A dissenting judge argued the College suffered a concrete injury through deprivation of its statutory right to notice and comment before HUD issued the interpretive memorandum.
key_cases_cited: Bostock v. Clayton County, 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020)
Lujan v. Defs. of Wildlife, 504 U.S. 555 (1992)
Abbott Lab'ys v. Gardner, 387 U.S. 136 (1967)

case_name: Krystal Theresa Davis v. Daniel B. Rubin; Shannon Leigh McGroarty
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request is described in the opinion; the case focuses on retaliation for reporting discrimination and general disability-based discrimination claims.
key_holding: The Third Circuit affirmed dismissal because Davis failed to adequately plead disability discrimination (her own exhibit contradicted her allegation that defendants mocked her disability) and failed to establish a causal connection between her HUD complaint and the adverse actions, which were almost exclusively prior to her HUD filing.
brief_summary: Krystal Davis, a Section 8 tenant, sued her landlords alleging disability discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act after being evicted following complaints about mistreatment and subsequent filing of a HUD complaint. The Third Circuit affirmed the dismissal, finding that Davis failed to adequately plead disability discrimination (her exhibits contradicted her claims) and failed to establish causation for her retaliation claim since the adverse actions predated her protected activity.
key_cases_cited: Revock v. Cowpet Bay W. Condo. Ass'n, 853 F.3d 96 (3d Cir. 2017)

source_file: 7854286_2022_Village Green at Sayville, LLC v. Town of Islip_ca2
case_name: Village Green at Sayville, LLC v. Town of Islip et al.
race_if_mentioned: African-American and Hispanic populations overwhelmingly concentrated in the hamlets of Brentwood, Bay Shore, and Central Islip, while Sayville is over 90% non-Hispanic white
accommodation_description: Developer Village Green alleged the Town of Islip's covenants and restrictions requiring owner-occupied condominiums discriminatorily excluded minorities from the predominantly white hamlet of Sayville.
key_holding: The Second Circuit vacated the district court's dismissal for lack of ripeness, holding that the Town of Islip's official resolution stating the motion to approve Village Green's application 'fails for lack of second,' combined with the town attorney's statement that no further proceedings would be held, constituted a final decision sufficient to ripen the developer's land-use discrimination claims.
brief_summary: Village Green at Sayville, LLC, a real estate developer, sued the Town of Islip alleging that the town's refusal to modify covenants and restrictions on its property constituted racial and ethnic discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and other laws. The district court dismissed for lack of ripeness under Williamson County's final-decision requirement. The Second Circuit vacated and remanded, holding that the town's December 2016 resolution stating the motion to approve 'fails for lack of second,' combined with the town attorney's representation that no further proceedings would be held, constituted a final decision sufficient to ripen the claims.
key_cases_cited: Williamson County Regional Planning Commission v. Hamilton Bank, 473 U.S. 172 (1985)
Knick v. Township of Scott, 139 S. Ct. 2162 (2019)
Sunrise Detox V, LLC v. City of White Plains, 769 F.3d 118 (2d Cir. 2014)
Murphy v. New Milford Zoning Commission, 402 F.3d 342 (2d Cir. 2005)
Mhany Management, Inc. v. County of Nassau, 819 F.3d 581 (2d Cir. 2016)

source_file: 7860243_2022_Sailboat Bend Sober Living v. City of Fort Lauderdale, FL._ca11
case_name: Sailboat Bend Sober Living, LLC v. City of Fort Lauderdale, Florida
accommodation_description: Request for waiver of automatic fire sprinkler installation requirement for a sober living home housing individuals with substance use disabilities who cannot afford higher rents.
key_holding: The reasonable accommodation claim failed because plaintiffs adduced no evidence establishing a causal relationship between residents' substance use disabilities and their inability to afford rent increases needed to fund a $30,000-$40,000 fire sprinkler system; the zoning ordinance does not facially discriminate because it treats disabled persons more favorably than non-disabled persons.
brief_summary: Sailboat Bend Sober Living, a for-profit substance use recovery home, sued the City of Fort Lauderdale under the FHA and ADA alleging that the City's zoning ordinance was facially discriminatory, the City failed to reasonably accommodate disability by waiving fire sprinkler requirements, and the City intentionally discriminated through code enforcement. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the City, holding that the zoning ordinance treats disabled persons more favorably than non-disabled persons and thus is not facially discriminatory, that the accommodation request was not necessary because plaintiffs failed to establish a causal link between residents' disabilities and their inability to afford rent increases, and that no evidence supported intentional discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Schaw v. Habitat for Humanity of Citrus Cnty., Inc., 938 F.3d 1259 (11th Cir. 2019)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, 473 U.S. 432 (1985)
Bostock v. Clayton County, 140 S. Ct. 1731 (2020)

source_file: 7860639_2022_Myers v. District of Columbia Housing Authority_dcd
case_name: Belinda Myers & Wanda Thomas v. District of Columbia Housing Authority et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege sexual harassment by the resident manager including quid pro quo propositions (offering to help avoid eviction or complete repairs in exchange for sex) and hostile environment conduct.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motions for summary judgment, finding sufficient evidence for a jury to find that the resident manager engaged in quid pro quo and hostile environment sexual harassment under the FHA and that DCHA is vicariously liable for his actions.
brief_summary: Two female tenants of public housing sued the District of Columbia Housing Authority and its resident manager alleging quid pro quo and hostile environment sexual harassment under the Fair Housing Act. The court denied Defendants' motions for summary judgment, finding sufficient direct evidence of harassment and genuine disputes of material fact regarding apparent authority and vicarious liability.
key_cases_cited: Honce v. Vigil, 1 F.3d 1085 (10th Cir. 1993)
Fox v. Gaines, 4 F.4th 1293 (11th Cir. 2021)
Quigley v. Winter, 598 F.3d 938 (8th Cir. 2010)

source_file: 7861582_2022_DeAnn Graham v. UMH IN Holiday Village, LLC_ca7
case_name: DeAnn Graham v. UMH IN Holiday Village, LLC
accommodation_description: Request to keep a dog as a registered emotional support animal for the plaintiff's daughter who has anxiety.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine bars federal courts from exercising subject-matter jurisdiction over claims that seek review of state court judgments, including federal Fair Housing Act discrimination claims challenging the outcome of eviction proceedings.
brief_summary: DeAnn Graham, a Black tenant, sued her former landlord UMH IN Holiday Village, LLC in federal court after an Indiana state court entered an eviction judgment against her based on an alleged lease violation concerning her daughter's emotional support dog. She alleged Fair Housing Act claims for race and disability discrimination. The Seventh Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine, holding that federal courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction to review state court judgments even when the plaintiff asserts federal statutory rights.
key_cases_cited: Rooker v. Fidelity Trust Co., 263 U.S. 413 (1923)

Andrade v. City of Hammond, Indiana, 9 F.4th 947 (7th Cir. 2021)

source_file: 8240500_2022_Tonca Watters v. Homeowners Association at the_ca7
case_name: Tonca Watters and Terence Watters v. The Homeowners' Association at the Preserve at Bridgewater, Kathryn Mamaril, and Edward Mamaril
accommodation_description: Requested installation of a six-foot vinyl privacy fence in the backyard as a reasonable accommodation for PTSD.
key_holding: The Watters' failure to accommodate claim fails because they provided no evidence the HOA knew about Terence's PTSD, as Terence did not mention PTSD in his accommodation request.
brief_summary: The Watters, an African-American couple, sued their HOA and individual members for race discrimination and failure to accommodate Terence's PTSD with a privacy fence under the Fair Housing Act. The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for defendants on the accommodation claim because the Watters failed to show the HOA knew about Terence's PTSD, but vacated judgment on the race discrimination claims against the Mamarils, finding sufficient evidence of intentional racial harassment for a jury to decide.

source_file: 8241798_2022_Jamal Akbar v. Interstate Realty Management Company_ca7
case_name: Jamal A. Akbar v. Interstate Realty Management Company
accommodation_description: Akbar alleged Interstate denied his rental application because of his disability (muscular damage to left shoulder) and low income.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment because Akbar presented no evidence that Interstate discriminated based on disability—the undisputed evidence showed Interstate applies its income policy consistently to both disabled and non-disabled applicants, rejecting Akbar solely due to his failure to meet the income threshold.
brief_summary: Jamal Akbar sued Interstate Realty Management Company and Legends A-2, LLC, alleging that they discriminated against him based on disability and low income when they denied his application to rent a unit at their Chicago apartment complex. The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Interstate, finding that Akbar presented no evidence of disability-based discrimination because the undisputed record showed Interstate consistently applies its income requirement policy to all applicants regardless of disability status.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Hous. & Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc., 135 S. Ct. 2507 (2015)
Khungar v. Access Cmty. Health Network, 985 F.3d 565 (7th Cir. 2021)

source_file: 8245021_2022_Steven Unger v. Majorca at Via Verde Homeowners Association Inc._ca11
case_name: Steven Unger v. Majorca at Via Verde Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with severe ankylosing spondylitis requested that the HOA either record its board meetings or provide transcripts of meeting minutes immediately after meetings so he could access community information despite being unable to attend meetings in person.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal because it erred in evaluating Majorca's alternative accommodations (Zoom access, designating a representative) before determining whether Unger's requested accommodations were facially reasonable under the Schaw framework, which requires courts to first assess whether a plaintiff's requested accommodation seems reasonable on its face before considering a defendant's counterproposals.
brief_summary: Steven Unger, who suffers from severe ankylosing spondylitis preventing him from attending homeowners association meetings, requested that Majorca record its meetings or provide immediate transcripts of meeting minutes as a reasonable accommodation under the FHA; when Majorca refused these requests but offered alternative accommodations, the district court dismissed his complaint. The Eleventh Circuit reversed, holding the district court erred by evaluating Majorca's alternative accommodations before determining whether Unger's requested accommodations were facially reasonable under the proper legal framework.
key_cases_cited: Schaw v. Habitat for Humanity of Citrus County, Inc., 938 F.3d 1259 (11th Cir. 2019)
Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)

source_file: 8509670_2022_Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_dcd
case_name: Sandpiper Residents Association v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Tenants requested HUD issue Tenant Protection Vouchers to Sandpiper Cove residents as a remedy for substandard housing conditions.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' Rule 59(e) motion for reconsideration because the sale of the property to a new owner rendered all claims moot—the statutory precondition for issuing Tenant Protection Vouchers (a Notice of Default against the current owner) was no longer satisfied.
brief_summary: Sandpiper Cove tenants and the Sandpiper Residents Association sued HUD seeking an order requiring HUD to issue Tenant Protection Vouchers due to substandard housing conditions at the PBRA-subsidized complex. The court denied plaintiffs' motion to reconsider its prior dismissal on mootness grounds, holding that because the property was sold to a new owner who had not received a Notice of Default, the statutory prerequisite for issuing vouchers was no longer satisfied.
key_cases_cited: Ciralsky v. CIA, 355 F.3d 661 (D.C. Cir. 2004)
Firestone v. Firestone, 76 F.3d 1205 (D.C. Cir. 1996)
Patton Boggs LLP v. Chevron Corp., 683 F.3d 397 (D.C. Cir. 2012)

source_file: 9328910_2022_The Religious Sisters of Mercy v. Xavier Becerra_ca8
9344939_2022_Joseph Phillips, Jr. v. City of Pittsburgh_ca3
case_name: Joseph D.S. Phillips, Jr. v. City of Pittsburgh
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; the complaint made disjointed and incoherent references to the Fair Housing Act in the context of alleged police misconduct, extortion, and property fraud, without identifying any accommodation denial or modification request.
key_holding: The Third Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal with prejudice of Phillips's pro se amended complaint because it failed to coherently allege any facts sufficient to state a plausible claim for relief, and further leave to amend would be futile.
brief_summary: Joseph Phillips, Jr. filed a pro se complaint that the district court found incomprehensible and dismissed without prejudice, granting leave to amend. Phillips's amended complaint remained incoherent, asserting causes of action including breach of duty, breach of contract, unjust enrichment, Commerce Clause violations, and passing references to the Fair Housing Act against HUD, the City of Pittsburgh, a Pittsburgh police officer, and the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, demanding tens of billions of dollars. The district court dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice for failure to state a claim, and the Third Circuit affirmed, finding the complaint failed to allege any coherent facts supporting a viable cause of action and that amendment would be futile.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Geness v. Cox, 902 F.3d 344 (3d Cir. 2018)

case_name: Corla Jackson v. Siegel Group, L.L.C.
accommodation_description: Jackson's claims stem from what she characterizes as wrongful eviction from her apartment, though the specific accommodation request or disability-related basis is not detailed in the opinion.
key_holding: The district court found no factual allegations to support Jackson's Fair Housing Act claims and dismissed all federal claims with prejudice, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed for the reasons stated in the district court's thorough opinion.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Corla Jackson appealed the district court's dismissal of her claims arising from what she characterized as wrongful eviction from her apartment, including Fair Housing Act claims. The Fifth Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment, which had found no factual allegations to support Jackson's FHA claims and dismissed all federal claims with prejudice while dismissing state claims without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Alabama Ass'n of Realtors v. Dep't of Health & Hum. Servs., 141 S. Ct. 2485 (2021)

source_file: 9368386_2023_Socal Recovery, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa_ca9
case_name: SoCal Recovery, LLC v. City of Costa Mesa
accommodation_description: Operators of sober living homes for persons recovering from addiction requested reasonable accommodations to waive the 650-foot separation requirement between sober living homes to continue operating their facilities.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit held that sober living home operators can satisfy the 'actual disability' prong by demonstrating they serve or intend to serve individuals with actual disabilities through collective evidence of policies and procedures, without providing individualized medical records of each resident; and that the 'regarded as disabled' prong does not require proof of the City's subjective belief that residents were disabled under the pre-ADAAA standard.
brief_summary: SoCal Recovery, LLC and RAW Recovery, LLC, operators of sober living homes for persons recovering from addiction, appealed summary judgment for the City of Costa Mesa, which had denied their permit applications and reasonable accommodation requests to waive a 650-foot separation requirement between sober living homes. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding that group home operators can establish the 'actual disability' prong by demonstrating through admissions criteria, house rules, and employee testimony that they serve persons with disabilities, without providing individualized medical records; and that operators need not prove the City's subjective belief to establish the 'regarded as disabled' prong under the amended ADA definition.
key_cases_cited: City of Cleburne v. Cleburne Living Center, Inc.
Olmstead v. L.C.
MX Grp., Inc. v. City of Covington
Toyota Motor Mfg., Kentucky, Inc. v. Williams
Nunies v. HIE Holdings, Inc.

case_name: Chris Langer v. Milan Kiser
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a paraplegic wheelchair user, requested that defendant property owners provide van-accessible parking spaces with access aisles to allow him to access the commercial tenants' businesses.
key_holding: A place of public accommodation violates Title III of the ADA by opening its parking lot to customers without disabilities without providing accessible van-accessible parking spaces, and district courts cannot use a plaintiff's extensive ADA litigation history to undermine their credibility or intent to return.
brief_summary: Chris Langer, a paraplegic who uses a wheelchair and drives a van with a side-deploying ramp, sued property owners Milan and Diana Kiser under Title III of the ADA, alleging their commercial property's parking lot lacked required van-accessible parking spaces, preventing him from accessing businesses on the property. The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's judgment for the defendants, holding that (1) the parking lot was a facility of a place of public accommodation because customers of the Lobster Shop actually used it regardless of lease terms, (2) Langer had Article III standing as a serial litigant with tester standing, and (3) the district court improperly relied on Langer's litigation history to discredit his testimony about intent to return.
key_cases_cited: Chapman v. Pier 1 Imports (U.S.) Inc., 631 F.3d 939 (9th Cir. 2011)
Civil Rights Education and Enforcement Center v. Hospitality Properties Trust, 867 F.3d 1093 (9th Cir. 2017)
Pickern v. Holiday Quality Foods Inc., 293 F.3d 1133 (9th Cir. 2002)
Doran v. 7-Eleven, Inc., 524 F.3d 1034 (9th Cir. 2008)

case_name: Elizabeth Fedynich; Nicole Fedynich v. Boulder Housing Partners
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of the plaintiffs' amended complaint alleging Fair Housing Act violations, finding no reversible error in the lower court's ruling.
brief_summary: Elizabeth and Nicole Fedynich, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's order granting motions to dismiss their amended complaint alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, the Rehabilitation Act, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and due process rights against Boulder Housing Partners and numerous other defendants. The Fourth Circuit per curiam affirmed the district court's dismissal, finding no reversible error in the lower court's ruling.

source_file: 9375420_2023_Asociacion Puertorriquena de Profesores Univ. v. University of Puerto Rico_ca1

case_name: Richard Wolf v. City of Millbrae
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought accommodation related to radiofrequency emissions from a T-Mobile cell tower, apparently due to claimed electromagnetic sensitivity disability.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal of Wolf's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because Wolf failed to allege that the requested accommodation was necessary to afford him equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
brief_summary: Richard Wolf sued the City of Millbrae, a homeowners association, and T-Mobile seeking reasonable accommodation under the Fair Housing Act related to radiofrequency emissions from a cell tower. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the dismissal, holding that Wolf failed to adequately plead that the requested accommodation was necessary to afford him equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling under § 3604(f)(3)(B).
key_cases_cited: United States v. Cal. Mobile Home Park Mgmt. Co., 107 F.3d 1374 (9th Cir. 1997)

case_name: Alejandro Hernandez v. Constable R.A. Sommers Precinct #7
accommodation_description: Plaintiff attempted to bring a Fair Housing Act claim based on familial status discrimination related to eviction proceedings, but failed to plead facts establishing he had children.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal of Hernandez's Fair Housing Act claim because he failed to plead facts claiming that he has children, and thus cannot be covered under the Act's familial status provision.
brief_summary: Alejandro Hernandez, proceeding pro se, appealed the dismissal of his claims including a Fair Housing Act claim related to his eviction and foreclosure. The Fifth Circuit affirmed, holding that Hernandez failed to state a familial status discrimination claim because he did not plead facts showing he had children, and his other claims under the Protecting Tenants and Foreclosure Act and 42 U.S.C. §§ 1985 and 1986 were also not cognizable.

case_name: Symon Mandawala v. Struga Management
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves claim that landlord refused to allow plaintiff to remain as an occupant and withheld mail/packages due to race
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit affirmed that the plaintiff failed to establish disparate treatment under the Fair Housing Act because he did not complete application requirements for housing and failed to rebut the defendant's legitimate, non-discriminatory reason (failure to provide verifiable proof of income) for its housing decisions.
brief_summary: Black tenant Symon Mandawala appealed the district court's take-nothing judgment after a bench trial, alleging Struga Management discriminated against him by refusing to allow him to remain as an occupant in an apartment and withholding his mail and packages because of his race. The Fifth Circuit affirmed, finding Mandawala failed to establish a prima facie case of disparate treatment under the FHA because he did not complete the required application process and failed to rebut the defendants' legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for denying housing.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Crain v. City of Selma, 952 F.3d 634 (5th Cir. 2020)
Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Prop. Co., 920 F.3d 890 (5th Cir. 2019)

case_name: Simmons v. Langston Lane Limited Partnership
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a ground-floor, three-bedroom apartment as a reasonable accommodation for her osteoarthritis and obesity to afford her equal opportunity to use and enjoy her dwelling.
key_holding: Defendants failed to meet their initial burden of demonstrating through undisputed evidence that accommodating Plaintiff's transfer request to a ground-floor three-bedroom unit was unreasonable or would impose undue hardship, leaving genuine issues of material fact for trial; Plaintiff's cross-motion for summary judgment on her retaliation claim also failed because she did not establish as a matter of law that Defendants' stated legitimate reasons for their actions were pretextual.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eloise Simmons sued her apartment building's management and owner alleging they discriminated against her by denying her request for a ground-floor, three-bedroom apartment as an accommodation for her osteoarthritis and obesity. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for partial summary judgment, finding that Defendants failed to meet their burden of showing the accommodation request was unreasonable or would cause undue hardship, while Plaintiff failed to establish as a matter of law that Defendants' actions were retaliatory.

9399510_2023_Queen'Prinyah Godiah Nmiaa Pa El-Bey v. Social 2700 Student Spaces_ca11
case_name: Queen'Prinyah Godiah Nmiaa Pa El-Bey v. Social 2700 Student Spaces
accommodation_description: The case text does not describe any specific accommodation requested. Plaintiff's complaint listed the ADA, the FHA, and a Florida employment discrimination statute without elaboration, and the court characterized the claims only generically as 'disability discrimination.' No facts regarding a particular accommodation request, modification, or denial are set forth in the opinion.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed the district court's sua sponte dismissal without prejudice of plaintiff's pro se disability discrimination complaint for failure to comply with court orders and failure to prosecute, finding no abuse of discretion even where plaintiff claimed she never received the pertinent orders due to a change of address.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff filed a civil action asserting vague disability discrimination claims under the ADA, the Fair Housing Act, and a Florida employment discrimination statute against an apartment complex, a property management company, and a former roommate, arising from alleged injuries in August 2021. The district court dismissed the case without prejudice after plaintiff failed to respond to an order requiring an amended complaint and a subsequent show-cause order, and plaintiff filed no objections to the magistrate judge's recommendation. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, holding the district court did not abuse its discretion because it mailed orders to the address plaintiff provided, and plaintiff had an ongoing duty to keep the court informed of her current address.

case_name: United States v. Louis A. Rupp, II
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - case involves familial status discrimination (eviction of family with children from rental housing).
key_holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of Rupp's motion to set aside or reduce the punitive damages award, concluding there was sufficient evidence of reckless indifference to submit punitive damages to the jury and that the $60,000 punitive award was not constitutionally excessive given the reprehensibility of evicting a family with a newborn infant.
brief_summary: The United States sued landlord Louis Rupp under the Fair Housing Act on behalf of Laura Erwin and Mack Teal, alleging he discriminated against them based on familial status by evicting them because they had children. After the district court granted summary judgment for the government on liability and a jury awarded compensatory and punitive damages, Rupp appealed the district court's denial of his motion to reduce the punitive damages award. The Eighth Circuit affirmed, holding there was sufficient evidence of reckless indifference to support punitive damages and that the $60,000 punitive award was not constitutionally excessive.
key_cases_cited: Quigley v. Winter, 598 F.3d 938 (8th Cir. 2010)
Badami v. Flood, 214 F.3d 994 (8th Cir. 2000)

source_file: 9402431_2023_Joelle Angel v. Charlestowne Condominium Association, Inc._ca4
case_name: Angel v. Charlestowne Condominium Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request analyzed; case addressed procedural remand jurisdiction only.
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court's order remanding the case to state court for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction, finding no reversible error in the procedural ruling.
brief_summary: Multiple individual unit owners appealed a district court order remanding their removed action to state court for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction and denying their sanctions motions against the Charlestowne Condominium Association. The Fourth Circuit found jurisdiction to review the remand based on the § 1443 removal statute but affirmed on the merits, with the substantive FHA claims remaining unresolved.

case_name: Theresa Thomas-Tupper v. Catholic Charities et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that Robert Kellett be permitted to serve as her live-in aide despite his disqualifying drug-related criminal conviction.
key_holding: Defendants did not deny Plaintiff a reasonable accommodation because they offered her the exact accommodation she sought—a stipulation permitting Kellett as a live-in aide—which Plaintiff refused to sign, and the eviction was based on legitimate lease violations rather than disability discrimination.
brief_summary: Theresa Thomas-Tupper sued Catholic Charities and related entities (operators of a federally funded independent living facility) alleging disability discrimination under the FHA for failing to accommodate her request to have Robert Kellett serve as a live-in aide despite his criminal history, and retaliation for engaging in protected activity. The Second Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Defendants, finding that Defendants offered Plaintiff the exact accommodation she sought via stipulation (which she refused to sign) and that the eviction proceedings were causally unrelated to any protected activity.
key_cases_cited: Sheng v. M&TBank Corp., 848 F.3d 78 (2d Cir. 2017)
Wright v. N.Y. State Dep't of Corr., 831 F.3d 64 (2d Cir. 2016)

source_file: 9408770_2023_Scott Thomas v. Broward County Sheriff's Office_ca11

case_name: Rosemarie Vargas v. Facebook, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs challenge Facebook's ad-targeting algorithm that allegedly allowed housing advertisers to exclude protected classes (including women of color, single parents, and persons with disabilities) from receiving housing ads.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that plaintiffs adequately alleged Article III standing by claiming deprivation of truthful information and housing opportunities through Facebook's discriminatory ad-targeting tools, and that Facebook was not immune from liability under 47 U.S.C. § 230(c)(1) because Facebook materially contributed to the alleged illegality by creating the targeting categories and providing exclusion tools to housing advertisers.
brief_summary: Named plaintiffs sued Facebook, Inc. alleging that Facebook's Ad Platform allowed housing advertisers to discriminate in housing advertising by excluding protected classes (including women of color, single parents, and persons with disabilities) from receiving housing ads through discriminatory targeting tools. The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that plaintiffs adequately alleged Article III standing and that Facebook was not immune from liability under Section 230 because Facebook materially contributed to the alleged discriminatory conduct by creating the targeting categories and providing exclusion tools to housing advertisers.
key_cases_cited: Fair Housing Council of San Fernando Valley v. Roommates.com, LLC, 521 F.3d 1157 (9th Cir. 2008) (en banc)

case_name: David Q. Webb v. State of Delaware
accommodation_description: Webb alleged he was denied housing based on race and familial status, seeking damages for discriminatory housing denial.
key_holding: The court held that Webb's claim of familial status discrimination failed because familial status under 42 U.S.C. § 3602(k) protects only individuals under age 18 living with a parent or guardian, not single adults without children, and his conclusory factual allegations were insufficient to state a plausible claim.
brief_summary: David Webb, proceeding pro se, appealed the District of Delaware's dismissal of his complaint alleging violations of constitutional rights, Title VI, the Fair Housing Act, and state law against the State of Delaware, state/local officials, and motels. The Third Circuit affirmed, holding that Webb failed to state a plausible familial status discrimination claim under the FHA because single adults without children are not protected by the familial status provision, and his other claims failed for insufficient factual allegations.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

source_file: 9416474_2023_Oxford House Inc v. Township of North Bergen_ca3
case_name: Oxford House, Inc. v. Township of North Bergen
accommodation_description: Oxford House sought a Certificate of Continuing Occupancy to operate a community residence for individuals recovering from substance use disorders in a two-family dwelling.
key_holding: Oxford House failed to demonstrate a reasonable probability of success on its discrimination claims because it did not adduce sufficient evidence showing that the prospective residents' disability status played any role in the Township's denial of the Certificate of Continuing Occupancy.
brief_summary: Oxford House, a nonprofit that establishes housing for individuals recovering from substance abuse, sued the Township of North Bergen after it denied a Certificate of Continuing Occupancy for a proposed group home, alleging the denial violated the FHA and ADA. The Third Circuit affirmed the denial of preliminary injunction, finding Oxford House failed to show the Township's denial was motivated by discriminatory intent rather than legitimate zoning concerns about the property's two-family dwelling classification.
key_cases_cited: Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Housing Development Corp., 429 U.S. 252 (1977)

case_name: James Darell Smith v. James K. Hein; Transition Projects, Inc.; Home Forward of Multnomah County
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation requested is not described in the disposition; the case was dismissed on procedural grounds.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit affirmed dismissal because claims against Home Forward were precluded by a prior state court settlement agreement, and claims against Hein and Transition Projects were barred by the two-year Fair Housing Act statute of limitations.
brief_summary: James Darell Smith, proceeding pro se, appealed the district court's dismissal of his disability discrimination claims under the Fair Housing Act against a public housing authority, a nonprofit organization, and an individual landlord. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that claims against the housing authority were precluded by a prior state court settlement, and claims against the other defendants were barred by the two-year FHA statute of limitations.

source_file: 9420585_2023_County of Cook v. Bank of America Corporation_ca7
case_name: County of Cook, Illinois v. Bank of America Corporation
accommodation_description: Cook County alleges banks targeted African American and Hispanic borrowers for predatory mortgages and discriminatory loan practices, causing the County economic harm through lost tax revenue and increased municipal costs.
key_holding: The FHA does not provide a remedy for Cook County because its economic injuries (lost tax revenue, increased municipal costs for vacant properties) are too remotely connected to the alleged discriminatory lending practices—the County suffered only tertiary injuries rather than the first-tier injuries proximately caused by the statutory violation.
brief_summary: Cook County, Illinois sued several banks under the Fair Housing Act alleging they engaged in discriminatory lending practices that targeted African American and Hispanic borrowers for predatory mortgages, and that the resulting foreclosures caused the County economic injuries including lost tax revenue and increased municipal costs. The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the banks, holding that the County's injuries were too remote from the alleged discrimination to establish proximate cause under the FHA.

source_file: 9420586_2023_County of Cook v. Bank of America Corporation_ca7
case_name: County of Cook, Illinois v. Bank of America Corporation
accommodation_description: Cook County alleges banks engaged in discriminatory lending targeting African American and Hispanic home buyers for predatory mortgages, but this is not a reasonable accommodation request case.
key_holding: The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the banks, holding that Cook County lacks standing to bring FHA claims because the County's injuries (lost property tax revenue and increased municipal service costs from foreclosures) are too attenuated from the alleged discriminatory lending practices to satisfy proximate cause under Bank of America Corp. v. Miami, which requires a direct relation between injury and injurious conduct.
brief_summary: Cook County, Illinois sued multiple banks under the Fair Housing Act alleging that the banks engaged in discriminatory predatory lending targeting minority borrowers, causing the County to suffer lost property tax revenue and increased municipal costs from resulting foreclosures. The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the banks, holding that the County lacks standing because its injuries are not proximately caused by the banks' alleged discrimination—under Bank of America Corp. v. Miami, the County is a tertiary injured party too far removed from the discriminatory conduct to satisfy the proximate cause requirement.

case_name: James Nathaniel Douse v. Sabrina Traeger
accommodation_description: Complaint was inadequate and incomprehensible, failing to articulate a specific accommodation request; claims related to HOA assessments and property deposit disputes rather than a discrete accommodation.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal because plaintiff's FHA complaint was wholly insubstantial and frivolous, containing no factual allegations establishing a violation of any FHA provision, and even construing the complaint generously, the claims regarding HOA fees and property deposits did not relate to discriminatory conduct on a protected basis.
brief_summary: James Douse, proceeding pro se, appealed the sua sponte dismissal of his Fair Housing Act complaint against private individuals and a homeowners association for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding Douse's complaint wholly insubstantial and frivolous because it failed to allege any factual content establishing that defendants engaged in conduct prohibited by the FHA, instead raising only contract claims regarding HOA assessments and a pool construction deposit.

source_file: 9425247_2023_Reese v. Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association I_dcd
case_name: Allison Reese v. Park Place Condominium Homeowners Association I
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged racial discrimination in the denial of access to the HOA's master insurance policy for foundation repairs, not a reasonable accommodation request.
key_holding: The court found Reese's racial discrimination claim under § 3605 survived PPCA's motion to dismiss because she alleged sufficient facts showing PPCA denied her insurance coverage while allowing White owners to make similar repairs, but dismissed her retaliation claim under § 3617 because reporting fraud and waste is not protected activity under the FHA.
brief_summary: Allison Reese, an African-American condo owner, sued her HOA alleging racial discrimination when PPCA denied her six requests to use the master insurance policy for foundation repairs while allowing White owners to make similar claims. The court granted MCM's motion to dismiss as time-barred, dismissed Reese's retaliation claim for failing to allege protected activity, but allowed her race discrimination claim to proceed finding she alleged sufficient facts supporting an inference of discrimination.

case_name: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Azalea Garden Properties, LLC
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was analyzed; the case concerned organizational standing to bring a race-based disparate impact claim challenging Azalea Garden's criminal background check policy.
key_holding: LaFHAC lacks organizational standing because it failed to allege facts showing that its diversion of resources to counteract Azalea Garden's alleged discriminatory practices perceptibly impaired its ability to achieve its mission of eradicating housing discrimination.
brief_summary: LaFHAC sued Azalea Garden Properties, LLC alleging that its criminal background check policy had a disparate impact on African American rental applicants in violation of the FHA. The Fifth Circuit dismissed the appeal after finding that LaFHAC, a nonprofit fair housing organization with no members, lacked organizational standing because its alleged injuries—diversion of resources to investigate and counteract the defendant's practices—did not constitute cognizable Article III injury.

case_name: Orlando Garcia v. Gateway Hotel L.P.
accommodation_description: ADA claim regarding hotel reservation policies and website accessibility for persons with disabilities (not an FHA reasonable accommodation case)
key_holding: The ADA's fee- and cost-shifting provision (42 U.S.C. § 12205) does not 'provide otherwise' than Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(d)(1), and therefore a prevailing ADA defendant may be awarded costs at the district court's discretion without a finding that the plaintiff's action was frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation.
brief_summary: Orlando Garcia sued Gateway Hotel L.P. under the Americans with Disabilities Act, challenging the hotel's reservation policies and website practices regarding accessible rooms. After the district court dismissed the case and awarded costs to Gateway, Garcia appealed arguing ADA defendants should only receive costs if the action was frivolous. The Ninth Circuit affirmed, holding that 42 U.S.C. § 12205 does not limit Rule 54(d)(1)'s discretionary cost award standard, effectively overruling prior precedent in Brown, and concluding the district court properly exercised discretion in awarding costs to the prevailing defendant.

source_file: 9427143_2023_National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_dcd
case_name: National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; NAMIC challenges HUD's Disparate-Impact Rule as exceeding statutory authority under the FHA.
key_holding: HUD's Disparate-Impact Rule does not conflict with the Fair Housing Act as applied to insurers' underwriting and rating practices; NAMIC's four arguments—that the Rule causes pervasive consideration of protected characteristics, is invalidated by state insurance laws, allows claims based solely on statistical disparities, and permits displacement of valid priorities—are all unpersuasive.
brief_summary: The National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies, a trade association whose members sell homeowners insurance, challenged HUD's Disparate-Impact Rule (which establishes a burden-shifting framework for disparate-impact claims under the FHA) as exceeding HUD's statutory authority under the APA and FHA as interpreted by Inclusive Communities. The court denied NAMIC's motion for summary judgment and granted HUD's cross-motion, finding the Rule does not conflict with the FHA and is a permissible construction of the statute.

case_name: Sonya Youvett McNeal v. Navy Federal Credit Union
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was substantively analyzed; the plaintiff alleged FHA violations in a foreclosure/mortgage dispute, but the case was dismissed for failure to state a claim and the court did not reach the merits of any accommodation request.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit lacked jurisdiction to review the district court's dismissal of the complaint and denial of preliminary injunction due to procedural defects (untimely appeal and mootness), and affirmed the denial of the motion to recuse and first motion to reconsider on the merits.
brief_summary: Sonya McNeal, proceeding pro se, appealed from a district court dismissal of her suit against Navy Federal Credit Union over a foreclosure dispute, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, CARES Act, and Due Process Clause. The Eleventh Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction over the dismissal order (untimely appeal) and preliminary injunction denial (mootness), and affirmed the denial of the motion to recuse and first motion to reconsider.

case_name: Rosemarie Vargas; et al. v. Facebook, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege Facebook's ad platform allowed housing advertisers to exclude protected classes from seeing housing advertisements, limiting access to housing opportunities.
key_holding: The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, holding that plaintiffs adequately alleged Article III standing and that Facebook is not immune from liability under Section 230(c)(1) because Facebook actively developed the discriminatory ad targeting tools rather than merely publishing third-party content.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs filed a class action against Facebook alleging that its advertising platform allowed housing advertisers to exclude protected classes from viewing housing ads, causing concrete injury. The Ninth Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal, finding that plaintiffs adequately alleged Article III standing and that Facebook is not immune from liability under Section 230(c)(1) because Facebook materially contributed to the alleged discrimination through its development of ad targeting categories and tools rather than acting as a mere publisher.

source_file: 9433324_2023_Southwest Fair Housing Council v. Wg Scottsdale LLC_ca9
case_name: Southwest Fair Housing Council v. WG Scottsdale LLC

key_holding: The court held that Southwest Fair Housing Council had organizational standing, sufficient evidence supported the jury's finding that an ASL interpreter was a necessary accommodation to provide a deaf applicant an equal opportunity to enjoy the housing, and the punitive damages award and permanent injunction were appropriate.
brief_summary: Southwest Fair Housing Council sued WG Scottsdale LLC (operator of Atria Sierra Pointe assisted-living facility) after testers were denied an ASL interpreter for a fictional deaf applicant, alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The Ninth Circuit affirmed the jury verdict in favor of Southwest, holding that the organization had standing, the ASL interpreter request was a necessary accommodation under § 3604(f)(3)(B), and the punitive damages award and permanent injunction were supported by evidence of the defendant's reckless indifference to disability accommodation requirements.

case_name: Mamberto Real v. Judith Moran
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged national origin discrimination during the rental process, but no specific accommodation request is described.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of the complaint as a shotgun pleading because each of the seven counts reincorporated vague factual allegations and legal conclusions, making it impossible to determine which allegations supported which claims, and plaintiff forfeited any challenge to dismissal without leave to amend.
brief_summary: Mamberto Real, proceeding pro se, appealed the dismissal of his Fair Housing Act claims alleging national origin discrimination and retaliation against Judith Moran, Frank Diaz Gines, and Presbyterian Homes & Housing Foundation of Florida, Inc. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed, finding the complaint was properly dismissed as a shotgun pleading because each count reincorporated the same vague factual allegations and legal conclusions, failing to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them.

case_name: Women's Elevated Sober Living L.L.C. v. City of Plano
accommodation_description: Request for a zoning accommodation to exceed the eight-resident capacity limit to allow 15-20 residents in a women's sober living home for individuals recovering from substance use disorders.
key_holding: The Fifth Circuit held that the district court applied the wrong legal standard by accepting that proof of greater therapeutic benefit from larger occupancy was sufficient to establish necessity under § 3604(f)(3)(B); rather, plaintiffs must prove the requested accommodation is indispensable or essential—not merely preferable—to ameliorate their disabilities.
brief_summary: Women's Elevated Sober Living LLC and its owner sued the City of Plano challenging the denial of a zoning accommodation request to allow 15-20 residents in their sober living home beyond the eight-person limit in the SF-7 zoning ordinance. The Fifth Circuit vacated the district court's finding of an FHA violation, holding that the district court improperly applied a standard accepting that therapeutically beneficial treatment constitutes necessity under the FHA, when plaintiffs must instead prove the accommodation is indispensable to recovery.

source_file: 9443643_2023_Dayton Veterans Residences Ltd. v. Dayton Metro. Housing Authority_ca6
case_name: Dayton Veterans Residences Ltd. Partnership v. Dayton Metro. Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority to amend its Administrative Plan to permit project-based HUD-VASH vouchers for a veteran homeless housing development serving disabled veterans.
key_holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed that the district court properly instructed the jury using the 'was necessary' standard for reasonable accommodation claims and that Freedom's Path failed to prove its accommodation claim; the court also upheld evidentiary rulings permitting testimony about whether GDPM knew or should have known its prospective tenants were disabled.
brief_summary: Dayton Veterans Residences Limited Partnership (Freedom's Path), a developer of housing for homeless veterans, sued Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority alleging GDPM failed to reasonably accommodate disabled veterans by refusing to amend its Administrative Plan to permit project-based HUD-VASH vouchers. After a remand from the Sixth Circuit, a jury found for GDPM, and Freedom's Path appealed challenging jury instructions and evidentiary rulings. The Sixth Circuit affirmed, holding the district court properly used the 'was necessary' standard and that GDPM's late disclosure of a witness and admission of evidence about prospective tenants' disabilities did not warrant reversal.

source_file: 9447936_2023_Lawrence T. Newman v. Heritage Village West Condominium Association, Inc._ca11
case_name: Lawrence T. Newman v. Heritage Village West Condominium Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for advance notice of toxic chemical use so Beverly Newman can avoid exposure due to her chemical sensitivity disability.
key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of retaliation and discriminatory harassment claims as barred by res judicata and statute of limitations, but reversed dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim (requiring proof of different facts than retaliation) and religious discrimination claim regarding housing services, which were allowed to proceed.
brief_summary: Lawrence and Beverly Newman, tenants in a Florida condominium, sued the Heritage Village West Condominium Association and board members under the Fair Housing Act alleging religious discrimination and failure to accommodate Beverly Newman's chemical sensitivity. The Eleventh Circuit affirmed dismissal of retaliation and discriminatory harassment claims as barred by res judicata and the statute of limitations, but reversed dismissal of the reasonable accommodation and religious discrimination claims regarding housing services, remanding for further proceedings.

case_name: Nagla Abdelhalim v. Andrew McDevitt
accommodation_description: N/A - harassment/interference claim under § 3617 alleging neighbors violated the FHA through a year-long campaign to force her out of her neighborhood based on her race, national origin, and religion; no reasonable accommodation was requested.
key_holding: The district court abused its discretion in awarding attorneys' fees to defendants because it applied post hoc reasoning, concluding the plaintiff's case was 'without foundation' merely because she did not prevail on summary judgment, without considering the circumstantial evidence she presented supporting her belief that defendants' harassment was motivated by discrimination.
brief_summary: Nagla Abdelhalim, an Egyptian Muslim woman who wears hijab, sued her neighbors alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by engaging in a year-long campaign of harassment including threats, intimidation, and interference intended to drive her out of her neighborhood based on her race, national origin, and religion. The district court granted summary judgment to defendants and awarded them attorneys' fees. On appeal, the Fourth Circuit vacated the fee award, holding the district court applied the wrong legal standard by engaging in post hoc reasoning and concluding the case was 'without foundation' merely because plaintiff did not prevail at summary judgment.

case_name: Nagla Abdelhalim v. Aaron Lewis
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested. This case involves interference and coercion claims under FHA § 3617, based on neighbors' alleged discriminatory harassment of plaintiff because of her race, national origin, and religion.
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit vacated the district court's attorneys' fees award to the prevailing defendants because the district court abused its discretion by applying post hoc reasoning—concluding plaintiff's FHA § 3617 claims were 'without foundation' solely because she did not prevail at summary judgment—rather than independently analyzing whether she knew or should have known her claims were groundless when filed.
brief_summary: Nagla Abdelhalim, an Egyptian immigrant and Muslim woman wearing a hijab, sued her neighbors under the FHA (42 U.S.C. § 3617), the Civil Rights Act (§ 1982), and 42 U.S.C. § 1985(3), alleging a year-long campaign of threats, intimidation, and harassment designed to drive her from her home because of her race, national origin, and religion. The district court granted summary judgment to the defendants for lack of evidence of discriminatory intent and then awarded them attorneys' fees, finding Abdelhalim's claims were 'without foundation.' The Fourth Circuit vacated the fee award, holding that the district court failed to engage with Abdelhalim's specific circumstantial evidence of discriminatory motive and improperly equated losing on the merits with having filed a frivolous or unfounded claim.

case_name: Nagla Abdelhalim v. Aaron Lewis
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested; the case involves claims of interference, threats, and intimidation under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 based on the plaintiff's race, national origin, and religion.
key_holding: The Fourth Circuit vacated the district court's award of attorneys' fees to the prevailing defendant-neighbors, holding that the district court abused its discretion by applying impermissible post hoc reasoning—equating plaintiff's failure to survive summary judgment with her claims being 'without foundation'—when plaintiff had presented sufficient circumstantial evidence to establish a reasonable basis for her FHA interference claim.
brief_summary: Nagla Abdelhalim, an Egyptian Muslim immigrant and homeowner, sued her immediate neighbors under the FHA (42 U.S.C. § 3617) and related civil rights statutes, alleging a year-long campaign of harassment intended to drive her from her home because of her race, national origin, and religion. The district court granted summary judgment for defendants on the merits (finding insufficient evidence of discriminatory intent) and then awarded defendants approximately $124,000 in attorneys' fees on the ground that plaintiff's claims were 'without foundation.' On appeal—limited solely to the fee award—the Fourth Circuit vacated the fee award, finding the district court had engaged in prohibited post hoc reasoning by failing to engage with plaintiff's circumstantial evidence arguments and instead inferring lack of foundation merely from her failure to prevail.

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Emmanuel Adeyinka filed suit against Project Home and others alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on disability, race, color, and national origin in connection with subsidized housing, but the District Court for the District of Columbia dismissed the complaint without prejudice because it failed to meet Rule 8(a)'s minimal pleading standard, providing no coherent statement of claims or adequate notice to defendants.

key_holding: The Eleventh Circuit affirmed that Oxford House's requested accommodation—waiving the business license requirement for utility accounts—was not necessary because plaintiffs failed to establish that the business license requirement actually affected residents' therapeutic recovery or created financial hardship directly tied to their addiction disabilities.
brief_summary: Oxford House, Inc. and three sober living group homes sued the City of Dothan, Alabama, alleging the City violated the Fair Housing Act by requiring them to obtain business licenses to open utility accounts. source_file: 9471209_2024_Jane Doe v. Allegheny County Housing Authority_ca3
case_name: Jane Doe v. Allegheny County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Pro se tenant in public housing alleging harassment and retaliation for filing HUD complaints, with claims under FHA and ADA regarding violation of address confidentiality protections
key_holding: The Third Circuit vacated in part the District Court's dismissal with prejudice, holding that the District Court erred in dismissing without granting leave to amend, while agreeing that Doe failed to adequately plead FHA retaliation for lack of causal connection between protected activity and adverse actions
brief_summary: Jane Doe, a pro se tenant in public housing managed by Allegheny County Housing Authority, appealed the District Court's sua sponte dismissal with prejudice of her amended complaint alleging violations of Pennsylvania's Address Confidentiality Program, the Fair Housing Act, and the ADA. The Third Circuit vacated in part and remanded, holding that while Doe failed to adequately plead an FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 for lack of causal connection, the District Court erred in dismissing without granting leave to amend.

source_file: 9475745_2024_BMG Monroe I, LLC v. Village of Monroe_ca2
case_name: BMG Monroe I, LLC v. Village of Monroe
accommodation_description: BMG Monroe I, LLC, a residential developer, claimed the Village of Monroe denied building permits for a 181-unit subdivision motivated by discriminatory animus toward the Hasidic Jewish community to whom the developer intended to market the development.
key_holding: The Second Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that the developer's FHA and Equal Protection claims were unripe because the developer failed to exhaust administrative remedies by not appealing to the Zoning Board of Appeals for Lots 1, 2, and 3 and not submitting a meaningful variance application after seeking to modify the conditions of its initial variance.
brief_summary: BMG Monroe I, LLC, a residential developer, sued the Village of Monroe under the Fair Housing Act and Equal Protection Clause, alleging discriminatory animus toward the Hasidic Jewish community motivated denials of building permits for a 181-unit subdivision. The Second Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal, finding the claims unripe because the developer failed to exhaust administrative remedies by not appealing permit denials to the Zoning Board of Appeals for all lots and not submitting a meaningful variance application after seeking to modify the conditions of its initial variance.

source_file: 9476529_2024_Miller v. First United Bank and Trust_ca10

brief_summary: Amia L. key_holding: The court affirmed dismissal because plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts showing his Crohn's disease substantially limits a major life activity to qualify as a disability under the FHA, and because his requested accommodation (delay of eviction) did not address the needs created by his alleged disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Dwight Smith sued American Homes 4 Rent alleging the landlord failed to reasonably accommodate his Crohn's disease by refusing to grant additional time to vacate the premises, and unlawfully retaliated by continuing eviction proceedings after he requested accommodations. brief_summary: Kalvin Schanz sued the City of Otsego, Michigan and city officials under the Fair Housing Act, claiming that officials' opposition to his speculative plan to house immigrant workers at JBS constituted discrimination and retaliation under § 3617. case_name: Neway Mengistu v. Forestview Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants apply to HACLA for a Section 8 exception payment standard—a government subsidy mechanism that could increase the monthly voucher payment above the standard—so that defendants could finance approximately $30,840 in wheelchair-accessibility modifications (including bathroom modifications and other alterations) and recoup those costs over time from the elevated subsidy payments, rather than paying for the modifications out-of-pocket.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment on two independent grounds: plaintiff's FHA and related claims were time-barred because they accrued on May 11, 2017—more than two years before suit was filed—and, on the merits, defendants were not required under the FHA to apply for a Section 8 exception payment standard as a reasonable accommodation, nor did plaintiff present evidence of discriminatory motive.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Neway Mengistu, a wheelchair user, applied to rent an apartment from Forestview Apartments using a Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher and requested that defendants apply for a Section 8 exception payment standard to fund approximately $30,840 in accessibility modifications; defendants cancelled his application after determining they could not cover the modification costs and HACLA would not directly fund them. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment on two independent grounds: the claims accrued on May 11, 2017 when the application was cancelled—over two years before the June 12, 2019 filing date—making them time-barred, and the court further held that no case law supports requiring a landlord to apply for federal exception payment standards as a reasonable accommodation under the FHA. The court also found no evidence of discriminatory animus, as defendants had repeatedly offered plaintiff the unit and cancelled only after he refused to sign the lease in a timely manner and neither party could cover the modification costs.

brief_summary: C.R., a minor with physical, mental, and emotional disabilities, sued Park La Brea apartment complex through his guardian, seeking a preliminary injunction to require defendants to assign him a specific parking space and fund upgraded windows as reasonable accommodations for his disabilities. key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel Richard Rice, finding that even assuming an attorney-client relationship existed between Rice and the SHA, defendants failed to demonstrate that the prior quasi-representation was substantially related to plaintiff's current employment discrimination and FHA retaliation lawsuit.
brief_summary: Michael Threatt, former CEO of the Sylacauga Housing Authority (SHA), filed suit alleging race discrimination, race retaliation under Title VII and § 1981, retaliation under the Fair Housing Act, and retaliation under the False Claims Act after the SHA terminated his employment following his complaints about the agency's discriminatory housing practices and HUD-identified segregation risks. The court denied disqualification, holding that the preliminary civil rights assessment discussions never ripened into a formal representation on a substantially related matter and that no current attorney-client relationship existed between Rice and the SHA.

source_file: 9524190_2022_Miller v. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama_alnd
case_name: Fredrika M. Miller v. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama
accommodation_description: No housing accommodation was requested. Miller asked Blue Cross to investigate pesticide use on her property and to provide specialized medical care for her and her mother following pesticide exposure and domestic violence; there was no request for a reasonable accommodation or modification in a housing context.
key_holding: The court dismissed all of Miller's claims because the cited ACA provisions lack private rights of action, her FHA claim failed to plead any discrimination in housing terms based on a protected class and was time-barred, and her Alabama Fair Housing Law claim similarly failed on the merits and was time-barred.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Fredrika Miller sued her health insurer, Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama, under the ACA, the FHA, and the Alabama Fair Housing Law, alleging that Blue Cross's failure to investigate pesticide overuse and domestic violence reports caused her and her mother to lose their home and that her mother subsequently died. The court dismissed the ACA claims because §§ 300gg-17 and 300gg-12 provide no express or implied private right of action and enforcement authority is vested in HHS and state agencies. The FHA and state housing law claims were dismissed both for failure to plead any discrimination in housing transactions based on a protected characteristic — Miller's theory was that unpaid medical bills caused her homelessness, not that Blue Cross discriminated against her as a housing provider — and because the claims were filed seven years after the 2014 events, well outside the applicable limitations periods.

brief_summary: Vinson sued on behalf of herself and her two minor daughters against their former landlord and property manager, alleging disability discrimination for denying over twenty requests to accommodate her autistic, deaf, and blind daughter Kaislee, and retaliation for evicting them after they made these requests. The court granted the motion to dismiss as to most of Vinson's individual claims as time-barred under the two-year FHA limitations period, but denied dismissal of the minor daughters' claims and the retaliation claims, finding sufficient temporal proximity and pretext allegations to survive dismissal.

accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was clearly articulated; plaintiff's complaint vaguely referenced air conditioner maintenance failures at his apartment, which the court characterized as possibly a state-law breach of contract claim rather than a cognizable FHA claim.
key_holding: The court granted all defendants' motions to dismiss because plaintiff's amended complaint failed to comply with the court's prior pleading order and failed to state a federal cause of action upon which relief could be granted.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Don Cash filed a largely indecipherable amended complaint against HUD, a property management company, and related defendants, vaguely invoking the Fair Housing Act, the Fourteenth Amendment, and the Civil Rights Act of 1964 in connection with alleged air conditioner maintenance failures at his apartment. The court had previously ordered plaintiff to file a compliant amended complaint with clear, specific allegations, but the amended pleading still failed to comply with Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 8(a), 8(d)(1), 10(b), and 11(b) and did not assert facts plausibly supporting any federal cause of action. All three motions to dismiss were granted, with the court noting plaintiff may have a viable state-court breach of contract claim.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Larry Arnold v. Elmington Property Management LLC
accommodation_description: Arnold requested a waiver of Elmington's policy not to accept housing choice vouchers so he could continue renting his apartment using his Section 8 voucher.
key_holding: The court denied Elmington's motion to dismiss Arnold's reasonable accommodation claim, finding Arnold's request that Elmington accept his Section 8 voucher facially reasonable and that Elmington had not demonstrated undue hardship at the pleading stage, emphasizing that the reasonableness inquiry is highly fact-specific and Elmington's motion was premature without discovery into specific hardships.
brief_summary: Larry Arnold, a disabled veteran with COPD, neuropathy, and heart disease who uses a Section 8 housing voucher, sued Elmington Property Management after it decided to no longer accept housing vouchers, effectively threatening his tenancy. The court denied Elmington's motion to dismiss Arnold's reasonable accommodation claim, finding Arnold adequately pleaded that his request for a voucher policy waiver was facially reasonable and that the undue hardship inquiry required discovery into Elmington's specific circumstances rather than a categorical rule.

case_name: Michael C. Threatt v. Sylacauga Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; plaintiff was an employee who claimed SHA retaliated against him for raising fair housing compliance issues.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on the FHA retaliation claim (Count Three) because plaintiff raised a good-faith, reasonable belief that SHA improperly designated Sylavon Court as elderly-only housing to the exclusion of families, which constitutes protected activity under the FHA's anti-retaliation provision.
brief_summary: Michael Threatt, former Executive Director of the Sylacauga Housing Authority, sued SHA and its commissioners alleging race discrimination, Title VII and FHA retaliation, False Claims Act retaliation, and Equal Protection violations. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on most claims but denied summary judgment on the FHA retaliation claim because Threatt raised a reasonable belief that SHA's elderly-only housing designation excluded families in violation of the Fair Housing Act.

case_name: Mueller v. Sylacauga Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs are former SHA executive officers who were fired after reporting alleged discriminatory housing practices and financial mismanagement to HUD and DOJ.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for SHA on the FHA retaliation claim because the plaintiffs failed to establish causation—they could not show the decision-maker (Royster) was aware of their protected complaints, and their cat's paw theory was unsupported by evidence showing Lozito's alleged financial motives were connected to retaliatory animus based on the plaintiffs' FHA-related reports.
brief_summary: Former executive officers of Sylacauga Housing Authority sued for retaliation under the FHA, alleging they were terminated after reporting discriminatory housing practices and financial mismanagement to HUD and DOJ. The court granted summary judgment for SHA, finding plaintiffs failed to establish causation because the decision-maker testified he was unaware of their complaints, and their cat's paw theory linking board influence to retaliatory animus was unsupported.

case_name: United States v. Hames
accommodation_description: This is a sexual harassment case alleging landlord demanded sexual favors from female tenants in exchange for housing and subjected them to unwelcome sexual contact, comments, and intrusions.
key_holding: The court granted the government's motion for partial summary judgment on vicarious liability but denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding the government's § 3614(a) pattern-or-practice claim is not time-barred and genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether the landlord engaged in a pattern of sexual harassment.
brief_summary: The United States brought a pattern-or-practice claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(a) against Randy Hames and Hames Marina, alleging the landlord sexually harassed female tenants by demanding sexual favors in exchange for rent and subjecting them to unwelcome sexual contact and intrusions. The court granted the government's motion for partial summary judgment on vicarious liability and denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding the government's claim was not time-barred and genuine disputes of material fact existed regarding the pattern-or-practice of discrimination.

case_name: Larry Arnold v. Elmington Property Management, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendant make an exception to its no-subsidy policy and continue accepting his Section 8 vouchers as an accommodation for his disabilities.
key_holding: Plaintiff's request for defendant to accept his Section 8 vouchers was facially reasonable under the low bar established in Schaw, and defendant failed to produce evidence demonstrating that granting the accommodation would impose an undue burden or fundamental alteration of its program.
brief_summary: Larry Arnold, a 72-year-old disabled veteran with COPD, neuropathy, and heart disease, sued Elmington Property Management after the company adopted a no-subsidy policy and refused his request for an exception to continue accepting his Section 8 vouchers as a reasonable accommodation for his disabilities. The court denied defendant's motion for summary judgment, finding that the accommodation request was facially reasonable under Schaw because Arnold was simply asking defendant to accept the same payment from a different source, and defendant failed to produce evidence of undue burden.
