source_file: 9642077_2021_Williams v. Tampa Bay Extended Stay Hotel_flmd
case_name: Brittany Williams v. Tampa Bay Extended Stay Hotel
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial discrimination during COVID-19 pandemic at extended stay hotel, but no specific accommodation request is described.
key_holding: The case was remanded to state court because removal statutes do not allow a plaintiff to remove her own case from state court, and the court lacked subject matter jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Brittany Williams sued Tampa Bay Extended Stay Hotel alleging racial discrimination during the COVID-19 pandemic under the Civil Rights Act and Fair Housing Act. The court granted remand because Williams improperly removed her own case from state court, as removal statutes permit only defendants to remove cases, and the court lacked subject matter jurisdiction.

case_name: Williams v. Aluna Largo
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was discriminatorily rejected as a rental applicant based on race, gender, nationality, and family status.
key_holding: The Court remanded the case to state court because removal was improper—only defendants may remove actions from state court, and plaintiff improperly removed her own case.
brief_summary: Brittany Williams sued Aluna Largo Apartments in federal court after removing her state court action, alleging she was discriminatorily rejected as a rental applicant based on race, gender, nationality, and family status in violation of federal civil rights laws. The Court remanded the case to state court for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because removal was improper—only defendants may remove an action from state court, and the plaintiff cannot remove her own case.

source_file: 9642893_2022_Suntree Master Homeowners Association, Inc. v. Frison_flmd
9643667_2022_Weekley Homes, LLC v. Board of County Commissioners_flmd

case_name: Mamberto Real v. Judith Moran, Frank Diaz Gines, and Presbyterian Homes & Housing Foundation of Florida, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request — case involves alleged discriminatory refusal to rent based on national origin (Cuban) and retaliation under § 3617.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint with prejudice as a shotgun pleading that failed to comply with Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, with plaintiff having had four prior opportunities to properly plead his national origin discrimination and retaliation claims.
brief_summary: Mamberto Real, a Cuban national origin individual, sued Presbyterian Homes and its employees alleging he was denied an apartment and subjected to ongoing delays as retaliation because of his national origin. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding Real's complaint was an impermissible shotgun pleading that failed to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them despite four prior opportunities to properly plead.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Office, 792 F.3d 1313 (11th Cir. 2015)
Boatman v. Town of Oakland, 76 F.3d 341 (11th Cir. 1996)
Philippeaux v. Apartment Inv. & Mgmt. Co., 598 F. App'x 640 (11th Cir. 2015)
Anderson v. District Bd. of Trustees of Cent. Fla. Cmty. Coll., 77 F.3d 364 (11th Cir. 1996)

case_name: James Nathaniel Douse v. Sabrina Traeger, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was made; plaintiff made vague references to discrimination under the Fair Housing Act without identifying a protected class or discriminatory conduct covered under the statute.
key_holding: Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims were dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because he failed to identify his membership in any protected class (race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, or national origin) and failed to describe any discriminatory conduct covered under the FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff James Douse sued his homeowners association and an employee over a disputed pool construction deposit and assessment charges, vaguely referencing the Fair Housing Act. The court dismissed the case for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding the FHA claims were wholly insubstantial because plaintiff failed to identify his membership in any protected class or allege discriminatory conduct covered under the statute.
key_cases_cited: Fountain v. Metro. Atlanta Rapid Trans. Auth., 688 F.2d 1038 (11th Cir. 1982)
Bell v. Hood, 327 U.S. 678 (1946)
Steel Co. v. Citizens for a Better Env't, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)

case_name: Marvin Lane and Shanita Lane v. Security National Mortgage Company, Tamara Perrin and Lisa Casanova
accommodation_description: Alleged racial discrimination during mortgage application process, including racially discriminatory remark and actions taken to delay and deter plaintiff due to race
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed for failure to state a plausible claim because plaintiffs failed to allege defendants knew of Shanita Lane's race, did not identify which FHA provisions were violated, provided no evidence of disparate treatment compared to other applicants, and failed to allege any cognizable injury.
brief_summary: Marvin and Shanita Lane sued Security National Mortgage Company and two employees alleging racial discrimination during their mortgage application process, claiming a racially discriminatory remark was made and improper actions were taken to delay and deter them due to race. The Court granted defendants' motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), finding plaintiffs failed to state a plausible Fair Housing Act claim because they did not adequately plead disparate treatment or any cognizable injury.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

source_file: 9645190_2023_Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc._flmd
case_name: Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Parisi requested a waiver of the Association's two-dog rule so that his emotional support dog Rokco (needed for depression and anxiety) could remain in the residence alongside co-plaintiff Clark's two pet dogs, totaling three dogs in the unit.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part plaintiffs' motion to strike affirmative defenses, striking the unclean hands (Third) and reasonableness-of-accommodation (Fourth) defenses as legally insufficient, while sustaining the Second Affirmative Defense because co-plaintiff Clark never requested a reasonable accommodation as required under the FHA.
brief_summary: Joseph Parisi, who relies on an emotional support dog (Rokco) for depression and anxiety, and co-resident Terry Clark, who owns two pet dogs, sued the Sabal Springs Homeowners Association under the FHA after the Association refused to waive its two-dog-per-unit rule to allow all three dogs to remain in the residence. The Amended Complaint asserted three counts: failure to reasonably accommodate (Count I), illegal intimidation and threats (Count II), and discriminatory terms and conditions of a dwelling (Count III). The court resolved plaintiffs' motion to strike five affirmative defenses, striking the Third (unclean hands) and Fourth (accommodation not reasonable) defenses while denying the motion as to the Second Defense because Clark—unlike Parisi—never made a request for accommodation.
key_cases_cited: Hawn v. Shoreline Towers Phase 1 Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 347 F. App'x 464 (11th Cir. 2009)
Loren v. Sasser, 309 F.3d 1296 (11th Cir. 2002)
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island, 544 F.3d 1201 (11th Cir. 2008)
Weiss v. 2100 Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 941 F. Supp. 2d 1337 (S.D. Fla. 2013)
Hunt v. Aimco Properties, L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)

source_file: 9645767_2023_Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc._flmd
case_name: Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Request that HOA waive its two-pet-dog rule to allow Parisi to reside with his assistance animal (Rokco) in the HOA-governed community.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion to strike the HOA's affirmative defense because the defense was in substance a denial rather than a true affirmative defense, and thus will be treated as a denial with particularity under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 9(c).
brief_summary: Joseph Parisi and Terry Clark sued Sabal Springs Homeowners Association under the Fair Housing Act, alleging the HOA discriminated by denying their request to waive the two-pet-dog rule so Parisi could keep his assistance animal. The court issued a procedural ruling denying plaintiffs' motion to strike the HOA's First Affirmative Defense, holding that the defense was actually a denial rather than a true affirmative defense and should be treated accordingly under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
key_cases_cited: Hunt v. Aimco Properties, L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Wright v. Southland Corp., 187 F.3d 1287 (11th Cir. 1999)
In re Rawson Food Serv., Inc., 846 F.2d 1343 (11th Cir. 1988)

case_name: David Wallace v. Carefree Shadowwood LLC
accommodation_description: Request to keep an emotional support animal (ESA dog named Zena) at the manufactured home community following a dog altercation incident.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss, holding that Mr. Wallace plausibly alleged Shadowwood made housing unavailable because of his disability by forcing him to choose between his home and his assistance animal, and that Shadowwood failed to conduct an individualized assessment before requiring Zena's removal.
brief_summary: David Wallace sued Carefree Shadowwood LLC, the owner of Bahia Vista Estates manufactured home community in Sarasota, Florida, alleging the housing provider violated the FHA by forcing him to choose between his home and his emotional support animal Zena after a dog altercation, and by failing to accommodate his disability-related need for the ESA. The court denied Shadowwood's motion to dismiss both claims, finding Wallace plausibly alleged that Shadowwood made housing unavailable because of his disability and improperly refused to consider his accommodation request without an individualized assessment.
key_cases_cited: Hunt v. Aimco Props., L.P., 814 F.3d 1213 (11th Cir. 2016)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Smith v. Powdrill, No. CV 12-06388 DDP RZX, 2013 WL 5786586 (C.D. Cal. 2013)
Friedel v. Park Place Cmty. LLC, 747 F. App'x 775 (11th Cir. 2018)

case_name: Brittany Williams v. Professional Marketing Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - The complaint does not clearly articulate a specific accommodation request; the FHA claim appears to be based on race discrimination rather than disability-related accommodation denial.
key_holding: The Court dismissed plaintiff's § 1983 claims because the private landlord was not a state actor and the claims were untimely under the four-year statute of limitations, and dismissed the FHA claim as untimely under the two-year limitations period in 42 U.S.C. § 3613(a)(1)(A).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Brittany Williams, a pretrial detainee, sued private landlord Professional Marketing Management, Inc. for evicting her in August 2018 after she fell behind on rent and allegedly attempted to pay three months late, asserting § 1983 constitutional claims and a Fair Housing Act claim. The Court dismissed all claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), finding the § 1983 claims failed because the private landlord did not act under color of state law and were untimely, and the FHA claim was time-barred under the two-year limitations period.
key_cases_cited: West v. Atkins, 487 U.S. 42 (1988)
Am. Mfrs. Mut. Ins. Co. v. Sullivan, 526 U.S. 40 (1999)
Chappell v. Rich, 340 F.3d 1279 (11th Cir. 2003)

source_file: 9646548_2023_Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc._flmd
case_name: Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for waiver of HOA Rule #11 limiting residences to two dogs and two household pets to allow plaintiff to keep his assistance animal dog named Rokco.
key_holding: The court granted the HOA's Rule 56(d) motion and deferred ruling on plaintiffs' summary judgment motion because discovery into plaintiff's disability status is necessary since disability is an essential element of the reasonable accommodation claim.
brief_summary: Joseph Parisi and Terry Clark, homeowners in a HOA community, sued the Sabal Springs Homeowners Association alleging the HOA violated the FHA by refusing to waive Rule #11's pet restrictions to accommodate Parisi's assistance animal. The court granted the HOA's Rule 56(d) motion to defer ruling on plaintiffs' summary judgment motion because discovery into whether Parisi has a qualifying disability has not been completed, and disability is an essential element of the reasonable accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Hawn v. Shoreline Towers Phase 1 Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 347 F. App'x 464 (11th Cir. 2009)
Loren v. Sasser, 309 F.3d 1296 (11th Cir. 2002)
Groner v. Golden Gate Gardens Apartments, 250 F.3d 1039 (6th Cir. 2001)
Snook v. Tr. Co. of Georgia Bank of Savannah, 859 F.2d 865 (11th Cir. 1988)
Burns v. Town of Palm Beach, 999 F.3d 1317 (11th Cir. 2021)

source_file: 9646692_2023_E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC v. Toll Bros., Inc._flmd
case_name: E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC v. Toll Bros., Inc.
accommodation_description: Indian business owner alleges defendant homebuilder refused to sell homes because of his Indian ethnicity.
key_holding: Court granted in part defendant's motion to compel, ordering plaintiff to produce documents responsive to Request No. 7 (communications between Trika and Johnson within past five years), but denied the motion to the extent it sought documents beyond the scope of that request.
brief_summary: Plaintiff E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC sued Toll Bros., Inc. alleging the homebuilder refused to sell homes to its Indian owner (Jeev Trika) because of his ethnicity, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The Court ruled on a discovery motion, granting in part defendant's motion to compel production of documents exchanged between Trika and sales agent Johnson, but denying relief as to documents beyond the scope of the propounded discovery request.

source_file: 9646737_2023_E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC v. Toll Bros., Inc._flmd
case_name: Jeev Trika and E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC v. Toll Bros., Inc.
accommodation_description: The underlying case alleges Toll Bros. refused to sell homes to plaintiff Jeev Trika because he is Indian (national origin discrimination). This order addresses a discovery motion to compel non-party witness compliance with a subpoena.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part the motion to compel, ordering non-party Johnson to comply with a second deposition (up to 3 hours) and produce documents, but denied sanctions, fees, costs, and contempt because Johnson was unrepresented, appeared under a reasonable belief about timing, and defendant had promised to accommodate her schedule.
brief_summary: Jeev Trika and E-Ventures Worldwide, LLC sued Toll Bros., Inc. alleging the homebuilder refused to sell them homes because Trika is Indian, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. This order resolves a discovery dispute, with the magistrate judge granting in part the motion to compel non-party witness Marjorie Johnson to comply with a subpoena (attending a second deposition and producing documents) but denying sanctions and fees because the circumstances did not warrant such sanctions.
key_cases_cited: Consumer Fin. Prot. Bureau v. Brown
Devaney v. Cont'l Am. Ins. Co.
Bailey Indus., Inc. v. CLJP, Inc.

case_name: City of Tampa ex rel. Bradley Toston v. D&M Assets 1 LLC
accommodation_description: Request to waive no-pets policy and pet deposit for a German Shepard service dog named Kai to assist with disabilities
key_holding: The federal FHA claims survived dismissal because it is not apparent from the face of the complaint that the statute of limitations has run, as the HUD complaint appears still pending providing tolling, while the local ordinance claims were dismissed as time-barred for lack of tolling provisions.
brief_summary: The City of Tampa sued D&M Assets 1 LLC and its owners on behalf of Bradley Toston, alleging they violated the FHA by refusing to waive their no-pets policy and pet deposit for his service dog. The court denied the motion to dismiss Counts I and II (federal FHA claims) because the statute of limitations question could not be resolved on the face of the complaint given the pending HUD proceeding, but granted dismissal of Counts III and IV (local ordinance claims) as time-barred due to the absence of tolling provisions.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Gonsalvez v. Celebrity Cruises Inc.
La Grasta v. First Union Sec.
Pielage v. McConnell

source_file: 9647011_2023_Parisi v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc._flmd
case_name: Joseph Parisi and Terry Clark v. Sabal Springs Homeowners Association Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that defendant accommodate their service animals, which defendant allegedly refused to do
key_holding: The court denied the motion to compel as moot (defendant had already provided discovery) but ordered defendant to pay plaintiffs' reasonable expenses incurred in bringing the motion under Rule 37(a)(5) because discovery was provided only after the motion was filed
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Joseph Parisi and Terry Clark sued their homeowners association under the Fair Housing Act, alleging the HOA refused to accommodate their service animals. The court resolved only plaintiffs' motion to compel discovery, finding that while the motion was moot because defendant had already provided the requested documents, defendant must nonetheless pay plaintiffs' reasonable expenses under Rule 37(a)(5) because the documents were produced only after the motion was filed.

source_file: 9647881_2023_Jones v. Tudor Cay Condominium Association, Inc._flmd
case_name: Jones v. Tudor Cay Condominium Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Tudor Cay failed to treat her fairly like other nonblack residents by not offering her a payment plan despite offering such plans to white and Hispanic owners who were delinquent on their dues.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state an FHA disparate treatment claim because it contains no factual allegations showing Tudor Cay had any role in offering payment plans to other residents or that any defendant acted with discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Terese E. Jones sued Tudor Cay Condominium Association and related entities alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on racial discrimination, claiming she was treated differently than white and Hispanic owners regarding payment plans for delinquent dues. The Court granted the motions to dismiss, finding the complaint was a shotgun pleading that failed to state an FHA claim because it contained no factual allegations establishing discriminatory intent or connecting Tudor Cay to any allegedly disparate treatment.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Tex. Dep't of Hous. and Cmty. Affs. v. Inclusive Cmtys. Project, Inc.
Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Off.
Schwarz v. City of Treasure Island

source_file: 9648267_2024_Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees_flmd
case_name: Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodation to keep his emotional support cat in his university dormitory room (already granted) and to take the cat outside his room into common areas of the dorm building. He also sought injunctive relief restoring access to his dorm room after defendants terminated his lease and changed his locks as a sanction for violating the policy restricting the animal to his room.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part plaintiff's emergency motion for a temporary restraining order, enjoining defendants from placing holds on plaintiff's academic records or preventing class registration, but denying all other requested injunctive relief — including relief related to housing — for failure to sufficiently demonstrate irreparable harm.
brief_summary: Daniel Frishberg, a USF student, brought a federal FHA suit alleging that defendants discriminated against him and retaliated by terminating his dorm lease and locking him out after he violated a policy restricting his emotional support cat to his room. He filed an emergency motion for a TRO, primarily seeking reinstatement to housing and the ability to register for classes before a January 12, 2024 deadline. The court partially granted the TRO only to prevent academic registration holds, finding that irreparable harm from missing the registration deadline outweighed minimal burden to defendants, while denying housing-related injunctive relief for failure to demonstrate sufficient irreparable harm.
key_cases_cited: Schiavo ex rel. Schindler v. Schiavo, 403 F.3d 1223 (11th Cir. 2005)

source_file: 9649187_2024_Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees_flmd
case_name: Daniel A. Frishberg v. University of South Florida Board of Trustees
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to keep his emotional support cat in common areas of the dorm building beyond his room.
key_holding: The court dismissed all FHA claims against USF Board of Trustees on Eleventh Amendment immunity grounds because the university is an arm of the state and neither the FHA nor FFHA contains a waiver of sovereign immunity for state entities.
brief_summary: Daniel Frishberg, a USF student, sued the University of South Florida Board of Trustees and its dormitory operator after being sanctioned, locked out, and having his lease terminated for allowing his emotional support cat outside of his dorm room. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing all FHA claims on Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity grounds because USF Board is an arm of the state and Congress did not abrogate state sovereign immunity in the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
University of South Fla. Bd. of Trustees v. CoMentis, Inc.

source_file: 9649579_2024_Warner v. School Board of Hillsborough County, Florida_flmd
case_name: Warner v. School Board of Hillsborough County, Florida
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; Warner alleged FHA claims related to school enrollment and housing proximity, which the court found too remote from housing to support FHA liability.
key_holding: The School Board's conduct in school enrollment and choice decisions is 'too remote' from housing to support Fair Housing Act claims, as the School Board lacks direct control over housing availability and Warner established no causal link to housing discrimination.
brief_summary: Blake Warner, proceeding pro se, sued the Hillsborough County School Board alleging Fair Housing Act claims related to his inability to enroll his child at a preferred school through school choice, along with equal protection and due process claims. The court adopted the magistrate judge's report, dismissing the FHA claims with prejudice because the School Board's decisions regarding school enrollment were too remote from housing to support FHA liability and Warner failed to establish any causal link between the Board's conduct and housing discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Bank of America Corp. v. City of Miami, Florida, 581 U.S. 189 (2017)
Stevenson v. Blytheville Sch. Dist. #5, 800 F.3d 955 (8th Cir. 2015)
Adkisson v. Blytheville Sch. Dist. No. 5, 2014 WL 6819729 (E.D. Ark. 2014)

case_name: Deborah Engle v. Royal Bahamian Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to use other areas of the condominium for her service dog, waiver of the pet fee, and access accommodations to the rear grounds due to mobility limitations from late-stage breast cancer
key_holding: The court denied RBA's motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel because RBA failed to show that prior representation was substantially related to the current FHA case or that counsel could use confidential information to RBA's disadvantage
brief_summary: Deborah Engle, a condominium owner with mobility disabilities from late-stage breast cancer, sued Royal Bahamian Association alleging failure to accommodate her service dog and retaliation. The court denied RBA's motion to disqualify plaintiff's counsel, finding RBA failed to meet its burden to show prior representation was substantially related to the current litigation or that counsel gained confidential information that could disadvantage RBA.
key_cases_cited: Woods v. Covington Cnty. Bank, 537 F.2d 804 (5th Cir. 1976)
In re BellSouth Corp., 334 F.3d 941 (11th Cir. 2003)
Herrmann v. GutterGuard, Inc., 199 F. App'x 745 (11th Cir. 2006)
Armor Screen Corp. v. Storm Catcher, Inc., 709 F. Supp. 2d 1309 (S.D. Fla. 2010)

source_file: 9652152_2021_Quality of Life, Corp. v. The City of Margate_flsd
case_name: Quality of Life, Corp. and MMJ Financial Services, Inc. v. The City of Margate
accommodation_description: This order concerns attorneys' fees and costs following summary judgment and appeal in an underlying case involving ADA and FHA claims; the accommodation request at issue in the underlying case is not described in this fee-motion order.
key_holding: The court denied the City of Margate's motions for attorneys' fees and appellate attorneys' fees because plaintiffs' claims were not frivolous, unreasonable, or without foundation, despite the grant of summary judgment in defendant's favor.
brief_summary: Quality of Life, Corp. and MMJ Financial Services, Inc. sued the City of Margate under the ADA and FHA; after summary judgment for the City and an unsuccessful appeal, the City moved for attorneys' fees and costs as a prevailing defendant. The court adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation to deny the fee motions but grant $23,458.04 in taxable costs, finding the plaintiffs' claims were not frivolous despite the adverse outcome.
key_cases_cited: Christiansburg Garment Co. v. Equal Emp. Opportunity Comm'n, 434 U.S. 412 (1978)
Bruce v. City of Gainesville, Ga., 177 F.3d 949 (11th Cir. 1999)
Sullivan v. Sch. Bd. of Pinellas Cnty., 773 F.2d 1182 (11th Cir. 1985)
Baker v. Alderman, 158 F.3d 516 (11th Cir. 1998)
Thomas v. Arn, 474 U.S. 140 (1985)

case_name: Elgin Hilliard, Sr. v. Rene Gutierrez
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; plaintiff brings false arrest and Fourth/Fourteenth Amendment civil rights claims arising from a 2016 arrest at the Hialeah Housing Authority office.
key_holding: The court granted Officer Gutierrez's motion to dismiss based on res judicata, finding that plaintiff's false arrest and constitutional violation claims were barred because they arose from the same nucleus of operative facts as claims in Hilliard I, involved parties in privity (employer-employee relationship), and could have been litigated in the prior action where final judgment on the merits was entered.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Elgin Hilliard, Sr. filed suit against Officer Rene Gutierrez asserting false arrest and § 1983 Fourth/Fourteenth Amendment claims arising from his May 17, 2016 arrest at the Hialeah Housing Authority. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding that plaintiff's claims were barred by res judicata because they arose from the same operative facts as claims in Hilliard I, defendant was in privity with HHA (his employer), and the claims could have been raised and were actually adjudicated in the prior action where final judgment was entered on the merits.

source_file: 9653018_2021_LaGrasso v. Seven Bridges Homeowners Association Inc_flsd
case_name: LaGrasso v. Seven Bridges Homeowners Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege the HOA discriminated against them based on their Christian/non-Jewish religious status through disparate treatment including fines, suspensions, and selective enforcement of community rules.
key_holding: The court grants in part and denies in part the motion in limine, excluding news articles about the litigation but allowing evidence related to the tennis court incident, Facebook posts, fines, and recordings to support Plaintiffs' disparate treatment religious discrimination claim at trial.
brief_summary: Jeffrey and Deborah LaGrasso sued Seven Bridges Homeowners Association alleging religious discrimination, claiming the HOA treated them disparately due to their Christian/non-Jewish status through fines, suspensions, and selective enforcement. The court denied most of the HOA's motion in limine to exclude evidence, allowing Plaintiffs to present circumstantial evidence of discrimination at trial while excluding news articles as inadmissible hearsay.
key_cases_cited: Smith v. Lockheed-Martin Corp., 644 F.3d 1321 (11th Cir. 2011)
Luce v. United States, 469 U.S. 38 (1984)

case_name: Rita Fox v. Dana James Gaines et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request at issue; case involves sexual harassment (quid pro quo and hostile housing environment) by landlord against tenant.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine issues of material fact exist on plaintiff's quid pro quo harassment, hostile housing environment, retaliation, and interference claims under the FHA.
brief_summary: Rita Fox sued her landlords Dana James Gaines and Lucille Gaines for sexual harassment and discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, alleging quid pro quo harassment and a hostile housing environment created by the landlord's sexual demands. The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact on all claims regarding whether sexual favors were conditioning on continued tenancy and whether defendant's post-relationship eviction proceedings constituted unlawful discrimination and retaliation.
key_cases_cited: Fox v. Gaines, 4 F.4th 1293 (11th Cir. 2021)
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973)
Quigg v. Thomas County Sch. Dist., 814 F.3d 1227 (11th Cir. 2016)

source_file: 9654135_2022_Gundogdu v. WDF-4 Wood Harbor Park Owner, LLC_flsd
case_name: Rengin Gundogdu v. WDF-4 Wood Harbor Park Owner, LLC
accommodation_description: The court never substantively analyzed any specific accommodation request; the complaint mentioned Fair Housing Act claims in passing but the case was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction before reaching the merits.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to dismiss and remanded the case because it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over the removed state-court eviction case, and alternatively would have abstained under Colorado River even if original jurisdiction existed.
brief_summary: Rengin Gundogdu, a pro se tenant facing eviction from a Broward County rental property, attempted to remove the consolidated state-court eviction case to federal court, raising Fair Housing Act and CARES Act claims. The Southern District of Florida granted the Defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction because Gundogdu improperly attempted to remove her own counterclaims rather than a complaint establishing federal jurisdiction, and alternatively would have abstained under Colorado River given the advanced state of the parallel state proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Caterpillar Inc. v. Williams, 482 U.S. 386 (1987)
Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. United States, 424 U.S. 800 (1976)
Younger v. Harris, 401 U.S. 37 (1971)

case_name: Eddy J. Philippeaux v. Miami Apartments Investors, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges he was retaliatorily evicted from his apartment in violation of the Fair Housing Act and Americans with Disabilities Act.
key_holding: The court dismissed Count I (ADA claim) with prejudice because the private residential apartment unit is not a place of public accommodation where Title III of the ADA applies, and dismissed Count II (FHA retaliation claim) without prejudice as the opinion contains no substantive analysis of the claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eddy J. Philippeaux, proceeding pro se, sued Miami Apartment Investors LLC, Baron Residential Management, and Sharon Fothergill alleging they retaliatorily evicted him in violation of the ADA, FHA, and civil rights statutes. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss Count I with prejudice, finding that a private residential apartment is not a place of public accommodation under the ADA, and dismissed Count II (FHA retaliation) without prejudice and Count III (§ 1981 and § 1985 conspiracy claims) with leave to amend for failure to state plausible claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Griffin v. Breckenridge, 403 U.S. 88 (1971)
Bailey v. Bd. of Cnty. Com'rs of Alachua Cnty., Fla., 956 F.2d 1112 (11th Cir. 1992)
Dean v. Warren, 12 F.4th 1248 (11th Cir. 2021)

case_name: Eddy J. Philippeaux v. Miami Apartments Investors, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled veteran, alleges landlord retaliated against him by evicting him and refusing to renew his lease after he filed prior ADA and FHA complaints.
key_holding: The court dismissed Counts I, III, IV, and V with prejudice, finding that plaintiff failed to adequately plead claims for ADA retaliation, § 1981 race discrimination, § 1985 conspiracy, intentional infliction of emotional distress, and negligent infliction of emotional distress, leaving only the FHA retaliation claim under § 3617 to proceed.
brief_summary: Eddy J. Philippeaux, a pro se disabled veteran tenant, sued Miami Apartments Investors and related defendants alleging retaliation under the ADA and FHA, race discrimination under §§ 1981 and 1985, and state law emotional distress claims after they evicted him and declined to renew his lease following his prior fair housing lawsuit. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss with prejudice on all claims except the FHA retaliation claim under § 3617, finding plaintiff failed to adequately plead race-based but-for causation, conspiracy, or viable emotional distress claims.

case_name: David Webb v. Miami-Dade County Government, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a homeless disabled individual, alleges discrimination by a shelter operator and county entities but does not articulate a specific accommodation request before the case was dismissed on procedural grounds.
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint as a shotgun pleading that failed to comply with Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 8 and 10, without reaching the merits of any FHA or ADA claims.
brief_summary: David Webb, a homeless Miami-Dade County resident with a heart disability, sued Camillus House, Miami-Dade County Government, and various officials alleging they violated his ADA, FHA, and constitutional rights by discharging him to the streets. The court denied his in forma pauperis motion and dismissed the complaint as a shotgun pleading that failed to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them or comply with Rule 10(b) requirements.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Chalissa Olivera Truesdale v. Venice Arms, Inc.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request at issue; case involves allegations of racial discrimination in cooperative housing rules enforcement
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because the amended complaint was a shotgun pleading failing to identify specific statutory provisions, and even interpreting the claims charitably, section 3604 claims failed as they apply only to buying/selling/leasing transactions (not cooperative rule enforcement against existing owners) while section 3617 claims required allegations of conduct severe or pervasive enough to be threatening or violent.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Chalissa Olivera Truesdale, a Hispanic woman and member of a 55-and-over housing cooperative, sued Venice Arms, Inc. alleging the Swedish-dominated cooperative association engaged in racially discriminatory housing practices including enforcement of no-renter rules, guest policies, and association with a racist board motion to exclude minorities. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss with leave to amend, finding the complaint was a shotgun pleading that failed to state viable FHA claims because section 3604 applies only to housing transactions and the section 3617 claim lacked allegations of severe or violent discriminatory conduct required to state a claim.

case_name: Eli Portnoy v. MEI Condominium Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodation to communicate with someone other than the Board President regarding residency business due to stress-related disability.
key_holding: The court denied the individual board member's motion to dismiss, finding that Florida state immunity statutes cannot bar federal FHA claims and that plaintiff adequately alleged individual liability against the board president for her personal involvement in discriminatory acts.
brief_summary: Eli Portnoy, a disabled condominium resident, sued MEI Condominium Association and its Board President Anna Strickstein-Zandman alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act, including failure to reasonably accommodate his request to communicate with someone other than the Board President due to his stress-related disability. The court denied the individual board member's motion to dismiss, rejecting her claims of immunity under Florida state statutes and finding that Portnoy adequately pleaded individual liability under the FHA for her personal involvement in discriminatory acts.

case_name: Eddy J. Philippeaux v. Miami Apartments Investors, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges retaliation through lease non-renewal after filing a prior lawsuit claiming disability discrimination, including requests for parking accommodations.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on the FHA retaliation claim because plaintiff failed to establish a causal link between filing the lawsuit and the lease non-renewal, as the approximately one-year gap between these events is insufficient under Eleventh Circuit precedent, and plaintiff failed to demonstrate that defendants' proffered legitimate reasons for non-renewal (resident complaints and disruptive behavior) were pretextual.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Eddy Philippeaux sued Miami Apartments Investors, LLC and Baron Residential Management alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by declining to renew his lease in retaliation for filing a previous lawsuit alleging disability discrimination. The court granted defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding that the approximately one-year gap between the lawsuit and non-renewal was insufficient to establish causation under controlling precedent, and plaintiff failed to rebut defendants' legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for non-renewal based on resident complaints about his disruptive behavior.
key_cases_cited: McCall v. Owens

case_name: Hannah Gorman v. Breeze Condominium Association, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for an emotional support dog for Mr. Tomlinson (a person with a disability) to ameliorate the effects of his disability, which was denied based on the dog's size and breed.
key_holding: Plaintiff, as a person associated with a disabled individual under § 3604(f), has standing to bring FHA claims including failure to accommodate; the complaint adequately alleges that Mr. Tomlinson is disabled, requested an ESA accommodation, and was denied, and that plaintiff suffered adverse actions causally connected to protected activity.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Hannah Gorman sued Breeze Condominium Association, its property management company Nautica Management, and property manager Richard Muller, alleging they denied her companion's request for an emotional support animal, refused to renew her lease, and denied approval of a second rental unit in retaliation for filing a HUD complaint. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss all counts, finding that Gorman, as a person associated with a disabled individual, has standing to assert FHA claims and that she adequately pled a failure to accommodate, retaliation, and interference with housing rights.

source_file: 9657400_2021_WODA COOPER DEVELOPMENT INC v. CITY OF WARNER ROBINS GEORGIA_gamd
case_name: Woda Cooper Development, Inc. et al. v. City of Warner Robins et al.
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; plaintiffs are developers challenging the City's refusal to permit an affordable housing development, alleging discriminatory intent based on race.
key_holding: The disparate treatment claim survives because the City enthusiastically solicited the affordable housing development then abruptly reversed course when faced with political opposition, and the sequence of events plausibly alleges intentional racial discrimination; however, the disparate impact claim fails because plaintiffs only allege a one-time decision rather than a policy causing disparate impact.
brief_summary: Woda Cooper Development sued the City of Warner Robins, Mayor Randy Toms, and the Development Authority after the City reneged on agreements to allow an affordable housing development at Perkins Field, allegedly due to racial animus against the African American residents who would occupy the housing. The court dismissed the Development Authority entirely, dismissed the disparate impact and Contract Clause claims, but allowed the disparate treatment claim to proceed based on the City's unusual sequence of enthusiastically soliciting then abruptly blocking the development in response to political pressure.

accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The Court denied plaintiff's motion for appointment of counsel, finding no exceptional circumstances, and deferred ruling on plaintiff's renewed summary judgment motion pending completion of discovery.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quincy Bernard Jones sued Featherstone Homeowners Association alleging Fair Housing Act failure-to-accommodate claims. case_name: Adonis Berle Whitby v. Macon-Bibb County, Georgia; Mayor Lester Miller; The Board of Commissioners; Henry C. Ficklin; Doctor Keith Moffett; Director Charles Brooks; and Director Tim Wilder
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requests that the county clear, establish right of way, repair, and maintain a 500-foot portion of road in Lizella, Georgia, claiming discriminatory denial of road maintenance services based on residents' race and other protected characteristics.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss based on res judicata, holding that Plaintiff's discrimination claims (including FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Fourteenth Amendment claims) were barred because they could have been raised in a prior state court suit seeking the same relief—court-ordered road maintenance.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Adonis Berle Whitby, an African American resident, sued Macon-Bibb County, Georgia and various officials under the Fair Housing Act, Fourteenth Amendment, and other statutes, alleging that the county's failure to fully maintain a road in Lizella constitutes racial discrimination against African American homeowners. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss on res judicata grounds, finding that Plaintiff's discrimination claims were barred because he previously sued in state court for the same relief—road maintenance—and could have raised these theories there but failed to do so.

case_name: Quincy Bernard Jones v. Featherstone Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - This order does not address the substantive accommodation request; it addresses procedural discovery matters only.
key_holding: The court denied Jones's motion to strike his deposition and motion to compel, finding no constitutional violation: Jones has no right to appointed counsel in civil cases, and his deposition was voluntary after the court properly advised him of his obligations.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quincy Bernard Jones sued Featherstone Homeowners Association alleging Fair Housing Act failure-to-accommodate claims; this order denies Jones's motion to strike his deposition and motion to compel production of letters, finding no constitutional violation in the deposition procedures and that Jones can review his transcript under Rule 30(e).
key_cases_cited: Wahl v. McIver, 773 F.2d 1169 (11th Cir. 1985)

case_name: Quincy Bernard Jones v. Featherstone Homeowners Association
accommodation_description: Request for installation of railings on the retaining wall in front of his duplex unit to address fear of falling while playing catch with relatives
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendant because plaintiff failed to establish he had a qualifying disability under the FHA, the requested retaining wall railings were neither reasonable nor necessary, and plaintiff refused to pay for the modification as required under § 3604(f)(3)(A).
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quincy Jones sued Featherstone Homeowners Association alleging failure to accommodate or modify under the FHA by refusing to install railings on a retaining wall, claiming his paranoia and schizophrenia made him fear falling while playing catch with relatives. The court granted summary judgment for the HOA, finding that Jones failed to establish a qualifying disability, the requested modification was not reasonable or necessary, and Jones refused to pay for the modification as required under § 3604(f)(3)(A).

case_name: Woda Cooper Development, Inc. v. City of Warner Robins
accommodation_description: Affordable housing developers allege the City rescinded support for a LIHTC-funded affordable housing development in retaliation for exercising FHA rights.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' disparate treatment claim because affordable housing developers cannot establish they were discriminated against 'because of' their race, but found genuine issues of material fact exist on the retaliation claim because defense counsel's threats of criminal prosecution and LIHTC revocation during litigation constituted adverse action taken in response to plaintiffs' pursuit of FHA claims.
brief_summary: Affordable housing developers sued the City of Warner Robins, Georgia alleging the City violated the FHA by rescinding support for a downtown affordable housing development (disparate treatment) and by making threatening statements during litigation in retaliation for pursuing FHA claims. The court granted summary judgment for the City on the disparate treatment claim, finding plaintiffs failed to establish intentional discrimination based on race, but denied summary judgment on the retaliation claim, finding genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether defense counsel's threats of criminal prosecution and LIHTC revocation constituted unlawful retaliation.

case_name: Tracy A. Miller v. Georgia Department of Community Supervision, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges his assignment to Bostick Nursing Center as discriminatory, arguing the Board made housing unavailable by not placing him in his preferred location.
key_holding: The Board did not discriminate against plaintiff under the FHA because it considered his disability and assigned him to Bostick specifically to accommodate his needs as an elderly, disabled parolee; the Board could not have placed him elsewhere because his parole application lacked that information.
brief_summary: Tracy A. Miller, a paraplegic parolee, sued the Georgia Board of Pardons and Paroles and Bostick Nursing Center officials under § 1983, the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and FHA, alleging disability discrimination in his placement at a nursing facility for parolees. The court found that because the Board assigned plaintiff to Bostick specifically to accommodate his disability-related needs rather than to exclude him from housing, and because his preferred housing information was not included in his parole application, plaintiff failed to state a viable disability discrimination or FHA claim.

case_name: Jean Paraison v. Nationstar Mortgage, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges race-based discrimination in a real estate transaction, claiming defendant attempted to discourage him from completing the purchase because he is African American with an accent
key_holding: The court dismissed Paraison's Fair Housing Act discrimination claim because his allegations were conclusory and speculative, failing to meet the Twombly/Iqbal pleading standard; the complaint did not allege sufficient facts to support a reasonable inference that Nationstar discriminated against him based on race.
brief_summary: Jean Paraison, an African American man, sued Nationstar Mortgage LLC alleging race-based discrimination under the Fair Housing Act after he claims the defendant's agent tried to discourage him from completing a real estate purchase by telling him to 'back out of the deal' and that he would lose money. The court granted Nationstar's motion to dismiss, finding Paraison's discrimination allegations were conclusory and failed to plausibly allege that race played a role in the defendant's conduct, as required by the pleading standards established in Twombly and Iqbal.

source_file: 9660196_2022_Fulton County, Georgia v. Wells Fargo _ Co._gand
case_name: Fulton County, Georgia v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request - case involves claims of discriminatory predatory lending and equity stripping targeting minority borrowers
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss on statute of limitations grounds but permitted plaintiffs to amend, while finding that plaintiffs adequately pled proximate cause for property tax injuries and statistical disparities to survive disparate impact claims.
brief_summary: Three Georgia counties (Fulton, DeKalb, and Cobb) sued Wells Fargo alleging a predatory lending scheme that targeted minority borrowers through discriminatory mortgage origination, servicing, and foreclosure practices in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss on statute of limitations grounds but allowed plaintiffs to file an amended complaint, while denying dismissal of plaintiffs' disparate impact claims after finding adequate statistical allegations and proximate cause for certain property-related injuries.

case_name: Charles Becoat II v. PNC Bank, National Association
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; plaintiff sought to assume his deceased mother's existing PNC mortgage loan and obtain a loan modification, temporary payment plan, or forbearance from PNC Bank after inheriting the Chicago property subject to the mortgage.
key_holding: The court granted PNC Bank's motion to dismiss plaintiff's FHA and civil rights claims with prejudice because plaintiff failed to allege any facts connecting PNC's denial of mortgage assumption to his race, and failed to identify any legal duty obligating PNC to allow him to assume his deceased mother's mortgage or provide loss mitigation options.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Charles Becoat II sued PNC Bank after it refused to allow him to assume his deceased mother's mortgage loan or provide loan modification or forbearance options following her death. Becoat alleged, among other things, that PNC violated the Fair Housing Act by engaging in practices targeting African Americans, but he offered no facts connecting PNC's denial to his race or showing PNC was even aware of his race. The court dismissed the federal civil rights claims with prejudice for failure to state a claim and declined to exercise supplemental or diversity jurisdiction over the remaining state-law claims.

case_name: Price v. Howard
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges landlord required her Black partner to undergo a background check and pay a $50 fee as a condition of leasing, based on discriminatory racial animus.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state a plausible claim for disparate treatment under the FHA because she did not allege any facts suggesting she was actually treated differently than similarly situated White prospective applicants, and her conclusory 'information and belief' allegations about Howard's treatment of White tenants lacked factual support.
brief_summary: Katie Price, a Black woman, sued her landlord Michael Howard alleging race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1981, claiming Howard required her Black partner to undergo a racially-motivated background check and pay a fee as a condition of leasing. The court granted Howard's motion to dismiss, finding Price's complaint consisted entirely of conclusory allegations that failed to plausibly allege disparate treatment because she did not plead any facts showing she was treated differently than similarly situated White prospective tenants.

case_name: Katia Price v. Michael Howard
accommodation_description: No accommodation request — the case involves a landlord's requirement that the Black plaintiff's partner submit to a background check and pay a fee, allegedly not imposed on similarly situated White tenants.
key_holding: The court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss, finding that the plaintiff adequately alleged disparate treatment by pleading sufficient facts showing she was treated differently than a similarly situated White tenant regarding the landlord's visitor background check requirement.
brief_summary: Katia Price, a Black woman, sued landlord Michael Howard alleging race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1981 after Howard required her partner to undergo a background check and pay a fee to lease his property. The court denied Howard's motion to dismiss, finding Price adequately alleged disparate treatment by providing sufficient facts supporting her belief that similarly situated White tenants were not subjected to the same background check requirements.

case_name: Jason Scutt v. Kelli Dorris, Xiayin (Gaoquiang) Lin, and Charlene Chen
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves claims of harassment based on transgender status and Jewish religion, and landlords' failure to prevent hostile housing environment.
key_holding: Dorris's claim dismissed because she is merely a co-tenant without agency authority over landlords; but claims against Lin and Chen may proceed for hostile housing environment under § 3617 because plaintiff adequately alleged Dorris harassed her based on sex/religion, harassment was severe or pervasive, and landlords knew of but failed to remedy the harassment.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jason Scutt sued his former landlords and co-tenant alleging they discriminated against him based on his transgender status and Jewish religion, and that landlords failed to prevent a hostile housing environment created by co-tenant Dorris. The court dismissed the claim against Dorris because she was merely a co-tenant without agency authority over the landlords, but allowed the hostile housing environment claims against the landlords to proceed because plaintiff adequately pled Dorris harassed him because of protected characteristics, the harassment was severe or pervasive, and landlords knew of but failed to remedy it.

key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish that defendant Ouansafi knew or should have known about the alleged harassment by other tenants or that he personally participated in or ratified the alleged retaliation, and mere supervisory authority is insufficient for individual liability under the FHA.
brief_summary: Tangee Renee Lazarus, a Black woman residing in public housing administered by the Hawaii Public Housing Authority, sued Executive Director Hakim Ouansafi and other HPHA employees alleging Fair Housing Act claims for hostile housing environment based on race and retaliation. The court granted Ouansafi's motion for summary judgment, finding plaintiff failed to provide evidence that Ouansafi knew of or personally participated in the alleged harassment or retaliation, and that mere supervisory authority is insufficient for individual FHA liability.

accommodation_description: In Spring 2016, a family residing at the Greenfield Apartment complex complained to the Council that defendants would not grant a reasonable accommodation for a parking permit; this incident was ultimately found to be outside the statute of limitations.
key_holding: The court partially granted and partially denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, allowing the FHA claims to proceed only for three timely incidents — racial steering in October 2018, discriminatory parking enforcement in summer 2020, and national origin discrimination against an Iraqi American tenant in summer 2021 — while barring all earlier incidents as time-barred and rejecting application of the continuing violations doctrine.
brief_summary: Intermountain Fair Housing Council sued Tomlinson & Associates and related defendants for FHA violations at two Boise apartment complexes, alleging racial steering, discriminatory enforcement of parking rules, and various other acts of discrimination against Black/African and Iraqi American tenants spanning 2015–2021. The court held that the vast majority of alleged incidents were outside the applicable statute of limitations and that the continuing violations doctrine of Havens Realty did not save them, because the plaintiff failed to identify a single, specific discriminatory practice occurring continuously into the limitations period. The court allowed three timely claims to proceed to trial, denied summary judgment on the negligence claim, and dismissed several entity defendants and one individual defendant.

brief_summary: Cook County brought a Fair Housing Act suit against Wells Fargo alleging discriminatory lending practices against minority borrowers. This opinion addresses a motion to compel production of consulting agreements between Wells Fargo and two former high-level County employees (former CFO Thomas Glaser and former Comptroller John Chambers), whom Wells Fargo had retained as consulting experts. The court granted the motion to compel on two independent grounds—Rule 26(b)(4)(D) applies only to interrogatories and depositions, not requests for production, and the County sought the agreements themselves rather than facts or opinions held by the experts—and also resolved multiple additional discovery disputes concerning document production scope, privilege, and cost-of-damages materials.

brief_summary: This case arises from a 21-year-old consent decree resolving Fair Housing Act claims brought by the Cabrini-Green Local Advisory Council against the Chicago Housing Authority, which had alleged that redevelopment of Cabrini-Green would displace residents and have a discriminatory impact on African Americans, women, and children. Following extensive settlement negotiations supervised by a magistrate judge, the court approved the resulting settlement over the objection of non-party Carol Steele and the CDC, holding that the LAC Board had properly recused conflicted directors with dual board membership and that the remaining directors had valid authority to approve the settlement.

key_holding: The court denied Wells Fargo's Rule 12(b)(1) motion to dismiss for lack of Article III standing, holding that even if the County's financial gains from Wells Fargo-related foreclosures exceeded its losses (Y ≥ X), Cook County retains standing so long as it suffered some concrete financial injury (X > 0), because injury-in-fact and recoverable damages are legally distinct concepts.
brief_summary: Cook County sued Wells Fargo under the Fair Housing Act alleging that discriminatory lending practices caused a disproportionate number of foreclosures in the county, resulting in concrete financial harm including increased sheriff, police, judicial, and infrastructure costs. Wells Fargo moved mid-discovery to dismiss for lack of Article III standing, arguing that evidence showed the County actually netted a financial benefit from the foreclosure boom. The court denied the motion, explaining that Wells Fargo conflated the merits question of net damages (X – Y) with the threshold standing question of whether any injury occurred at all (X > 0), and that Wells Fargo made no attempt to show X equaled zero.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges landlord retaliated against him for reporting housing code violations to the health department by calling him racial slurs and attempting to evict him
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state a retaliation claim under § 3617 because reporting housing code violations to a health department is not a protected activity under the Fair Housing Act; plaintiff's allegations about being called racial slurs do not save the claim because retaliation focuses on what the plaintiff did, not who he is.
brief_summary: Richard Johnson, a white tenant, sued his landlord Barry Flannery alleging retaliation under the Fair Housing Act for reporting building code and health violations to a government agency. accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Defendants violated § 3617 by using unlawful eviction proceedings aided by the state court judicial system to threaten, intimidate, and coerce him into remortgaging or leaving his property; no specific reasonable accommodation request is identified.
key_holding: The court lacks subject matter jurisdiction under the Rooker-Feldman doctrine because Satterfield's alleged injuries—loss of his home, failure to maintain the property, and failure to pay property taxes—were completed only when the state court ordered eviction, making his FHA claim not independent of the state court judgment; moreover, Satterfield had a reasonable opportunity to raise his FHA claims as equitable defenses in the state court eviction proceedings.
brief_summary: Nathaniel Satterfield sued HSBC Bank USA, N.A. and related defendants alleging they wrongfully obtained possession of his home through meritless state court eviction proceedings and violated the Fair Housing Act by intimidating him using the threat of unlawful eviction. case_name: Andy Hope Williams, Jr., and Vonita Cruz v. Heartland Realty Investors, Inc., Heartland Willowbrook, LLC, d/b/a Willowbrook Apartment Homes, and Starr, Bejgiert, Zink, and Rowells
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs Andy Williams and Vonita Cruz, proceeding pro se, brought Fair Housing Act claims against Heartland landlords and FDCPA claims against Heartland's law firm SBZR; the FHA claims are not substantively analyzed in this ruling dismissing only the FDCPA claims against SBZR.
key_holding: The Court granted SBZR's motion to dismiss the FDCPA claims because SBZR did not make actionable misrepresentations: Heartland Realty Investors, Inc. had authority to bring the eviction as agent for Heartland Willowbrook, LLC, the lease permitted attorney's fees for the prevailing party, the federal lawsuit did not constitute a pending eviction proceeding under Illinois law, and SBZR properly attached the required demand notice to the eviction complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se tenants Andy Williams and Vonita Cruz sued their landlord Heartland Realty Investors and its law firm SBZR, alleging Fair Housing Act violations against the landlord and FDCPA violations against the law firm for misrepresentations in a state court eviction proceeding. The Court granted SBZR's motion to dismiss the FDCPA claims because SBZR did not violate the FDCPA—Heartland Realty had authority to pursue eviction as the landlord's agent, the lease permitted attorney's fees, and SBZR attached all required documents to the eviction complaint.

case_name: Andy Hope Williams, Jr. v. Heartland Realty Investors, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request—case involves alleged selective enforcement of lease rules (grill prohibition) based on plaintiffs' race and national origin.
key_holding: Plaintiffs adequately stated FHA and § 1981 claims by alleging they were the only Hebrew Israelite and Puerto Rican family in the apartment complex and were selectively targeted with grill enforcement while other tenants were permitted to use grills.
brief_summary: Black and Puerto Rican tenants sued their private apartment complex alleging race and national origin discrimination when the landlord selectively enforced a grill prohibition against them while allowing other tenants to use grills, then refused to renew their lease. The court denied the motion to dismiss plaintiffs' FHA disparate treatment, interference, and § 1981 claims, finding sufficient allegations of selective enforcement based on protected characteristics.

source_file: 9681431_2022_Talley v. The Housing Authority of Cook County_ilnd
case_name: Charles Talley, Jr. and Christopher J. Bonds v. The Housing Authority of Cook County, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested a voucher for a two-bedroom dwelling and moving papers to transfer to accessible housing as a reasonable accommodation for their disabilities.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' failure-to-accommodate claims because plaintiffs never formally requested repairs as an accommodation, and the Housing Authority did not have authority to compel landlords to make repairs; additionally, the Housing Authority approved the voucher request and exhibits show it issued the moving papers, defeating the claim that plaintiffs were denied the requested accommodation.
brief_summary: Two Black disabled tenants using Section 8 Housing Choice Vouchers sued their landlord and the Housing Authority of Cook County for disability discrimination (failure to accommodate) and race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act. The district court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing all federal claims with prejudice, finding that plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege failure-to-accommodate claims because they never requested repairs as an accommodation and the Housing Authority approved their transfer request and issued moving papers, and also failed to adequately plead race discrimination claims.

source_file: 9681456_2022_County of Cook, IL v. Wells Fargo _ Co._ilnd
case_name: County of Cook, Illinois v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: N/A - this is a third-party standing case where Cook County claims Wells Fargo's discriminatory mortgage lending and servicing practices caused minority borrowers to default, increasing the County's foreclosure-related expenditures
key_holding: The County's FHA claims failed because its key expert witnesses were excluded under Rule 702 for unreliable methodologies, leaving the County without evidence to establish that Wells Fargo intentionally discriminated against minority borrowers or that such discrimination proximately caused the County's claimed injuries.
brief_summary: Cook County sued Wells Fargo alleging that the bank's mortgage lending and servicing practices discriminated against minority borrowers, causing higher default and foreclosure rates that increased the County's expenditures on foreclosure-related services. The court granted Wells Fargo's summary judgment motion after excluding the County's expert witnesses under Rule 702 for unreliable statistical methodologies, finding the County lacked sufficient evidence of intentional discrimination or proximate cause.

accommodation_description: Not applicable - this case involves national origin discrimination in refusal to pay for property damage, not a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: The court granted the defendants' motion to stay the federal case pending resolution of the parallel state court proceedings, finding that Colorado River abstention factors weighed in favor of staying the case to avoid piecemeal litigation given the state court's significantly advanced progress.

case_name: Emily Evans v. 210 East Pearson Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that defendants deliver packages directly to her apartment door as they do for other residents, as her disabilities prevent her from retrieving packages from the lobby.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the reasonable accommodation claim (Count I) because plaintiff sufficiently alleged she requested package delivery accommodation before defendants initiated state court proceedings, rejecting defendants' ripeness argument; however, the court dismissed the interference claims (Counts II and IV) without prejudice for failure to allege intentional discrimination.
brief_summary: Emily Evans sued her condominium association and property management company alleging they violated the FHA by refusing to provide package delivery service to her apartment as a reasonable accommodation for her disabilities. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the failure to accommodate claim, finding plaintiff's claim ripe because she requested the accommodation before defendants initiated eviction proceedings, but dismissed the interference and retaliation claims without prejudice for failure to plead intentional discrimination.

case_name: Amanda Quist v. Park Tower Condominium Association and The Habitat Company
accommodation_description: Permission to keep an emotional support dog in a building with a no-dog policy, supported by documentation from her care provider including an offer of a three-way call, email/fax/phone contact information, and receipts from doctor visits demonstrating an ongoing therapeutic relationship.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss plaintiff's IIED claim (Count VII), holding that the totality of allegations—including two uses of a racial slur, denial of an emotional support animal accommodation, an escort of three security officers to retrieve packages, and refusal to return plaintiff's furniture—plausibly stated extreme and outrageous conduct under Illinois law.
brief_summary: Amanda Quist, a Black woman with documented mental health disabilities requiring an emotional support dog, applied to purchase a Chicago condominium but was denied her reasonable accommodation request by the Association and its property manager. During the process, Association employees twice referred to Quist using a racial slur, forced her to be escorted by three security officers to retrieve her packages, and refused to return her furniture, causing her to forfeit her earnest money and incur significant additional costs before purchasing a substitute unit. Defendants moved to dismiss Quist's nuisance claim (Count VI, voluntarily dismissed) and IIED claim (Count VII); the court denied dismissal of the IIED claim, finding that the combination of accommodation denial, racially derogatory treatment, and withholding of property plausibly constituted extreme and outrageous conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Williams v. Village of Hazel Crest
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - case involves alleged race discrimination in municipal sewage flooding rather than a disability accommodation request under § 3604(f)(3)(B)
key_holding: The FHA claim was dismissed because Williams's allegations that the Village jetted sewage into her property because she is Black were conclusory and unsupported by factual allegations suggesting discriminatory intent.
brief_summary: Deanna Williams, a Black property owner, sued the Village of Hazel Crest and Mayor Vernard Alsberry alleging the Village repeatedly flooded her property with sewage and discriminated against her because of her race in violation of § 3604(b). The court dismissed the FHA claim with prejudice, finding Williams failed to allege sufficient factual support for her conclusory allegation that the Village acted with discriminatory intent based on her race.

accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege Fair Housing Act and racial discrimination claims arising from fraudulent inducement to sign a lease for student housing, but no specific disability accommodation request is made or analyzed.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(2) for lack of personal jurisdiction and Rule 12(b)(3) for improper venue because Defendants lacked minimum contacts with Illinois and the lease contained a Pennsylvania forum-selection clause.
brief_summary: Illinois-resident plaintiffs sued California-domiciled defendant property owners and managers alleging fraud, consumer protection violations, and Fair Housing Act claims stemming from alleged misrepresentations about the condition of a Pennsylvania student apartment leased by their son. The court dismissed the case under Rule 12(b)(2) for lack of personal jurisdiction because Defendants had no minimum contacts with Illinois, and alternatively under Rule 12(b)(3) because the lease contained a Pennsylvania forum-selection clause and venue was improper in Illinois.

source_file: 9682801_2023_Huskey v. State Farm Fire _ Casualty Company_ilnd
case_name: Huskey v. State Farm Fire & Casualty Company
accommodation_description: Black homeowners allege State Farm's algorithmic claims-processing system creates racial disparities in homeowners insurance claim handling
key_holding: The court allowed Plaintiffs' disparate-impact claim under § 3604(b) to proceed, finding the complaint adequately alleged statistical disparities, a specific policy (algorithmic claims-processing), and a plausible causal connection; but dismissed § 3604(a) for failure to allege constructive eviction and § 3605 based on Seventh Circuit precedent that insurers are not in the business of covered real estate transactions.
brief_summary: Black homeowners Jacqueline Huskey and Riian Wynn sued State Farm Fire & Casualty Company alleging that its use of algorithmic decision-making tools in claims processing created statistically significant racial disparities in how it handled their homeowners insurance claims. The court granted in part and denied in part State Farm's motion to dismiss, dismissing the § 3604(a) claim for failure to allege constructive eviction and the § 3605 claim based on Seventh Circuit precedent, but allowed the § 3604(b) disparate impact claim to proceed because Plaintiffs adequately pleaded a statistical disparity, a specific policy, and a causal connection.

source_file: 9682870_2023_County of Cook, IL v. Wells Fargo _ Co._ilnd
case_name: County of Cook v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: This is a discriminatory lending/equity stripping case, not a reasonable accommodation case under § 3604(f)(3)(B). The County alleges Wells Fargo engaged in predatory and discriminatory loan origination, servicing, and foreclosure activities targeting minority communities.
key_holding: Following Seventh Circuit precedent in County of Cook v. Bank of America Corporation, the court held that the County lacked standing to bring FHA claims because the harm to individual borrowers was too remote, and the proper plaintiffs would be the borrowers themselves; accordingly, the motion to alter or amend summary judgment was denied.
brief_summary: The County of Cook sued Wells Fargo & Co. under the Fair Housing Act alleging predatory and discriminatory lending practices ('equity stripping') targeting minority communities through loan origination, servicing, and foreclosure activities dating back to 2003. The court denied the County's motion to alter or amend summary judgment entered in Wells Fargo's favor, following Seventh Circuit precedent holding that the County lacked proximate causation because the discriminatory harm to individual borrowers was too remote to be cognizable under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: County of Cook v. Bank of America Corp., 584 F. Supp. 3d 562 (N.D. Ill. 2022)

case_name: Vinzella Trimuel v. Chicago Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a domestic violence survivor with disabilities affecting her communication abilities, requested reinstatement to the public housing voucher waitlist from which she was removed for failing to complete a required survey.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim because CHA approved the accommodation request but failed to implement it, and the court rejected CHA's argument that providing the accommodation would fundamentally alter its policies as inappropriate for resolution at the motion to dismiss stage.
brief_summary: Vinzella Trimuel, a domestic violence survivor with anxiety, depression, and PTSD, sued the Chicago Housing Authority for disability discrimination after CHA removed her from its housing voucher waitlist in 2013 and then failed to reinstate her despite approving her 2020 reasonable accommodation request. The court denied CHA's motion to dismiss the reasonable accommodation claim, holding that CHA's approval of the request followed by failure to implement it stated a viable claim and that administrative burden arguments were improper at the motion to dismiss stage, while dismissing sex discrimination and promissory estoppel claims.

case_name: Kathleen Bankhead v. Wintrust Financial Corporation
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification; it concerns alleged racial discrimination in the origination, pricing, and terms of residential mortgage loans.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss all claims without prejudice, holding that statistical data showing racial disparities in mortgage lending rates, fees, and approvals was insufficient, standing alone, to plausibly allege either disparate treatment (which requires factual allegations connecting the disparity to discriminatory intent) or disparate impact (which requires a robust causal connection between a specific identified policy and the alleged disparities) under the ECOA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, or the FHA.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Kathleen Bankhead, an African American attorney, sued Wintrust Financial Corporation and Barrington Bank & Trust Co. on behalf of a putative class of Black and/or African American borrowers, alleging race discrimination in mortgage lending under the ECOA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, and the FHA, based on HMDA data showing that Black borrowers received higher interest rates, paid higher fees, and were approved at lower rates than white borrowers. The court dismissed disparate treatment claims because the complaint offered no factual allegations tying the statistical disparities to discriminatory intent, and dismissed disparate impact claims because plaintiff identified only broad categories of policies without establishing the requisite robust causal link between any specific policy and the alleged racial disparities. All counts were dismissed without prejudice to allow plaintiff an opportunity to replead with additional factual support.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
