source_file: 9683084_2023_Chicago Housing Initiative v. The United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_ilnd
case_name: Chicago Housing Initiative v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs did not request a specific accommodation; rather, they sought an injunction requiring HUD to conduct a full civil rights review before approving the CHA's disposition of 23 acres of vacant public housing land via a long-term lease to the Chicago Fire Football Club, arguing the lease would disproportionately harm racial minorities and people with disabilities by permanently removing land designated for future affordable public housing development.
key_holding: The court dismissed without prejudice the fair housing organizations' challenge to HUD's approval of the CHA's lease of public housing land to the Chicago Fire Football Club because plaintiffs failed to establish Article III standing under either representational or direct standing theories.
brief_summary: Three fair housing organizations — Chicago Housing Initiative, Coalition to Protect Chicago Housing Authority Land, and Lugenia Burns Hope Center — challenged HUD's approval of the Chicago Housing Authority's 60-year lease of a vacant public housing lot in the Roosevelt Square neighborhood to the Chicago Fire Football Club for a training facility, alleging violations of the Administrative Procedure Act, the Fair Housing Act, and the Rehabilitation Act. Plaintiffs sought a TRO/preliminary injunction to halt construction and challenged HUD's failure to conduct a formal civil rights review, arguing the lease would deprive racial minorities and persons with disabilities of land designated for affordable housing. The court denied the injunction and granted defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that plaintiffs lacked Article III standing because they could not demonstrate a concrete, particularized, non-speculative injury that was fairly traceable to defendants' conduct and redressable by a favorable ruling.
key_cases_cited: Warth v. Seldin, 422 U.S. 490 (1975)
Havens Realty Corp. v. Coleman, 455 U.S. 363 (1982)

source_file: 9683510_2024_Haymarket DuPage, LLC v. Village of Itasca_ilnd
case_name: Haymarket DuPage, LLC v. Village of Itasca
accommodation_description: Haymarket sought municipal zoning approval (via a special use permit as a healthcare facility and/or a planned development designation) to convert a former Holiday Inn hotel in Itasca into a comprehensive substance abuse treatment and mental health facility offering inpatient treatment, outpatient treatment, detoxification services, recovery home services, GED classes, and employment placement for persons with substance use disorders and mental health disabilities.
key_holding: The court granted the Fire District's and School District defendants' motions to dismiss for lack of Article III standing because Haymarket's injury—denial of its zoning applications—was not fairly traceable to those defendants' conduct, as the Village Board held exclusive decision-making authority and the opposing defendants merely voiced concerns without a vote or determinative control over the outcome.
brief_summary: Haymarket DuPage, LLC, a nonprofit substance abuse treatment provider, purchased a former Holiday Inn in Itasca, Illinois, and spent two years seeking zoning approval from the Village of Itasca to operate a treatment center; after the Village Board unanimously denied the applications, Haymarket sued six defendants under the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and state law. The Fire Protection District and School District defendants (along with Superintendent Benes) moved to dismiss, arguing Haymarket lacked Article III standing to sue them. The court granted the motions, holding that while those defendants vocally opposed the project, the denial was traceable only to the Village Board—the actual decisionmaker—not to the Fire District or School District, who had no vote and no determinative or coercive control over the Board.

case_name: Edwards v. Alexander County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case. Plaintiffs alleged racial discrimination, segregation, and deplorable housing conditions—including infestations, lead poisoning, and inadequate security—at public housing developments where approximately 97% of residents were Black, while white residents received better-maintained units with security cameras and guards.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims against HUD and Ben Carson on sovereign immunity grounds and dismissed plaintiff Jamika Sueing's FHA and Illinois Civil Rights Act claims as time-barred, while denying dismissal of the remaining plaintiffs' claims against the Housing Authority defendants.
brief_summary: Six former African-American residents of the racially segregated McBride and Elmwood public housing developments in Cairo, Illinois sued the Alexander County Housing Authority, HUD, and associated officials for disparate treatment, perpetuation of racial segregation, and failure to affirmatively further fair housing, alleging that Black residents were subjected to deplorable living conditions while white residents received better-maintained units with security. The court granted HUD and Ben Carson's motion to dismiss entirely on sovereign immunity grounds, finding that neither the FHA, Title VI, nor the Illinois Civil Rights Act contained an unequivocal waiver of federal sovereign immunity. The court granted in part the Housing Authority's motion, dismissing plaintiff Sueing's FHA and Illinois Civil Rights Act claims as untimely since she moved out in 2015 and did not sue until 2019, but allowed her Title VI claim and all other plaintiffs' claims against the Housing Authority to proceed.

case_name: Karnes v. Bank of Whittington/Whittington Bancorp, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's vague complaint alleges water shutoff violates the Fair Housing Act but does not articulate a specific accommodation request; she claims the water shutoff 'feels like discrimination' due to her disability.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed without prejudice for failing to satisfy Rule 8 pleading requirements, as plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts explaining who, what, when, where, why, and how her water was shut off and how any defendant discriminated against her because of disability.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Giasemi Karnes sued Bank of Whittington/Whittington Bancorp, Mohammad Ardehali (her former landlord), and the City of Benton, alleging her water was turned off and this violated the Fair Housing Act and ADA due to her disability. case_name: Carolina Prejean v. Jen Dischbein, Kim Schaltenbrand, and Metro Landing Apartments

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Carolina Prejean sued Metro Landing Apartments and individual property managers alleging racial discrimination in housing after they refused to lower her rent or allow her fiancée on the lease, claiming racially motivated animus. case_name: Sandra Black v. Naomi Friedrichsen, et al.

key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's motion to compel discovery responses, finding her requests vague and overly broad, and granted Defendants' motion to compel her deposition, finding no legal basis for her refusal to attend.
brief_summary: Sandra Black, an African-American tenant with a Section 8 voucher, sued her landlord and property management company alleging race discrimination under the Fair Housing Act, claiming defendants falsely accused her of lease violations and pursued eviction to force her out. case_name: Norman v. Northwest Indiana CA Section 8
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested in this case; the plaintiff alleged FHA violations relating to the administration of her Section 8 housing assistance payments after her rental building was sold to a new owner, arguing that payments were made to the new owner without her consent and that she was being harassed for rent she did not owe.
key_holding: The court dismissed pro se plaintiff's Fair Housing Act complaint under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim because she did not allege membership in a protected class or that any adverse treatment occurred because of such membership, and granted leave to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff LaSandra Norman, a Section 8 voucher recipient, sued her housing authority, the new owner of her rental property, and associated lenders, alleging FHA violations arising from the sale of her building and the subsequent redirection of her Housing Assistance Payments to the new owner without her consent. The court screened the complaint under the in forma pauperis statute and dismissed it for failure to state a claim, finding that the plaintiff neither identified herself as a member of a protected class nor alleged that any discrimination was based on protected-class membership. The court also found she lacked standing for her general allegations about Section 8 recipients being denied homeownership opportunities, and granted her until June 14, 2021 to file an amended complaint.

case_name: Pinnacle Treatment Centers, Inc. v. City of Crown Point, Indiana
accommodation_description: Pinnacle sought to continue operating a group home providing temporary lodging for more than five unrelated recovering substance abuse patients in an R-1 single-family residential zone, which the City treated as a zoning violation subject to daily fines; the FHA reasonable-accommodation framework underlies Pinnacle's claim that the City must exempt the home from these restrictions.
key_holding: A group home operator for recovering substance abusers has standing under the Fair Housing Act as an 'aggrieved person' because the concrete injury of municipal fines levied against it satisfies the injury-in-fact requirement, even if Pinnacle itself is not a member of the protected class.

brief_summary: Kiontay Smith, a former maintenance technician and tenant of Kittle Property Group, was terminated and evicted after returning from sick leave, allegedly due to a confrontation with a white resident over a parking policy. source_file: 9700858_2021_FAIR HOUSING CENTER OF CENTRAL INDIANA, INC. v. NEW_insd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, Inc. v. New
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves racial harassment by a neighbor and HOA/property management's failure to enforce covenants to stop the discriminatory conduct
key_holding: The court denied judgment on the pleadings for the FHA claims because plaintiffs adequately alleged direct liability against the HOA and property management for failing to take prompt action to correct and end New's discriminatory harassment under 24 C.F.R. § 100.7(a)(1)(iii), despite having the authority and power to intervene.
brief_summary: The Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana and Donata Banks sued the Twin Creeks HOA, Kirkpatrick Management Company, and Vicki New for racial harassment, alleging the Association Defendants knew of New's race-based harassment of minority residents but failed to enforce HOA covenants to stop it. The court granted the Association Defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings as to the voluntarily abandoned § 1981 claim and the negligence claim, but denied the motion as to the FHA and § 1982 claims, finding plaintiffs sufficiently alleged direct liability under 24 C.F.R. § 100.7 for the Association Defendants' failure to take prompt action to correct the discriminatory conduct.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

9701099_2021_FAIR HOUSING CENTER OF CENTRAL INDIANA, INC. v. NEW_insd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, Inc. v. New
accommodation_description: The specific accommodation or modification requested by the plaintiffs is not described in this procedural order; the order addresses only the entry of default judgment as a sanction against defendant Vicki New for failure to participate in litigation.
key_holding: The court found defendant Vicki New in contempt and entered default judgment against her on all claims as a sanction for her brazen and persistent refusal to participate in litigation, comply with discovery, and respond to the Order to Show Cause.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, Inc. and individual plaintiff Donata Banks filed suit against Vicki New, Kirkpatrick Management Company, and Twin Creeks Homeowners Association for violations of the Federal Fair Housing Act, the Indiana Fair Housing Act, the Federal Civil Rights Act, and related state law claims. Defendant Vicki New evaded service, refused to file an answer, refused to participate in discovery, acted in a disruptive and belligerent manner during a telephonic court conference, and repeatedly refused to receive court mailings or respond to an Order to Show Cause. The court, exercising its inherent authority to sanction conduct that abuses the judicial process, found Ms. New in contempt and entered default judgment against her on all claims, with the amount of damages to be determined at a later date.

case_name: Diego Felipe Barbosa Vasquez v. Hunter Bloomington Properties, LLC
accommodation_description: Not specified in the case text; the underlying nature of the alleged discriminatory housing practices was not addressed because the case was dismissed on procedural/venue grounds before reaching the merits.
key_holding: The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss without prejudice because the parties' lease agreement contained a valid and enforceable forum selection clause designating Monroe County, Indiana state courts as the exclusive venue, which the court enforced through the doctrine of forum non conveniens.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Diego Felipe Barbosa Vasquez and Angiee Liliana Rocha Parra filed suit in federal court alleging discriminatory housing practices in violation of the Fair Housing Act, breach of contract, and negligence against their landlord and related defendants. Defendant Hunter Bloomington Properties moved to dismiss based on a forum selection clause in the parties' July 2020 lease agreement requiring all claims to be litigated in the courts of Monroe County, Indiana. The court, applying Atlantic Marine and Seventh Circuit precedent, found the forum selection clause valid and enforceable and dismissed the case without prejudice so it could be refiled in Monroe County state court.

case_name: David DeBoard v. Elmwood One, LLC
accommodation_description: This is a design and construction accessibility case under § 3604(f)(3)(C), not a reasonable accommodation case under § 3604(f)(3)(B); the plaintiff's underlying complaint alleged defendants failed to design and construct Redwood Brownsburg Apartments to be accessible to persons with disabilities.
key_holding: The court granted in part plaintiff's motion to strike, striking the portion of expert Torkelson's report that relied on a prior confidential settlement agreement because it was not based on objective scientific standards; granted plaintiff's motion to preclude expert Dement from testifying due to defendants' failure to provide required Rule 26 disclosures; and granted defendants' motion to maintain the prior settlement agreement under seal.
brief_summary: David DeBoard sued Elmwood One, LLC and related defendants alleging they failed to design and construct the Redwood Brownsburg Apartments to be accessible to persons with disabilities in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(C). This order addresses only procedural discovery matters, granting in part plaintiff's motion to strike expert Torkelson's report (striking the portion relying on a prior settlement agreement as not based on objective scientific standards), granting plaintiff's motion to preclude expert Dement (for failure to provide Rule 26 disclosures), and granting defendants' motion to seal the prior settlement agreement.

accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation request was made; this case involves racial harassment by a neighbor (Vicki New) and claims that the HOA and property management company failed to take prompt action to address the discriminatory conduct.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendants on § 3604(a) and § 3604(c) claims but denied summary judgment on § 3604(b) hostile housing environment and § 3617 interference claims because genuine factual disputes exist regarding whether the HOA and property management company knew of racial harassment in 2016 and whether their response was sufficient under 24 C.F.R. § 100.7(a)(1)(iii).
brief_summary: The Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana and Donata Banks sued the Twin Creeks HOA, Kirkpatrick Management Company, and neighbor Vicki New for racial harassment and discriminatory housing practices under the FHA. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on claims under § 3604(a) and § 3604(c) but denied summary judgment on § 3604(b) hostile housing environment and § 3617 interference claims because factual disputes exist about whether defendants knew of racial harassment as early as 2016 and whether their response was reasonable.

source_file: 9702623_2022_LYONS v. GENE B. GLICK COMPANY, INCORPORATED_insd
case_name: Christina G. Lyons v. Gene B. Glick Company, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged she had exercised her right to a 'modification accommodation' of her apartment unit, and that Glick retaliated against her for doing so by denying maintenance requests, entering her unit unannounced, and conducting construction projects in a hostile and unprofessional manner.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendant Glick because plaintiff Lyons, by failing to respond to requests for admissions, conclusively admitted facts negating discriminatory intent, and alternatively because her state law claims were barred by Indiana's res judicata doctrine.
brief_summary: Pro se tenant Christina Lyons sued her former landlord Gene B. Glick Company under the FHA and Indiana state law, alleging retaliation and interference under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 for acts occurring between October and December 2017—specifically denial of maintenance requests, unannounced entries, and hostile construction—taken in retaliation for her exercising her right to a modification accommodation. The case returned on remand from the Seventh Circuit, which had held that a narrow subset of retaliatory claims survived Rooker-Feldman and the statute of limitations. The district court granted Glick's unopposed motion for summary judgment, finding that Lyons' failure to respond to requests for admissions constituted conclusive admissions negating discriminatory intent, and that her state law claims were separately barred by Indiana claim preclusion.
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317 (1986)

case_name: Debra Dunnivan v. Camille Mitchell, Karen Mitchell, Kirkpatrick Management Co., Grandville Cooperative Board of Directors
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested in this case; plaintiff challenged the termination of her lease as racially discriminatory and retaliatory, and sought relief from allegedly discriminatory eviction proceedings following a shooting incident involving her grandson.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that plaintiff's FHA claims—based on racial discrimination, hostile environment, disparate impact, and retaliation—consisted entirely of conclusory allegations insufficient to state a plausible claim under Rule 8 and Rule 12(b)(6), and that her Fourteenth Amendment claims failed because defendants are private actors.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Debra Dunnivan, an African American cooperative apartment resident, sued management and the board of directors after receiving a notice to vacate following a shooting incident involving her grandson, alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act and the Fourteenth Amendment based on a pattern of racial discrimination, a hostile housing environment, and retaliation for her sister's prior FHA lawsuit against defendants. The court dismissed the Fourteenth Amendment claims because the Fourteenth Amendment does not apply to private actors, and dismissed all FHA claims for failure to state a claim, finding plaintiff's allegations were bare conclusory statements unsupported by any factual detail regarding discriminatory intent, the five elements of disparate impact, or a causal connection for retaliation. Plaintiff was granted 30 days to seek leave to amend her complaint.

key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to stay discovery because Defendants' pending Motions to Dismiss raise a threshold standing issue that could dispose of the entire case, satisfying the factors for a stay of discovery under the court's discretion to manage discovery.

accommodation_description: Motion to compel property inspection to document design and construction accessibility barriers under FHA and ADA
key_holding: The court granted in part plaintiff's motion to compel inspection, allowing inspection of one of each type of unit and all FHA/ADA-covered aspects of the property within one day, but denied plaintiff's request for two units of each type, finding that balancing discovery needs with disruption to operations warranted limiting inspection to one unit per type.
brief_summary: David DeBoard, a wheelchair user, sued Union at Crescent, LP and related entities alleging the apartment complex in Bloomington, Indiana was not designed and constructed with accessible features in violation of the FHA and ADA. source_file: 9703505_2023_FAIR HOUSING CENTER OF CENTRAL INDIANA, INC. v. NEW_insd
case_name: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana, Inc. and Donata Banks v. Vicki New
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was at issue in this case; the claims centered on alleged racial harassment and discriminatory conduct by defendant Vicki New toward her neighbors in the Twin Creeks neighborhood, in violation of the Fair Housing Act and the Civil Rights Act of 1866.
key_holding: The court denied defendant Vicki New's three duplicative motions for reconsideration of the default judgment entered against her, finding she failed to establish any basis for relief under Rule 60(b) because she was properly served, acknowledged notice on multiple occasions, and voluntarily chose to ignore the litigation rather than participate in her own defense.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Center of Central Indiana and individual plaintiff Donata Banks sued Vicki New (along with a homeowners association and property management company) for violations of the Federal Fair Housing Act, Indiana Fair Housing Act, and Federal Civil Rights Act, alleging racial harassment and discrimination by Ms. New against neighbors in the Twin Creeks neighborhood. Ms. New evaded service, refused to participate in discovery, behaved disruptively at a status conference, and ignored court orders, resulting in a Clerk's Entry of Default in November 2020 and a Default Judgment in April 2021 with damages awarded in June 2022. This order concerns Ms. New's three duplicative post-judgment motions for reconsideration, all of which the court denied because she failed to satisfy the high standard under Rule 60(b), having been properly served and given repeated opportunities to defend herself that she willfully refused.

case_name: David DeBoard v. Union at Crescent, LP
accommodation_description: Plaintiff seeks to amend complaint to add allegations about independent injuries and unit rental offer related to accessibility claims at Union at Crescent property
key_holding: The court grants plaintiff leave to amend because he filed before the July 28, 2023 case management deadline, has not previously amended his complaint, and under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 15(a)(2), leave to amend should be freely given when justice requires.
brief_summary: David DeBoard filed a motion for leave to amend his Fair Housing Act complaint against Union at Crescent, LP and related defendants to add allegations about independent injuries and rental offer related to accessibility/design claims. The court granted the motion because DeBoard filed before the case management deadline and under Rule 15(a)(2), leave to amend must be freely given when justice requires.

key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for leave to file second amended complaint because plaintiff failed to establish good cause under Rule 16(b)(4), having filed the motion almost six months after the deadline without demonstrating diligence.

key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim at screening because her complaints about apartment odors were not related to unlawful discrimination and therefore did not constitute protected activity under 42 U.S.C. § 3617.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff April Royal sued Pedcor Management Corporation alleging retaliation under the Fair Housing Act's anti-retaliation provision after she was evicted for non-payment of rent following complaints about odors in her apartment. The court dismissed her complaint without prejudice, finding that her complaints about general housing conditions did not constitute protected activity under 42 U.S.C. § 3617 because they were not related to discrimination.

case_name: Quinn Ngiendo v. University Partners, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested waiver of defendants' policies barring prospective tenants from inspecting actual rental units and barring staff from cleaning apartments, due to her allergic rhinitis triggered by mold.
key_holding: Plaintiff sufficiently stated a reasonable accommodation claim for rhinitis because she requested to inspect units for mold and requested mold removal, both of which were refused by defendants under their no-showing and no-cleaning policies, plausibly alleging a reasonable accommodation that was denied.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Quinn Ngiendo sued multiple apartment complex owners and managers alleging they failed to accommodate her rhinitis by refusing to allow unit inspections or mold remediation, placed her in mold-infested units in retaliation for seeking accommodations, and discriminated against her based on her race (Black) and national origin (Kenyan). The court dismissed her PTSD accommodation claims but allowed her rhinitis accommodation, retaliation, and disparate treatment claims to proceed against Asset and Everest.

case_name: Quinn Ngiendo v. University Partners, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she experienced racial harassment by a white neighbor, including knife-stab marks on her door and a racial slur scratched into another Black tenant's car, creating a hostile housing environment based on race and national origin.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's hostile housing environment claim because she failed to plausibly allege that Waypoint knew or should have known she was being harassed due to her race or national origin, and adopted the Second Circuit's position that landlords are not liable under the FHA for tenant-on-tenant harassment.
brief_summary: Quinn Ngiendo, a Black pro se plaintiff, sued private landlords University Partners and Waypoint alleging a hostile housing environment based on race and national origin under the FHA, claiming the landlords failed to remedy racial harassment by her white neighbor. The court granted the motions to dismiss, finding plaintiff failed to plausibly allege the landlords knew the harassment was racially motivated, and declined to extend FHA liability to landlords for tenant-on-tenant harassment.

case_name: Melissa Wren v. City of Cherryvale Kansas, The Housing Authority of the City of Cherryvale, Kansas
accommodation_description: Request to remain in a two-bedroom public housing unit rather than being transferred to a one-bedroom unit, to provide a separate bedroom for nighttime personal assistance aides who provide disability-related care.
key_holding: The court found that Plaintiff was likely to succeed on her FHA failure-to-accommodate claim because CHA's occupancy policy requiring transfer to a one-bedroom unit was a rule that must yield to reasonable accommodation when Plaintiff needed a bedroom for her nighttime aides to provide disability-related care, and CHA failed to make such accommodation.
brief_summary: Melissa Wren, a mobility-impaired tenant using a wheelchair due to leg amputations, sued the Cherryvale Housing Authority after being ordered to transfer from a two-bedroom to a one-bedroom unit, claiming the transfer violated the FHA by failing to accommodate her need for a separate bedroom for her nighttime personal assistance aides. The court granted a temporary restraining order, finding Plaintiff likely would succeed on the merits because CHA's occupancy policy must yield to reasonable accommodation when Plaintiff needed the larger unit for disability-related aide care.

case_name: Quinn Ngiendo v. Asset Campus USA, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested accommodations for mold allergies and breathing sensitivities, including cleaning and remediation by Everest, and for PTSD-related noise sensitivity including ground floor transfer and quiet environment from Cardinal.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment to all three defendants because plaintiff failed to submit evidence supporting her reasonable accommodation claims—she never provided medical documentation to Everest for her accommodation request, and her request for accommodation from excessive noise was not shown to be necessary or reasonable.
brief_summary: Quinn Ngiendo, a pro se Black immigrant from Kenya, sued three property management companies (Asset Campus, Everest Campus West, and Cardinal Group Management) alleging Fair Housing Act violations including failure to accommodate her disabilities (mold allergies and PTSD-related noise sensitivity) and disparate treatment based on race and national origin. case_name: Coe v. Cross-Lines Retirement Center, Inc.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; plaintiffs allege generally that elderly and disabled tenants are captive to poor housing conditions (bedbugs, flooding, mold).
key_holding: Defendants' motion for reconsideration of the court's order excluding expert testimony regarding tenant cooperation was denied as moot because the court did not rely on that testimony when granting class certification, and defendants did not move for reconsideration of the class certification order itself.
brief_summary: Elderly tenants sued Cross-Lines Retirement Center (a nonprofit housing provider for elderly) and its property manager alleging poor housing conditions including bedbug infestations, flooding, and mold. case_name: Donald Coe, Linda Smith, and Edward Yost v. Cross-Lines Retirement Center, Inc. and Young Management Corp.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested in this case. The FHA claim arises from defendants' alleged failure to maintain habitable conditions free of pervasive bed bug infestations in an apartment complex housing elderly and disabled residents, rather than from a denial of any particular accommodation or modification request.
key_holding: The court grants in part and denies in part plaintiffs' motion for class certification, certifying issue classes for five of the six proposed issues concerning bed bug infestations (issues 2–6) under Rule 23(c)(4), while denying certification of issue 1 because it is dominated by individualized questions of fact.
brief_summary: Elderly and disabled tenants of Cross-Lines Retirement Center, a federally subsidized nonprofit apartment complex, sued the owner and property manager over pervasive and persistent bed bug infestations, asserting claims including FHA violations, negligence, breach of the implied warranty of habitability, breach of contract, and Kansas Consumer Protection Act violations. Plaintiffs moved to certify a class for six specific issues related to the bed bug infestations. The court granted the motion as to five issues addressing defendants' standard of care, bed bugs' effect on habitability and fair market value, and the essentialness of extermination services, but denied certification of the first proposed issue—whether every tenant was affected—because it was inherently dominated by individualized factual questions.

case_name: Garry Adam v. Andmark White Lakes Apartments, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought repairs and maintenance as a reasonable accommodation for his visual disability, along with communication in 18-point font and ability to pay rent via check instead of online portal (as specified in a prior conciliation agreement).
key_holding: The court held that repair requests do not constitute a reasonable accommodation under the FHA because the accommodation framework requires a change to an existing rule or policy, not merely a request for maintenance; the court dismissed the failure to accommodate and modification claims but allowed the retaliation claim to proceed.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Garry Adam, a visually disabled tenant at White Lakes Plaza Apartments in Topeka, Kansas, sued the property owner, management company, and subsequent owners alleging Fair Housing Act violations including failure to accommodate, failure to permit modifications, misrepresentation of dwelling availability, and retaliation after the parties had previously entered into a conciliation agreement regarding his disability accommodations. The court dismissed most claims but allowed the retaliation claim to proceed, holding that repair requests are not reasonable accommodations under the FHA and that post-agreement discriminatory conduct could form the basis of a retaliation claim.
key_cases_cited: Asbury v. Brougham, 866 F.2d 1276 (10th Cir. 1989)
Bangerter v. Orem City Corp., 46 F.3d 1491 (10th Cir. 1995)
Ngiendo v. Univ. Partners, LLC, No. 22-2393-HLT, 2021 WL 5038780 (D. Kan. Oct. 27, 2021)
Hatfield v. Cottages on 78th Cmty. Ass'n, No. 21-4035, 2022 WL 2452379 (10th Cir. July 6, 2022)

case_name: Coe v. Cross-Lines Retirement Center, Inc.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested; the case concerns habitability conditions (bed bug infestations, rodent bodies, flooding, leaking, and mold) affecting elderly and disabled residents of a retirement center.
key_holding: The court conditionally certified a settlement class of approximately 332 residents of Cross-Lines Retirement Center and granted preliminary approval of the class settlement resolving claims related to habitability conditions including bed bug infestations, rodent infestations, flooding, and mold, finding the settlement fair, reasonable, and adequate under Rule 23(e).
brief_summary: Elderly and disabled tenants of Cross-Lines Retirement Center brought a class action against the facility and its property manager alleging that neglected conditions—including bed bug infestations, decaying rodents, flooding, and mold—violated the Fair Housing Act and state law claims including negligence, implied warranty of habitability, breach of contract, and the Kansas Consumer Protection Act. After class certification of issue classes, the parties reached a settlement providing class members approximately $208.04 per month of residency during the class period (September 1, 2016 through December 31, 2023), plus injunctive relief to remedy ongoing conditions. The court conditionally certified the 332-member settlement class and granted preliminary approval of the settlement, finding it the product of serious, non-collusive negotiations with immediate value outweighing continued litigation.
key_cases_cited: DG ex rel. Stricklin v. DeVaughn, 594 F.3d 1188 (10th Cir. 2010)
Shook v. El Paso Cnty., 386 F.3d 963 (10th Cir. 2004)

source_file: 9711727_2024_Adam v. Andmark White Lakes Apartments, LLC_ksd
case_name: Garry Adam v. Andmark White Lakes Apartments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who is blind, requested that defendants put the offer to transfer units in writing, and argued that his repair requests constituted reasonable accommodation requests.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiff failed to allege that defendants OPG and 37North knew or reasonably should have known of his disability, and because plaintiff's requests for repairs did not constitute requests for accommodation of an otherwise valid policy.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Garry Adam, who is legally blind due to a retinal dystrophy, sued his former landlords and property managers alleging Fair Housing Act violations including failure to accommodate, refusal to rent, and retaliation. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff failed to state a claim because the new property managers (OPG and 37North) lacked knowledge of his disability and because plaintiff's repair requests did not constitute valid accommodation requests under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

source_file: 9714170_2023_Garvey Farm LP v. City of Elsmere, Kentucky_kyed
case_name: Garvey Farm LP v. City of Elsmere, Kentucky
accommodation_description: Mobile home park operator seeks to expand by rezoning adjacent vacant land for manufactured housing development, alleging discriminatory denial based on protected class composition of prospective residents
key_holding: The city council members have absolute legislative immunity for their zoning decisions regardless of alleged discriminatory motive; the vacant land satisfies the FHA definition of 'dwelling'; and plaintiffs failed to show the taking was pretextual since parks and public facilities constitute legitimate public use.
brief_summary: Garvey Farm LP, a mobile home park operator, sued the City of Elsmere, Kentucky after the city denied its zoning amendment to expand the park onto adjacent vacant land and passed an ordinance making such expansion more difficult. The court dismissed the claims against individual council members based on legislative immunity, found that vacant land qualifies as a dwelling under § 3604(b), and dismissed the takings and conspiracy claims because the city's stated public use (park and public works facility) was not pretextual.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Bogan v. Scott-Harris
Kelo v. City of New London

case_name: Miller v. Alco Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Alco Defendants discriminated against him based on gender and disabled status in the terms, conditions, and privileges of his rental and services in connection with his tenancy at Southern Oaks apartment complex.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations, finding the alleged discriminatory housing practices occurred no later than July 24, 2020 (when plaintiff moved out) but the complaint was not filed until August 11, 2022.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ron Miller sued Alco Management, Inc. and related entities (property management) and Georgetown Police Department, alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on gender and disability discrimination in the terms and conditions of his tenancy at Southern Oaks apartment complex. The court overruled plaintiff's objections and adopted the magistrate judge's recommendation, granting defendants' motions to dismiss because the FHA claims were time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowners Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Alberto James Santiago, Sr. v. Elishia Chill, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that management repair a broken door that caused him physical injury and prevented him from entering and exiting his apartment due to his mobility disability and arm condition.
key_holding: The court allowed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims alleging discrimination based on national origin and disability, retaliation, and failure to make reasonable accommodation to proceed against defendants Chill, Hext, and Key Property Management, while dismissing claims against other defendants for failure to meet pleading standards.
brief_summary: Alberto James Santiago, a 57-year-old tenant in a wheelchair with a mobility-related arm injury, sued Key Property Management and individual managers alleging discrimination, failure to accommodate (broken door not repaired for years causing physical injury and trapping him in his apartment), retaliation for filing HUD complaints, and discriminatory eviction based on his national origin (Puerto Rican) and disability. The court dismissed claims against some defendants for failing to meet pleading standards but allowed claims for discrimination, retaliation, and failure to make reasonable accommodation to proceed against the primary defendants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Groner v. Golden Gate Gardens Apartments, 250 F.3d 1039 (6th Cir. 2001)
Larkin v. State of Mich. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 89 F.3d 285 (6th Cir. 1996)

case_name: Ruth Castro Uribe v. Cynthia Ramser, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff made vague references to housing rights violations affecting minorities, elderly, and persons with disabilities but did not clearly request any specific reasonable accommodation; her filings challenged secondhand smoke exposure, rent payment practices, and sought an air purifier.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss because plaintiff failed to establish federal subject matter jurisdiction by relying solely on Maine and Kentucky state law, and to the extent she attempted to raise federal claims including Fair Housing Act claims, those claims were dismissed without prejudice for failure to comply with Rule 8's pleading requirements.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ruth Castro Uribe sued landlords Cynthia Ramser, Tom Ramser, and EER Investments, LLC alleging housing rights violations, human rights violations, and financial exploitation under Maine and Kentucky state law, complaining about secondhand smoke exposure and requiring twelve advance rent checks. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction, finding plaintiff failed to identify any viable federal cause of action despite vague references to housing discrimination affecting minorities, elderly, and disabled persons.
key_cases_cited: Twombly, 550 U.S. 544
Kensu v. Corizon, Inc., 5 F.4th 646

case_name: Rodney L. Nance, Sr. v. Mayfield Plaza Apartments Management et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a convicted felon released from incarceration, alleges he was threatened with eviction from his fiancée's apartment based on his criminal history.
key_holding: Plaintiff lacks standing to bring FHA claims because he is not a lessee, and even construing the complaint liberally, his status as a felon is not a protected class under the FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Rodney Nance sued Mayfield Plaza Apartments Management alleging he was threatened with eviction from his fiancée's apartment because he is a convicted felon. The court dismissed the case, finding plaintiff lacks standing because he is not a lessee and his status as a convicted felon is not a protected class under the Fair Housing Act.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife

case_name: Yusef Abdullah Bilal Ali v. Louisville Metro Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested permission to keep his 120-pound pit bull-Mastiff emotional support animal off leash during surgical recovery from knee surgery.
key_holding: The court denied Plaintiff's Emergency Motion for Injunction Pending Appeal, finding Plaintiff failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits because his requested off-leash accommodation was unreasonable given the dog's documented aggressive behavior, and his transfer request was properly denied because he failed to provide required medical documentation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Yusef Abdullah Bilal Ali, a public housing tenant with mobility impairments requiring knee surgery, sued Louisville Metro Housing Authority alleging failure to accommodate his requests to keep his emotional support animal off leash and to transfer to a two-bedroom single-family unit. The court denied Plaintiff's Emergency Motion for Injunction Pending Appeal, finding he could not demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits because the off-leash request posed unacceptable safety risks given the dog's documented aggressive history, and LMHA properly denied the transfer request after Plaintiff failed to provide required medical documentation.
key_cases_cited: Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Hollis v. Chesnut Bend Homeowner's Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)

case_name: Watkins v. Commonwealth of Kentucky
accommodation_description: Plaintiff references Fair Housing Act violations in challenging an eviction proceeding but does not specify a particular accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claim because her complaint was written solely as a legal conclusion unsupported by facts, failing to state a claim upon which relief may be granted.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Rita Watkins, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued the Commonwealth of Kentucky, her mobile home park landlord, an attorney, and two state court judges challenging an eviction proceeding for failure to pay rent and alleging Fair Housing Act and constitutional violations. The court dismissed the action for failure to state a claim, finding that while Plaintiff referenced the FHA, she provided only legal conclusions without factual support for any discrimination claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Brenda L. Alexander v. CS/KY/LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff complained about secondhand cigarette smoke from a neighboring tenant and sought enforcement of HUD's Smoke Free Rule against that neighbor
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's claims because the HUD Smoke Free Rule does not create a private right of action for a tenant to sue the landlord for a neighbor's smoking, and the Fair Housing Act and ADA do not apply to this secondhand smoke exposure claim.
brief_summary: Brenda L. Alexander, a pro se plaintiff residing in HUD-subsidized public housing, sued her landlord and property management company seeking damages for secondhand cigarette smoke exposure from a neighboring tenant and alleging violations of the HUD Smoke Free Rule, Fair Housing Act, and ADA. The court dismissed all claims for failure to state a claim because the HUD Smoke Free Rule does not create a private right of action for tenants, and neither the FHA nor ADA apply to this type of secondhand smoke complaint.

case_name: Ronnie Joe Forte v. Hopkinsville Housing Authority et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; plaintiff applied for Section 8 subsidized rental housing and sought damages and injunctive relief after his application was denied based on pending drug charges under a blanket criminal-history ban.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claim for failure to state a claim because the FHA does not prohibit discrimination based on criminal history, and federal law expressly permits public housing agencies to deny admission to federally assisted housing for drug-related criminal activity.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Ronnie Joe Forte sued the Hopkinsville Housing Authority and a Section 8 housing specialist under the FHA after his housing application was denied based on a blanket ban tied to his pending drug-related criminal charges. Conducting mandatory § 1915(e)(2) screening, the court found that the FHA does not cover discrimination based on criminal history and that 42 U.S.C. § 13661(c) expressly authorizes housing authorities to deny admission to applicants engaged in drug-related criminal activity. The lawsuit was dismissed for failure to state a claim upon which relief could be granted.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Robertson v. Olsen 2023 WL 5284480
Smith v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urb. Dev. 2022 WL 18107588
Nickell v. Metro. 2018 WL 2392849

case_name: Yusef Abdullah Bilal Ali v. Louisville Metro Housing Authority, et al.
accommodation_description: Request to keep emotional support dog off leash on LMHA property and common areas during recovery from knee surgery.
key_holding: Ali cannot show his request to keep his dog off leash was a reasonable accommodation given the dog's documented history of aggression, and his transfer request fails because he never provided the required physician's certification verifying medical necessity.
brief_summary: Ali, a public housing tenant recovering from knee surgery, sued LMHA alleging disability discrimination for denying his request to keep his emotional support dog off leash and to transfer to a single-family unit. The court granted summary judgment to defendants, finding Ali cannot show the off-leash request was reasonable given the dog's documented aggression history and that LMHA engaged in an extensive interactive process but Ali never provided required medical documentation for the transfer.
key_cases_cited: Overlook Mut. Homes, Inc. v. Spencer, 415 F. App'x 617 (6th Cir. 2011)
Hollis v. Chestnut Bend Homeowner's Ass'n, 760 F.3d 531 (6th Cir. 2014)

case_name: Aicha Bouchgl v. Suleiman Ibrahim
accommodation_description: No disability-related accommodation requested; plaintiffs allege discrimination based on national origin, religious beliefs, and color including excessive security deposits, late fees, threats of eviction, and harassment.
key_holding: Louisiana enjoys Eleventh Amendment sovereign immunity from Fair Housing Act claims brought in federal court, and Congress did not clearly intend to abrogate state sovereign immunity under the FHA; accordingly, the state defendants (Louisiana Department of Justice and Attorney General) are dismissed without prejudice.
brief_summary: Tenants Aicha Bouchgl and Suleiman Ibrahim sued their landlord Tonti Management Co. and the Louisiana Department of Justice and Attorney General, alleging housing discrimination based on national origin, religious beliefs, and color under the Fair Housing Act and Louisiana Equal Housing Opportunity Act. The federal court granted Louisiana's motion to dismiss the state defendants without prejudice, holding that the Eleventh Amendment bars FHA claims against unconsenting states in federal court and that Congress did not abrogate state sovereign immunity under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: McCardell v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 794 F.3d 510 (5th Cir. 2015)
Edelman v. Jordan, 415 U.S. 651 (1974)
Cozzo v. Tangipahoa Par. Council-President Gov't, 279 F.3d 273 (5th Cir. 2002)

case_name: Russell Andre Briley v. Ignatius Barreca, Jr. et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identified; plaintiff failed to state any coherent Fair Housing Act claim.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's federal claims with prejudice because he failed to allege any facts to state a claim under the FHA, ADA, Title VI, or Title VII, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Russell Briley sued landlords Ignatius Barreca Jr., David Barreca Sr., and Josephine Broadwater alleging violations of the ADA, Title VI, Title VII, and Fair Housing Act, though the complaint contained no factual allegations supporting any claim. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff failed to state any claim under federal law, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2008)

source_file: 9719738_2021_Treece v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc._laed
case_name: Dwayne Treece, et al. v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, a family of six with four children, sought to rent a condominium unit but were subject to occupancy limits (250/400 square feet per person) and attempted eviction based on familial status.
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to establish robust causation required for a disparate impact claim under § 3604(a) because they offered no evidence that the occupancy limits caused families with children to be the dominant group of renters affected, as families with children already comprised larger households prior to the challenged policy.
brief_summary: The Treece family of six sued the Perrier Condominium Owners Association alleging that occupancy limits (250/400 square feet per person) violated the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on families with children based on familial status. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for partial summary judgment and granted defendants' cross-motion, finding plaintiffs failed to establish the robust causation element of their disparate impact claim because families with children already had larger households before the challenged policy, and the 400 square foot rule was never actually enforced.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing & Cmty. Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc.
Inclusive Communities Project, Inc. v. Lincoln Property Co.
Reyes v. Azucar Bakery

source_file: 9720571_2021_Treece v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc._laed
case_name: Dwayne Treece, et al. v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was at issue; the case concerns familial status discrimination in which the condominium association and unit owners adopted and enforced occupancy limits (first a 250-sq-ft-per-person rule, then a proposed 400-sq-ft-per-person rule), threatened eviction, levied daily fines against the landlord, and otherwise pressured the Treece family—a family of six with four young children—to vacate their unit because of their familial status.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motion to modify its prior partial summary judgment order to clarify that disparate treatment claims under § 3604(a) and interference/coercion claims under § 3617 were never adjudicated and remain pending, while only disparate impact claims under § 3604(a) and discriminatory-statement claims under § 3604(c) had been dismissed, and denied defendants' motion for entry of partial final judgment.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs—a family of six (the Treeces), their landlord (Harlan), and others—sued a four-unit condominium association (PCOA) and individual unit owners alleging familial status discrimination after the Treeces moved in and faced occupancy-limit enforcement, proposed bylaw amendments, fines against Harlan, and pressure to evict the family. The court had previously granted summary judgment dismissing disparate impact claims under § 3604(a) and all § 3617 claims, but the order was later challenged as having erroneously swept in disparate treatment claims that were never briefed or decided on the merits. The court modified the prior summary judgment order to reflect that intentional disparate treatment claims under § 3604(a), Harlan's § 3604(b) claims, and all § 3617 claims remain pending, while simultaneously denying defendants' motion to enter partial final judgment on the adjudicated claims due to the risk of piecemeal appellate review.
key_cases_cited: Treece v. Perrier Condo. Ass'n, Inc., 519 F. Supp. 3d 342 (E.D. La. 2021)

source_file: 9720727_2021_Winston v. Housing Authority of Jefferson Parish_laed
case_name: Nadia Winston v. Housing Authority of Jefferson Parish
accommodation_description: Alleged discriminatory comment by housing authority employee regarding plaintiff's eight children and her children's disability status
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss without prejudice and granted leave to amend because the complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to state a claim, and individual employees cannot be held personally liable under the Fair Housing Act under vicarious liability principles.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Nadia Winston sued the Jefferson Parish Housing Authority and individual employees alleging she is owed $45,000 under the Family Self Sufficient Program and suffered discrimination based on disability and familial status, plus retaliation for reporting the housing authority to HUD. The court denied the motion to dismiss without prejudice, granting leave to amend because the complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations and individual defendants cannot be held personally liable under the FHA.
key_cases_cited: Meyer v. Holley, 537 U.S. 280 (2003)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

source_file: 9720836_2022_Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Plantation Management Company, LLC_laed
case_name: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center Inc. v. Plantation Management Co. LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Deaf prospective residents requested video remote interpreting (VRI) services as a reasonable accommodation to enable effective communication with staff at a nursing home/assisted living facility.
key_holding: The court found that the plaintiff adequately alleged ownership interest and agency relationship, sufficient to state claims for discriminatory refusal to provide interpretive services under the FHA and ADA, rejecting defendants' arguments that conclusory ownership allegations and agency relationship were insufficient at the pleading stage.
brief_summary: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center sued nursing home owners for refusing to provide video remote interpreting services to deaf prospective residents, alleging violations of the FHA and ADA. The court denied the owners' motion to dismiss, finding the plaintiff's allegations of direct ownership and agency relationship were sufficient to put defendants on notice and survive a 12(b)(6) motion.

case_name: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Plantation Management Company, LLC et al.
accommodation_description: Fair housing organization alleges on behalf of prospective deaf residents that nursing home staff refused to provide ASL interpretation or video remote interpreting (VRI) services.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that the fair housing organization had standing based on diverted organizational resources and adequately stated FHA reasonable accommodation claims against the facility owners/operators for refusing to provide interpretive services to deaf prospective residents.
brief_summary: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center sued CommCare Corporation and CommCare Management Corporation (owners/operators of Greenbriar Community Care Center nursing facility in Slidell, Louisiana), alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to provide ASL interpretation or VRI services to prospective deaf residents. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the fair housing organization had standing to sue and adequately stated reasonable accommodation claims under the FHA.

source_file: 9721018_2022_Treece v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc._laed
case_name: Dwayne Treece, et al. v. Perrier Condominium Owners Association, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case involves familial status discrimination challenge to occupancy limits and eviction threats directed at family with four children.
key_holding: The court denied summary judgment on plaintiffs' § 3604(a) disparate treatment claim because material facts regarding defendants' intent to discriminate against families with children are in genuine dispute, but granted summary judgment on Harlan's claim that defendants blocked prospective buyers from purchasing his unit.
brief_summary: Dwayne and Phallon Treece (with their four children) and their landlord Clifford Harlan sued the Perrier Condominium Owners Association and individual unit owners for discriminatory actions including threatening eviction, changing occupancy rules from 250 to 400 square feet per occupant, and harassment based on the family's size. The court denied summary judgment for defendants on the familial status discrimination claim under § 3604(a) because disputed facts about intent preclude summary judgment, but granted summary judgment on Harlan's separate claim that the occupancy rules prevented him from selling his unit to families.

source_file: 9721118_2022_Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Azalea Garden Properties, LLC_laed
case_name: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center, Inc. v. Azalea Garden Properties, LLC
accommodation_description: Blanket criminal background screening policy allegedly having disparate impact on persons with disabilities (recovering from drug addiction) by excluding them without individualized assessment
key_holding: The disability-based disparate impact claim was dismissed because LaFHAC failed to allege any statistical data showing that individuals with drug convictions are likely to be recovering from an addiction that substantially limits major life activities, failing to establish the requisite causal connection for a disparate impact claim.
brief_summary: Louisiana Fair Housing Action Center sued Azalea Garden Properties, LLC alleging that its blanket criminal background screening policy violates the FHA by having a disparate impact on African American renters and persons recovering from drug addiction. The court denied the motion to dismiss as to the race-based disparate impact claim, finding sufficient statistical allegations, but granted dismissal as to the disability claim because LaFHAC failed to allege any data connecting drug convictions to individuals with qualifying disabilities.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

source_file: 9721277_2022_Winston v. Housing Authority of Jefferson Parish_laed
case_name: Winston v. Housing Authority of Jefferson Parish
subsidy_program: Housing Choice Voucher Program (HCVP), Family Self-Sufficiency Program (FSSP)
accommodation_description: Plaintiff asserts she was discriminated against based on disability in her termination from the Housing Choice Voucher Program and Family Self-Sufficiency Program, which resulted in forfeiture of funds owed to her.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for JPHA because the plaintiff, proceeding pro se, failed to file an opposition to the motion and therefore failed to present any evidence of discriminatory intent, discriminatory effect, or retaliation under the Fair Housing Act.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Nadia Winston, proceeding pro se, sued the Jefferson Parish Housing Authority alleging she was owed $45,000 in Family Self-Sufficiency Program funds after being terminated from the HCVP and that she was discriminated against based on disability and retaliation. The court granted JPHA's motion for summary judgment because Winston failed to file an opposition and thus presented no evidence of discriminatory intent, discriminatory effect, or retaliation under the Fair Housing Act.

accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case involves refusal to rent to family with children based on policy against opposite-gender children sharing a bedroom.
key_holding: The court denied Mai's motions to dismiss and for summary judgment without prejudice under Rule 56(d), finding that genuine issues of material fact exist regarding Mai's involvement in setting and enforcing an allegedly discriminatory policy against families, and that Plaintiff needs additional discovery time to adequately oppose the motions.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Velma Lee sued J.M. Property Holdings, LLC, Thao P. Mai, and Tammy Sponberg alleging familial status discrimination after a property manager refused to rent her a unit because her two children of opposite genders were allegedly too old to share a bedroom. The court denied Mai's motions to dismiss and for summary judgment without prejudice, finding disputed facts exist regarding Mai's involvement in managing the property and setting the allegedly discriminatory policy, and that plaintiff needs additional discovery time.

case_name: Victor Cagara Ortiguerra, et al. v. Grand Isle Shipyard, LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was requested. The FHA claim alleged that defendants discriminated against Filipino workers on the basis of national origin by segregating them in substandard bunkhouse and COVID-19 quarantine accommodations, refusing to allow them to evacuate during and after Hurricane Ida while non-Filipino workers were permitted to leave, and confining them in a damaged bunkhouse without clean water or electricity for weeks.
key_holding: The court held that the narrow POEA employment contract arbitration clause—covering only disputes 'arising from' employment—required arbitration of plaintiffs' FLSA wage and overtime claims, but did not compel arbitration of plaintiffs' TVPA and FHA claims because those claims could be maintained independently of the employment relationship and did not arise from it.
brief_summary: Filipino welders and fitters employed on offshore oil rigs sued their employer, Grand Isle Shipyard, alleging violations of the Fair Labor Standards Act (unpaid wages and overtime), the Trafficking Victims Protection Act (forced labor and confinement), and the Fair Housing Act (national-origin discrimination in housing assignments and Hurricane Ida evacuation). Defendants moved to dismiss and compel arbitration of all three claims pursuant to a POEA seafarer employment contract incorporating a Philippine arbitration clause. The court granted the motion as to the FLSA claims, finding a valid arbitration agreement that covered wage disputes arising from employment, but denied it as to the TVPA and FHA claims, concluding that the arbitration clause was 'narrow' and that housing discrimination and forced labor claims could be maintained independently of the employment contract and did not arise from it.

case_name: Turnipseed v. APMT, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested waiver of the apartment's animal fee and 35-pound weight restriction to allow her emotional support animal dog to live in her apartment.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal with prejudice because the record did not show contumacious conduct and the arbitration order did not specify a deadline, but warned that plaintiff must initiate arbitration within 30 days or face dismissal.
brief_summary: Dory Turnipseed sued her landlord APMT LLC, alleging the property management company violated the Fair Housing Act by denying her accommodation request to waive animal fees and weight restrictions for her emotional support animal. The court previously ordered the parties to arbitrate, but four years later the plaintiff had not initiated arbitration; the court denied the defendant's motion to dismiss with prejudice for failure to prosecute, finding insufficient evidence of contumacious conduct and ordering plaintiff to initiate arbitration within 30 days.

key_holding: The Court granted Defendant's motion to compel arbitration because the parties had a valid arbitration agreement with a delegation clause, and Plaintiff's challenges to the agreement's enforceability and constitutionality must be submitted to the arbitrator rather than the Court.

The Court granted the motion to compel arbitration, holding that the valid arbitration agreement contained a delegation clause that assigned questions of the agreement's scope, validity, and enforceability to the arbitrator.

case_name: Jason Allen James, et al. v. Tangipahoa Parish
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs requested that Tangipahoa Parish grant a reasonable accommodation under the FHA to allow their sober home—housing up to ten persons in recovery from substance abuse—to continue operating in a single-family zoning district without being required to comply with the Parish's burdensome permit requirements for 'addictive disorder treatment facilities,' which included 24-hour on-site supervisory personnel, regular access to health care providers, significant general liability insurance, and handicap accessibility standards that plaintiffs alleged were financially impossible to satisfy.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, holding that the Anti-Injunction Act barred injunctive relief on the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act claims, and that plaintiffs failed to demonstrate a substantial likelihood of success on the merits of their Section 1983 First Amendment retaliation claim because the Parish's enforcement actions predated any reasonable accommodation request.
brief_summary: Three residents of a sober home in Hammond, Louisiana filed FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Section 1983 claims against Tangipahoa Parish, which was seeking to shut down their sober living facility for operating without a permit as an 'addictive disorder treatment facility' under the Parish Code of Ordinances. Plaintiffs moved for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to prevent the Parish from enforcing its ordinance and to stay a state court injunction authorizing closure. The court denied the motion, finding the Anti-Injunction Act barred injunctive relief on the federal civil rights housing claims, and independently that plaintiffs could not show a likelihood of success on the Section 1983 retaliation claim because the Parish's enforcement efforts began before plaintiffs had made any indication they would seek a reasonable accommodation.

case_name: Lisa N Carey v. St. Charles Parish
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request identifiable; plaintiff appears to allege disparate treatment discrimination based on race when parish enforcement actions intensified after learning she, a Black woman, owned the property.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims because she failed to plead a prima facie case of disparate treatment (no facts showing she applied for housing, was rejected, or that housing remained open to similarly situated applicants), and alternatively, all claims were barred by res judicata as they arose from the same transaction as prior state court litigation.
brief_summary: Lisa N. Carey, proceeding pro se, sued St. Charles Parish in federal court alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on the Parish's enforcement of unsafe structure ordinances against her property after learning she, a Black woman, owned it. The court granted the Parish's motion to dismiss with prejudice, finding Carey failed to state a prima facie disparate treatment claim and that res judicata barred relitigating claims arising from the same transaction as prior state court proceedings.

key_holding: The court granted plaintiffs' motion to dismiss defendants' defamation counterclaim because the claim was not yet ripe—defamation claims arising from judicial proceedings cannot be brought until the underlying proceedings are terminated—and defendants failed to provide sufficient factual allegations to state a defamation claim.

case_name: Jessica Bush v. Broad Management Group, et al.

key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to strike plaintiff's jury demand because three of five factors weighed in favor of finding the jury waiver clause in the lease to be knowing and voluntary, despite plaintiff not being represented by counsel when she signed.
brief_summary: Jessica Bush sued Broad Management Group and Cristina Perez alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by failing to provide a reasonable accommodation for her emotional support animals. The court granted defendants' motion to strike Bush's jury demand, finding that the jury waiver clause in her lease was a knowing and voluntary waiver of her Seventh Amendment right to trial by jury.

key_holding: The court denied summary judgment because genuine issues of material fact exist as to whether defendants had sufficient notice of plaintiff's disability and whether their April 5 denial letter, combined with the subsequent eviction notice citing unauthorized animals, constituted a refusal to provide a reasonable accommodation.

case_name: Hughes v. Bouchon Properties LLC
accommodation_description: Hughes alleged in conclusory terms that Bouchon refused to permit or make reasonable modifications and failed to make reasonable accommodations necessary to afford him equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling, but the complaint never identified any specific accommodation requested, any specific modification sought, or any nexus between his disability and the eviction beyond reciting statutory language under § 3604(f)(3).
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss, allowing Hughes's § 1982 and FHA § 3604(a) racial discrimination claims to proceed while dismissing the § 3604(c) discriminatory advertising and § 3604(f) disability discrimination claims for insufficient factual allegations, with leave to amend the dismissed claims.
brief_summary: Trashawn Hughes, a disabled African-American tenant at 1602 Clearview Parkway in Metairie, Louisiana, was evicted by his new landlord Lester Bouchon in August 2023 and alleged racial remarks, racial slurs via text, and discriminatory eviction in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 1982 and the FHA. The court denied dismissal of the § 1982 and FHA § 3604(a) racial discrimination claims, finding that allegations of racial epithets and discriminatory eviction plausibly stated claims, but granted dismissal of the § 3604(c) discriminatory advertising claim (no advertising conduct alleged) and the § 3604(f) disability discrimination claims (no specific accommodation requested, no nexus between disability and eviction alleged). Hughes was granted fifteen days to move for leave to amend the dismissed claims.

key_holding: The court granted St. Tammany's motion to dismiss BCP's claims as moot and Military Road's due process claims as unripe, but denied the motion to dismiss Military Road's Fair Housing Act claims, finding the claims are ripe and not barred by Colorado River abstention.
brief_summary: Military Road Revitalization Company and BCP (developers) sued St. Tammany Parish Government alleging that a moratorium ordinance blocking an affordable housing development violated the Fair Housing Act by having a disparate impact on African Americans, Hispanics, and persons with disabilities, and constituted intentional race-based discrimination. source_file: 9725785_2022_Discovery Real Estate and Development, LLC v. Town of St. Francisville_lamd
case_name: Discovery Real Estate and Development, LLC v. Town of St. Francisville
accommodation_description: No accommodation or modification was requested. This case involved a real estate developer seeking to construct a 155-unit multifamily residential development (the Parker District–St. Francisville) on a 13-acre parcel, which was allegedly blocked by the Town's discriminatory amendments to its Commercial Zoning Ordinance.
key_holding: The court dismissed Discovery's FHA claim without prejudice for lack of standing and ripeness, holding that plaintiff's alleged harm was not traceable to the challenged 2022 CZO amendments because an independent, unchallenged Sewer Capacity Ordinance already prohibited the multifamily development until at least June 2023, making any injury speculative and non-redressable by the relief sought.
brief_summary: Discovery Real Estate and Development, LLC sued the Town of St. Francisville and its Mayor under the FHA, alleging that 2022 amendments to the Town's Commercial Zoning Ordinance were enacted with discriminatory intent and effect to block Discovery's planned 155-unit multifamily development. The court dismissed the FHA claim without prejudice for lack of standing and ripeness, finding that the plaintiff's injury was not traceable to the challenged CZO changes because a separate Sewer Capacity Ordinance—which imposed a moratorium on all major developments and which had not been challenged in the case—independently precluded the development from proceeding until at least June 2023. The court also denied Discovery's motion for a temporary restraining order on the alternative ground that any injury was not imminent and remained speculative given the existing development moratorium.

brief_summary: Plaintiffs Wilbert Aron and Katlin Morris sued G. Lewis-Louisiana No. 2, L.L.C. and Garry Lewis d/b/a Garry Lewis Properties, alleging Defendants violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to make a reasonable accommodation for Aron's disability (recovering drug addiction) by waiving their criminal background policy, resulting in Morris and her children's eviction. The court denied Defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding that Plaintiffs adequately pleaded Aron has a 'handicap' under the FHA because he has a record of impairment from his addiction.

accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was described; the complaint cited Fair Housing Act violations (42 U.S.C. § 3601 et seq.) in a conclusory fashion with no factual allegations identifying any particular accommodation request or discriminatory act.
key_holding: The court dismissed the case without prejudice for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the pro se plaintiffs' complaint contained no factual allegations supporting jurisdiction under the Fair Housing Act or any other cited statute.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Cheryl Fenelon and Barbara Jackson filed a four-sentence complaint against 21 defendants—including federal agencies, federal judges, and private entities—citing Fair Housing Act violations, conspiracy to violate civil rights, and antitrust violations, but included no factual allegations describing how any statute was violated or what any defendant did. case_name: Clinton-Brown v. Hardick
accommodation_description: African American plaintiffs sought to purchase a home in Rhode Island but were refused sale based on their race.
key_holding: The court lacks personal jurisdiction over the Florida-resident defendants under Massachusetts's long-arm statute and venue is improper in Massachusetts because the discriminatory refusal to sell occurred in Rhode Island, so the case must be transferred to the District of Rhode Island.
brief_summary: African American plaintiffs Ebony Clinton-Brown and Todd Brown sued Florida residents Helene and John Hardick, alleging the Hardicks refused to sell them a Rhode Island property because of their race in violation of the Fair Housing Act.
