case_name: Vanderburgh House, LLC v. City of Worcester
accommodation_description: Operators of sober recovery houses requested that the City treat their properties as single-family residences under the State Building Code to continue operating sober housing in residentially zoned areas.
key_holding: The court denied the motion to dismiss on the FHA reasonable accommodation and disparate treatment claims, finding plaintiffs plausibly alleged that the City's enforcement actions were motivated by animus toward disabled persons in recovery; however, the court granted qualified immunity to individual defendants and dismissed the MZA and MCRA claims.
brief_summary: Vanderburgh House and Southbridge RE, operators of two sober living houses in Worcester, sued the City of Worcester after receiving cease-and-desist orders requiring them to reclassify their properties from single-family residences to higher-occupancy categories. The court denied the City's motion to dismiss the FHA reasonable accommodation and disparate treatment claims, finding plaintiffs adequately stated claims that enforcement was motivated by discriminatory animus toward disabled persons in recovery, while dismissing the MZA claim and granting qualified immunity to individual defendants.
key_cases_cited: Astralis Condo. Ass'n v. Sec., U.S. Dept. of Hous. and Urb. Dev., 620 F.3d 62
Summers v. City of Fitchburg, 325 F. Supp. 3d 203
Crossing Over, Inc. v. City of Fitchburg, 98 Mass. App. Ct. 822
Oxford House-C v. City of St. Louis, 843 F. Supp. 1556
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662

source_file: 9733029_2021_Paulsen v. Great Bridge Attleboro Limited Partnership_mad
case_name: Paulsen v. Great Bridge Attleboro Limited Partnership
accommodation_description: The case involves sexual harassment by a maintenance worker rather than a reasonable accommodation request; plaintiff alleges sex discrimination under the FHA's post-acquisition provisions.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that post-acquisition sexual harassment is actionable under § 3604(b) and § 3617 of the FHA, and that sexual harassment may constitute sex-based discrimination under the FHA, following the weight of authority from other circuits.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Sara Paulsen sued Great Bridge Attleboro Limited Partnership and others alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on sexual harassment by a maintenance worker at her Attleboro, Massachusetts apartment building. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that post-acquisition sexual harassment constitutes discriminatory conduct under the FHA and that sexual harassment claims are cognizable under 42 U.S.C. §§ 3604(b) and 3617.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Rosa v. Lawrence Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Rosa requested permission to modify family composition to add her grandchildren to her household and additional time extensions on her Section 8 voucher search period as an accommodation for her multiple psychiatric and medical disabilities.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the housing authority because Rosa failed to establish a causal link between her disabilities and her inability to find housing, and indefinite requests for additional time beyond the substantial extensions already provided are not reasonable accommodations under the FHA.
brief_summary: Gricely Rosa, a Section 8 voucher holder with mental health disabilities, sued the Lawrence Housing Authority alleging failure to accommodate her requests to modify family composition to add grandchildren and to extend her voucher search time. The court granted summary judgment for the Authority, finding Rosa failed to establish the necessary causal link between her disability and her housing difficulties, and that the Authority had already provided substantial accommodations including multiple extensions totaling fifteen months beyond the standard sixty-day voucher period.

source_file: 9733179_2021_Bellus Real Estate and Management Corporation v. Brodeur_mad
case_name: Bellus Real Estate Services and Management Corporation v. Brodeur
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Bellus sought to lease property for use as sober housing for individuals in recovery from substance abuse; defendant Brodeur refused after learning the intended use.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiff pled sufficient facts to plausibly allege disability discrimination under § 3604(f)(1) where defendant abruptly terminated lease negotiations after learning the property would house individuals in recovery from substance abuse.
brief_summary: Bellus Real Estate Services, a property management company that operates sober housing, sued individual landlords Brodeur alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to rent after learning the property would house individuals in recovery from substance abuse. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the allegations sufficient to state a plausible claim for relief under § 3604(f)(1) because defendant's sudden termination of negotiations upon learning the intended use permitted an inference that the disability of prospective occupants motivated the refusal.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Steele v. HAPHousing
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges race-based harassment by neighbors and failure of landlord to intervene; no accommodation request at issue.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claim against Pedro is barred by res judicata from prior state small claims proceedings, and Way Finders cannot be liable because it had no legal relationship to the alleged harassers and no ability to control their conduct.
brief_summary: Tanya Steele, a Black woman, sued landlord John Pedro Jr. and Section 8 administrator Way Finders alleging they failed to protect her from racial harassment by tenants at a neighboring property in violation of the FHA. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding Steele's claims against Pedro are barred by res judicata from prior small claims proceedings, and Way Finders cannot be liable because it had no legal relationship with the alleged harassers and no power to control their behavior.
key_cases_cited: Francis v. Kings Park Manor, Inc., 992 F.3d 67 (2d Cir. 2021)
Wetzel v. Glen St. Andrew Living Cmty., LLC, 901 F.3d 856 (7th Cir. 2018)

case_name: Linda Valentin, Joel Valentin, and Grace Gable Manoors, LLC v. Town of Natick, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request—this case involves permit denial allegedly based on race, analyzed as intentional discrimination under § 3604 rather than reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: Plaintiffs adequately alleged discriminatory intent under the FHA where the Board subjected them to 29 hearings over 16 months, reversed its interpretations of the New Bylaw after racist neighborhood opposition, and denied their permit while approving comparable projects by white applicants.
brief_summary: Black Haitian couple Linda and Joel Valentin, along with their development company, sued the Town of Natick and its Planning Board alleging racial discrimination in denying their permit to develop a historic property into condominiums, citing racist neighborhood opposition and disparate treatment compared to a similar white-sponsored church project. The court denied in part defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs stated plausible FHA disparate treatment and interference claims under § 3604 and § 3617 based on procedural irregularities, discriminatory intent, and Board acquiescence to racist private opposition.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Kelechi Linardon v. Boston Housing Authority et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges BHA intentionally prevented her from renting housing because of her disability and race while she searched for housing using a MRVP voucher.
key_holding: The City of Boston and Governor Baker were properly dismissed because plaintiff failed to plead specific factual allegations linking either defendant to the housing decisions, and plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction was denied for failure to show likelihood of success on the merits.
brief_summary: Kelechi Linardon, a disabled individual, sued the Boston Housing Authority, City of Boston, and former Governor Charlie Baker alleging they delayed and prevented her from renting housing with a disability accommodation voucher due to her disability and race. The court denied her preliminary injunction and dismissed the City of Boston and Governor Baker for failure to plead sufficient factual allegations to support any claims against them.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

case_name: United States v. Chicopee Housing Authority
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was at issue for the proposed intervenor Fitzgerald; her claim concerned denial of public housing placement as retaliation for refusing to provide favorable testimony in a HUD investigation. The underlying case includes disability discrimination claims on behalf of Clover King, though the specific accommodation requested by King is not described in this opinion.
key_holding: Jean Fitzgerald has an unconditional right to intervene under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(e) as an aggrieved person because she claims injury from the defendants' alleged pattern or practice of coercion, intimidation, and retaliation in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3617, which is among the discriminatory housing practices already alleged by the United States in its amended complaint.
brief_summary: The United States brought suit against the Chicopee Housing Authority and its Executive Director Monica Blazic for a pattern or practice of discrimination based on race, national origin, and disability under the Fair Housing Act, Section 504, and the ADA. Jean Fitzgerald, a former CHA board member who applied for public housing, sought to intervene after Blazic allegedly threatened to withhold housing from Fitzgerald unless she testified favorably for defendants in a HUD investigation, and a board member later reiterated that she would have received housing had she cooperated. The court granted Fitzgerald's motion to intervene as of right, finding she was an 'aggrieved person' under 42 U.S.C. § 3614(e) because her retaliation and coercion claim fell within the § 3617 violations already pleaded by the United States.
key_cases_cited: United States v. Marsten Apartments, Inc., 175 F.R.D. 265 (E.D. Mich. 1997)
United States v. Henry, 519 F. Supp. 2d 618 (E.D. Va. 2007)
B. Fernandez & Hnos., Inc. v. Kellogg USA, Inc., 440 F.3d 541 (1st Cir. 2006)

case_name: René Flores v. First Cambridge Realty Corporation
accommodation_description: No accommodation requested; case concerns refusal to rent based on race and color
key_holding: The plaintiff's motion for judgment on the pleadings was denied because the defendant denied the discriminatory allegations, presenting genuine issues of material fact that must be resolved at trial or after discovery.
brief_summary: Hispanic plaintiff René Flores sued First Cambridge Realty Corporation alleging race and color discrimination when the rental management company's administrative assistant allegedly made discriminatory statements and sent a citizenship questionnaire in December 2022; the court denied the plaintiff's partial motion for judgment on the pleadings because the defendant denied the discriminatory allegations, creating genuine issues of material fact that preclude judgment at this early stage.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dep't of Hous. & Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

case_name: Jeffrey D. Summers v. City of Fitchburg
accommodation_description: Summers requested a reasonable accommodation on August 27, 2021, on behalf of Jeffrey's House's eight disabled residents living on the third floor of 69 High Street, asking that those residents be permitted to remain on the third floor notwithstanding a zoning violation notice; he also subsequently sought ZBA approval to increase total occupancy at the property to 22 residents and to permit use of the third floor for sleeping purposes.
key_holding: The court granted the City of Fitchburg's motion to dismiss all eight counts without prejudice, finding that the FHA/ADA reasonable accommodation claims belonged to Jeffrey's House Inc. (a corporation that Summers cannot represent pro se), and all remaining claims failed on substantive and procedural grounds including municipal immunity for intentional torts, lack of a Monell policy or custom, and absence of a private right of action under the HCDA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jeffrey Summers, President and Director of Jeffrey's House Inc. (operator of sober living homes in Fitchburg, Massachusetts), sued the City of Fitchburg alleging violations of the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act arising from the city's denial of a reasonable accommodation to allow eight disabled residents to occupy the third floor of 69 High Street, as well as racial discrimination in zoning and enforcement decisions. The court dismissed all counts: the FHA/ADA accommodation claims were dismissed because they belonged to Jeffrey's House (a corporation that cannot appear pro se through Summers), the racial discrimination/equal protection claims failed under Monell for lack of an alleged municipal policy or custom, the intentional tort claims were barred by municipal governmental immunity, and the HCDA claim failed because no private right of action exists under that statute.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of N.Y.
In re Victor Publishers, Inc.
Latinos Unidos de Chelsea en Accion v. Secretary of HUD

case_name: Dawn Thompson v. Evolve Bank & Trust and PennyMac Loan Services, LLC
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation is described in this opinion; the ADA claim (42 U.S.C. § 12101) is listed among the federal causes of action in the mortgage origination and servicing context, but the court does not address its substance in this procedural memorandum limited to the remand motion.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion to remand, holding that PennyMac's pre-service removal was procedurally proper because service is not a prerequisite for removal under 28 U.S.C. § 1446(b), and that federal question jurisdiction existed based on the multiple federal law claims alleged in the complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Dawn Thompson sued her mortgagee Evolve Bank & Trust and mortgage servicer PennyMac Loan Services in Worcester County Superior Court, alleging eleven counts of federal and state law violations arising from the origination of her mortgage and the subsequent sale of her Worcester, Massachusetts property. PennyMac removed the action to federal court before either defendant had been served, prompting Thompson to move for remand on the grounds that pre-service removal was procedurally improper. The court denied remand, relying on First Circuit precedent establishing that service is generally not a prerequisite for removal and finding that federal question jurisdiction was plainly established by Thompson's federal claims under the 14th Amendment, ECOA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, FHA regulations, CARES Act, and the ADA.
key_cases_cited: Novak v. Bank of N.Y. Mellon Trust Co., N.A., 783 F.3d 910 (1st Cir. 2015)

case_name: Islam Faisal M.I. Abdelrasoul v. Trustees of Boston University
accommodation_description: Ph.D. student requested to transfer from a studio apartment to a one-bedroom apartment for the next academic year as a disability accommodation for mental health needs.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on his reasonable accommodation claim because he did not explain why a one-bedroom apartment was necessary to ensure equal opportunity to use and enjoy his housing.
brief_summary: A Ph.D. student at Boston University sued the university for failing to accommodate his disability by denying his request to transfer from a studio to a one-bedroom apartment and by refusing to renew his graduate residence lease. The court denied his motion for preliminary injunction, finding he failed to show likelihood of success on the merits because he did not explain why a one-bedroom was necessary for equal housing opportunity, and also failed to demonstrate irreparable harm.
key_cases_cited: Summers v. City of Fitchburg, 940 F.3d 133 (1st Cir. 2019)

case_name: Keating v. Commonwealth of Massachusetts
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint references disability discrimination regarding real estate transactions but does not articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request; court dismissed FHA claim on procedural pleading grounds.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss because plaintiff's 72-page amended complaint failed to comply with federal pleading standards (Rules 8, 9(b), 10) and applicable statutes of limitations, and failed to articulate a coherent FHA claim with specific factual allegations connecting each defendant to the alleged discriminatory conduct.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Michelle Keating sued the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, Town of Groveland, and Edward Jones entities alleging a decades-long fraudulent scheme involving predatory lending, fictitious employment, and discriminatory real estate transactions based on gender, familial status, and disability in connection with properties at 7 Pinewood Lane and 4 Parker Road in Groveland, MA. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss because the amended complaint failed to comply with basic pleading standards, did not specify which defendant did what and when, and was substantially time-barred under applicable statutes of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

source_file: 9738216_2021_Prince George's County, Maryland v. Wells Fargo _ Co._mdd
case_name: Prince George's County, Maryland v. Wells Fargo & Co.
property_city: Prince George's County and Montgomery County
accommodation_description: Discriminatory residential mortgage lending and servicing practices targeting racial minority communities, resulting in foreclosures that allegedly harmed the Counties' tax base and municipal services.
key_holding: The Counties plausibly alleged proximate cause for tax-base and municipal expenditure claims through regression analysis linking Wells Fargo's discriminatory lending to concentrated foreclosures, but the lost municipal income claim (franchise taxes and utility revenue) was dismissed as too attenuated from the alleged discriminatory conduct.
brief_summary: Prince George's County and Montgomery County, Maryland sued Wells Fargo alleging predatory and discriminatory residential mortgage lending practices targeting minority communities violated the FHA, causing concentrated foreclosures that injured the Counties' tax base and increased municipal expenditures. The Court granted in part and denied in part Wells Fargo's motion to dismiss, allowing the tax-base and municipal expenditure claims to proceed based on the Counties' regression analysis showing direct traceable injury, but dismissed the lost municipal income claim as too attenuated from the alleged discriminatory conduct.

case_name: Adam W. E. Stemmons v. Georgia Corso
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested that the landlord provide one week's advance notice with a specific date and time before entering his apartment to make repairs, as an accommodation for his PTSD-related anxiety.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's Motion for Stay seeking injunctive relief requiring the landlord to provide specific entry times, finding plaintiff failed to satisfy the four-prong test for preliminary injunction, particularly failing to demonstrate irreparable harm or likelihood of success on the merits.
brief_summary: Adam Stemmons sued his landlord Georgia Corso under the Fair Housing Act and ADA, alleging he needed one week's advance notice with a specific date and time before landlord entry as an accommodation for his PTSD-related anxiety. The court denied his Motion for Stay seeking injunctive relief because he failed to establish irreparable harm or likelihood of success on the merits, without reaching the substantive merits of his reasonable accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Winter v. Natural Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
Monsanto Co. v. Geertson Seed Farms, 561 U.S. 139 (2010)

case_name: Prince George's County, Maryland v. Wells Fargo & Co.
accommodation_description: N/A - case involves discriminatory mortgage lending practices targeting racial minority communities, not a disability accommodation request
key_holding: The court denied Wells Fargo's motion to certify an interlocutory appeal on the question of proximate cause, finding the proposed question was not a controlling question of law, would not materially advance litigation, and did not present substantial ground for difference of opinion.

The court denied Wells Fargo's motion to certify an interlocutory appeal on proximate cause, concluding the proposed question did not meet the statutory requirements for interlocutory appeal.

source_file: 9738715_2021_Williams v. Arora Hills Homeowners Association Inc._mdd
case_name: Daborah Williams v. Arora Hills Homeowners Association Inc.
subsidy_program: Housing assistance voucher from Montgomery County Housing Opportunities Commission
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; claims are for discriminatory treatment based on race and familial status, retaliation, and hostile environment.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the HOA because plaintiff failed to provide sufficient evidence of discriminatory animus to support her discrimination claim, failed to demonstrate objectively material adverse action for her retaliation claim, and failed to show conduct sufficiently severe or pervasive to constitute hostile environment harassment.
brief_summary: Daborah Williams, an African American mother of eight children renting a home in Clarksburg, Maryland with a Section 8 voucher, sued Arora Hills Homeowners Association alleging discrimination based on race and familial status, retaliation for protected complaints, and hostile environment harassment. The court granted summary judgment for the HOA, finding no evidence of discriminatory animus, no objectively material adverse action for the retaliation claim, and conduct insufficiently severe or pervasive for hostile environment liability.

case_name: Michael Manley, et al. v. Evette L. Threeths, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was requested; plaintiffs alleged general harassment and landlord-tenant disputes rather than a denial of reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The FHA claim was dismissed because plaintiffs failed to allege facts establishing a causal connection between the alleged incidents and their protected characteristics, and explicitly did not claim they were denied any reasonable accommodation.
brief_summary: Michael and Susan Manley sued their landlord Evette Threeths and her agent Baltimore Rent Court Agents, LLC, alleging discrimination based on race, age, disability, and religion under the FHA, ADA, Section 1981, and Rehabilitation Act, along with state law abuse of process claims. The court granted the motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to state a plausible FHA claim because they did not allege a causal connection between the alleged incidents and their protected characteristics, and expressly did not claim they were denied a reasonable accommodation.

case_name: Adam Stemmons v. Georgia Corso
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges defendant refused to permit rent payment via cash or check and refused to address an electricity issue in his apartment.
key_holding: Court denied multiple premature motions including motions to amend, motions for summary judgment, motion to dismiss, discovery motions, and motion for appointed counsel without reaching the merits of plaintiff's FHA or ADA claims.
brief_summary: Adam Stemmons sued landlord Georgia Corso alleging Fair Housing Act and ADA violations arising from her refusal to accept cash/check rent payments and failure to address apartment electricity issues. The court denied numerous procedural motions as premature or moot—including motions to amend, summary judgment motions, a motion to dismiss, discovery requests, and plaintiff's motion for appointed counsel—without conducting any substantive analysis of the underlying housing discrimination claims.

case_name: Dollie Truesdale v. Isabel Mercedes Cumming, et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff challenges Baltimore City's water billing practices and property lien sales, alleging disparate treatment compared to Baltimore County residents — not a disability accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed the action for lack of standing because plaintiff failed to allege a causal connection between the named defendants (city inspectors and solicitors) and the injuries she suffered from water billing and property sales — the officials were not responsible for installing water meters, placing liens, or selling properties.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Dollie Truesdale sued Baltimore City Inspector General and City Solicitor officials alleging Fair Housing Act and Civil Rights Act claims challenging disparities in water billing and property lien sales compared to Baltimore County. The court dismissed the action for lack of standing because the named defendants were not causally connected to the injuries alleged — they neither caused the water billing practices nor ordered the property sales.

case_name: Lawrence Bailey et al. v. PHH Mortgage Corporation et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, African American homeowners, allege that mortgage servicers' policies regarding forced place insurance, loan servicing, and implementation of loan modification agreements discriminated against them based on race.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' disparate treatment claim for failure to allege they were treated differently than similarly situated borrowers of a different race, and dismissed the disparate impact claim for failure to provide statistical evidence establishing a robust causal connection between defendants' policies and disparate effects on African-American homeowners.
brief_summary: Lawrence and Deborah Bailey, African American homeowners, sued PHH Mortgage Corporation, HSBC Bank USA, and Ocwen Loan Servicing alleging racial discrimination in mortgage servicing practices, including forced place insurance policies and failure to honor loan modification agreements. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act claims, finding plaintiffs failed to plead a prima facie case of disparate treatment (no comparison to similarly situated borrowers) and disparate impact (no statistical evidence of causation).

case_name: Adams v. Cameron
accommodation_description: Black employee alleged that defendant employer assigned him to substandard, unsanitary employee housing while non-Black employees received better housing; no disability accommodation request was made.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of the FHA race discrimination claim (Count 6) because Adams adequately alleged disparate treatment theory by claiming Black employees were restricted to substandard housing while non-Black employees received better housing conditions.
brief_summary: Damon Adams, a Black man formerly employed by Rod and Reel, Inc., sued his employer and individual managers alleging race discrimination in housing, wrongful termination for complaining about unsanitary housing conditions, and violations of state housing and employment laws. The court denied dismissal of Adams's FHA race discrimination claim under § 3604(b) based on allegations that Black employees were assigned only to substandard housing while non-Black employees received better units, but granted dismissal of the hostile work environment claim and certain state law claims.

brief_summary: Prince George's County and Montgomery County, Maryland sued Wells Fargo alleging the bank engaged in predatory and discriminatory mortgage lending, servicing, and foreclosure practices in violation of the FHA, causing property tax revenue losses and increased municipal expenditures. Wells Fargo & Co.

case_name: Stemmons v. Corso
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to pay rent in cash instead of electronically via Zelle, as a reasonable accommodation for his PTSD requiring schedule consistency and limited disruption.
key_holding: The preliminary injunction motion was denied as moot because the plaintiff had voluntarily vacated the premises, rendering any eviction-related injunction request non-justiciable; additionally, the plaintiff failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits of his FHA reasonable accommodation claim regarding rent payment method.
brief_summary: Adam Stemmons, a tenant with PTSD, sued his landlord Georgia Corso alleging violations of the Fair Housing Act for failing to accommodate his disability regarding rent payment methods and notice requirements. The court denied Stemmons' motion for preliminary injunction to block evictions, finding the motion moot because Stemmons had voluntarily vacated the property in September 2021, and alternatively that Stemmons failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits.

case_name: Tamara Johnson, et al. v. City of Annapolis
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege the City failed to inspect and license public housing properties, creating discriminatory conditions in violation of the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The court denied the City's motion to dismiss, finding that the Johnson plaintiffs' claims are not precluded by the White consent decree, the absent parties are not indispensable, and the suit is not an impermissible collateral attack; the court also declined to dismiss based on statute of limitations, finding questions of fact about whether the non-inspection policy constituted a continuing violation.
brief_summary: Public housing residents filed a class action against the City of Annapolis alleging the City's longstanding policy of not inspecting and licensing public housing properties disparately impacted African American residents in violation of the Fair Housing Act and civil rights laws. The court denied the City's motion to dismiss, rejecting arguments that the claims were barred by the prior White consent decree, that indispensable parties were missing, and that the suit was an impermissible collateral attack.

case_name: Mian v. LoanCare Servicing Company
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a mortgage forbearance from his loan servicers after defaulting on three months of payments in 2019, claiming it was denied due to his race; defendants' own documentation showed forbearance was available only to borrowers intending to keep their homes, whereas plaintiff had expressly stated his intention to sell.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings, holding that plaintiff failed to state cognizable claims under ECOA, FHA § 3605, or 42 U.S.C. § 1981 because he did not allege facts showing he was qualified for a forbearance or that discriminatory animus motivated its denial, and also dismissed his Maryland Consumer Protection Act and Paperwork Reduction Act claims.
brief_summary: Mohammad Aslam Mian, a retiree who defaulted on his mortgage held by LoanCare/NewRez/Fannie Mae, sued alleging racial discrimination in the denial of his forbearance request, violations of the Maryland Consumer Protection Act (Md. Code Ann. § 13-316), and violations of the Paperwork Reduction Act. The court granted defendants' motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding that Mian's discrimination claims under ECOA, FHA § 3605, and § 1981 were insufficiently pled because he never alleged his qualifications for a forbearance, failed to identify any comparators or discriminatory policy, and offered only conclusory assertions of racial animus. His MCPA claim failed for lack of alleged economic damages, and his PRA claim failed because no private right of action exists under that statute.

case_name: Hesman Tall v. Commissioner of the Howard County Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an extension of the Housing Choice Voucher term beyond the standard expiration date to allow time to repair credit damaged by identity theft before securing a lease.
key_holding: The court granted the motion to dismiss because plaintiff failed to allege any facts demonstrating he has a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities, which is required to state a claim under both the ADA and FHA.
brief_summary: Hesman Tall, a Black pro se plaintiff who receives Social Security disability benefits, sued the Howard County Housing Authority seeking an extension of his Section 8 voucher term as a reasonable accommodation for disability-related circumstances caused by identity theft. The court granted the motion to dismiss, finding that while plaintiff submitted evidence of receiving disability benefits, he failed to allege any facts showing he has a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits major life activities as required to state a claim under the ADA or FHA.

case_name: Jerome Want v. Saundra Jones, Wayne Jones, City of Hagerstown, MD., Michael Sabol, Salvatore & Morton
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested by the plaintiff; his allegations centered on the landlord's failure to make physical repairs to the apartment (holes in the bathroom floor, plumbing leaks from an upper unit, dirty wooden floors, and holes allowing mice to enter), which the court found did not constitute a request for or denial of a reasonable accommodation under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B).
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because the plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts to support his FHA or ADA claims, and diversity jurisdiction was unavailable as the parties were not citizens of different states.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jerome Want sued his landlord, the City of Hagerstown, a city housing inspector, and a law firm over his deteriorating apartment, alleging violations of the FHA, ADA, and various state law claims. The court found Want's ADA claim failed because his landlord is not a public entity and his apartment is not a public accommodation, and his FHA claim failed because he alleged no discriminatory conduct in leasing and no refusal of a reasonable accommodation. Lacking viable federal claims and unable to establish diversity jurisdiction because most parties were Maryland citizens, the complaint was dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

key_holding: The court found plaintiffs adequately alleged group pleading and standing to sue the corporate defendants, but dismissed certain claims including breach of management contract (no third-party beneficiary status) and discriminatory advertising; the court permitted disparate impact and perpetuation of segregation claims to proceed past the motion to dismiss stage.
brief_summary: CASA de Maryland and seven Hispanic tenant plaintiffs sued Arbor Realty Trust and related entities alleging that defendants' financialization, harvesting, divestment, and outsourcing policies result in discriminatory maintenance and repair of multifamily housing in Langley Park, Maryland, constituting disparate impact based on national origin and perpetuation of segregation in violation of the Fair Housing Act. case_name: Ronald Satish Emrit v. Hagerstown Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requests priority placement on Section 8 housing voucher waiting list based on his schizoaffective and bipolar disorder.
key_holding: The complaint was dismissed for failure to state a cognizable claim because plaintiff provided no factual narrative supporting his conclusory Fair Housing Act allegations and HUD regulations do not create a right to a particular position on a housing voucher waiting list.
brief_summary: Ronald Satish Emrit, proceeding pro se, sued the Hagerstown Housing Authority and HUD seeking a Section 8 housing voucher priority based on his schizoaffective and bipolar disorders, alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The court dismissed the complaint as frivolous for failure to state a claim, finding the allegations conclusory and unsupported by factual narrative, and noting that HUD regulations do not grant applicants any right to a particular position on a housing waiting list.

case_name: Ronald Satish Emrit v. Queen Anne's Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff with schizoaffective and bipolar disorder seeks priority placement on Section 8 housing waiting list as a reasonable accommodation for disability.
key_holding: HUD regulations do not grant applicants any right to a particular position on a housing authority waiting list, and courts have consistently held that housing authorities have discretion to determine waiting list placement, so plaintiff's claim that he should receive priority due to disability fails to state a cognizable claim.
brief_summary: Ronald Emrit, a self-represented plaintiff with schizoaffective and bipolar disorder, sued the Queen Anne's Housing Authority and HUD seeking priority placement on Section 8 waiting lists and a housing voucher as a reasonable accommodation. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, holding that HUD regulations expressly provide no right to a particular waiting list position and housing authorities have sole discretion in managing waiting lists.

brief_summary: Ms. Cooper, a tenant receiving housing assistance through the Housing Authority of Baltimore City, sued ten HABC employees in their individual capacities alleging they retaliated against her for filing prior lawsuits including a 2015 sexual harassment complaint and 2018 race discrimination complaint. key_holding: The court denied the defendants' motions for summary judgment, finding that genuine issues of material fact exist regarding the validity of the plaintiffs' investigation methodology, whether a specific policy caused the statistical disparity, and whether robust causation exists between the defendants' practices and the observed racial disparities.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to rent an apartment at Oaklee Village and was denied after submitting income verification including Social Security Disability Award Letter.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege that Defendants knew of the nature of his impairment or that they were motivated by his disability in denying his rental application, as the documented income requirements—rather than disability status—appeared to be the basis for the denial.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Travis Jones sued Blue Ocean Realty LLC and Oaklee Village Baltimore LLC alleging Fair Housing Act and ADA claims after being denied rental of an apartment when his income verification (including Social Security Disability benefits) did not satisfy the property's income requirements. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding Plaintiff failed to plausibly allege disability discrimination because he did not identify his impairment, did not allege Defendants knew of the nature of his impairment, and provided no facts suggesting disability motivated the denial rather than documented income deficiencies.

case_name: Tamara Johnson, et al. v. City of Annapolis
subsidy_program: Public Housing (Capital Fund and Operating Fund)
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it involves a class of public housing residents challenging the City of Annapolis's non-inspection policy as racially discriminatory under the Fair Housing Act.
key_holding: The court denied HACA's motion to dismiss the City's third-party indemnification and contribution claims because the City plausibly alleged that HACA's failure to maintain properties was the primary cause of plaintiffs' injuries, but granted HUD's motion to dismiss because the City lacked Article III standing—failing to show injury-in-fact separate from residents' harm, causation between HUD's actions and the City's alleged injuries, and redressability of any injury through a favorable ruling.
brief_summary: Named plaintiffs Tamara Johnson and Tyonna Holliday, representing a class of Annapolis public housing residents, sued the City of Annapolis alleging its non-inspection policy for HACA properties disproportionately impacted African American residents in violation of the Fair Housing Act; the City subsequently filed third-party complaints against HACA and HUD seeking indemnification and contribution. The court denied HACA's motion to dismiss the City's third-party claims but granted HUD's motion to dismiss, finding the City lacked Article III standing because it failed to demonstrate injury-in-fact separate from the residents' harm, causation between its alleged injuries and HUD's conduct, and redressability.

key_holding: The court denied defendant's motion to dismiss, holding that FHA exemptions under § 3603(b) are affirmative defenses that defendant bears the burden of pleading and proving, and plaintiff sufficiently alleged a quiet enjoyment claim based on sexual harassment and stalking by the landlord.

case_name: Nathan Connolly & Shani Mott v. Shane Lanham, et al.
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification; rather, it concerns allegations of intentional racial discrimination in a home appraisal conducted in connection with a mortgage refinance application.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that plaintiffs plausibly alleged intentional race discrimination in a home appraisal and mortgage refinancing transaction under the FHA (§ 3605), ECOA, Civil Rights Act (§§ 1981, 1982), and Maryland Fair Housing Laws, while dismissing the § 3604 FHA claim and Count V, and denying plaintiffs' motion to dismiss the appraiser's defamation counterclaims.
brief_summary: Dr. Nathan Connolly and Dr. Shani Mott, a Black married couple in Baltimore, sued appraiser Shane Lanham and lender loanDepot after their home was appraised at $472,000 during a 2021 refinance application—only to be appraised at $750,000 seven months later after plaintiffs removed markers of Black identity and had a white colleague stand in as the homeowner. The court found plaintiffs plausibly alleged intentional racial discrimination, pointing to Lanham's selection of comparable properties from majority-Black census blocks and loanDepot's failure to properly process plaintiffs' discrimination complaint, and allowed most claims to proceed. The court also denied plaintiffs' motion to dismiss Lanham's counterclaims for defamation and false light invasion of privacy arising from plaintiffs' media statements about the alleged discrimination.

case_name: Edward Siguel v. King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc.

brief_summary: Edward Siguel, a disabled individual with mobility limitations causing pain and bleeding with movement, sued King Farm Citizens Assembly, Inc. (a homeowners' association) and others, alleging the HOA violated the Fair Housing Act by denying his requests for modifications including storage sheds, a brick patio, trellis, and modifications to a balcony structure. On motion to dismiss, the court dismissed most claims finding the requests lacked direct nexus to his disability, but allowed the storage shed claims to proceed because Plaintiff adequately alleged the sheds would reduce his painful movement when accessing gardening tools.

accommodation_description: Class action settlement for tenants alleging Defendants failed to maintain and repair apartments, with discrimination through deficient housing conditions as the basis for FHA claim
key_holding: The court granted preliminary approval of the $3,000,000 settlement fund, finding the settlement terms fair, reasonable, and adequate in comparison to potential per-apartment damages of $18,798 per year under Maryland law, given the risks of litigation and the strength of the case.
brief_summary: CASA de Maryland and individual tenants sued Arbor Realty Trust and related entities alleging that Defendants failed to maintain and repair Bedford and Victoria Station apartment complexes, and discriminated against tenants through deficient housing conditions in violation of the Fair Housing Act, Prince George's County Code, and Maryland common law. The court granted preliminary approval of a $3,000,000 class settlement, finding the settlement terms fair and adequate given the $18,798 potential per-year recovery at trial versus the estimated average recovery of $4,750 per year under the settlement, and certified the settlement class of approximately 2,356 current and former tenants.
key_cases_cited: Amchem Prods., Inc. v. Windsor, 521 U.S. 591 (1997)

source_file: 9742748_2023_Group Home on Gibson Island, LLC v. Gibson Island Corporation_mdd
case_name: Group Home on Gibson Island, LLC v. Gibson Island Corporation
accommodation_description: Request to waive restrictive covenant prohibiting 'business purpose' use to permit operation of a state-licensed assisted living group home for nine seniors with disabilities on Gibson Island
key_holding: Plaintiffs failed to establish that removing the four disputed conditions in the accommodation agreement (Guarantor Provision, Dispute Resolution Provision, Septic Provision, and Arbitration Escrow Provision) was 'necessary' to provide disabled residents an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the Banbury Property under the reasonable accommodation analysis.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Group Home on Gibson Island and Assisted Living Well Compassionate Care sued Gibson Island Corporation seeking a reasonable accommodation to waive restrictive covenants prohibiting business use, so they could operate an assisted living group home for disabled seniors on the private island community. The court granted GIC's motion for summary judgment, finding plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that removing four disputed conditions from the proposed accommodation agreement was 'necessary' to provide disabled residents equal housing opportunity under the Fair Housing Act.

case_name: Rosanna Bailey v. The Queen's Landing Council of Unit Owners, Inc.
accommodation_description: Request for installation of video cameras and motion detecting lights (not framed as disability accommodation)
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint because her FHA claims are barred by claim preclusion from prior state court litigation, time-barred by the two-year statute of limitations, and fail to allege sufficient facts to state plausible claims of racial discrimination or retaliation.
brief_summary: Dr. Rosanna Bailey, a Black woman with disabilities, sued her condominium association alleging race, sex, and disability discrimination and retaliation under the FHA regarding unequal maintenance, delayed door repairs, and differential treatment compared to white neighbors. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, finding most claims precluded by a prior state court judgment, time-barred, or failing to state plausible claims without sufficient factual allegations of discriminatory intent.

source_file: 9742964_2024_Affinity Recovery Center LLC v. Town Commissioners of Sudlersville_mdd
case_name: Affinity Recovery Center LLC v. Town Commissioners of Sudlersville
accommodation_description: Affinity Recovery Center, a substance abuse treatment facility operator, requested a special exception to the Town of Sudlersville's zoning permit to operate a 16-bed residential treatment facility, which would exceed the zoning code's 8-resident limit for group homes.
key_holding: The court dismissed Affinity's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because the complaint failed to allege facts showing that a 16-bed facility was necessary to afford disabled persons equal housing opportunity—the only proffered reason was economic non-viability, not a direct linkage to disability needs.
brief_summary: Affinity Recovery Center LLC sued the Town Commissioners of Sudlersville, Maryland, alleging that the town's denial of a special exception to operate a 16-bed residential substance abuse treatment facility violated the ADA and FHA. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that the zoning code's 8-resident limitation applied equally to all group homes and did not facially discriminate against substance abuse treatment facilities, and that Affinity failed to plausibly allege a reasonable accommodation claim because economic non-viability does not establish that a 16-bed facility is necessary to afford disabled persons equal housing opportunity.

source_file: 9742978_2024_CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor and City Council Of Baltimore_mdd
case_name: CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore
accommodation_description: Permit approval to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility for persons with disabilities, framed as a reasonable accommodation from zoning requirements rather than an individual tenant accommodation
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the City on the estoppel claim because CMDS failed to establish reliance on the zoning verification letter and building permit, dismissed the judicial review claim under Burford abstention, and denied both parties' motions on the discrimination claims because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether the City denied the permit based on discriminatory animus toward persons with substance use disorders.
brief_summary: CMDS Residential, LLC sued Baltimore City after the City denied its permit to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility, claiming the denial violated the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, Fair Housing Act, and constitutional protections for persons with disabilities. The court granted summary judgment for the City on the estoppel claim (finding CMDS failed to prove reliance), dismissed the state-law judicial review claim under Burford abstention, but allowed the federal disability discrimination and equal protection claims to proceed because genuine factual disputes exist regarding whether community opposition was based on discriminatory animus toward the facility's future patients.

source_file: 9743091_2024_Estate of DaMon R. Fisher v. City of Annapolis_mdd
case_name: Estate of DaMon R. Fisher, et al. v. City of Annapolis, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request was made; this is a disparate impact challenge to the City's policy exempting HACA properties from licensing and inspection requirements.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motions for partial summary judgment because the statistical evidence comparing HACA property populations to the general City population used an improper comparator; the proper comparison should be between HACA renters and all City renters, and additional discovery is needed to establish proximate cause for the certified class period.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs, including the Estate of DaMon R. Fisher and a certified class of HACA tenants, sued the City of Annapolis alleging that the City's policy of exempting Housing Authority properties from rental licensing and inspection requirements violated the Fair Housing Act by disproportionately affecting Black residents who comprise over 90% of HACA populations. The court denied plaintiffs' motions for partial summary judgment, finding that while statistical evidence demonstrated significant racial disparity, the expert analysis used an improper comparator population and insufficient evidence linked the non-enforcement policy to specific harms during the class period, warranting additional discovery.

case_name: Tamara Johnson, et al. v. City of Annapolis
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - The case challenges the City's non-enforcement policy of HACA property inspections as racially discriminatory under disparate impact theory; the accommodation at issue is not a traditional reasonable accommodation but rather municipal enforcement of housing code requirements.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motions for partial summary judgment because they failed to establish a prima facie disparate impact case—their statistical analysis improperly compared HACA property populations to the general City population rather than to other rental households subject to the licensing policy, and they lacked sufficient evidence of harmful conditions during the class period (May 2019 to May 2021).
brief_summary: HACA residents and class members sued the City of Annapolis alleging the City's policy of exempting HACA public housing properties from rental licensing and inspection requirements violated the Fair Housing Act on a disparate impact theory. The court denied plaintiffs' motions for partial summary judgment, finding their statistical analysis compared the wrong populations and failed to establish sufficient evidence of harm during the relevant class period.

case_name: Deborah Morris, et al. v. Memorial Development Partners, LP, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged defendants failed to provide critical services to elderly and disabled residents, including failing to maintain functioning elevators, failing to install a stairway chair lift, and failing to provide support services and dispute resolution procedures for disabled tenants.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss—rejecting both the two-dismissal rule and failure-to-prosecute arguments—but granted the motion for a more definite statement, ordering plaintiffs to file a second amended complaint within 28 days that clearly identifies the jurisdictional basis, applicable statutes, and factual support for each claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Deborah Morris and Arnell Mason sued their Baltimore apartment complex's owner, developer, and management company alleging widespread habitability deficiencies and failure to provide critical services to elderly and disabled residents, citing the Fair Housing Act and ADA among other statutes. Defendants moved to dismiss based on the two-dismissal rule and failure to prosecute, or alternatively for a more definite statement. The court denied outright dismissal, finding the two-dismissal rule inapplicable because the Maryland case was dismissed by court order (not voluntarily) and finding no bad faith failure to prosecute, but granted the motion for a more definite statement because the amended complaint was excessively long, disorganized, and insufficiently clear as to the legal and jurisdictional basis for each claim.

source_file: 9743192_2024_CASA de Maryland, Inc. v. Arbor Realty Trust, Inc._mdd
case_name: CASA de Maryland, Inc. v. Arbor Realty Trust, Inc.
accommodation_description: This is a housing conditions class action (poor maintenance and repair), not a disability accommodation case; the surviving claims were breach of contract and breach of implied warranty of habitability under state law, not reasonable accommodation claims.
key_holding: The court granted final approval of the $3 million class settlement, approved $900,000 in attorneys' fees (30% of the fund), $78,965.18 in litigation expenses, $27,701 in settlement administration costs, and $7,500 incentive payments to each of seven named plaintiffs, finding the settlement fair, reasonable, and adequate.
brief_summary: CASA de Maryland and seven named tenants sued Bedford United, LLC, Victoria United, LLC, and related parties alleging that defendants failed to maintain and repair apartments at Bedford Station and Victoria Station complexes, initially bringing Fair Housing Act and state law claims. After the court dismissed the FHA claims, the parties reached a $3 million settlement covering current and former tenants who resided at the properties between July 2018 and May 2022, and the court granted final approval of the settlement, attorneys' fees, expenses, and incentive payments.

case_name: CMDS Residential, LLC v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore
accommodation_description: CMDS sought to operate a residential substance-abuse treatment facility at 6040 Harford Road, which was denied when the city required City Council approval after community opposition.
key_holding: The court denied the City's motion for reconsideration, adhering to its prior ruling that the 'motivating factor' causation standard applies to ADA Title II and FHA claims, and finding that Gentry did not abrogate Baird's controlling precedent.
brief_summary: CMDS Residential, LLC sued the City of Baltimore after the city denied its application for a use and occupancy permit to open a residential substance-abuse treatment facility, claiming the denial was motivated by discriminatory community opposition based on stereotypes about people with substance use disorders. The court denied the City's motion for reconsideration, adhering to its prior ruling that the 'motivating factor' causation standard governs ADA Title II and FHA claims and that Gentry v. E.W. Partners Club Management Co. did not abrogate Baird's controlling precedent establishing that standard.

case_name: Iguade v. First Home Mortgage Corporation
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation requested; this is a race discrimination claim in mortgage lending under ECOA and FHA § 3605.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' race discrimination claims under ECOA and FHA because plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts showing intentional race-based discrimination or that similarly situated non-minority applicants received more favorable treatment, and also failed to identify a neutral policy causing disparate impact.
brief_summary: Black plaintiffs Oseghae and Maurice Iguade sued First Home Mortgage Corporation alleging race discrimination under ECOA and FHA when their mortgage loan application to purchase a home in Baltimore, Maryland was denied. The court granted First Home's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to state plausible discrimination claims because they did not allege facts showing discriminatory intent, establish they were qualified for the loan, identify similarly situated non-minority applicants treated more favorably, or identify a neutral policy causing disparate impact.

key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' reasonable accommodation claim as moot because the County returned the dogs to plaintiffs and the administrative commission determined the dogs are not Pit Bull Terriers subject to the ordinance.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Denise Venero and others sued Prince George's County Maryland challenging the County's Pit Bull Ordinance and seeking to keep their dogs (Bella and Mimi), classified as emotional support animals, without enforcement of the ordinance. The court granted the County's motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs lacked standing because their dogs were returned and the Commission determined the dogs are not Pit Bull Terriers, and further finding the reasonable accommodation claim moot.

case_name: Karen Lundregan v. Housing Opportunities Commission
accommodation_description: Request for reinstatement of Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher as reasonable accommodation for mental health disabilities (PTSD, Borderline Personality Disorder) following alleged improper termination.
key_holding: The court found genuine disputes of material fact exist as to whether HOC violated the FHA by improperly determining, without objective evidence and based only on unverified allegations from a biased former landlord, that plaintiff posed a direct threat, and by attaching unduly invasive conditions to the accommodation approval, thereby delaying restoration of her voucher for several months.
brief_summary: Karen Lundregan, a disabled tenant with PTSD and Borderline Personality Disorder, sued the Housing Opportunities Commission of Montgomery County and employee Ethan Cohen alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by improperly delaying or denying her reasonable accommodation request to reinstate her Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher for approximately five months (April-September 2018) without sufficient evidence and without providing her a hearing. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact remain as to whether defendants relied improperly on unverified allegations from a biased landlord without conducting an individualized assessment before concluding plaintiff posed a direct threat, and whether the delay in reinstating her voucher constituted constructive denial of her accommodation request.
key_cases_cited: Corey v. Secretary, HUD ex rel. Walker, 719 F.3d 322 (4th Cir. 2013)

case_name: Dr. Paul C. Clark, Sr., et al. v. Council of Unit Owners of the 100 Harborview Drive Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege the defendant HOA took retaliatory actions (removal of possessions, imposition of unauthorized fees, publication of litigation updates) in response to plaintiffs' prior exercise of Fair Housing Act rights.

brief_summary: Dr. Paul Clark and family sued the 100 Harborview Drive Condominium Association alleging the HOA retaliated against them for exercising Fair Housing Act rights in connection with disputes over unit conditions and remediation. This opinion addresses discovery disputes regarding search of Board Members' private email accounts and sufficiency of Defendant's privilege log. The court ordered Defendant to conduct a limited search of current Board Members' private emails for responsive communications and to produce documents the court found were not protected by attorney-client privilege or work product.

brief_summary: Deborah Morris and Arnell Mason, pro se elderly/disabled tenants at Linden Park Apartments in Baltimore, sued their landlord and property management company alleging Fair Housing Act violations, ADA claims, and RICO claims based on various housing conditions and business practices. accommodation_description: Plaintiff's Amended Complaint references failure to provide reasonable accommodations in violation of 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(1), but no specific accommodation request is clearly identified in the opinion; the complaint mentions Plaintiff requested a walk-through inspection given his disability.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA housing discrimination claims were dismissed as time-barred because they were filed nearly eleven months after the two-year statute of limitations expired, and neither equitable tolling based on COVID-19 nor the continuing violation doctrine applied to excuse the late filing.
brief_summary: Travis R. Jones, a physically disabled individual, sued Blue Ocean Realty, LLC and Oaklee Village Baltimore, LLC alleging they refused to rent him an apartment and failed to provide reasonable accommodations in violation of the FHA. accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer to a different apartment unit and ultimately to a subsidized apartment due to her disabilities including cardiomyopathy, hypertension, and anxiety disorder.
key_holding: Vantage satisfied its reasonable accommodation obligation by offering comparable units at comparable prices; the FHA does not require landlords to accommodate changes in a tenant's financial status or roommate situation.

key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for defendant because plaintiff, proceeding pro se, failed to respond to defendant's summary judgment motion and failed to file objections to the Magistrate Judge's Report and Recommendation, thereby waiving her right to appeal and releasing the court from its duty of independent review.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Shana Smallwood sued IA Properties alleging the company refused to rent her an apartment because of her race, bringing claims under the Fair Housing Act, Fair Credit Reporting Act, and Equal Credit Opportunity Act. case_name: Larry Lee v. Washtenaw County et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested placement in a shelter that would either allow separation from men or have a security system (on-site employee or camera), due to recent sexual assault and mental health conditions.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim fails because CMH is a mental health agency that assists clients in accessing housing rather than a housing provider itself, and the FHA applies only to providers of housing.
brief_summary: Larry Lee, a transgender individual with mental health conditions including PTSD and depression, sued Washtenaw County, its Community Mental Health agency (CMH), and two social workers after being directed to sleep in a parking garage and subsequently sexually assaulted. The court granted summary judgment for defendants on the Fair Housing Act claim, finding that CMH is a mental health agency that assists clients in accessing housing rather than a housing provider to whom the FHA's reasonable accommodation requirements apply.

case_name: Douglas J. Johnson v. East Tawas Housing Commission

key_holding: Plaintiff failed to state an FHA claim because he did not identify any physical or mental impairment that substantially limits major life activities, and his complaints about apartment maintenance are not cognizable federal claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Douglas Johnson, a Section 8 tenant at Bay Park Tower North, sued East Tawas Housing Commission alleging discrimination and failure to accommodate his disability by not fixing heavy doors and maintaining the garbage chute. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to identify any qualifying disability under the FHA, ADA, or Rehabilitation Act, and complaints about apartment maintenance are not individually enforceable federal rights.

brief_summary: Tenants sued their landlord and property management company alleging race discrimination (refusing to rent to Black tenants, providing preferential repairs to white tenants), retaliation for protesting discriminatory practices, and related state law claims. source_file: 9750016_2021_Tranchmontagne v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development_mied
case_name: Tranchmontagne v. United States Department of Housing and Urban Development
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation is described in the case text; the complaint references 'prior accommodation requests' only as the predicate for the retaliation claim, without identifying the nature or content of those requests.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims against HUD on sovereign immunity grounds and for failure to state a claim, and dismissed all claims against MSHDA and its Acting Director under Eleventh Amendment immunity (with limited ADA/Rehabilitation Act exceptions that still failed on the merits), because plaintiff did not plausibly allege that her voucher was terminated because of her disability rather than due to documented program violations.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Deanna Tranchmontagne challenged the termination of her Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher by MSHDA, alleging her voucher was terminated because of her disabilities and in retaliation for prior accommodation requests, in violation of the Fair Housing Act, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and the Constitution. The court dismissed all claims against federal defendant HUD for lack of subject matter jurisdiction based on sovereign immunity and failure to state a claim, and dismissed all claims against state defendants MSHDA and Acting Director Heidel under Eleventh Amendment immunity and Rule 12(b)(6) failure to state a claim. Plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction was also denied because she had no likelihood of success on the merits.

case_name: Geoffrey Leonard, et al. v. Nokel LLC, et al.
accommodation_description: This is a race discrimination case, not a reasonable accommodation case; plaintiffs allege defendants discriminated against Black tenants and prospective tenants by refusing to rent to them and providing unequal repair services.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state plausible claims for intentional race discrimination, disparate impact, or retaliation under the FHA because plaintiffs' allegations are conclusory and unsupported by specific factual allegations demonstrating how defendants' actions were motivated by race.
brief_summary: Non-Black tenants (Leonard, Misumi, Messer) sued their landlords (Nokel LLC and individuals) alleging race discrimination against Black tenants and prospective tenants, claiming defendants refused to rent to qualified Black applicants and provided unequal repair services to force Black tenants to move out. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to allege sufficient facts to plausibly support claims for intentional race discrimination, disparate impact, or retaliation under the Fair Housing Act.

case_name: Rhonda Henderson, et al. v. Vision Property Management, LLP, et al.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case. The claims center on racial discrimination through a predatory lease-with-option-to-purchase (LOP) program that allegedly targeted Black prospective homebuyers with abusive credit terms and had both disparate impact and discriminatory intent against Black communities in Southeast Michigan.
key_holding: The court denied Atalaya Capital Management and ACM Vision V's motion to dismiss, holding that plaintiffs adequately alleged plausible claims under the Fair Housing Act (§§ 3604, 3605), the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, and the Truth in Lending Act based on their alleged participation in a predatory lease-with-option-to-purchase scheme that discriminatorily targeted Black homebuyers in Southeast Michigan.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Black homebuyers filed a class action alleging that Vision Property Management and related entities, including funders Atalaya Capital Management and ACM Vision V, operated a predatory lease-with-option-to-purchase program that intentionally targeted Black communities in the greater Detroit area with abusive credit terms and virtually no realistic path to homeownership. Atalaya and ACM moved to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), arguing the complaint failed to state plausible claims against them. The court denied the motion in full, finding plaintiffs adequately pleaded FHA, ECOA, and TILA claims by alleging Atalaya funded and helped design the discriminatory scheme, and ACM held title to properties acquired through it.

case_name: McCree v. KMG Prestiege Company
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request was identified; complaint broadly alleged stigma discrimination, harassment, threats to evict, and refusal to renew lease without specifying any accommodation request.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's complaint with prejudice for failure to state a claim because plaintiff failed to allege facts demonstrating she is disabled, failed to connect any landlord action to a protected characteristic, and failed to identify any specific statute or constitutional right violated.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Herlandos McCree, a Section 8 voucher recipient, sued KMG Prestige Company and individual defendants alleging housing discrimination based on stigma and disability, including threats to evict and refusal to renew her lease. The court granted in forma pauperis status but dismissed the complaint with prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim, finding plaintiff failed to identify her disability, connect any landlord action to a protected characteristic, or identify a valid legal theory under the FHA or ADA.

case_name: Williams v. Huron Pines Condominium Association
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a request for reasonable accommodation or reasonable modification under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f). The FHA claims rest on alleged racial disparate treatment in the enforcement of condominium assessment collection procedures and maintenance obligations under § 3604(b) and § 3617.
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part defendants' Rule 12(b)(6) motion to dismiss, allowing all four federal claims (FHA §§ 3604(b) and 3617, and 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982) and two state law claims (breach of fiduciary duty and membership oppression) to proceed because plaintiff's allegations of racial disparate treatment were facially plausible, while dismissing both breach of contract claims because the bylaws unambiguously authorized the challenged conduct.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Alf Williams, the only African American resident in a 38-unit condominium community, sued the Huron Pines Condominium Association and its three board directors alleging racial discrimination after the new board filed a lien and pursued a money judgment against him for unpaid annual assessments—while prior boards had allowed white co-owners to fall years behind without similar consequences—and also refused to perform storm water retention maintenance and septic tank cleaning required by the bylaws. The court found plaintiff plausibly alleged disparate treatment under the FHA's continuing violations doctrine, surviving the statute of limitations challenge, and that the McDonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework does not apply at the pleading stage. The court dismissed both breach of contract claims because the bylaws expressly authorized the board's enforcement actions and the discontinuation of services for defaulting members, but allowed the fiduciary duty and membership oppression claims to survive due to defendants' underdeveloped briefing.

case_name: Thornton v. Caramagno
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges that defendants refused to sell her a property and sold it to another buyer for $25,000 less after learning she is African American.
key_holding: The court found sufficient factual allegations to state a plausible claim of racial discrimination under the FHA, noting that defendants reversed the sale after learning plaintiff's race and sold the property for $25,000 less than plaintiff's offer, permitting a reasonable inference of racial animus.
brief_summary: Kiara Thornton, an African American prospective purchaser, sued Sam Caramagno, Susan Gottlieb, and Gottlieb Group Real Estate alleging they refused to sell her a property after learning her race and instead sold it to another buyer for $25,000 less than her offer, in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA and related race discrimination claims, finding Thornton's factual allegations sufficient to plausibly infer racial discrimination.

case_name: Bonnie Bright v. Cheryl Flaisher and State Farm Fire and Casualty Company
accommodation_description: Landlord refused to rent to tenant because she had a child, allegedly in violation of the Fair Housing Act's familial status protections.
key_holding: The court granted State Farm's motion for summary judgment on its declaratory judgment claim, holding that State Farm has no duty to defend or indemnify Flaisher because intentional discrimination based on familial status does not constitute an 'accident' or 'occurrence' under the insurance policies, and therefore falls outside policy coverage.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Bonnie Bright sued landlord Cheryl Flaisher alleging Fair Housing Act violations for refusing to rent her property because Bright had a child; Bright also named State Farm as defendant. State Farm moved for summary judgment on its declaratory judgment claim seeking a ruling that it had no duty to defend or indemnify Flaisher under her insurance policies. The court granted State Farm's motion, concluding that intentional familial status discrimination is not an 'accident' or 'occurrence' covered under the insurance policies, and therefore State Farm owes no defense or indemnification duties.

source_file: 9752353_2022_Amber Reineck House v. City of Howell_mied
case_name: Amber Reineck House, et al. v. City of Howell, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs operate sober living/transitioning housing for women in recovery seeking reasonable accommodation from Howell's zoning ordinances and special use requirements.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to exclude Jeffery Van Treese's expert opinion as irrelevant, held in abeyance the motion regarding damages expert Patrick O'Keefe, granted in part/denied in part motions to exclude experts Carlisle and Arroyo (excluding impermissible legal conclusions), denied Defendants' motion to exclude Plaintiffs' expert Brian Connolly, and granted in part/denied in part the motion to exclude Gerald Fisher.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Amber Reineck House and related sober living/transitioning housing operators sued the City of Howell alleging the city's zoning ordinances and handling of their special use applications violated the Fair Housing Act's reasonable accommodation requirements. This order resolved cross-motions to exclude expert witnesses under Daubert standards, excluding certain impermissible legal conclusions while qualifying planners Connolly and Fisher to testify about zoning practices.

case_name: Brenda K. Sanders v. Detroit Housing Commission
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought immediate priority placement in Detroit Housing Commission public housing, requesting that DHC prioritize her on the housing waitlist based on her age, disability, homelessness, and history of being subjected to gender-based violence, in accordance with HUD regulations and applicable housing preference rules.
key_holding: The court adopted the magistrate judge's report and recommendation dismissing pro se plaintiff's complaint sua sponte under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) for failure to state a plausible claim under the Iqbal/Twombly standard, overruling all of plaintiff's objections.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Brenda Sanders sued the Detroit Housing Commission alleging it failed to prioritize her for housing placement based on her age, disability, homelessness, and history of gender-based violence, in purported violation of the Fair Housing Act, HUD regulations, VAWA, and Michigan's Elliott-Larsen Civil Rights Act, and additionally alleged breach of an oral contract. Magistrate Judge Stafford recommended sua sponte dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e) for failure to state a claim, finding each claim legally deficient. The district court overruled all eight of Sanders' objections and adopted the report and recommendation in full, concluding that none of Sanders' claims met the Iqbal/Twombly pleading standard.
