key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding claims for equitable relief moot because Local Law 4 was repealed and site plan approval was granted, and rejecting the futility argument for remaining damages claims because the developer's ultimate approval demonstrates seeking a variance would not have been futile.
brief_summary: Cedar Development East sued the Town Board of Hurley, Planning Board, and individual members alleging violations of the Equal Protection Clause and Fair Housing Act, claiming the town enacted discriminatory zoning legislation and obstructed permit approvals based on anti-Semitic and racial animus toward the developer's principals. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss on mootness and ripeness grounds, finding equitable relief claims moot since the zoning law was repealed and project approved, and rejecting the futility exception because the developer's eventual approval showed seeking variances would not have been futile.

case_name: CNY Fair Housing, Inc. v. Swiss Village, LLC

case_name: Kevin V. Byng v. Bob Kelly
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation request is described in the complaint; plaintiff alleged disability-based discrimination under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act generally, but the court found the complaint devoid of any facts showing defendants' actions were taken because of plaintiff's disabilities or that they were even aware of his disabilities.
key_holding: On IFP initial review, the court recommends that plaintiff's First Amendment freedom of association claims against both defendants and his FHA racial discrimination claim against defendant Kelly survive and require a response, while recommending dismissal of his Eighth Amendment, substantive due process, § 1437d(l)(3), and disability-based ADA/RA/FHA claims.
brief_summary: Kevin Byng, a sixty-two year old pro se plaintiff with multiple disabilities, sued the Executive Director and security officer of the Utica Municipal Housing Authority under § 1983, the ADA, the Rehabilitation Act, and the FHA, alleging that defendants repeatedly threatened him with eviction, harassed him, and denied him overnight guest privileges because of his associations with African American women, while also failing to maintain building security. The court conducted an IFP initial review and found that plaintiff's First Amendment intimate association claims and FHA racial discrimination claim against defendant Kelly plausibly survived, while his disability-based discrimination claims failed for lack of factual allegations connecting the adverse actions to his disability. The court recommended dismissal with prejudice of the Eighth Amendment, § 1437d, and substantive due process claims, and dismissal without prejudice of the remaining ADA/RA/FHA disability claims and the FHA racial discrimination claim against defendant Connelly, with leave to amend.

case_name: Weilburg v. Castellane
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs alleged they were unlawfully evicted from their apartment because they are Jehovah's Witnesses, constituting religious discrimination under the FHA.
key_holding: Defendant is entitled to summary judgment because the property qualifies for the Mrs. Murphy exemption under 42 U.S.C. § 3603(b)(2), which excludes owner-occupied dwellings with four or fewer families from FHA coverage, regardless of whether plaintiffs' allegations of religious discrimination are true.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Daro and Maria Weilburg sued landlord Richard Castellane alleging they were unlawfully evicted because they are Jehovah's Witnesses, asserting religious discrimination under the Fair Housing Act. accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges HUD's no-reasonable-cause determination regarding her underlying housing discrimination complaint alleging discrimination based on sex, race, and national origin.

The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that sovereign immunity bars the suit against federal agencies and officials, and that the Fair Housing Act provides no private right of action to challenge HUD's administrative determinations.

Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Marinoff v. U.S. Dep't of Hous. & Urban Dev., 892 F. Supp. 493 (S.D.N.Y. 1995)
Weisberg v. Leon, 1999 WL 1216663 (S.D.N.Y. Dec. 20, 1999)

case_name: Mohamed Samura v. Maria Figueroa; Castleton Park Management; Castleton Preservation LLC
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this case concerns an alleged discriminatory denial of a housing application, with defendants citing plaintiff's full-time student status as the basis for the denial.
key_holding: The Southern District of New York transferred pro se plaintiff's FHA housing application denial claim to the Eastern District of New York because all defendants and the operative events were located in Staten Island (Richmond County), which falls within the Eastern District.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mohamed Samura filed an FHA claim alleging defendants denied his housing application on discriminatory grounds, while defendants asserted a non-discriminatory reason—his status as a full-time student at the College of Staten Island. The Southern District of New York found venue was improper because the underlying events occurred in Staten Island and defendants' addresses were in Staten Island, both of which are in Richmond County within the Eastern District of New York. The court sua sponte transferred the action to the Eastern District of New York pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) in the interest of justice.

case_name: Sister E. Jones Bey v. Dana La Casse, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff asserted vague housing discrimination allegations against her landlord for discrimination based on nationality, family size, religion, and source of income, but no specific accommodation request or disability-related claim was alleged or analyzed.
key_holding: The Court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim against her landlord because she failed to allege facts connecting Powell's conduct to any animus against a protected characteristic, relying instead on conclusory allegations insufficient to state a claim under Rule 8.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Sister E. Jones Bey, proceeding pro se, sued her landlord Vicknell Powell and numerous government defendants alleging constitutional violations under § 1983 and Fair Housing Act claims. The Court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claim against Powell for failure to state a claim, finding she failed to allege facts showing a connection between Powell's conduct and any protected characteristic, and granted leave to replead the housing discrimination claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly

case_name: Donald A. Lord v. City of New York et al.
accommodation_description: The case text does not specifically describe any discrete accommodation request; rather, Plaintiff asserts broadly that conditions in homeless shelters and actions of shelter staff and city agency employees violated the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act, suggesting disability-related accommodation or equal-access claims arising from shelter living conditions.
key_holding: The court dismissed DHS and HRA as improper defendants because New York City agencies cannot be sued in their own name, directed identification of Doe defendants, and ordered service on newly added defendants, while denying Sera Security's earlier motion to dismiss as moot.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Donald Lord, who had been living in New York City homeless shelters since March 2017, brought claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the ADA, the FHA, and the Rehabilitation Act against the City of New York, shelter operators (Project Renewal and CORE Services Group), a private security firm (Sera Security), and various individual employees, based on conditions in those shelters and the conduct of staff. The court dismissed DHS and HRA as improper defendants because city agencies cannot be named as defendants under New York City Charter § 396, with claims relating to those entities preserved against the City of New York itself. The court then issued procedural directives regarding identification of Doe defendants and service of process on newly added defendants.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly
Valentin v. Dinkins

case_name: Donald A. Lord v. City of New York et al.
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request is analyzed by the Court; the order addresses procedural matters including service, identification of Doe defendants, and dismissal of agency defendants.
key_holding: The Court dismissed claims against DHS and HRA (City agencies not subject to suit), ordered identification of unidentified defendants, directed service on newly added defendants, and denied Sera Security's motion to dismiss as moot after the Second Amended Complaint was filed.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Donald Lord, a homeless individual living in various shelters since March 2017, brings claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, the ADA, the Fair Housing Act, and the Rehabilitation Act against the City of New York, shelter operators (Project Renewal, CORE Services Group), and security personnel regarding conditions at homeless shelters. The Court issued an amended order dismissing agency defendants DHS and HRA, ordering identification of unidentified defendants, directing service on newly added defendants, and denying Sera Security's motion to dismiss as moot.
key_cases_cited: Valentin v. Dinkins, 121 F.3d 72 (2d Cir. 1997)

source_file: 9864995_2021_Xia v. 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation_nysd
case_name: Eva Xia and Paul Privitera v. 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation, Christine Elbert, Samantha Pinkowitz, Anthony Sarmiento, and Angela Rojo
accommodation_description: This order does not address a reasonable accommodation request; it addresses work product privilege regarding a recorded conversation in an underlying Fair Housing Act case concerning denial of a cooperative housing purchase application.
key_holding: The court found that portions of the May 18, 2020 conversation between Pinkowitz and Pannkoke discussing the merits of the Fair Housing Act lawsuit are protected by attorney work product privilege under Rule 26(b)(3), while portions limited to insurance coverage discussions are not privileged, and the Coop did not waive the privilege through disclosure by a third-party witness.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Eva Xia and Paul Privitera sued 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation and its board members under the Fair Housing Act regarding denial of their application to purchase a cooperative apartment unit; this order resolves a discovery dispute over whether a recorded telephone conversation between board member Pinkowitz and an insurance claims adjuster discussing the lawsuit is protected by attorney work product privilege.

In re Grand Jury Proceedings, 219 F.3d 175 (2d Cir. 2000)

source_file: 9865041_2021_Brock v. The City of New York_nysd
case_name: Mandela Brock v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a homeless person, alleged discrimination because he is homeless, seeking placement in a particular type of shelter.
key_holding: Being homeless is not a protected characteristic under the Fair Housing Act, and plaintiff failed to allege facts connecting the alleged discriminatory conduct to a protected class, thus the FHA discrimination claim fails for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Mandela Brock, proceeding pro se and seeking shelter services for himself and his minor son, sued the City of New York, the Department of Homeless Services, private shelter operators, and individual employees under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, alleging discrimination based on homelessness and retaliation for exercising his rights. The court dismissed the FHA claim, holding that homelessness is not a protected characteristic under the FHA, and denied the motion for a temporary restraining order because the complaint failed to state viable claims.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs. of City of New York, 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
Connick v. Thompson, 131 S. Ct. 1350 (2011)

case_name: Daryl J. Davis v. Port Jervis Community Development; Nora Gallagher/Goetz; Valerie Maginsky
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges discrimination causing termination of Section 8 benefits but does not clearly articulate a specific reasonable accommodation request; the complaint is dismissed for failure to state a claim.
key_holding: The court dismissed the Fair Housing Act claim because Plaintiff failed to allege facts suggesting that Defendants discriminated against him on the basis of any prohibited factor under the FHA, and granted no further leave to amend.
brief_summary: Daryl J. Davis, proceeding pro se, sued Port Jervis Community Development and individual defendants alleging discrimination that resulted in termination of his Section 8 benefits. The S.D.N.Y. dismissed his Fair Housing Act claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) for failure to state a plausible claim, finding the amended complaint failed to allege facts showing discrimination on the basis of any protected characteristic, and denied further leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

source_file: 9865413_2021_Mercer v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Robert Mercer v. New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Specific accommodation request not stated in this order; original complaint alleged FHA violations against NYCHA.
key_holding: Pro se plaintiff's motion for leave to amend is denied because his response failed to cure deficiencies by not identifying what major life activity is impaired by his condition or alleging defendant knew of his disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Robert Mercer, a Black public housing tenant, sued NYCHA alleging Fair Housing Act violations. The Court denied plaintiff's motion for leave to amend his complaint after a prior order dismissed his claims, finding he failed to adequately plead that his condition substantially limits a major life activity or that NYCHA knew of his disability.

source_file: 9865899_2021_Dodd v. City University of New York_nysd

case_name: Joshua Kellier v. Billups
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged that defendants attempted to place him in a 'smaller facility' because of his disability, framing this as disability discrimination under the FHA and ADA; the court observed that, if anything, such conduct suggested an attempt to accommodate his disability rather than to discriminate against him.
key_holding: The court dismisses claims against previously-named defendants under res judicata and grants pro se plaintiff leave to file an amended complaint within 60 days as to claims against new defendants and more recent events, while denying motions for pro bono counsel and injunctive relief.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Joshua Kellier brought claims under the FHA, ADA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1983, and state law against numerous defendants connected to New York City homeless shelters, alleging race discrimination, retaliation for complaining about shelter conditions, disability-based placement in a smaller facility, destruction of property, and denial of grievance rights. The court dismissed claims against defendants who were also named in a prior action (Kellier I) under the doctrine of claim preclusion, finding that earlier dismissal constituted a judgment on the merits. For claims against new defendants or arising from more recent events, the court granted leave to amend, noting the current complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations to state viable FHA, ADA, or § 1981 claims, and that defendants' attempt to place plaintiff in a smaller facility due to disability appeared more like an accommodation effort than discrimination.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

source_file: 9866577_2021_Paynes El-Bey v. ADT Security Services, Inc._nysd
case_name: Queen Prinyah Godiah P. Paynes El-Bey v. ADT Security Services, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who states she is disabled, alleges her landlord installed cameras to surveil her and subjected her to harassment, claiming differential treatment because she is not Spanish.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff leave to amend her complaint to properly allege Fair Housing Act claims, construing her pro se filings as potentially asserting discrimination based on disability and national origin.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Queen Prinyah Godiah P. Paynes El-Bey sued her landlord Sheila L. Robinson-Zenon, ADT Security Services, Inc., and Federal Savings Bank alleging privacy violations related to cameras installed to surveil her in her Poughkeepsie rental apartment. The court construed her complaint as potentially raising Fair Housing Act claims based on disability and national origin discrimination and granted her sixty days' leave to file an amended complaint to properly allege these claims.
key_cases_cited: Gladstone Realtors v. Vill. of Bellwood, 441 U.S. 91 (1979)

case_name: Madison v. Graham
subsidy_program: New York City Department of Homeless Services
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation was formally requested; the court construed the complaint as potentially asserting a reasonable accommodation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B) based solely on plaintiff's allegation that he has a long history of mental illness and takes medication for it, but no particular accommodation was identified or requested in the complaint.
key_holding: The court dismissed claims against District Attorney Vance for failure to state a claim and prosecutorial immunity, replaced NYPD with City of New York as proper defendant, and granted pro se plaintiff 60 days leave to file an amended complaint because the original complaint was insufficient to state claims under § 1983, the FHA, § 1981, or the ADA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Malcolm Madison, a Black Muslim man with mental health issues residing at Fort Washington Men's Shelter, brought claims arising from an alleged assault by another shelter resident, the DA's failure to investigate, and alleged targeting by both the shelter and NYPD based on his race, religion, and disability. The court dismissed all claims against DA Vance on prosecutorial immunity and discretion grounds, substituted the City of New York for the non-suable NYPD, and found the FHA, § 1983, § 1981, and ADA claims factually deficient but potentially viable. Plaintiff was granted 60 days to file an amended complaint with additional factual support.

case_name: Samuel Indig, et al. v. The Village of Pomona, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege religious discrimination—Orthodox Jewish residents claim Village Defendants engaged in harassment and discriminatory enforcement of code violations against them based on their religion.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiffs' Third Claim (state equal protection) and Fourth Claim (unconstitutional conditions) with prejudice, dismissed punitive damages claims against Pomona with prejudice, but denied dismissal of First and Second Claims against Harris for lack of personal involvement.
brief_summary: Samuel Indig and other Orthodox Jewish residents sued the Village of Pomona and individual officials alleging religious discrimination and harassment, including discriminatory code enforcement, in violation of the Fair Housing Act and constitutional rights. The court granted in part Defendants' motion to dismiss, dismissing state constitutional and unconstitutional conditions claims with prejudice while allowing First and Second Claims against one individual defendant to proceed.

case_name: TAL Properties of Pomona, LLC v. Village of Pomona
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege anti-religious discrimination against Orthodox Jewish community affecting real estate transactions, not a traditional disability accommodation request
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss on res judicata grounds, finding that the claims arose from the same transactions as a prior action and could have been raised therein, with limited exception for allegations regarding Mayor Banks's 2019 conduct which was dismissed without prejudice for failure to state a claim.
brief_summary: TAL Properties and Avrohom Manes sued the Village of Pomona and individual officials alleging anti-religious discrimination against the Orthodox Jewish community under the FHA, First Amendment, RLUIPA, and constitutional provisions. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss on res judicata grounds, finding the claims were precluded by a prior action involving the same parties and transactions.

case_name: Wood v. Mutual Redevelopment Houses, Inc.
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; claims involve religious discrimination, familial status discrimination, and retaliation in housing application process
key_holding: Summary judgment granted because plaintiff Wood failed to qualify financially for the cooperative apartment, never provided required income documentation despite multiple opportunities, and could not establish a prima facie case of housing discrimination.
brief_summary: Tzvee Wood and Andrea Malester sued Mutual Redevelopment Houses, Inc. and related defendants alleging religious discrimination, familial status discrimination, and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act arising from Wood's unsuccessful 2012 application to purchase a cooperative apartment in Manhattan. The court granted summary judgment for defendants, finding Wood failed to provide required income documentation demonstrating he met the cooperative's financial eligibility requirements and therefore could not establish a prima facie case of housing discrimination.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green

case_name: Sister E. Jones-Bey v. Pamela K. Chen, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation request is substantively analyzed; the court references that FHA claims were dismissed in a prior related action.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's amended complaint for failure to state claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B), denied habeas corpus relief, and granted only limited leave to amend state law diversity claims, while noting that prior related case No. 20-CV-9171 had already dismissed plaintiff's FHA claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Sister E. Jones-Bey brought claims against 57 defendants including federal and state judges, NYPD officers, ACS employees, and private landlord Vicknell Powell, alleging violations of constitutional rights, including reference to Fair Housing Act claims that were previously dismissed in a related case. The court dismissed the amended complaint for failure to state a claim, denied habeas corpus relief for child custody matters, and granted only limited leave to amend state law claims under diversity jurisdiction.

key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' claims because they failed to plead facts sufficient to show they were qualified for a Mutual apartment, failed to specify the nature of Wood's disability, and failed to adequately plead discrimination or retaliation claims under the FHA.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Wood and Malester sued Mutual Redevelopment Houses and related defendants alleging disability discrimination, reasonable accommodation denial, and retaliation related to their application for an income-limited cooperative apartment in New York City. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiffs failed to plead facts showing they were qualified for an apartment, failed to specify the nature of Wood's disability, and failed to adequately plead any cognizable claim under the FHA or related statutes.

case_name: Fair Housing Justice Center, Inc. v. Lighthouse Living LLC
accommodation_description: Design and construction accessibility requirements for multifamily housing - alleged lack of wheelchair accessible features including entrances, mailboxes, light switches, environmental controls, doorways, and floor space in dwelling units and common areas.
key_holding: The court denied both motions to dismiss, holding that (1) the plaintiff sufficiently alleged Realty's involvement in design and construction despite information and belief allegations, and (2) the continuing violation doctrine applies to design and construction FHA claims, making the claims against Papp timely.
brief_summary: Fair Housing Justice Center, a fair housing nonprofit, sued Lighthouse Living LLC entities and Papp Architects alleging that three newly constructed multifamily apartment buildings in Westchester County, New York lack wheelchair accessible features in violation of the FHA's design and construction requirements. The court denied both defendants' motions to dismiss, finding that plaintiff sufficiently pled Realty's involvement in the design and construction despite conclusory information and belief allegations, and that the continuing violation doctrine applied to make Papp's claims timely.

case_name: Ronald W. Harris, Sr. v. Community Housing Management Corp.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a double-amputee who uses two mechanical legs, requested an accessible/handicapped parking space near the entrance of Huguenot House where he resides.
key_holding: The case was dismissed as moot because the plaintiff no longer holds a valid driver's license due to his medical conditions, rendering his request for an accessible parking space no longer needed.
brief_summary: Ronald W. Harris, Sr., a double-amputee tenant at Huguenot House in New Rochelle, sued the property owner and management company under the Fair Housing Act, alleging disability discrimination for failing to provide him with an accessible parking space. The court granted summary judgment for defendants and dismissed the case as moot because the plaintiff's driver's license was not renewed due to medical conditions, and he could no longer drive, so he no longer needed the requested parking accommodation.

source_file: 9868754_2021_Congregation Rabbinical College of Tartikov, Inc. v. Village of Pomona, NY_nysd
case_name: Congregation Rabbinical College of Tartikov, Inc. v. Village of Pomona, NY
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs seek to build a rabbinical college with family housing on their property, requesting that zoning ordinances defining 'educational institutions' and 'dormitories' be invalidated or waived as applied to them.
key_holding: The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss because Plaintiffs lack Article III standing and their claims are not ripe for review, as they never submitted a formal development proposal, applied for a permit, or sought variances from the Village regarding the proposed rabbinical college.
brief_summary: Congregation Rabbinical College of Tartikov, Inc. and individual plaintiffs sued the Village of Pomona, New York challenging zoning ordinances that prohibit non-accredited educational institutions and limit dormitory-style housing, alleging violations of RLUIPA, the Fair Housing Act, and the New York State Constitution. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss on standing and ripeness grounds, finding that Plaintiffs failed to submit a formal development proposal, apply for permits, or seek variances from the Village, rendering their claims merely conjectural and not ripe for federal review.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiffs Jama M. Tasfay and Desmond Rolle sued Acacia Network Inc. and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations and constitutional claims arising from their removal from a DHS homeless shelter based on alleged race-based discrimination. Nathan granted defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA claims, finding plaintiffs' complaint contained only conclusory allegations of discriminatory intent without sufficient factual support to state a plausible claim, while denying dismissal of the § 1983 claims against the corporate defendant.

accommodation_description: Request to transfer from a studio apartment to a two-bedroom unit in a building with a pool and safe location to accommodate mobility disability and provide space for a live-in medical assistant
key_holding: The court dismissed Currin's FHA and ADA claims because he failed to plausibly allege that building accessibility deficiencies deprived him of equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling, and because Glenwood had attempted to accommodate his transfer request by placing him on a waiting list, offering a live-in medical assistant, and providing access to a pool in another building.
brief_summary: Charlie G. Currin, a pro se plaintiff who suffered a stroke causing mobility impairments, sued his landlord Glenwood Management Corp. alleging violations of the ADA and FHA for failing to transfer him to a larger apartment and accommodate his disability-related needs at Crystal Green. The court granted Glenwood's motion to dismiss, finding Currin failed to state a plausible claim because he did not adequately plead that building accessibility issues deprived him of equal housing opportunity and because Glenwood had attempted to accommodate his transfer request by placing him on a waiting list and offering alternative accommodations.

key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claims were properly dismissed because the complaint alleged only negligent care and inadequate supervision, not intentional discrimination or discriminatory animus against the disabled; plaintiff failed to plead facts showing defendants treated Zlotnick worse than other residents due to his disability.

case_name: Joanne Noel Higgins v. 120 Riverside Boulevard at Trump Place Condominium
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested (1) advance notice of renovation and construction work throughout the building that would generate loud noises and vibrations, so she could manage the triggering of her disability-related symptoms (vertigo, headaches, PTSD), and (2) remediation of water leaks and mold growth in her bedroom, which she alleged aggravated her respiratory conditions and other disabilities stemming from her traumatic brain injury.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because she failed to plead that she communicated to defendants that her requests for construction notice and mold remediation were linked to her disability rather than general grievances shared by all residents, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Joanne Higgins, a condominium owner with a traumatic brain injury causing vertigo, hearing and vision impairment, severe headaches, and PTSD, sued the condominium board and related defendants under the FHA for failing to make reasonable accommodations related to construction noise, vibrations, noxious odors, and mold in her unit. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss the FHA reasonable accommodation claim, finding that Higgins failed to allege that she informed the Condominium Defendants her requests—including advance notice of construction and mold remediation—were linked to her disability rather than general complaints equally shared by all unit owners. The court declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims, dismissing the FHA claim without prejudice to replead.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested access to cleaning supplies, medical equipment, refrigeration for medication, and bed rest passes as reasonable accommodations for his disabilities (burns, lymphedema, Von Willebrand disease) while living in a homeless shelter.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim fails because he was not a 'buyer or renter' under the FHA as a homeless shelter resident, and even if he were, his claim for injunctive relief is moot since he no longer resides at the shelter.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Brandon Jones, a homeless shelter resident with disabilities including burns and lymphedema, sued Volunteers of America Greater New York alleging the shelter denied him reasonable accommodations by refusing to allow him cleaning supplies, medical equipment, and refrigeration for medication. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, holding that as a homeless shelter resident directed to live there by authorities, Jones was not a 'buyer or renter' under the FHA and lacked standing to bring FHA claims, and even if he could proceed, his reasonable accommodation claim would fail as moot since he no longer resided at the facility.

case_name: Wilshire v. L&M Development Partners
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer to a different accessible parking space after her assigned handicap parking space became obstructed and inaccessible.
key_holding: Plaintiff's disparate treatment claim survives because she adequately alleged that Defendants terminated her parking license while not terminating similarly situated non-Black and non-disabled tenants who violated the same agreement; Plaintiff's reasonable accommodation claims survive because Defendants raised no merits challenge until their reply brief, waiving the argument.
brief_summary: Coanne Wilshire, a Black woman with a disability, sued L&M Development Partners and related entities (collectively, Larkspur) under the FHA and other statutes, alleging disparate treatment and reasonable accommodation denial based on her race and disability in connection with termination of her handicap parking space license. The court dismissed Wilshire's ADA claims for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and dismissed time-barred FHA claims based on incidents before February 3, 2018, but allowed Wilshire's timely disparate treatment and reasonable accommodation claims to proceed because defendants failed to timely challenge the reasonable accommodation claims on the merits.

source_file: 9873146_2022_Sykes v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Derry Sykes v. New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a disabled NYCHA tenant residing in a retrofitted/Section 504 apartment, seeks emergency repairs to address water leaks, mold, electrical hazards, and other deteriorated conditions that he alleges require higher priority completion as a reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA reasonable accommodation claim because he failed to allege facts showing that the requested repairs were necessary to afford him an equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling, rather than merely preferential treatment, and failed to allege that discriminatory animus was a factor in NYCHA's failure to make repairs.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Derry Sykes, who is disabled and suffers from major depression, sued NYCHA alleging the housing authority failed to make repairs to his Manhattan apartment and failed to provide reasonable accommodations under the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Section 1983. The court granted leave to amend, finding that Sykes failed to state a plausible FHA claim because he did not allege facts showing that repairs were necessary to afford him equal opportunity to use and enjoy his dwelling, nor did he allege discriminatory animus was a motivating factor in NYCHA's failure to repair.

source_file: 9873811_2022_BMG Monroe I, LLC v. Village of Monroe_nysd
case_name: BMG Monroe I, LLC v. Village of Monroe
accommodation_description: Developer BMG alleges Village of Monroe refused building permits and enacted discriminatory laws to exclude the Hasidic Jewish community from housing in the Village.
key_holding: The court dismissed BMG's claims without prejudice because BMG lacks standing to assert third-party claims on behalf of the Hasidic Jewish community and because BMG's claims are unripe—BMG failed to seek a variance from the ZBA and failed to adequately allege futility of doing so.
brief_summary: BMG Monroe I, LLC, a developer, sued the Village of Monroe alleging the Village denied building permits and enacted discriminatory laws motivated by anti-Hasidic Jewish animus in violation of the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. § 1983. The court granted the Village's motion to dismiss, finding BMG lacks standing to assert claims on behalf of third-party members of the Hasidic Jewish community and that BMG's claims are unripe because it failed to seek variances from the Zoning Board of Appeals.

key_holding: The court found the complaint failed to state a reasonable accommodation claim because Plaintiff did not allege that her landlord knew of her disability, that she requested the ramp accommodation, or that the landlord denied such request, but granted leave to file a second amended complaint.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Queen Prinyah Godiah Paynes El-Bey sued her landlord Sheila L. Robinson-Zenon and others alleging Fair Housing Act violations, including that the landlord failed to accommodate her mobility disability by not installing a wheelchair ramp. The court dismissed claims against all defendants except Robinson-Zenon, finding the complaint failed to state a claim because Plaintiff did not allege the landlord knew of her disability, requested the accommodation, or that it was denied, but granted 30 days leave to amend.

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Robert Mercer sued NYCHA alleging constitutional violations and housing code violations stemming from lead paint detection in his NYCHA apartment. case_name: Jose Antonio Ramos v. Department of Homeless Services
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, a senior with handicaps, requests installation of safety features in showers and bathrooms as a disability accommodation at his temporary homeless shelter residence.
key_holding: This is an order of service construing the complaint as asserting FHA claims and directing service; the court has not yet reached the merits of the reasonable accommodation claim.
brief_summary: Jose Antonio Ramos, a senior with mobility handicaps residing in temporary homeless shelter housing in New York City, brought this action against Breaking Ground (a supportive housing operator) and the City of New York alleging failure to install safety features in showers and bathrooms as a reasonable accommodation. The court construed the complaint as asserting Fair Housing Act claims, dismissed the Department of Homeless Services as a non-suable entity, added the City of New York as a defendant, and directed service on the remaining parties.

case_name: Jack Bizelia et al. v. Clinton Towers Housing Co., Inc. et al.
accommodation_description: Request to transfer from a one-bedroom to a two- or three-bedroom apartment to accommodate tenant's claustrophobia, anxiety, and cardiac conditions
key_holding: Because there are factual disputes regarding when plaintiffs' FHA reasonable accommodation claim accrued—whether defendants' delay in responding constituted constructive denial—the court denied defendants' motion to dismiss on statute of limitations grounds.
brief_summary: Three tenants of Clinton Towers, a federally subsidized apartment complex in Manhattan, sued the property management companies alleging disability discrimination under the FHA based on defendants' failure to accommodate their requests to transfer to a larger apartment to manage tenants' mental health and cardiac conditions. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss on statute of limitations grounds, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to when the claim accrued—whether defendants' multi-year delay in processing the transfer request and subsequent commencement of eviction proceedings constituted constructive denial.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

source_file: 9875225_2022_Highview Properties D.H.F. Inc. v. Town of Monroe_nysd
case_name: Highview Properties D.H.F. Inc. v. Town of Monroe
accommodation_description: Plaintiff developer claims town zoning actions (moratorium, denial of exemption/variance, accessory apartment restrictions) were motivated by anti-Hasidic Jewish animus to make housing unavailable to that religious community.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's Fair Housing Act claims because a corporate developer lacks religious affiliation and cannot assert third-party standing to bring religious discrimination claims on behalf of Hasidic Jewish community members.
brief_summary: Highview Properties, a developer, sued the Town of Monroe and its officials under the Fair Housing Act and constitutional law, alleging that town zoning legislation (a development moratorium, denial of exemption from the moratorium, and accessory apartment restrictions) was enacted with discriminatory animus against Hasidic Jews to prevent them from obtaining housing in the town. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that Highview lacks standing to assert religious discrimination claims because it has no religious affiliation and cannot bring claims on behalf of third parties.

source_file: 9875229_2022_Doe v. New York City Housing Authority_nysd
case_name: Jane Doe v. New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer to a different building within NYCHA housing due to disability-related safety concerns following a violent assault and diagnosis of PTSD and anxiety.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion to proceed pseudonymously, finding the risk of retaliatory physical and mental harm from gang members, combined with her PTSD and anxiety vulnerability, outweighed the presumption against anonymity and the government defendants' minimal prejudice.
brief_summary: Jane Doe, a NYCHA public housing resident at Linden Houses diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety following a violent gang assault, sued NYCHA and its CEO alleging they constructively denied her request for transfer to a safer location as a reasonable accommodation under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act. The court granted her motion to proceed pseudonymously, finding the substantial risk of retaliatory harm from gang members and her psychological vulnerability outweighed the public's interest in knowing litigant identities.

case_name: Frank Ditto; Julie Ditto v. Peterson Properties; Peterson Property Management; Ted Peterson; Steve Peterson; Does 1-10
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - the complaint vaguely mentions 'possibly' the Fair Housing Act but does not specify the accommodation requested
key_holding: The court transferred the case to the Northern District of California because the operative events (rental of an Oakland, California apartment) occurred there, making venue more appropriate in that district under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a).
brief_summary: Pro se tenants Frank and Julie Ditto sued their Oakland, California landlord (Peterson Properties) and associated parties in the Southern District of New York, alleging violations of the ADA and possibly the Fair Housing Act in connection with their rental apartment. accommodation_description: No specific accommodation request; plaintiff makes vague allegations of race-based housing discrimination against HPD representative and landlord
key_holding: The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because federal courts lack jurisdiction over state landlord-tenant matters, the plaintiff failed to state a viable FHA claim (no facts plausibly suggesting discrimination on the basis of race), and diversity jurisdiction was lacking since all parties were citizens of New York.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Rene Belmar sued G&M Realty and others arising from a Bronx Housing Civil Court landlord-tenant case, alleging fair housing violations and race-based discrimination against an HPD representative. The court dismissed the complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding that federal courts lack jurisdiction over state landlord-tenant matters, plaintiff failed to allege facts plausibly stating an FHA claim, and diversity jurisdiction was lacking, but granted plaintiff thirty days leave to amend.

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Derry Sykes sued NYCHA under the FHA, ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Section 1983, alleging that NYCHA's failure to repair dangerous conditions in his apartment (mold, water leaks, electrical hazards, collapsed ceiling) constituted disability discrimination and failure to provide reasonable accommodations. key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA disparate impact claim because they failed to plausibly allege that the occupancy limits resulted in underrepresentation of Orthodox Jews or families with children in affordable housing, lacking statistical or factual comparisons to similarly situated groups.
brief_summary: Orthodox Jewish couple Chaim and Channa Katz sued New York City housing agencies and private developers after being denied affordable housing twice due to occupancy limits that capped units at two persons per bedroom, claiming the policy had a disparate impact on their religion and familial status. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the complaint lacked sufficient factual allegations or statistics showing that the occupancy limits disproportionately affected Orthodox Jews or families with children compared to similarly situated groups.

race_if_mentioned: Not specified; plaintiffs alleged removal was based on their race but no specific racial identity is named in the text

case_name: Jose Antonio Ramos v. Department of Homeless Services
accommodation_description: Request for safety strips or safety bars in showers and bathrooms at a homeless shelter for seniors with handicaps
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's TRO/PI motion because plaintiff failed to demonstrate irreparable harm, noting that defendants offered plaintiff multiple housing opportunities which he refused, and that plaintiff never filed any grievances or requested reasonable accommodations for any disability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jose Antonio Ramos, a homeless shelter resident, moved for a preliminary injunction and TRO against the NYC Department of Homeless Services and Breaking Ground, alleging denial of safe housing and reasonable accommodations for seniors with handicaps, as well as racial discrimination in housing allocation. case_name: Jane Doe v. Related Companies, LLP
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation or modification was requested. key_holding: The court denies plaintiff's motion to proceed anonymously and grants her 60 days' leave to file an amended complaint, finding the original complaint fails to state claims under Section 1983, Title VII, and the Fair Housing Act because the allegations are conclusory and lack specific factual support.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jane Doe filed suit against the owners and managers of her Manhattan apartment building (456 Washington Street), alleging racial discrimination, harassment, and retaliation under the FHA, Section 1983, and Title VII. key_holding: The jury waiver provision in Plaintiff's proprietary lease was enforceable because Plaintiff was represented by counsel during negotiations, the waiver was sufficiently conspicuous, and Plaintiff had sufficient business acumen as a real estate developer to understand the waiver's effect.

key_holding: The court dismissed the amended complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because plaintiff failed to allege any facts sufficient to state a viable FHA claim under § 3604 or § 3617, and no diversity jurisdiction existed, warranting dismissal without further leave to amend.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Rene Belmar filed suit against his landlord, management company, attorney, a fellow tenant, and others, alleging various grievances arising from a landlord-tenant proceeding in Bronx Housing Civil Court, including race and housing discrimination. case_name: Dante Malik Sullivan v. City of New York, et al.
accommodation_description: Pro se plaintiff in a homeless shelter alleges shelter staff retaliated against him for advocating about living conditions and mental safety, including calling police on him and labeling him as emotionally disturbed due to his mental illness.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act retaliation claims without prejudice because plaintiff failed to allege that his complaints involved discrimination based on protected characteristics and failed to identify specific state actors responsible for the alleged retaliation, granting leave to amend.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Dante Malik Sullivan, a mentally ill resident of a New York City homeless shelter operated by Project Renewal, sued the City of New York and multiple officials alleging retaliation under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act after he complained about shelter conditions. The court dismissed the claims for failure to state a viable retaliation theory because plaintiff did not allege his complaints concerned discrimination based on a protected characteristic and failed to identify specific state actors, granting plaintiff 60 days leave to amend.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Bernadette Skorupska v. 525 West 52 Property Owner LLC
accommodation_description: Request for a two-bedroom accessible apartment under disability set-aside program for plaintiff's son with developmental disabilities.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for reconsideration because she failed to demonstrate standing for her ADA accessibility claim, did not establish that she and comparator Anna Hernandez are similarly situated, and improperly raised new arguments regarding deposition discrepancies.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Bernadette Skorupska moved for reconsideration of this Court's September 2022 summary judgment order dismissing her claims that defendants discriminated against her and her son with developmental disabilities by failing to provide a two-bedroom accessible apartment. The Court denied the motion, finding plaintiff failed to demonstrate standing for her ADA claim, failed to show she and comparator Anna Hernandez were similarly situated, and improperly raised new arguments about deposition discrepancies.
key_cases_cited: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 141 S. Ct. 2190 (2021)
Calcano v. Swarovski N. Am. Ltd., 36 F.4th 68 (2d Cir. 2022)

case_name: Keisha A. Jones v. City of New York
accommodation_description: The accommodation request is not described in this procedural order granting an extension of time to amend.
key_holding: The Court granted Plaintiff's request for an extension of time to file an amended complaint by December 5, 2022, without making any substantive determination on the merits of the dismissed Fair Housing Act claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Keisha A. Jones, proceeding pro se, filed an action against the City of New York alleging Fair Housing Act claims that were previously dismissed for failure to state a claim. The Court now grants Plaintiff's request for an extension of time to file an amended complaint by December 5, 2022.

case_name: Keisha A. Jones v. City of New York, et al.
accommodation_description: Cannot be determined from this procedural order addressing only an extension of time to file an amended complaint.

brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Keisha A. Jones, who was previously granted leave to replead claims under the Fair Housing Act following dismissal for failure to state a claim, requested an extension of the filing deadline due to illness; the Court granted the extension allowing Plaintiff until December 15, 2022, to submit an amended complaint.

case_name: Stone v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who has unspecified mental illness and chronic asthma, alleged retaliation for complaining about shelter conditions that exacerbated his disabilities; the court found the complaints did not constitute protected activity under the FHA because they concerned general conditions rather than disability discrimination.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA retaliation claim with leave to amend because plaintiff failed to allege facts showing his complaints involved disability-based discrimination, as required to establish protected activity under the FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff John Stone, a homeless individual with mental illness and asthma residing in New York City shelters, sued the City of New York and various officials and shelter operators alleging retaliation under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act for complaining about shelter conditions. The court dismissed the claims with leave to amend, finding plaintiff failed to allege protected activity because his complaints concerned general shelter conditions rather than disability-based discrimination, and failed to establish personal involvement of individual defendants or state action by private shelter operators.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal

case_name: Housing Rights Initiative v. Compass, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff challenges landlords' policy of refusing to rent to Housing Choice Voucher holders as having a disparate impact on disabled, Black, and Hispanic individuals.
key_holding: Although the court denied defendants' motions to dismiss, finding HRI had organizational standing and adequately pleaded disparate impact claims, this is a procedural ruling denying dismissal—the case proceeds to discovery rather than ruling on the merits of the FHA claims.
brief_summary: Housing Rights Initiative, a fair housing nonprofit, sued landlords and brokers for refusing to rent to Housing Choice Voucher holders, alleging disparate impact on disabled, Black, and Hispanic individuals under the FHA and state/local source-of-income discrimination laws. The court denied all defendants' motions to dismiss and for judgment on the pleadings, finding HRI had organizational standing based on diversion of resources and adequately pleaded disparate impact claims against each defendant.

case_name: Michael Reeves v. CMP Consultants, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial discrimination in housing and retaliation for filing a NYSDHR complaint; no reasonable accommodation request is at issue.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's request for preliminary injunctive relief because plaintiff failed to allege facts sufficient to state a plausible FHA discrimination claim—specifically, plaintiff did not identify his own race or allege facts showing discriminatory animus caused the leasing delays.
brief_summary: Michael Reeves, proceeding pro se, sued CMP Consultants, Inc. and other defendants alleging they discriminated against him on the basis of race by obstructing his access to a NYC Housing Lottery apartment and retaliating against him for filing a NYSDHR complaint. The court denied plaintiff's motion for preliminary injunction and temporary restraining order, finding the complaint failed to state a plausible FHA claim because plaintiff did not identify his own race or allege facts demonstrating discriminatory animus caused the leasing delays, and granted plaintiff 60 days leave to amend.

case_name: Jimmy Avila v. Acacia Network, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer from BASICS to a one-bedroom apartment at an alternate site as a reasonable accommodation for his medical condition (infection/osteomyelitis requiring bed rest).
key_holding: The court found plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts showing the accommodation was necessary to afford equal opportunity to use the dwelling, was reasonable, and was refused by defendant, but granted plaintiff 60 days' leave to amend.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Jimmy Avila, proceeding pro se, sued Acacia Network, Inc., Lorraine Coleman, and Bronx Addiction Services Integrated Concepts System, Inc. (BASICS), alleging disability discrimination under the FHA, including failure to accommodate his request to transfer to a different apartment as recommended by his physician. The Southern District of New York found the complaint failed to adequately plead the elements of a reasonable accommodation claim under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(f)(3)(B) but granted plaintiff 60 days' leave to amend his complaint.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal

case_name: Baltazar v. Goldfarb Properties Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested an emergency transfer from his current apartment in Far Rockaway to Manhattan or the Bronx, claiming isolation at his current location was exacerbating his disability.
key_holding: The court found plaintiff's complaint failed to allege sufficient facts to state a claim for reasonable accommodation under the FHA because he did not allege facts showing the accommodation was necessary to afford him an equal opportunity to enjoy the dwelling, that the accommodation was reasonable, or that defendants refused to make the requested accommodation.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Mynor Federico Nunez Baltazar sued Goldfarb Properties Management and related defendants under the FHA and ADA, alleging disability discrimination and failure to accommodate his request for emergency transfer from Far Rockaway to Manhattan or the Bronx to address isolation exacerbating his medical condition. The court denied the preliminary injunction request and dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding plaintiff failed to allege sufficient facts showing the accommodation was necessary, reasonable, or denied, but granted leave to amend within 60 days.
key_cases_cited: Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)

case_name: Jane Doe v. Anthony Pistilli et al.
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation requested; claim concerns denial of lease renewal after plaintiff rebuffed sexual advances from building superintendent.
key_holding: The S.D.N.Y. transferred the case to the Eastern District of New York because all parties reside in the EDNY and the operative facts occurred there, making transfer appropriate under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a).
brief_summary: Jane Doe sued Anthony Pistilli and related defendants alleging sex discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act, claiming her lease was not renewed after she rejected sexual advances from her building superintendent. The S.D.N.Y. granted transfer to the Eastern District of New York, finding that all parties reside there and the operative facts occurred there, making transfer appropriate for convenience of parties and witnesses and in the interests of justice.
key_cases_cited: Corley v. United States, 11 F.4th 79 (2d Cir. 2021)

case_name: Elaine Williams Bethea v. NYCHA Law Department
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint concerns denial of a two-bedroom apartment assignment in 2001 and substandard housing conditions, which she characterizes as race-based discrimination under the FHA.
key_holding: The complaint fails to state a claim under the FHA because Plaintiff does not allege facts plausibly suggesting that Defendant discriminated against her based on race, exercised FHA rights, or was subjected to retaliation under § 3617.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Elaine Williams Bethea sued NYCHA Law Department alleging Fair Housing Act violations based on race discrimination and intimidation. The court dismissed her complaint for failure to state a claim, finding she failed to allege facts plausibly suggesting discrimination based on race or retaliation under the FHA. The court granted Plaintiff 30 days' leave to file an amended complaint to cure the deficiencies, including addressing timeliness concerns under the FHA's two-year statute of limitations.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Jimmy Avila v. Sun River Health, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a safety transfer from his current housing unit to a one-bedroom apartment at an alternate location based on medical documentation.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's ADA and Rehabilitation Act claims without prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim, granting plaintiff sixty days leave to amend his complaint to allege sufficient facts.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jimmy Avila sued Sun River Health, Inc. and individual defendants alleging they failed to provide required medical accommodations, specifically a safety transfer to a different apartment unit. The Southern District of New York dismissed the ADA Title II and Rehabilitation Act claims without prejudice for failure to state a plausible claim, granted plaintiff leave to amend within sixty days, and denied his preliminary injunction request without prejudice.

case_name: Joaquin Dean v. Jeremy Doberman and Marc Wohlgemuth
accommodation_description: No specific accommodation requested; plaintiff primarily seeks to enjoin foreclosure sale and eviction, with claims of discriminatory statements by attorneys during litigation.
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss because plaintiff's claims to enjoin the sale and eviction are barred by Rooker-Feldman and Younger abstention doctrines, and plaintiff's FHA discrimination claim fails because he did not plausibly allege defendants acted with discriminatory intent in connection with the sale or rental of a dwelling.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Joaquin Dean sued attorneys Jeremy Doberman and Marc Wohlgemuth, alleging they made discriminatory statements during quiet title and holdover proceedings in state court in violation of the Fair Housing Act, and sought to stop the sale of his foreclosed property and his eviction. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff's claims to reverse the sale and eviction are barred by the Rooker-Feldman doctrine and Younger abstention, and that his FHA discrimination claim fails because he did not plausibly allege defendants acted with discriminatory intent regarding housing.

case_name: Katz, et al. v. New York City Housing Preservation & Development, et al.
accommodation_description: This case does not involve a disability accommodation request; it challenges occupancy limits applied to a large family based on family size (number of occupants) rather than familial status (presence of children under 18).
key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion for an extension of time to file a motion to dismiss and stayed discovery pending resolution of the anticipated motion, finding that the dispositive motion may eliminate all claims and that plaintiffs have not been prejudiced given delays caused by plaintiffs.
brief_summary: The Katz family sued NYC HPD and HDC alleging the occupancy limits in affordable housing lotteries discriminated against them based on familial status; defendants moved to dismiss and stay discovery, arguing the amended complaint conflated family size (not protected) with familial status (protected). The court granted the extension and stay pending the motion to dismiss, finding the dispositive motion may resolve all claims.

case_name: McKins v. Pye
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: This procedural order vacates the Order to Show Cause and directs the Clerk to issue summonses and complete service through the U.S. Marshals Service; the substantive FHA claims have not been analyzed.
brief_summary: Plaintiff John McKins, proceeding pro se, filed a Fair Housing Act complaint in May 2019 against Tara Pye, Joanne Russo-Lanza, and United Hebrew Soundview Senior Living; the case was initially dismissed, reopened by the Second Circuit, and this Court issued an Order to Show Cause for failure to prosecute. The Court vacated the Order to Show Cause and directed service of process through the U.S. Marshals Service; the substantive merits of the FHA claims remain unadjudicated.

source_file: 9883432_2023_Xia v. 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation_nysd
case_name: Xia v. 65 West 87th Street Housing Development Fund Corporation
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case does not involve a reasonable accommodation or modification request; it involves a discriminatory denial of a cooperative apartment purchase application.
key_holding: The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding genuine disputes of material fact as to whether the HDFC cooperative board's repeated rejection of plaintiffs' purchase applications was motivated by racial animus against Eva Xia as a Chinese American woman.
brief_summary: Eva Xia, a Chinese American woman, and her husband Paul Privitera attempted to purchase a cooperative apartment at 65 West 87th Street in Manhattan, an HDFC building, but were rejected by the board's special committee on multiple occasions. Plaintiffs brought claims under the Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. § 1981/1982, and state and city human rights laws, alleging the rejections were motivated by racial discrimination. The court denied defendants' motion for summary judgment, finding sufficient evidence of pretextual reasons for rejection and potential racial animus—including board member Rojo's contemporaneous comments, disparate treatment compared to prior applicants, and evidence of prior hostility toward Asian tenants—to require resolution by a jury.

case_name: Chanel Moody, Ayanda Carmichael, and Ronnie Clark v. The Related Companies, L.P., and Ery South Residential Tower LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs, Black low-income individuals selected for affordable housing units, alleged they were treated less favorably than market-rate tenants, raising disparate treatment and disparate impact claims under § 3604(a) based on race.
key_holding: The court declined to impose Rule 11 sanctions against plaintiffs' counsel because, despite finding the underlying racial discrimination claims had no chance of success under Second Circuit precedent, counsel's good faith belief in extending civil rights law to address the intersection of race and economic status warranted protection from sanctions in light of the potential chilling effect on civil rights litigation.
brief_summary: Black low-income plaintiffs sued private developers of a mixed-use building in Hudson Yards alleging they were treated less favorably than market-rate tenants based on race in violation of § 3604(a). The court denied defendants' motion for Rule 11 sanctions against plaintiffs' counsel, finding that while the racial discrimination claims had no chance of success under Second Circuit precedent, counsel's good faith effort to extend civil rights law merited protection from sanctions given the importance of avoiding chilling effects on civil rights advocacy.

case_name: Felicia Rosa v. Pathstone Corporation
accommodation_description: Termination of Section 8 housing subsidy allegedly based on race and disability; plaintiff is African-American and identifies as Bipolar
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claims because she failed to allege specific facts showing Defendants terminated her Section 8 subsidies because of her race or that Defendants violated her rights under the FHA, though the court granted her 60 days leave to amend.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Felicia Rosa, an African-American woman participating in Section 8, sued Pathstone Corporation (Section 8 program administrator), its employees, her landlord, and the landlord's attorney alleging discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act after her Section 8 subsidy was terminated for allegedly not using her apartment as her primary residence. The court dismissed her FHA claims for failure to state a claim, finding she did not allege sufficient facts showing Defendants acted because of her race, but granted her 60 days leave to amend and denied her motion for preliminary injunctive relief.

case_name: Shauna Noel and Emmanuella Senat v. City of New York
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; case challenges City of New York's community preference policy in affordable housing lottery as discriminatory on basis of race.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment for the City on the disparate impact claim because plaintiffs failed to show members of their protected class are disproportionately impacted (the policy advantages and disadvantages different racial groups depending on community district demographics), but denied summary judgment on the intentional discrimination claim because genuine disputes of fact exist regarding whether the City's maintenance of the policy was motivated by racial animus rather than legitimate concerns about displacement.
brief_summary: African-American plaintiffs sued the City of New York challenging its community preference policy for affordable housing lottery allocation, alleging the policy causes disparate impact on the basis of race and constitutes intentional discrimination. The court granted summary judgment for the City on the disparate impact claim, finding plaintiffs failed to show members of their protected class are disproportionately impacted, but denied summary judgment on the intentional discrimination claim because genuine disputes of material fact exist regarding whether the City's proffered justifications (preventing displacement) are pretextual for racial animus.

case_name: Noel v. City of New York
accommodation_description: Challenge to the City's community preference policy in affordable housing lottery that allegedly perpetuates residential segregation
key_holding: The court granted in part and denied in part defendant's motion to exclude expert testimony, allowing Professor Orfield's opinions on segregation patterns and dynamics but excluding his opinions on City officials' intent and less discriminatory policy alternatives as unreliable, irrelevant, and improper legal conclusions.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Shauna Noel and Emmanuella Senat sued the City of New York alleging that its community preference policy for affordable housing distribution creates a disparate impact on the basis of race and constitutes intentional discrimination. key_holding: The Court granted Plaintiff leave to amend because the complaint failed to comply with Rule 8's requirement of a short and plain statement showing entitlement to relief, as it lacked factual allegations from which the Court could discern the specific claims being alleged.
brief_summary: Alphonso Syville, a pro se plaintiff, brought suit against the City of New York and two municipal employees alleging violations of multiple federal statutes including the Fair Housing Act regarding events occurring in DHS shelters during COVID-19. brief_summary: Pro se public housing tenant Elaine Williams Bethea sued NYCHA alleging she was selected for a two-bedroom apartment in 2001 but was placed in a one-bedroom unit, with available two-bedroom apartments allegedly given to Spanish-speaking residents; the court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a racial discrimination claim under the Fair Housing Act.

case_name: Gambaro v. 1917 ACP Owner LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege Defendants failed to reasonably accommodate their disability while the sole building elevator was inoperable, effectively restricting their access to their apartment.
key_holding: The court stayed the action pending Plaintiffs' application for leave to sue the temporary receiver, finding that suing a temporary receiver without leave from the appointing court is a condition precedent that must be satisfied, though it does not affect federal jurisdiction.
brief_summary: Jeanette and Joseph Gambaro sued their landlord and related parties under the Fair Housing Act, alleging Defendants failed to reasonably accommodate their disabilities while the building's sole elevator was inoperable. The court stayed the action pending Plaintiffs' application for leave from the New York Supreme Court to sue the temporary receiver, without reaching the merits of the FHA accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: McIntire v. China MediaExpress Holdings, Inc., 113 F. Supp. 3d 769 (S.D.N.Y. 2015)
Blanchard v. Landis, 2002 WL 1933819 (S.D.N.Y. 2002)
Copeland v. Salomon, 56 N.Y.2d 222 (1982)
Halpern v. Wilf, 2000 WL 1277300 (S.D.N.Y. 2000)

case_name: Ayala v. Saw Mill Lofts, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Victor Rios, a wheelchair user requiring a respirator, alleges that Saw Mill Lofts was designed and constructed with numerous architectural barriers in violation of federal accessibility requirements.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for reconsideration because plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that the Temporary Certificates of Occupancy they obtained post-ruling were truly newly discovered evidence—they could have obtained them with due diligence prior to the original motion, and even assuming relevance, the certificates would not alter the court's conclusion that production of all leases over a 7-year period was not relevant to whether any specific apartments complied with FHA accessibility requirements.
brief_summary: Jessica Ayala and Victor Rios, a wheelchair user, sued Saw Mill Lofts and Ginsburg Development Companies alleging the apartment complex was designed and constructed with architectural barriers in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for reconsideration of the court's earlier discovery ruling, holding that documents plaintiffs obtained after the ruling (Temporary Certificates of Occupancy) were not truly newly discovered evidence because plaintiffs could have obtained them with due diligence, and even if relevant, they would not change the conclusion that demanding all leases over a 7-year period was overbroad and irrelevant to plaintiffs' accessibility claims.

case_name: Gayle Leslie, et al. v. The Corcoran Group, et al.
accommodation_description: Lease application allegedly denied based on race and income
key_holding: Plaintiffs abandoned their federal race discrimination claims by failing to address Defendants' summary judgment arguments, resulting in deemed admissions of Defendants' unrefuted evidence.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Gayle Leslie and Michael Jackson sued Craig Hollander and The Corcoran Group alleging race and income discrimination in connection with their apartment lease application. The court granted summary judgment for Defendants because Plaintiffs abandoned their federal claims by failing to respond to Defendants' summary judgment arguments on the race discrimination claims, and the court declined supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state and local claims.
key_cases_cited: McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green
Carzoglio v. Adams, 2022 WL 2193376
Mirza v. Garnet Health, 2022 WL 826410
United Mine Workers v. Gibbs, 383 U.S. 715

case_name: Richard Blitz v. BLDG Management Co., Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to be transferred to a similar rent-regulated apartment elsewhere in the building at the same or lower rent to escape disturbances from neighbor's barking dog.
key_holding: Defendants did not fail to provide reasonable accommodations under § 3604(f)(3)(B) because they offered plaintiff multiple reasonable accommodations (transfer to other units, rent-stabilized apartment options, soundproofing) that plaintiff refused, and the FHA does not require landlords to subsidize rent as an accommodation.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Richard Blitz, a disabled tenant, sued BLDG Management Company alleging failure to accommodate his disability by not transferring him away from a neighbor's barking dog that exacerbated his anxiety and sleep deprivation. The court granted summary judgment to defendants, finding that BLDG offered reasonable accommodations including transfers to multiple units and soundproofing, which plaintiff unreasonably refused, and that the FHA does not require landlords to provide rent subsidies as accommodations.
key_cases_cited: Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242 (1986)
Reyes v. Krasdale Foods, Inc., 945 F. Supp. 2d 486 (S.D.N.Y. 2013)
Rodriguez v. 551 West 157th St. Owners Corp., 992 F. Supp. 385 (S.D.N.Y. 1998)

Logan, 57 F. Supp. 3d at 257 (S.D.N.Y. 2014)

case_name: Mark Liboy v. Gregory Russ, Lisa Bova-Hiatt, and New York City Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for transfer to a two-bedroom apartment in lower Manhattan or nearby Brooklyn to accommodate mobility disabilities and proximity to medical providers
key_holding: The court dismissed Liboy's reasonable accommodation claims because requiring NYCHA to provide housing at a specific geographic location would constitute a fundamental alteration of the Section 8 program, which does not offer participants a place to live as a benefit and does not guarantee housing in any particular location.
brief_summary: Mark Liboy, a NYCHA tenant with mobility disabilities, sued NYCHA and its officials seeking a transfer to lower Manhattan or Brooklyn as a reasonable accommodation for his disabilities after Baychester converted from public housing to project-based Section 8 under the RAD/PACT Program. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, ruling that requiring NYCHA to provide housing at a specific geographic location would fundamentally alter the Section 8 program, which does not guarantee housing in any particular location as a benefit.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Louis v. N.Y.C. Hous. Auth., 152 F. Supp. 3d 143 (S.D.N.Y. 2016)

case_name: Felicia Rosa v. Pathstone Corporation
accommodation_description: Plaintiff Felicia Rosa sought a TRO or preliminary injunction to enjoin a state court eviction proceeding, alleging it would violate the Fair Housing Act and Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act.
key_holding: The court declined to rule on the motion for TRO/injunction because plaintiff failed to address the elements required for injunctive relief, granting her leave to supplement her motion.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Felicia Rosa filed an action against Pathstone Corporation and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act and Rehabilitation Act violations, and separately moved for a TRO or preliminary injunction to enjoin a state court eviction proceeding for non-payment of rent. The court declined to rule on the TRO motion because Rosa failed to address the required elements for injunctive relief, including likelihood of success on the merits, balance of hardships, and public interest, granting her leave to supplement her submission.
key_cases_cited: Benihana, Inc. v. Benihana of Tokyo, 784 F.3d 887 (2d Cir. 2015)
Winter v. Natural Res. Def. Council, Inc., 555 U.S. 7 (2008)
