case_name: Felicia Rosa v. Pathstone Corporation
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to enjoin eviction proceedings and reinstate Section 8 housing assistance as an accommodation for her disability, while alleging discrimination based on race, source of income, and parental status.
key_holding: Plaintiff failed to establish likelihood of success on the merits because her own evidence showed defendants' termination of Section 8 assistance was based on federal regulations; additionally, the Anti-Injunction Act bars federal courts from enjoining state eviction proceedings.
brief_summary: Felicia Rosa, proceeding pro se, sued Pathstone Corporation and individual defendants seeking injunctive relief to prevent her eviction and reinstate her Section 8 housing assistance, alleging discrimination under the FHA and Rehabilitation Act based on race, source of income, and disability. The court denied her TRO and preliminary injunction motions without prejudice because she failed to demonstrate likelihood of success on the merits, as her own evidence showed the Section 8 termination was based on federal regulations, and the Anti-Injunction Act bars enjoining state eviction proceedings.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic v. Twombly
Village of Arlington Heights v. Metropolitan Hous. Dev. Corp.
Fulton v. Goord
Logan v. Matveevskii

case_name: Alphonso Syville v. City of New York, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested a transfer from the Help Meyer homeless shelter to a hotel room during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic based on his medical conditions (lower back disability, mental illness, anxiety, and major depression), which DHS official Hargrow denied by asserting plaintiff had nothing wrong with him; plaintiff also sought access to mental health services and medication following Defendant Kodali's refusal to complete his psychological evaluation.
key_holding: The court dismissed all claims for failure to state a claim, finding that claims against Hargrow and Kodali were barred by claim preclusion, that shelter supervisor Estrada was a private actor not subject to § 1983, and that plaintiff failed to allege facts showing any defendant acted with discriminatory or retaliatory animus based on disability under the ADA, Rehabilitation Act, or FHA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Alphonso Syville, a former NYC homeless shelter resident with physical and mental disabilities, sued the City of New York and shelter staff alleging disability discrimination, retaliation for his advocacy and prior lawsuits, and civil rights violations arising from conditions in the shelter system during the COVID-19 pandemic from 2020–2021. The court dismissed claims against Hargrow and Kodali as precluded by a prior judgment in Syville II, dismissed § 1983 claims against Defendant Estrada because she was an employee of a private shelter operator rather than a state actor, and dismissed ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and FHA claims because plaintiff did not allege facts plausibly showing that any defendant deprived him of services or housing because of his disability or that he requested and was denied a reasonable accommodation. The court also dismissed HIPAA claims for lack of a private right of action and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
key_cases_cited: Brown v. Felsen, 442 U.S. 127 (1979)
Lucky Brand Dungarees, Inc. v. Marcel Fashions Grp., Inc., 140 S. Ct. 1589 (2020)
In re Motors Liquidation Co., 943 F.3d 125 (2d Cir. 2019)
Mazzocchi v. Windsor Owners Corp., No. 11-CV-7913 (LBS), 2012 WL 3288240 (S.D.N.Y. Aug. 6, 2012)
Lindsey v. Normet, 405 U.S. 56 (1972)

case_name: Carol Noe v. Ray Realty, et al.
accommodation_description: Cannot be determined from this procedural order, which addresses only which filing constitutes the operative complaint.
key_holding: The court granted plaintiff's motion to deem ECF 95 (her earlier proposed amended complaint) as the operative complaint, finding she did not intend ECF 114 to serve as her amended complaint and that justice requires allowing a pro se litigant every opportunity to demonstrate a valid claim.
brief_summary: Carol Noe, a pro se plaintiff who is permanently disabled, sued Ray Realty under the Fair Housing Act, and this procedural order resolves a dispute about which filing constitutes the operative complaint. The court granted plaintiff's motion to deem her earlier proposed amended complaint (ECF 95) as the operative complaint, declining to treat her later filing (ECF 114) as the operative complaint since she did not intend it to serve that purpose.
key_cases_cited: State Teachers Retirement Bd. v. Fluor Corp., 654 F.2d 843 (2d Cir. 1981)
Matima v. Celli, 228 F.3d 68 (2d Cir. 2000)
Chavis v. Chappius, 618 F.3d 162 (2d Cir. 2010)

case_name: Felicia Rosa v. Pathstone Corporation
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED - This order addresses only a motion for appointment of pro bono counsel; the underlying accommodation request is not analyzed.
key_holding: The court denied without prejudice the plaintiff's application for pro bono counsel because she failed to demonstrate an inability to obtain counsel and failed to show that prudential factors warranted appointment.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Felicia Rosa filed suit against Pathstone Corporation and individual defendants alleging Fair Housing Act and other claims, and sought appointment of pro bono counsel. The court denied the application without prejudice, finding Rosa failed to demonstrate she was unable to retain counsel and that prudential factors under the Hodge test did not warrant appointment of counsel at this juncture.
key_cases_cited: Hodge v. Police Officers, 802 F.2d 58 (2d Cir. 1986)
Ferrelli v. River Manor Health Care Ctr., 323 F.3d 196 (2d Cir. 2003)

case_name: Mynor Federico Nunez Baltazar v. Pelican Management, Inc.
accommodation_description: The order mentions failure to accommodate disability but does not specify the nature of the accommodation requested.
key_holding: This is a procedural service order directing the U.S. Marshals Service to effect service on defendants; the court has not reached the merits of the Fair Housing Act reasonable accommodation claim.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Baltazar, proceeding in forma pauperis, filed suit against Pelican Management, Inc. and affiliated defendants alleging discrimination and failure to accommodate his disability under the ADA, FHA, and state law. The Court granted IFP status and ordered the U.S. Marshals Service to effect service on defendants.

case_name: Shauna Noel v. City of New York
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; plaintiffs challenge the City of New York's community preference policy in affordable housing lotteries as having a disparate impact on Black applicants.
key_holding: The motion for reconsideration was properly denied because plaintiffs failed to demonstrate that the community preference policy causes a disparate impact by race, as whether an applicant benefits or is harmed depends on the community district typology where the housing is located rather than race itself.
brief_summary: Individual Black applicants for affordable housing sued the City of New York challenging the community preference policy in housing lotteries as having a discriminatory disparate impact. The Court denied plaintiffs' motion for reconsideration of the summary judgment ruling, concluding that plaintiffs failed to demonstrate the policy causes a disparate impact by race because the alleged racial disparities depend on community district location rather than applicants' race.
key_cases_cited: Texas Dept. of Housing and Community Affairs v. Inclusive Communities Project, Inc., 576 U.S. 519 (2015)

source_file: 9890323_2023_Lost Lake Holdings LLC v. Town of Forestburgh_nysd
case_name: Lost Lake Holdings LLC v. Town of Forestburgh
accommodation_description: Developers claim municipal denial of building permits and imposition of supplemental SEQRA review constitutes religious discrimination under FHA, preventing construction of housing development intended for Hasidic Orthodox Jewish families
key_holding: Court denied preliminary injunction because private commercial developers failed to establish irreparable harm—their economic losses from denial of building permits are compensable by money damages, and the FHA's presumption of irreparable harm applies only when plaintiffs face threat of homelessness or serve vulnerable populations in immediate need of housing, not when profit-motivated developers seek to construct housing for eventual sale
brief_summary: Lost Lake Holdings LLC and Hasidic Orthodox Jewish developers sued the Town of Forestburgh, alleging the municipality violated the Fair Housing Act and constitutional rights by denying building permits and imposing supplemental environmental review to prevent construction of a housing development targeted to Hasidic Orthodox families, motivated by anti-Semitic animus. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction, finding they failed to establish irreparable harm because private commercial developers seeking economic gain cannot presume irreparable harm under FHA—their alleged injuries are compensable by money damages, and the FHA's presumption of irreparable harm applies only when plaintiffs face imminent homelessness or serve vulnerable populations in immediate need, not when profit-motivated developers seek to construct housing for eventual sale.
key_cases_cited: Congregation Rabbinical Coll. of Tartikov, Inc. v. Village of Pomona, 945 F.3d 83 (2d Cir. 2019)
Vill. Green at Sayville, LLC v. Town of Islip, 43 F.4th 287 (2d Cir. 2022)
Ateres Bais Yaakov Acad. of Rockland v. Town of Clarkstown, 2023 WL 8494453 (2d Cir. 2023)
City of New York v. Golden Feather Smoke Shop, Inc., 597 F.3d 115 (2d Cir. 2010)
Elrod v. Burns, 427 U.S. 347 (1976)

case_name: Gonzalez v. Tejada
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges she was denied an apartment by Berkshire Hathaway because her son has autism, which she frames as housing discrimination based on disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA claim for failure to state a claim because Plaintiff's single-sentence allegation that Berkshire Hathaway denied her an apartment because her son has autism lacked sufficient factual detail to suggest even a minimal inference of discriminatory motivation, but granted Plaintiff 30 days leave to replead.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Omayra Gonzalez sued Berkshire Hathaway Homeservices, alleging she was denied an apartment because her son has autism, along with claims against a gang leader and the Westchester District Attorney. The court dismissed the complaint for failure to state a claim, finding Plaintiff's single-sentence FHA allegation lacked sufficient factual detail to plausibly suggest discriminatory motivation, but granted Plaintiff 30 days leave to amend her complaint against Berkshire Hathaway.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Rodriguez v. Vill. Green Realty, Inc.

case_name: Yaya Jallow v. Edward I. Geffner, Project Renewal, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleged racial discrimination in housing (shelter system) but court found no facts plausibly suggesting FHA violation.
key_holding: The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claims for failure to state a claim because Plaintiff did not allege facts plausibly suggesting that any defendant subjected him to discrimination or retaliation in housing based on any protected characteristic.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Yaya Jallow sued multiple defendants including Project Renewal shelter staff, NYPD officers, DOC correction officers, and others alleging a wide-ranging conspiracy involving racketeering, constitutional violations, and discrimination in housing. The court dismissed Plaintiff's FHA claims because he failed to allege facts plausibly suggesting housing discrimination, dismissed his § 1981 claims for lack of race-based factual allegations, and granted leave to amend only the excessive force claim arising from Manhattan Central Booking.

case_name: Harold Warren, MD v. 111 Tenants Corporation
accommodation_description: No accommodation request is described in the case text; the complaint is construed as raising general FHA discrimination and retaliation claims arising from conduct in the 1980s, with no specific reasonable accommodation or modification at issue.
key_holding: The court dismissed all of plaintiff's federal claims — including FHA discrimination and retaliation, and civil rights conspiracy claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1985, and 1986 — as time-barred because the alleged conduct occurred in the 1980s and the applicable statutes of limitations had expired decades prior, and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Harold Warren, MD, sued 111 Tenants Corporation, a cooperative, alleging discrimination and retaliation under the Fair Housing Act and 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981, 1982, 1985, and 1986, based on conduct the complaint itself placed in the 1980s. The court issued an order to show cause why the federal claims should not be dismissed as untimely, twice extending Warren's deadline to respond, but Warren filed no response. The court sua sponte dismissed all federal claims as untimely and declined to exercise supplemental jurisdiction over the state and city law claims.

case_name: Omayra Gonzalez v. Danci Tejada Jr.; Westchester District Attorney; Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices
accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges Berkshire Hathaway refused to rent her an apartment because her son has autism.
key_holding: The court dismissed the amended complaint for failure to state an FHA claim because Plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual details showing her son's autism qualifies as a disability under the FHA and that the disability was a motivating factor in Berkshire Hathaway's decision to deny her an apartment.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Omayra Gonzalez, proceeding pro se, sued Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices under the Fair Housing Act, alleging the real estate agency denied her an apartment because her son has autism. The court dismissed the amended complaint for failure to state a claim, finding the plaintiff failed to allege sufficient factual details to plausibly suggest her son's autism qualifies as a disability under the FHA and that it was a motivating factor in the denial.
key_cases_cited: Ruotolo v. City of New York, 514 F.3d 184 (2d Cir. 2008)
Salahuddin v. Cuomo, 861 F.2d 40 (2d Cir. 1988)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

case_name: Jeanette Gambaro and Joseph Gambaro v. 1917 ACP Owner LLC, Bruce Lederman, Sharp Management Corp., and The Clearstone Group Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs allege Defendants failed to reasonably accommodate them while the sole elevator in their apartment building was inoperable, but the court's order does not substantively analyze the specific accommodation request.
key_holding: The Court dismissed the case without prejudice because Plaintiffs failed to make a strong showing they are likely to succeed on the merits of their appeal of the state court decision denying them leave to sue the court-appointed receiver, and Plaintiffs will not suffer irreparable injury from dismissal since they may refile after obtaining the necessary leave.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Jeanette and Joseph Gambaro sued Defendants 1917 ACP Owner LLC and related parties under the Fair Housing Act alleging failure to reasonably accommodate them while the sole elevator was inoperable. The Court dismissed the case without prejudice because Plaintiffs failed to obtain leave from the appointing court to sue the court-appointed receiver and did not demonstrate a strong likelihood of success on the merits of their state court appeal.

case_name: Jane Doe v. Related Companies, LLP
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's vague Fair Housing Act complaint references hostile housing environment but no specific accommodation request is described in the dismissed complaint.
key_holding: The court dismissed the action without prejudice under Rule 41(b) for failure to prosecute because Plaintiff failed to respond to a show cause order within the allotted time despite receiving explicit warning that non-compliance could result in dismissal.
brief_summary: Pro se Plaintiff Jane Doe filed a Fair Housing Act complaint against Related Companies, LLP and related defendants alleging a hostile housing environment, but the court dismissed the action without prejudice for failure to prosecute after Plaintiff ignored a show cause order directing her to explain why the complaint should not be dismissed for failing to name all parties and failing to state a plausible claim.

source_file: 9890940_2024_Town of Newburgh, New York v. Newburgh EOM LLC_nysd

case_name: Cynthia Monterroso v. City of New York, et al.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested physical modifications and features in her Build-It-Back reconstructed home—including wider driveway, properly functioning bathtub, lower toilet, adequate attic access, proper HVAC, and generator space—to accommodate her mobility and chronic pain disabilities.
key_holding: The FHA claim was dismissed because many requests were unrelated to Plaintiff's disabilities, the complaint failed to allege that requested accommodations were reasonable or that Defendants refused to make them, and Defendants had already made accommodations including installing a lift and ADA-compliant kitchen.
brief_summary: Cynthia Monterroso, a disabled homeowner whose home was rebuilt through the City's HUD-funded Build-It-Back Program after Hurricane Sandy, sued the City of New York alleging the reconstructed home contained features incompatible with her mobility disabilities and that the City failed to provide reasonable accommodations. The court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, finding the FHA reasonable accommodation claim failed because many requests were unrelated to disability, the complaint did not sufficiently allege requested accommodations were reasonable, and Defendants had already made accommodations including installing a lift and ADA-compliant kitchen.
key_cases_cited: Olsen v. Stark Homes, Inc., 759 F.3d 140 (2d Cir. 2014)
Brooklyn Ctr. for Indep. of the Disabled v. Metro. Transp. Auth., 11 F.4th 55 (2d Cir. 2021)

source_file: 9891340_2024_Ball v. Hope East of Fifth HDFC Inc._nysd
case_name: Raymond Ball v. Hope East of Fifth HDFC Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested transfer to a lower-level apartment as a reasonable accommodation for his physical disability.
key_holding: Plaintiff's FHA claims were dismissed because he failed to allege facts showing how his disability was at least a motivating factor in the landlord's alleged failure to transfer him to a lower-level apartment, failure to protect him from assault, or refusal to perform repairs.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Raymond Ball sued his landlord Hope East of Fifth HDFC Inc. alleging disability-based housing discrimination for refusing to transfer him to a lower-level apartment, failing to protect him from assault in a hallway with non-functioning security cameras, and refusing repairs. The court dismissed the complaint with leave to amend, finding that while Ball alleged he was physically disabled, he failed to plead facts showing his disability was at least a motivating factor for the alleged discriminatory conduct.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)
Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Sandra L. Cullum and Deirdre Saleh v. Wyndham Hotels & Resorts Corp., Wyndham Destinations Inc., Geoffrey A. Ballotti, Elisabeth Gale, Broadridge Corporate Issuer Solutions
accommodation_description: This is a timeshare consumer fraud case, not a reasonable accommodation case; plaintiffs allege deceptive sales practices and fraudulent inducement into a retail installment contract.
key_holding: The court granted WDI's motion to dismiss and noted the arbitration clause in the contract, granted WHR Defendants' motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction, granted Broadridge's motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Sandra Cullum and Deirdre Saleh sued Wyndham Hotels & Resorts Corp. and related entities alleging fraudulent inducement and deceptive practices related to a timeshare purchase made in December 2019, asserting claims under TILA, RESPA, FCRA, RICO, and other federal and state consumer protection laws. The court granted defendants' motions to dismiss for failure to state valid claims and lack of personal jurisdiction, dismissed federal claims against Broadridge, and declined supplemental jurisdiction over state law claims, while granting plaintiffs 30 days leave to amend claims against the unserved defendant Elisabeth Gale.
key_cases_cited: Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly
Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Nicosia v. Amazon.com, Inc.
Local Union 97, Int'l Brotherhood of Elec. Workers v. Niagara Mohawk Power Corp.
Spinelli v. Nat'l Football League

source_file: 9891560_2024_Katz v. New York City Housing Preservation _ Development_nysd
case_name: Chaim Y. Katz and Chana Katz v. New York City Housing Preservation & Development, New York City Housing Development Corporation, Site 5 Residential Owner LLC, C&C Apartment Management LLC, and NRT New York LLC d/b/a Citi Habitats
accommodation_description: Plaintiffs challenged occupancy limits in affordable housing lotteries that restricted three-bedroom units to six persons, claiming the policy discriminated against families with children.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiffs' FHA disparate-treatment claim for failure to plausibly allege discriminatory intent, finding plaintiffs did not adequately plead a comparator showing similarly-sized households without children were treated more favorably under the occupancy policy.
brief_summary: The Katz family sued New York City housing agencies and private developers after being denied affordable housing through the city's lottery system due to occupancy limits, alleging the two-person-per-bedroom policy discriminated against families with children under the Fair Housing Act. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to plausibly allege discriminatory intent because they did not identify similarly situated comparators without children who were treated more favorably.

case_name: Morris Glen Levine v. Project Renewal
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested waiver of shelter food policies to bring in special food for his Crohn's disease and accommodation from exposure to cigarette/K2 smoke due to his asthma.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiff failed to plead facts showing defendants were aware of his disabilities (Crohn's disease, asthma) or that he requested accommodations for these disabilities.
brief_summary: Morris Glen Levine, a pro se plaintiff with Crohn's disease and asthma residing in Project Renewal's Anna's Place homeless shelter, sued the private shelter operator alleging failure to accommodate his disabilities by refusing to allow him to bring special food and failing to enforce no-smoking rules. The court dismissed his ADA, Rehabilitation Act, and Fair Housing Act claims with prejudice for failure to state a claim because he did not plead facts showing defendants knew of his disabilities or that he requested accommodations, but granted him 60 days leave to amend.

source_file: 9892170_2024_Tiffany Simone Fulton v. City of New York_nysd
case_name: Central Harlem Community (District 10); Silent Voices United Inc.; St. Nicholas Houses Resident Association; Tulinde LLC; Breaking the Chains of Your Mind v. City of New York; James Equities LLC; Douglas C. James; John and Jane Does
accommodation_description: Not described in the case text; the substance of the underlying Fair Housing Act claims is not set forth in this order, which addresses only the procedural issue of pro se representation by artificial entities.
key_holding: Artificial entities (corporations, nonprofits, and associations) cannot proceed pro se in federal court under 28 U.S.C. § 1654 and must be represented by licensed counsel, so the court directed plaintiffs to obtain legal representation within 30 days or face dismissal without prejudice.
brief_summary: Several organizational plaintiffs — including Silent Voices United Inc., St. Nicholas Houses Resident Association, Tulinde LLC, and Breaking the Chains of Your Mind — along with Central Harlem Community District 10, filed pro se Fair Housing Act claims against the City of New York and private defendants, seeking injunctive relief and class certification. The court determined that, as artificial entities, none of the plaintiffs could proceed pro se, and that the non-lawyer individuals who signed the complaint could not represent the organizations' legal interests. The court ordered plaintiffs to retain licensed counsel by April 8, 2024, warning that failure to do so would result in dismissal without prejudice.
key_cases_cited: Rowland v. California Men's Colony, Unit II Men's Advisory Council, 506 U.S. 194 (1993)

case_name: Roland Elliott v. City of New York
accommodation_description: The case involves an FHA claim for race discrimination in housing services, not a disability accommodation request; plaintiff references 'reasonable accommodation' only in the context of the United States Housing Act, not the FHA.
key_holding: NYCHA's motion to dismiss the Fair Housing Act claim is granted because plaintiff failed to adequately allege that NYCHA, as opposed to the NYPD, maintained a discriminatory practice attributable to the housing authority.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Roland Elliott, a Black NYCHA public housing resident in the Bronx, sued the City of New York, NYCHA, and NYPD officers under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 and the Fair Housing Act, alleging that NYPD selectively enforced COVID-19 social distancing policies against Black and Latinx communities, resulting in his arrest and use of force. The court granted NYCHA's motion to dismiss all claims against it, finding Elliott failed to allege NYCHA's own discriminatory policy separate from NYPD's actions, while allowing certain constitutional claims against the individual officers to proceed.

Monell v. Dep't of Soc. Servs., 436 U.S. 658 (1978)
City of Los Angeles v. Lyons, 461 U.S. 95 (1983)

case_name: Cynthia Monterroso v. City of New York

key_holding: Leave to amend was denied because the supplemental allegations failed to describe each requested accommodation, state when requests were made, or provide facts showing each accommodation is reasonable, as required to state a plausible FHA failure-to-accommodate claim.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Cynthia Monterroso, a disabled homeowner who received assistance through the City of New York's post-Hurricane Sandy Build It Back program, sued the City alleging disability discrimination claims including failure to accommodate under the FHA. After the Court granted Defendants' motion to dismiss, Plaintiff sought leave to amend her complaint, but the Court denied this motion as futile because the supplemental allegations failed to adequately describe the specific accommodations requested, when they were made, or why they were reasonable.

accommodation_description: Plaintiff alleges racial harassment including being falsely accused of theft by a security officer and subjected to race-based insults as an African American resident.
key_holding: The plaintiff failed to plead facts sufficient to establish that the alleged harassment was sufficiently severe or pervasive, or that it was motivated by discriminatory intent, to sustain a hostile housing environment claim under the FHA.
brief_summary: Gloria Dickerson, an African American woman residing in Peter Cooper Village, sued BPP PCV Owners LLC alleging racial discrimination and a hostile housing environment claim under the Fair Housing Act after a security officer falsely accused her of theft. The court granted the defendant's motion to dismiss, finding the plaintiff failed to plead sufficient facts showing the alleged harassment was severe or pervasive enough to constitute a hostile housing environment or that it was motivated by discriminatory intent.

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Franklin Mendez, proceeding in forma pauperis, filed this action under the ADA, FHA, and state law against NYC Department of Social Services officials and agencies. key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's claims as barred by claim preclusion from her prior action and for failure to state a constitutional claim under Section 1983, finding no general constitutional duty for the government to provide shelter assistance under DeShaney v. Winnebago.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Helen West, a former homeless shelter resident with mental health conditions, sued the City of New York and various social services agencies and employees alleging constitutional violations and Fair Housing Act claims arising from her placement in NYC homeless shelters from 2011-2021. The court dismissed all federal claims under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B)(ii) for failure to state a claim, finding claims barred by claim preclusion from her prior action and that no constitutional right to shelter assistance exists under DeShaney.

key_holding: The court ordered pro se plaintiff to address in her opposition brief why claims against non-appearing defendants should not be dismissed on the same grounds applicable to appearing defendants, warning that failure to do so may result in a sua sponte recommendation of dismissal.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Carol Noe filed a Fair Housing Act complaint in 2019 alleging disability discrimination and retaliation against Ray Realty and a large number of individual and entity defendants. Multiple defendant groups filed motions to dismiss, and Magistrate Judge Tarnofsky issued a procedural order noting that the arguments supporting those motions appeared to apply equally to certain non-appearing defendants. The court required plaintiff to include arguments in her upcoming opposition as to why the claims against non-appearing defendants should not also be dismissed, signaling the court's willingness to act sua sponte if she failed to do so.

key_holding: The motion for reconsideration is denied because Olsen and De La Fuente were in privity for purposes of res judicata—their interests were virtually identical, and Olsen received the assignment with full knowledge of impending litigation, distinguishing this case from Gramatan Home Investors.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Olsen, as assignee of Roque De La Fuente, moved for reconsideration of this Court's order dismissing his claims that the Sherry cooperative board denied De La Fuente's apartment purchase application because of his Mexican American heritage. The Court denied the motion, finding that Olsen and De La Fuente were in privity for res judicata purposes because their interests were virtually identical, and Olsen received the assignment with knowledge of impending litigation, making him bound by the prior judgment.

case_name: Jerry W. Moore v. Capital Realty Group, Inc.

The court granted in forma pauperis status and allowed the claims against the private defendants to proceed past screening, while dismissing claims against HUD because Moore failed to state viable claims against it and no private right of action exists against HUD for failure to investigate discrimination under the FHA.

case_name: Jerry W. Moore v. Capital Realty Group, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought to enjoin the installation of new patio/balcony sliding doors at St. John Tower Apartments that he alleged were no more accessible than the existing doors and would prevent wheelchair-bound tenants from accessing their balconies.
key_holding: The court grants Moore's motion to amend his complaint, allows his ADA/FHA design-and-accessibility claims against the property manager and realty group to survive screening, but dismisses all claims against HUD because no private right of action exists against HUD for failure to investigate FHA violations and because HUD is not subject to suit under Titles II or III of the ADA.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jerry Moore, a resident of St. John Tower Apartments, moved for a preliminary injunction to halt the installation of new patio/balcony sliding doors he contends will prevent wheelchair-bound tenants from accessing their balconies in violation of the FHA and ADA. The court treated the motion as one to amend the complaint, allowed the amended claims against Capital Realty Group and property manager Felecia Pryor to survive § 1915(e)(2) screening as colorable, but dismissed all claims against HUD on the grounds that HUD is not suable under ADA Titles II or III and that the FHA provides no private right of action for HUD's failure to investigate discrimination. The court ordered Pryor and Capital Realty Group to respond to the preliminary injunction motion within ten days.

brief_summary: Plaintiff Carolette Meadows, proceeding pro se, sued her neighbor Rachel Eckert, the Buffalo Police Department, Erie County prosecutors, and others alleging constitutional violations, ADA claims, and Fair Housing Act claims stemming from a long-running neighborhood dispute involving property disputes and physical altercations. case_name: Jerry W. Moore v. Capital Realty Group, Inc.
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought reasonable modifications and accommodations to ensure wheelchair accessibility throughout St. John Apartments, including in individual apartment units and common areas; specific inaccessible features identified included sliding balcony doors with a 3-inch step rendering balconies inaccessible to wheelchair-dependent tenants, as well as features affecting tenants with vision impairments.
key_holding: The court granted HUD Secretary Fudge's motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, finding that plaintiff failed to establish standing because his alleged injuries were not traceable to HUD (which was not a party to the relevant HAP contract) and failed to demonstrate a waiver of sovereign immunity under 42 U.S.C. § 1404a.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Jerry Moore, a wheelchair-dependent tenant with 100% total and permanent disability residing in HUD-subsidized housing at St. John Apartments in Buffalo, New York, sued Capital Realty Group, property managers, and HUD Secretary Marcia Fudge under the FHA, ADA, and Rehabilitation Act, alleging defendants failed to reasonably modify and maintain the property for wheelchair accessibility and disability accommodations. HUD Secretary Fudge moved to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction on grounds of lack of standing and sovereign immunity. The court granted the motion, holding that plaintiff could not trace his injuries to HUD—which was not a party to the HAP contract governing the property—and could not establish a waiver of sovereign immunity under 42 U.S.C. § 1404a because HUD had no contractual relationship with or substantial control over the St. John Apartments.

case_name: Meadows v. Buffalo Police Department
accommodation_description: No reasonable accommodation was formally requested. Meadows's FHA claim under § 3617 was based on her neighbor Eckert allegedly coercing, intimidating, and interfering with Meadows's enjoyment of her home through physical assaults, harassment, surveillance, false complaints, and racially charged social media posts—not a request for a specific housing accommodation.
key_holding: The court dismissed all FHA and civil rights claims against neighbor Eckert and the Erie County defendants, finding Eckert was not a state actor under § 1983, that Meadows failed to plead a sufficient nexus between racial animus and an adverse housing action under FHA § 3617, and that Erie County prosecutors' charging decisions were immune from Monell liability.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Carolette Meadows brought claims under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981–1983, 1985–1986, the ADA, and the FHA against her neighbor Rachel Eckert, the Buffalo Police Department, Erie County, and Erie County prosecutors, arising from a years-long neighbor feud in which Eckert allegedly harassed, physically assaulted, and racially targeted Meadows while police and prosecutors gave undue deference to Eckert's complaints. The court granted motions to dismiss filed by Eckert and the Erie County defendants, finding that Eckert was not a state actor, that Meadows failed to connect Eckert's racial animus to any adverse housing action as required for a viable FHA § 3617 claim, and that the Erie County prosecutors' charging decisions could not support a Monell claim. The action continues against the City of Buffalo and BPD defendants who answered the second amended complaint.

brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Tedric Kewon Jones sued Homestate Asset Management LLC alleging Fair Housing Act violations, claiming defendant refused to accept his Emergency Rental Assistance Program benefits, denied maintenance requests, harassed him, and attempted to evict him. case_name: Donald Davis v. Mary Z. Cornely, et al.
accommodation_description: No disability accommodation was requested; this case involves allegations of racial discrimination in housing conditions, a racially derogatory verbal attack, retaliation for complaining about property conditions and filing a civil stalking protection order, and interference with plaintiff's foster-care arrangements.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion to dismiss defendants' amended state law counterclaims, holding that 28 U.S.C. § 1367 confers supplemental jurisdiction over those counterclaims because they arise from the same landlord-tenant relationship and share a common nucleus of operative facts with plaintiff's federal FHA and civil rights claims.
brief_summary: Donald Davis, an African American tenant, sued his landlord Mary Cornely and property manager Carl Wood alleging race-based discrimination and retaliatory conduct in violation of the Fair Housing Act (§§ 3604(a), 3604(b), 3604(c), 3617) and the Civil Rights Acts of 1866 and 1870, stemming from an incident in which Wood allegedly used a racial slur and threatened him, as well as Defendants' failure to make repairs and interference with his foster-care placements. Defendants filed amended state law counterclaims for bad-faith rent deposit, tortious interference, civil liability for false alarms, abuse of process, defamation, and assault. The court denied Davis's Rule 12(b)(1) motion to dismiss the counterclaims, concluding that all counterclaims derive from the same disputed landlord-tenant relationship and conduct underlying the federal claims, satisfying the 'common nucleus of operative facts' standard for supplemental jurisdiction.

brief_summary: African-American customers of Cleveland Water sued the City of Cleveland alleging that the city's water lien policy, which converts overdue water bills into tax liens on properties, disproportionately impacts Black homeowners and violates the Fair Housing Act. accommodation_description: Sexual harassment by property manager/owner including making housing benefits contingent on sexual acts, unwanted touching, and eviction threats against female tenants who rejected advances.
key_holding: The court denied Defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the complaint plausibly alleges YLP's vicarious and direct liability for Pedaline's sexual harassment, direct § 3617 interference claims against Pedaline personally, and a timely-filed pattern-or-practice claim.
brief_summary: The United States sued property owner/manager Joseph Pedaline and YLP LLC under the FHA's pattern-or-practice provision, alleging that from 2009-2020 Pedaline sexually harassed female tenants by conditioning housing benefits on sexual acts, making unwanted advances, and evicting those who rejected him. The court denied both defendants' motions to dismiss, finding the complaint sufficiently pleaded vicarious liability against YLP, direct liability for YLP's failure to respond to complaints, personal liability against Pedaline under § 3617, and that the complaint was timely filed.

key_holding: Mindale Farms failed to state an FHA or ADA claim because it attempted to use age as a proxy for disability without establishing a sufficient nexus, and the court refused to effectively rewrite the FHA and ADA to include age as a protected class.
brief_summary: Mindale Farms Co., a land developer, sued the City of Tallmadge, Ohio alleging the city's denial of its rezoning application and subsequent repeal of the R-6 District violated the Fair Housing Act and ADA by reducing housing available to disabled individuals. The court granted the city's motion for judgment on the pleadings, finding that Mindale Farms failed to state a valid FHA or ADA claim because it improperly attempted to use age (55 and older housing) as a proxy for disability without establishing a sufficient causal nexus between age and disability.

source_file: 9910433_2021_Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority_ohsd
case_name: Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff sought that defendant housing authority apply for 60 VASH project-based vouchers on behalf of the veterans housing project and/or amend its Administrative Plan to permit award of vouchers based on prior third-party competition without competitive RFP process.
key_holding: The requested accommodation lacked sufficient nexus to disability because defendant would have denied the voucher application request regardless of the disabled status of prospective tenants—disabled and non-disabled veterans were equally affected by defendant's RFP policy requirements.
brief_summary: Freedom's Path, a developer of supportive housing for homeless veterans, sued Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority alleging violations of the ADA and FHA for refusing to apply for VASH project-based vouchers on its behalf and refusing to amend its Administrative Plan to permit voucher awards based on prior third-party competition. The court granted summary judgment to defendant, finding no genuine issue of material fact because plaintiff failed to establish the required nexus between the accommodation request and any disability, as defendant's policy denial would have applied equally to disabled and non-disabled housing projects.

case_name: UFM Realty Corporation v. Matthews
accommodation_description: No formal reasonable accommodation request is central to this case; Matthews invoked a CDC Declaration order to seek a stay of the eviction proceedings based on her alleged status as an individual at risk for COVID-19, and she had separately filed HUD administrative complaints alleging discriminatory housing practices by the property owner.
key_holding: The court recommended remanding the improperly removed state eviction case to Middletown Municipal Court for lack of federal subject matter jurisdiction, because the plaintiff's complaint relied exclusively on state law and a defendant's assertion of federal defenses or counterclaims—including FHA, HUD complaints, and the CDC order—is legally insufficient to confer removal jurisdiction.
brief_summary: UFM Realty Corporation filed a state court eviction action against pro se defendant Rashawnda Matthews for failure to comply with her month-to-month lease. Matthews removed the case to federal court, alleging the eviction constituted racial and civil-rights discrimination and retaliation for HUD complaints she had filed regarding discriminatory housing practices. The magistrate judge recommended dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and remand to state court, finding that the well-pleaded complaint rule bars removal based solely on a defendant's federal defenses or counterclaims when the plaintiff's own complaint invokes only state law.

case_name: Vanessa McQueen v. City of Cincinnati
accommodation_description: Not described in the case text; the specific nature of the alleged Fair Housing Act violation or any accommodation requested is not identified in the order.
key_holding: The court adopted the Magistrate Judge's Report and Recommendation and dismissed the pro se plaintiff's Fair Housing Act complaint with prejudice under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) because plaintiff failed to include sufficient factual context from which the court could reasonably infer that any defendant discriminated against her.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Vanessa McQueen filed a Fair Housing Act complaint against the City of Cincinnati and other defendants, alleging unspecified FHA violations. The Magistrate Judge recommended dismissal with prejudice for failure to state a claim, finding the complaint lacked the factual context necessary to support any inference of discrimination. After a de novo review of plaintiff's timely objections and applying a liberal construction to her filings, the district court agreed with the Magistrate Judge and dismissed the action with prejudice, also denying plaintiff leave to appeal in forma pauperis.

source_file: 9911698_2021_Seattle House LLC v. City of Delaware, Ohio_ohsd
case_name: Seattle House, LLC v. City of Delaware, Ohio
accommodation_description: This is not a reasonable accommodation case; it concerns whether municipal water and sewage capacity fees that allegedly prevent affordable housing development constitute a disparate impact under the FHA.
key_holding: The developer plausibly alleged standing by claiming financial injury from allegedly discriminatory fees and stated a cognizable disparate impact claim by alleging the City's fee policy causes an affordable housing crisis disproportionately impacting racial minorities, surviving dismissal on the FHA claim while constitutional claims were dismissed.
brief_summary: Seattle House LLC, an apartment developer, sued the City of Delaware, Ohio alleging the City's water and sewage capacity fees create an affordable housing crisis that disproportionately impacts racial minorities in violation of the Fair Housing Act. On the City's motion for judgment on the pleadings, the court dismissed the Equal Protection and Substantive Due Process claims but allowed the FHA disparate impact claim to proceed, finding the developer adequately pleaded standing and sufficient facts showing the City's fee policy causes a disparate impact.

brief_summary: African-American homeowners in Cincinnati sued the City of Cincinnati alleging its Residential Tax Abatement Program violates the Fair Housing Act by disproportionately directing tax benefits to Caucasian neighborhoods, causing racial segregation and economic harm to African-American communities. case_name: United States v. Klosterman
accommodation_description: N/A - this case involves enforcement of a consent decree regarding sexual harassment of female tenants, not a reasonable accommodation request
key_holding: The court found clear and convincing evidence that defendant John Klosterman violated multiple provisions of the Consent Decree including making false affirmations about property holdings, personally interacting with tenants in violation of injunctive provisions, failing to complete required Fair Housing Act training, and failing to establish a required interest-bearing escrow account for monetary damages; the court recommended finding civil contempt and imposing prospective sanctions.
brief_summary: The United States and intervenor HOME sought to enforce a Consent Decree against landlord John Klosterman for violations of the Fair Housing Act's prohibition on sex discrimination through sexual harassment of female tenants, alleging defendant made false affirmations about property holdings, continued prohibited contact with tenants, failed to complete required FHA training, and failed to establish required escrow accounts for monetary damages. case_name: Dayton Veterans Residences Limited Partnership v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Request for project-based housing vouchers as a reasonable accommodation for homeless disabled veterans seeking housing at a VA Medical Campus development.
key_holding: The court denied DMHA's motion to withdraw its jury demand, finding that Freedom's Path is entitled to a jury trial because it seeks monetary damages under the FHA, which constitutes a legal remedy triggering Seventh Amendment rights.
brief_summary: Freedom's Path, a developer seeking to create housing for homeless veterans on a VA campus, sued DMHA for allegedly reneging on a commitment for project-based housing vouchers and denying reasonable accommodation requests for disabled veterans. case_name: Dennis Howell, et al. v. City of Cincinnati
accommodation_description: This is a systemic challenge to the City of Cincinnati's Residential Tax Abatement program, not a reasonable accommodation request; plaintiffs allege the program has discriminatory effects on Black communities.
key_holding: The City's motion for reconsideration of the Court's Notation Order requiring the City Manager to submit a proposed nonbinding calendar for RTA program reform is denied because the order did not violate separation of powers—it merely requested a proposed timeline, not mandatory legislative action.
brief_summary: Black residents of Cincinnati sued the City of Cincinnati alleging that the Residential Tax Abatement program, which provides property tax benefits for home renovations, has deepened racial segregation and disproportionately benefits white neighborhoods in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The Court denied the City's motion to reconsider a Notation Order requiring the City Manager to submit a proposed timeline for presenting RTA reform legislation to City Council, finding no separation of powers violation because the order merely requested a nonbinding proposed schedule for legislative consideration.

brief_summary: Tasha Chapman, a Muslim pretrial detainee with Bipolar Disorder II, sued the Franklin County Sheriff alleging violations including First Amendment free exercise, Fair Housing Act, ADA, and state law claims arising from being forced to remove her hijab at the county jail. case_name: Dayton Veterans Residences Limited Partnership, d/b/a Freedom's Path at Dayton v. Dayton Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Freedom's Path requested that DMHA provide 33 project-based housing vouchers (later revised to 60) as a reasonable accommodation to allow disabled homeless veterans to obtain housing in the Dayton community on equal footing with non-disabled persons, in connection with a housing development on the VA Medical Campus.
key_holding: The court denied DMHA's motion for $250,000 in attorney's fees because Freedom's Path's FHA and ADA claims were not frivolous, as demonstrated by the Sixth Circuit's reversal allowing the reasonable accommodation theory to proceed to trial.
brief_summary: Freedom's Path, a developer of affordable housing for disabled homeless veterans on the Dayton VA Medical Campus, sued DMHA under the FHA and ADA, alleging DMHA reneged on a commitment of 33 project-based housing vouchers and denied reasonable accommodation requests. case_name: Dennis Howell, et al. v. City of Cincinnati
accommodation_description: No accommodation request; plaintiffs challenge the City's Residential Tax Abatement program as having a disparate impact on African American communities.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction because they failed to demonstrate immediate, irreparable harm, and granted in part the City's motion to dismiss by dismissing plaintiffs' disparate treatment claims while denying dismissal of other claims.
brief_summary: African American homeowners sued the City of Cincinnati alleging the City's Residential Tax Abatement program disadvantages African American communities and perpetuates racial segregation in violation of the Fair Housing Act. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction for failure to show irreparable harm and dismissed their disparate treatment claims while allowing disparate impact claims to proceed.

case_name: Isis Rudolph v. Michael Green, et al.
accommodation_description: No specific reasonable accommodation was requested. Plaintiff alleged that Defendants refused to provide her with a trash can and moved a trash can placed by the city after she requested one, and made it difficult for her to renew her lease — conduct she characterized as retaliatory in connection with her unidentified disability.
key_holding: The magistrate judge recommended dismissal of all of plaintiff's federal claims — under the FHA, Rehabilitation Act, Civil Rights Act, and ADA — pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2) for failure to state a claim, finding the allegations too threadbare and conclusory to raise a plausible inference of actionable discrimination, and further recommended declining supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state-law claims.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Isis Rudolph sued her landlord, Green Quarters LLC, and its manager Michael Green, alleging disability discrimination under the FHA, Rehabilitation Act, Civil Rights Act, and ADA. Her allegations included harassment via repeated eviction threats and discriminatory comments about her disability, and retaliation for refusing to provide her a trash can and making lease renewal difficult. The magistrate judge recommended dismissal of all federal claims as legally and factually insufficient — the FHA harassment/interference claim lacked allegations of discriminatory animus, the Rehabilitation Act claim failed to allege federal funding, the Civil Rights Act does not cover disability, and the ADA does not apply to private landlords — and recommended that state-law claims be dismissed without prejudice for lack of jurisdiction.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662 (2009)

case_name: Tasha Chapman v. Columbus Metropolitan Housing Authority
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's landlord requested documentation for plaintiff's emotional support animal and sought to rekey locks, which plaintiff characterized as discriminatory retaliation for disability.
key_holding: The court recommended dismissal because plaintiff failed to allege that defendants' statements indicated a preference, limitation, or discrimination based on disability or family status; the landlord's requests for ESA vaccination records and lock rekeying were legitimate property management requests, not discriminatory statements under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c).
brief_summary: Tasha Chapman, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, sued Columbus Metropolitan Housing Authority, Heels Homes Ltd., and related defendants under the Fair Housing Act alleging family status and disability discrimination based on statements regarding her ESA and alleged housing code violations. The court recommended dismissal of the entire complaint, finding that plaintiff failed to allege any statements indicating discrimination based on protected characteristics under 42 U.S.C. § 3604(c).

case_name: Consuella Oliver et al. v. Etna Township, Ohio
accommodation_description: Property owners sought zoning approval to construct a 20-unit multi-family residential development; the court analyzed this as an equal protection challenge to zoning decisions rather than a traditional reasonable accommodation claim.
key_holding: The court granted summary judgment to Etna Township on all claims, finding that plaintiffs failed to demonstrate discriminatory intent under the Arlington Heights framework and that the Township's zoning decisions were rationally related to legitimate interests in preserving rural character and minimizing urban development.
brief_summary: African American property owners Consuella and Phillip Oliver sued Etna Township over denial of their use variance application to construct a 20-unit multi-family development, asserting Fair Housing Act, Equal Protection, Substantive Due Process, and regulatory takings claims. The court granted summary judgment to the Township, finding that the Township's zoning decisions were rationally related to legitimate government interests in preserving rural character and that plaintiffs failed to establish discriminatory intent under the Arlington Heights framework.

case_name: April Clark v. Blueprint Investments, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff's complaint mentions Fair Housing Act claims but no specific accommodation request is analyzed due to lack of subject matter jurisdiction.
key_holding: The Court lacks subject matter jurisdiction because (1) a plaintiff cannot remove their own state court action to federal court, and (2) federal claims asserted as counterclaims do not confer federal question jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule.
brief_summary: Plaintiff April Clark, proceeding pro se and in forma pauperis, attempted to remove four state court actions (including eviction proceedings) to federal court, citing the Fair Housing Act, ADA, and other federal laws as bases for jurisdiction. The Court granted in forma pauperis status but recommended remand because (1) plaintiffs cannot remove their own cases under 28 U.S.C. § 1441(a), and (2) federal counterclaims do not establish federal question jurisdiction under the well-pleaded complaint rule.

case_name: Watkins v. Housing Authority of the City of Hugo
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested reinstatement of terminated rental assistance with retroactive benefits and emergency injunctive relief to prevent eviction from public housing as an accommodation for disability.
key_holding: The court denied the motion for TRO and preliminary injunction without prejudice because Defendants had not been served and therefore could not be properly enjoined, as Rule 65 requires notice to adverse parties.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Ronesha Watkins, individually and on behalf of minor children, sued the Housing Authority of the City of Hugo and related defendants alleging Fair Housing Act violations and seeking emergency injunctive relief including reinstatement of terminated rental assistance to prevent eviction. The court denied the motion for temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction without prejudice on procedural grounds, finding that the housing authority defendants had not been served and therefore could not be bound by an injunction, and that plaintiff failed to meet the procedural requirements for ex parte relief under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 65.

case_name: Metropolitan Fair Housing Council of Oklahoma, Inc. v. Feiock
accommodation_description: Request for a one-year lease renewal as a reasonable accommodation for the tenant's terminal illness (stage 4 cancer) to avoid displacement during end-of-life care.
key_holding: The requested one-year lease renewal was neither necessary nor reasonable because it offered better housing terms than other tenants received (one-year vs. six-month standard leases) rather than equal opportunity, and plaintiffs provided no evidentiary support that such a lengthy renewal was required to accommodate the disability.
brief_summary: Metropolitan Fair Housing Council of Oklahoma and individual tenants James and Marta McNamee sued landlords Frank and Glenna Feiock alleging failure to accommodate under the FHA when they refused to renew the McNamees' lease for one year as an accommodation for James McNamee's terminal cancer. The court granted partial summary judgment for defendants, finding the accommodation request was neither necessary (because it provided better terms than other tenants received) nor reasonable (because indefinite lease extensions for disabled tenants are not required).

case_name: Joseph Backus v. I.Q. Data International, Inc., Tulsa Greenbriar I, LLC, and Gaines Investment Trust
accommodation_description: Request to transfer to an apartment closer to the mailbox due to difficulty walking (uses a cane)
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiff failed to adequately allege he actually requested an accommodation separate from submitting a notice to vacate, and the notice to vacate did not independently serve as a request for accommodation.
brief_summary: Joseph Backus, a 74-year-old tenant with mobility limitations requiring use of a cane, sued his former landlord and collection agency alleging he was denied a reasonable accommodation when the property manager allegedly refused his request to transfer to an apartment closer to the mailbox, and that defendants retaliated by collecting alleged fraudulent debts. The district court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding that plaintiff failed to state a failure to accommodate claim because his notice to vacate did not constitute a proper accommodation request and he did not adequately allege he engaged in an interactive process before vacating the apartment.

case_name: Joseph Backus v. Tulsa Greenbriar I, LLC and Gaines Investment Trust
accommodation_description: Plaintiff requested to be transferred to an apartment closer to the mailbox due to mobility limitations from a leg injury requiring use of a cane.
key_holding: Although plaintiff adequately stated a failure to accommodate claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B), the claim was barred by the two-year statute of limitations because plaintiff filed suit on May 20, 2020—more than two years after the April 24, 2018 denial of his accommodation request.
brief_summary: Joseph Backus sued Tulsa Greenbriar I, LLC and Gaines Investment Trust alleging they violated the Fair Housing Act by denying his request to transfer to an apartment closer to the mailbox due to his mobility limitations. The court found that while plaintiff adequately pleaded a failure to accommodate claim, the claim was dismissed as time-barred because it was filed more than two years after the April 24, 2018 denial of his accommodation request.

case_name: Gina Gotcher v. PC Woodland Manor, LLC and RPM Living, LLC
accommodation_description: Plaintiff, who has a severe brain injury affecting her mobility, requested to be transferred from her second floor apartment to a first floor apartment as a reasonable accommodation.
key_holding: The Court granted plaintiff's motion to amend her complaint, denied her motion for default judgment against RPM Living for failure to properly effect service, and found her TRO motion moot due to the proposed amended complaint potentially naming different defendants.
brief_summary: Gina Gotcher, a tenant with a severe brain injury, sued PC Woodland Manor, LLC and RPM Living, LLC alleging disability discrimination for denying her request to transfer from a second floor to a first floor apartment and for alleged retaliation through eviction attempts. The Court granted plaintiff's motion for leave to amend the complaint to add new defendants, denied her motion for default judgment against RPM for improper service, and dismissed her TRO motion as moot without ruling on the merits of her reasonable accommodation claim.

case_name: Stephany Webster v. Fairway Management, Inc., et al.
accommodation_description: The complaint references Fair Housing Act violations based on Webster's physical and mental disabilities, but the accommodation request itself is not described in the motion to dismiss analysis.
key_holding: The court denied JES's motion to dismiss regarding agency relationships and denied Webster's motion to dismiss Walnut Park's counterclaim, without reaching the merits of the FHA reasonable accommodation claims.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Stephany Webster, a senior citizen with physical and mental disabilities, sued Fairway Management, Walnut Park Manor, and JES Holdings alleging Fair Housing Act violations and other claims. The court denied JES's motion to dismiss for failure to adequately plead agency relationships and denied Webster's motion to dismiss Walnut Park's counterclaim for breach of contract, without reaching the merits of any FHA reasonable accommodation claim.
key_cases_cited: Ashcroft v. Iqbal
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly

case_name: Idalys Torres Rivera v. Charo Naifeh, Casa Light Realty, LLC, and Platinum Investment Group, LLC
accommodation_description: The accommodation request is not described in this procedural remand order.
key_holding: The court lacked subject matter jurisdiction because defendants' removal was untimely, as plaintiff alleged a Fair Housing Act violation in her initial petition filed eight months before removal, triggering the thirty-day removal deadline.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Idalys Torres Rivera sued defendants Charo Naifeh, Casa Light Realty LLC, and Platinum Investment Group LLC in Tulsa County, Oklahoma state court, alleging among other claims a Fair Housing Act violation. The case was removed to federal court, but plaintiff moved to remand arguing the removal was untimely. The court granted the motion to remand, finding that plaintiff's initial petition clearly presented a federal FHA claim, starting the thirty-day removal clock eight months before defendants filed their notice of removal.

case_name: United States v. Johnson
accommodation_description: UNDETERMINED
key_holding: The court ordered a hearing under Rule 55(b)(2) to determine whether to grant default judgment regarding the fair-housing training requirement, while the $5,000 damages claim could likely be entered by the Clerk without a hearing.
brief_summary: The United States moved for default judgment against property manager Will Johnson for breaching a HUD conciliation agreement arising from a disability discrimination complaint filed by Donna Winfrey regarding a rental property; the court ordered a hearing to determine whether to grant the motion regarding the fair-housing training requirement, finding procedural requirements for default judgment satisfied.

case_name: United States v. Johnson
accommodation_description: The enforcement action does not analyze a specific accommodation request; this is a breach of conciliation agreement proceeding regarding an underlying fair housing complaint.
key_holding: Because defendant defaulted and failed to respond to the enforcement action, the court granted default judgment enforcing the conciliation agreement, awarding $5,000 in damages and requiring completion of HUD fair housing training.
brief_summary: The United States brought this enforcement action against a private landlord for breach of conciliation agreements entered into through HUD regarding a fair housing complaint. The court granted default judgment after the defendant failed to appear or respond, awarding $5,000 in damages to the underlying complainant and ordering the defendant to complete HUD fair housing training.

case_name: Watson v. Vici Community Development Corp.
accommodation_description: Tenant with permanent mobility impairments due to knee disorders requested to pay rent on the third Wednesday of each month to coincide with receipt of Social Security disability benefits.
key_holding: The court denied dismissal of the reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B), finding Watson plausibly alleged that defendants terminated her third Wednesday payment privilege without notice and then denied the accommodation in practice by issuing lease violation notices even after reinstating it on paper.
brief_summary: Arleta Watson, a 79-year-old tenant with permanent mobility impairments at Vici Manor Apartments in Vici, Oklahoma, sued Vici Community Development Corp. and property manager Cindy Arnold alleging Fair Housing Act violations after defendants terminated her accommodation allowing rent payment on the third Wednesday of each month and issued lease violations when she had third parties deliver rent payments. The court denied defendants' motion to dismiss the reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B), finding Watson plausibly alleged that terminating the accommodation without notice and issuing repeated lease violation notices after reinstatement constituted a failure to accommodate, while dismissing claims under § 3604(f)(1)(C) and § 3604(f)(2)(C) as insufficiently pled.

case_name: Sarah Melton v. State of Oklahoma ex rel. University of Oklahoma
accommodation_description: Student with heightened sensitivity to toxic mold requested professional remediation of mold infestation in her university dormitory room as a reasonable accommodation for her disability.
key_holding: The court dismissed the FHA reasonable accommodation claim because plaintiff failed to plausibly allege a refusal to accommodate; the University began remediation efforts within days of the request, which did not constitute a refusal.
brief_summary: Sarah Melton, a student at the University of Oklahoma, sued the University and individual officials alleging that her dormitory's toxic mold infestation caused her serious health problems and that the University violated the Fair Housing Act by refusing to accommodate her disability (heightened susceptibility to mold) through professional remediation. The court dismissed the FHA claim, finding that the University's prompt initiation of remediation efforts within days of the request did not constitute a refusal to accommodate.

case_name: Marquise Miller v. Legacy Bank
plaintiff_type: OTHER: Individual property owner and loan applicant
accommodation_description: No accommodation request - case concerns discriminatory denial of a loan application based on race and neighborhood demographics.
key_holding: The court dismissed plaintiff's FHA, § 1981, and § 1982 claims as time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations, and dismissed his ECOA claim for failure to adequately plead he was qualified for the loan or that similarly situated applicants received loans.
brief_summary: Plaintiff Marquise Miller, an African American pastor, sued Legacy Bank alleging the bank denied his loan application to remodel a property based on his race and because the property was located in a predominately Black neighborhood. The court granted defendant's motion to dismiss, finding the FHA, § 1981, and § 1982 claims time-barred under the two-year statute of limitations and the ECOA claim failed for insufficiently alleging plaintiff was qualified for the loan.

case_name: Miller v. Legacy Bank
accommodation_description: Not applicable; this case involves a denied loan application, not a request for a disability-related accommodation.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion for reconsideration of the dismissal of his FHA, § 1981, § 1982, and ECOA claims because plaintiff failed to present any recognized grounds for reconsideration—intervening change in law, newly available evidence, or need to correct clear error—and instead merely reargued issues already decided.
brief_summary: Pro se plaintiff Marquise Miller brought suit against Legacy Bank alleging discriminatory denial of his loan application on October 19, 2015, asserting claims under the FHA, 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, and the ECOA. In a prior November 3, 2021 order, the court dismissed the FHA and §§ 1981/1982 claims with prejudice as time-barred (filed nearly five years after the loan denial) and granted leave to amend the ECOA claim. In this order, the court denied plaintiff's motion for reconsideration because he offered no new grounds—only rearguing limitations-period calculations already addressed—and failed to satisfy any of the three recognized bases for reconsideration.

case_name: Watson v. Vici Community Development Corp.

key_holding: The court found that Watson raised genuine issues of material fact as to whether her requests to pay rent on the third week of the month were necessary to afford her an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the dwelling, were reasonable, and were refused by defendants.
brief_summary: Arleta Watson, a tenant at Vici Manor Apartments with mobility impairments from knee surgeries, sued the property owner and manager alleging Fair Housing Act violations including failure to accommodate her disability by allowing her to pay rent on the third week of each month. The court denied both parties' cross-motions for summary judgment, finding genuine issues of material fact exist on Watson's reasonable accommodation claim under § 3604(f)(3)(B), her discrimination claims under § 3604(f)(1)(A) and (f)(2)(A), and her retaliation claim under § 3617.

case_name: Miller v. Legacy Bank
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested; this case involves an alleged racially discriminatory denial of an $80,000 commercial renovation loan with a 10-year maturity and 6.5% interest rate.
key_holding: Plaintiff's ECOA claim that Legacy Bank denied his loan application because of his race survived the motion to dismiss, as his factual allegations were minimally sufficient to state a plausible claim, though his FHA, § 1981, and § 1982 claims remained dismissed with prejudice as time-barred.
brief_summary: African American pastor Marquise Miller alleged that Legacy Bank denied his 2015 loan application to remodel a property in a predominantly Black neighborhood in Oklahoma City based on his race, citing pretextual reasons such as crime rate and neighborhood vacancy. case_name: Miller v. First United Bank and Trust Co.
accommodation_description: No accommodation was requested in this case; the dispute concerned the alleged race-based denial of a commercial loan application submitted by CDMR, LLC (backed by four individual Black plaintiffs as guarantors/co-borrowers) to finance the purchase of a 160-unit apartment complex in Oklahoma City.
key_holding: The court denied the defendant bank's motion for attorney fees under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 and its inherent power without prejudice, extending leeway to pro se plaintiffs who persistently and unsuccessfully pursued race-based loan denial claims while warning that any further such conduct would warrant fee-shifting.
brief_summary: Four Black individual plaintiffs and their LLC (CDMR, LLC) alleged that First United Bank denied their loan application to purchase a 160-unit Oklahoma City apartment complex on the basis of race, asserting claims under the FHA, the ECOA, and 42 U.S.C. § 1981. All claims were dismissed on standing and procedural grounds—the individuals lacked standing as guarantors under the ECOA, and CDMR's action was dismissed for failure to retain counsel—after which the individual plaintiffs repeatedly and unsuccessfully sought to reenter the case through motions to add parties, amend the complaint, and alter the judgment. The court denied the bank's motion for attorney fees without prejudice, finding that while plaintiffs' persistent pursuit of meritless and internally inconsistent claims was troubling, pro se litigants deserved some leeway, and warning that further such conduct would remove all doubt as to unreasonable and vexatious prosecution.
key_cases_cited: Baca v. Berry, 830 F.3d 1262 (10th Cir. 2015)

case_name: Marquise Miller v. Legacy Bank
accommodation_description: Not applicable — this case involves an alleged discriminatory denial of a remodel loan, not a request for a reasonable accommodation or modification.
key_holding: The court denied plaintiff's motion to strike (construed as a motion for leave to amend the complaint after the scheduling order deadline) because plaintiff failed to demonstrate good cause under Fed. R. Civ. P. 16(b)(4).
brief_summary: Plaintiff Marquise Miller sued Legacy Bank alleging it denied his home remodel loan application because he is African American and because the property is located in a predominantly Black neighborhood, asserting claims under the FHA, ECOA, and 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982. The FHA, § 1981, and § 1982 claims were dismissed with prejudice as time-barred, while the ECOA claim survived after plaintiff filed a second amended complaint adding financial qualification allegations. The court denied plaintiff's post-deadline motion to strike those qualification paragraphs from the complaint—treated as a motion to amend—because plaintiff failed to show good cause for modifying the scheduling order under Rule 16(b)(4), as defendant had not admitted plaintiff was qualified for the loan.

key_holding: The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss because plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient factual matter to state a plausible claim of racial discrimination under § 3604(a) or § 3604(b), as they did not allege facts showing similarly situated neighbors were treated differently or that the housing opportunity remained available.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Blackburn and Freeman, proceeding pro se, sued landlords Kelly Webb and Rent King, LLC alleging racial discrimination in violation of the Fair Housing Act based on disputes over property repairs, non-renewal of tenancy, and an FED (forcible entry and detainer) action. The court granted defendants' motion to dismiss, finding plaintiffs failed to plead sufficient facts to establish a plausible claim of racial discrimination under § 3604(a) or § 3604(b) because they did not adequately allege similarly situated neighbors were treated differently or that the housing opportunity remained available.

brief_summary: Donald Watkins, a Black male, sued Property Management Services, Inc. alleging racial discrimination in denial of access to rent-to-own housing and FHA retaliation after he complained about discriminatory practices and was subsequently evicted from his month-to-month tenancy. accommodation_description: Request to prevent euthanasia of dog Lladk, claimed as a service animal/ESA/assistance animal assisting plaintiffs with emotional disabilities, so they can retain the animal despite the County's dangerous dog designation.
key_holding: The court denied the preliminary injunction because plaintiffs failed to show likelihood of success on the merits, the state court judgment had preclusive effect, Rooker-Feldman doctrine barred constitutional challenges, and the dog's serious bite of plaintiffs' child undermined any reasonable accommodation claim under the FHA and ADA.
brief_summary: Plaintiffs Lanea and Caleb Kollenburn sued Clackamas County seeking to prevent euthanasia of their dog Lladk, which the County designated as a dangerous dog after it seriously bit one of their children; plaintiffs claimed the dog was a service animal/ESA protected under the FHA and ADA. The court denied plaintiffs' motion for preliminary injunction, finding the constitutional claims barred by res judicata and Rooker-Feldman doctrine, and the accommodation claims unlikely to succeed because allowing a dangerous dog that had bitten a child did not constitute a reasonable accommodation.
